item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Brazil? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Brazil

Summary. Brazil is one of the clearest LEGAL jurisdictions in the world for the roof rat — and unusually, it names the species in law as a domestic animal. IBAMA Portaria 93/1998 (Anexo I) lists BOTH 'Rato' (Rattus rattus) and 'Ratazana' (R. norvegicus) as fauna doméstica, and Art. 13 declares domestic fauna 'isentos de quaisquer tramitações junto ao IBAMA' (exempt from any procedure with IBAMA). So keeping and amateur-breeding a captive-bred roof rat needs no IBAMA registration, no SISFAUNA entry, no environmental licence, and no criadouro permit — the same legal channel through which fancy rats ('rato twister') are sold in Brazilian pet shops. The Environmental Crimes Law (Lei 9.605/1998) reaches only 'fauna silvestre,' not domestic-listed species, though its Art. 32 animal-cruelty ban applies to all animals. R. rattus is also recognized as a synanthropic pest (IBAMA IN 141/2006) and an invasive alien species (CONABIO Res. 7/2018), but those target free-living/feral management and eradication and do NOT revoke the domestic-fauna exemption for captive pets. Commercial selling needs ordinary state/municipal pet-trade licensing plus a veterinary Responsável Técnico registered with the CRMV (not IBAMA); interstate transport needs a GTA animal-movement certificate; international import needs MAPA/VIGIAGRO authorization and a bilateral International Veterinary Certificate. Releasing a roof rat into the wild is strictly prohibited.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

IBAMA Portaria 93/1998 Anexo I lists 'Rato' (Rattus rattus) as fauna doméstica, and Art. 13 declares domestic fauna 'isentos de quaisquer tramitações junto ao IBAMA' — so keeping a captive-bred roof rat needs no IBAMA registration, no SISFAUNA entry, no Autorização de Uso e Manejo, and no environmental licence. Lei 9.605/1998 (Crimes Ambientais) Art. 29 reaches only 'fauna silvestre,' so a domestic-listed roof rat is outside it. Federal possession is fully legal and effectively unregulated; the only residual friction is local municipal public-health (Código de Posturas / CCZ) nuisance rules aimed at free-roaming pest infestations, not securely caged captive pets.

Sources: IBAMA, Presidência da República (Planalto)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Because R. rattus is fauna doméstica under Anexo I of Portaria 93/1998, the IBAMA criadouro (breeding-facility) licensing regime — which applies only to wild/exotic fauna (criador amadorista / criadouro comercial under Lei 9.605/1998 Art. 29) — does not apply, and Art. 13 exempts the species from all IBAMA procedures. An individual may breed roof rats in a private residence with no federal environmental permit, no litter registration, and no government pedigree tracking; there is no numeric hobbyist/commercial threshold in environmental law. Breeding remains subject to the universal animal-cruelty prohibition (Lei 9.605/1998 Art. 32; Decreto 24.645/1934). The invasive/synanthropic designations target free-living animals, not captive breeding.

Sources: IBAMA, Presidência da República (Planalto), IBAMA

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Non-commercial transfer, donation, or gifting of a roof rat by a hobbyist is completely unregulated. Commercial sale (pet shop / for-profit rattery) is legal but requires ordinary business licensing — NOT IBAMA, which has no jurisdiction over domestic-fauna trade (no fauna-dealer licence, not CITES-listed): a CNPJ business registration with the Receita Federal, a municipal Alvará de Funcionamento, a Licença Sanitária from the municipal Vigilância Sanitária, and — most significantly — registration with the regional veterinary council (CRMV) plus a contracted veterinarian acting as Responsável Técnico (RT) under Lei 5.517/1968 Art. 27. The 'permit' layer is commercial/sanitary/professional, not environmental.

Sources: IBAMA, Presidência da República (Planalto), Conselho Federal de Medicina Veterinária (CFMV)

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Domestic fauna is exempt from IBAMA transport permits, so movement defaults to the agricultural-defence framework. Interstate movement requires a Guia de Trânsito Animal (GTA) issued by the state animal-health agency (OESA), preceded by an Atestado Sanitário from a vet within 3 days attesting the animal is healthy and free of ectoparasites. IN MAPA Nº 18/2006 exempted ONLY dogs and cats from the GTA, so domestic rodents (including R. rattus) still need one. International import requires prior MAPA authorization, an International Veterinary Certificate (CVI) endorsed by the origin country, and VIGIAGRO clearance; importing as a pet is hard in practice because no bilateral CVI protocol for 'domestic rodents' may exist yet, requiring a slow MAPA risk-analysis petition via SEI. Never release a roof rat (invasive-species containment + abandonment is maus-tratos).

Sources: Ministério da Agricultura e Pecuária (MAPA), Ministério da Agricultura e Pecuária (MAPA), IBAMA

Restrictions & responsibilities

Selling roof rats commercially (pet shop or for-profit rattery) requires ordinary business/sanitary/veterinary licensing — not IBAMA. You must register a business (CNPJ), obtain a municipal operating licence (Alvará) and a sanitary licence (Vigilância Sanitária), register with the regional veterinary council (CRMV), and contract a veterinarian as Responsável Técnico (RT) under Lei 5.517/1968. Hobbyist donation / free rehoming needs none of this.
  • Register a business entity (CNPJ) with the Receita Federal to issue notas fiscais
  • Obtain the municipal Alvará de Funcionamento (zoning for animal breeding/retail)
  • Obtain the Licença Sanitária from the municipal Vigilância Sanitária
  • Register the establishment with the regional CRMV and contract a veterinarian as Responsável Técnico (pay the annual ART fee)

Forms: CNPJ registration (Receita Federal), Alvará de Funcionamento (município), Licença Sanitária (Vigilância Sanitária municipal), Anotação de Responsabilidade Técnica (ART) — CRMV · Where: Receita Federal (CNPJ); município (Alvará); Vigilância Sanitária municipal (Licença Sanitária); regional CRMV (RT/ART) · Fees: Varies by município and state; annual ART fee to the CRMV for the Responsável Técnico

Source: Presidência da República (Planalto), Conselho Federal de Medicina Veterinária (CFMV)

Interstate movement requires a Guia de Trânsito Animal (GTA) from the state animal-health agency (OESA), preceded by an Atestado Sanitário from a vet within 3 days (animal healthy, ectoparasite-free). IN MAPA 18/2006 exempts only dogs and cats, so domestic rodents still need a GTA. International import requires MAPA/VIGIAGRO authorization + an international vet certificate (CVI); no R. rattus protocol may exist yet, so import can require a slow MAPA risk analysis via SEI. No IBAMA permit (R. rattus is domestic fauna). Never release a roof rat.
  • Get an Atestado Sanitário from a registered veterinarian within 3 days before the trip
  • Request a GTA from the state agricultural-defence agency (OESA) or a MAPA-habilitated vet; pay the state emission fee (DAE)
  • For international import: obtain MAPA prior authorization + a bilateral CVI endorsed by the origin country, then clear VIGIAGRO at a designated port

Forms: Atestado Sanitário (vet health certificate), Guia de Trânsito Animal (GTA), Certificado Veterinário Internacional (CVI) — international import · Where: State animal-health authority / OESA (GTA); MAPA/VIGIAGRO (international import) · Fees: State GTA emission fee via DAE (varies by state, typically per head/batch)

Source: Ministério da Agricultura e Pecuária (MAPA), Ministério da Agricultura e Pecuária (MAPA)

Releasing or abandoning a captive roof rat into the wild or urban environment is strictly prohibited. R. rattus is a recognized invasive alien species (CONABIO Res. 7/2018) and synanthropic pest; intentional or negligent release crosses from animal abuse (maus-tratos, Lei 9.605/1998 Art. 32) into severe environmental degradation with IBAMA administrative fines and possible criminal prosecution. The law permits private ownership but demands absolute containment — keep enclosures secure and never release.

Source: Presidência da República (Planalto), Ministério do Meio Ambiente (CONABIO)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Portaria IBAMA Nº 93/1998 — Anexo I lists 'Rato' (Rattus rattus) & 'Ratazana' (R. norvegicus) as FAUNA DOMÉSTICA; Art. 13 exempts domestic fauna from any IBAMA procedure — IBAMA
  • Lei Federal Nº 9.605/1998 (Lei de Crimes Ambientais) — Art. 29 (offenses apply only to fauna silvestre); Art. 32 (animal cruelty, all species) — Presidência da República (Planalto)
  • Lei Federal Nº 5.517/1968 — veterinary profession; Art. 27 mandates a Responsável Técnico for commercial animal establishments — Presidência da República (Planalto)
  • IN MAPA Nº 18/2006 — Guia de Trânsito Animal (GTA); exempts only dogs & cats, so domestic rodents still require a GTA — Ministério da Agricultura e Pecuária (MAPA)
  • MAPA — Importação de animais vivos (VIGIAGRO; CVI; no IBAMA permit for domestic fauna) — Ministério da Agricultura e Pecuária (MAPA)
  • IN IBAMA Nº 141/2006 — control/management of harmful synanthropic fauna (free-living management/eradication; NOT a captive-keeping ban) — IBAMA
  • Resolução CONABIO Nº 7/2018 — National Strategy for Invasive Alien Species (recognizes feral R. rattus as invasive; targets free-living populations, not captive domestic specimens) — Ministério do Meio Ambiente (CONABIO)
  • CFMV — Responsável Técnico (RT) requirement for establishments that breed/sell/exhibit live animals (CRMV registration + ART) — Conselho Federal de Medicina Veterinária (CFMV)
  • Fanratics Rattery (São Paulo) — active captive breeding of R. rattus in Brazil (practice precedent) — Brazilian rattery (secondary, practice evidence)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, rato-preto, ratazana-preta, rato-de-telhado.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Canada? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Canada

Summary. Canada has no single national rule for keeping a roof rat — it is decided province by province, and the provinces diverge sharply. Alberta bans the entire genus Rattus outright (a famously 'rat-free' province); Saskatchewan explicitly lists the black rat on its captive-wildlife allowed list; Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia all allow it (BC under a tame-captive exemption, Quebec with an import notice that the fancy rat is exempt from). Federally, the CFIA lets you import a pet rat with no permit or health certificate as long as it does NOT come from Africa. Check your province (below) AND your municipality.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The federal government does not regulate the day-to-day keeping of companion animals — that is left entirely to the provinces and municipalities, and the answer changes drastically at provincial borders. Alberta PROHIBITS keeping any rat (genus Rattus) with no pet exemption; Saskatchewan EXPLICITLY allows the black rat as captive wildlife; Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia allow it. So there is no single Canadian answer — see your province below.

Sources: Canadian Food Inspection Agency

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Federally unregulated; follows provincial possession rules. Prohibited where keeping is banned (Alberta), legal where the species is allowed (SK/ON/QC/BC). Commercial breeders everywhere also face municipal business-licensing, zoning, and provincial animal-welfare standards.

Sources: Canadian Food Inspection Agency

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Federally unregulated within Canada; follows provincial rules and municipal pet-shop / commercial-breeder licensing. Prohibited in Alberta (sale/distribution of a declared pest is banned); legal in SK/ON/QC/BC subject to local business rules.

Sources: Canadian Food Inspection Agency

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Bringing a pet rat INTO Canada is permissive federally: the CFIA does not require an import permit or veterinary health certificate for pet rodents — you simply declare the animal to the Canada Border Services Agency. The big exceptions: any rodent originating from the continent of Africa is barred (plague/monkeypox rule), airlines may demand their own vet certificate, and exporting live rodents to the Eurasian Economic Union is currently suspended. Critically, your destination PROVINCE's rules still apply — you may not bring a rat into (or, arguably, through) Alberta at all.

Sources: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, CFIA, CFIA

Restrictions & responsibilities

Federal import is permit-free for pet rodents NOT from Africa — but a Rattus rattus originating from any African country is barred entry (and may be seized or destroyed). Airlines often require a veterinary health certificate even though the government does not, and exporting live rodents to the Eurasian Economic Union (Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Armenia, Kyrgyzstan) is suspended until further notice.
  • Declare the animal as a pet to the CBSA at the border
  • Confirm it is not African-origin
  • Check your airline's own health-certificate rule

Forms: Bringing animals to Canada — CFIA · Where: Canada Border Services Agency / CFIA National Import Service Centre · Fees: No CFIA fee for pet rodents

Source: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, CFIA

The answer depends entirely on your province. Alberta bans all rats (do NOT bring one in); Saskatchewan, Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia permit them. Always check your province (below) and your municipal bylaws (which can cap the number of animals or require a breeder licence).
  • Find your province below
  • Check your city/municipal animal bylaws

Source: Canadian Food Inspection Agency

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Help change this

How to help in Canada

Canada has no single national rule for keeping a pet roof rat (Rattus rattus); it is decided province by province, and the provinces diverge sharply. Saskatchewan explicitly lists the black rat as allowed captive wildlife; Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia all permit it; and federally the CFIA allows import of a pet rat with no permit or health certificate, with one hard exception (no rodents originating from Africa). The outlier, and the one true prohibition in Canada, is Alberta. Under the Agricultural Pests Act and its Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, the entire genus Rattus is a declared pest, and the Government of Alberta states that it is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta. There is no exemption for a tame, captive-bred animal kept indoors. The rule was written to keep wild Norway rats (Rattus norvegicus) from establishing breeding colonies on Alberta's farmland, but as written it also covers domesticated pet rats that pose none of that agricultural risk and have never founded a wild population.

The ask: Ask Alberta to add a narrow exemption to the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation for tame, captive-bred companion rats kept indoors, the same kind of carve-out that lets neighbouring provinces allow them safely. The case rests on a cost-benefit judgment that is Alberta's to make. The province already permits cats and dogs, which are themselves non-native and documented to harm native wildlife, because their companionship is judged worth the trade-off. Whether the limited additional risk of a few sterile, tame, indoor-only pet rats, which have never founded a wild colony, is similarly outweighed by their value as companions is a question to put to the decision-makers, not a conclusion to assert. The change is to the regulation itself (a matter for the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation and your MLA), not a favour the rat-control program can grant, because the program is correctly applying the law as written. Outside Alberta, no change is needed to keep a pet roof rat; confirm your province's rule and your municipal bylaws.

Where the lever really is: Branch (b): the law as written. The barrier is a deliberate statutory and regulatory listing, not a clerk's misreading. Alberta's Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, made under the Agricultural Pests Act, declares the whole genus Rattus a pest, and the Government of Alberta's rat-control page states that it is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta, with no pet exemption. The rat-control program is applying that regulation as drafted, so emailing the program to ask permission, or appealing its decision, will not work. The fix is to amend the regulation to add a captive-bred companion-animal exemption, a decision for the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation acting on public and political input. The correct lever is the legislature: your MLA and the Minister. For the other relevant provinces (SK, ON, QC, BC) there is no law-as-written problem to fix; the roof rat is already permitted, so they are a confirm-your-province check, not advocacy targets. On the species-not-domestication point, the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over: https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Members of the Legislative Assembly of Alberta — official MLA directory / 'find your MLA' (legislature) — official contact page
    The prohibition lives in a regulation the Minister and Cabinet control, so the change must come through the political/legislative branch. This official Legislative Assembly page lets any Alberta resident look up and contact their own MLA — the representative who can raise a regulatory amendment or relay constituent demand to the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation. Use it to write your own MLA; never address an individual member by name picked at random.
  • Elections Alberta — Member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) search (legislature) — official contact page
    An independent official tool to confirm which MLA represents your address, in case you are unsure of your constituency before contacting them via the Assembly directory above.
  • Alberta Rat Control Program (Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation) — official program inbox (executive / agency) — rats@gov.ab.ca
    Secondary channel. This is the official inbox of the program that administers the declared-pest rule. It cannot grant a pet exemption on its own (the regulation must change first), but a polite written request for the government's current position on tame captive-bred companion rats, and for whether a narrow exemption could be recommended to the Minister, puts the ask on record with the administering body and can be cited when you write your MLA. Verified on the Government of Alberta rat-control program page.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To my MLA / the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation,

I am writing about Alberta's prohibition on keeping pet rats. Under the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, the entire genus Rattus is a declared pest, so even a tame, captive-bred companion rat is illegal to own here.

I understand and support the goal of keeping wild Norway rats from establishing in Alberta's farmland. But the regulation as written also bans domesticated pet rats that are captive-bred, hand-tame, kept entirely indoors, and never released, animals that pose none of the agricultural risk the rule was designed to stop and that have never founded a wild colony.

Saskatchewan, Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia all allow these pets safely. The issue is not whether a rat can be domesticated; it plainly can. The dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised as domestic because of generations bred for tameness. The fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred pet rat is the same case. The issue is simply that the species is on a list with no exemption for companion animals.

This is a cost-benefit judgment that belongs to Alberta. The province already permits cats and dogs, themselves non-native and documented to kill native wildlife, because their companionship is judged worth the trade-off. The narrow question is whether the limited additional risk of a few sterile, tame, indoor-only pet rats, which have never founded a wild colony, is outweighed by their value as companions. I am not asking you to reach a particular conclusion, only to weigh that question, which neighbouring provinces have already answered by allowing these pets while keeping their own wild-rat controls in place.

I respectfully ask you to support adding a narrow exemption to the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation for tame, captive-bred rats kept indoors as pets, while leaving the wild-rat controls fully in place.

Thank you for considering this.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your town and constituency]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Bringing animals to Canada: importing and travelling with pets — CFIA (rodents need no import permit/health certificate) — Canadian Food Inspection Agency
  • Terrestrial animal products and by-products import policy — CFIA (Africa-origin rodent restriction) — CFIA
  • Export of live rodents to the Eurasian Economic Union — CFIA (health certificates suspended) — CFIA

Search terms: Rattus rattus, black rat, roof rat, ship rat, rat noir, rat des toits.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Switzerland? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Switzerland

Summary. Switzerland is legal for the roof rat, confirmed in writing by the federal veterinary office (BLV) on 15 June 2026. Keeping and breeding house rats (Rattus rattus) are permitted, and keeping small rodents needs no permit and no proof of competence (Art. 89 let. a of the Animal Welfare Ordinance, TSchV). The same welfare rules as for the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) apply: rats are social, so at least two must be kept, and the enclosure must meet the Annex 2 minimum dimensions (the BLV points to the German Säugetiergutachten 2014, about 2 square metres for two house rats). A cantonal permit plus recognised training is required only to breed and give away more than 300 rats per year to third parties (Art. 94 para. 2, Art. 101 let. c para. 4 TSchV), so an ordinary private keeper or hobby breeder needs nothing. R. rattus is on no CITES appendix and no Swiss invasive-species list. Import and transport depend on the country of origin (EU or non-EU) and whether the owner travels with the animals, so check the BLV travel guidance. Never release a roof rat.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • The BLV (Swiss Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office), Katrin Nydegger of Customer Communication, confirmed in writing on 15 June 2026 that keeping and breeding house rats (Rattus rattus) are permitted in Switzerland.
  • Keeping small rodents needs no permit (Art. 89 let. a of the Animal Welfare Ordinance, TSchV). A cantonal permit is required only to breed and give away more than 300 rats per year to third parties (Art. 94 para. 2 and Art. 101 let. c para. 4 TSchV).
  • Husbandry follows the minimum requirements in Annex 2 of the TSchV. Because the Ordinance sets no species-specific minimums for Rattus rattus, the BLV advises meeting at least the same requirements as for the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus), including keeping them in pairs or groups, and points to the German Säugetiergutachten 2014 (about 2 square metres for two house rats) as a guide.
  • Import and transport requirements depend on the country of origin (EU or non-EU) and whether the owner travels with the animals; the BLV refers to its 'travelling with pets' page for the conditions.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-15

The BLV confirmed in writing (2026-06-15) that keeping house rats (Rattus rattus) is permitted in Switzerland and that keeping small rodents needs no permit (Art. 89 let. a TSchV). Mandatory welfare conditions apply: rats are social, so keep at least two (TSchV Art. 13 and Annex 2), and meet the Annex 2 minimum husbandry requirements, at least the same as for the fancy rat R. norvegicus (the BLV points to the German Säugetiergutachten 2014, about 2 square metres for two house rats). No cantonal permit and no proof of competence are needed for private keeping.

Sources: Swiss Confederation / Fedlex, BLV (Federal Food Safety & Veterinary Office), Swiss Confederation / Fedlex

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-15

Private breeding for personal use or occasional rehoming is permit-free. A cantonal Bewilligung + recognised training (Sachkundenachweis/FBA) is required only above the commercial threshold, 300 rats given away (or used as feeder animals) per year, or for any 'gewerbsmässiger' (commercial) pet dealing. A normal hobby rattery stays well under 300/yr. (Same Wildtier-classification caveat as keeping.)

Sources: Swiss Confederation / Fedlex, BLV (Federal Food Safety & Veterinary Office)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-15

Gratuitous transfer (giving away) of captive-bred rats with no commercial element is lawful without a permit below 300 animals/year. Commercial trade ('gewerbsmässiger Handel') at any scale needs a cantonal Bewilligung + BLV-recognised training; organised animal swaps (Tierbörsen) have their own permit/training rule. No price cap; the test is whether the activity is commercial.

Sources: Swiss Confederation / Fedlex, BLV

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-15

Internal transport needs only welfare-compliant conditions (TSchG Art. 3). Non-commercial personal import of up to 5 healthy rodents from a non-EU country needs no import permit and no health certificate (BLV travel rules; checks possible at Zürich/Geneva). Commercial import (resale/breeding stock) needs a BLV import authorization + possibly an origin health certificate. R. rattus is not on any CITES appendix, so no CITES permit. Never release.

Sources: BLV, Swiss Confederation / Fedlex

Restrictions & responsibilities

Switzerland legally requires rats to be kept in groups, keeping a single rat is an offence (TSchV social-species rule). Meet the minimum enclosure dimensions (~0.5 m²/0.5 m³ for up to 5 rats). Private keeping/breeding is permit-free; a cantonal permit + training is needed only for commercial trade or giving away 300+ rodents/year. ⚠️ Confirm with your cantonal veterinary office that R. rattus is treated as a permit-free small rodent (not a Wildtier). Never release.
  • Confirm R. rattus's small-rodent (permit-free) status with your Kantonstierarztamt before acquiring

Where: Cantonal veterinary office (Kantonstierarztamt)

Source: BLV (Federal Food Safety & Veterinary Office), Swiss Confederation / Fedlex

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Tierschutzgesetz (TSchG, SR 455), Federal Animal Welfare Act — Swiss Confederation / Fedlex
  • Tierschutzverordnung (TSchV, SR 455.1), Art. 2 (Wildtier/Heimtier), Art. 13 (social), Anhang 2 Tab.1 (rats), Art. 101–102 (permits) — Swiss Confederation / Fedlex
  • BLV Merkblatt 'Ratten im Recht', private keeping permit-free; group rule; enclosure minimums; 300/yr threshold — BLV (Federal Food Safety & Veterinary Office)
  • BLV Fachinformation, Bewilligungs- und Ausbildungspflicht für den gewerbsmässigen Handel mit Heimtieren — BLV
  • BLV, Travelling with pets / import of rodents (≤5 personal, no permit/health cert) — BLV
  • BLV, EU-zugelassene Einrichtungen (lists Hausratte / R. rattus as a 'Domestizierte Form') — BLV (Switzerland)
  • BLV, Erläuterungen zur EDAV-Ht (companion-animal import; ≤5 rodents non-commercial) — BLV (Switzerland)
  • Freisetzungsverordnung (FrSV, SR 814.911), R. rattus NOT on the invasive-organism annexes — Fedlex (Switzerland)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, Hausratte, rat noir, ratto nero.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Chile? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Chile

Summary. Chile has no blanket ban on keeping captive-bred rats as pets, and in practice a roof rat is treated like the openly-sold fancy rat (R. norvegicus). Both are established commensal exotics classified as invasive (MMA's 2017 naturalized/invasive catalogue) and cited as 'especie dañina' in the agricultural-pest context, but NO SAG decree under the Ley de Caza (Ley 19.473) formally lists either Rattus species or bans keeping them. The Ley de Caza's wildlife-keeper registry (RNTFS) and criadero licensing are built for genuinely wild/protected exotic fauna (parrots, reptiles), not ubiquitous commensal rodents — so captive-bred pet rats sit in a practical gray zone (neither licensed nor expressly prohibited), and fancy rats are sold across Chilean platforms with no reported enforcement. For R. rattus there's an extra layer: its pest/invasive designation creates theoretical friction with private breeding, though no statute prohibits captive-bred specimens. IMPORT of any live exotic rodent needs a case-by-case SAG Art. 25 internment permit (which SAG could refuse on ecological grounds given the invasive status); internal transport of lawfully-held animals is unregulated. Not CITES-listed. ⚠️ Watch: the MMA is building a formal official invasive-species list under Ley 21.600 (2023) that, if it attaches possession provisions, could flip this to prohibited (Spain-style).

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

No Chilean statute prohibits a private individual from keeping captive-bred R. rattus. The Ley de Caza (19.473) governs 'fauna silvestre' via RNTFS registration aimed at exotic WILDLIFE (parrots, caimans) — a ubiquitous commensal like R. rattus doesn't neatly fall into that permit pipeline. The MMA EEI catalogue documents R. rattus as naturalized/invasive but prescribes no keeping ban. The strongest signal: R. norvegicus, in the same pest registers, is openly sold. No SAG resolution banning tenencia of captive R. rattus exists.

Sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional (BCN), SAG, Ministerio del Medio Ambiente

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-11

Breeding exotic fauna can in principle require SAG criadero-de-fauna-silvestre-exótica registration under the Ley de Caza, but that pathway targets genuinely wild/protected exotics; no regulation clearly extends criadero licensing to commensal rodents. Ley 21.020 ('Ley Cholito') requires companion-animal breeders/sellers to register with SAG but its guidance focuses on dogs/cats. Chilean vendors openly breed/sell rats (no active enforcement); the 'unenforced vs legal' gap is unresolved.

Sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional (BCN), BCN

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-11

Domestic rats are actively sold on Chilean platforms/specialist stores with no reported enforcement. Chilean law bars commercial sale of wild-captured native fauna but doesn't clearly reach captive-bred exotic commensal rodents. Ley 21.020 requires companion-animal vendors/breeders to hold SAG registration + per-animal vet health cards (the closest affirmative obligation). No statute prohibits selling/donating captive-bred R. rattus; the 'especie dañina' tag affects pest-control authorization, not a commercial ban under Ley 19.473's current text.

Sources: Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional (BCN), BCN

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

IMPORT of any live exotic animal (incl. rodents) needs two SAG authorizations under Ley 19.473 Art. 25: (1) an Exotic Fauna Internment Permit from DIPROREN; and (2) a species-specific zoosanitary protocol from PROPEC — ~60–90 days' notice. ⚠️ Because R. rattus is an established feral pest in Chile, SAG MAY refuse the import permit on ecological grounds (real risk; confirm). Not CITES-listed. INTERNAL transport of lawfully-held pets has no specific permit (Ley Cholito imposes only normal vet care) — practically unregulated. Never release.

Sources: SAG, Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional (BCN)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Keeping a captive-bred roof rat in Chile is in a gray zone (no licence, no express ban — treated like the openly-sold fancy rat). IMPORTING one needs a SAG Art. 25 exotic-fauna internment permit (DIPROREN) + a PROPEC zoosanitary protocol, applied 60–90 days ahead — and SAG could refuse it given R. rattus's invasive status. Internal transport of a lawful animal is unregulated. ⚠️ Watch the MMA's forthcoming EEI list (could add a possession rule). Never release.
  • For import: SAG DIPROREN exotic-fauna internment permit (Art. 25) + PROPEC zoosanitary protocol

Where: SAG — DIPROREN (import permit) / PROPEC (zoosanitary)

Source: SAG

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Help change this

How to help in Chile

Chile is currently an unclear case. It is building its invasive-species rules under Ley 21.600 (2023) and the new Biodiversity Service (SBAP). The 2025 public consultation on the draft regulation for qualifying invasive species and prevention plans has closed, but the invasive-species catalogue (the actual list) and further rules are still to come. How Rattus rattus is classified there could restrict keeping it as a pet.

The ask: When the MMA/SBAP opens its next public consultation (consulta pública), especially on the invasive-species catalogue, submit a comment asking that domesticated, captive-bred R. rattus kept as pets be distinguished from wild invasive populations: a keeping pathway rather than a flat ban. The fancy rat already kept and sold in Chile is itself the wild brown rat (R. norvegicus), domesticated only in the 19th century; a captive-bred R. rattus is the same case one species over (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/). Dogs and cats are also non-native introduced species documented to harm native wildlife, yet are permitted as pets. Whether the limited additional risk of a few tame, indoor-only, never-released roof rats is similarly outweighed by their companionship and educational value is a cost-benefit judgment for the MMA to make. Watch the consultation portal for the next window.

Where the lever really is: This is decided by the executive regulator (MMA / SBAP) through formal public-consultation windows. The lever is submitting a comment when a window is open, and writing the MMA, not the courts or Congress. No window is open now; the move is to watch for the next one.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministerio del Medio Ambiente (MMA) — consulta pública (EEI / Ley 21.600) (public comment) — official contact page
    The draft regulation qualifying invasive exotic species and prevention plans is run here for public comment under Ley 21.600. Comment while a window is open.
  • Servicio Agrícola y Ganadero (SAG) (executive / agency) — diproren@sag.gob.cl
    SAG coordinates invasive-species control on the agricultural side; a useful second touchpoint.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Ministry of the Environment (MMA),

I am writing about how the roof rat (Rattus rattus) is classified in the invasive-species work under Ley 21.600.

I ask that domesticated, captive-bred roof rats kept as pets be treated separately from wild invasive populations. These are tame animals bred over generations, kept indoors in cages and never released. A fully closed indoor colony poses no realistic invasive risk. A keeping pathway (registration or a simple permit) would protect biodiversity goals without criminalising responsible pet owners.

The fancy rat already kept and sold in Chile is itself the wild brown rat (R. norvegicus), domesticated only in the 19th century; a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over. Dogs and cats are also non-native introduced animals documented to harm native wildlife, yet are permitted as pets because their companionship is judged worth the trade-off. Whether the limited additional risk of a few tame, indoor-only, never-released roof rats is similarly outweighed by their companionship and educational value is a cost-benefit judgment for the Ministry to make.

Please consider this distinction in the EEI catalogue and any prevention plan.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
Español
Al Ministerio del Medio Ambiente (MMA),

Escribo en relación con la clasificación de la rata negra (Rattus rattus) en el trabajo sobre especies exóticas invasoras que se desarrolla en el marco de la Ley 21.600.

Solicito que las ratas negras domesticadas, criadas en cautiverio y mantenidas como mascotas se traten de forma separada de las poblaciones silvestres invasoras. Son animales mansos, criados durante generaciones, mantenidos en jaulas en interiores y nunca liberados. Una colonia totalmente cerrada y en interiores no representa un riesgo invasor realista. Una vía de tenencia (un registro o un permiso sencillo) permitiría proteger los objetivos de biodiversidad sin criminalizar a las personas responsables que las tienen como mascotas.

La rata domesticada (Rattus norvegicus) que ya se mantiene y se vende en Chile es la propia rata parda silvestre, domesticada solo en el siglo XIX; una Rattus rattus criada en cautiverio es el mismo caso una especie más allá. Los perros y los gatos también son especies introducidas, no nativas, documentadas como dañinas para la fauna silvestre nativa, y aun así se permiten como mascotas porque se juzga que su compañía vale la pena. Si el riesgo adicional, limitado, de unas pocas ratas mansas, mantenidas solo en interiores y nunca liberadas, se ve igualmente compensado por su valor de compañía y educativo es una ponderación de costo-beneficio que corresponde al Ministerio.

Le pido que considere esta distinción en el catálogo de EEI y en cualquier plan de prevención.

Atentamente,
[Su nombre]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Ley 19.473 (Ley de Caza, 1996) — Arts. 1–5, 25 (internación), 26(e) (especie dañina) — Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional (BCN)
  • DS 5/1998 — Reglamento de la Ley de Caza (mod. DS 53) — SAG
  • MMA — Catálogo de Especies Exóticas Asilvestradas/Naturalizadas (2017): R. rattus + R. norvegicus naturalized invasives — Ministerio del Medio Ambiente
  • Ley 21.020 ('Ley Cholito', 2017) — tenencia responsable; breeder/seller registration — BCN
  • Ley 21.600 (2023) — crea SBAP; mandates a formal EEI list (not yet gazetted for this) — BCN / MMA
  • SAG — Internación de fauna exótica (Art. 25 permit; DIPROREN; ~60-day timeline) + non-traditional pet protocol (PROPEC) — SAG
  • SAG - Registro Nacional de Tenedores de Fauna Silvestre (RNTFS), procedimientos — SAG (Chile)
  • SAG - Ingreso de otros animales/mascotas no tradicionales (PROPEC) — SAG (Chile)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, rata negra, rata de los tejados.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Colombia? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Colombia

Summary. Colombia prohibits private keeping, breeding, selling, and transport of the roof rat. R. rattus is formally cataloged a High-Risk Exotic Invasive Species (Especie Exótica Invasora) under Resolución MAVDT 0848/2008 (+ 0207/2010) on the strict-invasive PROHIBITIVE track — NOT the closed-cycle 'zoocría' track — so Decreto 1076/2015 Art. 2.2.2.3.2.2 bans its 'introduction, commercialization, mobilization, promotion and possession (tenencia)' outright. The captive-bred-as-pet loophole is now permanently closed: Ley 2473 de 2025 (8 Jul 2025) amended Civil Code Art. 687 to declare that exotic/wild fauna CANNOT be a 'domestic companion animal,' regardless of how tame or how many generations captive-bred — every R. rattus stays under environmental law where possession is banned. Breeding is a CRIME (Penal Code Art. 330A: 48–108 months prison + heavy fines). Import is administratively impossible (the genus Rattus is absent from the ICA pet-import whitelist, Resolución 842/2010). A confiscated roof rat is not rehomed — as an Angiostrongylus cantonensis (rat lungworm) and plague vector it is administratively euthanized. The ONLY legal holders are institutions under scientific/zoological permits (ANLA/CAR) — never private hobbyists. (Note: even the fancy rat R. norvegicus has only a narrow lab/bioterium import route, not a pet route; R. rattus has neither.)

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

Private possession (tenencia) of a declared invasive species is banned by Decreto 1076/2015 Art. 2.2.2.3.2.2; R. rattus is on the strict-invasive track of Resolución 0848/2008 (High Risk). Ley 2473/2025 amended Civil Code Art. 687 with a paragraph stating exotic/wild fauna are NOT 'domestic companion animals,' permanently defeating the captive-bred/'tame' argument. The state does not distinguish a feral roof rat from a multi-generation captive-bred one. Enforcement (Ley 1333/2009) = preventive confiscation by the environmental authority (CAR) + Environmental Police/GELMA; a seized R. rattus is administratively euthanized (Angiostrongylus/plague vector), not rehomed; fines scale up to 5,000 SMLMV. Only institutional scientific/zoological permit-holders may hold the species — never a private individual.

Sources: Presidencia de Colombia, Ministerio de Ambiente (MAVDT/MADS), Congreso de la República, Congreso de la República

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

Breeding R. rattus — hobby or commercial — is a criminal offense. Penal Code Art. 330A (Ley 599/2000, added by Ley 1453/2011) penalizes propagating an invasive exotic species without authorization with 48–108 months prison + fines of 133–15,000 SMLMV. The zoocría (captive-breeding) framework of Ley 611/2000 has no hobbyist exemption and cannot license a declared-invasive species (Decreto 1076/2015 bars its commercialization), so no commercial/scientific zoocría permit will issue for the pet trade. There is no closed-cycle (Art. 4) pathway for R. rattus — it sits on the prohibitive Art. 1 track.

Sources: Congreso de la República, Congreso de la República, Presidencia de Colombia

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

Decreto 1076/2015 Art. 2.2.2.3.2.2 explicitly bans the commercialization and promotion of declared invasive species; the ICA pet-trade whitelists exclude the genus Rattus. Even gratuitous transfer (giving away) is barred because no one can legally possess the animal (tenencia ban), so any transfer just facilitates a further infraction. A licensed pet dealer caught selling R. rattus faces confiscation, fines under Ley 1333/2009, and definitive closure of the establishment.

Sources: Presidencia de Colombia, Congreso de la República, Instituto Colombiano Agropecuario (ICA)

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

IMPORT: administratively impossible — Resolución ICA 842/2010 limits 'other pets' import to ferrets, rabbits, chinchillas, hamsters, guinea pigs and gerbils; the genus Rattus is absent, so the ICA SISPAP system cannot generate the Documento Zoosanitario de Importación (DZI) needed before shipment, and an animal arriving without it is rejected/confiscated/euthanized at the border. INTERNAL movement: needs a Salvoconducto Único Nacional (SUN) under Decreto 1076/2015 Title 2, which requires proof of legal origin (a licensed-zoocriadero receipt or valid ICA import docs) — impossible for R. rattus, so no CAR issues one; illegal transport triggers Penal Code Art. 328 (illicit use of renewable natural resources). Not CITES-listed (irrelevant — the invasive ban governs). Never release.

Sources: Instituto Colombiano Agropecuario (ICA), Presidencia de Colombia, Congreso de la República

Restrictions & responsibilities

Colombia bans keeping/breeding/selling/transporting R. rattus as a declared High-Risk Exotic Invasive Species. There is NO private or hobbyist pathway: possession is an environmental infraction (confiscation + administrative euthanasia), breeding is a crime (48–108 months prison), import is administratively impossible (genus Rattus off the ICA whitelist), and internal transport requires a salvoconducto that cannot be issued. Ley 2473/2025 forecloses any 'it's a tame captive-bred pet' argument. Do not acquire one; if you already hold one, a Derecho de Petición to MADS is the only way to ask about an amnesty/scientific-transfer alternative to seizure.
  • Do not import, buy, breed, or accept an R. rattus in Colombia — all are prohibited (breeding is criminal).
  • If you already possess one: consider a Derecho de Petición (Constitution Art. 23) to MADS asking about a grandfather/amnesty registration or transfer to an authorized scientific bioterium rather than euthanasia.
  • Institutions only: scientific/zoological holding requires an ANLA/CAR environmental license (biosecurity containment) — not available to individuals.

Where: MADS (policy/amnesty Derecho de Petición); regional CAR (enforcement/SUN); ICA (import)

Source: Presidencia de Colombia, Ministerio de Ambiente (MAVDT/MADS), Congreso de la República

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Colombia. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Colombia

In Colombia there is no legal way for a private individual to keep, breed, buy, sell, give away, import, or transport a roof rat (Rattus rattus), including a tame, captive-bred one. The roof rat is officially cataloged as a High-Risk Exotic Invasive Species (Resolución MAVDT 0848 de 2008), so Decreto 1076 de 2015 (Art. 2.2.2.3.2.2) bans its introduction, sale, transport, promotion, and possession (tenencia). In July 2025, Ley 2473 amended Civil Code Art. 687 to declare that exotic and wild fauna are not domestic companion animals, regardless of how tame the animal is or how many generations it was bred in captivity, which closes the captive-bred-pet argument. Breeding is a criminal offense (Penal Code Art. 330A: 48 to 108 months in prison plus fines). Import is administratively impossible because the genus Rattus is not on the ICA pet-import whitelist (Resolución ICA 842/2010, which lists only ferrets, rabbits, chinchillas, hamsters, guinea pigs, and gerbils). A confiscated roof rat is not rehomed: as a potential rat-lungworm (Angiostrongylus cantonensis) and plague vector, it is administratively euthanized. Only institutions with a scientific or zoological permit (ANLA/CAR) may legally hold the species, never a private hobbyist. The ban is grounded in ecological and public-health concerns (island ecosystems such as San Andrés and Gorgona; rat lungworm spread via the Giant African Snail), so asking the agency to reinterpret the rule will not work.

The ask: In Colombia today there is no private pathway to keep a roof rat, and a letter will not change that. If you do not already hold one, do not acquire, import, or breed one; breeding is a crime. The realistic, lawful actions are: (1) If you already possess a pre-2025 captive-bred roof rat, file a Derecho de Petición to MinAmbiente (MADS) asking whether any amnesty or pre-existing-possession registration exists to keep it strictly non-breeding until natural death, or whether you may voluntarily surrender it to an authorized scientific bioterium instead of having it euthanized. (2) Optionally ask ICA in writing to confirm whether any administrative exception or tariff code exists to import domestic-line Rattus as a companion animal. The expected answer is none, which documents the gap for the public record. (3) Broadening the law itself (creating a regulated captive-bred companion-rodent category, or distinguishing biosecure indoor lines from feral invasives) is a matter for the Congreso de la República, not the environmental agency, which is correctly applying the current statute. The point to raise with Congress concerns the Ley 2473/2025 line between domestic and exotic fauna: domestication, not wild ancestry, is what makes an animal a domestic companion. The dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic. The fancy rat (R. norvegicus), kept openly as a pet worldwide, is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/), so a captive-bred animal can be domesticated regardless of its species' wild origin. That is a legislative question for Congress to weigh against the species' zoonotic and island-ecosystem record, not a basis to ask the agency to disregard the statute it must apply.

Where the lever really is: This is the law as written, not a bureaucratic misreading. The agency (MinAmbiente) is applying the statute correctly: (a) Resolución MAVDT 0848 de 2008 puts R. rattus on the strict-invasive (prohibitive) track as High-Risk, not the closed-cycle 'zoocría' track; (b) Decreto 1076 de 2015 Art. 2.2.2.3.2.2 bans possession of any declared invasive species; (c) Ley 2473 de 2025 amended Civil Code Art. 687 to state that exotic and wild fauna are not domestic companion animals regardless of taming or captive breeding; and (d) the import whitelist (Resolución ICA 842/2010) does not contain the genus Rattus. The ban rests on a documented zoonotic and ecological record (rat lungworm via the Giant African Snail; plague; island-ecosystem damage). Appealing to MinAmbiente to reinterpret the rules will not change anything: the agency has no discretion to authorize private possession of a declared High-Risk invasive, and a de-cataloging petition is a non-starter given the documented harm. The genuine levers are two, both narrow: (1) For someone who already holds a pre-2025 captive-bred animal, a Derecho de Petición to MinAmbiente is appropriate, but it asks only about amnesty/registration or surrender to a bioterium as a humane alternative to seizure and euthanasia, not a general right to keep pet roof rats. (2) Any change to who may keep the species would require the Congreso de la República to amend the statutory framework (for example, a regulated biosecure captive-line category). There is no private route today, and the agency cannot create one.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (MinAmbiente / MADS) — Atención y Servicios a la Ciudadanía (PQRSDF / Derecho de Petición) (executive / agency) — servicioalciudadano@minambiente.gov.co
    The environmental ministry is the authority that catalogs invasive species and governs possession. It is the correct address for a Derecho de Petición (Constitution Art. 23; Ley 1755 de 2015) — but ONLY for the narrow, honest questions: does an amnesty/pre-existing-possession registry exist for an animal already held, and can a voluntarily surrendered animal go to an authorized scientific bioterium instead of being euthanized. Use the official PQRSDF channel (online portal linked from this page, or the servicioalciudadano inbox). It cannot and will not authorize general private keeping — the law forecloses that.
  • Instituto Colombiano Agropecuario (ICA) — Cuarentena Animal / Importación de animales de compañía diferentes a perros y gatos (executive / agency) — cuarentena.animal@ica.gov.co
    ICA controls animal import. A short written query asking ICA to confirm whether any tariff code or administrative exception exists to import domestic-line Rattus as a companion animal documents the regulatory gap on the public record (expected answer: none — the genus Rattus is absent from the Resolución 842/2010 whitelist). Useful only as evidence-gathering, not as a route to a permit.
  • Congreso de la República de Colombia — Cámara de Representantes (contacto ciudadano / atención al ciudadano) (legislature) — official contact page
    Because the prohibition is statutory (Decreto 1076/2015 + Resolución 0848/2008 + Ley 2473/2025), the only body that could ever create a regulated pathway for biosecure captive-bred companion rodents is the legislature, not the agency. This is the official citizen-contact channel for raising that idea with representatives. Realistically a long, uphill ask given the species' genuine invasive/zoonotic record — included for honesty, not false hope.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To: Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development (MinAmbiente), Citizen Services / Right of Petition
Subject: Right of Petition regarding an already-held captive-bred Rattus rattus: possible amnesty/registration or transfer to a scientific facility

Dear Sir or Madam,

I write respectfully under the right of petition (Constitution Art. 23; Law 1755 of 2015). I understand that Rattus rattus is listed as a High-Risk Exotic Invasive Species (Resolution 0848 of 2008), that its possession is prohibited (Decree 1076 of 2015), and that Law 2473 of 2025 confirms exotic fauna are not companion animals. I am not contesting that framework or the genuine ecological and public-health concerns behind it.

My questions are narrow: (1) Does any amnesty, pre-existing-possession registry, or special authorization exist that would let a citizen keep a captive-bred specimen acquired before 2025 strictly as a non-breeding, indoor-only animal until its natural death? (2) If not, may such an animal be voluntarily surrendered to an authorized scientific facility (bioterio) rather than being euthanized? The animal in question is captive-bred, tame, kept indoors, and never released.

I request a written reply within the legal term. Thank you for your guidance.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your city / contact details]
Español
Para: Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (MinAmbiente), Atención al Ciudadano / Derecho de Petición
Asunto: Derecho de Petición sobre un ejemplar de Rattus rattus nacido en cautiverio ya en tenencia: posible amnistía/registro o traslado a un bioterio científico

Respetados señores:

En ejercicio del derecho de petición (Art. 23 de la Constitución; Ley 1755 de 2015) me dirijo a ustedes de manera respetuosa. Entiendo que Rattus rattus está catalogada como Especie Exótica Invasora de Alto Riesgo (Resolución 0848 de 2008), que su tenencia está prohibida (Decreto 1076 de 2015) y que la Ley 2473 de 2025 confirma que la fauna exótica no es animal de compañía. No controvierto ese marco ni las legítimas preocupaciones ecológicas y de salud pública que lo sustentan.

Mis preguntas son puntuales: (1) ¿Existe algún mecanismo de amnistía, registro de tenencia preexistente o autorización especial que permita a un ciudadano mantener un ejemplar nacido en cautiverio adquirido antes de 2025, en tenencia estricta, sin reproducción, exclusivamente al interior del hogar y hasta su muerte natural? (2) De no existir, ¿puede dicho ejemplar entregarse voluntariamente a un bioterio científico autorizado en lugar de ser sometido a eutanasia? El animal es nacido en cautiverio, manso, mantenido dentro del hogar y nunca liberado.

Solicito respuesta escrita dentro del término legal. Agradezco su orientación.

Atentamente,
[Su nombre]
[Su ciudad / datos de contacto]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Ley 2473 de 2025 — modifica Código Civil Art. 687: la fauna exótica/silvestre NO es 'animal doméstico de compañía' (cierra el vacío de la mascota cautiva) — Congreso de la República
  • Decreto 1076/2015 — Art. 2.2.2.3.2.2 (prohíbe introducción/comercialización/movilización/promoción/tenencia de invasoras) + Título 2/Sec. 22 (salvoconducto SUN) — Presidencia de Colombia
  • Resolución MAVDT 0848/2008 (+ 0207/2010) — lista de especies exóticas invasoras; R. rattus 'Alto Riesgo' (track Art. 1 prohibitivo) — Ministerio de Ambiente (MAVDT/MADS)
  • Ley 599/2000 (Código Penal) Art. 330A (+ Art. 328) — propagación de especie exótica invasora: 48–108 meses prisión + multa 133–15.000 SMLMV — Congreso de la República
  • Ley 1333/2009 — procedimiento sancionatorio ambiental (decomiso + multas hasta 5.000 SMLMV + cierre de establecimientos) — Congreso de la República
  • Resolución ICA 842/2010 — requisitos importación 'otras mascotas' (hurones/conejos/chinchillas/hámsteres/cobayos/jerbos; género Rattus AUSENTE) — Instituto Colombiano Agropecuario (ICA)
  • Ley 611/2000 — manejo sostenible de fauna silvestre / zoocriaderos (sin exención para aficionados; no licenciable para invasoras) — Congreso de la República

Search terms: Rattus rattus, rata negra, rata de techo, especie exótica invasora, fauna exótica, tenencia.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Czechia? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Czechia

Summary. Czechia is cleanly permissive for the roof rat, and the verified statutory texts make it cleaner than the preliminary note implied. Czech law is a negative-list (civil-law) system: what is not forbidden is allowed, and an exotic animal needs a permit only if its species is expressly named on the 'special care' list. The Animal Protection Act (Zákon č. 246/1992 Sb.) and its implementing Decree č. 451/2021 Sb. enumerate the species requiring special care, and the mammal entries are limited to primates, carnivores (incl. pinnipeds), elephants, and odd- and even-toed ungulates. No rodent at all appears on that list, so both Rattus rattus (Czech: krysa obecná) and the fancy rat Rattus norvegicus (Czech: potkan) are default unregulated companion animals (zvířata v zájmovém chovu) with identical standing. R. rattus is also NOT on the EU Union list of invasive alien species (Reg. 1143/2014 / Implementing Reg. 2016/1141) and not on any Czech national invasive list under Zákon č. 364/2021 Sb. (which implements the EU IAS regime; the regulated rodents are the muskrat and nutria, not Rattus), and it is not CITES-listed. A hobbyist may keep, breed, and sell or give captive-bred roof rats with no permit, subject only to baseline welfare duties; running it as a continuous business adds a standard 'free trade' (živnost volná) notification to the Trade Licensing Office plus veterinary oversight of commercial breeders/dealers under the Veterinary Act (Zákon č. 166/1999 Sb.). Non-commercial intra-EU movement of up to five owner-accompanied pet rodents needs no harmonized health certificate or pet passport. Never release a roof rat into the wild (general nature-protection and welfare law forbid abandoning any animal).

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Private keeping of a captive-bred roof rat needs no permit, registration, or fee. Section 13 of the Animal Protection Act (Zákon č. 246/1992 Sb.) makes a permit from the Regional Veterinary Administration (Krajská veterinární správa, KVS) mandatory only for a 'species of animal requiring special care' (druh zvířete vyžadující zvláštní péči), and the species so designated are enumerated in the implementing Decree č. 451/2021 Sb. The State Veterinary Administration's own published list of special-care mammals is limited to primates (Primates), carnivores incl. pinnipeds (Carnivora vč. Pinnipedia), elephants (Proboscidea), odd-toed ungulates (Perissodactyla) and even-toed ungulates (Artiodactyla); no rodent (Rodentia) is named at all. Because R. rattus is absent, it is a default companion animal (zvíře v zájmovém chovu), keepable without proactive authorization. It is not CITES-listed and not on any invasive list. Only the universal welfare duties of Act 246/1992 Sb. apply (adequate food/water, an environment that does not cause suffering, and reasonable measures to prevent escape).

Sources: e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws), e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws), Státní veterinární správa (SVS), FAO FAOLEX (mirror of CZ statute)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Hobby breeding of roof rats is fully legal with no permit: the species is outside the special-care Decree 451/2021 Sb., Czech law imposes no reproductive quota or sterilization rule on genus Rattus, and the IAS framework (Zákon č. 364/2021 Sb. implementing EU Reg. 1143/2014) does not list R. rattus. The only obligation is the general anti-cruelty standard of Act 246/1992 Sb. (no breeding practice that causes foreseeable suffering or harm). Breeding at a continuous, systematic, profit-seeking scale becomes a business: it is an 'unqualified free trade' (živnost volná) under the Trade Licensing Act (Zákon č. 455/1991 Sb., Annex 4 item 'Chov zvířat a jejich výcvik', animal breeding and training, excluding livestock production), needing only a notification to the municipal Trade Licensing Office (živnostenský úřad), with no required veterinary degree or zoological qualification. A commercial breeder/dealer of animals is additionally subject to veterinary-hygiene oversight under the Veterinary Act (Zákon č. 166/1999 Sb., § 5) and to KVS inspection. So: hobby breeding = legal, no permit; commercial breeding = legal but with a free-trade notification plus veterinary oversight.

Sources: e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws), e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws), e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws), e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws), Zákony pro lidi (CZ legal database)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Transferring a captive-bred roof rat, whether by sale or as a gift, is unrestricted for a hobbyist; there is no species permit, dealer license, or quota for R. rattus. The welfare conditions of Act 246/1992 Sb. § 13 apply: the animal must be healthy and fit, the recipient must receive adequate care information, and the animal may not be sold or given to a person under 15 (or to a person whose legal capacity is restricted) without the consent of a parent or legal guardian. Rodents are expressly outside the Czech pet-shop sale bans that cover dogs, cats, and primates, so licensed pet shops may stock and sell roof rats. Selling continuously as a business is the same 'free trade' (živnost volná) as commercial breeding, needing a Trade Licensing Office notification; occasional hobbyist-to-hobbyist transfer does not. No veterinary health certificate, microchip, or quarantine is required for a domestic (within-Czechia) hobbyist transfer.

Sources: e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws), e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws), e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws)

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-14

Domestic transport within Czechia is unregulated administratively, no permit or health certificate, subject only to welfare-in-transit standards (escape-proof, ventilated, adequately sized enclosure) under Act 246/1992 Sb. and the transport decree. Non-commercial intra-EU movement of pet rodents is highly permissive: rodents are 'other pet animals' (not in the dog/cat/ferret regime and outside the EU Pet Passport), so up to five owner-accompanied animals may move with no harmonized EU health certificate, pet passport, or rabies vaccination, provided the origin is not under an animal-health alert; the SVS confirms Czechia imposes no supplementary national conditions on EU-origin pet rodents. The same five-animal, owner-accompanied, non-commercial allowance is applied to third-country (non-EU) imports of 'other pet animals' (the heavy import conditions target pet birds, not rodents). Commercial movement (more than five animals, unaccompanied, or for sale/transfer) is instead handled as a commercial consignment in the EU TRACES system with an official animal-health certificate. R. rattus is on no prohibited-import or CITES list. Never release.

Sources: Státní veterinární správa (SVS), European Union (EUR-Lex), e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Private keeping, hobby breeding, and hobbyist sale/gift of captive-bred roof rats are legal in Czechia with NO permit or registration (R. rattus is on no special-care, invasive, or CITES list). The only formalities attach to running it as a continuous BUSINESS: commercial breeding or selling of animals is an 'unqualified free trade' (živnost volná) under the Trade Licensing Act, which requires only a notification to the municipal Trade Licensing Office (živnostenský úřad); a commercial breeder/dealer is then also subject to veterinary-hygiene oversight and KVS inspection under the Veterinary Act. There is no per-transfer registration for hobbyists and no reproductive quota. Never release a roof rat.
  • Keeping / hobby breeding / occasional hobbyist sale or gift: nothing to file.
  • To breed or sell as a continuous business: notify the municipal Trade Licensing Office (živnostenský úřad) of the free trade 'Chov zvířat a jejich výcvik' (excluding livestock production) and obtain a trade-registration (IČO).
  • As a commercial breeder/dealer: comply with the veterinary-hygiene and traceability duties of Zákon č. 166/1999 Sb. § 5 and accept KVS inspection.
  • No special-care (zvláštní péče) permit applies to rodents.

Where: Municipal Trade Licensing Office (živnostenský úřad) for the free trade; Krajská veterinární správa (KVS) / SVS for commercial-breeder/dealer veterinary oversight. · Fees: Trade notification fee per the Trade Licensing Act (standard administrative fee, e.g. CZK 1000 for a new trade notification); no special-care permit fee applies because no permit is required.

Source: e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws), e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws)

Movement health documents apply only above the non-commercial threshold. Non-commercial intra-EU or third-country movement of up to five owner-accompanied pet rodents needs NO harmonized health certificate, pet passport, or rabies vaccination, and Czechia adds no national conditions on EU-origin pet rodents (origin must not be under an animal-health alert). A movement is commercial, and then needs an official animal-health certificate via the EU TRACES system, if it exceeds five animals, is unaccompanied, or is for sale/transfer of ownership. Domestic transport within Czechia needs no documents (welfare in transit only).
  • Domestic (within Czechia): no documents; transport welfare only (escape-proof, ventilated, adequately sized enclosure).
  • Non-commercial intra-EU or third-country: keep within five animals, owner-accompanied, not for sale; confirm the origin is not under an animal-health alert; no certificate required for rodents.
  • Commercial (over five, unaccompanied, or for sale): obtain an official animal-health certificate and notify the movement in the EU TRACES system (confirm the current certificate model with SVS, given the 22 April 2026 EU framework change).

Where: Státní veterinární správa (SVS) for commercial movement certification / TRACES; no filing for non-commercial pet-rodent movement. · Fees: None for non-commercial pet-rodent movement; official-vet examination/certification fees apply to commercial consignments.

Source: Státní veterinární správa (SVS), European Union (EUR-Lex)

Never release or abandon a roof rat into the wild. It is illegal to intentionally release a non-native or companion animal into the Czech environment under the Nature and Landscape Protection Act (Zákon č. 114/1992 Sb.) and the Animal Protection Act (Zákon č. 246/1992 Sb.). Indoor captive keeping is fully legal; facilitating establishment in the local ecosystem is a prohibited offense. Rehome responsibly and check local municipal ordinances.

Source: e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws), e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Zákon č. 246/1992 Sb. na ochranu zvířat proti týrání, Animal Protection Act (welfare duties; § 13 special-care-permit trigger + transfer/welfare conditions incl. minor-recipient consent; ban on releasing animals) — e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws)
  • Vyhláška č. 451/2021 Sb. o ochraně druhů zvířat vyžadujících zvláštní péči, exhaustive special-care species list (mammal entries: primates, carnivores incl. pinnipeds, elephants, perissodactyls, artiodactyls; NO rodents; R. rattus absent) — e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws)
  • Státní veterinární správa, Chov zvířat vyžadujících zvláštní péči (SVS published list of special-care species under Decree 451/2021 Sb.; mammals limited to primates/carnivores/elephants/ungulates; no rodents) — Státní veterinární správa (SVS)
  • Vyhláška č. 451/2021 Sb. (FAOLEX PDF mirror of the full decree text incl. annexes) — FAO FAOLEX (mirror of CZ statute)
  • Zákon č. 166/1999 Sb. o veterinární péči, Veterinary Act (§ 5: veterinary-hygiene and traceability duties of commercial animal breeders/dealers; KVS oversight) — e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws)
  • Zákon č. 455/1991 Sb. o živnostenském podnikání (Trade Licensing Act), Annex 4, 'Chov zvířat a jejich výcvik' (animal breeding and training, excl. livestock production) is an unqualified free trade (živnost volná) — e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws)
  • Zákon č. 364/2021 Sb., amends Czech laws to implement the EU invasive-alien-species regime (Reg. 1143/2014); the regulated rodents are muskrat/nutria, R. rattus is not listed — Zákony pro lidi (CZ legal database)
  • Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2016/1141 (the EU Union list of invasive alien species, under Reg. 1143/2014), no species of genus Rattus is listed (verified against the consolidated annex) — European Union (EUR-Lex)
  • Zákon č. 114/1992 Sb. o ochraně přírody a krajiny, Nature and Landscape Protection Act (prohibits intentional release of non-native animals into the wild) — e-Sbírka (official State Collection of Laws)
  • SVS (English), Requirements for travelling with other pet animals (rodents = 'other pet animals'; 5-animal owner-accompanied non-commercial limit; no harmonized health certificate/passport/rabies for rodents; no Czech national add-ons for EU-origin rodents; notes 22 April 2026 EU framework change) — Státní veterinární správa (SVS)
  • EU Animal Health Law (Reg. 2016/429) + Pet Passport Reg. 576/2013 (rodents excluded from the Pet Passport; non-commercial 'other pet animals' move with no harmonized certificate; new pet-movement framework effective 22 April 2026) — European Union (EUR-Lex)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, krysa obecná, potkan (= Rattus norvegicus, the fancy rat, contrast), roof rat, black rat, ship rat, zvíře v zájmovém chovu (companion animal), druh vyžadující zvláštní péči (species requiring special care).
