item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Germany? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Germany

Summary. Germany is one of the cleanest 'yes' countries for keeping a roof rat. It uses a negative-list system (any animal may be kept unless a law bans it), and the black rat (Hausratte, Rattus rattus) is named-and-excluded by binomial from the federal species-protection annex. Although wild R. rattus is a Red List native mammal, Anlage 1 of the Bundesartenschutzverordnung (BArtSchV) lists both Rattus rattus and Rattus norvegicus as exceptions (mit Ausnahme von) to the 'specially protected' status that covers other native mammals, so a captive specimen has the exact same unregulated standing as the common fancy rat (R. norvegicus), with no registration, no origin certificate, and no CITES paperwork. Neither species is on the EU list of invasive alien species of Union concern (Reg. 1143/2014), so no EU keep/breed/sell/transport ban applies. No Bundesland dangerous-animal ordinance (Gefahrtierverordnung) covers small rodents, so keeping is uniform across all 16 states. The only live conditions sit at the welfare and commercial tiers: §2 TierSchG requires species-appropriate, behaviour-appropriate housing (R. rattus is strongly arboreal, so tall climbing enclosures), and crossing into a commercial operation triggers a §11 TierSchG Erlaubnis (the threshold for rodents is more than 300 young per year under the AVV TierSchG, or any business-like trading for profit). Hobby keeping, hobby breeding, and free or occasional private transfer need no permit. The one genuinely unclear point is importing a roof rat from a non-EU third country, because rodents fall outside the EU pet-travel rules and national veterinary-certificate requirements vary by port. Never release a roof rat into the wild.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Germany operates a negative-list system: any animal may be privately kept unless a specific law bans it, and no law bans R. rattus. The Bundesartenschutzverordnung (BArtSchV) Anlage 1 designates mammals (Mammalia spp. / Saeugetiere) as specially protected but lists an explicit exception block, and both 'Rattus norvegicus' (Wanderratte) and 'Rattus rattus' (Hausratte) appear by name in that 'mit Ausnahme von' exclusion, so the roof rat carries zero special protection despite wild populations being Red-Listed. Consequently no registration with the lower nature-conservation authority and no origin/CITES certificate is required. No EU bar applies either: neither Rattus species is on the EU list of invasive alien species of Union concern (Reg. 1143/2014). No Bundesland dangerous-animal ordinance (Gefahrtierverordnung) covers small rodents. The only keeping rule is §2 TierSchG: the keeper must provide species-appropriate and behaviour-appropriate feeding, care, and housing and have the necessary knowledge and skills; because R. rattus is arboreal, this implies tall climbing enclosures, enforced ex-post by the local Veterinaeramt only on complaint.

Sources: Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de (federal statute portal), Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de, Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de, European Commission, DG Environment

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Hobby breeding is unregulated: a private citizen may breed roof rats without a permit, registration, fee, or inspection. All breeders are still bound by §11b TierSchG (the Qualzucht / torture-breeding prohibition), but R. rattus is rarely bred for the extreme mutations (hairlessness, tailless, etc.) that trigger it. Breeding only becomes regulated when it is gewerbsmaessig (commercial): §11(1) sentence 1 No. 8(a) TierSchG requires a prior Erlaubnis from the local Veterinaeramt to commercially breed or keep vertebrates. The threshold is set in the AVV TierSchG (No. 12.2.1.5.1), which assumes commercial activity for rodents (Maeuse, Hamster, Ratten, Gerbils) at more than 300 young animals (Jungtiere) per year. A commercial breeder must pass a Sachkundenachweis (proof of competence), a Zuverlaessigkeitspruefung (reliability check), and an on-site facility inspection. This commercial layer applies identically to every vertebrate species, not just R. rattus.

Sources: Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de, Bundesregierung / verwaltungsvorschriften-im-internet.de, Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Private, occasional, non-business transfer (giving away a litter, an occasional small-scale sale) is unregulated: no health certificate, registration, bill of sale, or species-protection paperwork is required, because the BArtSchV exemption removes any CITES/origin-document duty for R. rattus. Regulation attaches only to commercial dealing: §11(1) sentence 1 No. 8(b) TierSchG requires an Erlaubnis from the local Veterinaeramt for anyone who commercially trades in vertebrates (gewerbsmaessiger Handel mit Wirbeltieren), defined by the AVV TierSchG by business-like intent (planmaessig, fortgesetzt und mit der Absicht der Gewinnerzielung) rather than a fixed volume. A commercial seller must also give the buyer written care information about the species. Because the predominant case for a hobbyist keeper is free or occasional private transfer, the headline status is legal, with the §11 permit applying only to a business-like dealer.

Sources: Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de, Bundesregierung / verwaltungsvorschriften-im-internet.de, Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de (federal statute portal)

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Domestic transport within Germany (including between Bundeslaender) is entirely unregulated: there are no internal border checks for pets and no movement documents, the only condition being general §2 TierSchG welfare during transit (appropriate carrier with adequate space, ventilation, and protection from temperature extremes). Moving a roof rat into Germany from another EU country is also simple: rodents are explicitly outside the EU pet-travel rules (Reg. 576/2013, which target rabies in dogs, cats, and ferrets), so no EU pet passport or microchip is required, and R. rattus is not on the EU invasive-species Union list (Reg. 1143/2014), so no IAS transport ban applies. The single open point is import from a non-EU third country, handled at activity level here but flagged as unclear in notes and routed to Zoll/BMEL. Never release a roof rat into the wild (intentional release of a captive animal is an offence under animal-welfare and ecological law).

Sources: Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de, Generalzolldirektion (German Customs), European Commission, DG Environment

Restrictions & responsibilities

Commercial (gewerbsmaessig) breeding or trading of vertebrates requires a prior Erlaubnis under §11(1) TierSchG from the local Veterinaeramt. For rodents, breeding is assumed commercial above more than 300 young animals per year (AVV TierSchG No. 12.2.1.5.1); trading is assumed commercial by business-like, profit-seeking intent. Hobby breeding and free/occasional private transfer are exempt.
  • Determine whether your activity is gewerbsmaessig: for breeding, more than 300 young/year (AVV TierSchG); for selling, regular business-like trading for profit.
  • If commercial, apply for the §11 TierSchG Erlaubnis at your local Veterinaeramt BEFORE starting operations.
  • Pass the Sachkundenachweis (proof of competence) via a vocational qualification or a Fachgespraech with the official state veterinarian (Amtstierarzt).
  • Pass the Zuverlaessigkeitspruefung (reliability check) and an on-site facility inspection (lighting, ventilation, hygiene, enclosure sizes; check local Baurecht/zoning).
  • Commercial sellers must additionally give each buyer written species-care information at the point of sale.

Where: Local Veterinaeramt (oertliches Veterinaeramt / Amtstierarzt) · Fees: No fixed national fee; permit processing scales with administrative effort and economic advantage, roughly 50 to 10,000 EUR plus travel costs of inspecting officials.

Source: Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de, Bundesregierung / verwaltungsvorschriften-im-internet.de

§2 TierSchG requires species-appropriate, behaviour-appropriate housing. Because R. rattus is strongly arboreal (longer balancing tail, larger ears, naturally lives in high places), a wide-but-short enclosure that might satisfy a terrestrial rodent can fall short, and the local Veterinaeramt may issue corrective orders. This is an ongoing welfare duty enforced ex-post (on complaint or observed cruelty), not a pre-acquisition permit or registration.
  • Provide a tall enclosure with vertical climbing space, multiple levels, secure bar spacing (commonly cited maxima around 1.5 cm, 1.0 cm for juveniles), ventilation, and social housing.
  • Use the BMEL Saeugetiergutachten and TVT Merkblatt 160 as the practical interpretive standard for §2 TierSchG.
  • Keep at least two rats together (rats are social); never single-house.

Where: Local Veterinaeramt (enforces §2 TierSchG; no filing required by a private keeper)

Source: Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de

Importing a roof rat from a NON-EU third country is the one unclear area. Rodents are outside the EU pet-travel rules (Reg. 576/2013, which cover dogs/cats/ferrets and rabies), so no EU pet passport applies, but the German border inspection post (Veterinaergrenzkontrollstelle) may require a national veterinary health certificate (Tiergesundheitsbescheinigung) depending on the origin country's epidemiological status and the port of entry. Domestic and intra-EU movement need no such document. Confirm the exact certificate with Zoll/BMEL before any third-country import.
  • Domestic / intra-EU: no passport, microchip, or permit for rodents; transport with §2 TierSchG welfare conditions only.
  • Non-EU import: contact German Customs (Zoll) and/or BMEL in advance for the required Tiergesundheitsbescheinigung and any zoonosis-testing requirements for the genus Rattus at your intended border inspection post.
  • Never release a roof rat into the wild.

Where: German Customs (Zoll) central information desk / BMEL; the Veterinaergrenzkontrollstelle at the port of entry.

Source: Generalzolldirektion (German Customs)

Never release a roof rat into the wild. Intentional release of a captive-bred animal is an offence under animal-welfare and ecological law, and R. rattus is an invasive species globally. Rehome responsibly through free adoption with vetting.

Source: Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Anlage 1 BArtSchV (Bundesartenschutzverordnung): Mammalia spp. specially protected, with explicit exception block naming 'Rattus norvegicus' and 'Rattus rattus' (mit Ausnahme von), removing both from 'besonders geschuetzt' status — Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de (federal statute portal)
  • § 11 TierSchG (Tierschutzgesetz): Erlaubnispflicht; §11(1) S.1 Nr. 8 requires a permit to gewerbsmaessig (a) breed/keep vertebrates (except farm animals and enclosed game) or (b) trade in vertebrates — Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de
  • § 2 TierSchG: anyone keeping an animal must feed, care for, and house it appropriately to its species and needs (verhaltensgerechte Unterbringung) and possess the necessary knowledge and skills — Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de
  • Allgemeine Verwaltungsvorschrift zur Durchfuehrung des Tierschutzgesetzes (AVV TierSchG), No. 12.2.1.5.1: rodents (Maeuse, Hamster, Ratten, Gerbils) assumed gewerbsmaessig at more than 300 Jungtiere per year — Bundesregierung / verwaltungsvorschriften-im-internet.de
  • § 39 BNatSchG (Bundesnaturschutzgesetz): general protection of wild-living animals and plants (the baseline that BArtSchV Anlage 1 modifies; R. rattus excepted) — Bundesministerium der Justiz / gesetze-im-internet.de
  • EU list of invasive alien species of Union concern (Regulation (EU) 1143/2014; consolidated Union list, 114 species as of the Aug 2025 update). NEITHER Rattus rattus NOR Rattus norvegicus is listed; listed rodents are squirrels/chipmunks, listed mammals include Myocastor coypus, Ondatra zibethicus, Procyon lotor — European Commission, DG Environment
  • Zoll (German Customs): rules for bringing pets (Heimtiere) from non-EU states; EU pet-travel rules (Reg. 576/2013) cover only dogs/cats/ferrets, so rodents fall under national veterinary rules confirmed via Zoll/BMEL/the border veterinary post — Generalzolldirektion (German Customs)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, Hausratte, Dachratte, Schiffsratte, black rat, roof rat, ship rat, Wanderratte (= Rattus norvegicus, the Norway/fancy rat, for contrast), Tierschutzgesetz (TierSchG), Bundesartenschutzverordnung (BArtSchV).

Last reviewed 2026-06-14. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

This page is part of Roof Rat Laws, a free resource built with Pet Freedom — a gift from the roof-rat community.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Denmark? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Denmark

Summary. Denmark is a genuinely conflicted and likely restrictive case for the roof rat, driven by a clash between two ministries. The forbidden-exotic-pets order (BEK nr 1261 of 17/11/2015, Fødevarestyrelsen) does NOT list Rattus rattus: its annex bans certain rodents (beavers, flying squirrels, Old World and New World porcupines) but the genus Rattus and the family Muridae are entirely absent, so there is no exotic-pet permit bar. The binding constraint is the rat-control order (Bekendtgørelse om forebyggelse og bekæmpelse af rotter, BEK nr 991 of 21/08/2024, in force 1 January 2025, under the Environmental Protection Act / Miljøbeskyttelsesloven), which names BOTH Rattus norvegicus AND Rattus rattus by Latin name in its scope. Section 3 imposes a duty on every person ('Enhver') who observes the occurrence (forekomst) of rats to report it immediately to the municipal council, and the municipality must then investigate and eradicate (bekæmpe). The order contains no written exemption or safe-harbour for a captive-bred, caged pet. The Danish Mammal Society states plainly that the house rat, like the brown rat, is covered by the rat-control legislation and must therefore be combated everywhere it occurs. The paradox is that the fancy rat (tamrotten), which IS Rattus norvegicus and is named in the same order, is kept freely as a pet across Denmark under unwritten administrative tolerance (sædvane), while the rarer Rattus rattus has no such established tolerance. Whether a securely caged pet roof rat actually counts as a reportable 'forekomst' has never been resolved by published agency guidance, which is the single most important open question and the basis for the advocacy ask.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-14

The rat-control order BEK nr 991 of 21/08/2024 (under Miljøbeskyttelsesloven, in force 1 January 2025) defines its scope as the prevention and eradication of rats and names both Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus by Latin name. Section 3 imposes a duty on every person ('Enhver, der konstaterer forekomst af rotter, skal straks anmelde dette til kommunalbestyrelsen' - anyone who observes the occurrence of rats must immediately report this to the municipal council), and the municipality must investigate and eradicate. There is no written carve-out for a captive specimen. The Danish Mammal Society (Dansk Pattedyrforening) states the house rat 'er ligesom den brune rotte medtaget i lovgivningen vedrørende bekæmpelse af rotter' and 'den må derfor bekæmpes alle steder, hvor den forekommer' (is covered by rat-control legislation like the brown rat, and must therefore be combated everywhere it occurs). The separate forbidden-exotic order BEK nr 1261 of 17/11/2015 does NOT list Rattus (the rodent annex bans beavers, flying squirrels and porcupines, not Muridae), so the restriction stems from rat-control law, not an exotic ban. Confidence is medium because no published guidance or enforcement ruling resolves whether a securely caged pet on private premises is itself a reportable 'forekomst,' and the fancy rat (R. norvegicus), named in the identical order, is kept freely by tacit tolerance.

Sources: Miljø- og Ligestillingsministeriet (Retsinformation), Miljøstyrelsen (Danish EPA), Miljø- og Fødevareministeriet / Fødevarestyrelsen, Dansk Pattedyrforening (Danish Mammal Society), Dansk Pattedyratlas / Lex (Den Store Danske)

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-14

Breeding compounds the keeping problem: if a single specimen triggers the rat-control report-and-eradicate duty, multiple specimens, nests and litters squarely meet the definition of a rat occurrence and would, on a textual reading, oblige municipal intervention; the property-owner duty under § 4 (and Miljøbeskyttelsesloven § 17) to limit rats' living conditions cuts directly against deliberately housing and propagating them. Hobby breeding of the domesticated tamrotte (R. norvegicus) needs no agricultural permit, but for R. rattus the species-level rat-control status is the binding constraint. Commercial breeding or selling of any animal requires a Fødevarestyrelsen authorisation under the commercial-trade order (BEK nr 686 of 31/05/2023), whose application requires species counts, enclosure plans and trained staff; a permit to propagate a species the state is mandated to eradicate is, in practice, a non-starter.

Sources: Miljø- og Ligestillingsministeriet (Retsinformation), Ministeriet for Fødevarer, Landbrug og Fiskeri / Fødevarestyrelsen, Dansk Pattedyrforening (Danish Mammal Society)

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-14

Transferring a live R. rattus, whether by sale or free gift, introduces a rat-control-regulated species onto another person's premises, where the recipient becomes subject to the § 3 report duty the moment they take possession; the same rat-control conflict applies regardless of whether money changes hands. Commercial sale carries an additional layer: trading animals commercially requires a Fødevarestyrelsen authorisation under BEK nr 686 of 31/05/2023, which it is highly improbable would be granted to formalise trade in a species under a national eradication mandate. The Danish pet-rat scene (e.g. Den Danske Tamrotteforening) is built entirely around R. norvegicus; R. rattus is practically unavailable in the trade.

Sources: Miljø- og Ligestillingsministeriet (Retsinformation), Ministeriet for Fødevarer, Landbrug og Fiskeri / Fødevarestyrelsen, Den Danske Tamrotteforening

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-14

Internal transport in a private vehicle needs no specific transit permit, but the underlying rat-control constraint travels with the animal: on arrival the destination premises host a 'forekomst,' triggering the § 3 report duty, and an escape or release would introduce a destructive non-native species into the wild. For movement into Denmark from another EU state, EU pet-travel harmonisation (Reg. 2016/429, Animal Health Law) standardises only dogs, cats and ferrets; for 'other animals' including rodents the Fødevarestyrelsen travel guidance says national rules apply, and no specific inbound health-certificate rule for pet rodents was found. Because keeping is restricted, the rat-control restriction attaches the moment the animal enters Denmark, which makes lawful transport precarious. No permit pathway was identified. Status is reclassified from the preliminary 'unregulated_unclear' to 'restricted' because transport is governed by the same binding rat-control constraint that restricts keeping, not because a distinct transport rule bars it. Never release.

Sources: Miljø- og Ligestillingsministeriet (Retsinformation), Fødevarestyrelsen, EU / EUR-Lex

Restrictions & responsibilities

Denmark's mandatory rat-control order (BEK nr 991 of 21/08/2024) names Rattus rattus by Latin name and requires anyone who observes a rat occurrence to report it to the municipality, which must then eradicate, with no written exemption for a caged pet. So keeping a roof rat is at best legally uncertain and likely restricted, even though R. rattus is not on the forbidden-exotic list. The fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is named in the same order yet kept freely by tacit tolerance. Get a written ruling from Miljøstyrelsen (and a cross-check from Fødevarestyrelsen) BEFORE acquiring a roof rat. Never release a roof rat.
  • Ask Miljøstyrelsen in writing whether an individually caged, captive-bred R. rattus is a reportable 'forekomst' under BEK nr 991 of 21/08/2024, or whether the report/eradicate duty reaches only free-living rats.
  • Ask whether Miljøstyrelsen offers a dispensation, or recognises a customary tolerance for a domesticated roof rat equivalent to the one the fancy rat (tamrotte) already enjoys.
  • Cross-check with Fødevarestyrelsen that the forbidden-exotic order (BEK nr 1261 of 17/11/2015) does not cover R. rattus and that the only bar is the rat-control law.

Where: Miljøstyrelsen (rat control) as primary; Fødevarestyrelsen (exotic-pet / import) as cross-check.

Source: Miljø- og Ligestillingsministeriet (Retsinformation), Miljø- og Fødevareministeriet / Fødevarestyrelsen

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Denmark. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Denmark

In Denmark the roof rat (Rattus rattus) is not on the forbidden-exotic-pets list, so there is no exotic-permit ban. The obstacle is the rat-control order (Bekendtgørelse om forebyggelse og bekæmpelse af rotter, BEK nr 991 of 21 August 2024, in force 1 January 2025, issued under the Environmental Protection Act / Miljøbeskyttelsesloven), which names BOTH the brown rat (Rattus norvegicus) AND the roof rat (Rattus rattus) by Latin name in its scope. Section 3 makes it every person's duty to report any 'occurrence' (forekomst) of these rats to the municipality, and the municipality's duty to investigate and eradicate them. The order contains no written exemption for a captive-bred, caged pet. Because the order targets the species, not wild behaviour, a tame indoor roof rat reads as caught by the same rule that targets pest infestations. No published guidance has resolved whether a single caged pet triggers the report-and-destroy duty. The brown rat (the fancy rat or tamrotte) is named in the same order yet is kept freely as a pet across Denmark; the roof rat is treated differently by reputation, not by any difference in the rule's wording. The already-permitted fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over.

The ask: Request one of two clarifications from Miljøstyrelsen (the Danish Environmental Protection Agency, which authors the rat-control order): (1) a written ruling or published guidance note stating that an individually captive-bred Rattus rattus kept in a secure cage indoors is not a reportable 'forekomst' under the rat-control order, so the report-and-eradicate duty reaches only free-living rat populations, not a contained pet; or (2) at the next revision of the order, a captive-pet carve-out exempting securely housed, captive-bred pet specimens, matching the practical treatment the brown rat (fancy rat) already receives under the identical wording. The order is aimed at the public-health and nuisance risk of free-living rat colonies, and that cost-benefit judgment is Denmark's to make. Cats and dogs are also non-native and documented to harm Danish wildlife, yet are permitted as pets. Whether the limited additional risk of a few tame, indoor-only roof rats, bred for generations in captivity and never released, is similarly outweighed by their value as companions is a judgment for the agency to make, not a conclusion for the keeper to assert. The species-level wording, with no pet carve-out, may be a drafting oversight worth flagging to the Folketing's Environment and Food Committee, since neighbouring countries (Netherlands, Sweden) allow roof-rat pets without this conflict.

Where the lever really is: This is principally a law-as-written problem with an agency-rulemaking lever: a hybrid, but the controlling fact is that the species sits in the scope clause of a ministerial order. The roof rat (Rattus rattus) is named by Latin name in the rat-control order (BEK nr 991 of 21 August 2024, under Miljøbeskyttelsesloven). The municipal eradication duty and the citizen report duty flow directly from that wording, so an enforcing municipality or the agency applies the rule correctly when it treats a roof rat as in scope. Appealing for mercy or arguing 'you are misreading the law' will not work, because the text says what it says. The lever is to change or clarify the text. In Denmark the rat-control order is a ministerial bekendtgørelse drafted and administered by Miljøstyrelsen, not primary legislation passed line by line by the Folketing, so the agency itself can fix it, either by a published scope clarification (confirming a caged pet is not a 'forekomst') or by adding a captive-pet exemption at the next revision. That makes Miljøstyrelsen the primary, legitimate target even though this is a 'law on a list' case. The one genuinely open agency-interpretation angle is the unresolved definitional question of whether a contained pet is a 'forekomst' at all, which is a clarification request, not a plea against correct enforcement. The Folketing's Environment and Food Committee is the legislative backstop if the agency declines to amend or clarify its own order. A single municipal caseworker is unlikely to grant a personal exemption to a written rule on the spot; the fix is a guidance note or a rule amendment, which is a policy step, not frontline discretion.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Miljøstyrelsen (Danish Environmental Protection Agency), rat-control / Rottebekæmpelse (executive / agency) — mst@mst.dk
    Miljøstyrelsen drafts and administers the rat-control order (BEK nr 991 of 21 August 2024) that names Rattus rattus by Latin name, so it is the body that can either publish a scope clarification (a caged pet is not a reportable 'forekomst') or add a captive-pet exemption at the next revision. This is the primary, correct target for both the clarification ask and the rule-amendment ask. The general agency inbox mst@mst.dk and the official contact page are the verified channels; ask to be routed to the rat-control unit (rottebekæmpelse). Inquiry can be in Danish or English.
  • Folketinget, Miljø- og Fødevareudvalget (Environment and Food Committee) (legislature) — official contact page
    Legislative backstop. If Miljøstyrelsen declines to amend or clarify its own order, the Folketing's Environment and Food Committee is the channel that can press the Minister to add a captive-pet carve-out at revision. Use this only as escalation, and contact the committee via its official page, never an individual member by name.
  • Fødevarestyrelsen (Danish Veterinary and Food Administration) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Secondary cross-check. The roof rat is NOT on Fødevarestyrelsen's forbidden-exotic list (BEK nr 1261 of 17 November 2015; the genus Rattus and family Muridae are absent from the rodent annex), so this agency can confirm in writing that the exotic-pet regime poses no bar, pinning the issue squarely on the rat-control order and strengthening the case put to Miljøstyrelsen. Useful for documenting that no exotic-permit pathway is even required, and for import questions (rodents are non-harmonised pets, so national rules apply).

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request for clarification / captive-pet exemption for Rattus rattus under the rat-control order (BEK nr 991 of 21 August 2024)

Dear Miljøstyrelsen,

I am writing about the keeping of captive-bred roof rats (Rattus rattus) as pets. The rat-control order names this species alongside the brown rat (Rattus norvegicus) but contains no written exemption for a tame, captive-bred animal kept in a secure cage.

The animals I am asking about are bred in captivity, hand-tame, kept permanently indoors in a closed enclosure, and never released. They pose none of the public-health risks the order is designed to address. This is the same case as the brown rat (the fancy rat / tamrotte), which is named in the same order yet is kept freely as a pet throughout Denmark. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated in the 19th century, so a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over.

The order is aimed at free-living rat colonies, and weighing their risk against any public benefit is Denmark's call to make. Cats and dogs are also non-native and documented to harm native wildlife, yet are permitted as pets. Whether the limited additional risk of a few tame, indoor-only roof rats is meaningfully greater is the narrow question I ask you to weigh. I do not ask you to reach any particular conclusion.

I respectfully request either: (1) written confirmation that an individually caged, captive-bred Rattus rattus is not a reportable 'forekomst' under the order; or (2) a captive-pet exemption at the next revision, matching the practical treatment the brown rat already receives.

Thank you for your consideration. I would be grateful for a written reply.

Kind regards,
[Your name]
[Your town/region, if you wish]
da
Emne: Anmodning om afklaring / undtagelse for kæledyr vedrørende Rattus rattus efter rottebekendtgørelsen (BEK nr 991 af 21. august 2024)

Kære Miljøstyrelse

Jeg skriver vedrørende hold af opdrættede husrotter (Rattus rattus) som kæledyr. Rottebekendtgørelsen nævner denne art sammen med den brune rotte (Rattus norvegicus), men indeholder ingen skriftlig undtagelse for et tamt, i fangenskab opdrættet dyr, der holdes i et sikkert bur.

De dyr, jeg spørger om, er opdrættet i fangenskab, håndtamme, holdes permanent indendørs i en lukket indhegning og sættes aldrig ud i naturen. De udgør ingen af de sundhedsrisici, som bekendtgørelsen skal imødegå. Det er samme tilfælde som den brune rotte (tamrotten), der er nævnt i samme bekendtgørelse, men holdes frit som kæledyr i hele Danmark. Tamrotten er selv den vilde brune rotte, domesticeret i 1800-tallet, så en i fangenskab opdrættet husrotte er samme tilfælde én art ved siden af.

Bekendtgørelsen retter sig mod frit levende rottebestande, og det er Danmarks egen afvejning at vurdere deres risiko over for en eventuel samfundsmæssig nytte. Katte og hunde er også ikke-hjemmehørende og dokumenteret at skade den hjemmehørende natur, men tillades som kæledyr. Om den begrænsede ekstra risiko ved nogle få tamme husrotter, der udelukkende holdes indendørs, reelt er større, er det snævre spørgsmål, jeg beder Dem afveje. Jeg beder Dem ikke om at nå frem til en bestemt konklusion.

Jeg anmoder respektfuldt om enten: (1) en skriftlig bekræftelse af, at en individuelt indburet, i fangenskab opdrættet Rattus rattus ikke udgør en anmeldelsespligtig 'forekomst' efter bekendtgørelsen; eller (2) en undtagelse for kæledyr ved næste revision, svarende til den praktiske behandling, den brune rotte allerede får.

Tak for jeres overvejelse. Jeg vil være taknemmelig for et skriftligt svar.

Med venlig hilsen
[Dit navn]
[Din by/region, hvis du ønsker det]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • BEK nr 991 af 21/08/2024 - Bekendtgørelse om forebyggelse og bekæmpelse af rotter (rottebekendtgørelsen; in force 1 Jan 2025; scope names R. norvegicus AND R. rattus; § 3 'Enhver, der konstaterer forekomst af rotter, skal straks anmelde dette til kommunalbestyrelsen'; § 4 property-owner duty; supersedes BEK nr 2307 af 06/12/2021) — Miljø- og Ligestillingsministeriet (Retsinformation)
  • Miljøstyrelsen - Rottebekæmpelse (official rat-control page: 'Det er Miljøministeriet, der har ansvaret... udmøntet i Miljøbeskyttelsesloven og bekendtgørelse nr. 991 om forebyggelse og bekæmpelse af rotter'; 'Hvis du ser en rotte, så anmeld det til din kommune') — Miljøstyrelsen (Danish EPA)
  • BEK nr 1261 af 17/11/2015 - Bekendtgørelse om forbud mod hold af særlige dyr (rodent annex bans Aplodontia, Castoridae, flying squirrels, Anomaluridae, Hystricidae, Erethizontidae; genus Rattus and family Muridae NOT listed; issued by Fødevarestyrelsen, j.nr. 2015-14-31-00127) — Miljø- og Fødevareministeriet / Fødevarestyrelsen
  • Husrotte (Rattus rattus) - Dansk Pattedyrforening: 'Husrotten er ligesom den brune rotte medtaget i lovgivningen vedrørende bekæmpelse af rotter' and 'den må derfor bekæmpes alle steder, hvor den forekommer'; notes the species is rare/sparse in Denmark — Dansk Pattedyrforening (Danish Mammal Society)
  • Husrotte (Rattus rattus) - Dansk Pattedyratlas / Lex: covered without exception by rat-control law; rare in modern Denmark, largely displaced by the brown rat — Dansk Pattedyratlas / Lex (Den Store Danske)
  • Den Danske Tamrotteforening - Danish fancy-rat association; the pet tamrotte is Rattus norvegicus (the domesticated brown rat), the only pet rat in the Danish trade — Den Danske Tamrotteforening
  • BEK nr 686 af 31/05/2023 - Bekendtgørelse om erhvervsmæssig handel med dyr (commercial animal-trade authorisation; application requires species counts, enclosure plans, trained staff; no numeric hobby threshold for rodents) — Ministeriet for Fødevarer, Landbrug og Fiskeri / Fødevarestyrelsen
  • Fødevarestyrelsen - Travelling with pet animals (dogs/cats/ferrets harmonised; for other animals incl. rodents, national rules apply) — Fødevarestyrelsen
  • Regulation (EU) 2016/429 (Animal Health Law) - non-commercial pet movement harmonised for dogs/cats/ferrets only; rodents non-harmonised. R. rattus also NOT on the EU Union list of invasive species (Reg. 1143/2014) — EU / EUR-Lex

Search terms: Rattus rattus, husrotte, tagrotte, sort rotte, tamrotte (Rattus norvegicus, the fancy/pet rat), rottebekendtgørelsen, forekomst af rotter, anmeldepligt.

Last reviewed 2026-06-14. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Spain? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Spain

Summary. Earlier research wrongly treated the roof rat as banned nationwide; the environment ministry has now corrected that. On the Spanish mainland (and everywhere outside the Canary Islands) Rattus rattus is NOT a cataloged invasive species, so the Real Decreto 630/2013 Art. 7.1 possession/breeding/transport/trade ban does not apply there — keeping is instead governed by the 2023 animal-welfare law (Ley 7/2023) and its forthcoming companion-animal 'listado positivo' (positive list), which is still pending and not yet in force. In the Canary Islands, by contrast, R. rattus IS listed in the Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras for that territory alone, so there the Art. 7.1 ban (possess/breed/sell/transport live specimens) does apply. Commercial breeding or sale anywhere in Spain requires a núcleo zoológico (establishment) authorization from the relevant Comunidad Autónoma, and animal health/identification/movement of bred or traded animals falls under the Ministry of Agriculture. So the country-level reality is split: not prohibited on the mainland (welfare-regulated, positive list pending) but cataloged-and-prohibited in the Canaries.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Spain's environment ministry for ecological transition (biodiversity mailbox), written reply June 2026, corrected the prior nationwide-ban reading: Rattus rattus is included in the Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras EXCLUSIVELY for the case of the Canary Islands, not nationwide. The ministry also set out the competence split: invasive-species catalogues and exotic/wildlife matters sit with the environment ministry (natural heritage and biodiversity); the animal-welfare framework for companion animals is Ley 7/2023, with competence mainly at the social-rights/consumer ministry (which is also building the companion-animal positive list); animal health, identification, movement, and the sanitary conditions of breeding, trade and transport sit with the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food; and authorization of núcleos zoológicos, breeding centres and establishment registries sits with the Comunidades Autónomas (regional governments). The practical effect: on the mainland R. rattus is not cataloged, so the Art. 7.1 ban does not reach it and keeping is permissible under the general welfare law pending the positive list; in the Canary Islands it is cataloged and the Art. 7.1 ban applies.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

On the Spanish mainland (and outside the Canary Islands), R. rattus is NOT in the Catálogo Español de EEI, so the RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1 possession ban does not apply and keeping is not prohibited; it is instead governed by the general animal-welfare framework of Ley 7/2023, with the companion-animal positive list still pending and not yet in force. In the Canary Islands, by contrast, R. rattus IS cataloged, so there Art. 7.1 prohibits possession of live specimens. The country-level reality is therefore 'legal on the mainland, prohibited in the Canaries'; confidence is medium because the forthcoming positive list could change mainland keepability once it takes effect.

Sources: BOE / Gobierno de España, MITECO, BOE / Gobierno de España

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

On the mainland R. rattus is not cataloged, so the RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1 breeding ban does not apply there; breeding for sale or as an establishment requires a núcleo zoológico authorization from the relevant Comunidad Autónoma (the regional government that authorizes breeding centres and establishment registries), and animal health/identification of bred animals falls under the Ministry of Agriculture. In the Canary Islands, where R. rattus IS cataloged, Art. 7.1 prohibits reproduction of live specimens, so breeding there is barred. Country-level best fit is legal_with_permit (regional núcleo-zoológico authorization on the mainland); confidence medium pending the positive-list outcome.

Sources: BOE / Gobierno de España, BOE / Gobierno de España

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

On the mainland R. rattus is not cataloged, so the RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1 trade/commerce ban does not apply there; selling or commercially supplying live animals requires a núcleo zoológico authorization from the Comunidad Autónoma, with animal-health/identification/movement conditions under the Ministry of Agriculture, and welfare/transfer requirements under Ley 7/2023. In the Canary Islands, where the species IS cataloged, Art. 7.1 prohibits 'tráfico y comercio de ejemplares vivos,' so sale/transfer there is barred. Private free rehoming on the mainland is not banned but is subject to the Ley 7/2023 welfare framework; commercial sale needs the establishment authorization — hence legal_with_permit at country level.

Sources: BOE / Gobierno de España, BOE / Gobierno de España

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

On the mainland R. rattus is not cataloged, so the RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1 transport ban does not apply there; movement of bred or traded animals is instead subject to the animal-health, identification and sanitary-movement rules administered by the Ministry of Agriculture (and ordinary welfare-in-transport requirements). In the Canary Islands, where the species IS cataloged, Art. 7.1 prohibits 'transporte' of live specimens. R. rattus is not on the EU Union list, so there is no EU-level border ban; non-commercial pet movement within the EU follows Reg. (EU) 576/2013, but the Canary-Islands catalogue prohibition takes effect on Canarian soil. Country-level best fit is legal_with_permit (sanitary/movement conditions on the mainland); never release.

Sources: BOE / Gobierno de España, EU / EUR-Lex

Restrictions & responsibilities

Territorial split. CANARY ISLANDS: R. rattus is a cataloged invasive species (RD 630/2013 Art. 7.1), so possessing, breeding, selling/giving or transporting a live one is prohibited there. MAINLAND (and elsewhere outside the Canaries): R. rattus is NOT cataloged, so it is not banned — keeping is governed by Ley 7/2023 (welfare; companion-animal positive list still pending/not in force), commercial breeding or sale needs a Comunidad-Autónoma núcleo zoológico authorization, and animal health/identification/movement fall under the Ministry of Agriculture. Never release anywhere.
  • Mainland: keep under the Ley 7/2023 welfare framework; watch for the forthcoming companion-animal positive list
  • Mainland commercial breeding/sale: obtain a núcleo zoológico authorization from the relevant Comunidad Autónoma; meet Ministry of Agriculture animal-health/movement rules
  • Canary Islands: do not acquire, breed, sell or move R. rattus (cataloged invasive, Art. 7.1 ban)
  • If advocating: ask the positive-list rulemaking ministry to include captive-bred R. rattus; for the Canaries, the formal exclusión/de-cataloguing procedure

Where: Comunidad Autónoma (núcleo zoológico authorization); environment ministry — biodiversity (Catálogo de EEI / Canaries de-cataloguing); social-rights/consumer ministry (positive list)

Source: BOE / Gobierno de España, BOE / Gobierno de España

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Spain

Spain's treatment of the roof rat (Rattus rattus) is territorial, not a blanket ban. The environment ministry confirmed this in writing in June 2026. The species is in the Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras (Real Decreto 630/2013) only for the Canary Islands. On the mainland and elsewhere it is not a cataloged invasive species, so the Article 7.1 possession/breeding/transport/trade ban does not reach it there. Mainland keeping is governed by the 2023 animal-welfare law (Ley 7/2023), under which the companion-animal 'listado positivo' (positive list) of species that may be kept as pets is still being written and is not yet in force. The concern is what happens when that list takes effect. The law generally excludes catalogue-listed invasive species from the positive list. Because R. rattus is cataloged in one territory (the Canaries), it is an edge case: a captive-bred domestic line that is legal to keep on the mainland today could be left off the national positive list by default unless the rulemaking treats it deliberately. The barrier is not a current prohibition. It is the risk that a future list closes the door that is open today. The already-permitted 'fancy rat' (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over.

The ask: Ask the ministry responsible for the Ley 7/2023 companion-animal positive list (social-rights/consumer) to include captive-bred Rattus rattus on the listado positivo, or, failing inclusion, to handle it through registration and welfare conditions, so that a species which is lawful to keep on the mainland today remains keepable once the list takes effect. Ask the rulemaking to address the partially-cataloged edge case explicitly: because R. rattus is cataloged only for the Canary Islands and is not an invasive species on the mainland, its captive-bred, indoor, never-released lineages should not be removed from the national positive list by the general 'no catálogo species' exclusion, which was designed for species cataloged across Spain. The already-permitted fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/ ). On the invasive-species concern that underlies the exclusion, the question is a cost-benefit one for Spain to decide. Cats and dogs are also non-native across most of Spain and are documented to harm native and especially island wildlife, yet are permitted everywhere as pets. Whether the limited additional risk of a few sterilized or altered, tame, indoor-only domesticated rats is similarly outweighed by their value as companions is a judgment for the ministry to make. Separately, for keepers in the Canary Islands, ask the environment ministry about the formal exclusión (de-cataloguing) procedure under Article 64 of Ley 42/2007 and RD 630/2013 to remove captive-origin R. rattus from the catalogue for that territory.

Where the lever really is: Two distinct levers, selected by territory and by question. (1) POSITIVE LIST is a rulemaking lever at the social-rights/consumer ministry (Dirección General de Derechos de los Animales), which owns the Ley 7/2023 'listado positivo' royal decree still in progress. The ask is inclusion of captive-bred R. rattus, with explicit treatment of the partial-catalogue edge case (cataloged only in the Canaries, not on the mainland). This is the primary lever because mainland keeping is otherwise already lawful and the only future risk is exclusion-by-default from the positive list. (2) CANARY-ISLANDS DE-CATALOGUING is an agency-procedure lever at the environment ministry (which owns the Catálogo de EEI). The formal exclusión procedure (Art. 64 Ley 42/2007 + RD 630/2013) is open to any citizen or organisation with scientific justification and is the route to lift the Art. 7.1 ban for the Canaries. It is secondary because it only matters for keepers in that territory. Authorization of breeding/sale establishments (núcleos zoológicos) is a separate Comunidad-Autónoma matter, and animal health/movement sits with the Ministry of Agriculture. Neither is an advocacy barrier, only the ordinary permitting layer. No front-desk clarification changes any of this, and the prior positive-list public-comment window is closed, so route the positive-list ask through the rulemaking ministry's mailbox and consider a keeper-rights ally to carry the scientific case.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministerio de Derechos Sociales, Consumo y Agenda 2030 — Dirección General de Derechos de los Animales (Ley 7/2023 listado positivo rulemaking) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    This is the ministry writing the Ley 7/2023 companion-animal positive list — the instrument that will decide, going forward, whether captive-bred R. rattus may be kept as a pet on the mainland once the list is in force. It is the correct office to ask that captive-bred R. rattus be INCLUDED on the positive list and that the partial-catalogue edge case (cataloged only in the Canaries) be resolved deliberately rather than by the default 'no catálogo species' exclusion. The prior public-comment window (17 Apr – 8 May 2026) is closed, so engage via the ministry's published rulemaking channel rather than as an open consultation.
  • Environment ministry — biodiversity sub-directorate (Catálogo Español de EEI): exclusión / de-cataloguing procedure for the Canary Islands listing (executive / agency) — buzon-sgb@miteco.es
    This office owns the invasive-species catalogue and confirmed in June 2026 that R. rattus is cataloged ONLY for the Canary Islands. Its formal 'Catalogación o descatalogación de taxones' procedure (Art. 64 Ley 42/2007 + RD 630/2013) is open to any citizen or organisation to request exclusión (de-listing) with scientific justification. This is the correct lever ONLY for the Canaries, where the Art. 7.1 ban actually applies — it is irrelevant on the mainland, where the species is not cataloged.
  • Federación FAUNA — keeper/breeder rights federation (advocacy ally, not a government body) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Spain's principal keeper/breeder federation, active in the listado-positivo rulemaking. As an organisation it can carry the scientific/husbandry case for INCLUDING captive-bred R. rattus on the positive list (and, for Canaries keepers, a de-cataloguing petition) more effectively than a lone keeper. Engage as an ally to the rulemaking ask, not as a substitute for it. (Do NOT route this to the conservation-aligned Coalición para el Listado Positivo.)

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To: Dirección General de Derechos de los Animales (Ministerio de Derechos Sociales, Consumo y Agenda 2030)
Re: Treatment of captive-bred Rattus rattus in the Ley 7/2023 companion-animal positive list (listado positivo)

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing regarding the welfare and legal status of domesticated roof rats (Rattus rattus). The environment ministry has confirmed that R. rattus is in the Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras only for the case of the Canary Islands, and is not a cataloged invasive species on the mainland, where keeping it is governed by Ley 7/2023 rather than by any catalogue ban.

My concern is the forthcoming companion-animal positive list. Because the law generally excludes catalogue-listed species from the positive list, a species cataloged in only one territory (the Canary Islands) risks being left off the national list by default, even though on the mainland it is not an invasive species and is lawful to keep today.

I ask: (1) that captive-bred Rattus rattus be included on the listado positivo, so that a domesticated, indoor, never-released line that is keepable on the mainland today remains keepable once the list is in force; and (2) that the rulemaking address the partial-catalogue situation explicitly, distinguishing the Canary-Islands listing from mainland status, rather than applying the general 'no catálogo species' exclusion to a species that is invasive in only one region. If full inclusion is not possible, please advise whether captive-bred lineages could instead be handled through registration and welfare conditions.

The already-permitted fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century. A captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over.

On the invasive-species concern that underlies the exclusion, this is a cost-benefit question for Spain to decide. Cats and dogs are also non-native across most of Spain and are documented to harm native and especially island wildlife, yet are permitted everywhere as pets. Whether the limited additional risk of a few sterilized or altered, tame, indoor-only domesticated rats is similarly outweighed by their value as companions is a judgment for the ministry to make.

Thank you for your time and for your work on animal welfare.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your town / province]
[Date]
Español
A: Dirección General de Derechos de los Animales (Ministerio de Derechos Sociales, Consumo y Agenda 2030)
Asunto: Tratamiento de la Rattus rattus criada en cautividad en el listado positivo de animales de compañía de la Ley 7/2023

Estimados señores:

Les escribo en relación con el bienestar y el estatus jurídico de las ratas domésticas (Rattus rattus). El ministerio competente en medio ambiente ha confirmado que la R. rattus está incluida en el Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras únicamente para el caso de las Islas Canarias, y no es especie catalogada invasora en la península, donde su tenencia se rige por la Ley 7/2023 y no por ninguna prohibición del Catálogo.

Mi preocupación es el futuro listado positivo de animales de compañía. Dado que la ley excluye con carácter general del listado positivo a las especies catalogadas, una especie catalogada en un solo territorio (las Islas Canarias) corre el riesgo de quedar fuera del listado nacional por defecto, pese a que en la península no es una especie invasora y hoy su tenencia es lícita.

Les ruego: (1) que la Rattus rattus criada en cautividad se incluya en el listado positivo, de modo que un linaje doméstico, mantenido en el interior del hogar y nunca liberado, que hoy puede tenerse en la península, siga pudiendo mantenerse cuando el listado entre en vigor; y (2) que el desarrollo reglamentario aborde de forma expresa la situación de catalogación parcial, distinguiendo la inclusión en Canarias del estatus peninsular, en lugar de aplicar la exclusión general de 'especies catalogadas' a una especie que es invasora en una sola región. Si la inclusión plena no fuera posible, les ruego me indiquen si los linajes criados en cautividad podrían regularse mediante registro y condiciones de bienestar.

La ya permitida rata doméstica (Rattus norvegicus) es la propia rata parda salvaje, domesticada solo en el siglo XIX. Una Rattus rattus criada en cautividad es el mismo caso una especie más allá.

Respecto a la preocupación por el carácter invasor que motiva la exclusión, se trata de una cuestión de coste-beneficio que corresponde decidir a España. Los gatos y los perros son también especies no autóctonas en casi toda España y está documentado que perjudican a la fauna autóctona, en especial a la insular, y aun así se permiten en todas partes como animales de compañía. Si el limitado riesgo adicional de unas pocas ratas domésticas esterilizadas o alteradas, dóciles y mantenidas siempre en interior queda igualmente compensado por su valor como animales de compañía es un juicio que corresponde hacer al ministerio.

Les agradezco su tiempo y la labor que realizan en favor del bienestar animal.

Atentamente,
[Su nombre]
[Su localidad / provincia]
[Fecha]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Real Decreto 630/2013 — Catálogo Español de Especies Exóticas Invasoras (Art. 7.1 prohibitions; R. rattus cataloged ONLY for the Canary Islands per MITECO June 2026) — BOE / Gobierno de España
  • MITECO — Ficha de especie Rattus rattus (Catálogo Español de EEI) — MITECO
  • Ley 7/2023 de protección de los derechos y el bienestar de los animales (companion-animal welfare framework; positive-list mandate, list still pending/not in force) — BOE / Gobierno de España
  • MITECO — Código de Conducta sobre comercio electrónico de flora y fauna exótica invasora (reaches cataloged species only — i.e. R. rattus in the Canaries) — MITECO
  • Proyecto de Real Decreto — listado positivo de animales de compañía (rulemaking pending; public-information window 17 Apr – 8 May 2026 now closed) — Ministerio de Derechos Sociales, Consumo y Agenda 2030
  • Regulation (EU) 1143/2014 + 2025/1422 update — Union list (R. rattus NOT listed; Spain's national catálogo applies only in the Canary Islands) — EU / EUR-Lex

Search terms: Rattus rattus, rata negra, rata campestre, rata de barco.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Finland? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Finland

Summary. Finland is permissive for the roof rat. There is no species-specific ban: R. rattus is on neither the EU invasive-species Union list (Reg. 1143/2014) nor Finland's national invasive list (Government Decree 1725/2015, whose mammals are alien carnivores, bats and chipmunks, not rats). On Finlands invasive portal it is classed only as an alien species (vieraslaji), not a harmful invasive alien species (haitallinen vieraslaji), so the bans and eradication duties that hit listed species do not apply. The Animal Welfare Act (Laki eläinten hyvinvoinnista 693/2023, in force 1 Jan 2024) sets welfare and husbandry standards for all kept animals but does not restrict keeping R. rattus, so a hobbyist is in the same position as a fancy-rat (R. norvegicus) keeper: both are small companion and hobby animals (pienikokoinen seura- ja harrastuseläin) under Government Decree 674/2010. A notification (ilmoitus) is required only at scale: 7 or more cages, terraria or aquaria for professional/commercial activity, or 20 or more for large-scale non-professional keeping, filed to Ruokavirasto at least 30 days before starting. Intra-EU non-commercial movement of pet rodents by an accompanying owner needs no import permit and no health certificate; commercial movement uses TRACES.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Keeping a captive-bred roof rat is lawful. R. rattus is absent from the EU Union list (Reg. 1143/2014; confirmed against Implementing Reg. 2016/1141, whose listed mammals are squirrels, mongoose, muntjac, coypu, coati, raccoon and chipmunk) and from Finland's national invasive decree 1725/2015 (national-concern mammals are alien carnivores, bats and chipmunks). Finland's invasive portal (vieraslajit.fi, SYKE) classes it only as an alien species (vieraslaji), not a harmful invasive alien species (haitallinen vieraslaji), so the keeping ban and eradication duties for listed species do not apply. As a synanthropic rodent it is treated as unprotected (rauhoittamaton) under wildlife law, so no Nature Conservation Act permit is needed. Finland keeps companion animals on a negative-list basis: anything not banned is keepable if welfare needs are met. The Animal Welfare Act 693/2023 and Government Decree 674/2010 apply welfare and housing standards to the rat (rotta) generically, with no distinction from R. norvegicus.

Sources: Eduskunta / Finlex, Finlex, Finlex, EU / EUR-Lex, Suomen ympäristökeskus (SYKE)

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Small-scale hobby breeding requires no registration; the breeder is bound only by the welfare and housing standards of the Animal Welfare Act 693/2023 and Decree 674/2010. A notification (ilmoitus) becomes mandatory only at scale. For small companion and hobby animals (which include rats), the Ruokavirasto thresholds are at least 7 cages, terraria or aquaria in regular use for professional/commercial activity, and at least 20 for large-scale non-professional keeping. The notification is filed to Ruokavirasto (via the animal-keeper and facility register) at least 30 days before starting. This is a notification, not a discretionary licence; a dedicated rattery can approach the 20-cage line, so flag it. This threshold is identical for R. norvegicus.

Sources: Eduskunta / Finlex, Ruokavirasto (Finnish Food Authority), Ruokavirasto (Finnish Food Authority)

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

No prohibition on selling or giving captive-bred R. rattus. Casual transfers between hobbyists below the notification threshold are unregulated. The same Ruokavirasto thresholds apply: professional/commercial activity is reached when the operator transfers at least three self-bred litters of cats/dogs/ferrets/rabbits per year, or at least 10 animals per year they did not breed themselves, or runs equivalent regular commercial activity in small companion and hobby animal species using at least 7 cages, terraria or aquaria; large-scale non-professional keeping is reached at 20 or more. At or above the threshold, file the notification to Ruokavirasto 30 days before starting; the premises then enter the keeper register and become subject to welfare inspection. Adoption given free below threshold needs no registration.

Sources: Eduskunta / Finlex, Ruokavirasto (Finnish Food Authority), Ruokavirasto (Finnish Food Authority)

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Internal transport within Finland carries no species restriction, only the fitness-for-transport welfare rules (Animal Welfare Act 693/2023; EU Reg. 1/2005). No internal health certificate or transit permit is needed. Intra-EU non-commercial movement by an owner accompanying the animals needs no import permit and no health certificate: Ruokavirasto guidance states imports of rodents from EU countries, Norway and Switzerland require neither an import permit nor a veterinary certificate. Customs (Tulli) may inspect for welfare and to confirm the animals are not a listed invasive species; R. rattus is on no invasive list, so the import bans do not apply. Commercial intra-EU trade uses the TRACES system with the rodent intra-trade health certificate (EU Reg. 2016/429); the receiving facility must be a registered Ruokavirasto importer. Extra-EU import requires entry via a Border Control Post with veterinary documentation. Never release a roof rat.

Sources: Ruokavirasto (Finnish Food Authority), EU / EUR-Lex, EU / EUR-Lex

Restrictions & responsibilities

Keeping, breeding or transferring rats at scale requires a NOTIFICATION (ilmoitus) to Ruokavirasto at least 30 days before you start: at 7 or more cages, terraria or aquaria in regular use this counts as professional/commercial activity, and at 20 or more as large-scale non-professional keeping. Below those thresholds, hobby keeping/breeding/rehoming is unregistered, subject only to the welfare standards. Filing puts the premises in the keeper register and open to welfare inspection. The threshold is the same for the fancy rat (R. norvegicus). Never release a roof rat.
  • If at or above 7 cages (professional) or 20 cages (large-scale), file the ilmoitus to Ruokavirasto via the animal-keeper and facility register at least 30 days before commencing
  • Below the threshold, keep no notification is required; meet the Decree 674/2010 welfare and housing standards

Where: Ruokavirasto (Finnish Food Authority), via the animal-keeper and facility register (eläintenpitäjä- ja pitopaikkarekisteri)

Source: Ruokavirasto (Finnish Food Authority), Ruokavirasto (Finnish Food Authority)

Government Decree 674/2010 sets minimum housing for the rat (rotta) generically, with no distinction between R. rattus and R. norvegicus: a minimum cage floor area and height, additional floor area per group-housed animal, a continuous nest box / shelter for concealment, species-suitable substrate for digging and foraging, continuous fresh water, and a balanced diet. Falling below these is an animal welfare offence. No microchipping or registration of pet rodents is required.

Source: Finlex

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Laki eläinten hyvinvoinnista 693/2023 (Animal Welfare Act, in force 1 Jan 2024; no prohibited pet-rodent list; notification-required keeping at scale) — Eduskunta / Finlex
  • Valtioneuvoston asetus 674/2010 koirien, kissojen ja muiden pienikokoisten seura- ja harrastuseläinten suojelusta (minimum husbandry standards for the rat, rotta) — Finlex
  • Valtioneuvoston asetus 1725/2015 kansallisesti merkityksellisistä haitallisista vieraslajeista (national invasive-species decree; mammals: alien carnivores, bats, chipmunks; R. rattus absent) — Finlex
  • Vieraslajit.fi (SYKE): Rattus rattus classified as an alien species (vieraslaji), not a harmful invasive alien species (haitallinen vieraslaji) — Suomen ympäristökeskus (SYKE)
  • Ruokavirasto: Ilmoitus ammattimaisesta tai laajamittaisesta seura- ja harrastuseläinten pidosta (7 / 20 cage thresholds; 30 days before; filed to Ruokavirasto) — Ruokavirasto (Finnish Food Authority)
  • Ruokavirasto: Ilmoituksenvarainen eläintenpito (notification system under AWA 693/2023; notification to Ruokavirasto) — Ruokavirasto (Finnish Food Authority)
  • Ruokavirasto: Rabbits and rodents, intra-EU movement (no import permit, no health certificate for non-commercial) — Ruokavirasto (Finnish Food Authority)
  • Regulation (EU) 1143/2014 on invasive alien species, Union list (Implementing Reg. 2016/1141; no Rattus species listed) — EU / EUR-Lex
  • Regulation (EU) 2016/429, Animal Health Law (intra-EU movement; TRACES for commercial rodent trade) — EU / EUR-Lex

Search terms: Rattus rattus, mustarotta, kattorotta, rotta, vieraslaji, pienikokoinen seura- ja harrastuseläin, ilmoituksenvarainen eläintenpito.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in France? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › France

Summary. In metropolitan France a captive-bred roof rat is legal to keep, hobby-breed, and give away, and the species-vs-domestication line does not, in practice, add a permit. The roof rat is non-domestic (the Arrêté du 11 août 2006 lists only 'les races domestiques du rat (Rattus norvegicus)' among the rodents), so it is governed by the Code de l'environnement and the Arrêté du 8 octobre 2018. But Annexe 2 of that order places Rattus rattus in the catch-all 'Toutes les autres espèces de Rodentia' row, which is column (a) 'Pas de formalité' (no formality) for 1 to 40 adult animals; only 41 or more triggers a certificat de capacité. Marking and I-FAP registration apply only to protected or CITES species (Article 3 of the same order), so they do not apply to the roof rat. A sale (vente) must come with a written document d'information (Art. L413-8); a free transfer between private persons does not. R. rattus is not on the EU Union list (Reg. 1143/2014) or France's metropolitan invasive Arrêté du 14 février 2018, so there is no keeping or sale ban. Commercial breeding or selling to the public is a separate, permitted-only regime (établissement authorization plus, for trade, Code rural Art. L214-6). Two limits: the species is managed as invasive in the French overseas territories (DROM-COM), where local decrees prohibit it; and the 2021 welfare law created a future 'positive list' (Art. L413-1A) whose implementing arrêté is still unpublished, a watch item rather than a current restriction.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

The roof rat is non-domestic (the Arrêté du 11 août 2006 lists only 'les races domestiques du rat (Rattus norvegicus)' among the Muridae), so it is governed by the Code de l'environnement (Art. L413-1 et seq.) and the Arrêté du 8 octobre 2018. Annexe 2 of that order places R. rattus in the catch-all row 'Toutes les autres espèces de Rodentia, hors espèces figurant en annexe A du règlement (CE) n° 338/97 susvisé et hors espèces protégées en application de l'article L. 411-1 du code de l'environnement', for which column (a) 'Pas de formalité' covers 'De 1 à 40' adults and only '41 et plus' triggers a certificat de capacité. So keeping 1 to 40 adult roof rats requires no declaration and no permit. Marking and I-FAP registration apply only to protected or CITES species (Article 3 of the order), not to R. rattus. The species is not on the EU Union list or the metropolitan invasive list, so there is no keeping ban. Overseas territories (DROM-COM) manage it as invasive and may prohibit it locally.

Sources: Ministère de l'Écologie, Ministère de la Transition écologique, Ministère de la Transition écologique

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Non-commercial hobby breeding (élevage d'agrément) follows the same Annexe 2 thresholds as keeping: below 41 adult animals R. rattus sits in column (a) 'Pas de formalité', so no declaration and no breeding permit are required; offspring count toward the threshold only once adult. Reaching 41 or more adults moves the keeper into column (c), requiring a certificat de capacité (Art. L413-2) and an autorisation d'ouverture d'établissement (Art. L413-3). Breeding for profit or systematically producing litters for the public is a separate matter: it requires opening a declared establishment (autorisation préalable under Art. R413-8) and, as a pet-trade activity, falls under Code rural Art. L214-6. The L413-1A 'élevage de conservation' carve-out awaits its implementing decree.

Sources: Ministère de la Transition écologique, Légifrance, Légifrance

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

A private person may give away or sell a small number of captive-bred roof rats without a permit. The attestation de cession and identification-document formalities of Art. R413-23-4 apply only 'pour les animaux des espèces mentionnées à l'article L. 413-6' (marked, i.e. protected or CITES species), which R. rattus is not, so they do not bind a roof-rat transfer. A sale (vente) of a live non-domestic animal must be accompanied by a written document d'information on the animal's characteristics, needs, and upkeep (Art. L413-8); a gratuitous transfer between private persons does not require it. Selling commercially or systematically to the public requires operating a declared pet-trade establishment (autorisation préalable, Art. R413-8; Code rural Art. L214-6). R. rattus is not on the EU Union list, so there is no sale ban.

Sources: Légifrance, Légifrance, Légifrance, EU / EUR-Lex

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-13

Moving a captive-bred roof rat within metropolitan France is legal for private individuals, subject to humane, escape-proof transport. There is no EU pet-passport or harmonised health-certificate scheme for rodents (Reg. (EU) 576/2013 does not cover them), so intra-EU non-commercial movement follows the destination country's national rules. Importing from outside the EU triggers veterinary controls: the Arrêté du 19 juillet 2002 (Annexe 18 model certificate for rodents) requires a health certificate from an official veterinarian of the exporting country and presentation at an approved Border Control Post. R. rattus is not on the EU Union list or the metropolitan invasive Arrêté du 14 février 2018, so there is no import ban for métropole. The French OVERSEAS territories (Réunion, Mayotte, Martinique, Guadeloupe and others) manage R. rattus as a damaging invasive species and local decrees prohibit its introduction, detention, transport, and sale, so transport into or within those territories is unlawful.

Sources: Ministère de l'Agriculture, EU / EUR-Lex, EU / EUR-Lex, Ministère de la Transition écologique

Restrictions & responsibilities

Below 41 adult animals there is no formality: the roof rat falls in column (a) 'Pas de formalité' of Annexe 2 of the Arrêté du 8 octobre 2018. Reaching 41 or more adults moves the keeper into column (c), which requires a certificat de capacité and an autorisation d'ouverture d'établissement. The certificat de capacité is a professional-grade credential (theory dossier, logged practical experience, defence before a departmental commission, facility inspection), so the practical ceiling for a hobbyist is 40 adults.
  • Stay at or below 40 adult animals to remain in the 'Pas de formalité' tier
  • To exceed 40 adults, obtain a certificat de capacité and an autorisation d'ouverture d'établissement

Where: Préfecture de département (DDETSPP / DREAL) for the certificat de capacité and establishment authorization

Source: Ministère de la Transition écologique

A sale (vente) of a live roof rat must be accompanied by a written document d'information on the animal's characteristics, needs, and upkeep (Art. L413-8). A free transfer between private persons does not require it. Selling commercially or systematically to the public requires operating a declared pet-trade establishment (autorisation préalable, Art. R413-8; Code rural Art. L214-6). The attestation de cession / I-FAP formalities of Art. R413-23-4 do not apply, because they are limited to marked (protected/CITES) species.
  • On a sale, give the buyer a written document d'information (Art. L413-8)
  • Do not sell commercially or systematically without a declared establishment

Source: Légifrance, Légifrance

Importing from outside the EU requires a veterinary health certificate (Arrêté du 19 juillet 2002, Annexe 18 model for rodents) issued by an official veterinarian of the exporting country, with presentation at an approved Border Control Post. There is no EU pet passport for rodents; intra-EU non-commercial movement follows the destination state's rules. Never release a roof rat into the wild.
  • For non-EU import, obtain the Annexe 18 veterinary health certificate and clear an approved Border Control Post
  • For intra-EU movement, check the destination country's national rules for rodents

Where: Border Control Post (Poste de contrôle frontalier)

Source: Ministère de l'Agriculture

In the French overseas territories (DROM-COM: Réunion, Mayotte, Martinique, Guadeloupe and others) R. rattus is managed as a damaging invasive species and local prefectural/ministerial decrees prohibit its introduction, detention, transport, reproduction, and sale. The metropolitan 'no formality' position does NOT apply there.

Where: Préfecture / DEAL of the territory concerned

Source: Ministère de la Transition écologique

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Arrêté du 11 août 2006, liste des espèces, races ou variétés d'animaux domestiques (Muridae: only 'les races domestiques du rat (Rattus norvegicus)'; R. rattus absent) — Ministère de l'Écologie
  • Arrêté du 8 octobre 2018, Annexe 2: 'Toutes les autres espèces de Rodentia' in column (a) 'Pas de formalité' De 1 à 40, 41 et plus = certificat de capacité (R. norvegicus = déclaration from 1) — Ministère de la Transition écologique
  • Arrêté du 8 octobre 2018, Article 3: mandatory marking + national-file registration limited to L411-1/L411-2 protected and CITES (Reg. 338/97 Annexes A-D) species; R. rattus exempt — Ministère de la Transition écologique
  • Code de l'environnement Art. R413-23-4: attestation de cession / identification document obligations limited to 'animaux des espèces mentionnées à l'article L. 413-6' (marked species) — Légifrance
  • Code de l'environnement Art. L413-8: 'Toute vente d'un animal vivant d'une espèce non domestique' must include a document d'information (applies to sales, not gratuitous gifts) — Légifrance
  • Code de l'environnement Art. L413-1 A: positive list for non-domestic companion animals fixed by arrêté du ministre chargé de l'environnement; 'toute personne physique ou morale' may request inclusion, reasoned reply within six months (arrêté still pending) — Légifrance
  • Code rural Art. L214-6: pet-trade establishment declaration (élevage / vente) — Légifrance
  • Regulation (EU) 1143/2014 on invasive alien species: Union list does NOT include Rattus rattus — EU / EUR-Lex
  • Regulation (EU) 576/2013 on the non-commercial movement of pet animals: rodents not covered by the EU pet-passport scheme — EU / EUR-Lex
  • Arrêté du 14 février 2018 (métropole), Annexe I: espèces exotiques envahissantes; 'Rattus norvegicus (Berkenhout, 1769): Rat surmulot' listed, R. rattus absent — Ministère de la Transition écologique
  • Arrêté du 19 juillet 2002: conditions sanitaires pour l'importation d'animaux vivants (Annexe 18: rongeurs / rodents health certificate) — Ministère de l'Agriculture
  • Sénat Question qSEQ251106679 (13 nov. 2025, en attente de réponse): confirms the L413-1A positive-list arrêté is still unpublished; cites April 2025 IGEDD-CGAAER report — Sénat de la République française

Search terms: Rattus rattus, rat noir, rat des toits, rat des champs.
