item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in the United Kingdom? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United Kingdom

Summary. In Great Britain, keeping and hobby-breeding a captive-bred roof rat is legal — it's omitted from the Dangerous Wild Animals Act 1976 and from the Invasive Alien Species (Enforcement and Permitting) Order 2019 possession bans. BUT the roof rat is on Schedule 9 of the Wildlife & Countryside Act 1981, so it's a strict-liability criminal offence to release it or let it escape into the wild (use escape-proof caging; you may not release a trapped one). Commercial breeding/selling needs a local-authority Animal Welfare licence (and inspectors may treat it as a non-domestic species). Sale is OUTRIGHT PROHIBITED in Northern Ireland (Wildlife (NI) Order 1985, Art. 15A). Importing one is excluded from the Pet Travel Scheme and needs an APHA rabies import licence (Form RM01) + up to 4 months quarantine.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

No statute bans mere possession of a captive-bred roof rat: the genus Rattus (family Muridae) is absent from the Dangerous Wild Animals Act 1976 schedule, it's not under the Destructive Imported Animals Act 1932, and it's not on Schedule 2 of the Invasive Alien Species (Enforcement and Permitting) Order 2019 (the possession-ban list). Owners owe the Animal Welfare Act 2006 duty of care. Because R. rattus IS on Schedule 9 of the WCA 1981, releasing it or letting it escape is a criminal offence — and a trapped one may not be released back to the wild.

Sources: UK Government / legislation.gov.uk, UK Government / Defra, UK Government / legislation.gov.uk

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Purely private, non-commercial hobby breeding is unregulated (no statutory litter limits), subject to the Animal Welfare Act 2006. The moment it becomes commercial (profit intent, >£1,000/yr gross from animal sales, dealing, or systematic advertising of litters), it requires a local-authority Animal Welfare licence under the Animal Welfare (Licensing of Activities Involving Animals) Regulations 2018 (England) / 2021 (Wales & Scotland). Never let breeding stock escape (Sch. 9).

Sources: Defra / local authorities, UK Government / legislation.gov.uk

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

GREAT BRITAIN: selling as a business needs a local-authority Animal Welfare licence (the 'business test' / £1,000 HMRC trading allowance); inspectors may classify the roof rat under 'Part I — other non-domestic mammals' (higher burden, invasive-species containment) rather than 'Part H — domestic small rodents'. Giving one away free is generally outside the commercial 'sale' test. NORTHERN IRELAND: selling, offering for sale, or transporting for sale is an OUTRIGHT CRIMINAL OFFENCE (Wildlife (NI) Order 1985, Art. 15A; R. rattus is on Sch. 9 Part 1) — no licensing pathway exists; even advertising is barred.

Sources: Defra / local authorities, DAERA / legislation.gov.uk

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

DOMESTIC: legal under the Welfare of Animals (Transport) Order 2006 — but use gnaw-proof, escape-proof carriers, because an escape in transit is a strict-liability offence (WCA 1981 s.14/Sch. 9). IMPORT: the roof rat is a rabies-susceptible non-native mammal EXCLUDED from the Pet Travel Scheme; you must apply for an APHA Rabies Import Licence (Form RM01) — non-EU origin means up to 4 months quarantine; EU origin may be exempt if captive-bred/kept since birth. Northern Ireland adds Windsor-Framework pre-notification. No CITES permit (not endangered).

Sources: APHA / UK Government, UK Government / legislation.gov.uk

Restrictions & responsibilities

The roof rat is on Schedule 9 of the Wildlife & Countryside Act 1981: it is a criminal offence (strict liability — intent doesn't matter) to release it or allow it to escape into the wild anywhere in the UK. Use secure, gnaw-proof caging; a trapped/escaped roof rat may NOT be released — only humane options or an exceptional licence apply.

Source: UK Government / legislation.gov.uk

In Great Britain, commercial breeding/selling (profit, >£1,000/yr, dealing, or systematic advertising) requires a local-authority Animal Welfare Activity Licence; expect possible 'Part I (non-domestic mammal)' treatment with specialist-knowledge + invasive-species containment requirements. In Northern Ireland, sale is prohibited entirely.
  • GB: apply to your local council for an Animal Activity Licence if you cross the business threshold
  • NI: do not sell/offer/transport-for-sale (Art. 15A)

Where: Local authority (GB); n/a (NI — prohibited) · Fees: Set by local authority

Source: Defra / local authorities, DAERA / legislation.gov.uk

Importing a roof rat needs an APHA Rabies Import Licence (Form RM01) — it's excluded from the Pet Travel Scheme. Non-EU origin = up to 4 months quarantine; EU origin may qualify for exemption if captive-bred and kept since birth. Apply to APHA Centre for International Trade (Carlisle) at least 4 weeks ahead.
  • Apply for APHA Form RM01 at least 4 weeks before import
  • Provide captive-bred-since-birth evidence to seek a quarantine exemption (EU origin)

Forms: APHA Rabies Import Licence (Form RM01) · Where: APHA Centre for International Trade, Carlisle · Fees: Quarantine at owner's expense

Source: APHA / UK Government

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Dangerous Wild Animals Act 1976 — Schedule (Muridae/Rattus absent, so no DWA licence) — UK Government / legislation.gov.uk
  • Invasive Alien Species (Enforcement and Permitting) Order 2019, Sch. 2 (R. rattus NOT listed) — UK Government / Defra
  • Wildlife & Countryside Act 1981 s.14 / Schedule 9 (R. rattus listed, no-release offence) — UK Government / legislation.gov.uk
  • Animal Welfare (Licensing of Activities Involving Animals) Regs 2018 — selling animals as pets / breeding licence (Part H vs Part I) — Defra / local authorities
  • Wildlife (Northern Ireland) Order 1985, Art. 15A & Sch. 9 Pt 1 — sale/transport-for-sale of R. rattus prohibited — DAERA / legislation.gov.uk
  • Bringing pet animals to Great Britain (rabies-susceptible mammals excluded from PETS; APHA RM01) — APHA / UK Government

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Greece? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Greece

Summary. Greece is permissive for the roof rat under a negative-list system: an animal is legal to keep unless a statute, invasive-species rule, or public-health directive bans it. Captive-bred R. rattus is a 'companion animal' (ζώο συντροφιάς) because Law 4830/2021 Art. 2(3) defines that term by reference to EU Reg. 2016/429 Annex I Part B, which includes 'rodents... other than those intended for food production' — and Greek law draws no distinction between the genus Rattus species (the fancy rat, R. norvegicus, is sold openly in Greek pet shops). The 'no wild fauna as pets' clause in the same article targets CITES/native-protected/Habitats-Directive wildlife; R. rattus is none of those (it is an introduced 'Least Concern' species, not protected under PD 67/1981) and a captive-bred specimen does not trigger it. Keeping and private/hobby breeding and free rehoming are legal with no permit or registry entry (microchip/National Companion Animal Registry rules apply to dogs/cats/ferrets, not small rodents); COMMERCIAL breeding and retail sale trigger standard pet-trade licensing (Law 4830/2021 Art. 8 + Law 4711/2020 + PD 184/1996). R. rattus is NOT on the EU Union IAS list (Reg. 1143/2014) and Greece's forthcoming National Catalogue of Invasive Alien Species (KYA 115162/3055/2021) is not yet gazetted as a possession ban. ⚠️ One real correction vs. the preliminary read: the DR finds that bringing a pet rodent INTO Greece (even intra-EU, owner-accompanied) is NOT certificate-free — Ministry Circular 3382/100752/2015 requires a veterinary declaration (κτηνιατρική βεβαίωση); commercial/third-country movement adds TRACES + Border Inspection Post.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Law 4830/2021 Art. 2(3) defines a 'companion animal' (ζώο συντροφιάς) as any animal kept in the home for affection OR any animal listed in EU Reg. 2016/429 Annex I; Annex I Part B expressly includes 'rodents... other than those intended for food production,' so captive-bred R. rattus kept as a pet falls squarely within it. No Greek statute, decree, or ministerial decision prohibits keeping it; PD 67/1981 protects NATIVE wild fauna and R. rattus is introduced (Red Data Book 'Least Concern'), not protected, and absent from the Habitats/Birds Directive annexes the law uses to define 'protected wild fauna.' The 'wild fauna cannot be kept as companion animals' clause targets indigenous/CITES/protected wildlife (e.g., native tortoises, raptors), not a captive-bred rodent of a genus already kept as a pet (cf. R. norvegicus sold openly). Private rodent owners are also exempt from the microchip/National Companion Animal Registry (EMZS) rules that apply to dogs, cats, and ferrets.

Sources: Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (ΦΕΚ Α 169/2021), European Union (EUR-Lex), Hellenic Republic (referenced via Univ. of Athens Zoological Museum / Red Data Book), European Union (EUR-Lex)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Private, non-commercial (hobbyist) reproduction of pet rodents is unregulated. Law 4830/2021 Art. 8's amateur-breeding cap (max two breeding females, one litter/year, prior club/registry authorization) is by its own text limited EXCLUSIVELY to 'female dogs or female cats' (θηλυκούς σκύλους ή θηλυκές γάτες) — by expressio unius the legislature excluded rodents, so a hobby roof-rat colony faces no quota, registry, or municipal permit. COMMERCIAL breeding (reproducing R. rattus to sell offspring for profit) crosses into the licensed pet-trade tier: Art. 8(1) requires the business to operate under Art. 3 of Law 4711/2020 with an operational licence from the Regional Directorate of Agricultural Economy & Veterinary Medicine (ΔΑΟΚ), facility/welfare inspections, and EU Reg. 2019/2035 traceability. So: legal (hobby) — a lawful no-permit pathway exists — with commercial breeding requiring a licence.

Sources: Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (ΦΕΚ Α 169/2021), Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (via NAWS legislation index), Greek Government (transposing Dir. 92/65/EEC), European Union (EUR-Lex)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Private, non-commercial gifting or rehoming between individuals (no profit, or merely covering vet costs) is entirely unregulated — no transfer form, municipal notification, or microchip protocol applies to rodents (unlike dogs/cats). COMMERCIAL retail sale requires a registered pet-shop or breeder licence and compliance with Law 4830/2021 Art. 8 + PD 184/1996; Art. 8's pet-shop window-display ban is limited to dogs and cats, so rodents may lawfully be displayed and sold in licensed shops. Online commercial sellers must include breeder-registration details. In practice R. rattus is essentially absent from Greek retail (market demand/reputation), not because the species is banned. So: legal (private transfer) with commercial sale requiring the standard pet-trade licence.

Sources: Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (ΦΕΚ Α 169/2021), Greek Government (transposing Dir. 92/65/EEC), Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (via NAWS legislation index)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Movement of a pet roof rat INTO Greece is lawful but documented — it is NOT certificate-free even intra-EU and owner-accompanied (correcting the preliminary read). EU Reg. 576/2013 leaves rodents (Annex I Part B) to national rules, and Greece's Ministry Circular 3382/100752/17.09.2015 requires that reptiles, rodents, and rabbits entering Greece be accompanied by an official veterinary declaration (κτηνιατρική βεβαίωση) from an authorized vet in the country of origin certifying the animal is clinically examined, healthy, free of contagious disease and external parasites, and fit to travel. To stay 'non-commercial' the animal must be owner-accompanied, ≤5 animals total, not for sale, with transit within five days of the owner's travel. COMMERCIAL/third-country movement (≥6 animals or for sale) is a veterinary consignment: intra-EU under the Balai Directive 92/65/EEC (PD 184/1996) via TRACES with an Intra-Trade Animal Health Certificate; third-country imports must clear an approved Border Inspection Post (Συνοριακός Σταθμός Ελέγχου) with third-country health certificates. A lawful pathway exists at every tier, so transport is restricted (documentation/permit), not prohibited. Never release.

Sources: European Union (EUR-Lex), Ministry of Rural Development & Food (ΥΠΑΑΤ), General Directorate of Veterinary Services, Greek Government (transposing Dir. 92/65/EEC)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Keeping a captive-bred roof rat, private/hobby breeding, and free rehoming are legal with NO permit (R. rattus is a companion-animal-category rodent under Law 4830/2021 Art. 2(3) + EU Reg. 2016/429 Annex I; not on the EU Union IAS list, CITES, or Bern; not a protected native; not subject to the dog/cat microchip/registry rules). Only COMMERCIAL activity is licensed: breeding R. rattus to sell, or running a pet shop/retail operation, requires a pet-trade/breeding establishment licence and veterinary/welfare compliance.
  • Keeping / hobby breeding / free rehoming: nothing required
  • Commercial breeding: operational licence from the Regional Directorate of Agricultural Economy & Veterinary Medicine (ΔΑΟΚ) under Law 4830/2021 Art. 8(1) + Law 4711/2020 Art. 3; facility/welfare inspection; EU Reg. 2019/2035 traceability
  • Commercial sale: registered pet-shop or breeder licence + veterinary welfare compliance (Law 4830/2021 Art. 8; PD 184/1996)

Where: Regional Directorate of Agricultural Economy & Veterinary Medicine (ΔΑΟΚ) of the relevant Regional Unit; Ministry of Rural Development & Food (ΥΠΑΑΤ) for veterinary oversight · Fees: Set by the licensing authority

Source: Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (ΦΕΚ Α 169/2021), Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (via NAWS legislation index), Greek Government (transposing Dir. 92/65/EEC)

Bringing a pet roof rat into Greece requires a veterinary declaration (κτηνιατρική βεβαίωση) — even intra-EU, owner-accompanied, non-commercial. The declaration is issued by an official/authorized vet in the country of origin shortly before travel (typically within 48-72 hours) certifying the rodent is clinically examined, healthy, free of contagious disease and external parasites, and fit to travel. Non-commercial status requires owner accompaniment, ≤5 animals, not for sale, transit within 5 days of the owner. Commercial (≥6 / for sale) or third-country movement needs TRACES registration and entry via an approved Border Inspection Post with the applicable EU/third-country health certificate.
  • Non-commercial entry (≤5, owner-accompanied): obtain the origin-country veterinary declaration within ~48-72h of travel; carry proof of owner travel (transit within 5 days)
  • Commercial / ≥6 animals (intra-EU): register in TRACES; obtain an Intra-Trade Animal Health Certificate (Balai Dir. 92/65/EEC / PD 184/1996); consign to a registered Greek entity
  • Third-country import: enter via an approved Border Inspection Post (Συνοριακός Σταθμός Ελέγχου) with third-country veterinary health certificates; documentary/identity/physical checks

Forms: Veterinary declaration (κτηνιατρική βεβαίωση) — origin-country official/authorized vet · Where: Origin-country official/authorized veterinarian (declaration); Greek Border Inspection Post + TRACES for commercial/third-country; Ministry of Rural Development & Food (ΥΠΑΑΤ) Animal Health Directorate for guidance

Source: Ministry of Rural Development & Food (ΥΠΑΑΤ), General Directorate of Veterinary Services, European Union (EUR-Lex), Greek Government (transposing Dir. 92/65/EEC)

Owners owe full animal-welfare duties under Law 4830/2021 (the 'Five Freedoms,' Arts. 2/9): a secure, hygienic enclosure suited to this arboreal, social species, fresh water, appropriate nutrition, veterinary care, and freedom from distress. Abuse or severe neglect (Arts. 34-35) carries administrative fines and possible criminal liability; deliberate release or abandonment of any companion animal — including a pet rat — into the Greek ecosystem is a serious criminal offense. Never release; rehome responsibly.

Source: Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (ΦΕΚ Α 169/2021)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Law 4830/2021 — companion-animal welfare framework ('Argos' Program; FEK A 169/18.09.2021). Art. 2(3) companion-animal definition via EU Reg. 2016/429 Annex I + 'no wild fauna' clause; Art. 8 breeding/sale & pet-shop rules; Arts. 34-35 penalties — Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (ΦΕΚ Α 169/2021)
  • EU Reg. 2016/429 (Animal Health Law) Annex I Part B — 'rodents... other than those intended for food production' = companion animals — European Union (EUR-Lex)
  • Circular 3382/100752/17.09.2015 — health rules for non-commercial movement of companion animals; reptiles/rodents/rabbits require a veterinary declaration (κτηνιατρική βεβαίωση) to enter Greece — Ministry of Rural Development & Food (ΥΠΑΑΤ), General Directorate of Veterinary Services
  • EU Reg. 576/2013 — non-commercial movement of pet animals; Annex I Part B leaves rodents to national rules — European Union (EUR-Lex)
  • Law 4711/2020 — establishment & operation of commercial breeding/companion-animal facilities (Art. 3, referenced by Law 4830/2021 Art. 8(1)) — Hellenic Parliament / Government Gazette (via NAWS legislation index)
  • Presidential Decree 184/1996 — commercial intra-EU trade in 'other animal species' (transposes Balai Dir. 92/65/EEC; TRACES/ITAHC for commercial consignments) — Greek Government (transposing Dir. 92/65/EEC)
  • Commission Delegated Reg. (EU) 2019/2035 — traceability/facility rules for kept terrestrial animals (commercial breeders) — European Union (EUR-Lex)
  • Presidential Decree 67/1981 — protection of native flora & wild fauna (R. rattus introduced/'Least Concern', NOT protected) — Hellenic Republic (referenced via Univ. of Athens Zoological Museum / Red Data Book)
  • EU Reg. 1143/2014 (invasive alien species) + Union List — neither R. rattus nor R. norvegicus is listed — European Union (EUR-Lex)
  • KYA 115162/3055/2021 (ΦΕΚ 5697/Β/2021) — national measures on invasive alien species; basis for Greece's forthcoming National Catalogue (not yet gazetted as a possession ban; R. rattus not confirmed listed) — Ministry of Environment & Energy (ΥΠΕΝ) / Government Gazette
  • HELLAS-ALIENS: the invasive alien species of Greece (Neobiota 2023) — R. rattus is a SCIENTIFIC alien-species record only (no legal force) — Neobiota / NECCA (scientific, secondary)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, μαύρος αρουραίος, αρουραίος των στεγών, roof rat, black rat.

Last reviewed 2026-06-10. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Hong Kong? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Hong Kong

Summary. Hong Kong is now DR-verified. Keeping a pet roof rat is legal — Rattus rattus is not protected wildlife (the family Muridae is omitted from Schedule 2 of the Wild Animals Protection Ordinance, Cap. 170), so no possession licence is needed — but it sits under a public-health overlay: the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department treats all rodents as 'vermin' under Cap. 132 with no carve-out for kept pets, enforced on a complaint/infestation basis rather than against sanitarily-caged pets. Private breeding is unregulated (Hong Kong licenses only dog breeders); selling 'by way of business' needs an Animal Trader Licence, though a hobbyist exemption covers selling a pet's offspring and giving one away free is unregulated. Importing any mammal needs an AFCD Special Permit + government-vet health certificate + rabies quarantine (the 2022 COVID small-mammal import ban was lifted by Jan 2023).

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-09

Rattus rattus is not a protected wild animal — the family Muridae is omitted from Schedule 2 of the Wild Animals Protection Ordinance (Cap. 170) — so no possession licence is required. Caveat: the Public Health and Municipal Services Ordinance (Cap. 132, s.47) defines all rodents as 'vermin' with no carve-out for caged pets, a public-health overlay the FEHD enforces on a complaint/infestation basis (elimination notices, not raids on kept pets).

Sources: Hong Kong e-Legislation, Hong Kong e-Legislation, Hong Kong e-Legislation

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

Private, non-commercial breeding is unregulated: Hong Kong created dedicated breeder licences only for dogs (Cap. 139B), deliberately leaving small mammals unregulated at the breeding stage. Oversight begins only at the point of commercial sale.

Sources: Hong Kong e-Legislation, HK Government

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

Selling 'by way of business' requires an Animal Trader Licence (Cap. 139B s.4), but a statutory HOBBYIST EXEMPTION covers selling an animal 'kept by him as a pet or any offspring thereof', and giving one away free (no consideration) is unregulated. Note: the ATL's permitted 'domestic rats' is widely read as the fancy R. norvegicus, so commercial sale of R. rattus is legally untested.

Sources: Hong Kong e-Legislation, HK Government

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

Internal movement of a lawfully-kept pet is unencumbered (subject only to anti-cruelty Cap. 169). IMPORT of any live mammal requires an AFCD Special Permit (Form AF240 commercial / AF242a personal) plus a government-vet Veterinary Health Certificate, with rabies quarantine set by the export country's risk group (Cap. 139; Cap. 421). The 2022 COVID small-mammal import ban was fully lifted by Jan 2023.

Sources: Hong Kong e-Legislation, AFCD, Hong Kong e-Legislation

Restrictions & responsibilities

Keeping a captive-bred roof rat is allowed in Hong Kong; selling needs an AFCD Animal Trader Licence, and importing needs an AFCD Special Permit (AF240) + health certificate — note AFCD has SUSPENDED commercial/unaccompanied rodent imports (owner-accompanied may still be approved). Keep proof your rat is captive-bred (re: the Cap. 132 'vermin' duty). Never release.
  • For import: apply for an AFCD Special Permit (Form AF240) in advance + origin health certificate
  • For sale: obtain an Animal Trader Licence

Forms: AFCD Special Permit (Form AF240) · Where: Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) · Fees: Import permit HK$432 first animal + HK$102 each additional

Source: AFCD, Hong Kong e-Legislation

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Cap. 170 — Wild Animals Protection Ordinance (Schedule 2 excludes Rattus spp.) — Hong Kong e-Legislation
  • Cap. 139 + Cap. 139B — Public Health (Animals & Birds) Ordinance & Trading/Breeding Regs (import permit; Animal Trader Licence) — Hong Kong e-Legislation
  • Cap. 132 — Public Health and Municipal Services Ordinance s.47 (vermin duty) — Hong Kong e-Legislation
  • Cap. 421 — Rabies Ordinance (mammal import/quarantine) — Hong Kong e-Legislation
  • AFCD — Import of Reptiles, Rodents and Miscellaneous Pet Mammals (Form AF240; rodent-import suspension) — AFCD
  • LCQ14 (28 Oct 2020) — government reply confirming 'domestic rats' on the Cap. 139B trade-species list — HK Government

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Hungary? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Hungary

Summary. Hungary treats the roof rat (Rattus rattus) as an ordinary pet rodent, and the preliminary 'protected-species' worry is resolved against any ban. Deep research confirms R. rattus is NOT protected ('védett') under KöM Decree 13/2001, NOT on the EU or national invasive-alien-species lists (Reg. 1143/2014 / Decree 408/2016), and NOT a dangerous animal (FM Decree 85/2015 — the whole family Muridae is absent) — so it defaults to the general pet-animal regime of Government Decree 41/2010, exactly like the fancy rat (R. norvegicus). Keeping and hobby breeding need no permit (only welfare/caging standards); only COMMERCIAL sale/breeding requires a FELIR identifier from NÉBIH, and cross-border movement requires EU/national veterinary paperwork (an Operator's Declaration intra-EU, a National Veterinary Import Certificate from third countries). One residual quirk — NM Decree 18/1998 lists the 'házi patkány' as a public-health pest subject to eradication of free-roaming infestations — does not reach a securely caged pet, but the burden is on the owner to maintain hygiene and prevent escape. Never release a roof rat.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

Keeping a roof rat as a private hobby pet is legal in Hungary with no permit or registration. R. rattus is not a protected species (absent from KöM Decree 13/2001 Appendices 2 and 8, so Decree 348/2006's nature-conservation keeping permit does not apply), not a dangerous animal (FM Decree 85/2015 — Muridae unlisted), and not an invasive alien species (absent from EU Reg. 1143/2014 and national Decree 408/2016), so by elimination it defaults to the general pet-animal (kedvtelésből tartott állat) regime of Government Decree 41/2010, which lists 'Patkány' generically and applies to R. rattus exactly as to the fancy rat. The keeper must meet that decree's welfare/caging standards (minimum 0.18 m² for one rat, +0.03 m² per additional animal, ≥0.3 m shortest side and height, daily checks, no constant light/dark) and the anti-cruelty duties of Act XXVIII of 1998. A municipality cannot cap pet numbers arbitrarily (Constitutional Court Decision 146/2011) provided welfare and hygiene standards are met.

Sources: Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár), Hungarian Parliament (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár), Hungarian Ministry of Environment, Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár), Hungarian Ministry of Agriculture

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

Private, non-commercial hobby breeding of roof rats is legal in Hungary and needs no breeder's licence — the same as the fancy rat, since R. rattus falls under the general pet-rodent regime of Government Decree 41/2010 rather than any protected-species (Decree 348/2006) or ecologically-dangerous-species (Act XXVIII of 1998 §24/F, Decree 408/2016) restriction, none of which list it. Breeders are bound by animal-welfare law: the Animal Protection Act prohibits over-breeding (túltenyésztés) and deliberately producing animals with debilitating genetic defects, enforceable as animal cruelty (állatkínzás) under Btk. §244. Breeding crosses into a regulated COMMERCIAL enterprise (triggering FELIR registration — see sell_give) once it becomes systematic with intent of regular financial gain; that threshold is defined by intent/systematic sale, not a codified litter quota.

Sources: Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár), Hungarian Parliament (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár), Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár), Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár)

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

Giving a roof rat away for free, or occasionally rehoming an accidental litter without profit motive, is unregulated. But anyone engaged in the regular COMMERCIAL sale or systematic breeding of pet animals must obtain a FELIR identifier (Food Chain Supervision Information System) from NÉBIH under Government Decree 578/2020 — a requirement that, since 1 April 2021, sweeps in all pet species including rodents. Registration is via the NÉBIH Client Profile System (ÜPR) through the Ügyfélkapu gateway and subjects the seller to possible inspection by the county government office. A pet shop must also notify the local municipal notary; mail-order/postal sale of live animals is prohibited (Decree 210/2009), and animals must be weaned before transfer. We classify this legal_with_permit because the lawful commercial pathway (FELIR registration) exists and is routine — there is no prohibition.

Sources: NÉBIH / Hungarian Government, Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár), Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár)

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

Moving a roof rat WITHIN Hungary needs no veterinary certificate for a private owner (only general welfare-in-transit standards). Intra-EU movement of pet rodents is non-harmonized under EU Animal Health Law (Reg. (EU) 2016/429): no official veterinary health certificate is required, but the transport must be accompanied by an Operator's Declaration (nyilatkozat) identifying origin/destination, transporter, and the animals (species Rattus rattus, quantity, health) — non-commercial if ≤5 animals accompany the owner with no ownership transfer. Importing from a non-EU third country is the most regulated: it requires the Hungarian National Veterinary Import Certificate (endorsed by an official state vet in the exporting country), entry through a designated Border Control Post, and TRACES-NT CHED pre-notification (Part I) at least one working day ahead, with documentary/identity/physical checks before NAV customs clearance. Because lawful documented pathways exist at every level (declaration / national import certificate), this is legal_with_permit, not prohibited.

Sources: EU / EUR-Lex, NÉBIH, NÉBIH

Restrictions & responsibilities

Commercial trade or systematic for-profit breeding of pet animals (including rodents) requires a FELIR identifier from NÉBIH (Government Decree 578/2020). Free gifting or occasional non-profit rehoming of an accidental litter does not. A pet shop must additionally notify the local municipal notary; mail-order/postal sale of live animals is banned.
  • Decide if your activity is commercial (regular sale / systematic breeding for profit) — if yes, register
  • Apply electronically for a FELIR identifier via the NÉBIH Client Profile System (ÜPR) using the Ügyfélkapu gateway
  • If running a pet shop, notify the local municipal notary (jegyző) of the commercial activity
  • Maintain welfare/caging and record-keeping standards for county-government-office inspection

Forms: FELIR registration via NÉBIH ÜPR (Ügyfélkapu) · Where: NÉBIH (National Food Chain Safety Office) — ÜPR / e-ügyintézés · Fees: No species permit fee; FELIR registration itself is administrative (no licence fee for the identifier)

Source: NÉBIH / Hungarian Government, Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár)

Cross-border movement needs paperwork: intra-EU, an Operator's Declaration (nyilatkozat) accompanying the animals (non-commercial if ≤5, owner-accompanied, no sale); third-country import, the Hungarian National Veterinary Import Certificate endorsed by an official state vet, entry through a designated Border Control Post, and TRACES-NT CHED pre-notification ≥1 working day before arrival. Domestic transport within Hungary needs no certificate.
  • Intra-EU: prepare and sign an Operator's Declaration with origin/destination, transporter, species (Rattus rattus) and quantity, and health statement
  • Third-country import: obtain the National Veterinary Import Certificate signed/stamped by an official state vet in the exporting country
  • Third-country import: pre-notify the Border Control Post via TRACES-NT (CHED Part I) at least one working day before arrival
  • Clear documentary/identity/physical checks at the BCP before NAV customs release

Forms: Operator's Declaration (intra-EU non-harmonized species), National Veterinary Certificate for Pet animals of Rodentia, Reptilia, Amphibia, Lagomorpha, Pisces (third-country import), Common Health Entry Document (CHED) via TRACES-NT · Where: NÉBIH (animal-health import) / designated EU Border Control Post; TRACES-NT for CHED · Fees: Standard veterinary/BCP inspection fees may apply on third-country import

Source: EU / EUR-Lex, NÉBIH, NÉBIH

A regulatory quirk to be aware of: NM Decree 18/1998 lists the 'házi patkány' (roof rat) as a public-health pest (egészségügyi kártevő) and obliges property owners to prevent infestation and eradicate free-roaming rats in inhabited areas. This targets uncontrolled, escaped, free-roaming populations — NOT a securely caged pet. A keeper of contained, captive-bred pets meeting Decree 41/2010 welfare standards is shielded by the Animal Protection Act, but the burden is on the owner to maintain impeccable hygiene and prevent escape so no nuisance/pest-control order is invoked by the local notary. Never release a roof rat.
  • Keep rats securely caged indoors — prevent any escape into the building or wild
  • Maintain strict hygiene/sanitation to avoid a neighbour nuisance complaint to the municipal notary (jegyző)
  • Never release or abandon a roof rat

Where: Local municipal notary (jegyző) handles nuisance/pest complaints; NÉBIH/local authority for welfare

Source: Hungarian Ministry of Welfare, Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Government Decree 41/2010 (II.26.) — keeping & trade of pet animals (covers rodents 'Patkány'; welfare/caging standards; no species permit) — Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár)
  • Act XXVIII of 1998 on the protection and humane treatment of animals (over-breeding ban; §24/F ecologically-dangerous species — R. rattus not listed; anti-cruelty) — Hungarian Parliament (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár)
  • KöM Decree 13/2001 (V.9.) — list of protected/strictly protected species (Apps. 2 & 8; R. rattus ABSENT → not protected) — Hungarian Ministry of Environment
  • Government Decree 348/2006 (XII.23.) — keeping/utilization of protected animal species (NOT triggered; R. rattus is not protected) — Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár)
  • FM Decree 85/2015 (XII.17.) — dangerous animal species (family Muridae NOT listed) — Hungarian Ministry of Agriculture
  • Government Decree 408/2016 (XII.13.) — IAS implementation of EU Reg. 1143/2014 (R. rattus NOT on the EU Union or national list) — Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár)
  • Government Decree 578/2020 (XII.14.) — Food Chain Supervision Information System (FELIR registration for commercial pet trade/breeding, incl. rodents) — NÉBIH / Hungarian Government
  • NM Decree 18/1998 (VI.3.) — epidemiological measures (classifies wandering & house rat as public-health pests subject to eradication of free-roaming infestations) — Hungarian Ministry of Welfare
  • Government Decree 210/2009 (IX.29.) — commercial-activity rules (prohibits mail-order/postal/mobile-vendor sale of live animals) — Hungarian Government (Nemzeti Jogszabálytár)
  • Regulation (EU) 2016/429 — Animal Health Law (Art. 151 Operator's Declaration for non-harmonized pet rodents intra-EU) — EU / EUR-Lex
  • NÉBIH — national veterinary import certificates for non-EU-harmonized live animals (third-country import via designated BCP + TRACES-NT CHED) — NÉBIH
  • NÉBIH — information on travelling/moving pet animals (intra-EU & non-commercial movement guidance) — NÉBIH

Search terms: Rattus rattus, házi patkány, fekete patkány, patkány.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Indonesia? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Indonesia

Summary. Indonesia is one of the more legally hostile places for a pet roof rat, and earlier preliminary research here was wrong to call it permissive. R. rattus is NOT on the protected-species list, so it isn't caught by the conservation-poaching law (Law No. 5/1990) — but that is where the good news ends. Indonesia explicitly lists the roof rat (tikus rumah / tikus atap, the black rat) as a high-priority INVASIVE species in Appendix I of Permen LHK P.94/2016, and three separate ministries are mandated to control or eradicate it: Environment & Forestry (invasive-species control), Agriculture (it is an official crop pest, targeted by a national rodent-eradication program, GERDAL OPT), and Health (a disease vector under Permenkes 50/2017). The practical results: IMPORTING a roof rat is flatly prohibited (P.94/2016 Art. 4(1) — border rejection), so even a captive-bred, certified pet cannot legally cross the border. SELLING is restricted — commercial wildlife trade needs a circulation license (Permen LHK 18/2024) the state will not issue for a species it is legally bound to destroy. KEEPING and hobby-BREEDING sit in a genuine legal vacuum: no clause specifically criminalizes caging one tame roof rat indoors, but there is also no 'pet permit' to legitimize it, and the invasive/vector designation gives officials authority to confiscate or euthanize it. Telling contrast: the fancy rat (R. norvegicus, 'tikus putih') is sold openly as a lab/feeder animal — not because the law exempts it, but because nobody enforces against it. The roof rat gets no such blind spot.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

R. rattus is absent from the protected-species list (Permen LHK P.106/2018), so Law No. 5/1990's poaching prohibitions do not apply — but escaping that list does NOT make it a recognized pet. It remains 'satwa liar' (wildlife) AND is codified as a priority invasive species (Permen LHK P.94/2016, Appendix I, entry 5) subject to state control/eradication, and a disease vector (Permenkes 50/2017). No penal clause specifically bans caging one tame specimen indoors (only the general KUHP Art. 302 animal-welfare duty applies), but there is no positive 'pet permit' to legitimize it, and officials retain authority to confiscate or euthanize on biosecurity grounds. A real, hostile legal vacuum — not 'legal.'

Sources: Ministry of Environment & Forestry (KLHK), KLHK / peraturan.go.id, Ministry of Health (Kemenkes)

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

Permen LHK No. 18/2024 requires a business license (Perizinan Berusaha Penangkaran Jenis TSL) to breed ANY wildlife, protected or not — so commercial roof-rat breeding is covered on paper. But BKSDA cannot lawfully approve propagation of a species officially designated for eradication (P.94/2016), and Agriculture funds a national program (GERDAL OPT) to exterminate it — so the mandatory permit is effectively unobtainable. Small, intra-household hobby breeding is uncodified and de facto invisible to enforcement (hence 'unregulated_unclear'); any attempt to scale or formalize it is blocked by the impossibility of the permit.

Sources: KLHK (Ditjen KSDAE), Ministry of Environment & Forestry (KLHK), Ministry of Agriculture (Kementan)

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

Commercial sale/circulation of wildlife requires a Perizinan Berusaha Peredaran Jenis TSL (Permen LHK No. 18/2024). For the roof rat that license is effectively unobtainable (an invasive species the state is bound to control), so organized commercial sale is restricted and unlawful without it. Casual, non-commercial gifting of a single animal is unmonitored in practice, but commercializing an officially listed invasive species cuts directly against federal biosecurity mandates. (Contrast: fancy rats sell openly through non-enforcement, not a legal exemption.)

Sources: KLHK (Ditjen KSDAE), Ministry of Environment & Forestry (KLHK)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

IMPORT is flatly PROHIBITED: Permen LHK P.94/2016 Art. 4(1) bans entry of listed invasive species ('Pemasukan jenis invasif dari luar negeri yang sudah tercantum... dilarang dan dikenakan tindakan penolakan'), and R. rattus is on Appendix I — Badan Karantina (Barantin) is mandated to reject, confiscate, or destroy a shipment at the border, regardless of captive-bred 'pet' status or origin health certificates. DOMESTIC inter-island movement legally requires BOTH an animal health certificate (SKKH) and a wildlife transport permit (SATS-DN from BKSDA, per Kepmenhut 447/Kpts-II/2003) — but the SATS-DN is effectively unobtainable because the applicant cannot prove legal origin from a licensed breeder (none exist for this invasive species). Never release a nonnative.

Sources: Ministry of Environment & Forestry (KLHK), Republic of Indonesia (BPK), Ministry of Forestry (now KLHK)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing a roof rat into Indonesia is prohibited. R. rattus is on Appendix I of the invasive-species regulation (Permen LHK P.94/2016), and Art. 4(1) bans the entry of listed invasive species — Badan Karantina will reject, confiscate, or destroy the shipment at the border, even for a captive-bred pet with an origin health certificate.
  • Do NOT attempt to import a roof rat — it will be rejected/confiscated at the port of entry.
  • The only narrow theoretical exception is a scientific/research permit under P.94/2016 Art. 7 (not a pet pathway).

Where: Badan Karantina Indonesia (Barantin) / KLHK

Source: Ministry of Environment & Forestry (KLHK)

Commercial breeding and sale of any wildlife (protected or not) require business licenses — Perizinan Berusaha Penangkaran Jenis TSL (breeding) and Peredaran Jenis TSL (circulation) under Permen LHK No. 18/2024. For the roof rat these are effectively unobtainable, because BKSDA will not license propagation or trade of a species the state is legally bound to eradicate. Inter-island transport additionally needs an SKKH (vet health certificate) plus a SATS-DN wildlife-transport permit that cannot realistically be issued for this species.

Where: Balai KSDA (BKSDA) regional office / KLHK KSDAE

Source: KLHK (Ditjen KSDAE), Ministry of Forestry (now KLHK)

The roof rat carries a triple eradication designation — invasive species (KLHK, Permen LHK P.94/2016), agricultural pest (Ministry of Agriculture, GERDAL OPT), and disease vector (Ministry of Health, Permenkes 50/2017). There is no 'pet permit' to legitimize ownership, and the state retains authority to confiscate or euthanize the animal on biosecurity grounds. Never release a roof rat into the wild.

Where: KLHK / Kemenkes / local Dinas

Source: Ministry of Environment & Forestry (KLHK), Ministry of Health (Kemenkes), Ministry of Agriculture (Kementan)

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Help change this

How to help in Indonesia

In Indonesia the roof rat (Rattus rattus, 'tikus rumah' / 'tikus atap' / black rat) is named as a high-priority invasive species in Appendix I of Ministry of Environment & Forestry regulation Permen LHK P.94/2016, and carries two further eradication mandates: an agricultural crop-pest designation (the GERDAL OPT control program) and a disease-vector designation (Permenkes 50/2017). The result is a hostile legal vacuum for keepers: importing a roof rat is banned at the border (P.94/2016 Art. 4(1)), no pet permit exists to legitimize keeping one, and officials retain authority to confiscate or euthanize on biosecurity grounds. This is a species classification, not a domestication problem: the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus, 'tikus putih'), an equally introduced, non-native congener with the same ecological profile, is sold openly across Indonesia as a pet, lab, and feeder animal. The difference is the species name on a list, not the animal's tameness or captive lineage. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over. Pet roof rats are captive-bred for generations, hand-tame, kept entirely indoors, and never released into the wild.

The ask: Ask the responsible ministries to recognize, in writing, a path for captive-bred, indoor-kept pet roof rats, the same de facto tolerance already extended to the pet fancy rat (R. norvegicus), and to clarify or amend how Permen LHK P.94/2016 treats a tame, captive-bred specimen kept indoors and never released. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/), so a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over. Cats and dogs are also non-native and documented to harm Indonesian and island wildlife, yet are permitted as pets. Whether the limited additional risk of a few sterile, tame, indoor-only roof rats, never released, is similarly outweighed by their value as companions is a cost-benefit judgment for the ministries to make. Specifically: (1) ask KSDAE for a written clarification on whether a private citizen may keep captive-bred R. rattus indoors as a pet, and whether a captive-bred carve-out or registration mechanism can be created; and (2) since the species is fixed in Appendix I by regulation, support a future revision of P.94/2016 that distinguishes wild invasive populations (which the state may control) from documented captive-bred indoor pets that pose no biosecurity risk.

Where the lever really is: Mixed, but the dominant lever is the law/list, not a bureaucrat's misreading. The hostile status is not an agency error: KSDAE, Agriculture, and Health are each applying a binding instrument. R. rattus is written by name into Appendix I of Permen LHK P.94/2016 (entry 5), with an Art. 3(5) control/eradication mandate and an Art. 4(1) import ban; it is a crop pest under the GERDAL OPT program and a disease vector under Permenkes 50/2017. An official cannot waive a species off a regulatory list by email, and BKSDA legally cannot license breeding or transport (SATS-DN) of a species the state is bound to eradicate. Asking an agency to allow it will not work, as that asks a civil servant to ignore a regulation they are mandated to enforce. The durable fix is regulatory: a revision of P.94/2016 (a ministerial regulation amendable by KLHK, not requiring parliament) that carves out documented captive-bred, indoor-kept specimens, or a formal de-listing/parity decision. There is also an agency-clarification angle worth pursuing in parallel, because the keep/hobby-breed status is a genuine vacuum: no clause specifically criminalizes caging one tame roof rat indoors, and the fancy rat's open pet trade shows the state already tolerates a congeneric introduced rat as a pet. The two-part approach is: (a) ask KSDAE for a written clarification on whether captive-bred indoor R. rattus may be kept, and press for parity with the fancy rat, which is useful even if it only confirms the vacuum; and (b) recognize that the durable fix is amending the regulation/list, which only KLHK (the rule-maker) can do. Indonesia has no fixed public-comment window for this, so the route is the official citizen-inquiry/aspiration channel (SP4N-LAPOR!) directed at KLHK, framed as a request to clarify and revise.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • SP4N-LAPOR! — National Public Aspiration & Complaint Portal (lapor.go.id) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Verified live, official 'no wrong door' federal portal jointly run by the Ministry of State Apparatus (PANRB), the Presidential Staff Office, and the Ombudsman. It routes a citizen inquiry or aspiration to the competent ministry (here: KLHK for the invasive-species rule; Kemenkes for the vector rule) and guarantees a tracked written response. The KSDAE site itself lists this as its public complaint channel. Best single channel for both the clarification ask (to KLHK) and the request to revise Permen LHK P.94/2016.
  • KLHK — Ditjen KSDAE (Directorate General of Conservation of Natural Resources & Ecosystems) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Verified live (June 2026). The federal authority that OWNS Permen LHK P.94/2016 and the invasive-species/wildlife-utilization rules — i.e. the only body that can issue a written clarification on keeping captive-bred R. rattus and the only rule-maker that can amend Appendix I to add a captive-bred carve-out. Address the clarify-and-revise request here (and via LAPOR! for a tracked reply). Submit in Bahasa Indonesia.
  • Badan Karantina Indonesia (Barantin) — National Quarantine Agency (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Verified live, official. The border-biosecurity authority enforcing the P.94/2016 Art. 4(1) import ban and domestic inter-area movement rules. Relevant only as a secondary touchpoint to confirm import/transport treatment of a captive-bred pet — NOT the body that can change the listing. Include only if your question is specifically about moving/importing an animal.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request to clarify and revise the treatment of captive-bred pet roof rats (Rattus rattus)

To the Directorate General of KSDAE, Ministry of Environment & Forestry,

I am writing to ask for a written clarification and a revision of the rules. Rattus rattus is listed by name as an invasive species in Appendix I of Permen LHK P.94/2016. I support controlling wild invasive populations. The rats I am asking about are captive-bred for generations, hand-tame, kept entirely indoors in cages, and never released into the wild; they pose no biosecurity, crop, or disease risk.

The issue is the species name, not the animal itself. The fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus, 'tikus putih') is an equally introduced, non-native rat that is openly kept and sold as a pet across Indonesia. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over, and the same tolerance should extend to it.

Cats and dogs are also non-native and documented to harm native and island wildlife, yet are permitted as pets. Whether the limited additional risk of a few sterile, tame, indoor-only roof rats, never released, is similarly outweighed by their value as companions is a judgment for the ministry to make.

I respectfully ask: (1) Please confirm in writing whether a private citizen may keep captive-bred R. rattus indoors as a pet, and whether any registration mechanism exists. (2) Please consider revising Permen LHK P.94/2016 to distinguish wild invasive populations from documented captive-bred, indoor-kept pets, creating a captive-bred carve-out.

Thank you for your consideration.

[Your name]
[Your city / contact]
id
Perihal: Permohonan klarifikasi dan revisi atas perlakuan terhadap tikus peliharaan hasil penangkaran (Rattus rattus)

Kepada Yth. Direktorat Jenderal KSDAE, Kementerian Lingkungan Hidup dan Kehutanan,

Saya menulis untuk memohon klarifikasi tertulis dan revisi atas peraturan. Rattus rattus tercantum secara eksplisit sebagai jenis invasif dalam Lampiran I Permen LHK P.94/2016. Saya mendukung pengendalian populasi invasif di alam liar. Tikus yang saya maksud adalah hasil penangkaran turun-temurun, jinak, dipelihara sepenuhnya di dalam rumah dalam kandang, dan tidak pernah dilepasliarkan, sehingga tidak menimbulkan risiko biosekuriti, pertanian, maupun penyakit.

Persoalannya terletak pada nama spesies, bukan pada hewannya. Tikus putih (Rattus norvegicus) adalah tikus yang sama-sama bukan asli Indonesia, namun dipelihara dan diperjualbelikan secara terbuka sebagai hewan peliharaan di seluruh Indonesia. Tikus putih itu sendiri adalah tikus cokelat liar yang baru didomestikasi pada abad ke-19, sehingga tikus atap hasil penangkaran adalah kasus yang sama, hanya berbeda satu spesies, dan toleransi yang sama sepatutnya juga berlaku baginya.

Kucing dan anjing pun bukan hewan asli Indonesia dan terdokumentasi membahayakan satwa liar asli maupun satwa di pulau-pulau, namun tetap diizinkan sebagai hewan peliharaan. Apakah tambahan risiko yang terbatas dari beberapa ekor tikus atap yang steril, jinak, dipelihara sepenuhnya di dalam rumah, dan tidak pernah dilepasliarkan, sebanding dengan manfaatnya sebagai hewan pendamping, adalah pertimbangan yang menjadi kewenangan kementerian.

Dengan hormat saya memohon: (1) Mohon konfirmasi tertulis apakah warga sipil diperbolehkan memelihara R. rattus hasil penangkaran di dalam rumah sebagai hewan peliharaan, dan apakah ada mekanisme pendaftaran. (2) Mohon dipertimbangkan revisi Permen LHK P.94/2016 untuk membedakan populasi invasif liar dari hewan peliharaan hasil penangkaran yang dipelihara di dalam rumah, dengan menciptakan pengecualian bagi hasil penangkaran.

Atas perhatian Bapak/Ibu, saya ucapkan terima kasih.

[Nama Anda]
[Kota / kontak Anda]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Permen LHK P.94/2016 — Invasive Species (Jenis Invasif): R. rattus on Appendix I (entry 5); Art. 4(1) import ban; Art. 3(5) eradication/control mandate; Art. 7 research exemption — Ministry of Environment & Forestry (KLHK)
  • Permen LHK No. 18/2024 — Utilization of Plant & Wildlife Species (Pemanfaatan TSL): Art. 4 business licenses (Penangkaran / Peredaran) for all wildlife, protected or not — KLHK (Ditjen KSDAE)
  • Law No. 5/1990 — Conservation of Living Resources (Art. 21 prohibitions apply only to protected species) — Republic of Indonesia (via FAOLEX)
  • Permen LHK P.106/2018 — protected plant & animal species list (R. rattus absent → not protected) — KLHK / peraturan.go.id
  • Law No. 21/2019 — Animal, Fish & Plant Quarantine (SKKH / quarantine clearance for movement) — Republic of Indonesia (BPK)
  • Kepmenhut 447/Kpts-II/2003 — administration of capture & circulation of wild flora/fauna (SATS-DN domestic transport permit) — Ministry of Forestry (now KLHK)
  • Permenkes No. 50/2017 — environmental-health standards for vectors & disease-carrying animals (rats as leptospirosis/typhus vectors; mandated control) — Ministry of Health (Kemenkes)
  • GERDAL OPT — national rat-pest eradication program (rodenticides + barn-owl biocontrol); R. rattus classified as a plant-pest organism (OPT) — Ministry of Agriculture (Kementan)
  • Lapak Satwa — open listing of pet white rats (R. norvegicus): the de-facto-tolerance contrast (market practice, not a legal exemption) — lapaksatwa.co.id (recognized pet-trade platform; secondary)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, tikus rumah, tikus atap, tikus hitam, jenis invasif, roof rat, black rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Ireland? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Ireland

Summary. Ireland is now DR-verified, and it is favourable for mainland keepers. S.I. 374/2024 lists the roof rat (Rattus rattus) as an invasive alien species of national concern, but its First Schedule restricts that designation to 'Offshore islands only' — so on the Irish MAINLAND keeping and breeding pet roof rats is fully legal and unregulated by possession bans, while on the offshore islands (critical seabird breeding grounds) keeping/breeding/transport are prohibited. Commercial supply on the mainland triggers DAFM rules: you must register as a seller/supplier if you transfer six or more pet animals in a year (sale OR free), and rats may not be transferred under 4 weeks of age. Importing rodents follows national 'non-harmonised species' rules (advance DAFM notice/permit + a government-vet health certificate). The earlier S.I. 477/2011 grey area is superseded.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • National Parks & Wildlife Service (NPWS) Wildlife Licensing Unit, Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, written reply June 2026: NPWS 'does not licence for such species' (roof rats, Rattus rattus) — i.e. it is not a species for which NPWS issues a keeping/wildlife licence — and indicated that animal-welfare questions fall to the Department of Agriculture (DAFM). This supports that keeping a pet roof rat on the Irish mainland is not gated by an NPWS wildlife permit; welfare, pet-sale registration, and import sit with DAFM. (The offshore-islands prohibition under S.I. 374/2024 is unaffected.)

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

On the Irish MAINLAND, keeping a pet roof rat is fully legal and unregulated by possession bans. S.I. 374/2024 lists Rattus rattus as an invasive alien species of 'national concern', but the First Schedule limits its geographical application to 'Offshore islands only' (Reg. 16), so the Reg. 17 keep/breed/transport prohibitions do NOT activate on the mainland. On offshore islands, keeping is prohibited. No domestication carve-out (the ban targets the species by binomial name, identical to R. norvegicus).

Sources: Irish Statute Book, Irish Statute Book, Invasive Species Ireland (NPWS / NBDC)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

Mainland: legal and unregulated by environmental law. Offshore islands: prohibited (S.I. 374/2024 Reg. 17(1)(c)). Commercial supply triggers DAFM registration (see Sell).

Sources: Irish Statute Book, National Parks & Wildlife Service

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

On the mainland, selling or even GIVING AWAY pet rats is legal but commercial law applies: supplying SIX or more pet animals in a calendar year (sale OR free supply) requires registration on the DAFM Register of Sellers and Suppliers of Pet Animals (S.I. 681/2019), which entails a private-vet premises inspection; rats may not be transferred under 4 weeks of age. Offshore islands: prohibited.

Sources: Irish Statute Book, Irish Statute Book, Irish Statute Book

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

Rodents are 'non-harmonised species' (outside the EU pet-passport system), so import follows Ireland's national rules: an EU-origin pet needs an Owner Declaration to DAFM at least one working day before arrival; a non-EU/GB pet needs an advance DAFM import permit (apply 1–2 months ahead) plus an official government-vet health certificate. Internal transport to an offshore island is an offence.

Sources: Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine, Irish Statute Book

Restrictions & responsibilities

MAINLAND: NPWS confirmed (June 2026) it does NOT licence roof rats, so keeping and breeding pet roof rats on the Irish mainland are legal and not gated by any NPWS wildlife licence. The only commercial layer is DAFM: supplying SIX or more pet animals in a calendar year (sale OR free) requires registration on the DAFM Register of Sellers and Suppliers of Pet Animals (S.I. 681/2019), with a private-vet premises inspection; rats may not be transferred under 4 weeks of age. OFFSHORE ISLANDS: keeping/breeding/transport of R. rattus are prohibited (S.I. 374/2024, 'Offshore islands only'). Never release — an escape is itself an offence.
  • Mainland: no NPWS licence needed to keep or breed (NPWS confirmed it does not licence the species)
  • If supplying >=6 pet animals per year (sale or free): register with DAFM (S.I. 681/2019) and meet the 4-week minimum transfer age
  • Offshore islands: do not keep, breed, or transport R. rattus (S.I. 374/2024)
  • Welfare/import questions: Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine (DAFM)

Where: DAFM (pet-sales registration; welfare; import). NPWS does not licence this species.

Source: Irish Statute Book, Irish Statute Book

Bringing a rat into Ireland from another EU state (including Northern Ireland) needs a DAFM import permit + a vet health certificate (within 48h) + TRACES notification. Non-EU import needs a DAFM permit applied for 1–2 months ahead. Never release a roof rat — an escape from confinement is itself an offence under S.I. 477/2011 Reg. 49.

Where: Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine (DAFM)

Source: Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • European Communities (Birds and Natural Habitats) Regulations 2011 (S.I. 477/2011) — Third Schedule + Regs 49–50 (R. rattus listed) — Irish Statute Book
  • Black rat (Rattus rattus) species account — Third Schedule listing under Regs 49 & 50; notes Reg 50 not yet enacted — Invasive Species Ireland (NPWS / NBDC)
  • European Union (Invasive Alien Species) Regulations 2024 (S.I. 374/2024) — national-concern schedule + market offence — Irish Statute Book
  • Animal Health and Welfare Act 2013 — general welfare duties — Irish Statute Book
  • Animal Health and Welfare (Sale or Supply of Pet Animals) Regulations 2019 (S.I. 681/2019) — DAFM registration ≥6/yr — Irish Statute Book
  • NPWS — Licences and Consents (Wildlife Licensing Unit) — National Parks & Wildlife Service
  • DAFM Pet Travel — rodent intra-EU / non-EU import (permit, health cert, TRACES) — Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine
  • Regulation (EU) 1143/2014 — Union list (coypu is the only listed rodent; R. rattus NOT listed) — EU / EUR-Lex

Search terms: Rattus rattus, black rat, roof rat, ship rat, francach dubh.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Israel? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Israel

Summary. Israel's regulation of roof rats is a paradox: the species is freely keepable precisely because it is legally branded a 'pest.' Under the Wildlife Protection Law 5715-1955, Section 8 bars holding, transferring, and trading a 'wild animal' WITHOUT an INPA permit — but only for animals that are NOT pests. The Wildlife Protection Regulations 5736-1976 (Reg. 2) explicitly declare Rattus rattus a pest (מזיק), listed right beside Rattus norvegicus, so both rat species are entirely exempt from INPA keeping, transfer, and internal-trade permits — and there is no White-List issue for domestic keeping. (This overturns the preliminary White-List assumption.) The fancy rat is sold freely for this exact reason, not because of any special 'domesticated' status. The catch is at the other end: as a declared pest and invasive species, R. rattus is NOT on the INPA Mammal White List, so commercial import is barred — deliberately, to keep exotic rat lineages out — with only a narrow, contested veterinary 'accompanied pet' exemption for personal import. Commercial breeding/selling needs a municipal business license, and municipal sanitation bylaws treat any rat on a property as a nuisance subject to eradication, a theoretical exposure that coexists with the federal exemption.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

Keeping a roof rat needs NO INPA permit. The Wildlife Protection Law 5715-1955 s.8(3) bars holding a 'wild animal that is not a pest' without a permit; the Wildlife Protection Regulations 5736-1976 Reg. 2(2) expressly declare Rattus rattus a pest (מזיק) — alongside R. norvegicus at Reg. 2(1) — so it is carved out of the s.8 permit regime entirely, exactly like the freely-kept fancy rat. The one wrinkle is tiered government: municipal sanitation bylaws (under the Municipalities Ordinance) classify rats on a property as a 'nuisance' subject to a removal/eradication notice, drawing no distinction between a feral infestation and a caged pet — a theoretical exposure that does not displace the federal exemption.

Sources: State of Israel / Knesset (via INPA), Ministry of Environmental Protection / INPA, Ministry of Interior / Local Municipalities

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

Private hobby breeding of lawfully-held roof rats is unregulated and lawful: because INPA requires no holding permit for declared pests (Wildlife Protection Law 1955 s.8; 1976 Regs Reg. 2), it does not track or restrict their reproduction, and the Animal Protection (Welfare) Law 5754-1994 sets only general welfare standards, not a breeding ban. The status shifts to RESTRICTED only at commercial scale: a systematic breeding operation triggers a mandatory municipal business license under the Business Licensing Order 5773-2013 Item 3.2(a) ('breeding, keeping and treating of animals'), with veterinary/sanitation/fire inspections. There is no fixed numeric hobby-to-business threshold; it is judged qualitatively (scale, public access, income, nuisance).

Sources: State of Israel / Knesset (via INPA), Ministry of Environmental Protection / INPA, State of Israel (translated text), Ministry of Interior (secondary: licensing-practice summary)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

Private sale or gifting of captive-bred roof rats is lawful and needs no INPA permit: the Wildlife Protection Law 1955 s.8(1)-(2) require trade/transfer permits only for a 'wild animal that is not a pest', and R. rattus is a declared pest (1976 Regs Reg. 2(2)), so it is exempt — which is why both rat species are sold openly on Israeli platforms (e.g. Yad2, Facebook groups) without violating any wildlife-trafficking statute. The status is RESTRICTED only for commercial retail: a pet shop or systematic seller needs a municipal business license under the Business Licensing Order 5773-2013 Item 3.2, plus Animal Protection (Welfare) Law 1994 housing standards. Not CITES-listed.

Sources: State of Israel / Knesset (via INPA), Ministry of Environmental Protection / INPA, Ministry of Interior (secondary: licensing-practice summary)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

Internal transport of lawfully-held stock is unregulated beyond general welfare. International IMPORT is the heavily restricted edge: Israel runs a 'White List' (רשימה לבנה) admitting only listed species, and the 2018 INPA Mammal White List omits ALL Rattus species while listing other pet rodents (hamsters, chinchilla, degu, gerbil) — so commercial import of roof rats is effectively prohibited, a deliberate policy (per a 2023/2025 draft amendment) to bar non-native rat lineages. A narrow lawful pathway survives: the Ministry of Agriculture Veterinary Services 'accompanied pet' exemption permits importing up to two rodents with an origin Veterinary Health Certificate (issued ≤7 days pre-export), a 90-day-ownership / non-commercial declaration (Annex B/C to vs-airport@moag.gov.il ≥48h before arrival), and an inspection fee — though its application to a declared 'pest' is unsettled and INPA inspectors may still confiscate at the border. Under the assume-a-pathway lens this is legal_with_permit/restricted, not flat-prohibited. Never release.

Sources: Israel Nature & Parks Authority, Israel Nature & Parks Authority, Israel Ministry of Agriculture — Veterinary Services, Israel Ministry of Agriculture — Veterinary Services (via USDA APHIS), State of Israel / Knesset (via INPA)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Commercial-scale breeding or a retail pet shop selling rats needs a municipal Business License (רישיון עסק) under the Business Licensing Order 5773-2013 Item 3.2 ('breeding, keeping and treating of animals'). Private hobby breeding and one-off/low-volume private sales need NO license. There is no numeric hobby/business threshold — municipalities judge it qualitatively (scale, public foot traffic, income, odor/refuse nuisance).
  • Determine whether the operation is qualitatively 'commercial' (scale, public access, income, nuisance) — private hobby placement is exempt
  • If commercial: apply to the local municipality for a Business License under Item 3.2
  • Pass prior/periodic inspections by the municipal veterinarian, Ministry of Health, and Fire & Rescue Authority (ventilation, drainage, escape-proof enclosures, disease control)

Where: Local municipality business-licensing department (רישוי עסקים) · Fees: Set by the municipality

Source: Ministry of Interior (secondary: licensing-practice summary)

Importing a roof rat as a personal pet runs through the Ministry of Agriculture Veterinary Services 'accompanied pet' exemption (no advance import license for up to two rodents), but R. rattus's absence from the INPA Mammal White List means INPA may still veto entry. The standard small-rodent pathway (hamster, etc.) does NOT clearly extend to a species declared a 'pest', so pre-clearance between MoAg-VS and INPA is advisable. Commercial import is effectively barred.
  • Obtain an original Veterinary Health Certificate (in English) from a government vet in the origin country, issued ≤7 days before export
  • Hold the animal(s) for ≥90 days pre-flight; limit to 2 rodents; non-commercial only
  • Submit the Annex B/C declaration to Veterinary Services at Ben Gurion (vs-airport@moag.gov.il) ≥48 hours before arrival
  • Pre-clear the species with INPA (off the White List) to avoid confiscation; pay the arrival inspection fee

Forms: MoAg Veterinary Services pet-arrival declaration (Annex B / Annex C) · Where: Ministry of Agriculture Veterinary Services, Ben Gurion Airport (vs-airport@moag.gov.il); coordinate with INPA (import@npa.org.il) · Fees: Arrival inspection fee, historically ~55 NIS (subject to adjustment)

Source: Israel Ministry of Agriculture — Veterinary Services, Israel Ministry of Agriculture — Veterinary Services (via USDA APHIS), Israel Nature & Parks Authority, Israel Nature & Parks Authority

Municipal sanitation bylaws (under the Municipalities Ordinance; model bylaw 1972, and e.g. Haifa, Nof HaGalil, Lod) classify the presence of rats on a property as an actionable 'nuisance' subject to a removal/eradication notice — with no legal distinction between a feral infestation and a caged pet. A complaint can trigger an inspector's notice; non-compliance can mean fines and forced extermination billed to the owner. There is no way to 'register' a pet rat to opt out. Separately, releasing a roof rat is strictly prohibited (invasive-species/ecological-hazard ban) — never release.
  • Keep rats fully indoors in secure, sanitary enclosures; avoid odor/escape that could draw a neighbor complaint
  • Never release a roof rat — release of an invasive pest is a prosecutable offense

Where: Local municipality (sanitation / nuisance enforcement)

Source: Ministry of Interior / Local Municipalities

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Wildlife Protection Law 5715-1955 (חוק להגנת חיית הבר) — s.1 'wild animal' definition; s.8(1)-(3) holding/transfer/trade permits exempt 'pests' — State of Israel / Knesset (via INPA)
  • Wildlife Protection Regulations 5736-1976 (תקנות להגנת חיית הבר) — Reg. 2 designates Rattus norvegicus (2(1)) and Rattus rattus (2(2)) as 'pests' (מזיקים) — Ministry of Environmental Protection / INPA
  • Draft Amendment to Wildlife Protection Regulations, 5783-2023 — explains the deliberate intent: keep only endemic rats on the pest list so non-native rat species cannot enter freely under the pest exemption — Ministry of Environmental Protection / Gov.il (tazkirim)
  • INPA Mammal White List (Sept. 2018) — permitted mammals for import/trade; omits ALL Rattus species (lists hamster, chinchilla, degu, gerbil) — Israel Nature & Parks Authority
  • INPA — Import of Mammals ('species not on the White List are prohibited for import, commerce and possession'; import@npa.org.il) — Israel Nature & Parks Authority
  • Ministry of Agriculture — Import of Pets (Veterinary Services; accompanied-pet exemption ≤2 rodents, health certificate) — Israel Ministry of Agriculture — Veterinary Services
  • MoAg Veterinary Services — Pet-arrival declaration (Annex B/C) for notifying Ben Gurion ≥48h before arrival — Israel Ministry of Agriculture — Veterinary Services (via USDA APHIS)
  • Business Licensing Order (Businesses Requiring Licensing) 5773-2013 — Item 3.2(a) license for breeding/keeping/treating animals (commercial breeders + pet shops) — Ministry of Interior (secondary: licensing-practice summary)
  • Animal Protection (Welfare) Law 5754-1994 — general vertebrate welfare standards (food/water/space); no rodent breeding ban — State of Israel (translated text)
  • Model Municipal Bylaw (Sanitation & Removal of Nuisances) 1972 + city bylaws (Haifa, Nof HaGalil, Lod) — rats classed as an actionable 'nuisance' subject to eradication notice — Ministry of Interior / Local Municipalities
  • IUCN GISD — Rattus rattus ('100 worst' invasive; underpins Israel's deliberate import bar) — IUCN

Search terms: Rattus rattus, חולדה מצויה (chuldah metzuyah — common/house rat, the statutory designation for R. rattus), חולדת העליות (chuldat ha-aliyot — attic rat), חולדה שחורה (chuldah shechorah — black rat, literal), מזיק (mazik — 'pest', the operative legal classification).

Last reviewed 2026-06-11. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.
