item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in India? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › India

Summary. India is permissive for the roof rat, with one commercial catch. R. rattus is NATIVE to the Indian subcontinent (its evolutionary cradle), so Indian law does NOT treat it as an invasive alien species. The Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act 2022 ABOLISHED the old Schedule V 'vermin' list (which had included rats), and R. rattus is on none of the protected schedules (I, II, IV) and not CITES-listed — so it carries no wildlife designation, and private keeping + non-commercial hobby breeding are UNREGULATED (only the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1960 welfare duties apply; the 2024 PARIVESH registration covers only CITES/Schedule-IV exotics, not native rats). Indian law draws NO distinction between the roof rat and the fancy rat — the Pet Shop Rules 2018 cover 'rodents of the rat or mice category' generically. The one real requirement is COMMERCIAL SALE: selling rats as a business (incl. online) needs registration with the State Animal Welfare Board under the PCA (Pet Shop) Rules 2018 (₹5,000, inspection, welfare standards). Internal transport is unregulated (anti-cruelty only); INTERNATIONAL IMPORT is heavily restricted (DGFT restricted-import licence + Sanitary Import Permit + vet certificate; cargo only, 6 airports). ⚠️ Local municipal sanitation bylaws (plague history) could theoretically limit keeping in dense housing.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

After the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act 2022 abolished Schedule V ('vermin', which had listed rats), R. rattus — a native species — is absent from Schedules I, II, and IV and is not CITES-listed, so it carries no wildlife designation and the WLPA's possession/registration prohibitions (Ch. V/VB) don't apply. The Living Animal Species (Reporting & Registration) Rules 2024 (PARIVESH 2.0) bind only CITES/Schedule-IV species, so a native rat owner is exempt. Possession is therefore governed only by the PCA Act 1960 §11 welfare duty (food/water/shelter, no abandonment). No permit to keep. 'Unregulated_unclear' (not 'legal') because legality is by statutory silence + a residual municipal-bylaw possibility, not an affirmative pet authorization.

Sources: Parliament of India (via PRS), Animal Welfare Board of India, MoEFCC (via PIB)

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

No federal statute requires a permit for private, non-commercial hobby breeding of non-scheduled small mammals. The Breeding of & Experiments on Animals (Control & Supervision) Rules 1998 (CPCSEA) govern only institutional/laboratory breeding and expressly exempt the pet trade; the PCA (Dog Breeding & Marketing) Rules 2017 cover dogs only — no analogous rodent-breeder rule exists. So hobby breeding of R. rattus falls through the gap (unregulated), bounded only by PCA Act §11 welfare. Ambiguity: there is no numerical 'hobby vs commercial' threshold — once offspring are sold for profit, the Pet Shop Rules (see sell_give) apply.

Sources: Animal Welfare Board of India, Parliament of India (via PRS)

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

COMMERCIAL sale requires registration. The PCA (Pet Shop) Rules 2018 define 'pet animal' to include 'rodents of the rat or mice category' (Rule 2(j)) — covering R. rattus and R. norvegicus identically — and Rule 3 bars operating a pet shop / trading in pet animals (incl. ONLINE: social media, e-commerce, classifieds) without a Certificate of Registration from the State Animal Welfare Board (Form I, ₹5,000, vet inspection, valid 5 yrs; caging/welfare standards + records). FREE, non-commercial gifting/rehoming is NOT a 'business' and doesn't trigger registration — but charging even a nominal 'rehoming fee' could be construed as commercial by a strict inspector.

Sources: Animal Welfare Board of India

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

INTERNAL (interstate/within India): unregulated beyond the Transport of Animals Rules 1978 / PCA Act anti-cruelty baseline (no transit permit/NOC, since R. rattus is non-scheduled). INTERNATIONAL IMPORT is heavily restricted: live rodents fall under ITC(HS) 01061900 ('Mammals: Other'), a 'Restricted' category — the DGFT pet-baggage route is for DOGS & CATS ONLY (Trade Notice 22/2022-23), so a pet rat must be imported as formal air cargo with (1) a DGFT restricted-import licence, (2) a Sanitary Import Permit (SIP) from DAHD via NSWS, (3) an official veterinary health certificate (DAHD SOP Annexure 12.1.1 for rodents), and (4) an Advance NOC from AQCS — entry only via 6 designated airports, with possible 30-day quarantine. Never release.

Sources: Directorate General of Foreign Trade, Department of Animal Husbandry & Dairying, Animal Welfare Board of India

Restrictions & responsibilities

To SELL roof rats as a business (including online), register as a pet shop with your State Animal Welfare Board under the PCA (Pet Shop) Rules 2018 (Form I, ₹5,000, vet inspection, 5-yr certificate; caging/welfare standards + records). Keeping, hobby breeding, and FREE rehoming need no registration. Internal transport is welfare-only.
  • For commercial sale: apply to your State Animal Welfare Board (Form I, ₹5,000) + pass the vet inspection
  • Free/non-commercial rehoming: nothing required

Where: State Animal Welfare Board (SAWB) · Fees: ₹5,000 (pet-shop registration)

Source: Animal Welfare Board of India

INTERNATIONAL IMPORT only: a pet roof rat must enter as air cargo with a DGFT restricted-import licence + a DAHD Sanitary Import Permit + a veterinary health certificate + an AQCS Advance NOC (6 designated airports; possible 30-day quarantine). The dog/cat pet-baggage route does NOT apply to rodents. Internal movement needs no permit. Never release.
  • Apply for the DGFT restricted-import licence (~2 months ahead)
  • Obtain a DAHD Sanitary Import Permit via NSWS
  • Get an origin-country veterinary health certificate (rodent SOP)
  • Submit to AQCS for an Advance NOC ≥7 days before arrival

Where: DGFT; DAHD (NSWS); AQCS

Source: Directorate General of Foreign Trade, Department of Animal Husbandry & Dairying

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Official sources

  • Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act 2022 — abolishes Schedule V ('vermin'); 4-schedule system; R. rattus on none of Sch. I/II/IV — Parliament of India (via PRS)
  • PCA (Pet Shop) Rules 2018 — 'rodents of the rat or mice category' = pet animal; State Board registration for sale/trade — Animal Welfare Board of India
  • Living Animal Species (Reporting & Registration) Rules 2024 — PARIVESH 2.0; applies only to CITES/Schedule-IV species (not native rats) — MoEFCC (via PIB)
  • DGFT Trade Notice 22/2022-23 — import of pets (baggage route = dogs & cats only; rodents = cargo, ITC(HS) 01061900 Restricted) — Directorate General of Foreign Trade
  • DAHD SOPs for Import of Live Animals (Sanitary Import Permit; Annexure 12.1.1 rodent veterinary health certificate) — Department of Animal Husbandry & Dairying

Search terms: Rattus rattus, chooha (चूहा), kala chooha (काला चूहा), roof rat, black rat, house rat.

Last reviewed 2026-06-08. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Italy? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Italy

Summary. Italy has no species-specific ban on keeping a captive-bred roof rat, but the framework that governs it is the wild/exotic-animal regime, not the ordinary-pet regime that covers the fancy rat. The 1996 dangerous-animals decree (DM 19 aprile 1996, under Legge 150/1992) lists five rodent families among the prohibited species (Hystricidae, Erethizontidae, Hydrochoeridae, Dinomyidae, Dasyproctidae) but NOT the family Muridae, so R. rattus is not a banned 'dangerous' species. R. rattus is not on the EU invasive-species Union list and is not CITES-listed. Under D.Lgs 135/2022 (Art. 3), keeping a wild/exotic companion species as a pet is allowed only for species named in a Ministry of Health decree drawn from Annex I of Reg. (EU) 2016/429, but a contingency clause makes that whole Annex I set (which includes rodents) lawful to keep, trade and import as long as the 'lista negativa' of banned species is not published. As of 2026 that banning list is still unpublished (overdue since March 2023), so keeping captive-bred R. rattus is currently lawful. Note: D.Lgs 135/2022 defines a 'specie selvatica' to include any wild species (native or exotic), so R. rattus falls under this regime, while the domesticated R. norvegicus (fancy rat) is treated as an ordinary companion animal. From 1 January 2026 private keepers of wild/exotic companion animals listed in Annex I Part B must complete a mandatory training course (D.Lgs 220/2025). Hobby breeding registers the activity with the local ASL; commercial breeding/sale needs ASL plus a municipal SUAP/SCIA authorization. The big caveat: if R. rattus is ever added to the lista negativa, keeping and breeding would become prohibited overnight (existing owners could keep the animal to natural death, with breeding barred).

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

No Italian law prohibits keeping captive-bred R. rattus. The 1996 dangerous-animals decree (DM 19 aprile 1996) lists five rodent families (Hystricidae, Erethizontidae, Hydrochoeridae, Dinomyidae, Dasyproctidae) but not the family Muridae, so the roof rat is not a banned 'dangerous' species; it is not on the EU IAS Union list or CITES. The roof rat is a 'specie selvatica' under D.Lgs 135/2022 (whose definition covers native wild species), so it sits in the wild/exotic regime, not the ordinary-pet regime that covers the domesticated fancy rat (R. norvegicus). Art. 3 of D.Lgs 135/2022 makes keeping the wild/exotic companion species in Annex I of Reg. (EU) 2016/429 (which includes rodents) lawful while the 'lista negativa' of banned species is unpublished. From 1 January 2026, private keepers of such animals must complete a mandatory training course (D.Lgs 220/2025). Note: the mandatory microchip + SINAC registration under D.Lgs 134/2022 applies to dogs, cats and ferrets, not to pet rodents. Status could shift if the lista negativa publishes and includes R. rattus.

Sources: Ministero dell'Ambiente / MIMIT (G.U. 3 ottobre 1996, n. 232), Gazzetta Ufficiale, FNOVI (Federazione Nazionale Ordini Veterinari Italiani), Gazzetta Ufficiale

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-13

Hobby breeding of captive-bred R. rattus is not expressly prohibited (it is on no published banning list). The Ministry of Health clarification of 27 June 2023 confirms the D.Lgs 135/2022 reproduction ban targets wild-caught exotic animals introduced after the decree, not captive-bred ones, so captive breeding is preserved. Under the EU Animal Health Law (Reg. 2016/429, implemented by D.Lgs 134/2022), the breeding establishment is registered with the local ASL; small amateur operations register directly at the ASL without a municipal SUAP step. Numeric thresholds separating amateur from commercial breeding are set regionally (for example ULSS 9 Scaligera in Veneto treats up to two to three breeding females as amateur). Commercial breeding triggers a SUAP/SCIA filing, structural and welfare standards, and stamped birth/death/transfer registers. Risk: a future lista negativa including R. rattus would prohibit breeding.

Sources: Gazzetta Ufficiale, Gazzetta Ufficiale, ASL / Servizio Veterinario regionale

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-13

No R. rattus-specific ban on sale or transfer. Gratuitous transfer by a hobbyist is unimpeded once the animal is lawfully held. Commercial sale requires an ASL establishment registration plus a municipal SUAP/SCIA authorization, a stamped load/unload register (registro di carico e scarico), and per-animal traceability. The exotic-animal decree (D.Lgs 135/2022) subjects distance/online selling (no immediate handover) to a prior veterinary health certification. Occasional hobby litters typically fall below the commercial-registration threshold (region-dependent). A future lista negativa including R. rattus would bar commercialization.

Sources: Gazzetta Ufficiale, Gazzetta Ufficiale, ASL / Servizio Veterinario regionale

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Intra-EU non-commercial movement of pet rodents falls under Reg. (EU) 576/2013 Annex I Part B. Rodents are not covered by the unified EU pet passport (which is for dogs, cats and ferrets); Italy requires an origin-country veterinary health certificate, owner accompaniment, no change of ownership, and a maximum of 5 animals, or the movement is reclassified as commercial. R. rattus is not CITES-listed, so no CITES permit is needed. Import from outside the EU must clear an Italian Border Inspection Post (PIF) with third-country health certification; rabies titer testing is generally waived for small rodents from low-risk countries. Release is prohibited (Art. 727 Codice Penale plus environmental control of the species). Never release.

Sources: EU / EUR-Lex, Gazzetta Ufficiale, EU / EUR-Lex

Restrictions & responsibilities

Captive-bred roof rats are not banned, but R. rattus is a 'specie selvatica' under D.Lgs 135/2022, so it sits in the wild/exotic-animal regime rather than the ordinary-pet regime that covers the fancy rat. Keeping is lawful today only through the Art. 3 contingency (Annex I species of Reg. (UE) 2016/429 permitted while the 'lista negativa' of banned species is unpublished). From 1 January 2026, private keepers of wild/exotic companion animals must complete a mandatory training course (D.Lgs 220/2025). Hobby breeding registers the establishment with the local ASL. The mandatory microchip + SINAC registration applies to dogs, cats and ferrets, not to pet rodents. Watch the pending lista negativa: confirm with the Ministry of Health / MASE before acquiring, as R. rattus's future status is uncertain. Never release.
  • Confirm R. rattus is not (and will not be) on the lista negativa via the Ministry of Health / MASE
  • If keeping as a wild/exotic companion animal, complete the mandatory training course required from 1 January 2026 (D.Lgs 220/2025)
  • For breeding, register the establishment with your local ASL (Azienda Sanitaria Locale)
  • Above the regional amateur threshold (commercial scale), file a SUAP/SCIA with the municipality and keep the required registers

Where: Local ASL (Azienda Sanitaria Locale); municipal SUAP for commercial scale; Ministry of Health DGSAF / MASE for lista-negativa status · Fees: Regional ASL tariff for breeding-establishment registration/inspection (borne by the breeder); municipal SUAP/SCIA fees for commercial scale

Source: Gazzetta Ufficiale, ASL / Servizio Veterinario regionale

Intra-EU non-commercial movement of pet rodents (Reg. (UE) 576/2013 Annex I Part B) requires an origin-country veterinary health certificate, owner accompaniment, no transfer of ownership, and a maximum of 5 animals. Import from outside the EU must clear an Italian Border Inspection Post (PIF) with third-country health certification. Distance/online selling (no immediate handover) requires a prior veterinary health certification under D.Lgs 135/2022. No CITES permit (R. rattus not listed).
  • Intra-EU non-commercial: carry an origin-country vet health certificate; owner-accompanied; max 5 animals; no sale on arrival
  • Third-country import: clear an Italian PIF with the required health certificate
  • Distance/online sale: obtain a prior veterinary health certification

Where: Origin-country authorized veterinarian; Italian Border Inspection Post (PIF) for third-country import

Source: EU / EUR-Lex, Gazzetta Ufficiale

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Italy
Time-sensitive: The "lista negativa" of banned species under D.Lgs 135/2022 has been overdue since 27 March 2023 and remains unpublished as of mid-2026; the government's correttivo (D.Lgs 220/2025, in force 6 February 2025) keeps the framework live and the decree could be issued at any time. The related "lista positiva" (the wild-capture list) was published in 2022 and updated to 71 species in February 2026, which shows the rulemaking is active. There is no formally announced public-comment window for the banning list, but the rule is actively being drafted now, so the window to influence its content is open and could close without notice. Write before the decree is published.

In Italy, keeping a captive-bred roof rat (Rattus rattus, "ratto nero") is currently lawful, but it sits in the wild/exotic-animal regime rather than the ordinary-pet regime that covers the fancy rat. The 1996 dangerous-animals decree (DM 19 aprile 1996 under Legge 150/1992) lists five rodent families (Hystricidae, Erethizontidae, Hydrochoeridae, Dinomyidae, Dasyproctidae) but not the family Muridae, so R. rattus is not a banned 'dangerous' species, and it is not on the EU invasive-species Union list or on CITES. Under Art. 3 of D.Lgs 135/2022, keeping a wild/exotic companion species is allowed only for species named in a Ministry of Health decree, but a contingency clause makes the whole Annex I set of Reg. (EU) 2016/429 (which includes rodents) lawful to keep while the 'lista negativa' of banned species is not published. That banning list, due since March 2023, is still unpublished in 2026. The agency is not misreading the law; under the law as it stands today, the captive-bred roof rat is permitted. The risk is a rule that has not been written yet. If R. rattus were added to the lista negativa, keeping and breeding would become illegal (existing owners could keep an animal to natural death, with breeding barred). The time to make the case is before the list is fixed. D.Lgs 135/2022 defines 'specie selvatica' to include native wild species, so the roof rat is swept in even though it is a small companion rodent. The already-permitted fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over.

The ask: Write to the two ministries that jointly draft the lista negativa (the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of the Environment / MASE) and ask them to confirm in writing that the captive-bred domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus), a small companion rodent and not a dangerous or wild-caught species, will not be included on the forthcoming lista negativa under D.Lgs 135/2022. The relevant test is domestication, not wild ancestry. The dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised as domestic animals, because what makes an animal domestic is generations of captive breeding for tameness. A captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense. The already-permitted fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/ ). Ask that small companion rodents bred in captivity be kept off the ban list, or, if any threshold applies, that a clear path to keep them legally be preserved.

Where the lever really is: The lever is the legislature/rulemaking side, not the front-line agency. Under the law as it exists today, the local ASL is applying it correctly: there is no species ban on R. rattus, so writing to an ASL to clarify or permit a rat will not change anything, and any ASL registration is a legitimate notification, not an error. There is no agency misreading to fix. The exposure is secondary legislation not yet enacted: the lista negativa mandated by D.Lgs 135/2022, drafted jointly by the Ministry of Health and MASE, overdue since March 2023 and still unpublished in 2026. Because that list is an interministerial decree (rulemaking) rather than an ASL decision, the correct touchpoint is the drafting ministries during the rulemaking window, to ensure captive-bred small companion rodents are not added, not a front-line health office. Appealing to a local ASL would be aimed at the wrong body. The advocacy is preventive: shape the rule before it is finalized, because once R. rattus is on a statutory ban list, no agency can exempt it.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministero della Salute — Direzione Generale della Sanità Animale e dei Farmaci Veterinari (DGSAF) (co-author of the D.Lgs 135/2022 implementing decrees, incl. the lista negativa) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    One of the two ministries that jointly draft and sign the lista negativa decree under D.Lgs 135/2022. The right body to ask that captive-bred small companion rodents (R. rattus) be kept off the ban list. Use the official contacts page; for a formal submission send to the institutional certified inbox (PEC) dgsa@postacert.sanita.it. Do not write to a named individual officer.
  • Ministero dell'Ambiente e della Sicurezza Energetica (MASE) — Ufficio Relazioni con il Pubblico (URP) (executive / agency) — urp@mase.gov.it
    The co-drafting ministry for the D.Lgs 135/2022 lista negativa and the authority that published the related positive list. The URP is the verified official intake channel; institutional PEC mase@pec.mase.gov.it for a formal submission. Writing to both ministries covers the two signatures the ban-list decree requires.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Direzione Generale della Sanità Animale e dei Farmaci Veterinari (Ministero della Salute) and to MASE,

I am writing about the forthcoming "lista negativa" of banned species under Legislative Decree 135/2022, which is still unpublished. I ask you to confirm that the captive-bred domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) will not be included on that list.

The roof rats kept by hobbyists are bred in captivity, tame, kept indoors as companion animals, and never released into the wild. They are small companion rodents, like the familiar fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus), not dangerous or wild-caught species. The decree's stated aim targets dangerous and exotic taxa, and the only rodent families on the 1996 dangerous-animals decree are porcupines and a few large hystricomorphs, not the mouse and rat family. The relevant test is domestication, not wild ancestry. The dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised as domestic animals, because what makes an animal domestic is generations of captive breeding for tameness, not its Latin name. A captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense. The already-permitted fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over.

I ask that captive-bred small companion rodents, including domesticated R. rattus, be excluded from the lista negativa, or that a clear legal path to keep them be preserved. Please confirm the current drafting status of the list and how the public may comment.

Thank you for your consideration.

[Your name]
[Your town/region, Italy]
Italiano
Alla Direzione Generale della Sanità Animale e dei Farmaci Veterinari (Ministero della Salute) e al MASE,

Scrivo in merito alla "lista negativa" delle specie di cui sarà vietata la detenzione, prevista dal D.Lgs 135/2022 e tuttora non pubblicata. Chiedo di confermare che il ratto nero domestico, allevato in cattività (Rattus rattus), non sarà incluso in tale lista.

I ratti neri tenuti dagli appassionati sono allevati in cattività, docili, custoditi in casa come animali d'affezione e non vengono mai rilasciati in natura. Sono piccoli roditori da compagnia, come il comune ratto domestico (Rattus norvegicus), e non specie pericolose o catturate in natura. La finalità dichiarata del decreto riguarda taxa pericolosi ed esotici, e le uniche famiglie di roditori presenti nel DM 19 aprile 1996 sugli animali pericolosi sono gli istrici e pochi grandi istricomorfi, non la famiglia dei topi e dei ratti. Il criterio rilevante è la domesticazione, non l'ascendenza selvatica. Il cane discende dal lupo e il gatto da un felide selvatico, eppure entrambi sono riconosciuti come animali domestici, perché ciò che rende domestico un animale sono generazioni di allevamento in cattività per la docilità, e non il suo nome latino. Un ratto nero allevato in cattività è domestico in questo stesso senso. Il ratto domestico già consentito (Rattus norvegicus) è esso stesso il ratto bruno selvatico, domesticato solo nell'Ottocento, sicché un Rattus rattus allevato in cattività è lo stesso caso una specie più in là.

Chiedo che i piccoli roditori da compagnia allevati in cattività, incluso il R. rattus domestico, siano esclusi dalla lista negativa, oppure che sia preservato un chiaro percorso legale per detenerli. Vi prego di confermare lo stato di redazione della lista e le modalità con cui il pubblico può presentare osservazioni.

Vi ringrazio per l'attenzione.

[Your name]
[Comune/Regione, Italia]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • DM 19 aprile 1996 — elenco specie pericolose di cui è proibita la detenzione (Allegato A, Rodentia: Hystricidae, Erethizontidae, Hydrochoeridae, Dinomyidae, Dasyproctidae; Muridae NON elencata) — Ministero dell'Ambiente / MIMIT (G.U. 3 ottobre 1996, n. 232)
  • D.Lgs 5 agosto 2022 n. 135 — animali di specie selvatiche ed esotiche; Art. 3 (detenzione consentita per le specie dell'Allegato I del Reg. (UE) 2016/429 in attesa della 'lista negativa') + correttivo D.Lgs 220/2025 — Gazzetta Ufficiale
  • FNOVI — 'Pubblicato decreto su specie selvatiche esotiche' (lista positiva pubblicata 11 ottobre 2022; 'lista negativa' non ancora pubblicata) — FNOVI (Federazione Nazionale Ordini Veterinari Italiani)
  • D.Lgs 5 agosto 2022 n. 134 — identificazione e registrazione (SINAC); microchip/registrazione obbligatori per cani, gatti e furetti (NON per i roditori da compagnia); Reg. (UE) 2016/429 — Gazzetta Ufficiale
  • ASL (es. ULSS 9 Scaligera, Veneto) — allevamento di animali da compagnia amatoriale e commerciale (soglie regionali; registrazione ASL; SUAP per il commerciale) — ASL / Servizio Veterinario regionale
  • Regolamento (UE) 576/2013 — movimenti non commerciali di animali da compagnia (Allegato I Parte B: roditori) — EU / EUR-Lex
  • Regolamento (UE) 2016/429 — Animal Health Law (Allegato I Parte B: roditori e conigli da compagnia) — EU / EUR-Lex
  • ISPRA / MASE — implementazione EU IAS Reg. 1143/2014 (R. rattus NON sull'elenco dell'Unione) — ISPRA

Search terms: Rattus rattus, ratto nero, ratto dei tetti, sorcio nero, animale da compagnia, animale d'affezione, specie selvatica, lista negativa.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Japan? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Japan

Summary. In Japan, keeping and hobby-breeding a captive-bred roof rat is legal and unregulated federally: the species is deliberately NOT a 'Specified Animal' (特定動物, hazardous) and NOT a 'Designated Invasive Alien Species' (特定外来生物) — a 2005 expert committee chose to exclude it because it's too long-established to regulate. Commercial activity (breeding for profit, retail sale, exhibition, or large-scale free rehoming) triggers registration as a First-Class (or Second-Class) Animal Handling Business with facility/welfare standards. The big restriction is IMPORT: bringing a roof rat into Japan is de-facto prohibited for the public — the Ministry of Health requires imported rodents to have lived since birth in a foreign-government-designated biosecure facility (homes/hobby breeders don't qualify). Never release one.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Private possession needs no federal permit: R. rattus is not a 'Specified Animal' (特定動物 — that list targets primates, big carnivores, large/venomous reptiles, not rodents), and it is not a 'Designated Invasive Alien Species' (特定外来生物). The 2005 Ministry of the Environment expert committee deliberately excluded it (long-established via maritime trade; eradication-vs-pet distinction). Domestic keeping is treated like keeping a fancy rat or guinea pig.

Sources: Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE), Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE), Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Private breeding without intent to profit/advertise/distribute commercially is entirely outside the commercial animal-handling law. (Commercial-scale breeding triggers First-Class Animal Handling Business registration — see sell_give.)

Sources: Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Selling for profit (or breeding to sell) requires registration as a First-Class Animal Handling Business (第一種動物取扱業) with the prefecture, plus facility/caging/disclosure standards and an Animal Handling Manager. Giving animals away free to 'a large number of unspecified people' on a continuing basis requires Second-Class (第二種) notification. Occasional free rehoming to friends/family is unregulated.

Sources: Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE), Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

DOMESTIC transport between prefectures is unregulated (subject only to carrier policies). IMPORT is de-facto prohibited for pets: under the Infectious Diseases Control Law's Animal Import Notification System, all live rodents need a health certificate from the EXPORTING government certifying the animal lived since birth in a government-designated disease-free facility — which homes and hobby breeders cannot obtain, so a pet roof rat cannot legally be imported. (R. rattus is not on the absolute-prohibition list, but the facility rule is an effective ban.) Export from Japan is legal with the destination country's health certificate (MAFF AQS). Never release.

Sources: Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW), Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Commercial selling/breeding (for profit) = First-Class Animal Handling Business registration (第一種動物取扱業) with the prefecture: facility floor plans, cleanable escape-resistant enclosures, space to 'stand/lie/move' naturally, an Animal Handling Manager, and written species/sex/origin disclosure at transfer. Large-scale non-commercial giveaway = Second-Class (第二種) notification (penalty up to ¥300,000 for failing to notify).
  • Register as a First-Class Animal Handling Business before any commercial sale/breeding
  • Or file a Second-Class notification for large-scale free rehoming

Where: Prefectural government (animal welfare center / public health dept)

Source: Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE), Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)

Importing a roof rat into Japan is effectively impossible for pet owners: imported rodents need an exporting-government health certificate proving the animal lived since birth in a government-DESIGNATED biosecure facility (homes/hobby breeders can't qualify). MHLW states such pets 'basically cannot be brought into Japan.'

Where: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (quarantine station at port of entry)

Source: Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW), Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Designated Invasive Alien Species list — Ministry of the Environment (R. rattus NOT listed) — Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)
  • List of Specified Animals (特定動物) — rodents excluded — Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)
  • MOE Expert Group minutes (July 2005) — rationale for excluding R. rattus (established; Watase/Blakiston lines) — Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)
  • Regulation of Animal Handling Business (動物取扱業の規制) — First-Class registration scope — Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)
  • Second-Class Animal Handling Business (第二種動物取扱業) — non-commercial large-scale transfer — Japan Ministry of the Environment (MOE)
  • Animal Import Notification System for rodents (designated-facility health certificate) — MHLW — Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW)
  • MHLW public warning — pet rodents 'basically cannot be brought into Japan' — Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, クマネズミ (kumanezumi), roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

Last reviewed 2026-06-07. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in South Korea? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › South Korea

Summary. South Korea has, as of December 14, 2025, become one of the most restrictive jurisdictions in the world for the pet roof rat — and earlier preliminary research here was wrong about why. The roof rat (Korean 곰쥐, R. rattus) is NOT an 'Alert Alien Species' (유입주의 생물); that label belongs to the Polynesian rat (R. exulans). Instead, Korea has flipped its entire exotic-animal regime from a 'negative list' (anything not banned is allowed) to a 'White List' (백색목록) positive list under the Wildlife Protection and Management Act: every mammal, bird, reptile and amphibian is now prohibited to import, breed, or sell by default unless the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment has expressly approved the species. Only 9 mammal species made the approved list — and the roof rat is not one of them. That makes R. rattus a 'Designated Managed Wild Animal' (지정관리 야생동물). The practical effect: importing one is banned outright (except for licensed academic research); breeding (증식) is prohibited; selling or even giving one away (거래/양도) is prohibited. People who already owned a roof rat before December 14, 2025 may keep that individual animal for the rest of its natural life ONLY IF they formally register it through the national WIMS portal by a hard deadline of June 13, 2026 — after which an unregistered animal becomes illegal contraband. There is no hobbyist exemption and no permit that reopens breeding or sale; the policy is deliberately designed to phase the species out of private hands by natural attrition.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

Keeping a roof rat is permitted ONLY under a transitional grandfather clause for animals already owned before the White List took effect (Dec 14, 2025). Such owners must file a possession declaration (보관 신고, Form 31-9) with their local mayor/county/district head through the national WIMS portal no later than June 13, 2026. A registered owner then receives a declaration certificate (신고확인증) and may keep that specific individual animal for the rest of its natural life. From June 14, 2026 onward, possessing an unregistered R. rattus is illegal harboring of contraband wildlife, subject to confiscation and penalties. No new acquisition is possible — the species is a 'Designated Managed Wild Animal' (지정관리 야생동물) because it is not on the 백색목록 White List.

Sources: National Law Information Center (법제처 국가법령정보센터), Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment (기후에너지환경부), Gimpo City Government (김포시청)

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

Breeding (증식) is unequivocally prohibited for both private citizens and commercial entities. The grandfather clause that allows continued possession of pre-existing animals expressly forbids breeding: municipal enforcement guidance states grandfathered Designated Managed Wild Animals 'may continue to be kept, but breeding and trading are not permitted' (증식·거래는 허용하지 않는다). The intent is biological containment — to eliminate the captive population over the lifespan of existing individuals. There are no hobbyist exemptions and no breeding permits available for a non-White-List species; even a Wild Animal Business Production License (생산업 허가) only applies to White-List species, so it cannot authorize breeding roof rats.

Sources: National Law Information Center (법제처 국가법령정보센터), Gimpo City Government (김포시청)

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

Commercial sale (판매) and private transfer or gifting (양도/양수) are prohibited under the same regime that bans breeding ('거래는 허용하지 않는다' — trading is not permitted). The grandfathered animal is legally tethered to the individual who filed the possession declaration. The 'transfer/acquisition' checkboxes on Form 31-9 exist for White-List animals or narrow state-approved exceptions (e.g., inheritance on the registered owner's death, or surrender to a licensed facility) — not for casual rehoming or sale of a roof rat between hobbyists. A Wild Animal Business Sales License does not help, because it covers only White-List species.

Sources: National Law Information Center (법제처 국가법령정보센터), Gimpo City Government (김포시청)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

Importation of R. rattus for the pet trade is banned outright — Designated Managed Wild Animals cannot be imported or brought into the country (Wildlife Act Art. 22-2), the only exemption being a rigorous permit for academic/scientific/state restoration purposes. A shipment intended for the pet trade would be denied entry or confiscated regardless of any origin health certificate. Internal transport of a legally grandfathered, WIMS-registered animal (e.g., to a veterinarian, or when the owner relocates) is generally tolerated as an inherent part of authorized possession, provided the animal is securely contained, never released, and the WIMS location data is updated on a permanent move — but the statute does not give explicit point-to-point transit rules, so confirm provincial-line movement with the Ministry.

Sources: National Law Information Center (법제처 국가법령정보센터), Animal and Plant Quarantine Agency

Restrictions & responsibilities

Since December 14, 2025, the roof rat is a 'Designated Managed Wild Animal' under Korea's White List positive-list system: importing, breeding, and selling/giving away the species are all prohibited. Only animals already owned before that date may be kept — and only if registered via the WIMS portal by June 13, 2026. After that deadline, an unregistered animal is illegal contraband subject to confiscation. There is no hobbyist exemption and no permit that reopens breeding or sale.
  • If you already own a roof rat (acquired before Dec 14, 2025): file the possession declaration (보관 신고, Form 31-9) via the WIMS portal https://wims.mcee.go.kr by June 13, 2026 to keep the animal lawfully for its natural life
  • Do NOT breed, sell, or give the animal away — these are prohibited even for grandfathered/registered animals
  • Do NOT import a roof rat — import for the pet trade is banned; a shipment would be confiscated regardless of health certificates
  • Update WIMS location data if you move; keep the animal securely contained and never release it

Forms: Form No. 31-9 — 지정관리 야생동물 (양도·양수·보관) 신고서 (Designated Managed Wild Animal Transfer/Acquisition/Possession Declaration) · Where: Local mayor / county governor / district head, filed through the national WIMS portal (야생동물종합관리시스템, https://wims.mcee.go.kr)

Source: National Law Information Center (법제처 국가법령정보센터), Gimpo City Government (김포시청)

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in South Korea. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in South Korea
Time-sensitive: Two live deadlines. (1) Possession registration: owners of a roof rat acquired before Dec 14, 2025 must file the possession declaration (보관 신고, Form 31-9) via the WIMS portal (wims.mcee.go.kr) by June 13, 2026; after that, an unregistered animal is illegal contraband. (2) The Ministry's 2026 White List revision public-comment process (2026 백색목록 개정 국민 의견수렴) is announced on the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment website; submit any species-inclusion or humane-treatment comment through this window. Confirm the exact closing date on the Ministry notice before relying on it.

As of December 14, 2025, South Korea switched from a 'negative list' (anything not banned is allowed) to a 'White List' (백색목록, positive list) under the Wildlife Protection and Management Act. Every mammal, bird, reptile, and amphibian is now banned to import, breed, or sell by default unless the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment has expressly approved the species. The approved White List names only 9 mammals, and the roof rat (곰쥐, Rattus rattus) is not one of them (neither is the fancy rat, R. norvegicus). The roof rat is therefore a 'Designated Managed Wild Animal' (지정관리 야생동물): importing it is banned, breeding (증식) is prohibited, and selling or giving one away (거래·양도) is prohibited. There is no hobbyist exemption and no permit that reopens breeding or sale. The only people who may keep a roof rat are those who already owned one before Dec 14, 2025 and who register that specific animal through the national WIMS portal (wims.mcee.go.kr) by the deadline of June 13, 2026; from June 14, 2026 an unregistered roof rat is illegal contraband. Korean law treats a captive-bred, hand-tamed roof rat as legally identical to a wild one. Domestication carries no legal weight here; only the species name on the list does.

The ask: There are two separate asks. (1) If you already own a roof rat (acquired before Dec 14, 2025): register that individual animal through the WIMS portal (wims.mcee.go.kr, Form 31-9) before June 13, 2026 so you can lawfully keep it for the rest of its natural life. Do not miss this deadline, and do not breed, sell, or give the animal away. (2) If you want the rule changed: the only lever is the Ministry's annual White List revision and its public-comment process (2026 백색목록 개정 국민 의견수렴). Submit a comment asking the Ministry to evaluate documented, long-domesticated captive-bred R. rattus lineages for inclusion against the four safety criteria (climate suitability, reproductive rate, hybridization risk, disease risk), and to recognize that domestication, not wild ancestry, is what should decide an animal's status: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/), so a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in the same way, one species over. A more realistically achievable ask is clear, humane rules for the grandfathered population (compassionate rehoming if an owner dies, and safe veterinary transport across provincial lines). A high-reproduction, climate-suited rodent is a long shot for the White List, so the achievable win is humane treatment of the animals already here.

Where the lever really is: This is a law/list problem, not a bureaucracy-misreading problem. The agency is applying the law correctly: under the positive-list ('White List') system effective Dec 14, 2025, every mammal is banned by default unless expressly listed, and the roof rat is not on the 9-mammal approved list (Ministry Notification No. 2025-55). There is nothing to clarify or reinterpret; the rule is unambiguous and the Ministry has no discretion to admit the species on request. An appeal asking the agency to treat a tame, captive-bred roof rat as exempt will not work, because the agency is doing what the statute and the list require. The only lever that can change the outcome is changing the list itself, through the Ministry's recurring White List revision and its public-comment process, and behind that the legislature that built the positive-list regime. The correct target is the public-comment/rulemaking window for the White List, not an inspector or help-desk. Two notes specific to Korea: (a) there is a live, recurring official comment process for the 2026 White List revision, so the petition channel is open even though success is unlikely for this species; (b) for owners of existing animals, the immediate action is administrative compliance (WIMS registration by June 13, 2026), which is separate from advocacy and is not a request the agency can deny if filed correctly.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment (기후에너지환경부) — Biodiversity Division (생물다양성과), White List public-comment / 2026 revision process (public comment) — official contact page
    The agency that owns the White List and runs the annual revision and public-comment process (2026 백색목록 개정 국민 의견수렴). Because the law is being applied correctly, the ONLY way to change the outcome is to change the list through this channel. Watch the Ministry's notice board for the live comment notice and its submission instructions/deadline. Division phone: +82-44-201-7245 / -7248.
  • e-People (국민신문고) — official government petition and opinion portal (public comment) — official contact page
    Korea's single official portal for submitting policy suggestions, opinions, and requests for interpretation to any government agency, including the Ministry. Its 'Petition for Foreigners' page accepts submissions and replies in English and 15 other languages, so a non-Korean speaker can lodge a formal, on-record comment directed to the Ministry's Biodiversity Division. Use this to submit the White List inclusion request or the humane-treatment ask.
  • WIMS — Wildlife Information Management System (야생동물종합관리시스템) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    NOT an advocacy channel — this is the mandatory portal for the administrative step: existing owners file the possession declaration (Form 31-9) here by June 13, 2026 to lawfully keep their animal. Included because it is the time-critical action for anyone who already owns a roof rat.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Biodiversity Division, Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment / Public comment on the White List (백색목록) revision

I am writing about the status of the roof rat (곰쥐, Rattus rattus) under the White List system in effect since 14 December 2025. Because the species is not on the approved list, it is treated as a Designated Managed Wild Animal, and keeping, breeding, and transfer are effectively prohibited.

The animals I am concerned with are captive-bred, hand-tamed companion rats kept entirely indoors. They are never released into the wild, never sold into the wild trade, and are descended from long-domesticated lines, biologically and behaviorally distinct from wild-caught roof rats. What should decide an animal's status is domestication, not wild ancestry: the dog descends from the wolf and the domestic cat from a wild felid, yet Korea recognizes both as domestic companion animals, not wildlife. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century; a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in the same way, as are the ferret and the fancy rat.

I respectfully ask the Ministry to (1) evaluate documented, captive-bred domesticated R. rattus lineages for inclusion on the White List against the four safety criteria, and (2) at minimum, adopt clear and humane rules for the already-registered grandfathered population, including compassionate rehoming when an owner dies or is incapacitated, and safe veterinary transport.

Thank you for considering this comment.

[Your name]
[Your city / country]
[Date]
한국어
기후에너지환경부 생물다양성과 귀중 / 백색목록(白色目錄) 개정 국민 의견 제출

2025년 12월 14일부터 시행된 백색목록 제도와 관련하여 곰쥐(Rattus rattus)의 분류에 대해 의견을 드립니다. 곰쥐는 백색목록에 포함되어 있지 않아 지정관리 야생동물로 취급되며, 사육·증식·양도가 사실상 금지되어 있습니다.

제가 말씀드리는 개체는 사람 손에서 번식하고 길들여져 실내에서만 기르는 반려 개체입니다. 자연에 방사하지 않으며, 야생 거래에 판매하지 않고, 오랫동안 가축화되어 온 혈통의 후손으로서 야생에서 포획된 곰쥐와는 생물학적·행동학적으로 구별됩니다. 동물의 지위를 결정해야 하는 것은 야생 조상이 아니라 가축화 여부입니다. 개는 늑대에서, 집고양이는 야생 고양잇과 동물에서 유래했지만, 한국은 이 둘을 야생동물이 아닌 반려동물로 인정하고 있습니다. 애완용 시궁쥐(R. norvegicus)도 본래 야생 시궁쥐이며 19세기에 이르러서야 가축화되었습니다. 사육 곰쥐 역시 가축화된 페럿이나 애완용 시궁쥐와 같은 방식으로 가축화된 동물이며, 야생 조상은 우리 앞에 있는 그 동물이 아닙니다.

이에 정중히 요청드립니다. (1) 문서로 입증된 가축화된 사육 곰쥐 혈통을 네 가지 안전성 기준에 따라 백색목록 등재 대상으로 검토하여 주시고, (2) 최소한, 이미 신고된 경과조치(유예) 대상 개체에 대해 명확하고 인도적인 관리 기준을 마련하여 주시기 바랍니다. 여기에는 소유자의 사망이나 중대한 장애 시 인도적 양도, 그리고 동물병원 진료를 위한 안전한 이동이 포함됩니다.

의견을 검토하여 주셔서 감사합니다.

[이름]
[거주 도시 / 국가]
[날짜]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Wildlife Protection and Management Act (야생생물 보호 및 관리에 관한 법률), as amended/enforced Dec 14, 2025 — Designated Managed Wild Animal definition (Art. 2), possession reporting (Art. 22-4), import prohibition (Art. 22-2) — National Law Information Center (법제처 국가법령정보센터)
  • White List Designation Notification (백색목록 지정 고시), Ministry Notification No. 2025-55 — 888 approved species; only 9 mammals; R. rattus excluded — Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment (기후에너지환경부)

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Mexico? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Mexico

Summary. Mexico governs Rattus rattus entirely through federal wildlife law, not ordinary pet law. Both R. rattus and R. norvegicus are on the official invasive-species list (SEMARNAT Acuerdo, DOF 07/12/2016, 'muy alto' risk), which makes the roof rat 'vida silvestre exótica invasora' regardless of how tame or captive-bred it is — domestication is not a legal shield in Mexican jurisprudence. The Reglamento de la LGVS (RLGVS Art. 2) expressly excludes invasive species from the legal definition of 'mascota,' so the simple free pet authorization (trámite SEMARNAT-08-056) is foreclosed; the remaining lawful pathway to keep or breed one is to register the premises as a wildlife-management facility (PIMVS, Art. 78 Bis, trámite SEMARNAT-08-045) under a SEMARNAT-approved Plan de Manejo. Any transfer (sale or gift) requires documented legal provenance (Art. 51) and a recipient who also holds legal facilities; internal transport requires the provenance documents to travel with the animal. Cross-border IMPORT is categorically prohibited — LGVS Art. 27 Bis 1 bars importing any listed invasive species, and SEMARNAT cannot issue an import permit even if SENASICA's zoosanitary requirements are met. In practice R. norvegicus is sold openly despite identical listing (de-facto tolerance from its commercial ubiquity), an asymmetry R. rattus does not enjoy. Not CITES-listed.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

R. rattus is on the 2016 invasive-species Acuerdo (DOF 07/12/2016), so it is 'vida silvestre exótica invasora' regardless of domestication, and the simple pet authorization is foreclosed: RLGVS Art. 2 expressly excludes invasive species from the legal definition of 'mascota,' barring trámite SEMARNAT-08-056 for this species. The one lawful pathway to keep one is to register the premises as a wildlife-management facility (PIMVS) under LGVS Art. 78 Bis (trámite SEMARNAT-08-045) with a SEMARNAT-approved Plan de Manejo and a certified Responsable Técnico — a heavy, facility-grade authorization rather than an ordinary pet permit. A pathway therefore exists (not prohibited), but it eliminates ordinary hobbyist keeping; PROFEPA enforces (LGVS Art. 122).

Sources: Cámara de Diputados / DOF, DOF / SEMARNAT (via FAOLEX), Diario Oficial de la Federación / SEMARNAT, gob.mx / SEMARNAT, gob.mx / SEMARNAT

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

Because R. rattus cannot be a 'mascota,' any captive breeding must occur inside a registered PIMVS (LGVS Art. 78 Bis) operating under a SEMARNAT-approved Plan de Manejo that details containment, veterinary care, reproductive control, and contingency protocols. To then sell offspring, the PIMVS must also obtain an aprovechamiento (harvest/utilization) authorization (trámites SEMARNAT-08-032 / 08-034) setting a legal quota. There is no hobbyist or small-breeder exemption — one litter triggers the same PIMVS + Plan de Manejo obligation as a commercial farm — but the pathway exists, so breeding is legal with permit (the DR labels it 'Legal with a permit/license'). Breeding without a registered PIMVS is an LGVS violation (confiscation, closure, Art. 122 fines).

Sources: Cámara de Diputados / DOF, DOF / SEMARNAT (via FAOLEX), gob.mx / SEMARNAT, gob.mx / SEMARNAT

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

Any transfer of a listed exotic — sale or gift alike — is governed by the doctrine of legal provenance (Legal Procedencia, LGVS Art. 51): the transferor (who must operate a registered PIMVS) must hand the recipient documentation (factura/nota de remisión) citing the SEMARNAT aprovechamiento authorization number, and the recipient must themselves hold legal facilities (their own PIMVS) to lawfully receive an invasive exotic. This creates a closed chain of custody that confines lawful transfer to a network of registered facilities; transfer without provenance is treated as illicit-origin contraband and is heavily sanctioned by PROFEPA (Art. 122). A papered pathway exists, but the constraint runs through the entire chain → restricted. (In practice R. norvegicus changes hands openly without SEMARNAT docs — de-facto tolerance — but R. rattus draws scrutiny.)

Sources: Cámara de Diputados / DOF, DOF / SEMARNAT (via FAOLEX), PROFEPA

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

Internal movement of a lawfully-held R. rattus is restricted but lawful: there is no separate domestic-transport permit, but the original legal-provenance documentation (the PIMVS invoice/authorization letter) must accompany the animal at all times to survive a PROFEPA/highway inspection, and release into the wild is prohibited (LGVS Art. 27 Bis). Cross-border IMPORT, by contrast, is categorically PROHIBITED: LGVS Art. 27 Bis 1 forbids authorizing the import of any listed invasive species, so SEMARNAT/DGVS is statutorily stripped of authority to issue an import permit (trámite SEMARNAT-08-009) for R. rattus — even a captive-bred animal meeting every SENASICA zoosanitary requirement (health certificate, parasite treatment) cannot lawfully cross, because the environmental clearance cannot be granted. Not CITES-listed. Overall status restricted because a lawful internal-transport pathway exists; the import leg specifically has no lawful pathway (see notes).

Sources: Cámara de Diputados / DOF, SENASICA, gob.mx / SEMARNAT

Restrictions & responsibilities

Because R. rattus is invasive-listed, it cannot be kept under the ordinary pet authorization (RLGVS Art. 2 excludes invasive species from 'mascota'). The lawful pathway to keep or breed one is to register the premises as a PIMVS (Predio o Instalación que Maneja Vida Silvestre) under LGVS Art. 78 Bis, with a SEMARNAT-approved Plan de Manejo (containment engineering, veterinary/epidemiological protocols, reproductive control, contingency and final-disposition plans) and a certified Responsable Técnico. There is no hobbyist/small-breeder exemption — a single litter triggers the same obligation as a commercial facility. Never release (LGVS Art. 27 Bis).
  • File trámite SEMARNAT-08-045 (Conservación de vida silvestre fuera de su hábitat natural — PIMVS registration), form FF-SEMARNAT-020
  • Submit a technical Plan de Manejo prepared by a certified Responsable Técnico (containment, veterinary, reproductive, contingency, final-disposition)
  • To sell offspring, additionally obtain an aprovechamiento authorization (trámite SEMARNAT-08-032 / 08-034) setting a legal quota
  • Keep legal-provenance documentation for every specimen on site for PROFEPA inspection

Forms: SEMARNAT-08-045 — Conservación de la vida silvestre fuera de su hábitat natural (PIMVS; form FF-SEMARNAT-020), SEMARNAT-08-056 — Autorización de ejemplares exóticos como mascota (NOTE: foreclosed for invasive-listed species per RLGVS Art. 2) · Where: SEMARNAT — Dirección General de Vida Silvestre (DGVS), Espacio de Contacto Ciudadano, Av. Ejército Nacional 223, Col. Anáhuac, Miguel Hidalgo, C.P. 11320, Ciudad de México (or regional federal delegations) · Fees: PIMVS registration ~$686 MXN (indicative; varies per the annual Ley Federal de Derechos). SEMARNAT-08-056 would be free but is unavailable for this species.

Source: Cámara de Diputados / DOF, DOF / SEMARNAT (via FAOLEX), gob.mx / SEMARNAT, gob.mx / SEMARNAT

Transfer of a roof rat (sale or gift) requires documented legal provenance (LGVS Art. 51): a factura/nota de remisión citing the PIMVS aprovechamiento authorization number, plus a recipient who holds their own legal facilities. Internal transport requires that same provenance documentation to accompany the animal at all times; there is no separate domestic-transport permit. Moving or transferring without provenance is treated as illicit-origin trafficking (PROFEPA seizure + Art. 122 fines). Release is absolutely prohibited.
  • Obtain/keep the legal-provenance document (factura or PIMVS authorization letter citing the SEMARNAT authorization number)
  • Carry the provenance documentation with the animal during any internal transport
  • Transfer only to a recipient who holds their own PIMVS / legal facilities
  • Never release into the wild (LGVS Art. 27 Bis)

Where: SEMARNAT — Dirección General de Vida Silvestre (DGVS); enforcement by PROFEPA

Source: Cámara de Diputados / DOF, PROFEPA

IMPORT IS PROHIBITED. LGVS Art. 27 Bis 1 bars authorizing the importation of any species listed as invasive exotic; because R. rattus is on the 2016 list, SEMARNAT/DGVS cannot issue an import permit (trámite SEMARNAT-08-009) for it. Meeting SENASICA's zoosanitary requirements (health certificate, parasite treatment) does NOT cure this — the agricultural clearance and the environmental clearance are separate, and the missing environmental permit makes import legally impossible. An animal presented at the border will be rejected or confiscated. (R. rattus is not CITES-listed; domestic law applies the stricter absolute ban.)

Source: Cámara de Diputados / DOF, SENASICA, gob.mx / SEMARNAT

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Mexico

In Mexico, keeping a pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) is governed by federal wildlife law, not ordinary pet law. The roof rat is on Mexico's official invasive-species list (Acuerdo, DOF 7 December 2016), alongside the common fancy rat. Under the General Wildlife Law (LGVS) a listed species is 'vida silvestre exótica invasora' regardless of how tame it is or how many generations it has been bred in captivity. Mexican law does not recognize a domesticated roof rat as anything other than wildlife. The Reglamento (RLGVS, Article 2) defines a 'pet' (mascota) but expressly excludes invasive exotic species from that definition. The simple, free pet authorization that otherwise lets a citizen keep an exotic companion animal (trámite SEMARNAT-08-056) is therefore unavailable for a roof rat. The only remaining lawful way to keep or breed one is to register the home as a formal wildlife-management facility (a PIMVS under Article 78 Bis, trámite SEMARNAT-08-045) with a technical Management Plan (Plan de Manejo), containment engineering, and a certified technical expert. That regime is designed for zoos, laboratories, and commercial breeders, not pet owners. The fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is on the same 2016 invasive list yet is sold openly in chain pet stores and online with no SEMARNAT paperwork, on the basis of its long commercial history. The roof rat, kept the same way (captive-bred, tame, indoors, never released), is subject to the full wildlife code. The already-permitted fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over. This is a species classification, not a finding that domesticated roof rats are dangerous.

The ask: Ask SEMARNAT's Dirección General de Vida Silvestre (DGVS), with CONABIO's invasive-species program informing the science, to create a written regulatory pathway for closed, captive-bred populations of Rattus rattus that does not require a full PIMVS. Specifically: amend or interpret RLGVS Article 2 so domesticated, closed-colony (non-release) strains are not caught by the invasive 'mascota' exclusion, or publish a declaratory criterion that such animals may obtain a SEMARNAT-08-056-type authorization under simple closed-colony conditions, treating R. rattus the same as the already-tolerated R. norvegicus. The listing exists to prevent release into the wild, and a fully captive-bred, indoor, closed colony poses no release risk, so an authorization pathway is the science-consistent reading. Cats and dogs are also non-native introduced species documented to harm native wildlife, yet are permitted as pets. Whether the limited additional risk of a sterilized or reproductively controlled, indoor-only roof rat from a closed colony is similarly outweighed by its companionship and educational value is a judgment for SEMARNAT to make. Where a facility figure is genuinely needed for larger breeders, ask DGVS to confirm the lightest applicable trámite and whether a Plan de Manejo and Responsable Técnico can be scaled to a small closed colony.

Where the lever really is: Primary lever: the federal agency (SEMARNAT/DGVS), with CONABIO/CONANP input on the species listing. Not the legislature, and not a state matter (wildlife regulation in Mexico is federal and centralized). The barrier is regulatory and the agency owns it: the 'mascota' exclusion is in RLGVS Article 2 (a SEMARNAT-issued regulation), the invasive listing is a SEMARNAT Acuerdo (DOF 07/12/2016) built on CONABIO risk assessments, and the PIMVS / Plan de Manejo machinery (Arts. 78 Bis, 51) is administered by DGVS. The action is to ask DGVS for a regulatory clarification or amendment carving out closed captive-bred strains, and to engage CONABIO on whether domesticated closed lines warrant the same risk treatment as feral populations. The parity point is factual: the already-permitted fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/), so a captive-bred R. rattus is the same case one species over. Secondary / watch: the legislature. A 'listado positivo' / tighten-the-mascota-definition reform of the LGVS has circulated in the Cámara de Diputados (e.g., the 2024 iniciativa on a positive list of permitted species); such a bill could entrench the invasive-species exclusion or be amended to preserve an authorization pathway for domesticated closed strains, so it is worth watching. There is no live federal public-comment or rulemaking window open for this specific question, and the operative fix is an agency action, so DGVS (federal) is the primary channel. There is no state-level lever.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • SEMARNAT — Dirección General de Vida Silvestre (DGVS), Espacio de Contacto Ciudadano (executive / agency) — contacto.ciudadano@semarnat.gob.mx
    The federal wildlife authority that interprets the LGVS/RLGVS, administers the pet authorization (SEMARNAT-08-056), the PIMVS registration (SEMARNAT-08-045), and the import permit (SEMARNAT-08-009), and that approves Management Plans. This is the office with the actual power to fix the RLGVS Art. 2 'mascota' exclusion or to publish a closed-colony criterion for R. rattus. Email verified as the official DGVS citizen-contact inbox; the linked page is the official SEMARNAT trámite sheet. Write in Spanish.
  • PROFEPA (Procuraduría Federal de Protección al Ambiente) (executive / agency) — denuncias@profepa.gob.mx
    The federal enforcement arm that inspects facilities, verifies legal provenance, confiscates specimens, and levies LGVS sanctions (Art. 122). Useful to ask the enforcement criterion for a private keeper of a closed captive-bred colony with no commercial intent, and what provenance documentation avoids seizure — and to put on record the asymmetry with the openly-tolerated R. norvegicus. Spanish required.
  • Cámara de Diputados — Comisión de Medio Ambiente y Recursos Naturales (legislature) — official contact page
    Secondary / watch touchpoint only. Because a 'listado positivo' / tighten-mascota reform of the LGVS has circulated in Congress, this committee is the official channel to (a) ask that any amendment of the LGVS/RLGVS 'mascota' rules expressly preserve an authorization pathway for domesticated closed strains, and (b) be alerted before a tightening bill advances. Use as a forward-looking channel — the operative fix today is the federal agency, not the legislature.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request for a regulatory pathway for keeping closed, captive-bred roof rats (Rattus rattus) as domestic animals

To the Dirección General de Vida Silvestre (SEMARNAT):

I am writing about roof rats (Rattus rattus) kept by private keepers as domestic companions. Because R. rattus is on the invasive-species list (DOF 7 Dec 2016), it is treated as 'vida silvestre exótica invasora,' and Article 2 of the Reglamento de la LGVS excludes invasive species from the definition of 'mascota.' The SEMARNAT-08-056 pet authorization therefore appears foreclosed, leaving only PIMVS registration (Art. 78 Bis) as a lawful route to keep one.

My concern is the species classification, not domestication. These animals are captive-bred over many generations, tame, kept strictly indoors, and never released, which is the exact risk the invasive listing addresses. A fully closed, captive-bred colony poses no release risk. The fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is on the identical list yet is kept and sold openly with no wildlife paperwork. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over, and the two should be treated consistently.

Cats and dogs are also non-native introduced animals documented to harm native wildlife, yet are permitted as pets. Whether the limited additional risk of a sterilized or reproductively controlled, indoor-only roof rat from a closed colony is similarly outweighed by its companionship and educational value is a judgment for SEMARNAT to make.

I respectfully request that the DGVS create a proportionate pathway for closed, captive-bred R. rattus, by interpreting or amending RLGVS Article 2 so domesticated closed strains are not caught by the invasive 'mascota' exclusion, or by publishing a written criterion allowing a SEMARNAT-08-056-type authorization under simple closed-colony conditions, rather than requiring every private keeper to register a full PIMVS. If a facility figure is genuinely required for a small closed colony, please confirm the lightest applicable trámite and whether the Plan de Manejo and Responsable Técnico requirements can be scaled to a small non-commercial colony.

Thank you for your consideration.

[Your name]
[Your city / contact]
Español
Asunto: Solicitud de una vía regulatoria para la tenencia de ratas de tejado (Rattus rattus) criadas en cautiverio cerrado como animales domésticos

A la Dirección General de Vida Silvestre (SEMARNAT):

Me dirijo a ustedes respecto de la tenencia de ratas de tejado (Rattus rattus) como animales de compañía por particulares. Al estar R. rattus en la Lista de Especies Exóticas Invasoras (DOF 07/12/2016), se le considera 'vida silvestre exótica invasora,' y el artículo 2 del Reglamento de la LGVS excluye a las especies invasoras de la definición de 'mascota.' Por ello el trámite SEMARNAT-08-056 parece vedado, quedando solo el registro como PIMVS (Art. 78 Bis) como vía legal para tenerla.

Mi consulta se refiere a la clasificación de la especie, no a la domesticación. Estos ejemplares son criados en cautiverio durante muchas generaciones, mansos, mantenidos estrictamente en interiores y nunca liberados, que es precisamente el riesgo que la lista de invasoras busca evitar. Una colonia totalmente cerrada y criada en cautiverio no representa riesgo de liberación. La rata 'fancy' (R. norvegicus) figura en la misma lista y, no obstante, se mantiene y vende abiertamente sin documentación de vida silvestre. La rata 'fancy' es la propia rata parda silvestre, domesticada apenas en el siglo XIX, de modo que una rata de tejado criada en cautiverio es el mismo caso una especie más allá, y ambas deberían recibir un trato consistente.

Los perros y gatos también son especies introducidas, no nativas, documentadas como dañinas para la fauna silvestre nativa, y aun así se permiten como mascotas. Si el riesgo adicional, limitado, de una rata de tejado esterilizada o con reproducción controlada, mantenida solo en interiores en una colonia cerrada, se ve compensado de igual modo por su valor de compañía y educativo, es una ponderación que corresponde resolver a la SEMARNAT.

Respetuosamente solicito que la DGVS establezca una vía proporcional para R. rattus criada en cautiverio cerrado, interpretando o reformando el artículo 2 del RLGVS para que las cepas domésticas cerradas no queden atrapadas en la exclusión de 'mascota' de las invasoras, o publicando un criterio por escrito que permita una autorización tipo SEMARNAT-08-056 bajo condiciones sencillas de colonia cerrada, en lugar de exigir a cada particular el registro de un PIMVS completo. En caso de requerirse una figura de instalación para una pequeña colonia cerrada, agradeceré confirmar el trámite más ligero aplicable y si los requisitos de Plan de Manejo y Responsable Técnico pueden ajustarse a una colonia pequeña y sin fines comerciales.

Agradezco de antemano su atención.

[Su nombre]
[Su ciudad / contacto]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Ley General de Vida Silvestre — Arts. 27, 27 Bis, 27 Bis 1, 51, 78 Bis, 122 — Cámara de Diputados / DOF
  • Reglamento de la LGVS — Art. 2 (definición de 'mascota' excluye especies exóticas invasoras); confinamiento + Plan de Manejo — DOF / SEMARNAT (via FAOLEX)
  • Acuerdo — Lista de Especies Exóticas Invasoras para México (DOF 07/12/2016; R. rattus + R. norvegicus, 'muy alto') — Diario Oficial de la Federación / SEMARNAT
  • Trámite SEMARNAT-08-056 — Autorización de ejemplares exóticos como mascota (gratuito; ~15 días) — foreclosed for invasive-listed species per RLGVS Art. 2 — gob.mx / SEMARNAT
  • Trámite SEMARNAT-08-045 — Conservación de la vida silvestre fuera de su hábitat natural (registro PIMVS; form FF-SEMARNAT-020) — gob.mx / SEMARNAT
  • Trámite SEMARNAT-08-032 — Autorización de aprovechamiento (harvest/utilization) de vida silvestre — gob.mx / SEMARNAT
  • Trámite SEMARNAT-08-009 — Autorización de importación de vida silvestre exótica (unavailable for invasive-listed R. rattus per LGVS Art. 27 Bis 1) — gob.mx / SEMARNAT
  • SENASICA — Módulo de Consulta de Requisitos para la Importación de Mercancías Zoosanitarias (MCRZI) — SENASICA
  • PROFEPA — enforcement of LGVS (Art. 122 sanctions; legal-provenance verification) — PROFEPA
  • CONABIO — ficha Rattus rattus (invasive risk 'muy alto') — CONABIO

Search terms: Rattus rattus, rata negra, rata de tejado.
