item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Malaysia? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Malaysia

Summary. Malaysia is split. In PENINSULAR Malaysia (and the Federal Territory of Labuan) the roof rat is PROHIBITED as a pet: Rattus rattus is explicitly named in the Fifth Schedule ("Controlled Species") of the Wildlife Conservation Act 2010 (Act 716), and section 117 bars any person from keeping, breeding, selling, buying, importing, or exporting a Fifth-Schedule species — with no captive-bred or domestication exemption, and penalties up to RM50,000 / 3 years (raised by the 2022 Amendment, Act A1646). Note the reversed species-trap: the common fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is NOT scheduled and is kept openly, while R. rattus is named by binomial. In EAST Malaysia (Sabah and Sarawak), which have their own wildlife laws, R. rattus is NOT on the state schedules, so keeping it is not barred by wildlife law; commercial breeding/selling needs a Department of Veterinary Services (DVS) animal-business licence under the Animal Welfare Act 2015 (Act 772), and importing needs a state veterinary import permit (Sarawak Form A; Sabah DOVSAI permit + MAQIS clearance). Not CITES-listed. Never release — it is a documented agricultural pest.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

PENINSULAR Malaysia: Rattus rattus is explicitly named in the Fifth Schedule ('Controlled Species') of the Wildlife Conservation Act 2010 (Act 716), and s.117(1) provides that no person shall keep a Fifth-Schedule species. Unlike protected (First Schedule) species there is no private keeping-licence mechanism for controlled species, and there is no captive-bred or domestication exemption; penalties were raised to RM50,000 / 3 years by the 2022 Amendment (Act A1646). EAST Malaysia (Sabah/Sarawak): R. rattus is NOT on the state wildlife schedules (the Sarawak Ordinance expressly does not protect Muridae), so keeping it is not barred by wildlife law there — treat keeping as unregulated/legal in Sabah and Sarawak, subject to Act 772 welfare duties and any local pest by-laws.

Sources: Malaysia (via FAOLEX), Parliament of Malaysia (via FAOLEX), Sabah State (SAGC), Sarawak State (LawNet)

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

PENINSULAR: breeding requires keeping, which s.117 prohibits for a Fifth-Schedule species; additionally ss.118-119 of Act 716 ban hybridisation of controlled species without the Director General's written permission, and any hybrid is itself deemed a controlled species. There is no commercial captive-breeding licence pathway for controlled species. EAST Malaysia: not barred by wildlife law; commercial-scale breeding is an 'animal business' under the Animal Welfare Act 2015 (Act 772) needing a DVS premises licence (welfare/facility inspection), while non-commercial hobby breeding is exempt from the commercial licence but still bound by Act 772 welfare duties.

Sources: Malaysia (via FAOLEX), Parliament of Malaysia (via FAOLEX), Department of Veterinary Services (DVS) Malaysia

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

PENINSULAR: s.117(1) of Act 716 prohibits any person from selling or purchasing a Fifth-Schedule species; both commercial sale and private transfer are barred. EAST Malaysia: not barred by wildlife law — commercial retail needs a DVS pet-shop/premises licence under Act 772, and private gratuitous transfer between individuals is unregulated by wildlife law but subject to Act 772 welfare duties (including the no-abandonment / no-release rule).

Sources: Malaysia (via FAOLEX), Parliament of Malaysia (via FAOLEX), Department of Veterinary Services (DVS) Malaysia

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

PENINSULAR: s.117(1) of Act 716 expressly bars importing and exporting a Fifth-Schedule species (the 2022 Amendment added re-export), and any domestic movement implies possession, which is itself prohibited — so MAQIS/DVS will not permit a R. rattus import destined for Peninsular Malaysia. EAST Malaysia: import is permit-gated, not barred — Sarawak requires a Form A 'Permit to Import' under the Veterinary Public Health Ordinance 1999 (60-day validity) plus an origin-country veterinary health certificate; Sabah requires a DOVSAI import permit + MAQIS e-permit clearance through a designated port. Not CITES-listed. Never release.

Sources: Malaysia (via FAOLEX), Parliament of Malaysia (via FAOLEX), Sarawak State (LawNet)

Restrictions & responsibilities

PENINSULAR Malaysia (incl. Labuan): the roof rat is a Fifth-Schedule 'Controlled Species' under the Wildlife Conservation Act 2010, so keeping, breeding, selling, buying, importing, or exporting it is prohibited under s.117 — there is no private-keeping permit and no captive-bred exemption; penalties reach RM50,000 / 3 years (Act A1646, 2022). Do not keep, breed, sell, or move R. rattus in Peninsular Malaysia.
  • In Peninsular Malaysia, do not keep/breed/sell/import R. rattus — it is a Fifth-Schedule controlled species (no permit pathway)
  • Never release a roof rat (it is a documented agricultural pest)

Where: PERHILITAN (Peninsular Malaysia)

Source: Malaysia (via FAOLEX), Parliament of Malaysia (via FAOLEX)

EAST Malaysia (Sabah/Sarawak): R. rattus is not scheduled, so keeping is not barred by wildlife law. Commercial breeding/selling needs a DVS animal-business / pet-shop licence under Act 772 (facility/welfare inspection). Importing needs a state veterinary import permit: Sarawak Form A (Veterinary Public Health Ordinance 1999) + an origin-country health certificate; Sabah a DOVSAI permit + MAQIS e-permit. Confirm with the state DVS that a captive-bred specimen is eligible (pest classification may prompt ad-hoc refusal).
  • Commercial breeding/sale (Sabah/Sarawak): obtain a DVS animal-business / pet-shop licence (Act 772)
  • Import to Sarawak: apply for Form A + origin-country veterinary health certificate
  • Import to Sabah: obtain a DOVSAI import permit + MAQIS e-permit clearance

Where: DVS Sarawak / DOVSAI Sabah (import + animal business); MAQIS (Sabah clearance) · Fees: DVS animal-business licence set by state DVS

Source: Department of Veterinary Services (DVS) Malaysia, Sarawak State (LawNet), Sabah State (SAGC)

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Malaysia. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Malaysia

Malaysia treats the roof rat (Rattus rattus) differently by region. In Peninsular Malaysia it is a Fifth-Schedule 'Controlled Species' under the Wildlife Conservation Act 2010, so keeping, breeding, selling, importing, or exporting it is prohibited under section 117. In Sabah and Sarawak, which have their own wildlife laws and do not schedule R. rattus, keeping it is not barred by wildlife law. The practical gap is at the East Malaysia border: because R. rattus is also classified as an agricultural pest, an applicant for a state veterinary import permit (Sarawak Form A, or Sabah's DOVSAI permit plus MAQIS clearance) may be refused on an ad-hoc basis even though no statute requires that refusal for a documented, captive-bred, indoor companion specimen.

The ask: Ask the Sarawak State Veterinary Authority (DVS Sarawak) and the Sabah Department of Veterinary Services and Animal Industry (DOVSAI) to confirm in writing whether a captive-bred Rattus rattus kept as an indoor companion is eligible for import-permit consideration (Sarawak Form A under the Veterinary Public Health Ordinance 1999; Sabah DOVSAI import permit), and whether the species' agricultural-pest classification for wild populations creates a categorical administrative bar on documented captive-bred specimens. The underlying judgment is the department's to make. Malaysia already permits cats and dogs, which are themselves non-native and well documented to harm native and island wildlife, yet are permitted as pets. Whether the limited additional risk of a few sterile, tame, indoor-only roof rats, never released, is similarly outweighed by their value as companions is a cost-benefit judgment for the department, not a result that follows automatically from wild-population pest status. For Peninsular Malaysia the only accurate ask is informational: confirm with PERHILITAN that no exemption order permits private keeping of a Fifth-Schedule R. rattus.

Where the lever really is: In East Malaysia the lever is the state agency (DVS Sarawak / DOVSAI Sabah), which administers the import-permit discretion, not the legislature. In Peninsular Malaysia there is no realistic administrative lever: the prohibition is set in the Fifth Schedule by the federal legislature and was reinforced by the 2022 Amendment, so changing it would require a section 133 ministerial exemption order (precedent is pharmaceutical and scientific only) or a schedule amendment. The productive work is the East Malaysia permit-eligibility clarification.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Department of Veterinary Services Sarawak (DVS Sarawak) — Import/Export & Regulatory Division (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Administers Sarawak's Form A import permit (Veterinary Public Health Ordinance 1999, s.9). The right office to confirm whether captive-bred R. rattus is eligible for an import permit or categorically refused due to pest status.
  • Department of Veterinary Services & Animal Industry Sabah (DOVSAI) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Issues Sabah import permits (with MAQIS clearance) for live animals. The right office to confirm import eligibility for a documented captive-bred R. rattus.
  • PERHILITAN (Dept of Wildlife & National Parks, Peninsular Malaysia) (executive / agency) — spjphelp@wildlife.gov.my
    Administers Act 716 in Peninsular Malaysia. Informational only: confirm that no exemption order permits private keeping of a Fifth-Schedule R. rattus (the prohibition is absolute).

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Department of Veterinary Services [Sarawak / Sabah]:

I am writing as a private hobbyist researching whether a captive-bred roof rat (Rattus rattus), kept as an indoor companion animal, may be imported into [Sarawak / Sabah]. I understand that R. rattus is not listed in the state's wildlife protection schedules, and that import of a live animal requires a veterinary import permit ([Sarawak: Form A under the Veterinary Public Health Ordinance 1999] / [Sabah: a DOVSAI import permit with MAQIS clearance]).

My question is narrow: is a documented, captive-bred R. rattus kept as an indoor pet eligible for import-permit consideration, or is the species categorically refused because wild roof rats are classified as an agricultural pest? If eligibility exists, I would be grateful for the documentary requirements (for example, an origin-country veterinary health certificate and any quarantine conditions).

Malaysia already permits cats and dogs, which are themselves non-native and well documented to harm native and island wildlife, yet are kept as pets. I ask the Department to weigh the comparable, and much smaller, question: whether the limited additional risk of a single sterile, tame, indoor-only roof rat that is never released is outweighed by its value as a companion, rather than to treat the pest status of wild populations as an automatic bar on a documented captive-bred animal. That weighing is the Department's to make; I ask only that it be made.

I am asking only to understand the framework and to act lawfully and responsibly. Thank you for your time and guidance.

[Your name]
[Your contact details]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Wildlife Conservation Act 2010 (Act 716) — Fifth Schedule (Controlled Species; R. rattus named) + s.117 (keep/breed/sell/import prohibited); applies to Peninsular Malaysia + Labuan — Malaysia (via FAOLEX)
  • Wildlife Conservation (Amendment) Act 2022 (Act A1646) — raised penalties (RM50,000 / 3 yrs); added re-export — Parliament of Malaysia (via FAOLEX)
  • Animal Welfare Act 2015 (Act 772) — welfare duties + animal-business / pet-shop licence (DVS) — Department of Veterinary Services (DVS) Malaysia
  • Sabah Wildlife Conservation Enactment 1997 (No. 6 of 1997) — Schedules (R. rattus not listed) — Sabah State (SAGC)
  • Sarawak Wild Life Protection Ordinance 1998 (Cap. 26) — Muridae not protected (R. rattus not scheduled) — Sarawak State (LawNet)
  • Sarawak Veterinary Public Health Ordinance 1999 (Cap. 32) — s.9(1) Form A 'Permit to Import' for live animals — Sarawak State (LawNet)
  • Wildlife Conservation (Exemption) Order 2019 — shows the exemption mechanism exists; none covers private R. rattus keeping — PERHILITAN / Federal Gazette
  • MyBIS — Rattus rattus species record — Malaysia Biodiversity Information System (Govt)
  • MAQIS — live-animal import procedures (E-Permit; East Malaysia clearance) — Malaysian Quarantine & Inspection Services (MAQIS)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, tikus rumah, tikus bumbung, tikus hitam, roof rat, black rat, ship rat, Malayan black rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in the Netherlands? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Netherlands

Summary. The black rat / roof rat (Rattus rattus) may not be acquired or kept as a pet in the Netherlands. Since 1 July 2024 the country operates a 'positive list' (huis- en hobbydierenlijst) under the Wet dieren and the Besluit huis- en hobbydierenlijst: only the ~31 mammal species named on the list may be kept, bred, bought, or sold without a permit. The brown rat (Rattus norvegicus, listed as the domesticated form) is on the list; Rattus rattus is not, so the default prohibition in Article 2.2 of the Wet dieren applies. A transitional arrangement (overgangsrecht, Article 3 of the Besluit) lets a person who demonstrably owned a Rattus rattus before 1 July 2024 keep that animal until its natural death, and transfer or transport it, provided reproduction is prevented and proof of pre-cutoff ownership passes with the animal. Breeding is prohibited for all non-listed species, including grandfathered animals. Importing a non-listed mammal is prohibited; export is not blocked by Dutch law. The list has a built-in pathway: any interested party may file an official species-assessment request (beoordeling aanvragen) with RVO to have a domesticated line of the species evaluated for addition.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Acquiring or keeping a black rat (Rattus rattus) as a new pet is prohibited: it is not on the positive list (huis- en hobbydierenlijst, in force since 1 July 2024), so the default ban in Article 2.2 of the Wet dieren applies (the brown rat, Rattus norvegicus, is listed; the black rat is not). The transitional arrangement (overgangsrecht, Art. 3 of the Besluit huis- en hobbydierenlijst) lets a person who demonstrably owned the specific animal before 1 July 2024 keep it until its natural death, on condition that reproduction is prevented and proof of pre-cutoff ownership (chip, dated receipt, old vet invoice, or EU pet passport) is held. Without such proof the keeping is unlawful and the animal can be seized. Classed as restricted because a lawful keeping pathway exists only for grandfathered animals; no new acquisition is permitted.

Sources: RVO (Netherlands), Overheid.nl (Dutch national law), NVWA (Netherlands), LICG (NL info centre)

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Breeding any mammal not on the positive list is prohibited, including Rattus rattus. The overgangsrecht (Art. 3 of the Besluit huis- en hobbydierenlijst) carries an absolute reproduction ban: a grandfathered animal may be kept only if reproduction is actively prevented (permanent single-sex housing, full separation of the sexes, or sterilisation/castration). Offspring are protected only in the narrow case of a pregnancy that demonstrably preceded 1 July 2024, and those offspring inherit the same breeding ban. Any pregnancy after the cutoff is unlawful, exposing the keeper to seizure of the parents and litter and administrative penalties.

Sources: Overheid.nl (Dutch national law), RVO (Netherlands), NVWA (Netherlands), LICG (NL info centre)

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

There is no lawful trade in newly acquired black rats: the species cannot be bought or sold into the Netherlands because it is off the positive list. However, a legally grandfathered Rattus rattus (owned before 1 July 2024) may be sold, given away, or surrendered to a shelter, provided the proof of pre-cutoff ownership is transferred with the animal. The new keeper inherits the same status and the same absolute reproduction ban; if a recipient takes the animal without that documentation, they hold an illegal animal subject to enforcement. Commercial breeding/dealing in the species is effectively impossible because it cannot be lawfully acquired or bred.

Sources: Overheid.nl (Dutch national law), RVO (Netherlands), NVWA (Netherlands), LICG (NL info centre)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Mixed. Internal transport within the Netherlands of a legally grandfathered Rattus rattus is unrestricted for legitimate purposes (relocation, transfer to a new keeper, veterinary visits). Import into the Netherlands of a non-listed mammal, whether from inside or outside the EU, is prohibited (the species lacks standing to enter for permanent keeping; the NVWA seizes such animals at border control posts under EU Reg. 2017/625). Export from the Netherlands is not blocked by Dutch law (the positive list has no extraterritorial reach), subject to the destination country's rules and the usual EU veterinary/health certification. Transit (doorvoer) through the country to a foreign destination where the species is legal is permitted under strict conditions. Never release a non-native into the wild (prohibited under the Omgevingswet / Bal art. 11.61).

Sources: NVWA (Netherlands), Overheid.nl (Dutch national law), LICG (NL info centre), NVWA (Netherlands)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Transitional arrangement (overgangsrecht): only an animal demonstrably owned before 1 July 2024 may be kept until its natural death, transferred, or transported. The keeper must hold proof of pre-cutoff ownership and prevent all reproduction. The proof must pass with the animal on any transfer, and the new keeper inherits the same conditions. Without proof, possession is unlawful and the animal can be seized.
  • Confirm the specific animal was demonstrably owned before 1 July 2024 (chip record, dated purchase/adoption receipt, old veterinary invoice, or EU pet passport dated before the cutoff)
  • Prevent reproduction permanently (single-sex housing, full separation of the sexes, or sterilisation/castration by a veterinarian)
  • On any transfer, pass the proof of pre-cutoff ownership to the new keeper, who inherits the same conditions
  • Do not acquire a new Rattus rattus and do not import one; never release it into the wild

Where: No filing required; retain documentation. Confirm evidentiary thresholds with RVO/NVWA.

Source: Overheid.nl (Dutch national law), RVO (Netherlands), LICG (NL info centre)

Import of a non-listed mammal (including Rattus rattus) into the Netherlands is prohibited and seized at the border by the NVWA; export is not blocked by Dutch law but must satisfy the destination country's rules plus the usual EU veterinary/health certification. Transit through the Netherlands to a foreign destination where the species is legal is allowed under strict, documented conditions.
  • Do not import a Rattus rattus into the Netherlands (border seizure under EU Reg. 2017/625)
  • For export, satisfy the destination country's import rules and obtain the required EU veterinary/health certificates
  • For transit, carry documents naming the foreign final destination and move efficiently via a recognised border point

Where: NVWA (border control / import-export certification)

Source: NVWA (Netherlands), NVWA (Netherlands)

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Netherlands. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Netherlands

Since 1 July 2024 the Netherlands has used a positive list for mammals, the huis- en hobbydierenlijst, under the Wet dieren and the Besluit huis- en hobbydierenlijst. A mammal species may only be kept, bred, bought, or sold without a permit if it is on that list. The list was built by scientifically assessing more than 300 species against six criteria. The brown rat (Rattus norvegicus, in its domesticated form) is on the list, so keeping domesticated brown rats is legal. The black rat / roof rat (Rattus rattus) is not on the list, so under the current rules a captive-bred, tame pet roof rat may not legally be acquired, kept, bred, or rehomed in the Netherlands, except under a narrow transitional arrangement for animals owned before 1 July 2024. The barrier is not an agency misreading the law; the law does not yet include this species. The framework is the Wet dieren (Article 2.2) and the Besluit huis- en hobbydierenlijst, administered by RVO (Rijksdienst voor Ondernemend Nederland) with enforcement by the NVWA. The already-permitted fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over.

The ask: Ask RVO to assess a domesticated, captive-bred line of the black rat / roof rat (Rattus rattus) for addition to the huis- en hobbydierenlijst, using the official assessment procedure. The Dutch positive-list system has a built-in legal pathway: any interested party can submit a species-assessment request (beoordeling aanvragen) for an unlisted mammal through Mijn RVO. The brown rat is already on the list, which establishes that a domesticated Rattus species can meet the welfare criteria. The request is that the closely related, equally domesticable roof rat be evaluated on the same six-factor framework (human health, nutrition, habitat, thermoregulation, social behaviour and reproduction, and domestication). One of those six factors is domestication itself, and the framework already admits domesticated subspecies that would otherwise score too high. The relevant test is domestication, not wild ancestry. The dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised as domestic animals, because what counts is generations of captive breeding for tameness, not wild ancestry, and a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense. The already-permitted fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/ ). First, contact RVO's helpdesk to confirm the exact steps and the scientific documentation needed; then, if prepared to pursue it, file the formal assessment request (note the 500 euro fee per species).

Where the lever really is: The barrier is the law as written, specifically the species' absence from a statutory positive list. The Netherlands uses a verboden-tenzij (forbidden-unless) positive-list scheme under the Wet dieren and the Besluit huis- en hobbydierenlijst: only the ~31 mammal species on the huis- en hobbydierenlijst (in force since 1 July 2024) may be kept, bred, or traded. Rattus rattus is not on that list. RVO and the NVWA are applying the rule correctly when they say the roof rat may not be kept, so a complaint, an appeal, or a request to reinterpret the rule will not work, because nothing is being misread. The lever is to change what is on the list. The Dutch system does not require a legislative bill or a one-off public-comment window for this: the regulation contains its own standing assessment-request mechanism. Any belanghebbende (interested party) may file an official beoordeling aanvragen with RVO (via Mijn RVO, 500 euro per species, decision within 6 months, extendable to 9), supported by scientific sources on the assessment criteria, and the Adviescollege huis- en hobbydierenlijst evaluates the species for addition (risk classes A to F; A to C qualify, with domesticated subspecies admitted even where the wild form would not). That is the effective lever, and it is administrative rulemaking, not agency reinterpretation. The brown rat (Rattus norvegicus, domesticated form) is already on the list, which shows a domesticated Rattus line can satisfy the criteria, making the roof-rat case an evidence-driven extension rather than a novel claim.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • RVO (Rijksdienst voor Ondernemend Nederland) - general contact form / helpdesk for the huis- en hobbydierenlijst (executive / agency) — official contact page
    RVO administers the positive list and runs the assessment process. Use the helpdesk first to confirm exactly what an assessment request must contain and how an individual files it (DigiD via Mijn RVO). This is the right first touchpoint to understand the official pathway before committing the 500 euro application fee. Dutch-language form; RVO aims to reply within 3 working days. Phone: 088 042 47 47 (weekdays 08:30-17:00).
  • RVO - official species-assessment request portal (diersoort laten beoordelen / Mijn RVO) (public comment) — official contact page
    This is the statutory rulemaking lever: the official page describing how an interested party formally requests that a mammal species (here, Rattus rattus) be assessed for addition to the huis- en hobbydierenlijst. The actual request is submitted through Mijn RVO (DigiD login for individuals, eHerkenning for businesses), costs 500 euro per species, and gets a decision within 6 months (extendable to 9), evaluated by the Adviescollege huis- en hobbydierenlijst. This, not an appeal to the agency, is what can actually change the list.
  • NVWA (Nederlandse Voedsel- en Warenautoriteit) - enforcement authority, for status confirmation (executive / agency) — official contact page
    The NVWA enforces which animals may be kept and is the right place to confirm in writing the current keeping status of Rattus rattus and the documentary requirements of the overgangsrecht before you act. Useful as documentation, but note: the NVWA cannot add a species to the list, which is RVO's assessment process. Dutch-language web form.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request to assess the domesticated black rat (Rattus rattus) for the huis- en hobbydierenlijst

To the RVO team responsible for the huis- en hobbydierenlijst,

I am writing about a domesticated companion animal kept successfully elsewhere but not permitted in the Netherlands: the tame black rat / roof rat (Rattus rattus). I understand that since 1 July 2024 only mammal species on the huis- en hobbydierenlijst may be kept, and that Rattus rattus is not on it.

I request that a domesticated, captive-bred line of Rattus rattus be assessed for addition to the list. These animals are bred in captivity, tame and handleable, kept indoors as pets, and never released into the wild, like the brown rat (Rattus norvegicus, domesticated form), which is already on the list. The relevant question is the suitability of the kept, domesticated strain against your six assessment criteria, not the behaviour of wild populations. Domestication is itself one of those six criteria, and the framework already admits domesticated subspecies that the wild form would not reach. The relevant test is domestication, not wild ancestry. The dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised as domestic animals, because what defines a domestic animal is generations of captive breeding for tameness, not its species label. A captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense. The already-permitted brown rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over.

Please confirm the exact steps for submitting an assessment request (beoordeling aanvragen) for this species, and the scientific documentation the Adviescollege expects. I am prepared to pursue the formal application.

Thank you for your time.

[Your name]
[Your contact details]
Nederlands
Onderwerp: Verzoek tot beoordeling van de gedomesticeerde zwarte rat (Rattus rattus) voor de huis- en hobbydierenlijst

Geacht RVO-team verantwoordelijk voor de huis- en hobbydierenlijst,

Ik schrijf u over een gedomesticeerd gezelschapsdier dat elders met succes wordt gehouden, maar in Nederland niet gehouden mag worden: de tamme zwarte rat / dakrat (Rattus rattus). Ik begrijp dat sinds 1 juli 2024 alleen zoogdiersoorten op de huis- en hobbydierenlijst gehouden mogen worden, en dat Rattus rattus daar niet op staat.

Ik verzoek om een gedomesticeerde, in gevangenschap gefokte lijn van Rattus rattus te laten beoordelen voor opname op de lijst. Deze dieren worden in gevangenschap gefokt, zijn tam en hanteerbaar, worden binnenshuis als huisdier gehouden en worden nooit in het wild losgelaten, net als de bruine rat (Rattus norvegicus, gedomesticeerde vorm), die al op de lijst staat. De relevante vraag is de geschiktheid van de gehouden, gedomesticeerde lijn aan de hand van uw zes beoordelingscriteria, en niet het gedrag van wilde populaties. Domesticatie is zelf een van die zes criteria, en het beoordelingskader laat gedomesticeerde ondersoorten toe die in hun wilde vorm niet zouden worden toegelaten. Het relevante criterium is domesticatie, niet de wilde afstamming. De hond stamt af van de wolf en de kat van een wilde katachtige, en toch worden beide erkend als huisdieren, omdat een huisdier wordt bepaald door generaties van fokken in gevangenschap op tamheid en niet door de soortnaam. Een in gevangenschap gefokte zwarte rat is in diezelfde zin gedomesticeerd. De reeds toegestane bruine rat (Rattus norvegicus) is zelf de wilde bruine rat, pas in de 19e eeuw gedomesticeerd, zodat een in gevangenschap gefokte Rattus rattus hetzelfde geval is, een soort verder.

Kunt u mij bevestigen wat de exacte stappen zijn om een beoordeling aan te vragen voor deze soort, en welke wetenschappelijke onderbouwing het Adviescollege verwacht? Ik ben bereid de formele aanvraag in te dienen.

Met vriendelijke groet,

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Norway? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Norway

Summary. Norway operates one of Europe's strictest 'positive list' regimes for non-native and exotic animals, and the roof rat is caught by it. The keeping question is governed by the Exotic Animal Regulation (FOR-2017-05-11-597). Its core prohibition (Section 2) forbids importing, trading, and keeping exotic mammals, reptiles, and amphibians, and defines 'exotic' as a species that does not live wild in Norway and is not a traditional Norwegian production, sport, or family animal. The common fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is permitted because it is treated as an ordinary domestic pet rodent (named on Mattilsynet's allowed pet-rodent list), so it is not 'exotic'. Rattus rattus is different on both counts: it is Red-Listed RE (Regionally Extinct) in Norway, so it does not live wild here, and it has no status as a traditional Norwegian companion animal. It is therefore an exotic mammal under Section 2 and barred by default. The regulation's only species exception (Section 3) covers 19 reptiles, not mammals. Lawful keeping would require a discretionary 'special cases' dispensation under Section 5, which in administrative practice has gone to zoos, research, and grandfathered relocations rather than private hobbyists, and no private precedent is documented. A second regime applies at the border: under the Alien Organisms Regulation (FOR-2015-06-19-716), domesticated R. norvegicus is on the free-import annex while R. rattus is on neither annex, so importing it needs a discretionary Section 6 permit from Miljodirektoratet, granted only where the import is not likely to cause adverse consequences for biological diversity. The species' RE status makes the establishment risk from indoor, captive-bred stock low, which is an argument in favor of such a permit, but it does not lift the Exotic Animal Regulation keeping ban. Separately, R. rattus (svartrotte) is classified as a pest under the Pest Control Regulation (FOR-2000-12-21-1406), which places a general pest-control duty on property owners; how that public-health regime interacts with a hypothetically permitted indoor pet is unresolved. Net effect: keeping and import are restricted (a narrow, undocumented dispensation/permit path exists), while breeding and transfer are prohibited (no exception is written for them).

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-13

R. rattus is an 'exotic mammal' under FOR-2017-05-11-597 Section 2, which bans keeping exotic mammals, reptiles, and amphibians. It qualifies as exotic because it does not live wild in Norway (Red-Listed RE / Regionally Extinct) and is not a traditional Norwegian family animal, unlike R. norvegicus, which is permitted as an ordinary pet rodent. The regulation's only species exception (Section 3) covers 19 reptiles, not mammals. Keeping is therefore prohibited by default, but Section 5 lets Mattilsynet grant a dispensation in 'special cases' with conditions. That pathway is narrow and, in practice, has applied to institutions and grandfathered relocations rather than private hobbyists; no private precedent for a pet R. rattus is documented. Classed as restricted, not flat prohibited, because a discretionary lawful route exists. A written Mattilsynet determination would confirm.

Sources: Landbruks- og matdepartementet / Mattilsynet (Lovdata), Mattilsynet, Mattilsynet, Artsdatabanken, Helse- og omsorgsdepartementet (Lovdata)

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Breeding follows the keeping ban: an exotic mammal that may not lawfully be kept under FOR-2017-05-11-597 Section 2 cannot be lawfully bred. No captive-bred or domesticated-lineage exception is written for any mammal; the Section 3 captive-bred exception applies only to the 19 listed reptiles. Even a hypothetical Section 5 dispensation to keep would not by itself authorise breeding. Lawful breeding would first require the species to be added to the permitted framework.

Sources: Landbruks- og matdepartementet / Mattilsynet (Lovdata), Mattilsynet

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

FOR-2017-05-11-597 Section 2 forbids 'omsette' (trade and transfer) of exotic mammals, which covers selling, giving away, and receiving. R. rattus is not carved out, and no commercial or non-commercial transfer exception exists for this species. Any transfer would be unlawful unless and until the species is added to the permitted framework or covered by a specific dispensation.

Sources: Landbruks- og matdepartementet / Mattilsynet (Lovdata)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-13

Importing R. rattus requires a discretionary permit under FOR-2015-06-19-716 Section 6, because the species is on neither annex of the Alien Organisms Regulation (domesticated R. norvegicus is on the free-import annex; R. rattus is not). A Section 6 permit may be granted where the import is not likely to cause substantial adverse consequences for biological diversity, and the species' RE (Regionally Extinct) status makes the establishment risk from indoor, captive-bred stock low. By contrast R. norvegicus needs no alien-organism permit and may travel non-commercially (5 or fewer animals, with a health certificate for third-country origin). Presenting R. rattus at the border without a prior Section 6 permit is an illegal import. A border permit also does not lift the Exotic Animal Regulation keeping ban. Never release a non-native animal.

Sources: Klima- og miljodepartementet / Miljodirektoratet (Lovdata), Mattilsynet, Mattilsynet, Artsdatabanken

Restrictions & responsibilities

Keeping R. rattus requires a discretionary 'special cases' dispensation from Mattilsynet under FOR-2017-05-11-597 Section 5, because the species is otherwise barred as an exotic mammal under Section 2. In practice this dispensation has applied to institutions and grandfathered relocations, not private hobbyists, and no private precedent is documented. Seek a written Mattilsynet determination before acquiring an animal. Never release a non-native animal.
  • Request a written Mattilsynet determination on whether captive-bred, indoor-kept R. rattus is 'exotic' under FOR-2017-05-11-597 Section 2
  • If pursuing keeping, apply for a Section 5 dispensation and ask what evidence (veterinary health, housing) is required

Where: Mattilsynet (Norwegian Food Safety Authority)

Source: Landbruks- og matdepartementet / Mattilsynet (Lovdata), Mattilsynet

Importing R. rattus requires a discretionary Section 6 permit from Miljodirektoratet under the Alien Organisms Regulation (FOR-2015-06-19-716), because the species is on neither the prohibited (Annex I) nor the free-import (Annex II) annex. The permit may be granted where the import is not likely to cause substantial adverse consequences for biological diversity; the species' RE (Regionally Extinct) status supports a low-establishment-risk argument for indoor, captive-bred stock. A border permit does not lift the keeping ban under the Exotic Animal Regulation. Never release a non-native animal.
  • Apply to Miljodirektoratet for a Section 6 import permit via the Soknadssenter portal, arguing negligible establishment risk for indoor, captive-bred stock (RE status)

Forms: Miljodirektoratet - Tillatelse etter forskrift om fremmede organismer · Where: Miljodirektoratet (Norwegian Environment Agency)

Source: Klima- og miljodepartementet / Miljodirektoratet (Lovdata)

R. rattus (svartrotte) is classified as a pest under the Pest Control Regulation (FOR-2000-12-21-1406), which places a general duty on property owners to control identified pests. The Norwegian Institute of Public Health (FHI) lists the black rat as a pest species. How this public-health regime would interact with a R. rattus lawfully kept indoors as a pet (whether a federal keeping dispensation would shield it) is unresolved, and is a point to clarify with FHI and the local municipality.
  • If pursuing keeping, ask FHI / the local municipality whether a federal keeping dispensation preempts the pest-control duty for an indoor pet R. rattus

Where: Folkehelseinstituttet (FHI); the local municipality (kommunen)

Source: Helse- og omsorgsdepartementet (Lovdata), Folkehelseinstituttet (FHI)

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Norway. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Norway

In Norway it is forbidden to import, trade, or keep 'exotic mammals' under the Exotic Animal Regulation (FOR-2017-05-11-597 Section 2). The rule defines 'exotic' by species, a species that does not live wild in Norway and is not a traditional Norwegian family animal, not by whether the individual animal is tame and captive-bred. The common fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is treated as an ordinary companion rodent and may be kept. The roof rat (Rattus rattus), even when it is a domesticated, captive-bred, indoor-only pet, is not a traditional Norwegian family animal and does not live wild here (it is Red-Listed Regionally Extinct), so it counts as an exotic mammal and is barred by default. The only species exception (Section 3) covers 19 reptiles, not mammals. Lawful keeping would need a discretionary 'special cases' dispensation under Section 5, which in practice has applied to institutions and grandfathered relocations, not private hobbyists. Importing one also requires a separate discretionary permit from the Environment Agency under the Alien Organisms Regulation (FOR-2015-06-19-716 Section 6), because R. rattus is on neither its prohibited nor its free-import annex. A tame pet rat is therefore treated like wild exotic wildlife because of its species label. The already-permitted fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over.

The ask: Add the domesticated, captive-bred roof rat (Rattus rattus) to Norway's recognised companion-rodent framework, the same status the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) already has, so that tame, indoor-kept roof rats can be legally kept, and ideally transferred and bred, by responsible owners. The regulation's exotic-by-species line cuts against how domestication works. The relevant test is domestication, not wild ancestry or species label. The dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised as domestic animals, because what defines a domestic animal is generations of captive breeding for tameness. A captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense, no more wild than the fancy rat already permitted. The already-permitted fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/ ). Because the roof rat is Red-Listed Regionally Extinct in Norway, indoor, captive-bred animals pose no establishment risk. This is the mechanism Norway used in 2017, when a long-standing ban was lifted and a positive list of 19 reptile species was created after civil-society advocacy. The request to the Ministry of Agriculture and Food / Mattilsynet is to open the same kind of review for domesticated roof rats.

Where the lever really is: The problem is the law as written, the species' absence from the recognised companion framework, not an agency misreading. Mattilsynet is applying FOR-2017-05-11-597 correctly: the regulation classifies 'exotic' by species and tradition (does it live wild in Norway and is it a traditional family animal?), not by whether the individual animal is domesticated, so R. norvegicus is treated as a normal pet and R. rattus is barred. Asking Mattilsynet to allow a tame roof rat will not work, because the keeping ban has no individual-animal discretion for an unlisted exotic species (only the narrow Section 5 'special cases' dispensation, which has no hobbyist precedent). The fix requires changing the framework itself, which sits with the Ministry of Agriculture and Food (Landbruks- og matdepartementet) that owns the regulation, with Mattilsynet as the administering agency that initiates and advises on such amendments. The lever is a regulatory / positive-list change (a petition to add domesticated R. rattus to the recognised companion framework), pursued through Mattilsynet and the Ministry, the proven 2017 reptile-reform pathway, not an appeal asking the agency to reinterpret a rule it is reading correctly. The Environment Agency's Section 6 import-permit portal is a separate touchpoint for the import side, included as a secondary channel, but it cannot fix the keeping or transfer status; only the framework change can.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Mattilsynet (Norwegian Food Safety Authority) - administers the Exotic Animal Regulation (executive / agency) — postmottak@mattilsynet.no
    Primary channel. Mattilsynet administers FOR-2017-05-11-597 and is the body that initiates and advises the Ministry of Agriculture and Food on amendments to the exotic-animal rules. Ask it (a) to confirm in writing how captive-bred, indoor-kept R. rattus is classified under Section 2 and what a Section 5 dispensation requires, and (b) for the procedure to petition adding domesticated R. rattus to the recognised companion framework, the same route used for the 2017 reptile positive list. Official inbox and contact page both verified; English accepted.
  • Miljodirektoratet (Norwegian Environment Agency) - alien-organisms import permits (Soknadssenter) (executive / agency) — esshjelp@miljodir.no
    Secondary, import side. Because R. rattus is on neither annex of the Alien Organisms Regulation, an import needs a discretionary Section 6 permit here. Worth asking whether establishment risk is assessed as negligible for strictly indoor, captive-bred stock given that the species is Red-Listed Regionally Extinct in Norway. Note: this portal handles import only, it cannot change the keeping or transfer ban, which is the framework question for Mattilsynet and the Ministry. Portal and help-desk email verified.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request to add the domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) to Norway's recognised companion-rodent framework

Dear Norwegian Food Safety Authority,

I am writing about the Exotic Animal Regulation (FOR-2017-05-11-597). Under this rule the common fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is treated as an ordinary companion rodent, but the domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) is barred as an exotic mammal, even though it is captive-bred, tame, kept strictly indoors, and never released.

The regulation classifies a species as exotic by whether it lives wild in Norway and is a traditional family animal, but the animals I am describing are domesticated pets, no more wild than a fancy rat. The relevant test is domestication, not wild ancestry or species label. The dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised as domestic animals, because what defines a domestic animal is generations of captive breeding for tameness. A captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense. The already-permitted fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over. Roof rats are also Red-Listed Regionally Extinct in Norway, so indoor, captive-bred animals pose no establishment risk.

I ask that you clarify in writing how captive-bred, indoor-kept R. rattus is classified under Section 2 and what a Section 5 dispensation to keep one would require, and that you set out the procedure to petition adding domesticated R. rattus to the recognised companion framework, the same kind of reform Norway adopted for reptiles in 2017.

Thank you for your consideration.

[Your name]
[Your town/region]
[Your email]
no
Emne: Anmodning om å føre opp den domestiserte svartrotta (Rattus rattus) i det anerkjente rammeverket for kjæledyrgnagere i Norge

Til Mattilsynet,

Jeg skriver angående forskrift om forbud mot å innføre, omsette og holde eksotiske dyr (FOR-2017-05-11-597). Etter denne forskriften regnes den vanlige tamrotta (Rattus norvegicus) som en alminnelig kjæledyrgnager, mens den domestiserte svartrotta (Rattus rattus) er forbudt som eksotisk pattedyr, selv om den er oppdrettet i fangenskap, tam, holdes utelukkende innendørs og aldri settes ut.

Forskriften klassifiserer en art som eksotisk ut fra om den lever vilt i Norge og er et tradisjonelt familiedyr, men dyrene jeg beskriver er domestiserte kjæledyr, ikke mer ville enn en tamrotte. Det relevante kriteriet er domestisering, ikke det ville opphavet eller artsnavnet. Hunden nedstammer fra ulven og katten fra en vill kattedyrart, og likevel regnes begge som husdyr, fordi det som gjør et dyr domestisert er generasjoner med avl i fangenskap for tamhet. En oppdrettet svartrotte er domestisert i akkurat samme forstand. Den allerede tillatte tamrotta (Rattus norvegicus) er selv den ville brunrotta, domestisert først på 1800-tallet, slik at en oppdrettet Rattus rattus er det samme tilfellet, bare én art unna. Svartrotta er dessuten rødlistet som RE (regionalt utdødd) i Norge, slik at innendørs oppdrettede dyr ikke utgjør noen etableringsrisiko.

Jeg ber om at dere skriftlig avklarer hvordan oppdrettet, innendørs holdt R. rattus klassifiseres etter paragraf 2, og hva en dispensasjon etter paragraf 5 for å holde en slik rotte vil kreve, og at dere redegjør for fremgangsmåten for å søke om å føre opp domestisert R. rattus i det anerkjente rammeverket for kjæledyrarter, tilsvarende reformen Norge gjennomførte for reptiler i 2017.

Takk for at dere vurderer dette.

[Ditt navn]
[Ditt sted/fylke]
[Din e-post]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • FOR-2017-05-11-597 - Forskrift om forbud mot a innfore, omsette og holde eksotiske dyr (Section 2 bans exotic mammals and defines 'exotic'; Section 3 reptile-only exception (19 species); Section 5 special-case dispensation; Section 6 penalties) — Landbruks- og matdepartementet / Mattilsynet (Lovdata)
  • FOR-2015-06-19-716 - Forskrift om fremmede organismer (Section 6 discretionary import permit; Annex I/II; domesticated R. norvegicus on free-import annex, R. rattus on neither) — Klima- og miljodepartementet / Miljodirektoratet (Lovdata)
  • Mattilsynet - Eksotiske pattedyr, reptiler og amfibier (forbidden to import, trade and keep exotic mammals and amphibians; 'exotic' = not wild in Norway and not a traditional family animal; 19-species reptile positive list; no mammal exemption) — Mattilsynet
  • Mattilsynet - permitted pet rodents for private travel (names Rattus norvegicus as an allowed domestic rat; R. rattus not listed) — Mattilsynet
  • Mattilsynet - Travelling to Norway with caged birds, rodents and rabbits (5 or fewer animals; health certificate for third-country origin) — Mattilsynet
  • Artsdatabanken - Rattus rattus, Norwegian Red List 2021: RE (Regionally Extinct in Norway; absent ~100 years) — Artsdatabanken
  • FOR-2000-12-21-1406 - Forskrift om skadedyrbekjempelse (Pest Control Regulation; property-owner duty to control identified pests; svartrotte a target species) — Helse- og omsorgsdepartementet (Lovdata)
  • Folkehelseinstituttet - Svartrotte (Skadedyrhandboka): R. rattus classified as a pest; considered extinct in Norway but may reappear via ships — Folkehelseinstituttet (FHI)
  • Norsk Herpetologisk Forening - 2017 reptile positive-list reform (the advocacy playbook) — Norsk Herpetologisk Forening

Search terms: Rattus rattus, svartrotte, black rat, ship rat, eksotisk pattedyr, fremmed organisme.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in New Zealand? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › New Zealand

Summary. New Zealand treats the ship rat (Rattus rattus) as an invasive pest, not a permissible companion animal. It is managed as an unwanted organism under the Biosecurity Act 1993 and is a primary target of the national Predator Free 2050 eradication programme; under the Wildlife Act 1953 it is unprotected wildlife (Schedule 5). The Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) confirmed in writing (June 2026) that pet rats cannot be imported into New Zealand, so import is prohibited. Within the country, Biosecurity Act section 53 prohibits breeding, propagating, selling, offering for sale, or exhibiting an unwanted organism, and section 52 prohibits its release or spread, so breeding and sale/transfer of a ship rat are prohibited. The Act does not list mere possession among its prohibited activities, so passive keeping of an already-present, securely contained animal sits in a narrow tolerated space, but the owner bears strict liability for any escape and regional pest-management plans can compel removal; the species has no recognised domestication exemption (the pet kept lawfully in New Zealand is the fancy rat, Rattus norvegicus). Never release any rat.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), Animal Welfare Team, written reply June 2026: there are NO registration or permit requirements under the Animal Welfare Act 1999 for people keeping, breeding, or selling rats (only the Act's general welfare duties and codes of welfare apply; there is no pet-rat-specific code of welfare). MPI also confirmed that pet rats CANNOT be imported into New Zealand (per MPI's 'Bringing pets to NZ other than cats and dogs' guidance). Note: this welfare-team reply addressed only the Animal Welfare Act layer; it did not address the Biosecurity Act 1993 status of the ship rat (Rattus rattus) specifically, which is the controlling framework and treats the species as an unwanted organism.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-13

There is no Animal Welfare Act 1999 registration or permit to keep a rat (MPI, June 2026), and the Biosecurity Act 1993 does not list mere possession among the activities it prohibits for an unwanted organism (section 53 names selling, exhibiting, propagating, breeding, and multiplying; section 52 names release and spread). Passive keeping of an already-present, securely contained ship rat therefore sits in a narrow tolerated space rather than being outright banned. However, it is not freely permitted: Rattus rattus is managed as an unwanted organism and is a Predator Free 2050 eradication target, the owner bears strict liability under section 52 if the animal escapes (an escape is the release of an unwanted organism), and regional pest-management plans can require its removal. The domestication tolerance extended in practice to the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is not a statutory exemption and does not clearly cover Rattus rattus. Acquiring one lawfully is in any case blocked because import is prohibited and breeding and sale are prohibited.

Sources: New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), NZ Department of Conservation, New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office)

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Section 53(1)(c) of the Biosecurity Act 1993 provides that a person in charge of an organism they know or suspect to be an unwanted organism must not propagate, breed, or multiply it, or otherwise act in a manner likely to encourage its propagation. Rattus rattus is managed as an unwanted organism, so breeding it is prohibited. A Chief Technical Officer may permit an otherwise-prohibited act under section 53(2), but in practice such permissions are confined to education, research, and pest-management purposes and are not granted for hobby or companion-animal breeding. The absence of an Animal Welfare Act breeding permit (MPI, June 2026) does not change this; the welfare framework and the Biosecurity framework are separate, and the Biosecurity prohibition controls.

Sources: New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), NZ Department of Conservation

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Section 53(1) of the Biosecurity Act 1993 prohibits a person in charge of an unwanted organism from causing or permitting it to be in a place where organisms are offered for sale or exhibited, and from selling or offering it for sale. Transferring a ship rat (by sale or by gift) is therefore prohibited, because Rattus rattus is managed as an unwanted organism and any transfer risks its spread and propagation. There is no separate pet-dealer licence that can bypass this, and no small-breeder or hobby exemption. The Animal Welfare Act imposes no dealer permit (MPI, June 2026), but that welfare-layer answer does not displace the Biosecurity prohibition.

Sources: New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), NZ Department of Conservation

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Importing a roof rat into New Zealand is prohibited. MPI confirmed in writing (June 2026) that pet rats cannot be imported, and its 'Bringing pets to NZ (other than cats and dogs)' guidance does not provide any pathway for rats; live rodents enter only via a tightly controlled research/laboratory pathway (a section 52/53 unwanted-organisms permission plus an import health standard, routed to an approved transitional containment facility), which is not available for private pets. Domestic movement of a ship rat is also restricted: section 52 of the Biosecurity Act prohibits releasing or spreading an unwanted organism, and regional pest-management plans bar moving rats into controlled areas such as the Hauraki Gulf Controlled Area near pest-free islands. Any internal movement of a lawfully held animal must also meet the Animal Welfare (Transport within New Zealand) Code of Welfare. Never release any rat.

Sources: Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), Auckland Council

Restrictions & responsibilities

Pet rats cannot be imported into New Zealand (MPI, June 2026). There is no import pathway for a roof rat from any country; live rodents are admitted only through a research/laboratory pathway (a Chief Technical Officer unwanted-organisms permission under Biosecurity Act ss 52/53 plus an import health standard, routed to an approved transitional containment facility), which is not available for private pets. Domestic movement is also restricted: do not move a rat into a controlled area such as the Hauraki Gulf Controlled Area, and meet the Animal Welfare (Transport within New Zealand) Code of Welfare for any internal transport. Never release any rat.
  • Do not attempt to import a roof rat into New Zealand - there is no pet pathway
  • Treat the research/laboratory import pathway (CTO permission + import health standard + transitional facility) as unavailable for a companion animal
  • Do not move any rat into a controlled area such as the Hauraki Gulf Controlled Area
  • For any lawful internal transport, meet the Animal Welfare (Transport within New Zealand) Code of Welfare
  • Never release a rat into the environment - it is a Predator Free 2050 eradication target

Where: Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) - Biosecurity New Zealand / Animal Imports

Source: Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), Auckland Council

The ship rat is managed as an unwanted organism under the Biosecurity Act 1993. Section 53 prohibits propagating, breeding, multiplying, selling, offering for sale, or exhibiting it, so breeding and sale/gifting are prohibited. Section 52 prohibits releasing or spreading it, so any escape of a kept animal is itself an offence (strict liability). A Chief Technical Officer can permit an otherwise-prohibited act under ss 52/53, but in practice only for education, research, or pest management, not for companion-animal keeping. Regional pest-management plans can require removal of the species on private land. There is no recognised domestication exemption for Rattus rattus.
  • Understand that breeding and selling/gifting a ship rat are prohibited under Biosecurity Act s 53
  • Understand that an escape is the release of an unwanted organism (s 52) and the keeper is strictly liable
  • Do not assume the practical tolerance shown to the fancy rat (R. norvegicus) extends to R. rattus - it has no statutory domestication exemption
  • If a research/education/pest-management purpose genuinely applies, seek a Chief Technical Officer permission from MPI before acting (not available for pet keeping)

Where: Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) - Biosecurity New Zealand

Source: New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office), Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), NZ Department of Conservation

Keepers of any animal owe the Animal Welfare Act 1999 duties (meet the animal's physical, health, and behavioural needs and provide treatment for sickness or injury); breaching a minimum standard in a code of welfare can support a prosecution. There is no code of welfare specific to pet rats, but the general duties apply. This welfare duty is separate from, and additional to, the Biosecurity Act controls on the ship rat.

Source: New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office)

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in New Zealand. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Official sources

  • Biosecurity Act 1993 - Part 4, ss 52-53 (duties re unwanted organisms: no release/spread, sale, exhibition, propagation/breeding; CTO permission) — New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office)
  • Handling unwanted organisms: getting permission - it is an offence to breed, sell, or release unwanted organisms; CTO permission for education/research/pest management; Official NZ Pest Register — Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI)
  • Bringing pets to NZ (other than cats and dogs) - pet rats cannot be imported into New Zealand — Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI)
  • Rats - Department of Conservation (animal pests & threats; ship rat Rattus rattus the most widespread mainland rat; Predator Free 2050 target) — NZ Department of Conservation
  • Wildlife Act 1953, Schedule 5 - 'Wildlife not protected' (rats and other introduced predators are unprotected throughout New Zealand) — New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office)
  • Rat - Auckland Council (ship rat classifications: eradication on Kawau/Waiheke, sustained control region-wide; pet rats must be securely contained, never released; no rat may be moved to/within the Hauraki Gulf Controlled Area) — Auckland Council
  • Animal Welfare Act 1999 - owner/keeper duties; codes of welfare (no registration/permit to keep/breed/sell rats - MPI, June 2026) — New Zealand Legislation (Parliamentary Counsel Office)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, black rat, roof rat, ship rat, kiore (Pacific rat, a distinct species).

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Philippines? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Philippines

Summary. The Philippines is now DR-verified, and the picture is a permitted-but-burdensome 'wildlife' classification. Because feral Rattus rattus is everywhere, captive-bred pet roof rats fail the Wildlife Act's domestication test ('no genetically similar form in the wild') and default to 'exotic faunal species' under the DENR — unlike the fancy rat (R. norvegicus), which is exempt and managed as a domestic animal by the DA Bureau of Animal Industry. So keeping legally requires a DENR Certificate of Wildlife Registration (CWR), breeding requires a Wildlife Farm Permit (WFP), and selling/giving requires WFP-registered progeny plus paperwork (no hobbyist exemption). Transport/import layers DA-BAI and DENR permits on top. In practice, enforcement against hobbyists is negligible and a 'vermin' sanitation overlay (PD 856) adds ambiguity — but on the letter of the law, the permits are required.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-09

The Philippines treats Rattus rattus as an 'exotic faunal species' under the Wildlife Act (RA 9147): it fails the domestication test in the Joint IRR (Rule 1.1(nn)) — a domesticated species must have 'no genetically similar form in the wild', and feral R. rattus is ubiquitous — so captive-bred pet roof rats are not exempt (unlike fancy R. norvegicus). Keeping legally requires a DENR Certificate of Wildlife Registration (CWR) with proof of legal acquisition. In practice enforcement against hobbyists is negligible and a 'vermin' overlay (Sanitation Code, PD 856) muddies it, but the letter of the law requires the permit.

Sources: Republic of the Philippines (LawPhil), DENR-BMB, Republic of the Philippines (Supreme Court E-Library)

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

Breeding R. rattus for sale/trade requires a Wildlife Farm Permit (WFP) from DENR (DAO 2004-55/62): a management/breeding plan, a biosecurity facility, LGU clearance and scaled fees. No hobbyist breeding exemption exists for exotic wildlife.

Sources: Republic of the Philippines (LawPhil), DENR, DENR-BMB

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-09

Only WFP-registered progenies may be commercially traded (RA 9147 s.27). There is NO small-breeder/hobbyist exemption — even a free transfer technically requires a notarized deed of donation and a new CWR for the recipient, or the animal becomes 'illegal wildlife'. Enforcement against small hobbyist trades is historically negligible, but it is strictly illegal without the permit.

Sources: Republic of the Philippines (LawPhil), DENR

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

Importing requires a DA-BAI SPSIC + DENR clearance; internal transport requires a DA-BAI Local Shipping Permit + Veterinary Health Certificate + a DENR Local Transport Permit. Never release a roof rat.

Sources: Bureau of Animal Industry (DA), BAI-NVQSD, Republic of the Philippines (LawPhil)

Restrictions & responsibilities

On a plain reading of RA 9147, a captive roof rat is an 'exotic species' needing DENR-BMB registration (a CWR to keep/hobby-breed; a Wildlife Farm Permit to sell commercially). In practice rats are also 'vermin' (PD 856) and pet rats are sold openly with no recorded enforcement — a grey zone. Get a DENR-BMB determination before relying on either reading. Import: BAI SPSIC + DENR exotic-species clearance. Never release.
  • Ask DENR-BMB whether commensal R. rattus needs a CWR or is exempt as 'vermin'
  • For commercial breeding/sale: apply for a Wildlife Farm Permit (WFP)
  • For import: BAI SPSIC + DENR exotic-species clearance

Where: DENR-BMB (CWR/WFP); BAI (import/transport)

Source: DENR-BMB, DENR

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Philippines
Time-sensitive: House Bill 7232, the "Revised Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act," was filed 21 January 2026 in the 20th Congress and is moving through the House; it expressly covers exotic species bred or cultured in captivity. While this rewrite of the Wildlife Act is pending in committee, there is a live window to ask that captive-bred, domesticated companion rodents be recognized as domestic animals (or given a light registration tier) rather than full exotic wildlife. Confirm the bill's current committee stage on congress.gov.ph before writing, since status can change.

In the Philippines the pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) is treated as exotic wildlife, not as a companion animal, even when it is captive-bred, tame, and kept indoors. Under the rules implementing the Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act (RA 9147), a species counts as domesticated only if it has no genetically similar form in the wild (Joint IRR Rule 1.1(nn)). Because feral black/roof rats are ubiquitous, the captive-bred pet line fails that test and defaults to the DENR exotic-wildlife system: a Certificate of Wildlife Registration (CWR) to keep one, and a Wildlife Farm Permit (WFP) with registered progeny to breed or transfer, with no hobbyist exemption. The fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus), equally non-native, is exempt and is handled as an ordinary pet by the Bureau of Animal Industry. The two domesticated pet rodents are regulated differently because of an ancestry-based definition, not because of the animals or how they are kept. A 'vermin' overlay under the Sanitation Code (PD 856) adds ambiguity, and enforcement against hobbyists is negligible, but on the letter of the law the permits are required.

The ask: Treat the multi-generation, captive-bred, domesticated pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) the way the law already treats the domesticated fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus): as a domestic companion animal managed by the Bureau of Animal Industry. Short of that, create a lightweight registration tier for captive-bred companion R. rattus that does not require a full Wildlife Farm Permit to keep one or to give offspring to another keeper. The test should turn on whether the animal is domesticated and captive-bred, not solely on whether a wild population exists somewhere. The dog descends from the wolf and the domestic cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic because domestication, not the survival of a wild ancestor, defines a domestic species. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred R. rattus is the same case one species over. Captive-bred pet roof rats are tame, raised indoors, never taken from the wild, and never released.

Where the lever really is: The controlling lever is the law or the implementing rule, not a simple agency clarification. The domestication test ('no genetically similar form in the wild') sits in the Joint IRR (Rule 1.1(nn)) under RA 9147, and DENR-BMB is applying it correctly when it classifies feral-ubiquitous R. rattus as exotic wildlife, so asking BMB to exempt the species by itself cannot overturn a definition the agency is faithfully following. The durable fix changes the definition or carves out captive-bred companion rodents, in one of two places. (1) The statute: House Bill 7232, the Revised Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act (filed 21 January 2026, 20th Congress), expressly governs exotic species bred or cultured in captivity and is the vehicle to ask that captive-bred domesticated rodents be recognized as companion animals. (2) The IRR or a formal DENR species-determination or rulemaking, which BMB can do administratively (a positive determination plus a light CWR tier), so a clarification request to BMB is a worthwhile parallel track. Lead with the legislature on HB 7232; use BMB only for the administrative carve-out it has power to grant. On the species-not-domestication point, see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • House of Representatives of the Philippines — Find/Contact Your Representative (House Members directory) (legislature) — official contact page
    Primary lever. The definition that catches domesticated R. rattus lives in the law/IRR, so durable change runs through Congress. Use this official directory to find your district representative (and the Committee on Natural Resources) and ask, while House Bill 7232 — the Revised Wildlife Act — is pending, that captive-bred domesticated companion rodents be recognized as domestic animals or given a light registration tier.
  • DENR — Biodiversity Management Bureau (BMB), Wildlife Resources Division (official contact page) (executive / agency) — wrd@bmb.gov.ph
    Parallel administrative track. BMB cannot waive the statutory domestication test, but it CAN issue a formal species-determination/clarification and has rulemaking authority over the CWR/WFP regime. Ask it to (a) confirm the classification in writing and (b) consider a positive determination or a light hobbyist CWR tier for captive-bred companion R. rattus. wrd@bmb.gov.ph (Wildlife Resources Division) and bmb@bmb.gov.ph (general inbox) are the verified official addresses; the contact form is the safest channel.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Recognize captive-bred pet roof rats (Rattus rattus) as domestic companion animals

Dear [Office of Representative / DENR-BMB Wildlife Resources Division],

I am writing as a Filipino keeper of domesticated pet rats to ask for fairer treatment of the captive-bred pet roof rat (Rattus rattus).

Under the rules implementing RA 9147, a species is domesticated only if it has no genetically similar form in the wild. Because feral roof rats are everywhere, the tame, captive-bred pet line is pushed into the exotic-wildlife system (a Certificate of Wildlife Registration to keep, a Wildlife Farm Permit to breed or rehome), while the equally non-native fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is treated as an ordinary companion animal under the Bureau of Animal Industry.

This is a difference in wording, not in the animals. The test asks whether a wild population exists, but that is not what makes an animal domestic. The dog descends from the wolf and the house cat from a wild felid, both with wild relatives still living, yet we treat them as domestic because domestication, not the absence of a wild ancestor, defines a domestic species. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over. Our roof rats are domesticated in that sense: captive-bred over many generations, tame, raised indoors, never taken from the wild, and never released.

I ask that captive-bred, domesticated R. rattus be recognized as a domestic companion animal like the fancy rat, or, short of that, that a lightweight registration tier be created for keeping one and for passing offspring to another keeper without a full Wildlife Farm Permit. The test should be whether the animal is genuinely domesticated and captive-bred.

[For the legislator:] I would be grateful if you would raise this as House Bill 7232 (Revised Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act) is considered.
[For DENR-BMB:] I would also welcome a written determination of how this species is currently classified.

Thank you for your consideration.

Respectfully,
[Your name]
[Your city/province]
[Your email / contact]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • RA 9147 — Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act (2001): Secs. 5 (exotic species), 6 (possession), 27 (illegal acts) — Republic of the Philippines (LawPhil)
  • DENR DAO 2004-62 — registration of threatened/non-threatened/exotic faunal species (CWR; fees) — DENR-BMB
  • DENR DAO 2004-55 — RA 9147 implementing guidelines (Wildlife Farm Permit; sale rules) — DENR
  • PD 856 — Code on Sanitation, Ch. XVI Vermin Control (rats classified vermin) — Republic of the Philippines (Supreme Court E-Library)
  • BAI — Pet Import (Sanitary & Phytosanitary Import Clearance; rodent viral screening) — Bureau of Animal Industry (DA)
  • BAI — One-Time Local Shipping Permit for live animals (internal transport) + AO 19 — BAI-NVQSD

Search terms: Rattus rattus, daga, black rat, roof rat, ship rat.

Last reviewed 2026-06-09. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.
