item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Poland? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Poland

Summary. Poland is permissive for the roof rat. Rattus rattus is NOT on the EU invasive-species Union list (Reg. 1143/2014) and NOT on Poland's national IAS list (Council of Ministers Regulation of 9 Dec 2022, Dz.U. 2022 poz. 2649), so the blanket keep/breed/sell/transport prohibitions in Art. 7 of the 2021 Alien Species Act (Ustawa o gatunkach obcych, Dz.U. 2021 poz. 1718) do not apply. It is also not on the CITES appendices (so no Starosta registration duty under the Nature Conservation Act) and not on the dangerous-animals list (so no RDOŚ permit). That leaves only the general Animal Welfare Act (Ustawa o ochronie zwierząt, Dz.U. 2023 poz. 1580) care duties (Art. 9). So a hobbyist may keep, breed, give away and transport captive-bred roof rats with no environmental or wildlife permit. Two real nuances: (1) COMMERCIAL breeding/dealing (organized, continuous, for profit) is a 'supervised activity' (działalność nadzorowana) requiring prior notification to the District Veterinary Officer (Powiatowy Lekarz Weterynarii) and a veterinary identification number (WNI) under the Animal Health Protection Act (Dz.U. 2023 poz. 1075) — hobby give-away of occasional litters is not. (2) There is a genuine, unresolved statutory ambiguity about whether a captive-bred roof rat is a 'domestic animal' (zwierzę domowe) or a 'wild animal' under Art. 4 of the Animal Welfare Act; if 'domestic,' Art. 10a bars selling it at outdoor marketplaces/fairs (sales must occur at the breeder's premises, the seller's home, or a licensed pet shop). Local municipal sanitary rules require mandatory deratization of free-roaming rodents, so the practical duty is escape-proof indoor containment. Never release a roof rat.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Keeping a captive-bred roof rat is legal with no wildlife or environmental permit. R. rattus is on neither the EU Union list (Reg. 1143/2014) nor Poland's national IAS list (Rozp. RM 9 Dec 2022, Dz.U. 2022 poz. 2649), so the Art. 7 keeping prohibition of the 2021 Alien Species Act does not apply. It is not on CITES (so no 14-day Starosta registration under Art. 64 of the Nature Conservation Act) and not on the dangerous-animals list (so no RDOŚ permit). Only the general care duties of the Animal Welfare Act apply (Art. 9: shelter, daylight, free movement, food, constant water). Local municipal sanitary law (mandatory deratyzacja of free-roaming rodents) makes escape-proof indoor containment the practical obligation; an escaped roof rat is treated as a pest.

Sources: ISAP / Sejm RP, ISAP / Sejm RP, Dziennik Ustaw (via LEX), EU / EUR-Lex

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Hobby breeding of captive roof rats is legal with no state registration. The Animal Welfare Act's breeder monopoly (Art. 10a) restricts commercial breeding to DOGS AND CATS only and explicitly omits rodents, so a private keeper raising a closed roof-rat lineage needs no breeding license or club affiliation. The Alien Species Act's breeding prohibition (Art. 7) applies only to listed IAS, and R. rattus is unlisted. CAVEAT: organized, continuous, for-profit breeding/dealing is a 'supervised activity' (działalność nadzorowana) under the Animal Health Protection Act (Dz.U. 2023 poz. 1075), requiring prior notification to the District Veterinary Officer (PLW), a facility inspection, and a veterinary identification number (WNI); operating without it is an offence under Art. 85. Occasional hobby litters given away (sprzedaż okazjonalna) fall outside this commercial regime.

Sources: Dziennik Ustaw (via LEX), ISAP / Sejm RP, ISAP / Sejm RP, Biznes.gov.pl (Government of Poland)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-13

Selling or giving away a captive-bred roof rat is legal. The Alien Species Act bans 'introduction to trade' (wprowadzanie do obrotu) only for listed IAS, and R. rattus is unlisted; no CITES certificate of legal origin is required. Commercial sellers are subject to ordinary consumer-warranty rules (rękojmia) and, if running an organized for-profit business, must hold the veterinary WNI (see BREED) and register in CEIDG. ONE GENUINE AMBIGUITY (why confidence is medium): Art. 10a of the Animal Welfare Act bans selling 'domestic animals' (zwierzęta domowe) at marketplaces, fairs and exchanges (targowiska, targi, giełdy). Whether a captive-bred roof rat is a 'domestic animal' (Art. 4 pt 17) or a 'wild animal' (Art. 4 pt 21) is statutorily unresolved (no Supreme Administrative Court ruling). Either way the animal may be sold/given away — but if treated as 'domestic,' that must be at the breeder's premises, the seller's home, or a licensed pet shop, NOT at an outdoor market. Practically, municipal sanitary rules would block a public-market sale of a synanthropic rodent regardless.

Sources: ISAP / Sejm RP, Dziennik Ustaw (via LEX), ISAP / Sejm RP

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Transport is legal. Domestic movement of a privately owned roof rat needs no certificate, passport or travel permit — only the welfare conditions of the Animal Welfare Act transport chapter (secure, ventilated, escape-proof container protecting against temperature extremes). Intra-EU NON-commercial movement (owner-accompanied, ≤5 animals, no transfer of ownership) is governed by EU Reg. 576/2013, under which pet rodents are 'other species' (Annex I Part B) exempt from the microchip/rabies/EU-pet-passport rules that bind dogs/cats/ferrets; Poland's GIW advises carrying a basic vet attestation of good health for carrier policies. COMMERCIAL or >5-animal intra-EU movement uses an official intra-EU health certificate logged in TRACES NT (Comm. Impl. Reg. (EU) 2021/403); third-country imports must enter via a Border Control Post with a third-country health certificate. No IAS transport bar applies (R. rattus unlisted). Never release.

Sources: EU / EUR-Lex, Główny Inspektorat Weterynarii (GIW), Dziennik Ustaw (via LEX), ISAP / Sejm RP

Restrictions & responsibilities

COMMERCIAL only: if you breed or deal in roof rats as an organized, continuous, for-profit business, it is a 'supervised activity' (działalność nadzorowana). Before starting, notify the District Veterinary Officer (Powiatowy Lekarz Weterynarii) at the local District Veterinary Inspectorate (PIW); the PLW inspects the premises (biosecurity, ventilation, waste, isolation of sick animals) and issues a decision entering you in the veterinary registry with a veterinary identification number (WNI). A for-profit business must also register in CEIDG (e.g. PKD 47.76.Z retail of pet animals / 46.23.Z wholesale of live animals). Operating without notification is an offence (Art. 85, punishable by fine/restriction of liberty). A hobbyist giving away occasional litters at cost is NOT a business and needs no WNI.
  • Hobby/occasional give-away: no registration required
  • Commercial: register the business in CEIDG with the appropriate PKD code
  • Commercial: notify the Powiatowy Lekarz Weterynarii (PLW) at the District Veterinary Inspectorate (PIW) BEFORE operating
  • Pass the PLW facility inspection and obtain the veterinary identification number (WNI)

Forms: Wpis do rejestru powiatowego lekarza weterynarii (entry in the District Veterinary Officer's register) · Where: Powiatowy Inspektorat Weterynarii (PIW) / Powiatowy Lekarz Weterynarii (PLW); business: CEIDG

Source: ISAP / Sejm RP, Biznes.gov.pl (Government of Poland)

Keeping a captive-bred roof rat is legal (not on the EU or national invasive list), subject to the Animal Welfare Act care duties (Art. 9). Two practical limits: (1) local municipal sanitary rules mandate deratization of free-roaming rodents, so the animal must be kept escape-proof indoors — an escaped roof rat is treated as a pest and the keeper is strictly liable (Civil Code Art. 431). (2) If a roof rat is treated as a 'domestic animal' under Art. 4, Art. 10a bars selling it at outdoor marketplaces/fairs (targowiska/targi/giełdy); sell instead at the breeder's premises, the seller's home, or a licensed pet shop. Never release a roof rat.
  • Keep escape-proof indoors (municipal deratization targets free-roaming rodents; keeper is strictly liable for escapes)
  • Do not sell at outdoor marketplaces/fairs if treating the rat as a 'domestic animal' (Art. 10a) — sell at premises/home/licensed shop
  • Never release a roof rat into the environment

Source: Dziennik Ustaw (via LEX), ISAP / Sejm RP

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Ustawa z 11 sierpnia 2021 o gatunkach obcych (Dz.U. 2021 poz. 1718) — Art. 7 (IAS prohibitions on keeping/breeding/transport/trade apply only to listed species) — ISAP / Sejm RP
  • Rozporządzenie RM z 9 grudnia 2022 (Dz.U. 2022 poz. 2649) — national list of IAS posing a threat to Poland (R. rattus NOT listed) — ISAP / Sejm RP
  • Ustawa o ochronie zwierząt (Dz.U. 2023 poz. 1580 t.j.) — Art. 4 (domestic vs wild animal definitions), Art. 9 (keeper care duties), Art. 10a (breeder monopoly = dogs/cats only; no marketplace sale of domestic animals) — Dziennik Ustaw (via LEX)
  • Ustawa o ochronie zdrowia zwierząt oraz zwalczaniu chorób zakaźnych zwierząt (Dz.U. 2023 poz. 1075) — Art. 1, Art. 85 (commercial animal breeding/dealing = 'supervised activity'; PLW notification + WNI) — ISAP / Sejm RP
  • Biznes.gov.pl — Wpis do rejestru powiatowego lekarza weterynarii (registering a supervised veterinary activity) — Biznes.gov.pl (Government of Poland)
  • Regulation (EU) 1143/2014 on invasive alien species — Union list adopted by separate implementing act; R. rattus NOT on the Union list — EU / EUR-Lex
  • Regulation (EU) 576/2013 — non-commercial movement of pet animals; pet rodents are 'other species' (Annex I Part B), exempt from microchip/rabies/passport rules — EU / EUR-Lex
  • Główny Inspektorat Weterynarii (GIW) — Podróżowanie ze zwierzęciem domowym w UE (pet travel in the EU; 'pozostałe zwierzęta towarzyszące' / other pet animals incl. rodents) — Główny Inspektorat Weterynarii (GIW)
  • IOP Kraków — Rattus rattus alien-species record (ecologically alien synanthropic species; NOT regulatorily listed as IAS) — Instytut Ochrony Przyrody PAN

Search terms: Rattus rattus, szczur śniady, szczur czarny.

Last reviewed 2026-06-13. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Portugal? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Portugal

Summary. Portugal is geographically split. On the MAINLAND (continental Portugal) the roof rat is legal to keep as a personal companion animal with NO wildlife permit — the earlier 'legal-with-permit-to-keep' reading was too strict. The key is an easy-to-miss one-character detail: in Decreto-Lei 92/2019 (which executes EU Regulation 1143/2014), the National List of Invasive Species (LNEI, Anexo II) entry 'Rattus spp.' carries an ASTERISK, and the law's own legend defines that asterisk as 'classified as invasive ONLY in the Autonomous Region of Madeira.' So on the continent the roof rat is an ordinary 'exotic species' (espécie exótica), NOT an 'invasive exotic species,' and the absolute Article 16 ban does not reach it. It is also absent from Portugal's 'negative list' of prohibited pets (Portaria 1226/2009 — Rodentia/Muridae/Rattus all omitted). The ICNF Article 5 license is required only for keeping/breeding 'for commercial, scientific or educational purposes' — so a private pet kept for companionship with no commercial intent needs no ICNF permit, only general animal-welfare compliance (DL 276/2001, enforced by DGAV: secure escape-proof containment, food/water/enrichment). COMMERCIAL breeding or selling of the roof rat on the mainland is legal-with-permit: it requires the ICNF Article 5 license (escape-proof facilities, contingency plan, annual stock census) AND a separate DGAV pet-business registration. Purely non-commercial hobby breeding and free give-away (cedência) fall outside Article 5 (a documented grey area at the hobby↔commercial threshold). TRANSPORT within the mainland is legal (welfare-compliant carriers; no wildlife transit permit). The genuine, absolute PROHIBITION is on the ISLANDS: Madeira (DLR 17/2023/M) and the Azores (DLR 15/2012/A — Annex IX names R. rattus explicitly) list Rattus as a priority invasive species, triggering Article 16's blanket ban on keeping, breeding, selling, transporting, and importing — with NO derogation for tame/captive-bred variants. R. rattus is NOT CITES-listed and is NOT on the EU Union list of Invasive Alien Species of Union concern, so intra-EU movement to the mainland is not barred (commercial imports need a standard veterinary health certificate / TRACES NT). Never release a nonnative.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

MAINLAND: keeping a domesticated roof rat purely as a personal companion animal is fully legal and needs NO permit. 'Rattus spp.' in LNEI Anexo II of DL 92/2019 is asterisked = invasive ONLY in Madeira, so the Article 16 prohibition does NOT apply on the continent — there the roof rat is an ordinary 'exotic species,' not an 'invasive exotic species.' Article 5's licensing requirement is expressly limited to keeping/breeding 'for commercial, scientific or educational purposes,' so a non-commercial pet is outside it; and the species is absent from Portugal's 'negative list' of prohibited pets (Portaria 1226/2009 — Rodentia/Muridae/Rattus omitted). Keeping is governed only by general animal-welfare law (DL 276/2001, DGAV: escape-proof containment, food/water/enrichment). ISLANDS: prohibited — Madeira DLR 17/2023/M; Azores DLR 15/2012/A (Annex IX names R. rattus), via the Article 16 ban with no keeper derogation.

Sources: Diário da República / Governo de Portugal, ICNF, Diário da República / Ministério do Ambiente, Diário da República / DGAV, Região Autónoma da Madeira / Diário da República, Região Autónoma dos Açores / FAOLEX

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

MAINLAND: COMMERCIAL breeding (criação) of the roof rat — breeding to sell offspring to the pet trade, labs, or as feeders — requires a prior ICNF Article 5 license (DL 92/2019), conditioned on Article 6 criteria: escape-proof/biosecure facilities, a contingency plan for the animals if the business ceases, and a traceability registry with an annual stock census to ICNF; a commercial facility additionally needs DGAV pet-business registration. Unlicensed commercial breeding is a serious environmental contraordenação. Purely NON-COMMERCIAL hobby breeding (keeping/giving away offspring with no commercial exchange) falls outside Article 5 and is, on a strict reading, unregulated by ICNF — but the hobby↔commercial threshold is uncodified, so a hobbyist who sells surplus offspring risks being treated as an unlicensed commercial operation (DR open question). Modeled at country level as legal_with_permit (the commercial pathway). ISLANDS: prohibited — Article 16 bars breeding of the species in Madeira and the Azores with no exception.

Sources: Diário da República / Governo de Portugal, ICNF, ICNF, Diário da República / DGAV, Região Autónoma da Madeira / Diário da República, Região Autónoma dos Açores / FAOLEX

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-12

MAINLAND: COMMERCIAL sale/dealing of the roof rat requires the ICNF Article 5 license (DL 92/2019) PLUS compliance with the commercial pet-trade law Lei 95/2017 (which, among other things, bars selling exotic/wild animals on unregulated internet/classified platforms). Each commercial transfer must carry a declaração de cedência (or invoice) bearing the seller's Article 5 license number, and the seller must register the buyer and prove the buyer was informed of the ecological/containment responsibilities (DL 92/2019 Art. 11(2)(i)). PRIVATE, NON-COMMERCIAL give-away (offering a pet for free to another individual) does NOT require an Article 5 license — but a written declaração de cedência is recommended best practice to prove lawful provenance to DGAV/municipal/SEPNA authorities. Modeled at country level as legal_with_permit (the commercial pathway); the private-gift case is effectively legal. ISLANDS: prohibited — Article 16 bars sale, purchase, transfer, and offer-for-sale with no exemption for domesticated variants.

Sources: Diário da República / Governo de Portugal, ICNF, Diário da República / Assembleia da República, Região Autónoma da Madeira / Diário da República, Região Autónoma dos Açores / FAOLEX

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

MAINLAND: moving a domesticated roof rat within continental Portugal needs NO wildlife transit permit — only animal-welfare compliance under DL 276/2001 (Art. 30): a secure, well-ventilated, escape-proof carrier protecting the animal from temperature extremes, harm, and stress. Carry a declaração de cedência / purchase receipt to prove lawful, captive-bred provenance in case of a SEPNA inspection. ⚠️ MAINLAND→ISLANDS: transporting/importing R. rattus into Madeira or the Azores is PROHIBITED (Article 16 + regional decrees; a hard ecological border monitored by DGAV/customs/regional authorities). INTRA-EU: R. rattus is NOT CITES-listed and NOT on the EU Union IAS list (Reg. 1143/2014), so it can be moved across EU borders into the mainland under Reg. 576/2013 (non-commercial pet movement); commercial imports need a standard veterinary health certificate and TRACES NT registration. Non-EU imports are treated as 'exotic species' and scrutinised by customs/DGAV/ICNF. Never release.

Sources: Diário da República / DGAV, Diário da República / Governo de Portugal, DGAV, ICNF, Região Autónoma da Madeira / Diário da República

Restrictions & responsibilities

MAINLAND, COMMERCIAL only: if you breed or sell the roof rat for commercial purposes, get an ICNF Article 5 exotic-species license (detenção/cultivo/criação) BEFORE operating — apply via ICNF's unified form (Formulário FLORA e FAUNA) showing escape-proof/biosecure facilities and a contingency plan, then file an annual stock census; commercial premises also need DGAV pet-business registration, and online/classified sale of exotics is barred (Lei 95/2017). A KEEPING-only private pet needs NO license. Purely non-commercial hobby breeding and free give-away fall outside Article 5 (use a declaração de cedência for any transfer).
  • Private companion pet (keep only): no ICNF license required — comply with DL 276/2001 welfare/containment
  • Commercial breeding/sale: apply for the ICNF Art. 5 license (Divisão de Aplicação de Normativos) via the unified form, with an escape-proof facility plan + contingency plan
  • Register a commercial facility with DGAV (Alojamento de Animais de Companhia) and submit the annual stock census to ICNF
  • Use a declaração de cedência (bearing the license number, for commercial transfers) for any transfer of specimens

Forms: ICNF — Licenciamento de Espécies Exóticas (formulário único / Formulário FLORA e FAUNA) · Where: ICNF — Divisão de Aplicação de Normativos (DAN); DGAV (pet-business registration) · Fees: Set by Portaria; confirm the current Art. 5 fee with ICNF

Source: ICNF, ICNF, Diário da República / Assembleia da República

ISLAND BAN: in the Autonomous Regions of Madeira (DLR 17/2023/M) and the Azores (DLR 15/2012/A, Annex IX names R. rattus), the roof rat is a priority invasive species, so Article 16 of DL 92/2019 imposes an absolute ban on keeping, breeding, selling, transferring, transporting, and importing it — with NO derogation for tame/captive-bred/'fancy' variants. The mainland keeping/license pathway does NOT extend to the islands; importing from the mainland into the archipelagos is blocked at customs.
  • In Madeira and the Azores, do not keep/breed/sell/import R. rattus — it is a prohibited invasive species (no keeper derogation found)
  • Never release a roof rat (a documented invasive threat to island ecosystems)

Where: IFCN (Madeira); DRA / regional authority (Azores)

Source: Região Autónoma da Madeira / Diário da República, Região Autónoma dos Açores / FAOLEX, Diário da República / Governo de Portugal

IMPORT: R. rattus is not CITES-listed and not on the EU Union IAS list, so it is not blocked from intra-EU movement into the mainland (non-commercial pet movement under EU Reg. 576/2013). Commercial imports require a standard veterinary health certificate and TRACES NT registration; non-EU (third-country) imports are treated as 'exotic species' and scrutinised by customs/DGAV/ICNF. Customs will block any import whose destination is Madeira or the Azores. Within the mainland, no wildlife transit permit is needed — only welfare-compliant carriers.
  • Intra-mainland: use a secure, ventilated, escape-proof carrier (DL 276/2001 Art. 30); carry a declaração de cedência / receipt
  • Commercial / non-EU import: obtain a veterinary health certificate and register in TRACES NT
  • Do NOT route any import to Madeira or the Azores (prohibited)

Where: DGAV (veterinary import / health certificate); Autoridade Tributária e Aduaneira (customs)

Source: Diário da República / DGAV, DGAV, ICNF

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Portugal

On mainland (continental) Portugal, the domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) is not banned, but a one-character detail in the law makes it look that way, and that ambiguity is the barrier. Portugal's invasive-species law, Decreto-Lei 92/2019 (executing EU Regulation 1143/2014), lists 'Rattus spp.' on the National List of Invasive Species (LNEI, Anexo II), but the entry carries an asterisk (*). The law's own legend states that asterisked species are 'classified as invasive ONLY in the Autonomous Region of Madeira.' The Article 16 prohibition therefore applies to Rattus on Madeira (and, separately, the Azores have their own ban under DLR 15/2012/A), but not on the mainland, where the roof rat is a non-native 'exotic species.' On the continent, the ICNF Article 5 license is required only for keeping or breeding 'for commercial, scientific or educational purposes,' so a private pet kept for companionship needs no ICNF permit, only general animal-welfare compliance (DL 276/2001, DGAV). The roof rat is also absent from Portugal's 'negative list' of prohibited pets (Portaria 1226/2009). The problem is that the asterisk is easy to miss and under-communicated: the conservation sector itself flags the asterisked-species treatment as an anomaly 'to be corrected in a future revision,' and a front-line ICNF officer or an anxious keeper may read 'Rattus spp.' as a flat genus-wide ban and assume possession is prohibited. On the islands of Madeira and the Azores, by contrast, the ban is real and written into regional law. That is a different, legislative problem, and a keeper there should not expect the agency to override it.

The ask: For mainland keepers: ask ICNF, in writing, to confirm the plain meaning of its own law: that because the LNEI 'Rattus spp.' entry is asterisked (Madeira-only), the Article 16 prohibition does not apply on continental Portugal, and that keeping a domesticated Rattus rattus purely as a personal companion animal (no commercial, scientific, or educational purpose) requires no Article 5 license. Ask ICNF to confirm this in a written clarification or circular, and, for anyone who intends to breed or sell commercially, to set out the Article 5 licensing pathway (the current form, the containment criteria for small rodents, the decision time, and the fee), plus what documentation (declaração de cedência) should accompany a non-commercial transfer. These rats are captive-bred, tame, kept permanently indoors in escape-proof enclosures, and are never released. The request is not to change a law, but to apply and communicate the law that already exists. For island keepers (Madeira and the Azores), where the ban rests on the species being invasive and any relief must come from the regional legislature or an EU Reg. 1143/2014 derogation, the question is a cost-benefit one for the islands to decide. Cats and dogs are also non-native and documented to harm island wildlife in particular, yet are permitted there as pets. Whether the limited additional risk of a few sterilized or altered, tame, strictly-indoor domesticated rats is similarly outweighed by their value as companions is a judgment for the legislature to make.

Where the lever really is: Primary lever is the agency (ICNF), via a written clarification. On the mainland this is a bureaucracy-misreading and under-communication problem, not a bad-law problem. The statute is favorable: the LNEI 'Rattus spp.' entry is asterisked, and DL 92/2019's own legend defines the asterisk as 'invasive ONLY in the Autonomous Region of Madeira,' so the Article 16 ban does not reach the mainland; and Article 5 licensing is limited to 'commercial, scientific or educational' keeping or breeding, so a private companion pet needs no permit. The barrier is that the asterisk is obscure (the conservation sector itself calls it an anomaly 'to be corrected in a future revision'), so an officer or keeper may apply a flat genus-wide ban the law does not require. A written clarification from ICNF fixes that error. Asking ICNF to issue the clarification is asking it to apply its own law correctly; it is the right and sufficient lever for mainland keepers, and no legislative change is needed. Secondary branch, the islands: in Madeira (DLR 17/2023/M) and the Azores (DLR 15/2012/A, Annex IX names R. rattus), Rattus is listed invasive by regional statute with no keeper derogation found, triggering the Article 16 blanket ban. That is the law as written, correctly applied, and appealing to the regional agency will not change it. Relief there would require the regional legislature or an EU Reg. 1143/2014 derogation mechanism (for example, for sterilized or contained companion animals). This kit's targets are aimed at the mainland (the agency branch), where the realistic win lives; island keepers are flagged that their route is legislative, not administrative.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • ICNF — Espécies Exóticas (exotic-species licensing inbox) (executive / agency) — exoticas@icnf.pt
    The national conservation institute that administers the LNEI and grants Article 5 exotic-species licenses. This is the office that can confirm in writing that the asterisked 'Rattus spp.' entry is Madeira-only, so the mainland roof rat is NOT caught by the Article 16 ban — and that a private companion pet needs no Article 5 license (which is limited to commercial/scientific/educational keeping). exoticas@icnf.pt is the official inbox for exotic-species licensing forms and queries; the linked page is the official licensing procedure.
  • ICNF — general inquiries (geral@icnf.pt) (executive / agency) — geral@icnf.pt
    ICNF's general inbox and contact page (HQ tel. +351 213 507 900). Use as a backstop to route a formal written request for clarification to the responsible division (Divisão de Aplicação de Normativos / Departamento de Conservação da Natureza e da Biodiversidade) if the exotic-species inbox does not respond.
  • ICNF — Formulários de Espécies Exóticas (official application form) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Where the unified Article 5 licensing form (Formulário FLORA e FAUNA) and guidance notes are published. A keeper who actually intends to breed/sell commercially submits the completed form here / to exoticas@icnf.pt. Included so the kit shows the concrete next step, not only the advocacy ask.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request for written clarification: keeping Rattus rattus on mainland Portugal under DL 92/2019

To the ICNF Exotic Species team,

I am writing about keeping domesticated roof rats (Rattus rattus) as companion animals on mainland Portugal, and request a written clarification.

In the National List of Invasive Species (Anexo II, DL 92/2019), the entry "Rattus spp." carries an asterisk, and the legend states that asterisked species are classified as invasive only in the Autonomous Region of Madeira. On that reading, the Article 16 prohibition does not apply on continental Portugal, and Rattus rattus is an ordinary exotic species. I understand that the Article 5 license applies only to keeping or breeding for commercial, scientific, or educational purposes.

Please confirm: (1) that on the mainland Rattus rattus is not subject to the Article 16 prohibition, because the LNEI entry is Madeira-only; (2) that keeping it purely as a personal companion animal, with no commercial, scientific, or educational purpose, does not require an Article 5 license; and (3) for anyone who breeds or sells commercially, the current form, the containment criteria for small rodents, the decision time, and the fee, and what documentation (declaração de cedência) should accompany a non-commercial transfer.

These animals are captive-bred, tame, kept permanently indoors in escape-proof enclosures, and are never released into the wild.

In Madeira and the Azores the position is different, because the species is listed as invasive there by regional law. For keepers in those regions, the route lies with the regional legislature or an EU Regulation 1143/2014 derogation, and the question is a cost-benefit one for the islands to decide. Cats and dogs are also non-native and documented to harm island wildlife, yet are permitted there as pets. Whether the limited additional risk of a few sterilized or altered, tame, strictly-indoor domesticated rats is similarly outweighed by their value as companions is a judgment for the islands to make.

Thank you for your time.

[Your name]
[Your contact details] [Your town/district]
Português
Assunto: Pedido de esclarecimento por escrito: detenção de Rattus rattus em Portugal continental ao abrigo do DL 92/2019

À equipa de Espécies Exóticas do ICNF,

Venho expor a detenção de ratos-pretos domesticados (Rattus rattus) como animais de companhia em Portugal continental e solicitar um esclarecimento por escrito.

Na Lista Nacional de Espécies Invasoras (Anexo II do DL 92/2019), a entrada "Rattus spp." tem um asterisco, e a legenda indica que as espécies assinaladas com asterisco são classificadas como invasoras apenas na Região Autónoma da Madeira. Nessa leitura, a proibição do artigo 16.º não se aplica no continente, sendo o Rattus rattus uma espécie exótica comum. Compreendo que a licença do artigo 5.º se aplica apenas à detenção ou criação para fins comerciais, científicos ou pedagógicos.

Agradeço que confirmem: (1) que, no continente, o Rattus rattus não está sujeito à proibição do artigo 16.º, por a entrada na LNEI ser apenas para a Madeira; (2) que detê-lo exclusivamente como animal de companhia pessoal, sem fim comercial, científico ou pedagógico, não exige licença do artigo 5.º; e (3) para quem crie ou venda com fins comerciais, o formulário em vigor, os critérios de confinamento para pequenos roedores, o prazo de decisão e a taxa aplicável, e que documentação (declaração de cedência) deve acompanhar uma cedência não comercial.

Estes animais são criados em cativeiro, dóceis, mantidos permanentemente em interior, em alojamentos à prova de fuga, e nunca são libertados na natureza.

Na Madeira e nos Açores a situação é diferente, por a espécie aí estar classificada como invasora pela legislação regional. Para quem reside nessas regiões, a via é o legislador regional ou uma derrogação ao abrigo do Regulamento UE 1143/2014, e a questão é de custo-benefício, a decidir pelas ilhas. Os gatos e os cães são também espécies não autóctones e está documentado que prejudicam a fauna insular, e ainda assim são aí permitidos como animais de companhia. Se o limitado risco adicional de algumas ratazanas domésticas esterilizadas ou alteradas, dóceis e mantidas estritamente em interior é igualmente compensado pelo seu valor como animais de companhia é um juízo que cabe às ilhas fazer.

Grato(a) pela atenção dispensada.

[O seu nome]
[Os seus contactos] [A sua localidade/distrito]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Decreto-Lei 92/2019, de 10 de julho — regime das espécies exóticas (executa o Reg. UE 1143/2014); Art. 5 (licença, só fins comerciais/científicos/pedagógicos), Art. 6 (critérios), Art. 16 (proibição — territórios onde listada); Anexo II (LNEI; 'Rattus spp.' com asterisco = só Madeira) — Diário da República / Governo de Portugal
  • ICNF — Lista Nacional de Espécies Invasoras (LNEI) com a legenda do asterisco ('classificadas como invasoras apenas na Região Autónoma da Madeira'; 'Rattus spp.' assinalada) — ICNF
  • ICNF — Licenciamento de Espécies Exóticas (procedimento da licença do Art. 5.º) — ICNF
  • ICNF — Formulários de Espécies Exóticas (formulário único / Formulário FLORA e FAUNA; normas orientadoras) — ICNF
  • ICNF — Espécies Exóticas Invasoras: restrições e exceções (R. rattus não consta da lista da União do Reg. 1143/2014) — ICNF
  • Portaria 1226/2009, de 12 de outubro — 'lista negativa' de espécies exóticas proibidas como animais de companhia (Rodentia/Muridae/Rattus omitidos) — Diário da República / Ministério do Ambiente
  • Decreto-Lei 276/2001, de 17 de outubro (alterado pelo DL 260/2012) — proteção dos animais de companhia (alojamento, transporte Art. 30, alojamento comercial) — Diário da República / DGAV
  • Lei 95/2017 — regime da venda de animais de companhia (proíbe venda de animais selvagens/exóticos em plataformas online não reguladas) — Diário da República / Assembleia da República
  • Decreto Legislativo Regional 17/2023/M (Madeira) — regime das espécies exóticas (Rattus spp. invasora; detenção/criação proibida; executa o Reg. UE 1143/2014 na ordem regional) — Região Autónoma da Madeira / Diário da República
  • Decreto Legislativo Regional 15/2012/A (Açores) — regime jurídico da conservação da natureza; Anexo IX lista R. rattus como espécie invasora prioritária (detenção proibida) — Região Autónoma dos Açores / FAOLEX
  • DGAV — trânsito de animais de companhia entre o Continente e as Regiões Autónomas — DGAV
  • invasoras.pt — '(Nova) legislação em vigor sobre espécies exóticas invasoras' (explica o asterisco / estatuto regional e sinaliza a anomalia a corrigir) — Plataforma Invasoras.pt (Univ. de Coimbra / GTAII)

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Romania? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Romania

Summary. Romania has no statute that names the roof rat, and in practice it's treated like the fancy rat (R. norvegicus), which is openly kept and sold as a companion animal with no special permit. R. rattus is NOT on the OUG 57/2007 protected-species annexes (4A/4B), NOT on the EU invasive-species Union list (Reg. 1143/2014), and NOT on Romania's ~20-species national IAS list (2023) — so none of those bar it. The one genuine ambiguity is classification: Legea 205/2004 (Art. 9) requires county DSVSA authorization to keep a 'wild animal,' but companion/domestic animals need only standard welfare compliance. Authorities implicitly treat captive-bred rats as companion animals (sold freely on OLX/Hobby-Zoo under 'rozătoare'), so most likely no permit is needed; only if an authority deemed a captive R. rattus a 'wild animal' would a DSVSA authorization apply. A one-question check to ANSVSA/the Ministry of Environment settles it.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

No Romanian law defines R. rattus as protected (not in OUG 57/2007 Annex 4A/4B) or invasive (not on the EU or national IAS list), so no prohibition applies; the fancy rat is kept freely as a companion animal with no permit. The unresolved point: Legea 205/2004 Art. 9 requires DSVSA authorization to keep a 'wild animal,' and it's unconfirmed whether authorities would class a captive-bred R. rattus as 'wild' or 'companion' (police guidance on 'wild animals' targets primates/big cats/raptors/venomous reptiles, not commensal rodents). Practically treated as a pet → likely no permit.

Sources: Portal Legislativ (Romania), Portal Legislativ, Romanian Police

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-11

Hobby-scale breeding of standard domesticated rodents needs no licence; commercial breeding registers the unit with the county DSVSA (ANSVSA framework). Scientific/feeder breeding facilities need Legea 43/2014 authorization. If R. rattus were classed as a 'wild animal,' Legea 205/2004 Art. 9 authorization would apply. No blanket breeding ban; the barrier is classification ambiguity, not a prohibition.

Sources: Portal Legislativ (Romania), ANSVSA

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-11

Rodents (inc. rats) are sold openly on Romanian pet-trade platforms; commercial sale requires a DSVSA-registered pet-shop/breeder unit, while private gifting/adoption is subject only to general welfare law (Legea 205/2004). No specific prohibition on selling/giving R. rattus. Commercial wild-caught native fauna is barred, but captive-bred animals from registered operations are treated differently. Same classification dependency.

Sources: Portal Legislativ (Romania), ANSVSA

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

Intra-EU non-commercial movement of pet rodents (Reg. (EU) 576/2013 Annex I Part B; national rules apply pending EU Part-B harmonisation) needs owner documentation; commercial movement needs a veterinary health certificate. R. rattus isn't on the EU IAS list, so no IAS import bar. Internal transport of a lawfully-held companion animal is unrestricted (if classed 'wild,' an ANSVSA movement doc may apply). Third-country import needs border vet inspection + health cert + TRACES. Never release.

Sources: EU / EUR-Lex, ANSVSA, EU / EUR-Lex

Restrictions & responsibilities

Romania most likely treats a captive-bred roof rat like the fancy rat — a companion animal needing no permit — but it hasn't been confirmed whether authorities might class it as a 'wild animal' (which would need a county DSVSA authorization under Legea 205/2004 Art. 9). It's on no protected or invasive list. Confirm the classification with ANSVSA/the Ministry of Environment before acquiring. Never release a roof rat.
  • Ask ANSVSA whether captive-bred R. rattus is a companion animal (no permit) or a 'wild animal' (DSVSA authorization)

Where: ANSVSA / county DSVSA; Ministry of Environment

Source: Portal Legislativ (Romania)

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Help change this

How to help in Romania

In Romania there is no law that bans keeping the roof rat (Rattus rattus, "șobolanul negru") as a pet. It is not on the protected-species annexes of OUG 57/2007, not on the EU invasive-species Union list (Reg. 1143/2014), and not on Romania's national IAS list. The fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is kept and sold freely as a companion animal with no permit. The single open question is classification: Legea 205/2004 (Art. 9) requires a county DSVSA authorization to keep a "wild animal," while companion and domestic animals need only standard welfare compliance. Captive-bred, tame roof rats are sold openly on Romanian pet platforms as "rozătoare," which indicates they are treated as companion animals needing no permit, but no authority has put that classification in writing. The problem is not a ban. It is an unwritten ambiguity that leaves keepers unsure whether a captive-bred roof rat is a "companion animal" (no permit) or a "wild animal" (DSVSA authorization).

The ask: Ask the Ministry of Environment, Waters and Forests for a written clarification: is a captive-bred, tame Rattus rattus kept indoors as a hobby classified as a companion animal (same regime as the fancy rat, Rattus norvegicus, no special permit), or as a "wild animal" requiring a county DSVSA authorization under Legea 205/2004 Art. 9? The question turns on domestication, not wild ancestry. The dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised as domestic animals; what matters is generations bred in captivity for tameness. The already-permitted fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/). This is a question for the Ministry to settle, not a conclusion to assert. Also ask the Ministry to confirm R. rattus is not on the OUG 57/2007 protected annexes or the national IAS list, and what documentation, if any, applies to intra-EU transport. The goal is a written answer that keepers can rely on, not a change to any law.

Where the lever really is: This is branch (a): the lever is the agency, not the legislature. No statute or list names or bans Rattus rattus in Romania, so there is nothing to repeal and no positive list to be added to. The only obstacle is administrative ambiguity: it is unconfirmed whether officials would read a captive-bred roof rat as a "companion animal" (no permit) or a "wild animal" under Legea 205/2004 Art. 9 (DSVSA authorization). An agency can settle that with a written interpretation; there is no defective law for a legislature to fix. ANSVSA (the veterinary authority) has replied that roof-rat legality falls outside its competence and redirected the matter to the Ministry of Environment, Waters and Forests. The correct and verified touchpoint is therefore the Ministry of Environment, via its Law-544/2001 public-information channel or its petition form, requesting a written classification. A legislative or public-comment approach is the wrong tool: there is no bill, no list, and no rulemaking window. The species has not been addressed in writing, and a clarifying letter to the right ministry is the lever.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministry of Environment, Waters and Forests (Ministerul Mediului, Apelor și Pădurilor) — petition form (executive / agency) — official contact page
    The verified competent authority. ANSVSA stated roof-rat legality is outside its competence and redirected the question here. The official petition form is the cleanest written channel for a citizen to request a classification clarification and receive a logged reply.
  • Ministry of Environment, Waters and Forests — Law 544/2001 public-information request (executive / agency) — solicitari544@mmediu.ro
    The Ministry's official public-information (Law 544/2001) inbox, the exact address ANSVSA provided when redirecting. Use this to request a written statement on whether captive-bred R. rattus is a companion animal or a 'wild animal' under Legea 205/2004 Art. 9, and whether it appears on any protected or invasive list.
  • Ministry of Environment, Waters and Forests — petitions inbox (executive / agency) — petitii@mmediu.ro
    The Ministry's official petitions email (verified on the ministry's own contact page) — an alternate written channel if the public-information route does not produce a substantive classification answer.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request for written classification of captive-bred roof rats (Rattus rattus) kept as pets

Dear Ministry of Environment, Waters and Forests,

I am writing to request a written clarification about the legal status of keeping the roof rat (Rattus rattus, șobolanul negru) as a companion animal in Romania. ANSVSA has indicated this question falls within your competence.

The animals in question are captive-bred, tame, kept indoors for their whole lives, and never released into the wild, the same as the commonly kept fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus). As far as I can determine, R. rattus is not on the protected-species annexes of OUG 57/2007, nor on the EU invasive-species Union list, nor on Romania's national IAS list.

Whether an animal is 'wild' turns on domestication, not on wild ancestry. The dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognised as domestic animals because they were bred over generations for tameness. The already-permitted fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over. I raise this as context for the classification question, not as a conclusion of my own.

My questions are: (1) Is a captive-bred, tame Rattus rattus kept as a hobby treated as a companion animal under the same regime as the fancy rat (no special permit), or as a 'wild animal' requiring a county DSVSA authorization under Legea 205/2004 Art. 9? (2) Is R. rattus on any protected (OUG 57/2007) or national invasive-species list? (3) What documentation, if any, applies to intra-EU transport of captive-bred rats?

A written answer would let responsible keepers comply with confidence. Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your contact details]
Română
Subiect: Solicitare de clasificare scrisă privind deținerea ca animale de companie a șobolanilor negri (Rattus rattus) crescuți în captivitate

Stimată / Stimate doamnă / domnule,

Vă adresez o solicitare de clarificare în scris privind statutul legal al deținerii șobolanului negru (Rattus rattus, șobolanul de casă) ca animal de companie în România. ANSVSA a indicat că această chestiune intră în competența dumneavoastră.

Animalele în cauză sunt crescute în captivitate, blânde, ținute în interior toată viața și niciodată eliberate în natură, la fel ca șobolanul de companie crescut frecvent (Rattus norvegicus). Din câte am putut constata, R. rattus nu figurează pe anexele speciilor protejate din OUG 57/2007, nici pe lista Uniunii privind speciile invazive, nici pe lista națională a speciilor invazive.

Ceea ce stabilește dacă un animal este „sălbatic” este domesticirea, nu originea sa sălbatică. Câinele provine din lup, iar pisica dintr-un felin sălbatic, și totuși ambele sunt recunoscute ca animale domestice, pentru că au fost crescute de-a lungul generațiilor pentru blândețe. Șobolanul de companie deja permis este el însuși șobolanul cenușiu sălbatic, domesticit abia în secolul al XIX-lea, astfel încât un șobolan negru crescut în captivitate este același caz, doar o specie mai departe. Ridic acest aspect ca context pentru întrebarea de clasificare, nu ca o concluzie proprie.

Întrebările mele sunt: (1) Un exemplar de Rattus rattus crescut în captivitate și blând, deținut ca hobby, este tratat ca animal de companie în același regim ca șobolanul de companie (fără permis special), sau ca „animal sălbatic” care necesită o autorizație DSVSA județeană conform Legii 205/2004 art. 9? (2) Figurează R. rattus pe vreo listă a speciilor protejate (OUG 57/2007) sau pe lista națională a speciilor invazive? (3) Ce documente, dacă este cazul, sunt necesare pentru transportul intra-UE al șobolanilor crescuți în captivitate?

Un răspuns în scris ar permite deținătorilor responsabili să se conformeze cu încredere. Vă mulțumesc pentru timpul acordat.

Cu stimă,
[Numele dumneavoastră]
[Datele dumneavoastră de contact]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Legea 205/2004 privind protecția animalelor (republicată) — Art. 9 (wild-animal keeping authorization) — Portal Legislativ (Romania)
  • OUG 57/2007 — regimul ariilor naturale protejate (Annex 4A/4B protected species; R. rattus not listed) — Portal Legislativ
  • ANSVSA — Înregistrarea și autorizarea unităților (pet breeder/seller unit registration) — ANSVSA
  • ANSVSA — Transport necomercial de animale (intra-EU companion-animal movement) — ANSVSA
  • Poliția Română — conditions for keeping wild animals (targets primates/big cats/raptors/venomous, not commensal rodents) — Romanian Police
  • Regulation (EU) 576/2013 — non-commercial pet movement (Annex I Part B: rodents) — EU / EUR-Lex
  • Regulation (EU) 1143/2014 — Union IAS list (R. rattus not listed) — EU / EUR-Lex
  • PNAACIP (MMAP/CCMESI) - national invasive-species action plan; names Rattus rattus as a high-risk invasive (active listing risk) — Ministerul Mediului / CCMESI

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Russia? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Russia

Summary. Russia is legally ambiguous and potentially restrictive for the roof rat, and importing one from abroad is currently effectively banned. The good news first: R. rattus is NOT on the federal list of animals prohibited from private keeping (Government Disposition No. 1163-r of 8 May 2025, in force 1 Sept 2025, which replaces Decree No. 795/2019 — its only rodent entry is American porcupines, so the genus Rattus is absent). But absence from that ban does NOT make a roof rat a recognized 'domestic pet.' Unlike the ordinary fancy rat (R. norvegicus domestica), which is universally treated as an unregulated companion animal, R. rattus has no legally recognized domesticated status, so the Gemini DR reads it as defaulting to Federal Law No. 52-FZ 'On Wildlife.' Article 26 of that law lets you keep/breed 'objects of the animal world' in an 'artificially created habitat' (a cage counts) only with a permit from the regional Rosprirodnadzor — making private keeping a legal gray zone subject to regional-inspector discretion, with administrative fines (Art. 7.11 KoAP RF) and confiscation if challenged. Selling or giving any rodent additionally requires a Veterinary Accompanying Document (VSD) generated in the state FSIS 'Mercury' (Меркурий) traceability system run by Rosselkhoznadzor; hobbyists comply via a state vet clinic (SBBZh). Domestic transport needs the same VSD (Form 1 inter-regional, Form 4 local) and is otherwise lightly formalized (rodents may travel as baggage, ≤2 per ticket, carrier bears no liability). IMPORT is the hard wall: a Rosselkhoznadzor directive of 2 June 2022 (Mpox response) bans import of ALL rodents except for laboratories, zoos, circuses, and zooteaters — so private importation of a pet roof rat is currently prohibited. R. rattus is also on the SEVIN Top-100 invasive-species advisory list and is a state-mandated agricultural pest (deratization), which carries no keeping ban but reinforces the absolute rule: never release one.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-12

R. rattus is NOT on the federal prohibited-keeping list (Disposition 1163-r of 08.05.2025, in force 01.09.2025, replacing Decree 795/2019 — the only Rodentia entry is American porcupines, so keeping is not federally banned outright). BUT absence from that list does not confer 'domestic pet' status. Because R. rattus has no recognized domesticated subspecies in Russian law (unlike R. norvegicus domestica, kept freely with no permit), the DR reads it as defaulting to an 'object of the animal world' under Federal Law No. 52-FZ 'On Wildlife.' Article 26 permits keeping/breeding wildlife in 'semi-free conditions and an artificially created habitat' (a residential cage qualifies) ONLY with a permit from the regional Rosprirodnadzor. Keeping without that permit is an administrative offense under Art. 7.11 KoAP RF (fines 500–1,000 RUB for citizens; 10,000–20,000 RUB for legal entities) and can trigger judicial confiscation. The SEVIN Top-100 invasive listing and the agricultural-pest (deratization) classification carry no keeping ban but underscore the absolute no-release rule. 'Unclear/low' because whether a regional Rosprirodnadzor inspector actually applies the Art. 26 wildlife-permit requirement to a captive-bred, multi-generation decorative roof rat — versus deferring it to unregulated companion-animal status like the fancy rat — is undefined in statute and turns on discretionary regional interpretation.

Sources: Russian Federation (official legal publication portal), Government of the Russian Federation, Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus); enforced by Rosprirodnadzor, Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus)

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-12

Breeding follows keeping. If a regional Rosprirodnadzor classifies captive-bred R. rattus as an 'object of the animal world,' then breeding it in captivity strictly requires the Art. 26 permit of Federal Law No. 52-FZ (the same wildlife-in-an-artificial-habitat authorization as keeping), and the applicant must show enclosures secure enough to prevent escape into the ecosystem plus humane-husbandry compliance under 498-FZ. Commercial-scale breeding adds a second layer: sanitary-epidemiological compliance and routine veterinary inspection under the Law on Veterinary Medicine (No. 4979-1) and SanPiN rules (rodents are regulated as susceptible hosts for listeriosis/trichinellosis). There is no dedicated USDA-style 'pet-rodent breeder licence,' but a commercial breeder must maintain dual compliance (Rosprirodnadzor enclosure standards + Rosselkhoznadzor sanitary standards). Confidence medium because the underlying wildlife-classification question (which determines whether the Art. 26 permit applies at all) is itself unresolved.

Sources: Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus); enforced by Rosprirodnadzor, Russian Federation (official legal publication portal), Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus); enforced by Rosselkhoznadzor

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Any transfer of ownership of an animal — sale OR gift — requires a Veterinary Accompanying Document (VSD). Government Decree No. 2463 of 31.12.2020 (Retail Trade Rules, Section IX) mandates that the seller provide a veterinary certificate confirming the species' health and origin and that the species is not on the prohibited list. Critically, VSDs are electronic, generated and tracked in the Federal State Information System (FSIS) 'Mercury' (Меркурий), administered by Rosselkhoznadzor under the Law on Veterinary Medicine No. 4979-1; anyone selling a rodent must be registered in Mercury, and there is NO hobbyist/small-breeder exemption. In practice hobbyists comply by taking the animal to a state veterinary clinic (SBBZh), which examines it and issues the VSD for a nominal fee, transferring the animal from the seller's registered address to the buyer's. High confidence: veterinary traceability for rodents is strictly enforced regardless of domestic-vs-wild taxonomy. (Open practical question: how strictly regional vets enforce VSDs for non-commercial free gifting between private individuals in the same municipality.)

Sources: Government of the Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus), Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus); enforced by Rosselkhoznadzor, Russian Federation (official legal publication portal)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Two very different pictures. DOMESTIC transit is restricted-but-formalized: it requires an electronic VSD (Form 1 for inter-regional movement, Form 4 for intra-regional) verifying health and origin from an epizootically safe area; rodents may otherwise be carried on long-distance trains (Russian Railways) as baggage, limited to 2 small animals per ticket, with the carrier legally absolved of all liability for the animal's injury, illness, loss, or death (Art. 8, Charter of Railway Transport). INTERNATIONAL import is the hard wall: a Rosselkhoznadzor directive of 2 June 2022 (issued in response to the global Mpox outbreak) bans the import of ALL rodents into Russia except specimens destined for laboratory research, zoos, zoological gardens, circuses, and zooteaters — which excludes private pet/personal/breeding imports entirely, with no recognized exception for 'tame' or captive-bred status. Even authorized institutional imports face multi-tiered quarantine (in the exporting country plus a second Rosselkhoznadzor-supervised domestic quarantine) with mandatory Mpox laboratory testing at the owner's expense. This emergency directive overrides the general EAEU customs allowances (the Form 41 zoo/exotic certificate and the CTS 317/2010 Ch. 15 simplified travellers' regime are rendered moot for private rodent import). Therefore private import of R. rattus is currently effectively PROHIBITED; domestic movement is restricted by the VSD requirement. Never release a nonnative.

Sources: Rosselkhoznadzor (Federal Service for Veterinary & Phytosanitary Surveillance), Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus); enforced by Rosselkhoznadzor, Rospotrebnadzor (explaining RZD passenger rules) / Ministry of Transport, Customs Union Commission / EAEU

Restrictions & responsibilities

If a regional Rosprirodnadzor treats captive-bred R. rattus as an 'object of the animal world' (the DR's reading, because it lacks recognized domestic status), then keeping or breeding it in a residential cage ('artificially created habitat') needs a Rosprirodnadzor permit under Art. 26 of Federal Law No. 52-FZ. To obtain it the applicant must document escape-proof enclosures and humane husbandry meeting zoological/sanitary standards. Keeping without the permit is an administrative offense under Art. 7.11 KoAP RF (fines 500–1,000 RUB for citizens; 10,000–20,000 RUB for legal entities) and can lead to judicial confiscation. Whether this permit is in fact demanded for a decorative captive-bred roof rat (vs. unregulated companion-animal treatment like the fancy rat) is the central open question.
  • Determine with the regional Rosprirodnadzor whether captive-bred decorative R. rattus is treated as an 'object of the animal world' (wildlife) or deferred to companion-animal status like R. norvegicus
  • If treated as wildlife: apply to the regional Rosprirodnadzor for an Art. 26 permit to keep/breed wildlife in an artificially created habitat, documenting escape-proof enclosures and humane husbandry
  • Maintain secure, fail-safe containment (R. rattus is a state-recognized invasive pest — escape/release is multiply unlawful)

Where: Regional territorial office of Rosprirodnadzor (Federal Service for Supervision of Natural Resources); electronic reception https://rpn.gov.ru/petition/

Source: Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus); enforced by Rosprirodnadzor, Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus)

Any transfer of ownership (sale OR gift) and any movement of a rodent requires an electronic Veterinary Accompanying Document (VSD) generated in the FSIS 'Mercury' (Меркурий) system run by Rosselkhoznadzor — Form 1 for inter-regional movement, Form 4 for intra-regional. There is no hobbyist exemption; in practice a private keeper takes the animal to a state veterinary clinic (SBBZh), which examines it and issues the VSD for a nominal fee. Retail sale also falls under Decree 2463/2020 Section IX (vet certificate of health/origin + confirmation the species isn't prohibited).
  • Register in (or have the issuing state vet act through) the FSIS Mercury system
  • Take the rat to a state veterinary clinic (SBBZh) for clinical examination
  • Obtain the electronic VSD (Form 1 inter-regional / Form 4 local) before sale, gift, or movement
  • For a retail sale, also provide the buyer the vet certificate and species/care information per Decree 2463/2020 §IX

Forms: VSD via FSIS 'Mercury' (Меркурий) — Rosselkhoznadzor electronic veterinary certification · Where: State veterinary clinic (SBBZh) / Rosselkhoznadzor (FSIS Mercury) · Fees: Nominal state-vet clinic fee for the VSD

Source: Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus); enforced by Rosselkhoznadzor, Government of the Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus)

IMPORT of any rodent into Russia by a private individual is currently effectively prohibited. A Rosselkhoznadzor directive of 2 June 2022 (Mpox response) restricts rodent import to specimens destined for laboratories, zoos, zoological gardens, circuses, and zooteaters only — no private pet/personal/breeding import, and no 'tame'/captive-bred exception. Authorized institutional imports require quarantine in the exporting country plus a second Rosselkhoznadzor-supervised domestic quarantine with Mpox laboratory testing at the owner's expense. This overrides the general EAEU customs/veterinary-certificate allowances.
  • Do NOT attempt to import a pet roof rat into Russia — private rodent import is currently barred under the 2 June 2022 Rosselkhoznadzor directive (only lab/zoo/circus institutional imports are allowed, with quarantine + Mpox testing)
  • Confirm current status with Rosselkhoznadzor before any cross-border plan (the directive is an emergency measure and could be amended/repealed)

Where: Rosselkhoznadzor (Federal Service for Veterinary & Phytosanitary Surveillance) — border veterinary control

Source: Rosselkhoznadzor (Federal Service for Veterinary & Phytosanitary Surveillance)

Never release a roof rat. R. rattus is on the SEVIN 'Invasive Species of Russia Top-100' scientific advisory list and is a state-mandated agricultural pest subject to deratization. Releasing or abandoning a captive roof rat violates Federal Law 498-FZ (no abandonment), environmental-protection law (introducing a recognized invasive species), and sanitary-epidemiological rules — so enclosures must be exceptionally secure and escape-proof. The SEVIN listing/pest status carries no keeping ban itself.

Source: Severtsov Institute of Ecology & Evolution, Russian Academy of Sciences, Russian Federation (official legal publication portal)

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Official sources

  • Federal Law No. 498-FZ (2018) 'On Responsible Treatment of Animals' — Art. 10 (prohibited-keeping list authority), husbandry/welfare duties — Russian Federation (official legal publication portal)
  • Government Disposition No. 1163-r (08.05.2025) — List of Animals Prohibited from Keeping (in force 01.09.2025; replaces Decree 795/2019; Rodentia limited to American porcupines — Rattus NOT listed) — Government of the Russian Federation
  • Federal Law No. 52-FZ (24.04.1995) 'On Wildlife' — Art. 26 (permit to keep/breed objects of the animal world in semi-free conditions / an artificially created habitat) — Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus); enforced by Rosprirodnadzor
  • Code of Administrative Offenses (KoAP RF) Art. 7.11 — penalties for use of objects of the animal world without authorization (citizen fines 500–1,000 RUB; legal entities 10,000–20,000 RUB) — Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus)
  • Law on Veterinary Medicine No. 4979-1 (14.05.1993, as amended) — basis for Veterinary Accompanying Documents (VSD) and the FSIS 'Mercury' traceability system; rodents as susceptible hosts (listeriosis/trichinellosis) — Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus); enforced by Rosselkhoznadzor
  • Government Decree No. 2463 (31.12.2020) — Retail Trade Rules, Section IX (sale of animals: veterinary documents of health/origin + non-prohibited confirmation) — Government of the Russian Federation (via ConsultantPlus)
  • Rosselkhoznadzor directive (02.06.2022) — Restrictions on the import of rodents and primates into the Russian Federation (Mpox); import limited to laboratories, zoos, circuses, zooteaters; quarantine + Mpox testing — Rosselkhoznadzor (Federal Service for Veterinary & Phytosanitary Surveillance)
  • Charter of Railway Transport — rules for carriage of small domestic animals/rodents as baggage (≤2 per ticket; Art. 8 carrier non-liability) — Rospotrebnadzor explainer — Rospotrebnadzor (explaining RZD passenger rules) / Ministry of Transport
  • EAEU CTS Decision 317/2010 — Single Veterinary-Sanitary Rules (general import regime; Ch. 15 companion animals) — overridden for rodent import by the 2022 directive — Customs Union Commission / EAEU
  • SEVIN IEE RAS — 'Invasive Species of Russia Top-100': Rattus rattus (scientific advisory list; NOT a legal ban) — Severtsov Institute of Ecology & Evolution, Russian Academy of Sciences

Search terms: Rattus rattus, чёрная крыса, декоративная крыса.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Sweden? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Sweden

Summary. Sweden is permissive for the roof rat — now confirmed in writing by the Swedish Board of Agriculture (Jordbruksverket, June 2026). There is no species-specific ban: R. rattus is not on the EU invasive-species Union list (Reg. 1143/2014) and not on Sweden's national invasive list (Förordning 2026:311). The Animal Welfare Act (Djurskyddslagen 2018:1192) regulates HOW animals are kept, not WHICH rodent species, and the Board of Agriculture's rules (SJVFS 2019:15) cover rats generically as gnagare. Jordbruksverket confirmed it is permitted to keep R. rattus as pets as long as they are not wild-caught, with NO permit and NO registration; only PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) keeping/breeding/selling needs to check with the county board (länsstyrelsen) — larger-scale but non-professional hobby activity is EXEMPT from the permit requirement (except breeding animals intended as feeder/feed animals). Welfare and enclosure standards apply (SJVFS 2019:15 ch. 1; enclosure size/enrichment per SJVFS 2019:29 ch. 11 §§17-18). Ironically R. rattus is classed as EXTINCT (RE) in the wild in Sweden, so captive pets pose essentially zero invasion risk. Cross-border transport of pet rodents needs no registration (commercial transport requires authorisation as an animal transporter); intra-EU commercial movement, or more than 5 pet animals, needs an Article 151 Animal Health Law self-declaration from a registered establishment — no TRACES notification and no health certificate. Non-EU import is tighter.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Swedish Board of Agriculture (Jordbruksverket), written reply June 2026: it is permitted to keep Rattus rattus as pets in Sweden as long as the animals are not caught in the wild, with NO permit and NO registration required (SJVFS 2019:15, ch. 1 §§4-5). Welfare and enclosure-size/enrichment standards apply (SJVFS 2019:15 ch. 1; SJVFS 2019:29 ch. 11 §§17-18). A permit is only relevant for PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) keeping, breeding, or selling — larger-scale but non-professional hobby activity is exempt (except breeding animals intended as feeder/feed animals); professional operators should ask their county administrative board (länsstyrelsen) whether a permit is needed. Cross-border transport of pet rodents needs no registration; commercial transport requires authorisation as an animal transporter, and intra-EU commercial movement (or more than 5 pet animals) needs an Article 151 Animal Health Law self-declaration from a registered establishment — no TRACES notification and no health certificate. The agency also confirmed the '6 enclosures' figure refers to the number of cages.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Jordbruksverket confirmed (June 2026) it is permitted to keep R. rattus as pets as long as they are not wild-caught, with no permit and no registration (SJVFS 2019:15 ch. 1 §§4-5). Djurskyddslagen 2018:1192 imposes welfare duties but no species ban; R. rattus is absent from the EU Union list and Sweden's national invasive list (Förordning 2026:311). Keepers must meet welfare/enclosure standards (SJVFS 2019:15 ch. 1; enclosure size/furnishing/enrichment per SJVFS 2019:29 ch. 11 §§17-18) and the social-species rule (keep ≥2 rats).

Sources: Sveriges Riksdag, Statens jordbruksverk, Sveriges Riksdag / Naturvårdsverket, EU / EUR-Lex

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Jordbruksverket confirmed (June 2026) that keeping, breeding, or selling pets other than dogs and cats at larger scale but NOT in a professional manner is EXEMPT from the permit requirement — so a private/hobby rattery needs no permit regardless of cage count. Only PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) breeding must ask the county administrative board (länsstyrelsen) whether a permit is required, and the exemption does NOT cover breeding animals intended to be sold as feeder/feed animals. (The agency clarified the '6 enclosures' figure refers to the number of cages.) Welfare standards apply throughout.

Sources: Sveriges Riksdag, Statens jordbruksverk, Statens jordbruksverk

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Free transfers and sales between hobbyists are permit-free: Jordbruksverket confirmed (June 2026) that larger-scale but non-professional keeping/breeding/selling of pets other than dogs and cats is exempt from the permit requirement (Sweden has no separate pet-shop licence). Only PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) selling must check with the county administrative board (länsstyrelsen). SJVFS 2019:15 sets sale conditions (health checks, documentation). No species ban or price cap on captive-bred R. rattus; the exemption excludes breeding animals sold as feeder/feed animals.

Sources: Sveriges Riksdag, Statens jordbruksverk

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Jordbruksverket confirmed (June 2026): cross-border transport of pet rodents needs NO registration. If animals are moved in connection with an economic activity, the carrier must be authorised as an animal transporter (SJVFS 2019:7; minimum rodent-container requirements in Annex/Bilaga 1.11). For intra-EU COMMERCIAL movement, or movement of more than 5 pet animals, no health certificate and no TRACES notification are required, but an Article 151 Animal Health Law (Reg. 2016/429) self-declaration is — issued by the operator at the place of origin, which must itself be registered as an establishment for terrestrial animals (Art. 84). There is no numeric cap on a single commercial movement and no fixed template for the self-declaration. Non-EU import follows different, tighter rules. Internal transport is unregulated beyond welfare. Never release.

Sources: Jordbruksverket, EU / EUR-Lex

Restrictions & responsibilities

Only PROFESSIONAL (yrkesmässig) keeping, breeding, or selling of pet rodents needs to check with your county administrative board (länsstyrelsen) about a permit — larger-scale but non-professional hobby activity is EXEMPT (Jordbruksverket, June 2026), except breeding animals intended to be sold as feeder/feed animals, which is not exempt. Transport in connection with an economic activity requires authorisation as an animal transporter (SJVFS 2019:7). Meet the welfare rules (minimum enclosure size, enrichment, and keep rats in groups of ≥2). Never release a roof rat.
  • If operating professionally, ask your länsstyrelsen whether a permit is required
  • For transport in connection with an economic activity, register as an authorised animal transporter with Jordbruksverket

Where: Länsstyrelsen (county administrative board); Jordbruksverket for transporter authorisation

Source: Statens jordbruksverk, Statens jordbruksverk

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Djurskyddslag (2018:1192) — Animal Welfare Act (no species ban for pet rodents; 6 kap. permit at scale) — Sveriges Riksdag
  • SJVFS 2019:15 — conditions for keeping/breeding/selling companion & hobby animals (covers rats/gnagare) — Statens jordbruksverk
  • SJVFS 2019:27 — permit obligation (tillståndsplikt); ~6-enclosure 'larger scale' threshold for rodents — Statens jordbruksverk
  • Förordning (2026:311) om invasiva främmande arter — national list (34 species, all plants/aquatic; R. rattus absent) — Sveriges Riksdag / Naturvårdsverket
  • Jordbruksverket — Gnagare som sällskapsdjur (rodents as pets; import + 5-animal intra-EU rule) — Jordbruksverket
  • Regulation (EU) 1143/2014 on invasive alien species — Union list (R. rattus not listed) — EU / EUR-Lex
  • Regulation (EU) 2016/429 — Animal Health Law (intra-EU movement framework) — EU / EUR-Lex
  • SLU Artdatabanken — svartråtta (Rattus rattus) Rödlista 2025: Utdöd (RE) in Swedish wild — SLU Artdatabanken
