item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Singapore? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Singapore

Summary. Singapore prohibits the roof rat as a pet, completely. It runs a closed 'positive list': only species the Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS, a cluster under the National Parks Board) has approved may be kept. The approved small-mammal list includes the domestic mouse (Mus musculus) alongside rabbits, hamsters, guinea pigs, gerbils and chinchillas — but NO species of the genus Rattus, so neither the roof rat (R. rattus) nor the ordinary fancy rat (R. norvegicus) may be kept. Because it is not a listed pet, R. rattus defaults to 'wildlife' under the Wildlife Act 1965, and s.5C(1) makes it a strict-liability offence to keep any wildlife without the Director-General's written approval (no such approval is available to the public). Breeding is separately barred by the Control of Vectors and Pesticides Act 1998 (CVPA), which defines any rodent 'capable of carrying' disease as a public-health vector and, under s.16, prohibits breeding vectors without permission; sale/transfer is blocked by the Wildlife Act (s.8) and the AVS pet-shop licensing rules (the hobbyist breeding exemption applies only to approved 'relevant pet animals'). The ONLY lawful pathway for any Rattus is institutional: an accredited Animal Research Facility (ARF) may import and keep lab rats — never a private pet keeper. One statutory quirk: the Wildlife (Exemption) Order 2020 cull-list names R. norvegicus and R. tanezumi (and Mus musculus castaneus, Suncus murinus) as exempt from the s.5C culling ban, but R. rattus is omitted, so a strict reading paradoxically gives the wild roof rat unpermitted-culling protection denied its cousins — an anomaly that offers a pet keeper nothing. Not CITES-listed; the closed positive list, not CITES, is the operative bar.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

R. rattus is not on the AVS approved-pet positive list (which permits mice, rabbits, hamsters, guinea pigs, gerbils, chinchillas — no Rattus), so it defaults to 'wildlife' under the Wildlife Act 1965. Section 5C(1) provides that 'a person must not intentionally kill, trap, take or keep any wildlife in any place unless the person has the Director-General's written approval to do so' — a strict-liability offence (belief that the animal is a domesticated pet is no defence), carrying up to S$20,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment for a first offence. The Wildlife Act's domestic-animal carve-outs (dogs, cats, livestock, poultry) do not include any rat, and no public permit/registration pathway exists to keep a roof rat. AVS guidance also treats rats as vermin that will not be allowed.

Sources: Singapore Statutes Online / Attorney-General's Chambers; administered by NParks, Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS (NParks)

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Breeding is interdicted by public-health law independent of the keeping ban. The Control of Vectors and Pesticides Act 1998 (CVPA) s.2 defines a 'vector' to include 'any rodent, including its young, which is carrying or causing, or capable of carrying or causing, any disease to human beings' — the test is the species' biological capacity, so a captive-bred, pathogen-free R. rattus is still a vector. CVPA s.16 ('Prohibition on breeding, etc., of vectors without Director-General's permission') makes it a strict criminal offence to intentionally breed vectors; no private hobbyist permit is ever issued (penalties under s.23 run to large fines and imprisonment). The only entities permitted to breed Rattus are licensed Animal Research Facilities. Keeping the animal to breed it is independently barred under the Wildlife Act s.5C, so a hobbyist breeding programme is doubly unlawful.

Sources: Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by NEA, Singapore Statutes Online / Attorney-General's Chambers; administered by NParks

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Sale or transfer (including giving away free) is blocked on two layers. (1) Wildlife Act 1965 s.8 prohibits selling, offering for sale, or exporting any wildlife without the Director-General's written approval; doing so in the course of an animal-related business is aggravated (s.5C(3)(b)(i): up to S$20,000 / 12 months even on a first offence). (2) The Animals and Birds (Licensing of Premises for Pet Shop and Other Purposes) Rules require an AVS pet-shop/breeding licence to distribute, breed, exhibit or sell pet animals (Rule 4), and AVS will not licence the sale of a non-positive-listed species. The Schedule 1 hobbyist 'breed-and-give-away-for-adoption' exemption applies only to a 'relevant pet animal or bird' — which excludes all Rattus — so it is legally void for the roof rat. Therefore one cannot lawfully sell, trade, or give away a roof rat in Singapore.

Sources: Singapore Statutes Online / Attorney-General's Chambers; administered by NParks, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS, Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Import/export of animals requires an AVS import licence under the Animals and Birds Act 1965 s.7 (no person may import any animal without the Director-General's licence). The framework bifurcates rodents into two mutually exclusive paths. PERSONAL PET import is allowed only for positive-listed small mammals — the AVS pet-import page lists rabbits, mice, hamsters, gerbils, guinea pigs and chinchillas, and the GoBusiness licensing system summarily rejects a personal pet application for any Rattus species; so personal import/transport of a roof rat is effectively PROHIBITED. The ONLY lawful pathway is institutional: an accredited Animal Research Facility (ARF) licensed under the Animals and Birds (Care and Use of Animals for Scientific Purposes) Rules may import lab 'rats' from an AVS-approved overseas facility, with a commercial veterinary health certificate, pre-arrival border inspection (≥5 days' notice) and quarantine (import licence ~S$174 express). That route is closed to private citizens. Not CITES-listed. Never release.

Sources: Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS (NParks), Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks, Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks

Restrictions & responsibilities

The roof rat cannot lawfully be kept, bred, sold, given away, or imported as a pet in Singapore. No Rattus species is on the AVS approved-pet positive list (only the mouse, Mus musculus, among small rodents), so the roof rat is 'wildlife' under the Wildlife Act 1965 — keeping it without the Director-General's written approval is a strict-liability offence under s.5C (up to S$20,000 / 12 months), breeding it is barred as a public-health 'vector' under CVPA 1998 s.16, and selling/transferring it is barred under Wildlife Act s.8 and the AVS pet-shop licensing rules. The ban is genus-wide (the ordinary fancy rat R. norvegicus is barred too). There is no private permit, licence, or hobbyist exemption. Never release.
  • Do not keep, breed, sell, give away, or import a roof rat in Singapore — no private permit pathway exists (Wildlife Act s.5C; CVPA s.16; Animals and Birds Act / pet-shop rules)
  • Never release a roof rat (it is a documented public-health vector and pest)

Where: Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), National Parks Board

Source: Singapore Statutes Online / Attorney-General's Chambers; administered by NParks, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by NEA, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS (NParks), Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks

The only lawful route by which any Rattus may be imported, bred or kept in Singapore is institutional research. An accredited Animal Research Facility (ARF) licensed under the Animals and Birds (Care and Use of Animals for Scientific Purposes) Rules — with an Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC), an attending veterinarian and AVS oversight — may import lab rats from an AVS-approved overseas facility under a commercial veterinary health certificate, with pre-arrival border inspection (≥5 days' notice) and quarantine. This pathway is closed to private individuals and confers no private pet-keeping right.
  • (Institutions only) Hold a valid AVS Animal Research Facility (ARF) licence with an IACUC and attending veterinarian
  • Import lab rats only from an AVS-accredited overseas facility, with a commercial veterinary health certificate
  • Book border-control inspection at least 5 days before arrival; complete inspection and quarantine on arrival

Forms: AVS — Importing and exporting laboratory animals, GoBusiness — Licence for Animal Research Facility · Where: Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks (ARF licence + import licence via GoBusiness) · Fees: Import licence for non-food animals/biologics ~S$174 (express, issued one working day after submission)

Source: Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks, Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Singapore. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Official sources

  • Wildlife Act 1965 (2020 Revised Edition) — s.5C (no keeping/killing/trapping/taking wildlife without Director-General approval), s.8 (sale/export of wildlife), s.2 'wildlife' definition, s.6 'defence of property' — Singapore Statutes Online / Attorney-General's Chambers; administered by NParks
  • Animals and Birds Act 1965 — prevention of epizootic disease; s.7 import licence; premises licensing power — Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS (NParks)
  • Control of Vectors and Pesticides Act 1998 — s.2 'vector' (rodent capable of carrying disease), s.16 (prohibition on breeding vectors without Director-General permission), s.23 (penalties) — Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by NEA
  • Wildlife (Exemption) Order 2020 — Schedule exempts R. norvegicus, R. tanezumi, Mus musculus castaneus, Suncus murinus from the s.5C culling ban; R. rattus omitted — Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; made under Wildlife Act 1965
  • Animals and Birds (Licensing of Premises for Pet Shop and Other Purposes) Rules — Rule 4 (pet-shop/breeding licence to distribute/breed/exhibit/sell) + Schedule 1 (hobbyist exemption limited to a 'relevant pet animal or bird') — Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS
  • Animals and Birds (Care and Use of Animals for Scientific Purposes) Rules — Animal Research Facility (ARF) licensing for laboratory animals — Singapore Statutes Online / AGC; administered by AVS
  • AVS — Animals that can be kept as pets (approved positive list: rabbits, mice, hamsters, guinea pigs, gerbils, chinchillas; no Rattus) — Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks
  • AVS — Importing small mammals (personal pet import allowed only for approved species: rabbits, mice, hamsters, gerbils, guinea pigs, chinchillas; AVS import licence + quarantine) — Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks
  • AVS — Importing and exporting laboratory animals (lab 'rats' permitted only for accredited Animal Research Facilities; commercial health certificate, border inspection, quarantine) — Animal & Veterinary Service (AVS), NParks

Search terms: Rattus rattus, black rat, roof rat, ship rat.

Last reviewed 2026-06-12. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Slovakia? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Slovakia

Summary. Slovakia is permissive for the roof rat, now grounded in the operative statutory texts. Slovak law uses a negative-list model — every species may be privately kept unless named on a prohibitive list — and R. rattus appears on NONE of them: not the EU Union list of invasive alien species (Reg. 1143/2014 + Implementing Reg. 2016/1141, no Rattus), not Slovakia's national invasive list (Government Reg. 449/2019 Z.z. Annex 2 as am. 396/2023, which names mink and similar mammals but no Rattus), not CITES, and not a protected native under Act 543/2002. Decree 283/2020 Z.z. §1(3)(a) expressly defines 'spoločenské zvieratá' (companion animals) to include rodents (hlodavce), and Slovak law draws no distinction between R. rattus and the fancy rat R. norvegicus (both are 'potkan' for spatial/welfare purposes). Net effect: keeping a captive-bred roof rat is fully legal with no permit or registration; breeding/selling/GIVING animals to another party triggers a Regional Veterinary & Food Administration (RVPS) breeder-facility registration under Act 39/2007 + Decree 283/2020; cross-border movement follows EU animal-health certificate rules (rodents are excluded from the EU Pet Passport).

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Keeping a captive-bred R. rattus purely as a private pet is fully legal and requires no permit, fee, or registration. The DR confirms R. rattus is absent from the EU Union list (Reg. 1143/2014 + Implementing Reg. 2016/1141) and from Annex 2 of Government Reg. 449/2019 Z.z. (as am. 396/2023) — the operative national invasive list names mink (Mustela vison) and the like but no member of genus Rattus. It is not CITES-listed and, as a synanthropic non-native, holds no protected-native status under Act 543/2002. Decree 283/2020 Z.z. §1(3)(a) expressly includes rodents (hlodavce) in the 'spoločenské zvieratá' (companion animal) definition, and ŠVPS SR guidance states the facility-registration mandate 'does not apply to households in which companion animals are kept exclusively for private non-commercial purposes' — only baseline welfare duties (Act 39/2007, Decree 283/2020) attach.

Sources: National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex), Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development SR (Slov-Lex), Government of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex), Government of the Slovak Republic, European Union (EUR-Lex), National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex)

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Breeding R. rattus and retaining ALL offspring within one's own household remains exempt from registration. But breeding with intent to transfer any offspring (sell, exchange, or donate) makes the keeper a 'chovné zariadenie' (breeding facility, Decree 283/2020 §1(3)(b)) and requires prior registration with the competent Regional Veterinary & Food Administration (RVPS) — a major 2022 amendment to Act 39/2007 ended unregulated hobby breeding of companion animals, and ŠVPS SR enforces it across rodents with no small-scale/accidental-litter exemption. Registration is by filing 'Ohlásenie začatia činnosti chovného zariadenia pre spoločenské zvieratá' to the local RVPS (hobbyists give rodné číslo; businesses give IČO) before bringing in breeding stock; the facility must meet Decree 283/2020 spatial/welfare standards (the rat — 'potkan,' both Rattus species — needs ≥0.20 m² for one animal, +0.10 m² per additional, ≥0.30 m height). So pure personal breeding with no transfer = legal (no permit); breeding-for-transfer = legal_with_permit.

Sources: National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex), Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development SR (Slov-Lex), ŠVPS SR

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Any domestic transfer of ownership of R. rattus — sale, exchange, OR free donation/adoption — is legal but classed as a regulated activity requiring the transferor to hold an active RVPS breeder registration; ŠVPS SR trade guidance is explicit that there is NO small-scale or accidental-litter exemption, and gifting is treated the same as selling (the rationale is epidemiological traceability of every transferred animal). No species-specific permit distinguishes R. rattus from R. norvegicus (both are rodents in one legal class) and no CITES permit applies. A person who buys from multiple breeders to resell is instead an animal-collection center ('stredisko na zhromažďovanie'), needing the stricter approval (schválenie) with pre-operational inspection rather than mere registration; a continuous for-profit seller additionally needs a Trade License (IČO) under Act 455/1991.

Sources: National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex), Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development SR (Slov-Lex), ŠVPS SR

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-10

DOMESTIC transport within Slovakia is essentially unregulated administratively — no passport, health certificate, or microchip — subject only to general welfare (ventilation, temperature, space). INTRA-EU: rodents are explicitly EXCLUDED from the EU Pet Passport (Reg. 576/2013, dogs/cats/ferrets only). Non-commercial movement (≤5 animals, no ownership transfer, owner travels within 5 days) needs an official rodent health certificate plus a clinical exam by an official vet at origin; commercial movement (a buyer across a border, or >5 animals) must be pre-notified in TRACES NT with an intra-Union veterinary certificate, from a registered facility to a registered RVPS facility (Reg. 2016/429 + Delegated Reg. 2020/692). THIRD-COUNTRY IMPORT is the most demanding: WOAH-member origin, entry only via a designated Border Control Post with a Common Health Entry Document (CHED), an official-vet health certificate (translated to Slovak), and origin from a registered/approved holding — no mandatory state quarantine if paperwork is flawless. R. rattus is on no prohibited-import or CITES list. Microchip nuance: imported rodents must carry an ISO 11784 transponder; a size-based derogation exists but BCP vets typically expect adult roof rats to be chipped, so a microchip should be treated as the default unless an official vet grants a written waiver. Never release.

Sources: National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex), ŠVPS SR, ŠVPS SR, European Union (EUR-Lex)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Keeping a captive-bred roof rat is legal with no permit (R. rattus is on neither the EU Union list nor the Slovak national invasive list, and rodents are companion animals under Decree 283/2020 §1(3)(a)). The ONE domestic formality: anyone who transfers animals to others — by sale, exchange, OR free gift — must first register the breeding facility ('chovné zariadenie') with their Regional Veterinary & Food Administration (RVPS) under Act 39/2007 + Decree 283/2020. There is no small-scale or accidental-litter exemption. Continuous for-profit selling additionally needs a Trade License (živnostenské oprávnenie, IČO).
  • Keeping only (household, non-commercial): nothing required
  • To breed-and-transfer / sell / give: file 'Ohlásenie začatia činnosti chovného zariadenia pre spoločenské zvieratá' with your local RVPS BEFORE bringing in breeding stock (hobbyist = rodné číslo; business = IČO)
  • Meet Decree 283/2020 spatial/welfare conditions (rat: ≥0.20 m² for one, +0.10 m²/animal, ≥0.30 m height; easy-to-clean, ventilated, lit, predator/parasite-protected enclosure)
  • Continuous for-profit sale: also obtain a Trade License (IČO) under Act 455/1991
  • Acting as a broker/collection center: apply for the stricter approval (schválenie) with pre-operational state-vet inspection

Forms: Ohlásenie začatia činnosti chovného zariadenia pre spoločenské zvieratá · Where: Local Regional Veterinary & Food Administration (RVPS) — one of 40 territorial offices · Fees: Companion-animal facility registration fee not explicitly published in the operative texts (the €33 individual / €100 corporate figures cited in bulletins are for FARM-animal holdings); confirm current fee with the RVPS

Source: National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex), Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development SR (Slov-Lex), ŠVPS SR

Cross-border movement needs EU animal-health documentation (rodents are excluded from the EU Pet Passport). Intra-EU non-commercial = an official rodent health certificate + clinical exam by an official vet at origin; intra-EU commercial = TRACES NT pre-notification + intra-Union veterinary certificate between registered facilities; third-country import = WOAH-member origin, entry via a designated EU Border Control Post with a CHED + official-vet health certificate (translated to Slovak) from a registered holding. ISO 11784 microchip generally required for imported rodents (size derogation is BCP-discretionary — default to chipping). Domestic transport needs no documents. Never release.
  • Domestic: no documents (welfare in transit only)
  • Intra-EU non-commercial: official rodent health certificate + origin clinical exam by an official vet
  • Intra-EU commercial: TRACES NT pre-notification + intra-Union veterinary certificate (registered → registered RVPS facility)
  • Third-country import: WOAH-member origin; pre-notify the Border Control Post (≥1 working day) via CHED; carry an official-vet health certificate translated to Slovak from a registered/approved holding; microchip (ISO 11784) unless an official vet grants a written size waiver

Forms: Rodent health certificate, Common Health Entry Document (CHED), Intra-Union veterinary certificate (TRACES NT) · Where: ŠVPS SR (competent authority for movement/import); EU Border Control Post for third-country entry · Fees: Per official-vet examination + certification; BCP/CHED handling fees for imports

Source: ŠVPS SR, ŠVPS SR, European Union (EUR-Lex)

Releasing or abandoning a roof rat is prohibited under Slovak animal-welfare law (Act 39/2007 + Decree 283/2020); severe neglect can escalate to criminal animal cruelty under the Criminal Code (fines, animal-keeping bans, asset forfeiture, possible imprisonment). Rehome responsibly; never release.

Fees: Administrative fines up to €1,000 (individuals) / €20,000 (legal entities) for veterinary-care violations under Act 39/2007

Source: National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Regulation (EU) 1143/2014 + Implementing Reg. 2016/1141 (Union list of invasive alien species; R. rattus NOT listed) — European Union (EUR-Lex)
  • Nariadenie vlády SR č. 449/2019 Z.z. — Slovak national list of invasive non-native species of concern (Annex 2: mink etc.; no Rattus) — Government of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex)
  • Nariadenie vlády SR č. 396/2023 Z.z. — amendment to the national invasive-species list (449/2019) — Government of the Slovak Republic
  • Zákon č. 150/2019 Z.z. — prevention & management of invasive non-native species (Art. 9 derogation framework) — National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex)
  • Zákon č. 39/2007 Z.z. o veterinárnej starostlivosti — Veterinary Care Act (companion-animal framework; breeder-facility registration on transfer; 2022 am.) — National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex)
  • Vyhláška č. 283/2020 Z.z. — companion-animal protection; §1(3)(a) defines rodents (hlodavce) as companion animals; §6+Annex spatial standards — Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development SR (Slov-Lex)
  • Zákon č. 543/2002 Z.z. o ochrane prírody a krajiny — Nature & Landscape Protection Act (R. rattus is not a protected native) — National Council of the Slovak Republic (Slov-Lex)
  • ŠVPS SR — Registrácia chovu spoločenských zvierat (companion-animal breeder-facility registration procedure) — ŠVPS SR
  • ŠVPS SR — Predaj, darovanie, adopcia, nákup a obchodovanie so zvieratami (any ownership transfer = registered activity; no small-scale exemption) — ŠVPS SR
  • ŠVPS SR — Zdravotné požiadavky na neobchodné premiestňovanie živých zvierat radu hlodavce do SR (Doc. 21-SVPS-010; rodent non-commercial movement health requirements) — ŠVPS SR
  • ŠVPS SR — Zdravotné požiadavky pre dovoz živých zvierat rádu hlodavce do SR (third-country rodent import health requirements; BCP/CHED, ISO 11784 microchip + size derogation) — ŠVPS SR
  • EU Animal Health Law (Reg. 2016/429) + Delegated Reg. 2020/692 + Reg. 576/2013 (Pet Passport excludes rodents) — rodent movement/import certificates — European Union (EUR-Lex)
  • Slovenský klub chovateľov drobných hlodavcov — RODENTIA (Slovak rodent fanciers' club; registered breeders) — practical-pathway evidence — RODENTIA club (secondary, practice evidence)
  • CITES — Slovakia party profile; Rattus rattus not on any appendix — CITES Secretariat

Search terms: Rattus rattus, potkan tmavý, potkan čierny, krysa, roof rat, black rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Thailand? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Thailand

Summary. Thailand is permissive by default for the roof rat. The Wild Animal Conservation and Protection Act B.E. 2562 (2019) regulates only species on its conserved/protected/controlled schedules — and R. rattus is on none of them. Thai law treats it 'functionally rather than nominally': it doesn't name 'domesticated rats' as exempt; rather, an unscheduled species simply falls outside the Department of National Parks (DNP) wildlife-permit system, so you never have to prove a roof rat is captive-bred vs. wild-caught. R. rattus is classified as a native/naturalized 'Least Concern' agricultural pest — pointedly NOT an Invasive Alien Species (that label, and its management mandates, fall on R. norvegicus), so there is no eradication/possession ban aimed at pet keepers. Keeping/breeding/giving a captive-bred roof rat is therefore unregulated at the federal level, subject only to the Cruelty Prevention & Welfare of Animals Act B.E. 2557 (2014) care duties; small rodents are sold openly (e.g., Chatuchak market). Bangkok's Animal Keeping Ordinance B.E. 2567 (2024) adds property-size pet-density quotas that textually include 'mammals' (so they could touch caged rats), but its registration/microchipping mandate is limited to dogs and cats, enforcement is nuisance-complaint driven, and the council DELAYED the whole ordinance one year — now effective 10 January 2027. The one hard permit step is IMPORT: bringing a live rodent into Thailand requires a Department of Livestock Development (DLD) import permit (Form R1/1), an origin-authority-endorsed veterinary health certificate, a 500 THB/animal fee, and a discretionary (often-waived) 30-day quarantine. Internal inter-province movement technically falls under the Animal Epidemics Act B.E. 2558 (2015) R-form chain, but that targets livestock and is not enforced against private pet rodents. No Thai law expressly prohibits private keeping/breeding/transfer of captive-bred R. rattus. Never release a nonnative.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

R. rattus is absent from every DNP conserved/protected/controlled wildlife schedule under WACPA B.E. 2562 (which regulates only scheduled species), so DNP wildlife jurisdiction simply does not attach — and because the test is scheduling, not 'domestication,' there is no requirement to prove a kept rat is captive-bred. It is classified as a native/naturalized 'Least Concern' agricultural pest, NOT an Invasive Alien Species (that designation falls on R. norvegicus under ONEP's IAS List 1), so no possession/eradication mandate targets private keepers. The Cruelty Prevention & Welfare of Animals Act B.E. 2557 (2014) imposes baseline care duties on any kept animal but bans no non-listed species. Bangkok's B.E. 2567 (2024) ordinance designates 'mammals' a controlled category with property-size density quotas (so it textually could reach caged rats), but registration/microchipping is dog/cat-only, enforcement is nuisance-driven, and the ordinance is delayed to 10 Jan 2027. 'Unclear' only because no official text affirmatively names R. rattus as a permitted pet; legality is derived from its absence on all prohibited schedules.

Sources: DNP (Thailand) / CITES MA, Thailand (via FAO FAOLEX), Office of Natural Resources & Environmental Policy and Planning (ONEP), Thailand, BMA (legal summary, ILCT), Bangkok Post (reporting BMA Council vote)

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

Breeding a non-scheduled, non-CITES species is outside the WACPA permit system, and there is no DNP/DLD 'rat-breeder licence' for domestic non-livestock rodents. Private, non-commercial breeding — keeping or giving away offspring — is entirely unregulated beyond welfare duties; small rodents are bred and sold openly (Chatuchak). The regulated layer attaches to the PREMISES and OPERATOR, not the species: under the Public Health Act B.E. 2535 (1992), local municipalities classify commercial animal breeding/boarding/retail as a 'hazardous activity to health' (กิจการที่เป็นอันตรายต่อสุขภาพ) needing a district-office premises permit (waste/ventilation/zoning inspection). Thai law sets no codified numeric threshold where a hobbyist becomes 'commercial,' so occasional give-away or cost-covering breeding is, in practice, ignored until scale generates waste/traffic/nuisance.

Sources: DNP (Thailand) / CITES MA, Thailand (municipal ordinance under the Public Health Act, illustrative)

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-11

Trade restrictions under WACPA apply only to scheduled/controlled wildlife, so no wildlife statute bars selling or gifting a captive-bred R. rattus, and non-commercial gifting between private parties is unrestricted (beyond welfare duties). Operating as a retail business adds general Department of Business Development (DBD) registration plus, at premises scale, the same municipal 'hazardous activity to health' permit as breeding — these attach to the business/premises, not to the species. Not CITES-listed. Ambiguity remains only over whether open-market sale of unlisted rodents needs a specific DLD animal-dealer licence or merely a local commercial-premises permit (the DR found the latter to be the practical answer).

Sources: DNP (Thailand) / CITES MA, Thailand (municipal ordinance under the Public Health Act, illustrative), CITES Secretariat

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-11

Regardless of its unlisted wildlife status, the Department of Livestock Development (DLD) holds absolute authority over the movement of all live animals under the Animal Epidemics Act B.E. 2558 (2015); for cross-border movement R. rattus is treated as a 'restricted live animal.' IMPORT requires: (1) an advance DLD import permit (Form R1/1), applied for at the Animal Quarantine Station at the port of entry no fewer than 7 and no more than 60 days before travel; (2) an Official Health Certificate from an accredited origin-country vet within 10 days of travel, formally endorsed (wet-ink) by the origin national veterinary authority (e.g., USDA APHIS) — electronic copies are routinely rejected; (3) a 500 THB/animal fee at the airport, after which the officer issues the Notice of Import Approval (R-6) and Import Licence (R-7). The DLD holds discretionary authority to impose a 30-day quarantine on imported rodents but frequently waives it for healthy private pets with flawless paperwork from low-risk origins. Microchipping is strictly mandated for dogs/cats and only ambiguously for rodents — strongly advised (or get written AQS confirmation that photographic ID suffices). INTERNAL inter-province movement technically falls under the Animal Epidemics Act R.3/R.4 movement-permit chain, but that text targets agricultural livestock and is not enforced against private pet rats (negligible-enforcement gray zone). Never release a nonnative.

Sources: Department of Livestock Development (Thailand), Department of Livestock Development (Thailand)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Keeping/breeding/giving a captive-bred roof rat in Thailand needs no wildlife permit (R. rattus is unscheduled), only welfare-law care. The one hard permit step is IMPORT: a DLD import permit (Form R1/1, applied for 7-60 days ahead at the port-of-entry Animal Quarantine Station) + an origin-authority-endorsed veterinary health certificate (issued within 10 days, wet-ink) + a 500 THB/animal fee, with a discretionary (often-waived) 30-day quarantine. Microchipping is advised for rodents (mandatory for dogs/cats; ambiguous for rats — confirm with the AQS).
  • Apply for the DLD import permit (Form R1/1) at the destination Animal Quarantine Station 7-60 days before travel
  • Obtain an Official Health Certificate from an accredited origin-country vet within 10 days, endorsed (wet-ink) by the origin national authority (e.g., USDA APHIS)
  • On arrival use the 'Goods to Declare' channel; pay 500 THB/animal; receive the R-6 (approval) and R-7 (import licence)
  • Microchip the rat if biologically safe, or get written AQS confirmation that photographic ID is accepted

Forms: DLD Import Permit (Form R1/1) — Animal Quarantine Station · Where: Department of Livestock Development (DLD) — Animal Quarantine Station (port of entry, e.g. Suvarnabhumi) · Fees: 500 THB per animal (airport processing); origin-country vet fee for the health certificate

Source: Department of Livestock Development (Thailand), Department of Livestock Development (Thailand)

Bangkok only: the Animal Keeping Ordinance B.E. 2567 (2024) sets property-size pet-density quotas (e.g., 1 pet in a 20-80 sq.m condo; up to 2 over 80 sq.m) for 'controlled' categories that textually include 'mammals,' so several caged rats could in principle count toward the limit. Registration/microchipping under the ordinance applies to dogs and cats only, and enforcement is nuisance-complaint driven — keep enclosures clean, secure, and odor-free. The ordinance's effective date was postponed one year to 10 January 2027. Commercial breeding/retail premises separately need a municipal 'hazardous activity to health' permit under the Public Health Act B.E. 2535.
  • In Bangkok, keep rat enclosures secure, ventilated, and sanitary to avoid nuisance complaints (the practical enforcement trigger)
  • If breeding/selling at commercial scale, obtain the district-office 'hazardous activity to health' premises permit

Where: Bangkok Metropolitan Administration district office (Veterinary Public Health) / your local municipality

Source: BMA (legal summary, ILCT), Bangkok Post (reporting BMA Council vote), Thailand (municipal ordinance under the Public Health Act, illustrative)

It is illegal to release/abandon any captive animal into the public domain under Thai urban animal-abandonment ordinances, and R. rattus is a documented agricultural pest — keep them contained and rehome responsibly; never release.

Where: Local district office

Source: Office of Natural Resources & Environmental Policy and Planning (ONEP), Thailand

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Official sources

  • Wild Animal Conservation & Protection Act B.E. 2562 (2019) — regulates only conserved/protected/controlled scheduled species; R. rattus on none — DNP (Thailand) / CITES MA
  • Cruelty Prevention & Welfare of Animals Act B.E. 2557 (2014) — care duties for any kept animal — Thailand (via FAO FAOLEX)
  • ONEP / TH-BIF — Invasive Alien Species registry: R. norvegicus is IAS List 1; R. rattus is native/naturalized 'Least Concern' (agricultural pest, not IAS) — Office of Natural Resources & Environmental Policy and Planning (ONEP), Thailand
  • Bangkok Animal Keeping Ordinance B.E. 2567 (2024) — property-size pet-density quotas; 'mammals' a controlled category; dog/cat-only microchip/registration — BMA (legal summary, ILCT)
  • Bangkok City Hall postpones the B.E. 2567 pet-control ordinance one year — now effective 10 January 2027 — Bangkok Post (reporting BMA Council vote)
  • Public Health Act B.E. 2535 (1992) — municipalities license commercial animal breeding/retail as a 'hazardous activity to health' (premises permit) — Thailand (municipal ordinance under the Public Health Act, illustrative)
  • DLD — Importation of live animals (rodents need a DLD permit; Form R1/1, AQS, 500 THB, discretionary 30-day quarantine) — Department of Livestock Development (Thailand)
  • Animal Epidemics Act B.E. 2558 (2015) — DLD authority over movement of all live animals; import R-forms + domestic R.3/R.4 movement permits — Department of Livestock Development (Thailand)
  • CITES appendices — Rattus rattus not listed — CITES Secretariat

Search terms: Rattus rattus, หนูดำ, หนูท้องขาว, black rat, roof rat.

Last reviewed 2026-06-11. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Turkey (Türkiye)? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Turkey (Türkiye)

Summary. Turkey is permissive-by-omission for the roof rat: under continental 'that which is not prohibited is permitted' doctrine (zımni izin), a private citizen needs no permit to keep captive-bred Rattus rattus. R. rattus is on no protected or huntable wildlife list under Law No. 4915 (Kara Avcılığı Kanunu) — it doesn't appear in the Central Hunting Commission (Merkez Av Komisyonu) EK-1 (strictly protected) or EK-2 (huntable) annexes — and it's not on CITES or the Bern Convention appendices; outside wildlife law, it's treated by health authorities as a pest rodent (zararlı kemirgen) when wild, but the moment it is captive-bred and kept as a pet it falls inside the broad 'ev ve süs hayvanı' (pet/ornamental animal) category of Law No. 5199 (Animal Protection Law) and is fully protected by its anti-cruelty provisions. Turkish law does not distinguish R. rattus from the fancy rat (R. norvegicus) — both are simply 'kemirgenler' — and an open pet-rodent trade runs on platforms like petcim.com. Private keeping, hobby breeding, and peer-to-peer gifting are unregulated and permit-free; COMMERCIAL breeding/selling needs a licensed facility (provincial establishment/operating permit + responsible veterinarian) under Regulation No. 15374 plus Law No. 5996. The one real barrier is cross-border IMPORT: Customs Circular 2011/39 limits duty-free passenger pet entry to cats/dogs/birds/aquarium fish only — rodents are excluded — so personal/passenger import is effectively blocked, leaving only a burdensome commercial-freight import pathway through GKGM with an origin veterinary health certificate and border-post inspection. Not CITES-listed; never release.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Private keeping of captive-bred R. rattus requires no permit. Under Turkish administrative law a private citizen may do anything not expressly prohibited (zımni izin / permissive-by-omission), and no statute names or bans the keeping of unlisted small rodents. Law No. 4915 (Land Hunting Law) reaches only listed game/protected wild species, and R. rattus is on neither the EK-1 nor EK-2 annex of the annual Merkez Av Komisyonu decision (it is classified as a pest, outside wildlife law); it is also unlisted on CITES and the Bern Convention. Once captive-bred and kept in a domicile, the animal falls within the intent-based 'ev ve süs hayvanı' (pet/ornamental animal) definition of Law No. 5199 (Art. 3(i), am. Law No. 7527/2024) and is comprehensively protected from abuse — so it is affirmatively lawful to own, not merely unregulated. The only realistic local touchpoint is municipal Zabıta enforcement of generic hygiene/nuisance ordinances, which cannot reach a sanitary, properly kept animal.

Sources: Grand National Assembly of Turkey, Grand National Assembly of Turkey, Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry / DKMP, CITES Secretariat, Council of Europe

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Private, non-commercial (hobby) breeding of captive-bred R. rattus is unregulated — Turkish law sets no numerical or licensing threshold for an individual breeding unlisted rodents in a private domicile, so an accidental litter given to friends is permit-free. COMMERCIAL breeding ('üretim' of kemirgenler for gain) requires a licensed facility under Regulation No. 15374 (Ev ve Süs Hayvanlarının Üretim, Satış, Barınma ve Eğitim Yerleri Hakkında Yönetmelik), which explicitly covers rodents: the operator must obtain a provincial establishment permit (Kuruluş İzni) with zoning-compliant blueprints and then an operating permit (the EK-4 İş Yeri Çalışma İzin Belgesi) after a government-veterinarian inspection, maintain disinfectable facilities with a separate quarantine unit, contract a Responsible Veterinarian (Sorumlu Veteriner Hekim), keep origin/health/disposition records, and submit to (at least quarterly) inspections; Law No. 5996 reinforces Ministry approval for commercial pet-animal production. So: legal (hobby/private) and legal_with_permit at commercial scale. The exact hobby-to-commercial threshold (litter volume, recurring sales, public advertising on e-commerce) is enforcement-discretionary and the one residual ambiguity.

Sources: Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry, Grand National Assembly of Turkey, Grand National Assembly of Turkey

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Private peer-to-peer transfer, gifting, or adoption of captive-bred R. rattus is unregulated — there is no registration, microchipping, or reporting requirement for unlisted rodents (governed only by the general Turkish Code of Obligations and Law No. 5199 welfare duties), and platforms like petcim.com openly host rodent sale/adoption listings ('kemirgen') without enforcement. COMMERCIAL sale requires a licensed physical facility (the same Regulation No. 15374 establishment/operating permit + Responsible Veterinarian) and the seller must complete a municipal animal-care training/certification program under Law No. 5199. Importantly, the 2021/2024 reform of Law No. 5199 (am. Law No. 7527) that BANNED pet-shop display/retail sale of cats and dogs DELIBERATELY EXEMPTED rodents (kemirgenler) — along with birds and aquarium fish — so a licensed urban pet shop may still breed, display in glass enclosures, and sell R. rattus. So: legal (private give/adopt) and legal_with_permit (commercial). Trade in LISTED wild species is separately restricted under Law 4915's wildlife-trade regulation, but that does not reach captive-bred, off-list R. rattus.

Sources: Grand National Assembly of Turkey, Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry, Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry / DKMP, petcim.com (secondary, market practice)

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

INTERNAL transport is effectively unregulated: no domestic movement permit, internal passport, or provincial check is required for pet rodents — only the general Law No. 5199 / Law No. 5996 welfare standard (secure, ventilated, temperature-protected enclosure) applies; commercial livestock-transport rules do not reach small numbers of pet rodents in a private vehicle. IMPORT is the real hurdle and is bifurcated. PASSENGER-accompanied import is effectively blocked: Customs Circular 2011/39 (Ministry of Trade), Annex 9, limits duty-free passenger pets to cats, dogs, birds and aquarium fish ('kedi, köpek ve kuş ile sınırlı'), max 2 pets / 10 fish — rodents are unequivocally excluded, with NO discretionary clearance, so a passenger-carried R. rattus is denied entry regardless of paperwork. COMMERCIAL import remains a lawful pathway: the animal must enter as live commercial freight through a Veterinary Border Inspection Post with prior GKGM (Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry) approval issued from Ankara, an origin-country official veterinary health certificate, documentary + physical border-vet inspection, a customs broker, and standard live-animal tariffs/VAT (Law No. 5996; Regulation No. 15541, drafted on EU 998/2003 lines). EXPORT uses a GKGM veterinary health certificate. So overall legal_with_permit. Never release (Law 5199 anti-abandonment).

Sources: Ministry of Trade (T.C. Ticaret Bakanlığı), Grand National Assembly of Turkey, Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry, USDA APHIS (secondary)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Private keeping, hobby breeding, and peer-to-peer gifting/adoption of captive-bred R. rattus need NO permit (the species is outside wildlife law and inside the general pet-rodent/'ev ve süs hayvanı' category). COMMERCIAL breeding or selling needs a licensed facility — a provincial establishment permit (Kuruluş İzni) plus the EK-4 operating permit (İş Yeri Çalışma İzin Belgesi) under Regulation No. 15374, with disinfectable premises, a quarantine unit, a contracted Responsible Veterinarian, record-keeping, and ≥quarterly inspections; commercial sellers must also hold a municipal animal-care training certificate (Law No. 5199). Personal/PASSENGER import is blocked (Customs Circular 2011/39 excludes rodents from duty-free passenger pets); the only lawful import is as commercial freight via GKGM (Ankara approval + origin veterinary health certificate + Veterinary Border Inspection Post). Export needs a GKGM veterinary health certificate. Never release a captive-bred rat (Law 5199 anti-abandonment).
  • Private owner: no permit, registration, or microchip required to keep, hobby-breed, or gift/adopt a captive-bred roof rat
  • Commercial breeding/sale: obtain the provincial Kuruluş İzni (establishment) + EK-4 Çalışma İzni (operating) permit for a rodent production/sale facility, with a contracted Responsible Veterinarian and a separate quarantine unit
  • Commercial seller: complete the municipal animal-care training and obtain the completion certificate (Law No. 5199)
  • Import (the only lawful route for a personal pet): secure prior GKGM (Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry) import approval from Ankara, an origin-country official veterinary health certificate, and clear the animal as live commercial cargo through a Veterinary Border Inspection Post with a customs broker (passenger-accompanied import is NOT available for rodents)
  • Export: obtain a GKGM veterinary health certificate (e-Devlet)

Forms: EK-4 İş Yeri Çalışma İzin Belgesi (Annex-4 Workplace Operating Permit) — commercial breeding/sale facility, issued by the Provincial Directorate of Agriculture & Forestry, Official veterinary health certificate (origin-country, endorsed) — required for commercial import via GKGM · Where: Provincial Directorate of the Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry + municipality (facility licensing); GKGM / Ankara + Veterinary Border Inspection Post (import/export); DKMP (wildlife-status confirmation, if requested) · Fees: Facility permit fees set provincially/municipally; commercial import subject to standard live-animal customs duties + VAT (no duty-free passenger exemption for rodents). Private keeping/gifting: none.

Source: Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry, Ministry of Trade (T.C. Ticaret Bakanlığı), Grand National Assembly of Turkey, Grand National Assembly of Turkey

Releasing or abandoning a captive-bred roof rat is prohibited. Law No. 5199 bars abandoning pets or releasing them into environments where they cannot survive; owners must rehome the animal or surrender it to an animal shelter. Releasing a domesticated R. rattus also conflicts with pest/invasive-control law (the wild roof rat is a 'zararlı kemirgen' that municipalities are mandated to suppress). Rehome responsibly; never release.

Source: Grand National Assembly of Turkey, Ministry of Health (T.C. Sağlık Bakanlığı)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Law No. 5199 — Hayvanları Koruma Kanunu (Animal Protection Law, 2004), am. Law No. 7527 (2024); 'ev ve süs hayvanı' definition (Art. 3(i)); anti-abandonment; cat/dog pet-shop display ban EXEMPTS rodents; seller training certificate — Grand National Assembly of Turkey
  • Law No. 4915 — Kara Avcılığı Kanunu (Land Hunting Law); regulates only listed game/protected wild species (R. rattus not listed) — Grand National Assembly of Turkey
  • 2025-2026 Merkez Av Komisyonu Kararı (Central Hunting Commission Decision; EK-1 strictly protected / EK-2 huntable — R. rattus absent), OG 6 Jul 2025 — Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry / DKMP
  • Ev ve Süs Hayvanlarının Üretim, Satış, Barınma ve Eğitim Yerleri Hakkında Yönetmelik (Reg. No. 15374) — covers kemirgenler; Kuruluş İzni + EK-4 Çalışma İzni facility licensing — Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry
  • Ev ve Süs Hayvanlarının Ticari Olmayan Hareketlerinde Uygulanacak Hayvan Sağlığı Şartlarına Dair Yönetmelik (Reg. No. 15541, OG 18 Feb 2020; drafted on EU Reg. 998/2003 lines) — non-commercial pet movement / animal-health conditions — Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry
  • Law No. 5996 — Veteriner Hizmetleri, Bitki Sağlığı, Gıda ve Yem Kanunu (Veterinary Services, Plant Health, Food & Feed Law, 2010); commercial live-animal import + production approval — Grand National Assembly of Turkey
  • Av ve Yaban Hayvanları İle Ürünlerinin Bulundurulması, Üretimi ve Ticareti Hakkında Yönetmelik (2005) — trade limits LISTED wild species only (does not reach captive-bred R. rattus) — Ministry of Agriculture & Forestry / DKMP
  • Customs Circular 2011/39 (Yolcu Beraberinde Getirilen Hayvanlar) — Annex 9 limits duty-free passenger pets to cats/dogs/birds/aquarium fish ('kedi, köpek ve kuş ile sınırlı'), max 2 pets/10 fish; rodents excluded — Ministry of Trade (T.C. Ticaret Bakanlığı)
  • Vektör, Kemirici ve Başıboş Hayvanların Kontrolü — Ministry of Health: wild R. rattus classified as 'zararlı kemirgen' (pest), municipal/agricultural eradication mandate (Law No. 1593) — Ministry of Health (T.C. Sağlık Bakanlığı)
  • Bern Convention Appendices (Council of Europe) — R. rattus not in App. II/III — Council of Europe
  • CITES Appendices (Feb 2025) — Rattus rattus not listed — CITES Secretariat
  • USDA APHIS — Pet Travel from the US to Turkey (reflects Turkish import rules) — USDA APHIS (secondary)
  • Petcim.com — open domestic rodent (kemirgen) sale/adoption listings (market reality) — petcim.com (secondary, market practice)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, çatı sıçanı, ev sıçanı, siyah sıçan, kemirgen, roof rat, black rat.

Last reviewed 2026-06-10. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Taiwan? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Taiwan

Summary. Taiwan is permissive to keep, breed, and give/sell a captive-bred roof rat domestically — but importing one is a near-absolute wall. The Gemini DR resolves the prior uncertainty: R. rattus is NOT on the March-2026 / 1-May-2026 list of 641 banned animals under Animal Protection Act (APA) Art. 8 (only the Myocastoridae family / nutria is named among rodents — the Muridae family, which includes R. rattus and R. norvegicus, is entirely absent), and it is NOT on the Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency's WCA Art. 55 captive-bred terrestrial-wildlife list (mammals there are limited to four ungulates/xenarthrans: Tibetan argali, argali, urial, hairy armadillo). So keeping a pet roof rat is LEGAL by statutory omission — no permit, registration, microchip, or health certificate. Breeding and selling/giving are UNREGULATED/UNCLEAR: the 'Specified Pet Business' licensing regime (特定寵物業管理辦法) covers ONLY dogs and cats, so hobbyist or even commercial rodent breeding/sale needs no specific animal-business licence (subject only to general civil/commercial law and APA anti-cruelty baselines), and the commercial-wildlife dealer regime (WCA Art. 36) doesn't apply because captive-bred R. rattus is not an Art. 55 species. Taiwan law draws NO distinction between R. rattus and the fancy rat (R. norvegicus) for keeping/breeding/selling. Domestic TRANSPORT is allowed (carrier containment rules only — secure, odor-free carrier). IMPORT is functionally PROHIBITED for private citizens: travellers may not hand-carry or check live rodents (only dogs, cats, rabbits are permitted, with prior APHIA approval), confiscation/euthanasia applies at the border, and the sole legal cargo pathway for Rodentia is the 'Quarantine Requirements for the Importation of Laboratory Animals' — open only to approved scientific institutions with an IACUC-approved experimental plan, plus a WCA Art. 24 general-wildlife import consent. R. rattus is an invasive pest and hantavirus vector subject to active state eradication campaigns, so import approval is realistically unobtainable. Never release.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Keeping a captive-bred R. rattus is legal by statutory omission. The Ministry of Agriculture's March-2026 amendment to 'Designated Animals Banned from Raising, Importing, or Exporting' (指定禁止飼養輸入或輸出之動物), in force 1 May 2026, lists 641 dangerous/venomous/invasive species — and among rodents names ONLY the Myocastoridae family (nutria/giant water rat); the Muridae family (R. rattus and R. norvegicus) is entirely absent, so APA Art. 8 does not ban keeping. R. rattus is also NOT on the Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency's WCA Art. 55 list of captive-bred terrestrial wildlife (whose mammalian entries are limited to the Tibetan argali, argali, urial, and hairy armadillo), so no Art. 55 wildlife registration/microchipping applies. No permit, registration, facility standard, or health certificate is required to keep a pet roof rat; the only duty is the APA's universal anti-cruelty baseline (food, water, space, safe environment, no abandonment). Taiwan law draws no distinction between R. rattus and the fancy rat R. norvegicus for keeping.

Sources: Ministry of Agriculture (Taiwan) — Laws & Regulations Database, Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC (Taiwan), Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency, Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Breeding R. rattus domestically sits in a structural regulatory gap. The 'Specified Pet Business Management Regulations' (特定寵物業管理辦法) under the APA — which impose facility standards, veterinary contracts, microchipping, and municipal inspection on breeders — define 'specified pets' (特定寵物) narrowly: dogs only, recently expanded to cats. All other small mammals, including rodents, are exempt, so a hobbyist or even a commercial operation breeding roof rats needs no Specific Pet Business Licence and alerts no central or municipal authority. Because R. rattus is not a WCA Art. 55 captive-bred-wildlife species, the WCA captive-breeding/registration regime also does not attach. 'Unclear' only in that no published rule affirmatively authorizes it (legality is by omission), and large-scale commercial breeding of a known public-health pest could in theory draw municipal zoning/sanitation scrutiny; the practical baseline is unrestricted, bounded only by APA anti-cruelty duties.

Sources: Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC, Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-12

Selling or gifting a captive-bred R. rattus domestically is legal by statutory silence. Because R. rattus is not a 'specified pet' (dogs/cats only), its sale needs no commercial pet-dealer licence under the Specified Pet Business Management Regulations — pet stores and hobbyists sell hamsters, guinea pigs, and fancy rats (R. norvegicus) without one, and roof rats fall under the same standard (the transaction is ordinary transfer of property under the Civil Code / Consumer Protection Act). The commercial-wildlife dealer regime under WCA Art. 36 ('Regulations for the Management of Commercial Wildlife Breeding, Trading and Processing') does NOT apply: Art. 2 of those regulations limits scope to wildlife taken directly from the wild or species announced under WCA Art. 55, and captive-bred R. rattus is neither. The one absolute prohibition is release/abandonment into the wild (WCA Art. 32 + APA): unwanted stock must be rehomed or surrendered to a municipal shelter, never released. 'Unclear' / medium because legality rests on omission and large-scale commercial sale of a public-health pest could draw municipal scrutiny.

Sources: Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC, Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency, Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

The operative question is IMPORT, which is functionally prohibited for private citizens. APHIA (Animal & Plant Health Inspection Agency) limits inbound passenger live-animal entry to dogs, cats, and rabbits only (and even those need a prior APHIA import-agreement letter); all other live animals — explicitly including pet rodents, hamsters, and rats — are forbidden in passenger cabins, checked baggage, or as personal effects, and unauthorized live animals found at the border are confiscated and euthanized. After the general 'Quarantine Requirements for the Importation of Animals and Animal Products' were abolished on 7 July 2022, the ONLY legal cargo pathway for Rodentia is the 'Quarantine Requirements for the Importation of Laboratory Animals' (實驗動物之輸入檢疫條件), available exclusively to approved 'animal scientific application institutions' that submit a scientific name/strain, an experimental plan, IACUC approval, and IATA-compliant sterilized containers — requirements a private hobbyist structurally cannot meet. Importing also triggers WCA Art. 24, which requires the Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency's prior consent for 'general wildlife' import. Given R. rattus's invasive-pest and hantavirus-vector status and active state eradication campaigns, approval is realistically unobtainable. DOMESTIC transport of a lawfully kept roof rat triggers no central permit — only individual carrier rules (e.g., THSR/MRT/TRA require a rigid escape-proof carrier within size limits and no offensive odor; staff retain discretion to refuse). Never release.

Sources: Animal and Plant Health Inspection Agency (APHIA), Animal and Plant Health Inspection Agency (APHIA), Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC, THSR carriage policy (summary)

Restrictions & responsibilities

IMPORT of a live roof rat by a private individual is functionally prohibited. Travellers may NOT hand-carry or check live rodents — APHIA permits only dogs, cats, and rabbits as passenger imports (with a prior APHIA agreement letter), and unauthorized live animals are confiscated and euthanized at the border. The sole legal cargo pathway for Rodentia is the 'Quarantine Requirements for the Importation of Laboratory Animals,' open only to approved scientific institutions with an IACUC-approved experimental plan; a pet owner cannot meet those requirements. A WCA Art. 24 general-wildlife import consent from the Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency is also required. Approval is realistically unobtainable given the species' invasive-pest/hantavirus status.
  • Do NOT attempt to hand-carry or check a live rodent into Taiwan — only dogs, cats, and rabbits are permitted as passenger imports (confiscation/euthanasia otherwise)
  • The only legal Rodentia import is institutional: an approved 'animal scientific application institution' applies under the Laboratory Animal quarantine conditions with scientific name/strain, experimental plan, IACUC approval, and IATA-compliant containers
  • Importing also requires the Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency's prior consent under WCA Art. 24 (general wildlife)
  • Never release a roof rat — it is a documented invasive pest subject to state eradication

Where: APHIA (Animal & Plant Health Inspection Agency); Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency (WCA Art. 24 consent)

Source: Animal and Plant Health Inspection Agency (APHIA), Animal and Plant Health Inspection Agency (APHIA), Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC

Domestic transport of a lawfully kept roof rat needs no permit — only the carriage rules of individual operators. Taiwan High Speed Rail (THSR), the Taipei/Kaohsiung MRT, and Taiwan Railways allow small pets in a rigid, escape-proof carrier within size limits (THSR: total length+width+height ≤ 210 cm, no single side > 70 cm) provided the animal is clean, contained, and not emitting an offensive odor; staff retain discretion to refuse a disruptive or smelly animal.
  • Use a rigid, escape-proof carrier within the operator's size limits (THSR: ≤210 cm total, no side >70 cm)
  • Keep the carrier clean and odor-free to avoid discretionary refusal by staff

Where: Individual transit operator (THSR / MRT / TRA)

Source: THSR carriage policy (summary)

Releasing or abandoning a captive roof rat into the wild is a criminal offense (WCA Art. 32 + Animal Protection Act). R. rattus is a documented invasive pest and hantavirus vector targeted by state eradication campaigns; unwanted animals must be rehomed to a capable owner or surrendered to a municipal animal shelter (which may legally euthanize), never released.
  • Never release or abandon a roof rat into the environment (criminal offense)
  • Rehome unwanted stock to a capable owner, or surrender to a municipal animal shelter

Where: Local municipal animal protection office / shelter

Source: Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Designated Animals Banned from Raising, Importing, or Exporting (指定禁止飼養輸入或輸出之動物) — 641-species list under APA Art. 8, eff. 1 May 2026; among rodents names only Myocastoridae (nutria), NOT Muridae/R. rattus — Ministry of Agriculture (Taiwan) — Laws & Regulations Database
  • Animal Protection Act (動物保護法) — Art. 3 (pet definition), Art. 8 (authority to designate banned species), anti-cruelty baseline — Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC (Taiwan)
  • Wildlife Conservation Act (野生動物保育法) — Art. 24 (general-wildlife import consent), Art. 32 (no release), Art. 36 (commercial-wildlife dealer permit), Art. 55 (captive-bred terrestrial wildlife) — Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC
  • Applicable terrestrial wildlife species artificially bred under the Wildlife Conservation Act (適用野生動物保育法之人工飼養繁殖陸域野生動物種類) — WCA Art. 55 list; mammals limited to Tibetan argali, argali, urial, hairy armadillo; R. rattus NOT listed — Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency
  • Specified Pet Business Management Regulations (特定寵物業管理辦法) — 'specified pets' = dogs and cats only; rodents exempt from animal-business licensing — Laws & Regulations Database of the ROC
  • Regulations for the Management of Commercial Wildlife Breeding, Trading and Processing (營利性野生動物飼養繁殖買賣加工管理辦法) — Art. 2 limits scope to wild-taken or WCA Art. 55 species (captive-bred R. rattus excluded) — Forestry & Nature Conservation Agency
  • Quarantine reference table for animals/plants carried by inbound passengers (入境旅客攜帶常見動植物或其產品檢疫規定參考表) — passenger live-animal imports limited to dogs, cats, rabbits; pet rodents/rats forbidden — Animal and Plant Health Inspection Agency (APHIA)
  • Quarantine Requirements for the Importation of Laboratory Animals (實驗動物之輸入檢疫條件) — sole legal Rodentia import pathway; approved scientific institutions + IACUC + experimental plan only (general import-quarantine conditions abolished 7 Jul 2022) — Animal and Plant Health Inspection Agency (APHIA)
  • Taiwan High Speed Rail / public-transit pet carriage rules — rigid escape-proof carrier within size limits, no offensive odor; staff discretion — THSR carriage policy (summary)

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in the United States? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States

Summary. Under U.S. federal law, KEEPING a roof rat as a pet is unregulated (left to the states). But the common belief that all rats are federally exempt is wrong for Rattus rattus: the Animal Welfare Act's rat exclusion covers only research-bred rats, so commercial BREEDERS and SELLERS can need a USDA license (small hobby breeders and face-to-face sales/giveaways are exempt), and because the USFWS classifies Rattus rattus as 'wildlife,' IMPORTING or EXPORTING one requires a Form 3-177 wildlife declaration even for a captive-bred pet.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The federal government does not regulate private, non-commercial possession of pet rats; under the Tenth Amendment this is left to state, county, and municipal law. Rattus rattus is not federally listed as injurious or endangered, so nothing federal stops you from keeping one (your state/city may).

Sources: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, USFWS

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Pet roof rats are NOT exempt from the Animal Welfare Act (its exclusion covers only rats 'bred for use in research,' 7 U.S.C. 2132(g); 9 C.F.R. 1.1), so they are regulated 'animals.' But a USDA license is needed ONLY if you sell the offspring WHOLESALE (to resellers) or SIGHT-UNSEEN (shipped to a buyer who has not seen the animal). Selling or placing rats face-to-face to the final owner, or giving them away, is exempt as a 'retail' transaction with NO limit on the number of breeding females (9 C.F.R. 2.1(a)(3)). The 'four or fewer breeding females' exemption only matters for sight-unseen/shipped sales.

Sources: USDA-APHIS / U.S. Code, USDA-APHIS

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

A USDA Class B dealer license is required only for WHOLESALE sales (to resellers/pet stores) or SIGHT-UNSEEN shipped sales. Selling face-to-face to the final owner (a 'retail pet store' transaction, which includes a home breeder selling directly), and giving rats away, are exempt — with NO limit on the number of breeding females (9 C.F.R. 1.1, 2.1(a)(3)). Only a wholesale or sight-unseen seller keeping 5 or more breeding females must be licensed.

Sources: USDA-APHIS / U.S. Code, USDA-APHIS

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Moving a roof rat between U.S. states needs no federal permit (and since U.S. v. Zinke (2017) even injurious species may move between contiguous states), BUT the Lacey Act (16 U.S.C. 3372) makes it a federal crime to transport one into a state where it is illegal. IMPORT/EXPORT is more involved: the USFWS classifies Rattus rattus as 'wildlife' (only Rattus norvegicus is on the domesticated-exemption list, 50 C.F.R. 14.4), so each shipment needs a USFWS Form 3-177 declaration, entry/exit through a designated wildlife port, and an inspection fee, even for a captive-bred pet (the personal-pet exemption waives only the commercial license). The CDC African-rodent import ban (42 C.F.R. 71.56) does not apply to roof rats sourced outside Africa, and USDA Veterinary Services has no health requirements for pet-rodent import.

Sources: U.S. Code, U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, USFWS, CDC, USFWS

Restrictions & responsibilities

A USDA APHIS license (Class A breeder / Class B dealer) is required ONLY for WHOLESALE selling or SIGHT-UNSEEN shipping by someone keeping 5 or more breeding females. Selling face-to-face to the final owner, or giving rats away, is EXEMPT no matter how many breeding females you keep (the 'retail pet store' exemption, 9 CFR 2.1(a)(3)).
  • Check whether you exceed the exemption thresholds (9 CFR 2.1(a)(3))
  • If not exempt, apply for the appropriate USDA license and meet the 9 CFR Part 3 housing/care standards

Forms: USDA AWA licensing rule & exemptions (9 CFR 2.1) · Where: USDA APHIS Animal Care · Fees: Varies by license type/size

Source: USDA-APHIS, USDA-APHIS / U.S. Code

Importing or exporting a roof rat requires a USFWS wildlife declaration (Form 3-177), clearance at a designated wildlife port, and a per-shipment inspection fee, because Rattus rattus is legally 'wildlife' (it is not on the 50 CFR 14.4 domesticated list). The personal-pet exemption waives only the commercial Import/Export license, not the declaration, port, or inspection.
  • File Form 3-177 via the USFWS eDecs system before the shipment
  • Route the shipment through a designated wildlife port (or get a Designated Port Exception Permit)
  • Give ~48-hour advance notice and pay the inspection fee

Forms: USFWS Form 3-177 (Declaration for Importation/Exportation of Wildlife) · Where: USFWS, at a designated wildlife port · Fees: Per-shipment inspection fee

Source: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, USFWS

Lacey Act: do not move a roof rat into (or out of) a state where keeping or importing it is illegal — interstate movement that violates a state's law is itself a federal crime.

Source: U.S. Code

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • 9 CFR 1.1 / 7 U.S.C. 2132(g) — AWA definition of 'animal' (Rattus excluded only if bred for research) — USDA-APHIS / U.S. Code
  • 9 CFR 2.1 — AWA licensing requirements & exemptions (≤4 females, <$500, retail/face-to-face) — USDA-APHIS
  • 50 CFR 14.4 — domesticated-animal list (R. norvegicus listed; R. rattus NOT → 'wildlife') — U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service
  • 50 CFR 14.61 — wildlife import/export declaration (Form 3-177) — USFWS
  • 50 CFR 16.11 — injurious live mammals (only Mastomys among rodents; R. rattus not listed) — USFWS
  • 16 U.S.C. 3372 — Lacey Act trafficking (federalizes state law) — U.S. Code
  • 42 CFR 71.56 — CDC African-rodent import ban (N/A to non-African roof rats) — CDC
  • Bring a Pet Rodent into the U.S. — USDA APHIS (no VS health requirements) — USDA-APHIS
  • Exporting a pet (rodent health certificate) — USDA APHIS — USDA-APHIS
