item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Vietnam? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Vietnam

Summary. Vietnam runs on a 'positive-list' model: an activity with a species is unauthorized unless that species is explicitly on a permitted schedule. The roof rat is on NO such list — not protected wildlife (Decree 06/2019, Decree 160/2013, not CITES), not permitted livestock/husbandry (Circular 66/2025/TT-BNNMT's 'other animals permitted for husbandry' list excludes ALL rodents), and not a recognized companion animal. So keeping a single pet roof rat sits in a regulatory void: not explicitly banned, currently unprosecuted, but with no statutory protection. Commercial breeding/selling is effectively illicit by omission (no way to obtain the required business/husbandry registration for an unlisted species) and exposed to the same enforcement used in the 2008 nationwide hamster crackdown (administrative fines up to 30 million VND + forced culling). Transport is the hardest layer: domestic inter-provincial movement needs a veterinary health certificate that can't readily be issued for an unlisted species, and IMPORT is practically prohibited — at the border R. rattus defaults to a 'wild animal' classification caught by Directive 29/CT-TTg's suspension of live wild-animal imports, and rodents are absent from the permitted-import list (Circular 14/2023). Vietnam draws NO legal distinction between R. rattus and the fancy rat R. norvegicus — both are equally unlisted. ⚠️ 2025: MARD + MONRE merged into one Ministry of Agriculture & Environment (MAE), centralizing veterinary + biodiversity enforcement.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

R. rattus is absent from every Vietnamese list: not in Group IB/IIB of Decree 06/2019 (am. 84/2021), not in Decree 160/2013, not CITES. The Law on Forestry Art. 9 keeping prohibitions are keyed to listed species, so they don't bite; Decree 06/2019 Art. 23's 3-working-day notification for 'ordinary forest animals' is not applied by rangers to commensal urban rats (they aren't treated as 'forest animals'). Result: personal possession is a pure regulatory void — neither prohibited nor affirmatively authorized as a 'pet.' Currently unprosecuted (an open hobby market exists), but with no statutory protection; the state retains discretionary biosecurity/sanitation power to confiscate. 'Unregulated_unclear,' tending tolerated-but-unprotected.

Sources: Government of Vietnam, Government of Vietnam, National Assembly of Vietnam (via FAOLEX), Ministry of Agriculture & Environment (Vietnam)

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

Under the positive-list paradigm, commercial breeding of any species not on the permitted-husbandry list is unauthorized/illicit. Circular 66/2025/TT-BNNMT (effective 5 Jan 2026) sets the exhaustive 'List of other animals permitted for animal husbandry' (earthworms, black soldier flies, crickets, scorpions, wild ducks, etc.) — and ALL rodents, R. rattus and R. norvegicus alike, are excluded. A would-be breeder therefore cannot obtain the business registration / facility-hygiene / biosecurity clearances required by Decree 13/2020. No hobbyist or small-breeder exemption exists. Hobby breeding is currently ignored but unprotected; any profit-making breeding operates in the black market and is exposed to the 2008-hamster-style enforcement (fines to 30M VND + culling). 'Unregulated_unclear' for the tolerated hobbyist; effectively illicit at commercial scale.

Sources: Ministry of Agriculture & Environment (Vietnam), National Assembly of Vietnam (via FAOLEX), Government of Vietnam

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-08

Commercial trade of an unlisted animal species is legally unsupported and exposed to discretionary enforcement. The direct proxy is the 2008 nationwide hamster crackdown: authorities used the pre-existing positive-list mechanism (hamsters 'not on the list of animals permitted for import/husbandry') to declare all trading/transport/keeping unauthorized, threatening administrative fines of 20–30 million VND plus forced culling/re-export — the exact same legal logic applies to R. rattus. Open Facebook-group and pet-shop sales currently proceed only on enforcement apathy. Free/non-commercial transfer has fewer hooks but no affirmative protection. Low confidence: highly volatile, subject to competitor reporting and localized biosecurity directives.

Sources: National Assembly of Vietnam (via FAOLEX), Government of Vietnam, Dept of Livestock Production (reported, CAND)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

DOMESTIC (inter-provincial): the Law on Animal Health 79/2015 + Circular 25/2016/TT-BNNPTNT require a veterinary health certificate + quarantine clearance to move terrestrial animals between provinces — but provincial vets have no protocol/health parameters to inspect an unlisted species, so the required certificate can't readily be issued; formal shipping risks confiscation at veterinary checkpoints. IMPORT (practically prohibited): (1) Directive 29/CT-TTg (23 Jul 2020) suspends imports of live WILD animals, and at customs R. rattus — not defined as a domestic husbandry animal — defaults to the 'wild animal' classification, so even a captive-bred specimen is rejected/re-exported; (2) rodents are absent from the permitted-import list (Circular 14/2023/TT-BNNPTNT), and importing unlisted terrestrial animals needs a prior biosecurity risk analysis + import permit the MAE does not issue for pet rodents (same rationale as the 2008 hamster import ban). Not CITES. Never release. Net: 'restricted' (high) — import operationally impossible, domestic formal transport blocked by the unlisted-species paperwork gap.

Sources: Prime Minister of Vietnam, Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development (Vietnam), Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development (Vietnam), National Assembly of Vietnam

Restrictions & responsibilities

Vietnam's positive-list system means R. rattus has no legal route to commercial husbandry, sale, or import — it's on no permitted list, so the required registrations/certificates can't be obtained, and authorities can invoke the 2008-hamster-ban precedent (fines to 30M VND + culling) at any time. Keeping a single pet is tolerated-but-unprotected. Import is practically impossible (Directive 29 wild-animal default + rodents off the Circular 14/2023 import list). Never release.
  • Understand there is currently NO legal pathway to commercially breed/sell/import R. rattus in Vietnam (it's on no permitted list)
  • For any movement, expect that a veterinary health certificate cannot readily be issued for an unlisted species
  • Constructive long game: petition the MAE to add captive-bred pet rodents to the Circular 66/2025 permitted-husbandry list

Where: Ministry of Agriculture & Environment (MAE) — Dept of Livestock Production / Dept of Animal Health

Source: Ministry of Agriculture & Environment (Vietnam), Prime Minister of Vietnam, Dept of Livestock Production (reported, CAND)

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Official sources

  • Circular 66/2025/TT-BNNMT — List of 'other animals' permitted for husbandry (effective 5 Jan 2026; EXCLUDES all rodents) — Ministry of Agriculture & Environment (Vietnam)
  • Law on Animal Husbandry 32/2018/QH14 — positive-list definition of permitted livestock; commercial-breeding requirements — National Assembly of Vietnam (via FAOLEX)
  • Decree 13/2020/ND-CP (am. 46/2022) — guidance to the Law on Animal Husbandry (commercial facility/registration requirements) — Government of Vietnam
  • Decree 06/2019/ND-CP (am. 84/2021) — endangered/precious/rare forest fauna (R. rattus unlisted; Art. 23 ordinary-animal notification) — Government of Vietnam
  • Decree 160/2013/ND-CP — species prioritized for protection (R. rattus absent) — Government of Vietnam
  • Directive 29/CT-TTg (23 Jul 2020) — suspension of live WILD-animal imports (R. rattus defaults to wildlife at customs) — Prime Minister of Vietnam
  • Circular 14/2023/TT-BNNPTNT — permitted livestock-import list (rodents absent) — Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development (Vietnam)
  • Circular 25/2016/TT-BNNPTNT — terrestrial-animal quarantine + inter-provincial health certificate — Ministry of Agriculture & Rural Development (Vietnam)
  • Law on Animal Health (Veterinary) 79/2015/QH13 — import quarantine + inter-provincial movement — National Assembly of Vietnam
  • Circular 35/2018/TT-BTNMT — invasive alien species list (R. rattus NOT listed; but Yersinia pestis listed as invasive microorganism) — Ministry of Natural Resources & Environment (now MAE)
  • 2008 nationwide hamster crackdown — positive-list rationale; fines 20–30M VND + culling (enforcement precedent for unlisted rodents) — Dept of Livestock Production (reported, CAND)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, chuột mái nhà, chuột đen, chuột cảnh, động vật gặm nhấm, roof rat, black rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in South Africa? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › South Africa

Summary. South Africa's status is now agency-confirmed (DFFE Biodiversity Risk Management, the Alien & Invasive Species Issuing Authority, June 2026). Rattus rattus is listed Category 1b under the 2020 NEMBA Alien & Invasive Species Regulations, a designation tied to offshore islands. DFFE's plain guidance for a private keeper: you MAY KEEP one as a pet with NO permit, but you may NOT breed or multiply them, NOT sell or give them away, and NOT transport them, except under a research permit. So keeping is open while breeding, trade and movement are effectively closed to hobbyists (a containment regime). A separate provincial layer can add a 'wild animal in captivity' permit in some provinces (liaise with your provincial environmental department), and international import is handled separately by the National Department of Agriculture's State Veterinary import permit. ⚠️ Live advocacy window: DFFE confirmed the AIS list amendment is under Law Reform review and will be gazetted for PUBLIC COMMENT this financial year — the moment to engage on how the species is treated.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • DFFE Directorate: Biodiversity Risk Management (the Alien & Invasive Species Issuing Authority), written reply June 2026: Rattus rattus is NEMBA AIS Category 1b (designated to offshore islands). KEEPING one as a pet requires NO permit. BREEDING/multiplying, SELLING or giving away, and TRANSPORTING are permitted ONLY under a research permit. The AIS amendment list is under Law Reform review and will be gazetted for public comment this financial year. Provincial environmental departments may also regulate (liaise with the relevant province), and veterinary import is handled by the National Department of Agriculture.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

DFFE (the AIS Issuing Authority) confirmed in writing (June 2026) that NO permit is required to keep Rattus rattus as a pet; permits for the species are issued only for research purposes. Note a separate provincial layer: some provinces (e.g., Western Cape, Eastern Cape, Northern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State) may require a general 'wild animal in captivity' permit, so confirm with your provincial environmental department.

Sources: DFFE, DFFE / South African Government, Absolute Exotics SA (secondary)

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

DFFE confirmed (June 2026): you cannot breed or multiply Rattus rattus unless it is for research purposes. There is no hobbyist/companion breeding permit; the only permits available for the species are research permits. This makes captive propagation by a private keeper effectively prohibited.

Sources: DFFE / South African Government

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

DFFE confirmed (June 2026) that selling or giving away Rattus rattus is not permitted ('No'); as with breeding, the only permits issued for the species are for research. Note the practical contrast: the fancy rat (R. norvegicus) carries the same island Cat 1b listing yet is openly traded — a species-not-domestication inconsistency to raise in the public-comment process.

Sources: DFFE / South African Government, African Journal of Ecology (Wiley)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

DFFE confirmed (June 2026) that you may transport Rattus rattus only for research purposes, so there is no ordinary pet-transport pathway. Inter-provincial movement also implicates provincial transport permits, and international import is handled separately by the National Department of Agriculture (State Veterinary import permit + health protocol). Never release a roof rat.

Sources: DFFE / South African Government, Absolute Exotics SA (secondary), National Dept of Agriculture (DALRRD)

Restrictions & responsibilities

DFFE (the AIS Issuing Authority) has confirmed that, for a privately kept Rattus rattus, you may keep one as a pet without a permit, but you may NOT breed/multiply or sell/give them away except under a research permit. There is no companion/hobbyist breeding or sales permit for the species. Never release a roof rat.
  • If your purpose is genuine research, apply to DFFE Biodiversity Risk Management for a research permit
  • Otherwise: keeping is allowed, but do not breed, sell, or give the animal away

Where: DFFE Biodiversity Risk Management (AIS Issuing Authority)

Source: DFFE / South African Government

No NATIONAL permit is needed to keep a roof rat as a pet (DFFE confirmed). But some provinces (Western Cape, Eastern Cape, Northern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Free State) may require a general 'wild animal in captivity' permit; the other four do not. Confirm with your provincial environmental department.
  • Check your provincial conservation authority (e.g., CapeNature in the Western Cape) on whether a captivity permit is required

Where: Provincial environmental department / conservation authority

Source: Absolute Exotics SA (secondary)

Transport of Rattus rattus is permitted only for research purposes (DFFE). International import is separately handled by the National Department of Agriculture's State Veterinary Import Permit (apply before shipment) + health certificate. Inter-provincial movement also implicates provincial transport permits.

Where: DFFE (research transport); National Dept of Agriculture / DALRRD (import); provincial authority (inter-provincial)

Source: National Dept of Agriculture (DALRRD), Absolute Exotics SA (secondary)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in South Africa
Time-sensitive: Act when the NEMBA Alien & Invasive Species amendment is gazetted for public comment (expected 2026 per DFFE).

South Africa's environment department (DFFE) confirmed in June 2026 that an amendment to the NEMBA Alien and Invasive Species lists is in Law Reform review and will be gazetted for public comment this financial year.

The ask: When the amended AIS list is gazetted for comment, submit a comment asking that domesticated R. rattus kept as pets be handled distinctly from wild invasive populations, for example a keeping or permit pathway rather than a blanket prohibition. The fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) carries the same island Category 1b listing yet is openly kept and sold in South Africa. The already-permitted fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over. See https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/. Cats and dogs are also non-native and well documented to harm indigenous and island wildlife, yet are permitted as pets because their companionship is judged worth the trade-off. Whether the limited additional risk of a few sterile, tame, indoor-only roof rats, never released, is similarly outweighed by that benefit is a cost-benefit judgment for DFFE to make.

Where the lever really is: This is executive rulemaking with a built-in public-comment step. The lever is the gazette comment window and a letter to DFFE's biodiversity directorate, not Parliament. On the species-not-domestication point, see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Dept. of Forestry, Fisheries & the Environment (DFFE) — Biodiversity / AIS (public comment) — AISpermits@dffe.gov.za
    DFFE runs the AIS listing and its comment process; the official comment address is published with the gazette notice.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE), Biodiversity,

I am commenting on the amendment to the NEMBA Alien and Invasive Species lists.

I ask that domesticated roof rats (Rattus rattus) kept as pets be handled distinctly from wild invasive populations. Captive-bred pet roof rats are tame, kept indoors in secure cages, and never released. A keeping or permit pathway would meet the conservation aim without penalising responsible pet owners.

The fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) carries the same island Category 1b listing yet is openly kept and sold. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over.

I put the underlying question as one for the Department to decide. South Africa already permits cats and dogs, which are themselves non-native and well documented to harm indigenous and island wildlife, because their companionship is judged worth the trade-off. The narrow question is whether the limited additional risk of a few sterile, tame, indoor-only roof rats, never bred for release and never set loose, is outweighed by the same companionship benefit. I do not ask the Department to assume the answer; I ask it to weigh that trade-off rather than close the question with a blanket prohibition.

Please consider this distinction in the amended list.

Sincerely,
[Your name]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • NEMBA Alien & Invasive Species Lists (GG 43726, GN 1003, 18 Sep 2020) — R. rattus Category 1b — DFFE
  • NEMBA Alien & Invasive Species Regulations (GG 43735, GN 1020, 2020) — s.71 restricted activities — DFFE / South African Government
  • Genetic diversity of rodent species sold in South African pet shops (Afr. J. Ecol. 2022) — fancy rat openly traded — African Journal of Ecology (Wiley)
  • Province-by-province exotic-pet permit overview (some provinces require captivity permits) — Absolute Exotics SA (secondary)
  • Traveling with an exotic pet in South Africa — inter-provincial transport permit — Absolute Exotics SA (secondary)
  • DALRRD — South African Veterinary Import Permit application process — National Dept of Agriculture (DALRRD)

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Alberta? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Canada › Alberta

Summary. Alberta is the strictest jurisdiction in Canada — and one of the strictest anywhere. Under the Agricultural Pests Act and the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation, the ENTIRE genus Rattus is a declared pest, and the law prohibits the import, purchase, sale, transport, and possession of any live rat. There is NO exemption for 'fancy', tame, or captive-bred rats. The only legal route is a special Ministerial permit reserved for accredited research institutions, zoos, or approved labs. A pet roof rat in Alberta may be seized and destroyed, and the keeper fined. Alberta has defended its 'rat-free' status since 1950.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Alberta-specific rules; Canada’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Alberta is silent. See Canada.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The Agricultural Pests Act declares the whole genus Rattus a pest, and possession of a live rat by a private citizen is unlawful — Alberta enforces a zero-tolerance 'rat-free' policy. There is explicitly no exemption for fancy, tame, or domesticated rats; a single caged pet is treated as an unacceptable escape risk. Wild sightings are reported to the 310-RATS line and eradicated.

Sources: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Breeding requires possession, which is prohibited, and the statute separately forbids the purchase, sale, or distribution of a declared pest. There is no legal hobby or commercial breeding of rats in Alberta.

Sources: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling, giving, or otherwise distributing a live rat is expressly prohibited as dealing in a declared pest. No pet-trade layer exists for rats in Alberta.

Sources: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Transporting a live rat into or within Alberta is prohibited except under a highly restricted Ministerial permit (research institutions, zoos, approved labs only). Whether a non-resident may drive a securely caged pet rat continuously THROUGH Alberta without stopping is not clearly addressed in the published rules — we have asked the province to clarify. Treat any presence of a rat in Alberta as prohibited unless you hold a permit.

Sources: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

Restrictions & responsibilities

The only lawful way to possess, breed, or transport a rat in Alberta is a special permit issued by the Minister of Agriculture, available only to accredited research institutions, major zoos, or government-approved laboratories — not to private pet keepers.
  • Pet keeping is not permitted — there is no pet-owner permit

Where: Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation (Ministerial permit)

Source: Government of Alberta, Government of Alberta

If you move to Alberta, you cannot bring a pet rat with you. Rehome it responsibly before relocating; do not transport it into the province. Rat sightings are reported to 310-RATS (310-7287) and acted on.

Source: Government of Alberta

Alberta's only legal route to hold any Rattus is a Ministerial Form-6 permit (AR 184/2001 s.11) limited to research facilities, zoos, and inspectors — no private/hobby pathway. Even the fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is prohibited for private keeping.

Forms: AR 184/2001 Form 6 — Ministerial permit to keep rats (research/zoo/inspector only) · Where: Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation — Inspection and Investigation Section

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Alberta. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Alberta

Alberta is one of the only places with a total ban on keeping any pet rat. Under the Agricultural Pests Act (RSA 2000, c. A-8) and the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation (AR 184/2001), the entire genus Rattus, every rat species including the tame fancy pet rat (Rattus norvegicus) and the roof rat (Rattus rattus), is a declared agricultural pest. The Government of Alberta states that it is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta. Possession, import, purchase, sale, transport, and breeding of any live rat are all prohibited. The only permit (a Ministerial permit under AR 184/2001) is reserved for accredited research institutions, zoos, and government labs; there is no private or hobby pathway, not even for a single captive-bred, tame rat kept indoors in a cage. Penalties can reach $5,000 per animal, and a pet rat found in the province can be seized and destroyed. The ban is the backbone of Alberta's 75-year rat-free status, and it makes no distinction between a wild invasive rat and a domesticated companion animal that has never lived outdoors.

The ask: Ask the Legislative Assembly (your MLA) to amend the Agricultural Pests Act and Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation to create a narrow, well-defined exemption for domesticated, captive-bred pet rats kept indoors under reasonable conditions (for example: spayed or neutered or single-sex housing, secure escape-proof caging, microchipping or registration, and a ban on outdoor release), distinct from Alberta's wild-rat eradication program, which would continue unchanged. Do not ask the rat-control program or Alberta Agriculture to make an exception, because that office is correctly applying a law it cannot rewrite. The change has to come from the Legislature.

Where the lever really is: Branch (b): the problem is the law as written, not a bureaucracy misreading it. The Agricultural Pests Act and AR 184/2001 declare the whole genus Rattus a pest at the statutory and regulatory level, and the rat-control agency is correctly applying that prohibition; the Government of Alberta's website confirms that it is illegal to own pet rats in Alberta. There is no exemption list a tame or captive-bred rat could be added to, and the sole permit category is statutorily confined to research, zoo, and lab operators. Appealing to the agency (rats@gov.ab.ca / 310-FARM) will not change anything: that line exists to report and eradicate rats, and the staff have no authority to legalize pet keeping. The only lever that can change this is the Legislature, by amending the Act or the Regulation to carve out a domesticated-pet-rat exemption, which means writing to your MLA and, where relevant, the Minister of Agriculture and Irrigation in their legislative and policy capacity. The single narrow thing the agency can properly answer is a factual clarification (for example, whether a non-resident may transit a securely caged pet rat through the province), included only as a secondary, agency-appropriate touchpoint, not as the reform lever. On the species-not-domestication point, the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred Rattus rattus is the same case one species over: https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Legislative Assembly of Alberta — Members of the Legislative Assembly directory (Find Your MLA / Member Contact list) (legislature) — official contact page
    The total ban is set in statute (Agricultural Pests Act) and regulation (AR 184/2001). Only the Legislature can amend it, so your own MLA is the correct first touchpoint. This official directory lists all 87 MLAs by name and constituency with individual contact pages and a downloadable contact list, letting you reach the representative who can raise or sponsor a change.
  • Legislative Assembly of Alberta — Find Your MLA by riding (Elections Alberta MLA search) (legislature) — official contact page
    Use this official Elections Alberta tool to identify exactly which MLA represents your address/riding before you write, so your letter reaches your own representative (constituent letters carry the most weight).
  • Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation — Rat Control Program inbox (factual clarification ONLY, not policy change) (executive / agency) — rats@gov.ab.ca
    Included only for a narrow factual question this office can legitimately answer — e.g., whether a non-resident may transit a securely caged pet Rattus through Alberta. Do NOT use this channel to request legalization: the rat-control program is correctly enforcing the statute and cannot amend it. (Phone: 310-FARM in Alberta / 403-742-7901 outside.)

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Please amend the Agricultural Pests Act to allow domesticated pet rats

Dear [MLA name / Member for [constituency]],

I am a constituent writing about Alberta's total ban on keeping pet rats. Under the Agricultural Pests Act and the Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation (AR 184/2001), the entire genus Rattus is a declared pest, so even a tame, captive-bred pet rat kept indoors is illegal.

I fully support Alberta's program against wild, invasive rats. But the current law makes no distinction between a wild rat and a domesticated companion animal that is captive-bred, hand-tame, housed in a secure escape-proof cage, kept entirely indoors, and never released. I am not claiming such a pet poses zero risk. I am asking the Legislature to weigh whether the limited, controllable risk of a securely caged, altered, indoor-only animal that cannot establish a wild population is outweighed by allowing Albertans the kind of companionship that cats and dogs, themselves non-native, are already permitted to provide. That balance is yours to strike, and Alberta's wild-rat eradication program would continue unchanged.

The fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred pet rat is the same case as the cats and dogs Alberta already permits.

Because this is set in statute and regulation, only the Legislature can fix it; the rat-control office is simply applying the law. I respectfully ask you to support amending the Act and Regulation to create a narrow exemption for domesticated pet rats kept under reasonable conditions (secure caging, no outdoor release, single-sex or altered housing), while Alberta's wild-rat eradication continues unchanged.

Thank you for considering this. I would welcome your reply.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your address / constituency]
[Your email]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Agricultural Pests Act (RSA 2000, c. A-8) — declares the genus Rattus a pest — Government of Alberta
  • Pest and Nuisance Control Regulation (AR 184/2001) — Government of Alberta
  • Rat prevention and control / rat-free Alberta — Government of Alberta

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in British Columbia? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Canada › British Columbia

Summary. In British Columbia, keeping a tame, captive-bred roof rat is legal. BC's Wildlife Act protects native and some designated non-native 'wildlife', but the Designation and Exemption Regulation (B.C. Reg. 168/90), section 8(h), exempts a non-native animal that 'is tame and kept in captivity for the use of man'. Rattus rattus is not a Controlled Alien Species (that list is for dangerous exotics like big cats and venomous snakes), so a captive-bred pet roof rat qualifies for the exemption and needs no provincial permit to keep, breed, or sell. Feral roof rats (e.g., on Haida Gwaii) are managed as invasive wildlife — never release one.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the British Columbia-specific rules; Canada’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where British Columbia is silent. See Canada.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • FrontCounter BC, Provincial Contact Centre, B.C. Ministry of Water, Land and Resource Stewardship (written reply June 2026): 'Rattus rattus is not designated as wildlife under the Wildlife Act. A provincial wildlife permit would not be required.' Keeping a roof rat therefore needs no provincial wildlife permit in British Columbia. (Releasing one remains prohibited — feral roof rats are managed as invasive wildlife; never release.)

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

FrontCounter BC (B.C. Ministry of Water, Land & Resource Stewardship) confirmed in writing (June 2026) that Rattus rattus is not designated as wildlife under the Wildlife Act, so no provincial wildlife permit is required to keep one. This matches the regulation: section 8(h) of the Designation and Exemption Regulation (B.C. Reg. 168/90) exempts a non-native animal that is tame and kept in captivity for human use, and R. rattus is not a Controlled Alien Species — so a captive-bred, tame roof rat needs no provincial captive-wildlife permit.

Sources: Province of British Columbia, Province of British Columbia

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

As an exempt tame species not listed as a Controlled Alien Species, breeding is legal without a provincial permit — subject to municipal bylaws, business licensing, and BC's animal-welfare law.

Sources: Province of British Columbia

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling or giving a tame, exempt roof rat is legal at the provincial level, subject to municipal pet-shop/business licensing and consumer-protection rules. No provincial dealer permit is required.

Sources: Province of British Columbia

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Moving a tame, securely-contained roof rat within BC is not restricted by provincial wildlife authorities, provided it is not released into the wild. Interprovincial transport follows the destination province's rules (you cannot bring one into Alberta).

Sources: Province of British Columbia

Restrictions & responsibilities

Releasing a roof rat into the wild is strictly prohibited under BC's ecological-protection rules — feral R. rattus are managed and eradicated as invasive wildlife (e.g., on the Haida Gwaii archipelago). Keep pets securely contained and rehome responsibly; never release.

Source: Province of British Columbia

Commercial breeding or selling is governed by municipal business licensing and zoning plus BC's Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act care standards — check your municipality.
  • Check municipal business-licensing/zoning if breeding or selling commercially

Where: Your municipality · Fees: Set locally

Source: Province of British Columbia

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Ontario? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Canada › Ontario

Summary. Ontario does not regulate roof rats at the provincial level — they are legal by default. Rattus rattus is not listed as prohibited or restricted under the Invasive Species Act, and as a non-native species it falls outside the Fish and Wildlife Conservation Act (which covers native 'game' and 'specially protected' wildlife). So keeping, breeding, selling, and transporting roof rats is unregulated by the province. The real rules are MUNICIPAL: city bylaws on exotic/pet animals, breeder/pet-shop licensing, animal limits, and the Provincial Animal Welfare Services Act (PAWS) care standards.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Ontario-specific rules; Canada’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Ontario is silent. See Canada.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Rattus rattus is not listed under the Invasive Species Act (unlike wild pigs or nutria) and is not native 'game' or 'specially protected' wildlife under the Fish and Wildlife Conservation Act, 1997 — so it is outside the Ministry of Natural Resources' regulatory scope. No provincial permit is needed to keep one. Your municipality may regulate exotic pets or cap animal numbers.

Sources: Government of Ontario, Government of Ontario

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The province has no jurisdiction over rat breeding. Breeding is governed by municipal bylaws, animal-control rules, and the Provincial Animal Welfare Services Act (PAWS) care standards. Operating commercially in a residential zone often needs a municipal kennel/pet-shop licence.

Sources: Government of Ontario

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling or giving roof rats is unregulated provincially. A retail storefront needs the municipality's pet-shop / commercial-establishment licence; private face-to-face placement and giveaways do not.

Sources: Government of Ontario, Government of Ontario

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

No provincial permit is required to move roof rats within or across Ontario's borders. Interprovincial transport is subject to the destination province's rules (you cannot bring one into Alberta).

Sources: Government of Ontario

Restrictions & responsibilities

The binding layer in Ontario is municipal: many cities license commercial breeders/pet shops, cap the number of animals per dwelling, or regulate 'exotic' pets. Check your city's animal bylaw. The Provincial Animal Welfare Services Act (PAWS) sets enforceable minimum care standards everywhere.
  • Check your municipality's animal/exotic-pet bylaw and any breeder/pet-shop licensing
  • Meet PAWS minimum care standards

Where: Your municipality; Animal Welfare Services (PAWS) · Fees: Set locally

Source: Government of Ontario

Never release a roof rat outdoors — it is a non-native species and release is both ecologically harmful and an animal-welfare concern. Rehome responsibly.

Source: Government of Ontario

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Quebec? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Canada › Quebec

Summary. In Quebec, keeping, breeding, and selling a roof rat is legal and largely unregulated at the provincial level: Rattus rattus is not a Schedule 1 prohibited species under the Règlement sur les animaux en captivité, so no captivity permit is needed for ordinary hobbyists. The one catch is IMPORT: section 13 requires anyone bringing an animal into Quebec to file a prior written import notice — and while the regulation explicitly exempts the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) and the house mouse from that notice, it does NOT name Rattus rattus. So importing a roof rat into Quebec appears to require a notice the fancy rat is spared. Captive facilities must also meet the regulation's housing standards.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Quebec-specific rules; Canada’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Quebec is silent. See Canada.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Neither Rattus rattus nor Rattus norvegicus is listed in Schedule 1 (prohibited/restricted species) of the Règlement sur les animaux en captivité, so keeping a roof rat as a pet needs no provincial captivity permit for normal hobbyist numbers.

Sources: Gouvernement du Québec, Gouvernement du Québec

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Breeding is legal without a wildlife permit, but facilities must meet the regulation's housing standards (enclosures free of injury hazards, allowing the animal to avoid its own waste, kept dry and clean). Commercial operations also need ordinary business licensing.

Sources: Gouvernement du Québec, Gouvernement du Québec

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling or giving roof rats is legal at the provincial level; commercial sale requires ordinary business licensing and compliance with the captive-animal housing standards. No species-specific dealer permit is required.

Sources: Gouvernement du Québec

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Section 13 of the Règlement sur les animaux en captivité requires a prior written import NOTICE to the Ministry (MELCCFP) — stating the species' scientific name, origin, planned import date, and place of captivity — before bringing an animal into Quebec. The regulation explicitly EXEMPTS the Norway rat (rat surmulot, R. norvegicus) and house mouse (Mus musculus) from this notice when imported by an individual for personal purposes, but it does NOT list Rattus rattus. On the face of the text, importing a roof rat into Quebec requires filing that notice. We have asked the Ministry to confirm. (This is a notice/declaration, not a discretionary permit.)

Sources: Gouvernement du Québec, Gouvernement du Québec

Restrictions & responsibilities

Before importing a roof rat into Quebec, file the section 13 import notice with MELCCFP (scientific name, origin, date, place of captivity). The fancy rat (R. norvegicus) and house mouse are exempt from this notice; R. rattus is not named, so file the notice unless the Ministry confirms otherwise.
  • Send the written import notice to MELCCFP before the animal arrives
  • Include the binomial name, origin, planned date, and place of captivity

Where: Ministère de l'Environnement, de la Lutte contre les changements climatiques, de la Faune et des Parcs (MELCCFP)

Source: Gouvernement du Québec, Gouvernement du Québec

Housing standards apply to anyone keeping animals in captivity: enclosures must prevent injury and aggression, let the animal avoid contact with its feces, and be kept dry and clean. These matter most for breeders and larger setups.

Source: Gouvernement du Québec

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Quebec

In Quebec, keeping, breeding, and giving or selling a pet roof rat (Rattus rattus, the "rat noir" / "rat des toits") is legal and needs no provincial captivity permit. The species is not on the prohibited list (Annexe I) of the Règlement sur les animaux en captivité (C-61.1, r. 5.1). There is one narrow snag. Section 13 of that regulation requires a person to file a prior written import notice with the Ministry (MELCCFP) before bringing certain captive animals into Quebec. The regulation explicitly exempts the fancy/Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus, "rat surmulot") and the house mouse (Mus musculus) from that notice when an individual imports them for personal purposes, but it does not name Rattus rattus. On the face of the text, a tame domestic roof rat is treated more strictly than the near-identical fancy rat. This appears to be a drafting oversight, since roof rats are rarer in the pet trade, not a deliberate choice to single them out.

The ask: Ask the Ministry (MELCCFP) to do one of two things: (1) confirm in writing that the section 13 import-notice exemption already granted to the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) and house mouse extends in practice to the domestic roof rat (Rattus rattus) kept as a pet; or (2) add Rattus rattus to the same section 13 exemption so the regulation treats the two domestic rat species the same. Both are domestic, captive-bred companion rats. Domestication, not which wild relative an animal descends from, is what the law recognises elsewhere: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are domestic animals. The already-exempt fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over and reasonably warrants the same paperwork treatment (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/). This is a one-line fix that closes a paperwork gap. It does not ask Quebec to legalize anything new, because keeping roof rats is already legal.

Where the lever really is: This is branch (a): the bureaucracy or drafting gap, and the correct lever is the agency (MELCCFP), either a written clarification or a one-species addition to the existing section 13 exemption. It is not a "law as written" prohibition. Keeping, breeding, and selling roof rats is already legal because Rattus rattus is absent from the prohibited-species schedule. The only friction is that section 13's import-notice exemption names Rattus norvegicus and Mus musculus but omits Rattus rattus. An agency can fix or interpret that omission; it is not the legislature having deliberately banned or listed the species. The Ministry administers C-61.1, r. 5.1 and can issue a written interpretation of the exemption's scope, and regulation amendments here are made by government or ministerial rulemaking rather than by a statute of the National Assembly. The productive move is to write the agency, not to lobby an MNA. If the Ministry responds that the omission is deliberate and it must apply the notice as written, the fallback would be a rulemaking or prepublication window. There is no open window now, and there is no statutory list of the National Assembly to repeal, so the legislature is not the lever.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Ministère de l'Environnement, de la Lutte contre les changements climatiques, de la Faune et des Parcs (MELCCFP) — official information-request form (Secteur de la faune et des parcs) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Official online intake for written questions to the Ministry; has a wildlife-and-parks routing category, so it lands the section 13 exemption question with the unit that administers the captive-animals regulation. Best first channel because it creates a tracked written record.
  • MELCCFP — Wildlife customer service (Service à la clientèle, secteur de la faune) (executive / agency) — renseignements.faune@environnement.gouv.qc.ca
    Verified official wildlife inquiry inbox (also listed on the quebec.ca general-contact page, phone 1-877-346-6763). Use it to email the same clarification/exemption request directly to the faune team.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Section 13 import notice: exemption for the domestic roof rat (Rattus rattus)

To the Wildlife sector, MELCCFP,

I am writing about an inconsistency in the Regulation respecting animals in captivity (C-61.1, r. 5.1). Keeping a domestic roof rat (Rattus rattus) as a pet is legal in Quebec; the species is not on the prohibited schedule. However, section 13's exemption from the prior import notice names the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) and the house mouse, but does not name Rattus rattus, even though the two are kept identically as pets.

These are captive-bred, tame animals, kept indoors as companions, never taken from or released into the wild. The roof rat is the less common of two domesticated rat species. Domestication, not wild ancestry, is what the law recognises elsewhere: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are treated as domestic. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over and reasonably deserves the same treatment.

Could you please (1) confirm in writing whether the section 13 exemption applies in practice to a domestic Rattus rattus imported by an individual for personal purposes, or (2) add Rattus rattus to that same exemption? This is a one-line fix that treats the two domestic rat species consistently.

Thank you for your time.

[Your name]
[Your municipality / region]
[Your email]
Français
Objet: Avis d'importation de l'article 13: dispense pour le rat noir domestique (Rattus rattus)

Au secteur de la faune, MELCCFP,

Je vous écris au sujet d'une incohérence dans le Règlement sur les animaux en captivité (C-61.1, r. 5.1). Garder un rat noir domestique (Rattus rattus) comme animal de compagnie est légal au Québec; l'espèce ne figure pas à l'annexe des espèces prohibées. Or, la dispense d'avis d'importation prévue à l'article 13 nomme le rat surmulot (Rattus norvegicus) et la souris commune, mais ne nomme pas le Rattus rattus, alors que les deux sont gardés de façon identique comme animaux de compagnie.

Il s'agit d'animaux nés en captivité, apprivoisés, gardés à l'intérieur comme compagnons, jamais prélevés dans la nature ni relâchés. Le rat noir est la moins répandue de deux espèces de rats domestiqués. C'est la domestication, et non l'ascendance sauvage, que la loi reconnaît ailleurs: le chien descend du loup et le chat d'un félin sauvage, et pourtant tous deux sont considérés comme domestiques. Le rat surmulot est lui-même le rat brun sauvage, domestiqué seulement au XIXe siècle, de sorte qu'un rat noir né en captivité est le même cas, à une espèce près, et mérite raisonnablement le même traitement.

Pourriez-vous (1) confirmer par écrit si la dispense de l'article 13 s'applique en pratique au Rattus rattus domestique importé par un particulier à des fins personnelles, ou (2) ajouter le Rattus rattus à cette même dispense ? Il s'agit d'une correction d'une seule ligne qui traiterait de façon cohérente les deux espèces de rats domestiques.

Je vous remercie de votre attention.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Saskatchewan? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › Canada › Saskatchewan

Summary. Saskatchewan is the clearest 'yes' in Canada. The province runs an aggressive feral-rat eradication program (landowners must destroy wild rats), yet it ALSO explicitly lists the Black Rat (Rattus rattus) on its official Captive Wildlife allowed list. Because the species is named on the allowed list, residents may keep, breed, and sell captive R. rattus as pets with NO captive-wildlife licence and no provincial registration. Large-scale breeding can still trigger municipal zoning or business-licensing rules.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Saskatchewan-specific rules; Canada’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Saskatchewan is silent. See Canada.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

The Black Rat (Rattus rattus) is explicitly named on Saskatchewan's Captive Wildlife allowed list (under The Wildlife Act, 1998 and the Captive Wildlife Regulations, 2021), which exempts listed species from the captive-wildlife licence requirement. So a resident may keep a captive-bred roof rat as a pet with no provincial licence — even though feral rats must be destroyed under the province's pest-control duty.

Sources: Government of Saskatchewan, Government of Saskatchewan / SVMA

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Because the species is on the allowed list, small-scale keeping and breeding are unregulated by wildlife law. A large commercial operation may meet a municipal 'commercial wildlife farm' / kennel definition or local business-licensing and zoning rules, so check your municipality if breeding at scale.

Sources: Government of Saskatchewan, Government of Saskatchewan / SVMA

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling or giving an allowed-list captive species is permitted; only large-scale commercial sale brings municipal pet-shop/business licensing into play. No provincial dealer licence is required for an allowed species.

Sources: Government of Saskatchewan

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Transport of a captive R. rattus within and into Saskatchewan is legal for an allowed-list species. Interprovincial transport is legal but subject to the destination province's rules — note you cannot transport one into (or, unresolved, through) Alberta.

Sources: Government of Saskatchewan

Restrictions & responsibilities

Feral rats are a different matter: under the Pest Control Act / pest declarations, every landowner and occupant has an affirmative duty to destroy and prevent the spread of wild rats. This applies to feral animals, not to your securely-caged, captive-bred pet — but never release a pet rat.

Source: Government of Saskatchewan

Operating a large-scale breeding or sales facility may require a municipal business licence and must comply with zoning and provincial animal-welfare standards, even though the species itself needs no wildlife licence.
  • Check your municipality's business-licensing and zoning rules if breeding/selling at scale

Where: Your municipality · Fees: Set locally

Source: Government of Saskatchewan / SVMA

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Alaska? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Alaska

Summary. Alaska is the most restrictive state in the nation for the roof rat — it's flatly PROHIBITED. Alaska uses a 'clean list' (whitelist): only species on 5 AAC 92.029 may be kept without a permit, and the Dept of Fish & Game is barred from issuing a permit for anything not on it. The ONLY rat on the list is the albino lab Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus var. albinus); Rattus rattus appears nowhere. On top of that, 5 AAC 92.141 makes it unlawful to harbor or transport live Muridae rodents (which includes the roof rat) — Alaska runs active 'rat-free' eradication programs. Anchorage adds a city-wide ban on the entire genus Rattus. Keeping/breeding/selling/importing are all prohibited (a class A misdemeanor, up to $25,000).

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Alaska-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Alaska is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Alaska's clean list (5 AAC 92.029) permits only listed species; the only rat on it is 'White rat Rattus norvegicus Var. albinus.' R. rattus is absent, and ADF&G is legally precluded from issuing a possession permit for an unlisted species. Independently, 5 AAC 92.141 prohibits harboring live Muridae rodents (defined to include true rats — 5 AAC 92.990(49)). ADF&G guidance states only albino rats are legal pets. Prohibited.

Sources: Alaska Board of Game / ADF&G (via Cornell LII), Alaska Dept of Fish & Game, Municipality of Anchorage / ADF&G

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Breeding presupposes lawful possession, which is barred; no permit pathway exists for unlisted species. The Municipality of Anchorage separately bans breeding any member of the genus Rattus without a Health Director research permit (AMC 16.90.030).

Sources: Alaska Board of Game / ADF&G (via Cornell LII), Municipality of Anchorage / ADF&G

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

The clean-list framework bars buying/selling/trading unlisted species, and giving one away facilitates unlawful possession by the recipient. Anchorage additionally bans import/buy/sell of any Rattus (AMC 16.90.030).

Sources: Alaska Board of Game / ADF&G (via Cornell LII), Municipality of Anchorage / ADF&G

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

5 AAC 92.141 makes it unlawful to enter Alaska (or operate any conveyance) while harboring live Muridae rodents — the roof rat is named in ADF&G guidance as covered. Import is also barred by the clean list (unlisted species can't be imported; no permit can issue). Class A misdemeanor (up to 1 yr / $25,000). Never release.

Sources: Alaska Dept of Fish & Game, Alaska Board of Game / ADF&G (via Cornell LII)

Restrictions & responsibilities

The roof rat is prohibited statewide in Alaska (clean-list exclusion + Muridae harboring ban), and Anchorage bans the whole genus Rattus. Do NOT bring one to Alaska — only the albino lab Norway rat is legal (and even that needs a permit in Anchorage). Violations are a class A misdemeanor (up to 1 year / $25,000). Never release.

Where: Alaska Dept of Fish & Game — Wildlife Permits

Source: Alaska Board of Game / ADF&G (via Cornell LII), Alaska Dept of Fish & Game

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Alaska. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Alaska
Time-sensitive: No proposal window is open now. The Board of Game's site currently shows it is not accepting proposals (the 2026/2027 cycle deadline of May 1, 2026 has passed and covered only certain regions). The next opportunity to file a statewide clean-list proposal is the upcoming statewide cycle, with proposals expected to be due around May 1, 2027. Watch the Board of Game site for the official "Call for Proposals" announcement (usually issued by January) and the online submission portal that opens with it. You can also ask to join the Board's notification list to be alerted when the window opens.

Alaska is the strictest state in the country for the pet roof rat (Rattus rattus). Alaska runs a "clean list" (a whitelist): under regulation 5 AAC 92.029, only the species on that list may be kept, and the only rat on it is the albino lab Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus var. albinus). The roof rat is not on the list. By law, the Department of Fish & Game is forbidden from issuing a possession permit for any species the list leaves off, so there is no permit to apply for. Separately, 5 AAC 92.141 bans harboring or transporting live Muridae rodents (which includes the roof rat), and the Municipality of Anchorage bans the entire genus Rattus. Keeping, breeding, selling, giving away, importing, or transporting a pet roof rat in Alaska is therefore prohibited and is a class A misdemeanor (up to one year and/or $25,000). This is not a case of the agency misreading the law. The agency is applying it as written. The list itself is the obstacle.

The ask: The fix is to add captive-bred Rattus rattus to the clean list (5 AAC 92.029), as the domesticated albino Norway rat already is. That is a regulation change, and the body with the power to make it is the Alaska Board of Game, through its public proposal-and-comment process. The realistic path is to file or support a Board of Game proposal in the next statewide cycle asking the Board to add the captive-bred, domesticated roof rat to the list as a permitted pet, documenting that it meets the same safety criteria the albino Norway rat already satisfies. The albino Norway rat on the list is itself the wild brown rat (R. norvegicus), domesticated only in the 19th century (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/), so a captive-bred R. rattus is the same case one species over. Asking ADF&G directly will not work: by statute it cannot permit an unlisted species, so the request must go to the Board that controls the list.

Where the lever really is: This is branch (b): the obstacle is the law and list as written, not an agency misreading. The Department of Fish & Game is applying 5 AAC 92.029 correctly. The regulation states that if a species is not on the list, ADF&G is forbidden from issuing a possession permit for it, and the roof rat is not on the list. A letter, appeal, or permit request to ADF&G will go nowhere, because there is no discretion to grant: the agency is barred by the regulation itself. The only thing that changes this is amending the list, which is controlled by the Alaska Board of Game through its public rulemaking (proposal-and-comment) process. The precedent is that the domesticated albino Norway rat is on the list, which shows the mechanism already exists to list a tame, captive-bred true rat. The ask is to extend the same treatment to captive-bred Rattus rattus, not to carve out an exception. The lever is therefore the rulemaking channel (Board of Game proposal plus public comment), not an administrative appeal. Even if listed statewide, Anchorage's separate genus-Rattus ban would still need a municipal fix, but the statewide list is the threshold issue and the right first target.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Alaska Board of Game — Proposal & Public Comment process (Boards Support Section) (public comment) — official contact page
    The Board of Game controls the 5 AAC 92.029 clean list and is the ONLY body that can add the roof rat to it. Its public proposal-and-comment process is the correct lever. Submit a proposal (or comment) through the official Board of Game portal when the Call for Proposals opens; until then, ask the Boards Support Section to add you to the notification list so you catch the next window.
  • Alaska Board of Game — regulatory proposal portal (boardofgame.adfg.alaska.gov) (public comment) — official contact page
    This is where the official proposal forms and the online submission option are posted once a Call for Proposals is issued, and where proposal books are opened for public comment. This is the channel through which a clean-list amendment for captive-bred Rattus rattus would actually be filed and commented on.
  • ADF&G Wildlife Permits / Possession program (executive / agency) — dfg.dwc.permits@alaska.gov
    Use this ONLY to request a written confirmation of the current status and to be pointed to the Board process — not as a place to win the change. By regulation this office cannot permit an unlisted species, so it cannot grant possession; a note here is useful to get the official statement in writing and to confirm the listing route, which strengthens a future Board proposal.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Alaska Board of Game / Boards Support Section,

I am writing about Alaska's clean list of animals that may be kept as pets, 5 AAC 92.029. I am asking the Board to add the captive-bred, domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) to that list as a permitted pet.

The domesticated albino Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus var. albinus) is already on the list. The pet roof rat is the same kind of animal: captive-bred for generations, hand-tame, kept entirely indoors as a companion, and never released to the wild. The distinction in the regulation is by species, not by whether the animal is domesticated. A tame, captive-bred roof rat poses no more risk than the listed lab rat.

Because the Department cannot issue a permit for a species the list leaves off, the only path is to amend the list, which is the Board's authority. I respectfully request that captive-bred Rattus rattus be added to 5 AAC 92.029, subject to the same indoor-only, no-release conditions, and I ask to be notified when the next Call for Proposals opens so I may submit a formal proposal.

Thank you for your consideration.

[Your name]
[Your city/region, Alaska]
[Your email / phone]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • 5 AAC 92.029 — Permit for Possessing Live Game (clean list; only 'White rat Rattus norvegicus Var. albinus') — Alaska Board of Game / ADF&G (via Cornell LII)
  • 5 AAC 92.141 + 92.990(49) — Muridae rodent transport/harboring prohibition (incl. roof rat) — Alaska Dept of Fish & Game
  • Anchorage Municipal Code 16.90.030 — genus Rattus banned except research permit — Municipality of Anchorage / ADF&G
