item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Alabama? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Alabama

Summary. Alabama doesn't name Rattus rattus anywhere, and the whole question turns on one classification: is your captive-bred roof rat a 'domestic animal' or a 'wild rodent'? State health rules (ADPH r. 420-4-4-.01(6)) define a 'domestic animal' as one bred through human association to the point of genetic changes in temperament/color/conformation — so a pedigreed, captive-bred, color-mutation roof rat can qualify, and if it does, keeping/breeding/selling are unregulated at the state level. If it's instead treated as a 'wild rodent,' the wildlife rule (Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.26) is harsh: it bans importing a wild rodent from out of state AND bans transporting one within the state at all (even an Alabama-born animal) except by a licensed game-breeder. There's no R. rattus-specific safe harbor, so the practical risk is an officer disagreeing that your animal is 'domestic.' Importing a domestic pet rat needs an electronic health certificate (eCVI); a 'semi-wild' classification adds a 10-day State-Veterinarian notice. Get a written ADCNR classification before importing or selling.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Alabama-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Alabama is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

No Alabama statute names Rattus rattus, and there is no state pet-rodent permit. Legality turns on classification: ADPH r. 420-4-4-.01(6) defines a 'domestic animal' as one bred through human association to a degree producing genetic changes (temperament/color/conformation) distinguishing it from wild animals of its species; 'wildlife' (r. 420-4-4-.01(12)) is everything else. A pedigreed, captive-bred, color-mutation roof rat can meet the 'domestic' test → keeping is unregulated, no permit. But if an officer deems it a 'wild rodent,' ADCNR r. 220-2-.26 bars possession of one imported from out of state (in-state-trapped wild rodents fall to unprotected-nongame rules but then can't be transported — see transport). No species-specific exemption names R. rattus, so the owner carries the evidentiary burden of domestication.

Sources: Alabama Dept of Conservation & Natural Resources, Alabama Dept of Public Health

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

Alabama has NO statewide commercial pet-breeder or small-rodent breeder license; if the animal is 'domestic,' non-commercial and hobby breeding are unregulated by the state. Commercial breeding is governed at the LOCAL/municipal level (e.g., the City of Gadsden's Commercial Breeder Permit + business license) — check your city/county. If the rat is instead classed as a 'wild rodent,' breeding it for transport/sale requires an ADCNR Game Breeder license (Code of Ala. §9-11-30; ~$250/yr non-cervid; facility inspections). Federally, USDA AWA exempts face-to-face/retail and small hobby sellers; the >4-breeding-female wholesale/sight-unseen threshold is the federal commercial demarcation (no Alabama state threshold).

Sources: City of Gadsden, Alabama, Alabama Legislature, Alabama Dept of Conservation & Natural Resources

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

Alabama has no state-level pet-dealer/pet-shop licensing act for domestic small animals; selling a 'domestic' pet rat needs only a standard retail revenue/business license for a storefront (Ala. Dept of Revenue 'Pet Shop' code), and private/free transfer is unregulated. BUT 220-2-.26 expressly prohibits the sale of a 'wild rodent' — so if the animal is classed wild, sale/transfer is banned. Everything again hinges on the domestic-vs-wild classification.

Sources: Alabama Dept of Conservation & Natural Resources, Alabama Dept of Revenue

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

INTRASTATE: ADCNR r. 220-2-.26(1) bans transporting a 'wild rodent' anywhere within Alabama — explicitly 'whether such member originated within or without the state' — EXCEPT by a properly licensed game-breeder. So if the animal is classed 'wild,' even a vet trip is unlawful; only the 'domestic animal' classification (or a game-breeder license) makes intrastate transport legal/unregulated. IMPORT (legal_with_permit): a domestic pet rat entering Alabama needs an electronic Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (eCVI via Global Vet Link or AgView; paper APHIS Form 7001 prohibited since 2019; valid 30 days). A 'semi-wild' classification additionally triggers a 10-day advance notice to the State Veterinarian (r. 80-3-6-.23); a 'wild rodent' classification = import banned. EXPORT: unregulated by Alabama (meet the destination state's rules; USFWS Form 3-177 for international, since the federal government treats R. rattus as wildlife). Never release. Net: 'restricted' because the binding intrastate ban + the import paperwork both turn on a classification the state hasn't settled for R. rattus.

Sources: Alabama Dept of Conservation & Natural Resources, Alabama Dept of Agriculture & Industries, Alabama Dept of Agriculture & Industries

Restrictions & responsibilities

Everything turns on whether your roof rat is a 'domestic animal' (ADPH genetic-change test, r. 420-4-4-.01(6)) or a 'wild rodent' (ADCNR r. 220-2-.26). If 'domestic': keeping/breeding/selling are state-unregulated and intrastate transport is legal; import needs an eCVI. If 'wild': import, sale, and ALL intrastate transport are barred except via a game-breeder license. Get a written ADCNR classification before importing or selling, and keep pedigree/photos documenting captive breeding + color mutations.
  • Ask ADCNR (WFF) in writing whether a pedigreed, captive-bred R. rattus is a 'domestic animal' or a restricted 'wild rodent' under 220-2-.26
  • For import: obtain an electronic CVI (Global Vet Link or AgView) from a USDA-accredited vet (valid 30 days); ask ADAI whether the 10-day State-Vet pre-report (80-3-6-.23) applies
  • For commercial breeding/sale: check your city/county for a local commercial-breeder permit + business license
  • Keep documentation (pedigree, photos of domestic color mutations) to support the 'domestic animal' classification

Where: Alabama DCNR (Wildlife & Freshwater Fisheries — classification); Alabama Dept of Agriculture & Industries (State Veterinarian — eCVI/import); local animal control (commercial breeding) · Fees: Game Breeder license ~$250/yr (only if 'wild')

Source: Alabama Dept of Conservation & Natural Resources, Alabama Dept of Public Health, Alabama Dept of Agriculture & Industries

Never release a roof rat — releasing any captive-raised/non-indigenous mammal into the wild in Alabama is illegal without express written ADCNR Commissioner permission, and it's ecologically harmful. Rehome responsibly.

Source: Alabama Dept of Conservation & Natural Resources

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Help change this

How to help in Alabama

Alabama law never mentions the roof rat (Rattus rattus) by name. There is no pet-rodent permit, no statewide ban, and no list that puts the species on or off limits. Everything hinges on one classification question: is a captive-bred, tame pet roof rat a "domestic animal" or a "wild rodent"? Alabama's public-health rule (Ala. Admin. Code r. 420-4-4-.01(6)) defines a "domestic animal" as one bred through human association to the point of genetic changes in temperament, color, or conformation that distinguish it from wild animals of the same species. A pedigreed, captive-bred, color-mutation roof rat that has never lived in the wild fits that test. If it is "domestic," keeping, breeding, and giving it away are unregulated by the state, and it can be taken to the vet freely. Alabama's wildlife rule (Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.26) is strict toward any "wild rodent": it bans importing one from out of state, bans selling one, and bans all transport within the state, even an Alabama-born animal and even a trip to the vet, except by a licensed game breeder. Because no Alabama rule names R. rattus as an exempt domestic pet, every owner carries the burden of proving their tame animal is "domestic," and a single officer could decide to treat the whole species as a restricted "wild rodent." That uncertainty is the problem.

The ask: Ask the Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources (Wildlife and Freshwater Fisheries Division) for a written interpretation confirming that a pedigreed, captive-bred Rattus rattus exhibiting domestication traits (genetic docility and domestic color mutations) is a "domestic animal" under ADPH Rule 420-4-4-.01(6), and therefore exempt from the possession, sale, and intrastate-transport bans of r. 220-2-.26, rather than a restricted "wild rodent." That classification turns on domestication, not wild ancestry. The dog descends from the wolf and the house cat from a wild felid, yet Alabama treats both as domestic animals because of generations bred for tameness, not their wild origins, which is the genetic-change test the ADPH rule describes. The fancy rat sold in pet stores is itself the wild brown rat (R. norvegicus), domesticated only in the 19th century (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/), and a pedigreed captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense, the same case one species over. The Division is asked to weigh that question, not to reach a particular result. The agency can also be asked to recognize pedigreed captive-bred Rattus as a category of domestic animal so individual owners no longer carry that burden case by case (New Jersey's genus-level exemption for Rattus is the model to cite). Separately, ask the Alabama Department of Agriculture and Industries (State Veterinarian) to confirm in writing that importing a captive-bred pet roof rat requires only a standard electronic Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (eCVI), not the 10-day "semi-wild animal" pre-report under r. 80-3-6-.23.

Where the lever really is: This is branch (a): a bureaucratic classification problem, and the lever is the agency, not the legislature. No statute and no administrative list names Rattus rattus. The restriction does not come from the species being placed on a prohibited list by the legislature; it comes from how an agency might read a generic, undefined phrase ("wild rodent" in r. 220-2-.26) against a separate definition of "domestic animal" (r. 420-4-4-.01(6)) that a captive-bred pet roof rat can already satisfy. The law as written contains the exemption sought, the "domestic animal" carve-out, so the request is not to change a law. It is to have the agency apply the existing definition correctly and say so in writing. The correct tool is therefore a written agency interpretation or declaratory ruling from ADCNR Wildlife and Freshwater Fisheries (the body that administers r. 220-2-.26), optionally backed by ADPH (which owns the "domestic animal" definition) and ADAI's State Veterinarian (for the import question). A legislative campaign would be the wrong tool: there is no bad statute to repeal and no species on a statutory list to remove. The honest caveat in the other direction: if ADCNR responds that it categorically treats R. rattus as a "wild rodent" regardless of captive-breeding history, it would be applying r. 220-2-.26 in a way the rule's text arguably permits, and the durable fix would then shift to a rulemaking petition (asking ADCNR to amend 220-2-.26 to add a captive-bred-Rattus exemption) rather than a one-off appeal, because an agency cannot be argued out of a reading the rule lets it hold; the rule has to change. Start with the clarification request and escalate to a rulemaking petition only if the agency confirms a categorical "wild rodent" reading.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources — Wildlife and Freshwater Fisheries Division (official Contact Us page) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    ADCNR Wildlife and Freshwater Fisheries administers r. 220-2-.26, the rule that defines and restricts a 'wild rodent.' This is the agency that can issue the written classification we need (domestic vs. wild). The official contact page routes to the Wildlife Section and to enforcement/permits — the right institutional doors for an interpretation request. Start here.
  • Alabama DCNR — Wildlife Section official inbox (executive / agency) — DCNR.Wildlife@dcnr.alabama.gov
    Verified official, role-based Wildlife Section mailbox (not an individual's personal address) listed on the DCNR Contact Us page. Use it to send the written request for a classification interpretation of captive-bred Rattus rattus under r. 220-2-.26 and ADPH r. 420-4-4-.01(6).
  • Alabama Department of Agriculture and Industries — Animal Industries Division / State Veterinarian (official contact) (executive / agency) — ask-me@agi.alabama.gov
    ADAI's Office of the State Veterinarian governs animal import into Alabama (eCVI) and the 10-day 'semi-wild animal' pre-report (r. 80-3-6-.23). Ask here, in writing, whether a captive-bred pet roof rat is treated as a standard domestic pet (eCVI only) or as a semi-wild animal. The contact form and ask-me inbox are the verified official channels.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Request for written classification of a captive-bred domestic roof rat (Rattus rattus)

To the Wildlife and Freshwater Fisheries Division:

I am writing to request a written interpretation of how Alabama classifies a pedigreed, captive-bred pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) kept as a household companion. My concern is the difference between a "domestic animal" under ADPH Rule 420-4-4-.01(6) and a restricted "wild rodent" under Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.26.

These animals are captive-bred over many generations, tame, kept indoors only, and never released. They show the genetic changes in temperament and color that the "domestic animal" definition describes, much like the fancy rat sold in pet stores. The issue is not whether a wild-caught rat is wild; it is that a domesticated, captive-bred animal should be recognized as domestic. The dog descends from the wolf and the house cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic animals because of generations bred for tameness, not their wild ancestry, and a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense.

Please confirm in writing that such an animal is a "domestic animal," and therefore exempt from the possession, sale, and intrastate-transport provisions of r. 220-2-.26, so an owner needs no game-breeder license to keep one or take it to a veterinarian. I would also welcome the Division recognizing pedigreed, captive-bred Rattus as a domestic category, as some other states have done, so owners are not left to prove this animal by animal.

Thank you for your time and guidance.

[Your name]
[Your city, Alabama]
[Your email / phone]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

  • Ala. Admin. Code r. 420-4-4-.01(6),(12) — ADPH definitions of 'Domestic animal' (genetic-change test) vs 'Wildlife' — Alabama Dept of Public Health

  • Ala. Admin. Code r. 80-3-6-.23 — Wild/semi-wild captive animals imported into Alabama (10-day State-Vet pre-report) — Alabama Dept of Agriculture & Industries

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Arkansas? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Arkansas

Summary. Arkansas uses a positive-list captive-wildlife system, and the roof rat falls through it. The Game & Fish Commission lists species as Unrestricted (R1.01), Permit-Required (R1.02), or Prohibited (R1.03) — and any species on NONE of the lists is 'prohibited by default until evaluated.' The fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is explicitly on the Unrestricted list and exempt from the possession/breeder/import rules; Rattus rattus is not on any list. So under a strict reading, keeping/breeding/selling/importing a roof rat is prohibited-by-default pending an AGFC species evaluation — another 'species-not-domestication' trap. There's a clear path: petition AGFC to add captive-bred R. rattus to the Unrestricted list (it poses no different risk than the fancy rat). We've queued that inquiry.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Arkansas-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Arkansas is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

AGFC's captive-wildlife framework (Code R1.00) classifies species as Unrestricted/Permit-Required/Prohibited and makes any UNLISTED species prohibited by default until evaluated. R. norvegicus is on the Unrestricted list (R1.01) and exempt from Code 09.02; Rattus rattus is on none of the lists, so a strict reading makes private possession prohibited-by-default pending an AGFC determination. (Genuine ambiguity: no enforcement names R. rattus and some sources treat 'rats' as unregulated pocket pets — but that rests on the R. norvegicus exemption.)

Sources: Arkansas Game & Fish Commission, Arkansas Game & Fish Commission, Arkansas Game & Fish Commission

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

The Wildlife Breeder/Dealer Permit (Code 09.07) is available only for species on the Permit-Required list (R1.02); R. rattus isn't on it, and unlisted species are prohibited by default — so there is currently no breeding-permit pathway for the roof rat under the AGFC framework (unless AGFC determines it's outside their jurisdiction).

Sources: Arkansas Game & Fish Commission, Arkansas Game & Fish Commission

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Sale/transfer of captive wildlife runs through the same AGFC framework; R. norvegicus is exempt from Code 09.07/09.10 by name, R. rattus is not. As an unlisted (prohibited-by-default) species, commercial sale has no permit pathway; gifting falls under the same possession framework. Resolve the possession classification with AGFC first.

Sources: Arkansas Game & Fish Commission, Arkansas Game & Fish Commission

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Importing wildlife needs an AGFC Wildlife Importation Permit (Code 09.10) unless the species is Unrestricted (R1.01) — R. rattus isn't, creating a circular bar. Separately, the Dept of Agriculture (ALPC Rule 125.00) requires an entry permit + CVI for 'zoo, wild, and/or exotic animals' (rodents not explicitly named). In-state transport of a lawfully-held animal isn't separately restricted, but the possession question controls. Never release a roof rat.

Sources: Arkansas Game & Fish Commission, Arkansas Dept of Agriculture

Restrictions & responsibilities

Because R. rattus is unlisted on AGFC's captive-wildlife lists (only the fancy rat is Unrestricted), it is prohibited-by-default until AGFC evaluates it. Request a species determination from AGFC (captivewildlife@agfc.ar.gov) BEFORE acquiring one, and consider petitioning to add captive-bred R. rattus to the Unrestricted list. Never release one.
  • Email AGFC captivewildlife@agfc.ar.gov for a species determination / petition to add R. rattus to R1.01

Where: Arkansas Game & Fish Commission — Captive Wildlife Program

Source: Arkansas Game & Fish Commission, Arkansas Game & Fish Commission

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Arkansas. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Arkansas

Arkansas regulates captive wildlife with a "positive list" system run by the Arkansas Game & Fish Commission (AGFC). Under AGFC Code R1.00, species are sorted into Unrestricted (R1.01), Permit-Required (R1.02), or Prohibited (R1.03), and any species on none of the lists is treated as prohibited-by-default until AGFC evaluates it. The common pet "fancy rat," Rattus norvegicus, is listed by name on the Unrestricted list and is exempt from the possession, breeder/dealer, and importation permit rules. The roof rat, Rattus rattus, is not on any of the lists. Under a strict reading, the captive-bred pet roof rat is therefore prohibited-by-default, not because anyone judged it dangerous, but because it was never added to a list, while its near-identical cousin the fancy rat already is. This is a classification gap, not a deliberate ban.

The ask: Ask AGFC to add captive-bred Rattus rattus to the Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List (R1.01), the same status the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) already holds, or, if AGFC views multi-generational captive-bred pet rats as outside its captive-wildlife jurisdiction, to say so in writing. A captive-bred, tame, indoor-only pet roof rat poses no different ecological or public-safety risk than the already-exempt fancy rat. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat (R. norvegicus), domesticated only in the 19th century (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/), so a captive-bred R. rattus is the same case one species over. The Commission is asked to weigh whether the same Unrestricted treatment is warranted. Send species-evaluation requests to the captive wildlife program inbox.

Where the lever really is: The lever is the agency (AGFC), not the legislature. This is a positive-list and species-evaluation gap, and AGFC is the body that maintains and amends those lists. AGFC's framework (Code R1.00 plus addenda R1.01/R1.02/R1.03) is administrative regulation written and revised by the Commission through a science-based species-evaluation process. It already added Rattus norvegicus by name to the Unrestricted list and exempted it from Codes 09.02/09.07/09.10, and the same body can add Rattus rattus the same way. The problem is therefore (a): the rules under-apply to the roof rat only because it was never evaluated and listed, not because a statute names it as banned. The correct move is a written species-evaluation request or petition to AGFC's captive wildlife program asking it to add captive-bred R. rattus to R1.01, or to confirm it is outside AGFC jurisdiction. The Arkansas General Assembly is not needed: the underlying statute (Ark. Code §15-43-201 et seq.) delegates captive-wildlife classification to the Commission, so AGFC can fix this by amending its own list. A legislative appeal would be the wrong door unless AGFC declines and points back to statute. Note that there is genuine ambiguity: some treat common pet rats as unregulated "pocket pets," and no known enforcement has targeted R. rattus, but that informal tolerance rests on the R. norvegicus exemption. Getting R. rattus formally listed removes the risk rather than relying on non-enforcement.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Arkansas Game & Fish Commission — Captive Wildlife Program (executive / agency) — captivewildlife@agfc.ar.gov
    This is the body that maintains the Unrestricted/Permit/Prohibited captive-wildlife lists and runs the science-based species-evaluation process. Its official captive-wildlife page directs species-evaluation requests for unlisted species to captivewildlife@agfc.ar.gov. This is exactly where to ask AGFC to add captive-bred Rattus rattus to the Unrestricted list (R1.01) — the status the fancy rat already holds — or to confirm captive-bred pet rats are outside its jurisdiction.
  • Arkansas Game & Fish Commission — Headquarters (executive / agency) — official contact page
    General AGFC headquarters touchpoint (phone 833-345-0325, 2 Natural Resources Drive, Little Rock) for routing or following up on a captive-wildlife species-evaluation request if the program inbox does not respond.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To: Arkansas Game & Fish Commission, Captive Wildlife Program
Subject: Species-evaluation request to add captive-bred roof rat (Rattus rattus) to the Unrestricted list

Dear Captive Wildlife Program,

I am writing about a gap in the captive-wildlife species lists under Code R1.00. The fancy rat, Rattus norvegicus, is on the Unrestricted list (R1.01) and exempt from Codes 09.02, 09.07, and 09.10. Its close cousin, the roof rat (Rattus rattus), is on none of the lists, so under a strict reading it is prohibited-by-default, only because it was never evaluated, not because anyone found it dangerous.

The animals I am describing are captive-bred and multi-generational tame, kept strictly indoors as pets, and never released to the wild. A captive-bred Rattus rattus poses no different ecological or public-safety risk than the already-exempt fancy rat.

Please evaluate captive-bred Rattus rattus and add it to the Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List (R1.01), giving it the same treatment as Rattus norvegicus. If AGFC considers captive-bred pet rats outside its captive-wildlife jurisdiction, please confirm that in writing. I am glad to provide further information.

Thank you for your consideration.
[Your name]
[Your city, Arkansas]
[Your email]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • AGFC Code R1.00 — Captive Wildlife framework (Unrestricted/Permit/Prohibited lists; unlisted = prohibited by default) — Arkansas Game & Fish Commission
  • AGFC Code 09.02 — Possession of Non-Native Wildlife Restricted (R. norvegicus exempt by name; R. rattus not) — Arkansas Game & Fish Commission
  • AGFC Addendum R1.01 — Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List (lists R. norvegicus; R. rattus absent) — Arkansas Game & Fish Commission
  • Arkansas Dept of Agriculture — Animal Entry Requirements (entry permit/CVI for exotic animals) — Arkansas Dept of Agriculture

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in American Samoa? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › American Samoa

Summary. American Samoa is effectively a closed door for a pet roof rat. IMPORT is functionally prohibited: the Department of Agriculture's quarantine code (ASAC Title 24, Ch. 3) bans the importation of 'miscellaneous pets' (ASAC 24.0318), the 'domestic animal' import list (ASAC 24.0320) is a closed list of agricultural/working animals that does NOT include any rat, and any non-domestic animal may be imported only with the Governor's prior written permission (ASAC 24.0315) — a waiver that is, in practice, reserved for scientific/laboratory use and essentially never granted for a pet rodent. There is no on-island quarantine facility, so a non-compliant animal is returned to origin at the owner's expense or destroyed. WITHIN the territory there is no wildlife-possession permit scheme for pet rats (keep/breed/sell are not separately licensed), so those activities sit in an unregulated legal void — but that void is legally perilous: ASAC Title 25, Ch. 21 (Rodent Control, ASAC 25.2101) imposes an affirmative duty on every building owner/occupant to eradicate rodents and to deny them food and harborage, with no carve-out for a caged, domesticated rat, and ASAC 24.1104 lists 'rats and mice' as pest species that may be killed at any time without a permit. The code makes NO distinction between wild R. rattus and a captive-bred 'fancy' rat (or even R. norvegicus) — taxonomically indifferent. Maintaining a public-health nuisance after a 10-day abatement notice is a class C misdemeanor (ASAC 25.0107). The traditional matai/village by-law system adds a further enforceable layer on communal land. Never release a roof rat (it is a documented, federally targeted invasive that devastates native Pacific birds).

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the American Samoa-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where American Samoa is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-12

No wildlife-possession permit or 'banned-to-keep' species statute exists for pet rats, so in-territory keeping is not separately licensed — BUT it is legally perilous, not safely permissive. ASAC 25.2101 (Rodent Control) imposes an affirmative duty on 'every owner, lessee, or occupant of an occupied building' to eradicate rodents 'by poisoning, trapping, fumigation or other appropriate means' and to keep premises 'free from foodstuffs... and other material which may serve as food or harborage for rodents,' with NO carve-out for a caged, domesticated rat — so a clean pet enclosure is textually indistinguishable from an illegal rodent harborage. ASAC 24.1104 separately classifies 'rats and mice' as pest species takeable at any time without a permit. Maintaining a public-health nuisance after a 10-day notice to abate is a class C misdemeanor (ASAC 25.0107). Whether Health actually treats a secure indoor pet as a 'harborage' is the open enforcement question.

Sources: American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR), American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR), American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR), American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR)

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-12

The ASAC contains no statute regulating or licensing the private propagation of small mammals, and no hobbyist-breeder carve-out for non-traditional pets — so breeding is technically unregulated. But it is the most legally hostile of the in-territory activities: intentionally increasing the population of a species the government is actively trying to suppress (ASAC 24.1104 lists rats/mice as pests takeable at will; federal eradication programs are underway) cuts directly against public policy, and breeding still requires keeping, which carries the ASAC 25.2101 harborage problem. A breeding operation would also be exposed to the broad public-health nuisance definition in ASAC 13.0203(31). With no legal way to import founder stock, establishing breeding stock is in any case a practical impossibility.

Sources: American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR), American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR), American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR)

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Low · Last verified 2026-06-12

There is no pet-dealer or rodent-specific licensing statute, and the quarantine chapter is silent on the local sale/gifting of an animal already lawfully present — so intra-territory transfer is unaddressed by specific point-of-sale law. Practically, however, selling/gifting a rat transfers the ASAC 25.2101 nuisance/eradication liability to the buyer, and any commercial enterprise would need a general business license from the Department of Commerce (DOC), whose issuance requires compliance with health/environmental rules and would trigger Department of Health / Environmental Quality Commission review — almost certainly denied given the territory's active rat-eradication posture. Because lawful import of founder stock is closed, a commercial breeding/sale operation is practically impossible to establish.

Sources: American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR), American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR), American Samoa Department of Commerce (ASDOC)

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Importing a roof rat into American Samoa is functionally prohibited. ASAC 24.0318 expressly prohibits the importation of 'miscellaneous pets' — a banned catch-all for non-traditional domestic animals into which pet rodents fall. The 'domestic animals' eligible for routine import are an exhaustive closed list (ASAC 24.0320: ruminants, horses/mules/asses, swine, domestic poultry) that does NOT include any rat. A non-domestic animal may be imported only with 'the prior written permission of the Governor' (ASAC 24.0315) — a waiver realistically reserved for scientific/laboratory imports, not pets. American Samoa has no quarantine facility (unlike Hawaii), so a non-compliant or unauthorized animal is immediately returned to origin at the owner's expense or destroyed. The species is treated firmly as an invasive pest at the border, not as a permissible companion animal. (American Samoa is outside the U.S. customs territory; a shipment routed through a U.S. designated port would also implicate federal USFWS rules, but the territorial import bar is dispositive.) Never release a roof rat.

Sources: American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR), FAO Legal Office archive (FAOLEX), PetTravel.com (secondary, summarizing DOA quarantine policy)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing a roof rat into American Samoa is functionally prohibited. Pet rodents fall under the banned 'miscellaneous pet' class (ASAC 24.0318); rats are absent from the closed 'domestic animal' import list (ASAC 24.0320); and a non-domestic animal can enter only with the Governor's prior written permission (ASAC 24.0315), which is realistically reserved for scientific/laboratory imports. There is no quarantine facility, so a non-compliant animal is returned to origin at the owner's expense or destroyed. Do not ship a pet rat to American Samoa expecting entry.
  • Treat import as effectively closed: a pet roof rat is a prohibited 'miscellaneous pet' and is not on the domestic-animal import list
  • The only theoretical route is the Governor's prior written permission (ASAC 24.0315) — confirm in writing with the Dept of Agriculture Quarantine office before any shipment; expect denial for a pet rodent
  • If denied or non-compliant: there is no on-island quarantine, so the animal is returned at your expense or destroyed — do not attempt entry on spec
  • Never release a roof rat (documented invasive; active eradication programs)

Where: American Samoa Dept of Agriculture — Plant & Animal Quarantine (PAQ) Division (and, for any waiver, the Governor's Office) · Fees: ASAC 24.0306 domestic-animal import permit nominal fee (N/A in practice — a pet rat is not an importable 'domestic animal')

Source: American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR), FAO Legal Office archive (FAOLEX), PetTravel.com (secondary, summarizing DOA quarantine policy)

Public-health 'rodent harborage' hazard. ASAC 25.2101 imposes an affirmative duty on every building owner/occupant to eradicate rodents and to keep premises free of food and harborage, with no exemption for a caged domesticated rat — so a pet enclosure can be read as an illegal rodent harborage. ASAC 24.1104 lists rats/mice as pest species takeable at any time without a permit. Maintaining a public-health nuisance after a 10-day notice to abate is a class C misdemeanor (ASAC 25.0107). Keep enclosures secure and sanitary; understand that enforcement could compel removal/destruction of the animal.
  • Understand that no possession permit exists, but the rodent-eradication duty (ASAC 25.2101) can be read to reach a caged pet rat
  • Keep any rat strictly contained, clean, and odor-free to minimize nuisance-complaint exposure
  • Confirm with the Dept of Health whether a secure indoor pet enclosure is treated as a regulated 'harborage' before relying on the gap

Where: American Samoa Dept of Health — Environmental Health Services

Source: American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR), American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR), American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR)

Traditional governance layer. Most land in American Samoa is communal native land under the matai (chief) system (ASAC Title 37), and villages enforce by-laws via Village Monitoring & Enforcement Committees. A matai or village council edict to clear 'isumu (rats/mice) harborage on communal land carries enforceable weight under the territorial statutes protecting traditional governance, and an individual without freehold rights has little recourse. This is a real, non-statutory hurdle to keeping a pet rat on communal land.

Where: Village council (fono) / matai with authority over the communal land

Source: American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR)

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Official sources

  • ASAC Title 24, Ch. 3 — Quarantine of Pets and Agricultural Products and Animals (24.0306 import permit; 24.0315 Governor's permission for non-domestic; 24.0318 'miscellaneous pet' import ban; 24.0320 closed 'domestic animal' list) — American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR)
  • American Samoa Administrative Code Title 24, Ch. 3 — full text (incl. 24.0320 closed 'domestic animal' definition) — FAO Legal Office archive (FAOLEX)
  • ASAC 24.1104 — Taking of pest species ('rats and mice' takeable at any time without a permit); ASAC 24.1101 (definition of 'wildlife') — American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR)
  • ASAC 25.2101 — Duty of owner/lessee/occupant of occupied building to eradicate rodents and deny food/harborage (Rodent Control) — American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR)
  • ASAC 25.0107 — Penalty for maintaining/allowing a public nuisance after notice to abate (class C misdemeanor; each day a separate offense) — American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR)
  • ASAC 13.0203(31) — Definition of a 'nuisance' affecting public health — American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR)
  • ASAC 37.0204 / 37.0201 — Restrictions on alienation of land; matai system and communal native-land definitions (village by-law enforcement layer) — American Samoa Administrative Code (via ASBAR)
  • American Samoa Pet Import Requirements — 'miscellaneous pets' barred; no quarantine facility; non-compliant animals returned or destroyed — PetTravel.com (secondary, summarizing DOA quarantine policy)
  • Savana Island Black Rat Eradication Program — Draft Environmental Assessment (Dec 2023): R. rattus active eradication target in American Samoa — USDA-APHIS (via Regulations.gov)
  • American Samoa Department of Commerce — business licensing (commercial breeding/retail must comply with health/environmental review) — American Samoa Department of Commerce (ASDOC)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat, 'isumu, le 'isumu.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Arizona? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Arizona

Summary. Arizona lets you keep, breed, and rehome a captive-bred roof rat with NO Game & Fish permit — but the legal basis is 'unrestricted wildlife,' not 'pet,' and that brings one big string attached. Arizona Game & Fish (AZGFD) restricts live wildlife by family, and the rat family (Muridae) is NOT on the restricted list (A.A.C. R12-4-406), so R. rattus is 'unrestricted wildlife.' Under A.A.C. R12-4-405(D) you may possess, propagate (breed), and sell/give away unrestricted wildlife and its offspring with no AZGFD license — PROVIDED the animal was lawfully imported from out of state (or is the offspring of one). The catch: because R. rattus also lives wild in Arizona and AZGFD's narrow definition of 'domestic' (R12-4-401) excludes it, you may NOT catch a feral Arizona roof rat and keep it — wild-caught local rats are illegal contraband (R12-4-402), and the burden is on you to prove your pet's captive-bred/imported provenance. Bringing a rat into Arizona requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) from the Dept of Agriculture (A.A.C. R3-2-602); intrastate transport needs no permit. Commercial sellers may meet the 'Pet Dealer' definition (A.R.S. Title 44) and must follow its care standards (e.g., a resting board over wire flooring). Bites from a caged pet rodent are statutorily exempt from rabies quarantine/testing (A.R.S. 11-1014(C)). Never release a roof rat — it is a strict-liability violation (R12-4-402(A)) and an active eradication target. R. rattus and the fancy rat R. norvegicus are treated identically (both unrestricted Muridae), so there is no species-trap.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Arizona-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Arizona is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

R. rattus (family Muridae) is not among the rodent families designated 'restricted live wildlife' in A.A.C. R12-4-406; under R12-4-405(D) a person may possess unrestricted wildlife and its offspring with no AZGFD license if it was lawfully imported/possessed. So keeping a captive-bred, out-of-state-sourced roof rat needs no Game & Fish license. The one limit: because R. rattus also lives wild in Arizona and the narrow 'domestic' definition in R12-4-401 excludes it, capturing a FERAL Arizona roof rat and keeping it is unlawful (R12-4-402(A) — no lawful take of a nongame mammal alive); the owner bears the burden of proving lawful (imported/captive-bred) provenance.

Sources: AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII), AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII), AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII), AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII), Arizona State Legislature

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

A.A.C. R12-4-405(D) expressly lets a person 'propagate' unrestricted wildlife and its offspring with no AZGFD license, provided the parent stock was lawfully imported/possessed. There is no Game & Fish hobby-breeder or small-mammal propagation license for an unrestricted species because no base license is required. The offspring of lawfully imported rats inherit the same unrestricted, lawful status.

Sources: AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII), AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

A.A.C. R12-4-405(D) lets a person 'trade, rent, lease, give away, sell, offer for sale, export' unrestricted wildlife and its offspring with no AZGFD license if the animal was lawfully imported/possessed — so selling or rehoming captive-bred roof rats is not barred by wildlife law. A commercial seller meeting the 'Pet Dealer'/'pet store' definition in A.R.S. 44-1799 ('selling at retail... other animals') must follow Title 44 care standards (sanitation, food/water, space, and a resting board over any wire flooring — A.R.S. 44-1799.04) and sourcing rules (44-1799.10); violations are a class 1 misdemeanor. The state preempts local bans on lawful retail pet sales (44-1799.11).

Sources: AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII), Arizona State Legislature, Arizona State Legislature

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Intrastate transport of an unrestricted species needs no permit (R12-4-405(D) authorizes transporting unrestricted wildlife). IMPORTING into Arizona requires no AZGFD wildlife license for an unrestricted mammal, BUT the Dept of Agriculture mandates that all animals moved into Arizona be accompanied by a valid official Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) from the state of origin (A.A.C. R3-2-602(A)); R. rattus is an 'exotic mammal not regulated as restricted live wildlife,' so it is an 'Animal' under R3-2-601. The CVI (issued by an accredited vet, typically valid 30 days) is the operative permit. The entry-permit-number requirement applies only to livestock and is waived for electronic CVIs (AZDA SP24-02). Animals entering without a CVI face mandatory quarantine at owner expense (R3-2-605). Never release a roof rat — release of any live wildlife is unlawful under R12-4-402(A)(3).

Sources: AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII), AZ Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII), AZ Dept of Agriculture, AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Bringing a pet roof rat INTO Arizona requires a valid official Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) from the origin state (A.A.C. R3-2-602(A)), issued by an accredited veterinarian (typically valid 30 days). No AZGFD import license is needed for an unrestricted species; no entry-permit number is required for an exotic small mammal when the CVI is submitted electronically (AZDA SP24-02). Animals entering without a CVI are subject to mandatory quarantine at the owner's expense (R3-2-605).
  • Before crossing into Arizona, have an accredited vet in the origin state issue a CVI for the rat (examination within ~30 days)
  • Carry the CVI during transport; e-CVI submission via USAHERDS removes any entry-permit-number requirement (SP24-02)
  • No AZGFD import permit is required (R. rattus is unrestricted wildlife)

Forms: Arizona Dept of Agriculture — Importing Animals into Arizona / CVI · Where: Issued by the origin-state accredited veterinarian; enforced by the Arizona Dept of Agriculture, State Veterinarian's Office · Fees: Veterinary fee for the CVI (no state CVI filing fee)

Source: AZ Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII), AZ Dept of Agriculture

Provenance burden: you may keep/breed/sell a roof rat only if it was lawfully imported (or is the offspring of one). Catching a feral Arizona roof rat and keeping it is unlawful (R12-4-402(A) — no lawful live take of a nongame mammal), and the owner bears the burden of proving lawful captive-bred/imported origin if questioned. Keep import receipts, breeder contracts, and CVIs indefinitely.
  • Acquire only captive-bred roof rats from a lawful out-of-state source (never a wild-caught Arizona rat)
  • Retain proof of provenance (purchase receipt, breeder contract, CVI) in case of an AZGFD inquiry

Where: Arizona Game & Fish Department (enforcement)

Source: AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII), AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII)

Commercial sellers/breeders who meet the A.R.S. 44-1799 'pet dealer / pet store' definition ('selling at retail... other animals') must meet Title 44 animal-care standards: sanitary facilities, continuous water and adequate food, adequate space, and — if rats are housed on wire flooring — a resting board/mat allowing the animal off the wire (A.R.S. 44-1799.04). They may not source from a USDA/AWA-noncompliant breeder (44-1799.10). Violations are a class 1 misdemeanor. Private (non-commercial) keepers/breeders are not 'pet dealers.'
  • If operating commercially, meet A.R.S. 44-1799.04 care standards (sanitation, food/water, space, resting board over wire flooring)
  • Source only from USDA/AWA-compliant breeders (44-1799.10)

Where: Arizona Dept of Agriculture (Animal Services) / local enforcement

Source: Arizona State Legislature, Arizona State Legislature

Never release a roof rat into the wild — releasing any live wildlife is an expressly unlawful act in Arizona (A.A.C. R12-4-402(A)(3)) and a strict-liability violation, whether intentional or via escape from an insecure enclosure. R. rattus is an active eradication target (citrus pest; vector). AZGFD may seize/euthanize even a lawfully possessed rat held in a way that threatens public health or other wildlife (R12-4-402(B)).
  • Keep rats in secure indoor enclosures; never release or allow escape into the environment

Where: Arizona Game & Fish Department

Source: AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • A.A.C. R12-4-401 — Live Wildlife Definitions (narrow 'domestic' definition; R. rattus is 'wildlife,' a nongame mammal) — AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII)
  • A.A.C. R12-4-402 — Live Wildlife: Unlawful Acts (no wild capture of a nongame mammal; no-release; seizure authority) — AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII)
  • A.A.C. R12-4-405 — Importing/Purchasing/Transporting Live Wildlife Without an Arizona License (subsection (D): possess/propagate/sell/transport unrestricted wildlife if lawfully imported) — AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII)
  • A.A.C. R12-4-406 — Restricted Live Wildlife (lists restricted Rodentia families; Muridae/Rattus deliberately absent) — AZ Game & Fish Commission (via Cornell LII)
  • A.A.C. R3-2-602 — Importation Requirements (CVI required for all animals moved into Arizona; rodents are 'Animals' per R3-2-601) — AZ Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII)
  • AZDA Substantive Policy Statement SP24-02 — waives the entry-permit-number requirement for electronic CVIs (USAHERDS) — AZ Dept of Agriculture
  • A.R.S. § 17-101 — Definitions ('wildlife' and 'take'; R. rattus is a nongame wild mammal) — Arizona State Legislature
  • A.R.S. § 44-1799 — Pet Dealers: Definitions ('pet store' = retail sale of 'other animals'; loops in exotic-mammal sellers) — Arizona State Legislature
  • A.R.S. § 44-1799.04 — Pet dealer animal-care requirements (sanitation, food/water, space, resting board over wire flooring; class 1 misdemeanor) — Arizona State Legislature
  • A.R.S. § 11-1014 — Biting animals; caged/pet rodents exempt from rabies quarantine/testing (11-1014(C)) — Arizona State Legislature
  • Roof Rat Control Around Homes and Other Structures (AZ1280) — R. rattus as invasive citrus/structural pest and disease vector in Arizona — University of Arizona Cooperative Extension

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in California? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › California

Summary. California restricts ALL rodents as 'detrimental' wild animals (14 CCR §671), and CDFW never issues possession permits for pets — so a normal wild-type roof rat is effectively illegal to keep. BUT the rule exempts 'domesticated races of rats or mice (white or albino; trained, dancing or spinning, laboratory-reared)', and that exemption is written by phenotype/origin, not by species — it doesn't name Rattus norvegicus. So a white/albino, trained, or documented laboratory-reared Rattus rattus may qualify, while a wild-type one does not. Whether a domesticated roof-rat line qualifies is the open question we've put to CDFW.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the California-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where California is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

California classifies every species of Order Rodentia as a 'detrimental' restricted wild animal (14 CCR §671; FGC §2118), and CDFW categorically refuses Restricted Species Permits for PET purposes (only research/exhibition/education). The one opening is the exemption for 'domesticated races of rats or mice (white or albino; trained, dancing or spinning, laboratory-reared)' (14 CCR §671(c)(2)(J)(1)(c)) — which is defined by phenotype/origin, NOT by species. A white/albino, trained, or documented laboratory-reared roof rat may qualify; a phenotypically wild-type (agouti/black) roof rat is presumed an illegal restricted pest. Wild-caught roof rats can never be kept (FGC §3005.5).

Sources: CA Code of Regulations, CA Fish & Game Code, CA Fish & Game Code, CA Dept of Fish & Wildlife

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Breeding restricted rodents is prohibited without research/exhibition permits. If the animals meet the 'domesticated races' exemption, breeding is outside CDFW's wildlife jurisdiction — but local animal-control/zoning rules apply, and any retail sale is governed by the Pet Store Animal Care Act.

Sources: CA Code of Regulations, CA Fish & Game Code

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling restricted wild rodents is prohibited. Selling EXEMPT domesticated rats is legal but regulated by California's Pet Store Animal Care Act (HSC §122350–122361), which sets enclosure, space, enrichment, and veterinary-care standards for anyone selling vertebrate pets.

Sources: CA Health & Safety Code, CA Code of Regulations

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Importing/transporting a restricted rodent needs a permit + Certificate of Veterinary Inspection. An EXEMPT domesticated rat may cross state lines without a restricted-species permit, but every animal entering California is still subject to inspection at CDFA border stations (the roof rat is a top agricultural pest), so carry documentation that the animal is an exempt domestic race. International movement is restricted federally (USFWS Form 3-177 — see United States).

Sources: CA Code of Regulations, CA Dept of Food & Agriculture

Restrictions & responsibilities

If the roof rat does NOT meet the 'domesticated races' exemption, it is a restricted species and CDFW issues permits only for research/exhibition/education — NOT pets — so keeping/breeding it as a pet is effectively prohibited (and wild-caught roof rats can never be kept, FGC §3005.5). Restricted-facility permits carry steep application + inspection fees and an emergency action plan.
  • Determine whether your animal meets the white/albino/trained/laboratory-reared exemption
  • If exempt, no CDFW permit is needed; if not, pet possession is not permitted

Forms: CDFW Restricted Species Permits · Where: CDFW License & Revenue Branch, Special Permits Unit · Fees: Restricted-species permits are not issued for pets

Source: CA Code of Regulations, CA Dept of Fish & Wildlife

Retail sale of an exempt domestic rat must meet the Pet Store Animal Care Act (HSC §122350–122361): structurally sound enclosures, adequate space, enrichment, separation of sick animals, and veterinary care.

Source: CA Health & Safety Code

All animals entering California pass CDFA border protection stations. Even an exempt domesticated roof rat may be stopped because it resembles a detrimental pest — carry proof (e.g., laboratory/breeder provenance) of its exempt domestic status.

Where: CDFA border protection stations

Source: CA Dept of Food & Agriculture

Never release or relocate a roof rat: relocating trapped wildlife is illegal (14 CCR §465.5), and releasing a nonnative species is prohibited. Wild roof rats may only be controlled lethally, never tamed/kept.

Source: CA Code of Regulations

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in California. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in California

California treats every rodent species as a "detrimental" restricted wild animal under Title 14 of the California Code of Regulations, section 671 (and Fish & Game Code section 2118), and the Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) does not issue possession permits for pets. A wild-type roof rat (Rattus rattus) is therefore effectively illegal to keep. The same animal, bred in captivity, can be as tame as the common pet "fancy rat" (Rattus norvegicus), which is kept freely in California. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated in the 19th century; a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over. Section 671 contains an exemption for "domesticated races of rats or mice (white or albino; trained, dancing or spinning, laboratory-reared)." That exemption is written by phenotype and origin, not by species. It says "rats or mice"; it does not name Rattus norvegicus and does not exclude Rattus rattus. A white/albino, demonstrably tame/trained, or documented laboratory-reared roof rat arguably fits the text, while a phenotypically wild-type one is presumed an illegal restricted pest. Whether CDFW reads the exemption to reach a domesticated roof-rat line, or treats it as fancy-rats-only, is the unresolved question, and it determines whether this is fixed by a clarification or by a rule change.

The ask: Two-track ask. (1) Ask CDFW's License & Revenue Branch / Special Permits Unit, in writing, to confirm whether the section 671(c)(2)(J)(1)(c) exemption for "domesticated races of rats or mice (white or albino; trained, dancing or spinning, laboratory-reared)" applies to a captive-bred, tame, domesticated line of roof rat (Rattus rattus), since the exemption is written by phenotype/origin and names no species, and to explain how the Department operationally defines "trained" and "laboratory-reared." (2) If CDFW answers that section 671 as written does not reach a domesticated roof rat, that is a question of the rule's text, which only the California Fish and Game Commission can change. The next ask is then a formal FGC 1 petition (and supporting public comment) to amend section 671 to add domesticated Rattus rattus to the exemption, the same path used to seek removal of the domestic ferret. The relevant question is domestication, not the wild ancestry of the species. The dog descends from the wolf and the house cat from a wild felid, yet California treats both as domestic animals because of generations bred for tameness, not their wild ancestry. The permitted fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated in the 19th century (https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/); a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense, one species over. The Department and the Commission are asked to weigh that question, not to reach a particular result.

Where the lever really is: This is both levers in sequence, and the order matters. First, it is plausibly a bureaucracy-reading problem (lever = the AGENCY): the exemption text in 14 CCR §671 is species-blind ("rats or mice"; no binomial; verified against the regulation), so a clarification or declaratory answer from CDFW could confirm a domesticated R. rattus already qualifies, with no rule change needed. Start by asking CDFW's License & Revenue Branch / Special Permits Unit for a written interpretation. There is a ceiling: if CDFW responds that §671 is meant to cover only fancy rats / lab-reared origin and a wild-type roof rat is excluded, the obstacle is the rule's text and the listing of all Rodentia as "detrimental," and CDFW cannot rewrite the regulation by email. The body that owns and can amend 14 CCR §671 is the California Fish and Game Commission (FGC), via its formal petition-for-regulation-change process (FGC 1 form) and the associated public-comment window, the same lever the domestic-ferret campaign uses. Appealing further to CDFW will not change a rule it is correctly applying; that step requires an FGC rulemaking petition. If the Commission concludes the blanket Rodentia restriction in Fish & Game Code §2118 ties its hands, the final backstop is the Legislature. The fancy rat already permitted in California is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated in the 19th century (https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/), and a captive-bred R. rattus is domesticated in the same sense one species over. Net: agency first for a clarification that may already exist in the text; Commission rulemaking if the text genuinely excludes the species.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • California Department of Fish and Wildlife — License & Revenue Branch / Special Permits Unit (Restricted Species) (executive / agency) — LRB@wildlife.ca.gov
    The Department that interprets and administers 14 CCR §671 and issues (and declines) restricted-species permits. This is the correct first stop for a written clarification on whether the species-blind 'domesticated races of rats or mice' exemption already reaches a captive-bred, tame roof rat. Verified official contact page; verified branch email LRB@wildlife.ca.gov and lines (916) 928-5805 / (916) 928-5846.
  • California Fish and Game Commission — Petition for Regulation Change (FGC 1) / Submit Comments (public comment) — fgc@fgc.ca.gov
    The rulemaking body that actually owns 14 CCR §671 and is the ONLY entity that can amend the restricted-species list or its exemptions. If CDFW reads the rule as excluding domesticated roof rats, this is where a formal FGC 1 petition (and public comment) to add domesticated Rattus rattus to the exemption must go — the same channel used for the domestic-ferret effort. Verified official petition page and inbox fgc@fgc.ca.gov.
  • California State Legislature — Find Your Representatives (legislature) — official contact page
    Backstop lever. The blanket classification of all Rodentia as restricted traces to Fish & Game Code §2118 (statute). If the Commission concludes the statute prevents it from exempting the species by regulation, only the Legislature can change the underlying law — so contacting your own Assembly Member and Senator becomes the route. Official legislative find-your-rep tool.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, License & Revenue Branch / Special Permits Unit:

I am writing to request a written clarification about the restricted-species exemption in 14 CCR §671(c)(2)(J)(1)(c). The rule restricts all rodents but exempts "domesticated races of rats or mice (white or albino; trained, dancing or spinning, laboratory-reared)." That exemption is written by phenotype and origin. It says "rats or mice" and names no species.

My question is whether this exemption applies to a captive-bred, domesticated and tame line of roof rat (Rattus rattus) that is white/albino, trained, or laboratory-reared, the same way it applies to the common pet rat (Rattus norvegicus). Domestication is a matter of an animal's breeding history and temperament, not its species. The dog descends from the wolf and the house cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic animals because of generations bred for tameness, not their wild ancestry. The permitted fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated in the 19th century, and a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense. These animals are captive-bred, hand-tame, kept strictly indoors as pets, and never released into the wild.

If the Department reads §671 as not reaching a domesticated R. rattus, please say so plainly, and please explain how the Department defines "trained" and "laboratory-reared" for this exemption. If a regulatory change is required, I intend to petition the Fish and Game Commission.

Thank you for your time and for a written reply.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your city, California]
[Your email]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • 14 CCR §671 — Restricted Animals (all Rodentia 'detrimental'; (c)(2)(J)(1)(c) domesticated-races exemption) — CA Code of Regulations
  • Cal. Fish & Game Code §2118 — prohibition on importing/possessing wild animals (incl. Rodentia) — CA Fish & Game Code
  • Cal. Fish & Game Code §3005.5 — no capture/possession of wild nongame mammals — CA Fish & Game Code
  • Restricted Species Permits — CDFW (not issued for pets) — CA Dept of Fish & Wildlife
  • Pet Store Animal Care Act — Cal. Health & Safety Code §122350–122361 — CA Health & Safety Code
  • California Border Protection Stations FAQ — CDFA (pest exclusion) — CA Dept of Food & Agriculture

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

Last reviewed 2026-06-06. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Colorado? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Colorado

Summary. Colorado is permissive for keeping a pet roof rat, and avoids the species-trap seen in other states. Colorado Parks & Wildlife's Domestic Animal List (2 CCR 406-11 §1103(A)) exempts 'Domesticated races of rats (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus)' from ALL wildlife licensing — the parenthetical names Norway rat and then the bare genus 'Rattus,' which is read to cover the whole genus, so a captive-bred roof rat is treated exactly like a fancy rat: no CPW permit, no inspection, no fee to keep one. (Wild-caught roof rats are NOT covered, and releasing any rat into the wild is illegal under §1100.) Breeding and selling/giving are legal as a hobby, but become RESTRICTED at commercial scale: producing, housing, or transferring more than 200 small mammals (rats/mice/gerbils/hamsters combined) per year requires a Colorado Dept of Agriculture PACFA 'Small Animal Breeder' license (~$425/yr + qualifying-education course + facility inspection). Transport within Colorado is unregulated, but IMPORTING a rat into the state requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) from the origin state — for a private pet, issued within 30 days of entry (the federal VS Form 7001 is not accepted). Colorado does NOT set a minimum transfer/weaning age for rats. Never release one.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Colorado-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Colorado is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Colorado Parks & Wildlife's Domestic Animal List (2 CCR 406-11 §1103(A)) exempts 'Domesticated races of rats (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus)' from all Parks & Wildlife Commission regulation — no wildlife license, exotic-pet permit, CPW registration, inspection, or fee is required to possess a captive-bred roof rat, and there is no numeric possession limit for personal use. The parenthetical names the Norway rat and then the bare genus 'Rattus,' which is read to extend the domestic exemption to the entire genus, so a captive-bred R. rattus is treated identically to a fancy rat. The exemption is conditional on the animal being a 'domesticated race' (captive-bred); a wild-caught/feral roof rat is NOT covered and remains subject to CPW's prohibition on possessing wild terrestrial wildlife.

Sources: Colorado Parks & Wildlife Commission (via Cornell LII), Colorado Parks & Wildlife Commission (via Cornell LII), Michigan State Animal Legal & Historical Center

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

No CPW wildlife breeding license applies to a domestic-list animal, and hobby breeding is legal. But breeding falls under the Colorado Dept of Agriculture's Pet Animal Care and Facilities Act (PACFA), under which 'pet animals' include rats and mice. 8 CCR 1202-15 §2.6.1.1 sets the small-mammal breeder threshold at 'producing, housing, or transferring more than 200' rats/mice/gerbils/hamsters combined per year — below that you are an exempt hobbyist; above it you must obtain a PACFA 'Small Animal Breeder' facility license before further transfers (the threshold aggregates across species, so you can't split it among multiple rodent types). Licensure adds a qualifying-education course, a pre-license inspection, and ongoing facility/sanitation/enclosure standards.

Sources: Colorado Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII), Colorado Dept of Agriculture (via Justia), Colorado Dept of Agriculture, Colorado Parks & Wildlife Commission (via Cornell LII)

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Transfers of a domestic-list animal need no CPW permit, and selling/giving/adopting-out is unregulated below the PACFA threshold — the law permits small-scale monetization of the hobby. But under 8 CCR 1202-15 §2.6, transferring (selling, giving away, or adopting out) more than 200 rats/mice/gerbils/hamsters combined per year makes you a PACFA-licensed commercial operation (~$425/yr small-animal breeder, or a Pet Animal Shelter/retail license at $450-$600 for rescues/retailers), triggering fees, qualifying education, and facility inspections. A separate rescue/shelter threshold (§2.6.6) applies if more than 200 rats/mice/gerbils are housed in a central facility. Operating or advertising a covered facility without a license is unlawful and can draw a cease-and-desist.

Sources: Colorado Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII), Colorado Dept of Agriculture (via Justia), Colorado Dept of Agriculture, Colorado Dept of Agriculture

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-12

Intrastate movement of a domestic-list animal needs no CPW transport permit, in-state health certificate, or wildlife transit document. But interstate IMPORT into Colorado is regulated by the CDA Animal Health Division: a roof rat is handled as a 'small animal'/'pocket pet' and, per the State Veterinarian's import directives (8 CCR 1201-19, pt. 2), must be accompanied by a valid Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) issued by a federally accredited veterinarian in the origin state within 30 days prior to entry — and the CVI must be an origin-state official form (the federal VS Form 7001 is NOT accepted). Animals arriving without a valid CVI may be quarantined at the owner's expense or ordered returned. Because the rat is on the CPW Domestic Animal List, NO wildlife importation permit is required. The §1100 no-release rule bars ever releasing one into the wild.

Sources: Colorado Dept of Agriculture, State Veterinarian, Colorado Dept of Agriculture, Animal Health Division (via Cornell LII), Colorado Parks & Wildlife Commission (via Cornell LII)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Producing, housing, or transferring more than 200 small mammals (rats/mice/gerbils/hamsters combined) per year makes you a PACFA 'Small Animal Breeder' and requires a Colorado Dept of Agriculture license (~$425/yr). A rescue/shelter housing more than 200 rats/mice/gerbils in a central facility, or a retail/wholesale pet operation, needs a Pet Animal Shelter/retail license ($450-$600/yr). Below the threshold, hobby breeding and free/low-volume adoption need no license.
  • Stay under 200 small mammals (rats+mice+gerbils+hamsters) produced/housed/transferred per year to remain an exempt hobbyist
  • If over the threshold: complete the PACFA Qualifying Education (QE) course
  • Apply for the PACFA license and pass a pre-license facility inspection
  • Meet ongoing facility standards (weatherproof structure, moisture-impervious surfaces, sanitation, adequate primary enclosures) and routine inspections

Forms: PACFA Licensing — Colorado Dept of Agriculture, PACFA Qualifying Education Summary · Where: Colorado Dept of Agriculture, Division of Animal Welfare — PACFA Program (305 Interlocken Pkwy, Broomfield, CO 80021) · Fees: ~$425/yr (Small Animal Breeder); $450-$600/yr (Pet Animal Shelter); $600/yr (retail/wholesale)

Source: Colorado Dept of Agriculture, Colorado Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII), Colorado Dept of Agriculture (via Justia)

Importing a pet rat into Colorado from another state requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) issued by a federally accredited vet in the origin state within 30 days prior to entry. It must be an origin-state official CVI form — the federal VS Form 7001 is NOT accepted. No CVI is needed for movement within Colorado. Arriving without a valid CVI risks quarantine at the owner's expense or return to the origin state.
  • Before crossing into Colorado, have an accredited origin-state veterinarian issue an official-state CVI within 30 days of entry (do not rely on VS Form 7001)
  • Carry the CVI with the animal during import
  • No CVI required for moving the rat within Colorado

Forms: Bringing Small Animals into Colorado — CDA Animal Health · Where: Colorado Dept of Agriculture, Animal Health Division / State Veterinarian's Office · Fees: Origin-state veterinary fee for the CVI; no Colorado import-permit fee

Source: Colorado Dept of Agriculture, State Veterinarian, Colorado Dept of Agriculture, Animal Health Division (via Cornell LII)

It is unlawful to intentionally release any animal on the Domestic/Unregulated list — including a pet roof rat — into the wild (2 CCR 406-11 §1100). The roof rat is a documented invasive pest and wild populations are actively targeted for control; keep them contained and rehome responsibly, never release. Local city/county ordinances may add limits, and the domestic exemption applies only to captive-bred 'domesticated races,' not wild-caught animals.

Where: Colorado Parks & Wildlife / your local code enforcement

Source: Colorado Parks & Wildlife Commission (via Cornell LII), Colorado Parks & Wildlife Commission (via Cornell LII)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • 2 CCR 406-11 §1103 — Exemptions From License Requirements (Domestic Animal List: 'Domesticated races of rats (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus)') — Colorado Parks & Wildlife Commission (via Cornell LII)
  • 2 CCR 406-11 — Chapter W-11, Wildlife Parks and Unregulated Wildlife (incl. §1100 no-release of domestic/unregulated wildlife) — Colorado Parks & Wildlife Commission (via Cornell LII)
  • CO — Exotic Pets and Wildlife — Chapter 11, Wildlife Parks and Unregulated Wildlife (domestic-list exemption explained) — Michigan State Animal Legal & Historical Center
