item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Hawaii? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Hawaii

Summary. Hawaii is legal-with-permit for a domesticated rat, including the roof rat. Hawaii runs four animal-import lists under HAR Chapter 4-71 (Prohibited; Restricted Part A; Restricted Part B; Conditionally Approved), and an unlisted animal is prohibited by default (HRS §150A-6.2). The Conditionally Approved list (HAR §4-71-6.5, Exhibit AR-71C) lists, under Family Muridae, the genus-level entry 'Rattus sp.' with common name 'rat, domesticated' (alongside 'Mus musculus - mice, domesticated'). Because the entry names the whole genus rather than only Rattus norvegicus, a domesticated/captive-bred R. rattus falls within it on the face of the rule, and Rattus does NOT appear on the Prohibited list (AR-71P). A domesticated rat may therefore be imported and kept WITH a prior HDOA Plant Quarantine import permit (Form PQ-7), entering the state only through the Daniel K. Inouye (Honolulu) International Airport and inspected at the Airport Animal Quarantine Holding Facility, accompanied by a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection. The genuine open point is administrative, not textual: HDOA's permit history and Board submittals discuss the 'domesticated rat' in terms of the laboratory/fancy Norway rat (R. norvegicus) and its 'degree of domestication,' and the Chief Plant Inspector has discretion at permit time, so whether HDOA will treat a captive-bred R. rattus as 'domesticated' under the genus entry is worth a written determination before importing. Breeding is restricted (the Board may attach permit conditions on reproduction, facility, and disposition of progeny). Intrastate sale/transfer is unregulated/unclear in the public code (the framework is import-focused). Wild/feral Rattus is separately managed as an invasive pest and disease vector (DOH HAR 11-26); never release one. For international (not mainland-to-Hawaii) movement, U.S. Fish & Wildlife treats R. rattus as wildlife under 50 CFR 14.4, which exempts only R. norvegicus and Mus musculus.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Hawaii-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Hawaii is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-13

A domesticated rat is on Hawaii's Conditionally Approved list (HAR §4-71-6.5 / Exhibit AR-71C), NOT the Prohibited list (AR-71P) - so it may be kept under a valid HDOA Plant Quarantine import permit (HRS §150A-6.2). The list entry under Family Muridae reads 'Rattus sp. - rat, domesticated' (genus-level, alongside 'Mus musculus - mice, domesticated'), and on the face of the rule that covers a domesticated/captive-bred R. rattus; Rattus does not appear on the Prohibited list. Possession of a non-domestic animal without a permit, or of an unlisted animal, is unlawful (an unlisted animal is prohibited by default). Confidence is medium because, although the text is genus-level, HDOA's permit submittals describe the 'domesticated rat' as R. norvegicus and the Chief Plant Inspector decides species coverage at permit time - a written HDOA determination should be obtained before relying on it.

Sources: Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity, Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity, Hawaii State Legislature (via Justia), HDOA Plant Quarantine Branch

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-13

The public HAR 4-71 text contains no express breeding prohibition for a conditionally approved pet, but each imported animal is permitted individually, and HRS §150A-6.2 (with HAR 4-71A standard/supplemental permit conditions) lets the Board attach conditions on time, place, use, and special precautions - in practice including conditions on reproduction, facility type, and disposition of any progeny. A permit issued for 'individual possession' authorizes a finite number of animals; producing unpermitted offspring changes that baseline, so a breeding intent should be stated on the Form PQ-7 and cleared with HDOA. Given feral R. rattus is highly invasive in Hawaii, HDOA is likely to impose strict conditions (e.g., segregation, sterilization, progeny records/disposition) on any approved breeding.

Sources: Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity, Hawaii State Legislature (via Justia), Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-13

HAR 4-71 is fundamentally an import/quarantine framework; the public code and guidelines are largely silent on routine intrastate sale or transfer of a conditionally approved animal already lawfully held. HAR 4-71A makes import permits 'nontransferable, unless otherwise specified in the permit,' so a permit holder cannot freely transfer the animal without coordinating with HDOA, and whether a Hawaii recipient needs their own permit/documentation is not specified publicly and likely turns on permit conditions. There is no published small/hobby-breeder transfer exemption. Confirm transfer mechanics with HDOA before selling or giving a domesticated rat to another resident.

Sources: Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity, Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Importing a domesticated rat requires an HDOA Plant Quarantine import permit (Form PQ-7) obtained in advance; non-domestic rodents enter ONLY through the Daniel K. Inouye (Honolulu) International Airport and are submitted by the carrier to the Airport Animal Quarantine Holding Facility for inspection, accompanied by a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) issued shortly before arrival and certifying freedom from disease and external parasites. The permit is the gatekeeping mechanism (HRS §150A-6.2; HAR §4-71-3). State agricultural law does not heavily regulate transport OUT of Hawaii (airlines set their own policies; the destination's import rules govern). For INTERNATIONAL movement only, USFWS treats R. rattus as wildlife under 50 CFR 14.4 (which exempts R. norvegicus and Mus musculus but not R. rattus), triggering federal wildlife-declaration requirements; mainland-to-Hawaii interstate moves do not trigger that federal layer. Never release one (feral Rattus is an invasive pest).

Sources: HDOA Plant Quarantine Branch, Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity, Hawaii State Legislature (via Justia), U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service (via Cornell LII)

Restrictions & responsibilities

To bring/keep a domesticated rat in Hawaii, get an HDOA Plant Quarantine import permit (Form PQ-7) BEFORE importing; the animal enters only via the Honolulu (Daniel K. Inouye) International Airport, is submitted by the carrier to the Airport Animal Quarantine Holding Facility for inspection, and must travel with a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (issued shortly before arrival, certifying freedom from disease and external parasites). The Conditionally Approved entry is genus-level ('Rattus sp. - rat, domesticated'), so a domesticated R. rattus is covered on the face of the rule - but because HDOA exercises species discretion at permit time, confirm in writing that the genus entry covers R. rattus (or seek a case-by-case HRS §150A-6.2 permit) before relying on it. Never release a roof rat (feral Rattus is an invasive pest).
  • Apply for an HDOA Plant Quarantine import permit (Form PQ-7) in advance (single-shipment vs unlimited; pay the fee with the application)
  • Confirm in writing that the genus-level 'Rattus sp. (rat, domesticated)' entry covers a domesticated R. rattus, or obtain a case-by-case HRS §150A-6.2 special permit
  • Obtain a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection from an accredited vet shortly before shipment (certifying no disease and no external parasites)
  • Ship so the animal enters only through Honolulu (Daniel K. Inouye) International Airport; the carrier submits it to the Airport Animal Quarantine Holding Facility for inspection
  • Maintain a secure, gnaw-proof, escape-proof enclosure and comply with any post-entry inspection / address-update conditions; never release the animal

Forms: HDOA Plant Quarantine - Application for Permit to Import (Form PQ-7) · Where: Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity - Plant Quarantine Branch (1849 Auiki St, Honolulu, HI 96819) · Fees: Import permit fee per HAR §4-71-3.1 (reported as $20 single-shipment / $100 unlimited-shipments / $250 expedited; confirm current schedule with HDOA). Plus origin-state veterinary fee for the CVI.

Source: HDOA Plant Quarantine Branch, Hawaii State Legislature (via Justia), Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity

Releasing a pet roof rat into the wild is prohibited and dangerous: feral R. rattus is among the most damaging invasive vertebrates in Hawaii and is separately managed as a public-health vector (DOH HAR 11-26, which bars conditions that harbor or breed rodents). Keep the animal contained at all times and rehome responsibly; never release. Breeding intent must be disclosed on the Form PQ-7 and cleared with HDOA, which may attach conditions on reproduction, facility, and disposition of progeny.
  • Never release a roof rat into the wild (invasive pest + public-health vector; multiple state violations)
  • Disclose any breeding intent on the Form PQ-7 and obtain HDOA approval/conditions before breeding

Where: Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity - Plant Quarantine Branch; Hawaii Dept of Health, Vector Control Branch

Source: Hawaii Dept of Health, Vector Control Branch, Hawaii State Legislature (via Justia)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Hawaii

Keeping a pet rat in Hawaii is not banned. Hawaii regulates animal imports through lists under Hawaii Administrative Rules (HAR) Chapter 4-71, and the Conditionally Approved Animals list (HAR §4-71-6.5, Exhibit AR-71C) names, under Family Muridae, the genus-level entry 'Rattus sp.' with the common name 'rat, domesticated' (alongside 'Mus musculus', common name 'mice, domesticated'). Because the entry is written at the genus level rather than naming only the Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus), a domesticated, captive-bred roof rat (Rattus rattus) falls within it on the face of the rule, and Rattus does not appear on the Prohibited list. So a domesticated rat may be imported and kept with a prior Hawaii Department of Agriculture & Biosecurity (HDOA) Plant Quarantine import permit (Form PQ-7); the animal enters only through Honolulu and is inspected at the Airport Animal Quarantine Holding Facility. The remaining issue is discretionary application, not the text. HDOA's permit submittals and approval justifications describe the 'domesticated rat' as the laboratory/fancy Norway rat, bred for generations under controlled conditions and unlikely to establish in the wild, and the Chief Plant Inspector decides species coverage when a permit is reviewed. An applicant for a captive-bred R. rattus therefore risks the agency reading the genus entry narrowly and treating the animal as a 'tame wild animal' rather than a 'domesticated' one; because an unlisted animal is prohibited by default, a narrow reading could foreclose the permit. A domesticated, captive-bred, hand-tame, indoor-only roof rat shares the same risk profile as the fancy Norway rat already covered. The fancy Norway rat is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated in the 19th century, and a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over.

The ask: Ask HDOA, in writing, to confirm coverage and, if it reads the entry narrowly, to provide an alternative: (1) Confirm whether the genus-level HAR §4-71-6.5 Conditionally Approved entry 'Rattus sp. (rat, domesticated)' covers a domesticated/captive-bred Rattus rattus, so a private resident may apply for a Form PQ-7 import permit for one as a pet. (2) If HDOA reads the entry to cover only Rattus norvegicus, confirm that a private keeper may obtain a case-by-case import permit for a domesticated R. rattus under HRS §150A-6.2, or that the domesticated R. rattus lineage can be recognized under the existing genus entry. The relevant question is domestication, not wild ancestry: the dog descends from the wolf and the house cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic animals because of generations bred for tameness. The fancy Norway rat the list already covers is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated in the 19th century (https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/), and a multi-generation captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense, one species over. The Department is asked to weigh that, not to reach any particular result. (3) State the standard permit conditions (including any breeding/disposition conditions), the fee, and the processing time for a few pet rats. Request a written determination you can rely on before importing.

Where the lever really is: Lever = THE AGENCY (HDOA), with a case-by-case permit and a rulemaking route in reserve; not the legislature first. The statute (HRS §150A-6.2) does not ban rats; it directs the Board of Agriculture to maintain the prohibited/restricted/conditionally-approved lists, to import conditionally-approved and restricted animals by permit, and to issue case-by-case special permits. The substantive lists live in administrative rule (HAR Chapter 4-71) and in the published Conditionally Approved list (Exhibit AR-71C), instruments HDOA owns. Here the published list already names 'Rattus sp. (rat, domesticated)' at the genus level, so on the face of the rule a domesticated R. rattus is covered and there is no statute banning pet rats that the agency is merely enforcing. The only live problem is whether the HDOA Plant Quarantine Branch, exercising its permit-time discretion, will read that genus entry to include a captive-bred R. rattus or will treat it as a 'tame wild animal.' That is an agency interpretation, fixable by the agency: a written determination that the entry covers domesticated R. rattus, or, if it reads the entry narrowly, a case-by-case import permit under HRS §150A-6.2. Because the lever is the agency's own list and permit power, the written HDOA inquiry is the right first move. Escalation to a HAR Chapter 4-71 amendment (which carries a public-comment/rulemaking window) becomes relevant only if HDOA both refuses to read the genus entry to cover domesticated R. rattus and declines a case-by-case permit. Start with the written agency inquiry and keep the rulemaking route in reserve.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Hawaii Department of Agriculture & Biosecurity - Plant Quarantine Branch (Import Permits / Form PQ-7) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    This is the office that maintains the Conditionally Approved Animals list and issues the import permits. It is the correct first stop to get a written determination on whether the genus-level 'Rattus sp. (rat, domesticated)' entry covers a domesticated Rattus rattus, and to apply for a permit (Form PQ-7). Verified live: it links the PQ-7 application and explains the conditionally-approved permit process.
  • Hawaii Department of Agriculture & Biosecurity - Plant Quarantine Branch Office Contacts (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Official contacts page for the Plant Quarantine Branch (Oahu main office phone 808-832-0566; airport line 808-837-8413; 1849 Auiki St, Honolulu, HI 96819). Use it to direct a written species-coverage inquiry to the branch that controls the list and issues permits. Listed because the branch's published page does not post a dedicated permit-inquiry email, so an official page/phone is the verified channel rather than an unconfirmed inbox.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To: Hawaii Department of Agriculture & Biosecurity, Plant Quarantine Branch

Re: Coverage of the genus-level Conditionally Approved entry 'Rattus sp. (rat, domesticated)' for a domesticated Rattus rattus

I am a Hawaii resident seeking to keep a domesticated, captive-bred pet rat as an indoor companion animal, in full compliance with state import rules. I understand the Conditionally Approved Animals list (HAR §4-71-6.5, Exhibit AR-71C) names, under Family Muridae, the entry 'Rattus sp.' with the common name 'rat, domesticated', and that conditionally approved animals may be imported with a Plant Quarantine permit (Form PQ-7).

My question is about how the Branch applies that genus-level entry. The animals I keep are domesticated, captive-bred, hand-tame Rattus rattus, multi-generation pet lineages kept strictly indoors in enclosures and never released, the same in behavior and risk as the fancy Norway rat. They are not wild-caught and pose no establishment risk. Because the list entry reads 'Rattus sp.' rather than naming only Rattus norvegicus, a domesticated R. rattus appears to fall within it. Domestication is a matter of an animal's breeding history, not its wild ancestry: the dog descends from the wolf and the house cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic animals because of generations bred for tameness. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated in the 19th century, and a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense.

Please confirm in writing: (1) Does the genus-level Conditionally Approved entry 'Rattus sp. (rat, domesticated)' cover a domesticated/captive-bred Rattus rattus, so a private resident may apply for a Form PQ-7 import permit to keep one as a pet? (2) If the Branch reads the entry to cover only Rattus norvegicus, may a private keeper obtain a case-by-case import permit for a domesticated R. rattus under HRS §150A-6.2? (3) What permit conditions (including any breeding or disposition conditions), fee, and processing time apply?

Thank you for a written determination I can rely on before importing.

[Your name]
[Your city, Hawaii]
[Your email / phone]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • HAR §4-71-6.5 - List of Conditionally Approved Animals (Exhibit AR-71C). Family Muridae entries verbatim: 'Mus musculus - mice, domesticated'; 'Rattus sp. - rat, domesticated' (genus-level, NOT species-specific). — Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity
  • HAR §4-71-6 - List of Prohibited Animals (Exhibit AR-71P). Order Rodentia includes Cricetidae, Erethizontidae, Hystricidae, Sciuridae but NOT Family Muridae and NO Rattus/Mus - the domesticated rat is not prohibited. — Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity
  • HRS §150A-6.2 - Animal import. Board maintains prohibited/restricted/conditionally-approved lists; conditionally-approved and restricted animals imported only by permit; unlisted animals prohibited until Board review; case-by-case special permits (incl. 90-day short-term). — Hawaii State Legislature (via Justia)
  • HAR Chapter 4-71A - Non-Domestic Animal permit conditions (standard & supplemental conditions; import permits 'nontransferable unless otherwise specified in the permit'; post-entry inspection authority). — Hawaii Dept of Agriculture & Biosecurity
  • HDOA - Importing Animals to Hawai'i + Application for Permits (Form PQ-7; conditionally-approved rats/mice/guinea pigs/chinchillas; Honolulu-only entry; Airport Animal Quarantine Holding Facility inspection; CVI). — HDOA Plant Quarantine Branch
  • 50 CFR 14.4 - USFWS definition of 'Domesticated animals' (names 'White lab rat - Rattus norvegicus' and 'White lab mouse - Mus musculus'; Rattus rattus NOT listed). Relevant to INTERNATIONAL movement only, not mainland-to-Hawaii. — U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service (via Cornell LII)
  • HAR Title 11 Chapter 26 - DOH Vector Control. Bars conditions that harbor or breed rodents; R. rattus managed as an invasive pest and disease vector (rat lungworm, leptospirosis, murine typhus). Never release. — Hawaii Dept of Health, Vector Control Branch

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat, 'iole.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Iowa? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Iowa

Summary. Iowa is one of the cleaner states for the roof rat, with no species-trap. The Dangerous Wild Animals law (Iowa Code ch. 717F) is a closed list — big cats, bears, wolves, primates, rhinos, elephants, crocodilians, venomous snakes, and feral swine — that contains NO rodents; and DNR jurisdiction (ch. 481A) reaches native 'wild animals found in this state,' game, and fur-bearers, not a captive-bred indoor pet rodent. Iowa's statutes use broad terms ('rodent,' 'vertebrate animal,' 'nonhuman vertebrate') and never split the genus Rattus by species, so a domesticated roof rat is treated exactly like a fancy rat (R. norvegicus). Keeping and breeding are legal and unregulated for a private owner (the IDALS 'commercial breeder' license applies only to dogs and cats). Selling/giving is legal: a producer who sells rats born and reared on their own premises is fully exempt from the IDALS 'pet shop' license regardless of volume, and a small reseller/broker is exempt below $1,000 in sales OR 12 animals per year. Importing a rat into Iowa does require a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (IAC 21-65.3) within 30 days of entry; intrastate movement is unregulated. Iowa's prohibited-import rodent list (the 2003 monkeypox seven — prairie dogs, Gambian rats, dormice, etc.) does NOT include Rattus. Releasing one into the wild is illegal (wildlife-introduction + animal-abandonment laws), and a kept rat is protected by the state animal-neglect statute.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Iowa-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Iowa is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Iowa Code §717F.1(5) defines 'dangerous wild animal' as a closed, exhaustive list of enumerated families/orders — Canidae, Hyaenidae, Felidae, Ursidae (incl. pandas), Rhinocerotidae, Proboscidea (elephants), non-human Primates, Crocodilia, specific Squamata (monitors, venomous snakes/lizards, certain large constrictors), and feral swine — and the order Rodentia is entirely absent, so by expressio unius a roof rat is not a regulated dangerous animal (no permit, insurance, or registration). DNR authority under Iowa Code ch. 481A reaches a 'wild animal' defined as wildlife 'found in this state' to which the state claims title (§481A.1(36)), plus game and fur-bearers (§481A.1(20)) — none of which covers a non-native, captive-bred indoor pet rodent. No state possession permit applies. (A kept rat is still protected from neglect under Iowa Code §717B, and wild-caught/released rats are a separate matter.)

Sources: Iowa Legislature, Iowa Legislature / Iowa DNR, Iowa Legislature

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Breeding roof rats is unregulated at the state level. The IDALS 'commercial breeder' license is defined (Iowa Code §162.2(8)) as applying only to a person 'engaged in the business of breeding dogs or cats,' so a rodent breeding operation — regardless of scale, revenue, or volume — cannot be classified as a commercial breeder. The DNR 'game breeder' license (Iowa Code §481A.60/§481A.61) covers only game birds, game animals, and fur-bearers, which exclude rats. And ch. 717F (dangerous animals) does not reach rodents. So there is no breeder license, facility cap, or breeding-volume limit for a roof-rat breeder. (A breeder who then resells rats NOT born on their premises can trigger the separate 'pet shop' license above a sales threshold — see sell_give.)

Sources: Iowa Legislature, Iowa Legislature / Iowa DNR, Iowa Legislature

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Selling or giving away captive-bred roof rats is legal. The only commercial touchpoint is the IDALS 'pet shop' license (Iowa Code §162.2(19)), defined as a facility where vertebrate animals 'not born and reared on the facility's premises' are sold at retail. Two large exemptions cover the typical keeper/breeder: (1) the 'born and reared on premises' exemption — a producer selling or giving away rats they bred themselves needs NO license, regardless of volume; and (2) a small-broker threshold — even someone reselling rats not born on their premises is exempt if they take in less than $1,000 OR transfer fewer than 12 vertebrate animals in a 12-month period. So a hobby breeder, a rescue, or a free-adoption program operates with no license. A pet-shop license (annual fee $175 via the IDALS Animal Welfare Bureau) is required only for a broker/retailer who exceeds the threshold, and that triggers IAC 21-67 welfare/caging standards and inspections.

Sources: Iowa Legislature, Iowa Legislature, Iowa Dept of Agriculture & Land Stewardship

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Intrastate transport (moving a roof rat within Iowa) is entirely unregulated. IMPORTING a rat into Iowa requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection: IAC 21-65.3(3) provides that 'Animals imported into the state must be accompanied by a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection, unless specifically exempted by this chapter,' and the chapter's exemptions cover certain livestock/poultry movements but NOT pocket pets or domesticated rodents — so a CVI is required. It must be issued by a licensed, USDA-accredited veterinarian in the origin state on an official state-of-origin form (or USDA equivalent), be no more than 30 days old at entry, and certify the animal free of infectious/communicable disease. Critically, Iowa's prohibited-import rodent embargo (IAC 21-65.3(1)(b) — the 2003 monkeypox seven: prairie dogs, tree/rope squirrels, dormice, Gambian giant pouched rats, brush-tailed porcupines, striped mice) does NOT include the genus Rattus, so roof rats may lawfully be imported with a CVI. (Vesicular-stomatitis certification under 65.3(4) is hoofed-animals-only and does not apply.) Never release a roof rat — outdoor introduction is separately illegal.

Sources: Iowa Dept of Agriculture & Land Stewardship, Iowa Legislature / Iowa DNR, Iowa Legislature

Restrictions & responsibilities

An IDALS 'pet shop' license is required ONLY for a broker/retailer who sells vertebrate animals NOT born and reared on their own premises AND exceeds the threshold ($1,000 in sales OR 12 vertebrate animals in 12 months, per Iowa Code §162.2(19) as amended by HF 666; the older IAC 21-67.1 still recites $500/6). A producer selling rats they bred themselves is exempt regardless of volume, and low-volume resellers and free-adoption programs are exempt. A licensed facility must meet IAC 21-67 animal-welfare/caging standards and pass inspections.
  • If you bred the rats yourself ('born and reared on premises'), no pet-shop license is required at any volume
  • If you resell rats not born on your premises, stay under the threshold (less than $1,000 in sales OR fewer than 12 vertebrate animals per 12 months) to remain exempt
  • If over the threshold as a broker/retailer: apply for the IDALS pet-shop license ($175/yr) and meet IAC 21-67 welfare/caging standards and inspections

Forms: Application to Operate in Iowa as a Licensed Animal Welfare Facility (IDALS Animal Welfare Bureau) · Where: Iowa Dept of Agriculture & Land Stewardship — Animal Welfare Bureau / Animal Industry Division (Hoover State Office Bldg, 1305 E. Walnut St, Des Moines, IA 50319) · Fees: $175/yr (pet-shop license) only if not exempt; $0 for exempt producers and low-volume/free transfers

Source: Iowa Legislature, Iowa Legislature, Iowa Dept of Agriculture & Land Stewardship, Iowa Dept of Agriculture & Land Stewardship

Importing a pet rat into Iowa from another state requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (IAC 21-65.3(3)) issued by a USDA-accredited veterinarian in the origin state, on an official origin-state form (or USDA equivalent), valid no more than 30 days before entry, certifying the animal free of infectious/communicable disease. The genus Rattus is NOT on Iowa's prohibited-import rodent list (IAC 21-65.3(1)(b)), so roof rats may be imported with a CVI. No CVI is needed for moving a rat within Iowa. Missing CVI can draw a civil penalty.
  • Before bringing the rat into Iowa, have a USDA-accredited origin-state veterinarian issue an official-state CVI within 30 days of entry
  • Carry the CVI with the animal to its final destination in Iowa (a copy goes to the origin state's livestock health official)
  • No CVI is required for moving the rat within Iowa

Where: IDALS Animal Industry Bureau / State Veterinarian (origin-state veterinarian issues the CVI) · Fees: Origin-state veterinary fee for the CVI; no Iowa import-permit fee

Source: Iowa Dept of Agriculture & Land Stewardship

Releasing a roof rat into the wild is illegal in Iowa: introducing any animal into the state's environment requires a DNR permit that will not be granted for a non-native nuisance species (Iowa Code §481A.47), and abandoning a pet is a crime (Iowa Code §717B.8). A kept roof rat is also protected from neglect (Iowa Code §717B.3 — adequate food, water, and sanitary housing). Keep them contained and rehome responsibly; never release. Local city/county ordinances may add limits.

Where: Iowa DNR (wild release) / local code enforcement (ordinances)

Source: Iowa Legislature / Iowa DNR, Iowa Legislature

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Iowa Code §717F.1 — Dangerous Wild Animals, Definitions (closed list of families/orders; order Rodentia absent; excludes domestic dog/cat) — Iowa Legislature
  • Iowa Code §481A.1 — Wildlife Conservation, Definitions ('wild animal' = wildlife found in state; game/fur-bearer lists exclude rats) — Iowa Legislature / Iowa DNR
  • Iowa Code §481A.47 — Importing fish and game; permits (DNR permit required to introduce/stock any animal; bars releasing a non-native rat) — Iowa Legislature / Iowa DNR
  • Iowa Code §481A.61 — Licensed game breeders (game birds/animals & fur-bearers only; does not reach rats) — Iowa Legislature / Iowa DNR
  • Iowa Code §162.2 — Care of Animals in Commercial Establishments, Definitions ('commercial breeder' = dogs/cats only §162.2(8); 'pet shop' §162.2(19) with 'born and reared on premises' exemption + $1,000/12-animal thresholds) — Iowa Legislature
  • House File 666 — amendment refining the Iowa Code §162.2(19) 'pet shop' definition (born-and-reared exemption; $1,000 / 12-animal thresholds) — Iowa Legislature
  • IAC 21-65.3 — Animal & Livestock Importation, general requirements (import CVI mandatory unless exempted, official origin-state form, valid <=30 days; prohibited-rodent embargo at 65.3(1)(b) — genus Rattus absent; VS rule hoofed-only) — Iowa Dept of Agriculture & Land Stewardship
  • IAC 21 ch. 67 — Animal Welfare (definitions & husbandry/caging standards for licensed facilities; pet-shop threshold recited as $500/6 pending HF 666 reconciliation) — Iowa Dept of Agriculture & Land Stewardship
  • Iowa Code ch. 717B / §717B.1, §717B.3, §717B.8 — Injury to Animals Other Than Livestock ('animal' = nonhuman vertebrate; neglect & abandonment crimes protect a kept rat / bar release) — Iowa Legislature
  • Application to Operate in Iowa as a Licensed Animal Welfare (Commercial Establishment) — IDALS Animal Welfare Bureau — Iowa Dept of Agriculture & Land Stewardship

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Idaho? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Idaho

Summary. Idaho is currently legal for a captive-bred pet roof rat, but it is the state to watch. Two state regimes govern the question and neither reaches R. rattus as a pet. The Idaho State Department of Agriculture (ISDA) bans possessing a 'deleterious exotic animal,' but its enumerated list (IDAPA 02.04.27.410, under Idaho Code Title 25, Chapter 39) names specific exotic rodents (Gambian pouched rats, prairie dogs, several African genera, South American rodents) and does NOT list the genus Rattus, so no ISDA possession permit is required. Idaho Fish & Game (IDFG) regulates 'wildlife,' but its rules (IDAPA 13.01.10) classify rodents as 'Conventional Pets' that are exempt from any IDFG permit to possess, breed, or sell. So keeping, hobby-breeding, and selling or giving a captive-bred roof rat is legal at the state level. Importing any pet into Idaho from out of state requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI); a June 2026 ISDA emergency order tightens this to a 5-day CVI (and an entry permit from infested zones) for warm-blooded animals, including pet rodents, originating from New World Screwworm states. Releasing a roof rat into the wild is prohibited. Advocacy watch: in the 2026 session the Idaho Senate passed S1271, the 'Rodents of Unusual Size Act,' which named both the Norway rat and the roof rat as a public-health nuisance for statewide abatement with no carve-out for caged pets; the House defeated it 32-38 on March 17, 2026, so it is dead for the 2026 session. A successor bill could return in 2027. The keep, breed, and sell/give answers reflect current law; they would be displaced if a future ban passes.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Idaho-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Idaho is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Two state regimes govern animal possession and neither reaches a captive-bred roof rat kept as a pet. (1) The ISDA bans possessing a 'deleterious exotic animal' without a permit (Idaho Code Title 25, Ch. 39; IDAPA 02.04.27), but the enumerated Rodentia list (IDAPA 02.04.27.410) names only specific exotic genera (Graphiurus, Funisciurus, Hybomys, Heliosciurus, Atherurus, Cricetomys, Cynomys, and all South American rodents except guinea pigs and chinchillas); the genus Rattus is absent, so no ISDA possession permit applies. (2) IDFG regulates 'wildlife' (Idaho Code Sec. 36-202) and generally requires a captive-possession permit (IDAPA 13.01.10.200), but rodents are listed 'Conventional Pets' (IDAPA 13.01.10.011.06: 'Privately owned companion animals not intended for research or resale... dogs, cats, ferrets, rabbits, rodents...'), and IDAPA 13.01.10.200.06 states no IDFG permit is needed to possess a conventional pet. A captive-bred roof rat fits both exemptions, so keeping one as a pet is legal with no state possession permit. Currently legal; see the 2026 S1271 advocacy watch for the legislative risk.

Sources: Idaho State Dept of Agriculture, Idaho Legislature, Idaho Department of Fish and Game, Idaho Legislature

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Hobby breeding of a captive-bred roof rat is legal and unregulated by the state. Because R. rattus is not a deleterious exotic animal, no ISDA propagation permit applies, and as a 'Conventional Pet' rodent it is exempt from the IDFG captive-wildlife/commercial-wildlife-facility regime (IDAPA 13.01.10). Idaho has no separate state pet-breeder or hobby-breeder license for small rodents. The federal Animal Welfare Act exempts businesses that breed or sell only rats, mice, or birds, so even commercial-scale rat breeding does not trigger USDA licensure. One textual ambiguity: the 'Conventional Pet' definition excludes animals 'intended for... resale,' so a strict reading could pull large-scale commercial breeding-for-resale out of the exemption and toward the IDFG 'commercial wildlife facility' rules; in practice the state treats domestic rats as pets, not wildlife, and does not apply that regime to rat breeders. Hobby breeding is clearly legal.

Sources: Idaho Department of Fish and Game, Idaho State Dept of Agriculture, U.S. Department of Agriculture, APHIS

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-13

Selling or giving away a captive-bred roof rat is legal at the state level. IDAPA 13.01.10.200.06 expressly states no IDFG permit is needed to 'sell' a conventional pet, and Idaho has no state pet-dealer license reaching private rodent sales or rehoming. Giving a rat away for free is unambiguously legal: there is no commercial transaction, so the animal plainly remains a 'privately owned companion animal not intended for... resale.' For paid sales there is a textual ambiguity in the IDFG rule: the 'Conventional Pet' definition (IDAPA 13.01.10.011.06) excludes animals 'intended for... resale,' which a strict reading could argue strips the exemption from an animal held for sale. In practice the retail and private sale of pet rats occurs routinely in Idaho without IDFG intervention, and the state maintains no pet-dealer licensing for rodents, so sale operates as unregulated. Confidence is medium for paid sales because of that unresolved drafting contradiction; free rehoming is high.

Sources: Idaho Department of Fish and Game, Idaho State Dept of Agriculture

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Moving a roof rat within Idaho is legal and unregulated (a conventional pet is exempt from IDFG transport permits under IDAPA 13.01.10.200.06). Importing one into Idaho from out of state is regulated by the ISDA: under the Rules Governing the Importation of Animals (IDAPA 02.04.21), all animals entering Idaho must be accompanied by an official Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI), normally issued within 30 days, and ISDA's household-pet import guidance confirms small pets/rodents require at least a CVI. A June 2026 ISDA emergency order in response to New World Screwworm tightens this for warm-blooded animals (expressly including companion animals) from affected states: a CVI issued within 5 days of entry, plus an ISDA entry permit if the animal originates from a designated infested zone. The deleterious-exotic import ban does not reach R. rattus. Releasing a roof rat into the wild is prohibited (it is a non-native species; the IDFG release exemption covers only native wildlife).

Sources: Idaho State Dept of Agriculture, Idaho State Dept of Agriculture, Idaho State Dept of Agriculture, State Veterinarian, Idaho Department of Fish and Game, Idaho State Dept of Agriculture

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing a roof rat into Idaho from another state requires an official Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI), normally issued within 30 days, listing the Idaho destination address. Under the June 2026 ISDA New World Screwworm emergency order, warm-blooded animals (including pet rodents) from affected states need a CVI issued within 5 days of entry, and an ISDA entry permit if from a designated infested zone. No paperwork is required to move a rat within Idaho. Never release a roof rat into the wild.
  • Before importing, have an accredited origin-state veterinarian issue an official CVI showing the Idaho destination address (standard validity 30 days)
  • If the animal originates from a New World Screwworm state, obtain a CVI within 5 days of entry; if from a designated infested zone, also obtain an ISDA entry permit
  • Confirm current pet-rodent import requirements with ISDA Animal Industries (rodents are not separately enumerated on the household-pet page)
  • No CVI or permit is required to move the rat within Idaho
  • Never release a roof rat into the wild (non-native species; release is prohibited)

Forms: Household Pet Imports - Idaho State Dept of Agriculture, ISDA New World Screwworm entry requirements (press release) · Where: Idaho State Dept of Agriculture, Division of Animal Industries (208) 332-8540 · Fees: Origin-state veterinary fee for the CVI; ISDA entry permit only if from a designated NWS infested zone

Source: Idaho State Dept of Agriculture, Idaho State Dept of Agriculture, Idaho State Dept of Agriculture, State Veterinarian

Legislative watch: 2026 Senate Bill S1271 ('Rodents of Unusual Size Act') would have declared the Norway rat and the roof rat a public-health nuisance for statewide abatement, with no exemption for caged pet rats. The Senate passed it 28-3-4 (Mar 5, 2026); the House defeated it 32-38 (Mar 17, 2026), so it is dead for the 2026 session. A successor bill could return in 2027. Idaho keepers should monitor the Legislature and be ready to testify that a captive-bred pet is not a wild pest, and to ask that any future bill exempt securely caged, captive-bred pets. The ISDA also has standalone authority (Idaho Code Title 25, Ch. 39) to add a species to the deleterious-exotic list by rule; no such rulemaking on Rattus has been initiated. Check local ordinances too.
  • Monitor the Idaho Legislature for a re-introduced rodent bill (successor to S1271), especially in the Senate and House Agricultural Affairs committees
  • If a bill is introduced, contact your Senator and Representative and sign up to testify at the committee hearing (captive-bred pet vs. wild pest; ask for a caged-pet carve-out)
  • Watch for any ISDA rulemaking to add Rattus to the IDAPA 02.04.27 deleterious-exotic list and comment if it opens
  • Check city/county ordinances for any local pet limits

Forms: S1271 (2026) - Idaho State Legislature, Find your Idaho legislator · Where: Idaho Legislature (your Senator/Representative; Agricultural Affairs committees)

Source: Idaho Legislature

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Idaho
Time-sensitive: S1271 is dead for the 2026 session (defeated in the House 32-38 on March 17, 2026). Watch for a 2027 successor bill and act when one is introduced, before its committee hearing.

Keeping a captive-bred roof rat (Rattus rattus) as a pet is currently legal in Idaho: the species is not on the ISDA deleterious-exotic-animal list (IDAPA 02.04.27.410) and rodents are exempt 'Conventional Pets' under the Fish & Game rules (IDAPA 13.01.10). In the 2026 session, Senate Bill 1271 (the 'Rodents of Unusual Size Act') would have declared the Norway rat and the roof rat a public-health nuisance, an invasive species, and an agricultural pest, and directed statewide abatement, with no exemption for caged, captive-bred pet rats. The Idaho Senate passed it 28-3-4 on March 5, 2026; the House defeated it 32-38 on March 17, 2026, so it is dead for the 2026 session. The margin and the underlying wild-rat concern in the Treasure Valley make a successor bill in 2027 plausible.

The ask: Ask your Idaho state legislators to oppose any future bill that bans or targets privately kept, captive-bred roof rats, and to distinguish domesticated pet Rattus rattus from wild pest populations. The fancy rat Idahoans already keep legally is itself the wild brown rat (R. norvegicus), domesticated only in the 19th century; a captive-bred R. rattus is the same case one species over (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/). Cats and dogs are also non-native and documented to harm native wildlife, yet are permitted as pets. Whether the limited additional risk of a few tame, indoor-only, captive-bred roof rats is similarly outweighed by their value as companions is a cost-benefit judgment for the Legislature. The narrow question is that trade-off, and whether any future bill can exempt securely caged, captive-bred pets while still addressing wild populations, not whether the wild species can be a pest.

Where the lever really is: This is a question of statute, not agency rule. The threat is a future law that would name the species, so the people who decide are your elected Senator and Representative, and testimony when a bill is in committee (S1271 was heard in the Senate and House Agricultural Affairs committees and decided on the House floor 32-38). Writing a state agency will not stop a bill. A secondary watch point is the ISDA, which has independent authority under Idaho Code Title 25, Chapter 39 to add a species to the deleterious-exotic list by rule; if it ever opens such a rulemaking on Rattus, the public-comment process is the place to respond.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Find & write your Idaho State Senator and Representative (legislature) — official contact page
    They cast the votes on any ban. S1271 was decided on the House floor, 32-38, on March 17, 2026.
  • Senate & House Agricultural Affairs committees (where rodent bills are heard) (legislature) — official contact page
    Bills are heard in committee before a floor vote; signing up to testify there is high-leverage. S1271 moved through the agricultural committees.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Dear Senator / Representative [name],

I am a constituent in [town]. I am writing to ask you to oppose any bill that would ban or target privately kept, captive-bred roof rats (Rattus rattus) as pets, such as the 2026 'Rodents of Unusual Size Act' (S1271), and to distinguish domesticated pet rats from wild pest populations in any future legislation.

Domesticated, captive-bred roof rats are not the wild pests such a bill is aimed at. They are kept in cages indoors, never released, and are no more an agricultural threat than the fancy pet rats Idahoans already keep legally. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat (R. norvegicus), domesticated only in the 19th century; a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over. A blanket ban would punish responsible pet owners without affecting wild populations.

The same trade-off already applies to other pets. Cats and dogs are non-native and documented to harm native wildlife, yet are permitted because their companionship is judged worth it. The question a rodent ban raises is that same cost-benefit judgment, which belongs to you as lawmakers: whether the limited additional risk of a few tame, indoor-only pet rats justifies banning them. I do not ask you to assume any particular answer, only to weigh it, and to consider exempting securely caged, captive-bred pets while still addressing wild rat populations.

Thank you for your time,
[Your name, town]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • IDAPA 02.04.27 - Rules Governing Deleterious Exotic Animals (Sec. 410 Rodentia list names Cricetomys, Cynomys, Graphiurus, Funisciurus, Hybomys, Heliosciurus, Atherurus, and South American rodents; genus Rattus NOT listed) — Idaho State Dept of Agriculture
  • Idaho Code Title 25, Chapter 39 (Sec. 25-3901 to 25-3904) - Importation or Possession of Deleterious Exotic Animals (authorizing statute; possession permit required only for listed species) — Idaho Legislature
  • IDAPA 13.01.10 - Rules Governing the Importation, Possession, Release, Sale, or Salvage of Wildlife (Sec. 011.06 defines 'Conventional Pets' to include rodents; Sec. 200.06 exempts conventional pets from any IDFG import/transport/possess/sell permit) — Idaho Department of Fish and Game
  • Idaho Code Sec. 36-202 - Definitions (defines 'wildlife' broadly as native or exotic animal life; basis for the IDFG captive-wildlife regime that the conventional-pet exemption carves rodents out of) — Idaho Legislature
  • IDAPA 02.04.21 - Rules Governing the Importation of Animals (official CVI required for animals entering Idaho) — Idaho State Dept of Agriculture
  • Household Pet Imports - Idaho State Dept of Agriculture (all household pets entering Idaho require at least a CVI; unlisted typical pets 'likely require only a CVI') — Idaho State Dept of Agriculture
  • ISDA Administrative Order (June 9, 2026) / press release - New World Screwworm entry requirements (warm-blooded animals incl. companion pets: 5-day CVI; entry permit from designated infested zones) — Idaho State Dept of Agriculture, State Veterinarian
  • USDA APHIS - Animal Welfare Act licensing (federal exemption for businesses that breed or sell only rats, mice, or birds) — U.S. Department of Agriculture, APHIS
  • Idaho Senate Bill S1271 (2026) - 'Rodents of Unusual Size Act' / Rats, health and safety nuisance (introduced Feb 10; Senate passed 28-3-4 on Mar 5; House FAILED 32-38 on Mar 17, 2026; dead for 2026) — Idaho Legislature
  • KTVB - 'Bill declaring rats a public health emergency fails in Idaho House' (House vote 32-38, March 17, 2026) — KTVB (news report)

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Illinois? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Illinois

Summary. Illinois is permissive for keeping a pet roof rat, and avoids the species-trap seen in other states because it does not use a taxonomic white-list. A captive-bred, cared-for roof rat is a 'companion animal' under the Humane Care for Animals Act (510 ILCS 70/2.01a), defined functionally as 'an animal that is commonly considered to be, or is considered by the owner to be, a pet.' That status keeps it outside the Wildlife Code's definition of 'wildlife' (520 ILCS 5/1.2t, which covers a mammal 'wild by nature... ordinarily living unconfined in a state of nature without the care of man'), so no Department of Natural Resources possession permit is required. The roof rat is on no prohibited list: the Dangerous Animals Act (720 ILCS 5/48-10) names only large carnivores and primates, and the Injurious Species list (17 Ill. Adm. Code 805.20) names the multimammate rat (genus Mastomys) but not the genus Rattus. Keeping and hobby breeding are legal. Selling or giving away only rats you produced and raised is exempt from pet-shop licensing under the Animal Welfare Act 'produced and raised' provision (225 ILCS 605/2); buying and reselling, or retailing as a business, requires a Department of Agriculture pet-shop/dealer license. In-state transport is unregulated. The one genuinely open point is the import CVI: the rule that mandates a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection and an entry permit (8 Ill. Adm. Code 25.47) is directed at 'Licensees' (commercial AWA licensees) and is silent on a private owner moving a personal pet across state lines. Never release a pet rat outdoors.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Illinois-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Illinois is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Keeping a captive-bred roof rat as a pet is legal with no state possession permit. It is not a 'dangerous animal' (720 ILCS 5/48-10 lists only large carnivores and primates, no rodent) and is on no injurious-species list (17 Ill. Adm. Code 805.20 names the multimammate rat, genus Mastomys, but not the genus Rattus). As a cared-for pet it is a 'companion animal' under the Humane Care for Animals Act (510 ILCS 70/2.01a: 'an animal that is commonly considered to be, or is considered by the owner to be, a pet'), and it falls outside the Wildlife Code's definition of 'wildlife' (520 ILCS 5/1.2t covers a mammal 'wild by nature... ordinarily living unconfined in a state of nature without the care of man,' which a tame, caged pet is not), so no DNR exotic-wildlife possession permit applies. Owners are bound by the Humane Care for Animals Act welfare and anti-hoarding standards (510 ILCS 70), and may never release the animal outdoors. The companion-animal status depends on the animal being kept as a pet; a wild-caught roof rat is a different matter.

Sources: Illinois General Assembly, Illinois General Assembly / IL DNR, Illinois General Assembly, Illinois Administrative Code / IL DNR

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Private hobby breeding is legal and not separately regulated. The roof rat is not 'wildlife,' protected, injurious, or a dangerous animal, so no DNR breeding permit applies. The Animal Welfare Act defines a 'pet shop operator' broadly (225 ILCS 605/2) but expressly exempts 'a person who sells only such animals that he has produced and raised,' which shelters a true hobby breeder who only distributes the offspring of their own animals from Department of Agriculture commercial licensing and inspection. Unlike dogs and cats, the rodent exemption turns on the home origin of the animals, not on a litter or intact-female count. Breeding only becomes regulated at commercial scale or when an individual sells rats they did not raise (see sell_give). Owners remain subject to the Humane Care for Animals Act welfare and anti-hoarding provisions (510 ILCS 70), which a large breeding colony must not run afoul of.

Sources: Illinois General Assembly / IL Dept of Agriculture, Illinois General Assembly, Illinois General Assembly / IL DNR

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Selling or giving away only rats you produced and raised is legal and exempt from licensing: the Animal Welfare Act says 'a person who sells only such animals that he has produced and raised shall not be considered a pet shop operator' (225 ILCS 605/2), so free vetted adoption or low-volume sale of home-bred rats needs no permit. No DNR sale permit applies, because the roof rat is not protected or injurious wildlife. The exemption ends if you buy rats from a third party and resell them, or operate as a retail pet shop, in which case you become a 'pet shop operator' and must hold a Department of Agriculture license (225 ILCS 605/3), with facility standards and unannounced inspections. A regulatory note specific to rodents: even a licensed dealer is exempt from the 12-month sales-record requirement for 'rats that were born in the United States' (8 Ill. Adm. Code 25.90), which covers domestic-bred R. rattus.

Sources: Illinois General Assembly / IL Dept of Agriculture, Illinois Administrative Code / IL Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII)

Transport & import   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-13

In-state movement of a legally kept pet roof rat is unregulated, with no transit permit or in-state health certificate required. Interstate import is the one open point. The import rule, 8 Ill. Adm. Code 25.47 ('Animals Imported Into Illinois'), mandates a health certificate (Certificate of Veterinary Inspection, issued within 30 days prior to entry by a USDA-accredited vet) and an Illinois Department of Agriculture entry permit number, but its operative text is directed at 'Licensees' (commercial AWA licensees such as pet-shop and kennel operators) and does not state that a private, non-licensed owner moving a personal pet across state lines must comply. USDA APHIS does not regulate interstate movement of pets by their owners and defers to the receiving state; the federal CDC African-rodent import ban does not reach a US-bred R. rattus (an Old World species not native to Africa). Because the state rule targets licensees and is silent on private owners, the private-owner obligation is genuinely unresolved; obtaining a CVI is the prudent course and a written answer from the State Veterinarian would settle it. Never release a pet rat outdoors (520 ILCS 5/2.2 bars liberating wild animals; abandonment is also barred under the cruelty statutes).

Sources: Illinois Administrative Code / IL Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII), USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, Illinois General Assembly / IL DNR

Restrictions & responsibilities

Selling rats you did NOT produce and raise, or retailing rats as a business, makes you a 'pet shop operator' and requires an Illinois Department of Agriculture pet-shop/dealer license under the Animal Welfare Act (225 ILCS 605/3), with facility standards and unannounced inspections. Selling or giving away only your own home-bred rats is exempt under the 'produced and raised' provision (225 ILCS 605/2) and needs no license.
  • Stay within the 'produced and raised' exemption (transfer only rats you bred and raised yourself) to remain license-free
  • If you resell purchased rats or operate a retail pet shop: apply for an Animal Welfare Act pet-shop/dealer license with the Department of Agriculture and meet facility/inspection standards

Where: Illinois Department of Agriculture, Bureau of Animal Health and Welfare

Source: Illinois General Assembly / IL Dept of Agriculture

Importing an animal into Illinois under 8 Ill. Adm. Code 25.47 requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (issued within 30 days prior to entry by a USDA-accredited veterinarian) and an Illinois Department of Agriculture entry permit number. The rule's operative text is directed at 'Licensees' (commercial AWA licensees) and does not state that a private owner moving a personal pet must comply, so the private-owner obligation is unresolved. No CVI is needed for movement within Illinois.
  • For in-state movement: no health certificate or permit is required
  • For interstate import as a private owner: the requirement is unresolved (the rule names 'Licensees'); obtaining a CVI is the prudent course, and confirm with the State Veterinarian whether a private pet-owner import CVI or entry permit is required
  • Commercial AWA licensees importing animals: obtain a CVI (within 30 days of entry) and an Illinois Department of Agriculture entry permit number before entry

Where: Illinois Department of Agriculture, Bureau of Animal Health and Welfare (Office of the State Veterinarian)

Source: Illinois Administrative Code / IL Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII)

Never release a pet roof rat outdoors. Liberating a wild animal is barred under the Wildlife Code (520 ILCS 5/2.2) and releasing a captive-bred companion animal also constitutes abandonment under the cruelty statutes (510 ILCS 70). Owners are bound by the Humane Care for Animals Act welfare and anti-hoarding provisions. Local city/county ordinances (for example, Chicago or Cook County) may add limits or public-health rules, so check yours.

Where: Illinois DNR / Department of Agriculture / your local code enforcement

Source: Illinois General Assembly / IL DNR, Illinois General Assembly

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • 510 ILCS 70/2.01a - Humane Care for Animals Act, 'companion animal' definition ('commonly considered to be, or is considered by the owner to be, a pet') — Illinois General Assembly
  • 520 ILCS 5/1.2t & 5/2.2 - Wildlife Code ('wildlife' = mammal 'wild by nature... living unconfined... without the care of man'; no liberation of wild animals) — Illinois General Assembly / IL DNR
  • 720 ILCS 5/48-10 - Dangerous animal or primate offense (lists only large carnivores and primates; no rodent) — Illinois General Assembly
  • 17 Ill. Adm. Code 805.20 - Listing of Injurious Species (names the multimammate rat, genus Mastomys; omits the genus Rattus) — Illinois Administrative Code / IL DNR
  • 225 ILCS 605/2 & 605/3 - Animal Welfare Act ('pet shop operator' definition; 'produced and raised' hobbyist exemption; Dept of Agriculture licensing) — Illinois General Assembly / IL Dept of Agriculture
  • 8 Ill. Adm. Code 25.47 - Animals Imported Into Illinois (CVI within 30 days + entry permit number; operative text directed at 'Licensees') — Illinois Administrative Code / IL Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII)
  • 8 Ill. Adm. Code 25.90 - Records Requirement (12-month sales records; exempts 'rats that were born in the United States') — Illinois Administrative Code / IL Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII)
  • USDA APHIS - Take a Pet From One U.S. State or Territory to Another (APHIS does not regulate interstate pet movement by owners; receiving state sets requirements) — USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Indiana? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Indiana

Summary. Indiana is permissive for the roof rat, and there is no species trap. The roof rat is not on any Indiana regulatory list: not a Class I, II, or III animal under the DNR Wild Animal Possession Permit rule (312 IAC 9-11), not an exotic mammal (312 IAC 9-3-18.5), not an endangered mammal (312 IAC 9-3-19), and not a prohibited invasive vertebrate. Under the residual clause 312 IAC 9-3-20, any mammal not identified in the article is an 'exempted wild animal,' which 312 IAC 9-1-6 defines as unprotected and possessable at any time without a permit. The roof rat (R. rattus) and the fancy rat (R. norvegicus) fall into that same residual category by negative taxonomy, so the two are treated identically. Keeping, breeding, and selling or giving are legal with no DNR permit and no state breeder license (Indiana's commercial-breeder law, IC 15-21, is dog-only, and its July 1 2024 retail-pet-store registration defines a retail pet store as selling dogs). Importing a pet roof rat needs no state CVI: the family Muridae is not among the wild families that require an entry CVI under 345 IAC 1-3-4, and rodents are not 'domestic animals' under IC 15-17-2-26. The DNR wild-animal import permit applies only to animals imported for release or sale for release, which does not cover the pet trade. Federal USDA Animal Welfare Act licensing can reach some wholesale or research breeders. Releasing a roof rat is prohibited (312 IAC 9-2-16); local ordinances may add limits.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Indiana-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Indiana is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

The DNR Wild Animal Possession Permit rule (312 IAC 9-11) requires a permit only for the exhaustively enumerated Class I, II, and III animals (rabbits and native squirrels; furbearers such as beaver, coyote, fox, raccoon, skunk; and dangerous wildlife such as bears, big cats, wolves, venomous reptiles, and large crocodilians). The roof rat and the genus Rattus appear on none of those lists. R. rattus is also absent from the exotic-mammal rule (312 IAC 9-3-18.5, which names 22 families, none of them Muridae) and the endangered-mammal list (312 IAC 9-3-19). Under 312 IAC 9-3-20, any mammal not identified in the article is an 'exempted wild animal,' which 312 IAC 9-1-6 defines as unprotected and possessable at any time. No state permit, facility inspection, registration, or fee is required to keep a roof rat, and the secondary-enclosure and perimeter-fence requirements for Class II and III animals (312 IAC 9-11-10) do not apply.

Sources: Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII), Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII), Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII), Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII), Indiana Code (via Justia)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Breeding follows keeping. Because the roof rat is an exempted wild animal that needs no possession permit, no DNR permit attaches to breeding it, and the Game Breeder's License (312 IAC 9-10-4) applies only to the listed native furbearers and game species, not to a non-listed pet rodent. Indiana's only commercial-breeder statute, the Commercial Dog Breeder Regulation (IC 15-21), applies solely to dogs, so there is no state breeding license for rats regardless of the number of animals kept or produced. Federal oversight can apply separately: under the USDA Animal Welfare Act, breeders who sell rodents at wholesale or for research, testing, or exhibition may need a USDA Class A or B license, while those who sell only at retail face to face to the final owner are generally exempt.

Sources: Indiana General Assembly / Indiana State Board of Animal Health, Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII), Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

No Indiana statute licenses or restricts selling or giving away pet rodents. The sale of an exempted wild animal is not permitted, tracked, or taxed by the DNR (the only limit being that animals may not be sold for release into the wild). The July 1 2024 retail-pet-store and animal-care-facility registration added to IC 15-21 defines a 'retail pet store' as a business that sells dogs, with sourcing rules targeting dog sellers, so a seller dealing only in roof rats, fancy rats, mice, or other small rodents is outside that scheme and need not register with the Board of Animal Health. Sellers are not required to provide a state health certificate, origin documents, or microchips. Federal USDA Animal Welfare Act dealer licensing can apply to some commercial sellers (wholesale or to research, testing, or exhibition).

Sources: Indiana General Assembly / Indiana State Board of Animal Health, Indiana State Board of Animal Health, Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII), Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII)

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

In-state transport is unregulated. For import into Indiana, no state CVI is required for a pet roof rat: 345 IAC 1-3-4 requires an entry CVI for 'domestic animals' (a list in IC 15-17-2-26 that omits rodents) and, for wild animals, only for the families bovidae, camelidae, cervidae, equidae, and suidae, so the family Muridae is not covered. The DNR wild-animal import permit (312 IAC 9-10-20) applies only to a mammal imported for release or sale for release in Indiana, which does not include the pet trade. No state entry permit or border health test is mandated to bring a pet roof rat into Indiana, although a destination state or country may impose its own rules on export, so confirm the receiving jurisdiction's requirements before moving an animal across a border. Releasing a roof rat into the wild is prohibited under 312 IAC 9-2-16.

Sources: Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII), Indiana Code (via Justia), Indiana Administrative Code (Indiana Register / IARP), Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII)

Restrictions & responsibilities

It is unlawful to release a captive-bred mammal into the wild (312 IAC 9-2-16), and an exempted wild animal may not be sold for release. The roof rat is a non-native species; keep it contained and rehome responsibly, never release it. Local city or county ordinances may independently restrict non-native or exotic pets (for example, some Indiana municipalities define an 'exotic animal' as any species not native to the United States, which would include the roof rat), so check your local code, county zoning, and any HOA covenants.
  • Never release a roof rat into the wild (312 IAC 9-2-16); rehome, surrender to a rescue, or seek humane euthanasia if you can no longer keep it
  • Do not sell or transfer a roof rat for release
  • Check your city and county ordinances and any HOA covenants for local exotic or non-native pet limits before keeping or selling

Where: Local code enforcement / county zoning office; Indiana DNR for wildlife questions

Source: Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII), Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • 312 IAC 9-3-20 - Exempted mammals ('Any mammal not identified in this article is an exempted wild animal') — Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII)
  • 312 IAC 9-1-6 - Definition of 'exempted wild animal' (unprotected; may be possessed at any time) — Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII)
  • 312 IAC 9-11 - Wild Animal Possession Permits (Class I/II/III lists; no Rattus) — Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII)
  • 312 IAC 9-3-18.5 - Exotic mammals (22 families enumerated; Muridae not listed) — Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII)
  • IC 14-8-2-318 - Definition of 'wild animal' — Indiana Code (via Justia)
  • IC 15-21 - Commercial Dog Breeder Regulation / Retail Pet Store registration (defines 'retail pet store' as selling dogs) — Indiana General Assembly / Indiana State Board of Animal Health
  • Indiana BOAH - Retail Pet Stores (registration effective July 1 2024; retail pet store = sells dogs) — Indiana State Board of Animal Health
  • 312 IAC 9-10-4 - Game breeder's licenses (listed native furbearers/game species only) — Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII)
  • 345 IAC 1-3-4 - CVI required for importation of domestic animals (wild families limited to bovidae, camelidae, cervidae, equidae, suidae; Muridae not listed) — Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII)
  • IC 15-17-2-26 - Definition of 'domestic animal' (enumerated list omits rodents/Muridae) — Indiana Code (via Justia)
  • 312 IAC 9-10-20 - Wild animal import permit (required only for import 'for release or sale for release in Indiana') — Indiana Administrative Code (Indiana Register / IARP)
  • 312 IAC 9-2-16 - Release of captive-bred mammals, reptiles, amphibians, and mussels prohibited — Indiana Administrative Code (via Cornell LII)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.
