item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Kansas? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Kansas

Summary. Kansas is among the most permissive states for the roof rat, and keeping, breeding, and selling a captive-bred R. rattus is legal. Three independent rules confirm it. The Dangerous Regulated Animals Act (K.S.A. 32-1301) defines a 'dangerous regulated animal' as only big cats, bears, and non-native venomous snakes, so no rodent is restricted. KDWP's exotic-wildlife rule (K.A.R. 115-20-3) affirmatively allows non-native species to be imported, possessed, sold, and purchased, with no permit and no limit in time or number, on one condition: confine the animal and never release it. R. rattus is non-native to Kansas, so it falls in this permissive class, and it does not appear on the KDWP prohibited-species list (K.A.R. 115-18-10). Kansas draws no R. rattus / R. norvegicus distinction; both are treated alike as non-native rodents. The Pet Animal Act (K.S.A. 47-1701) does reach rodents at commercial scale, but it exempts a resident home breeder who sells only animals produced and raised on their own premises, and its breeder and distributor licenses are written for dogs and cats only. So hobby keeping, breeding, and private sale or gifting are unregulated. The only open edge is import: the Department of Agriculture exempts 'pocket pets' from the exotic-animal import permit, but its general rule (K.A.R. 9-7-1) requires imported exotic animals to carry a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection, and how strictly that applies to a single pet rodent is best confirmed with the KDA Import Desk.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Kansas-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Kansas is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

No Kansas statute restricts keeping a captive-bred roof rat. The Dangerous Regulated Animals Act defines a 'dangerous regulated animal' as only lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs, mountain lions and hybrids, bears and hybrids, and all non-native venomous snakes (K.S.A. 32-1301), so no rodent is covered. KDWP's exotic-wildlife rule (K.A.R. 115-20-3) then governs: a non-native species 'may be possessed without limit in time and number' with no permit, and is not on the prohibited-species list (K.A.R. 115-18-10). The only obligation is confinement: exotic wildlife 'shall be confined or controlled at all times and shall not be released onto the lands or into the waters of this state' (K.A.R. 115-20-3). No registration, microchipping, insurance, or quantity limit applies. Local ordinances can still impose stricter rules, so check the municipality.

Sources: Kansas Office of Revisor of Statutes, Kansas Department of Wildlife and Parks (via Cornell LII), Kansas Department of Wildlife and Parks (via Cornell LII)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Breeding is authorized under the exotic-wildlife rule, which allows non-native species to be raised and possessed without a KDWP permit (K.A.R. 115-20-3). At commercial scale the Pet Animal Act (K.S.A. 47-1701) can apply to rodents, but a resident home breeder is exempt: a 'pet shop' excludes animals 'that are produced and raised on such premises and are sold, or offered or maintained for sale, by a person who resides on such premises' (K.S.A. 47-1701(t)(1)(B)). The Act's breeder licenses ('animal breeder', 'retail breeder', 'hobby breeder') and its 'animal distributor' license are all defined in terms of dogs or cats only, so no rodent-specific breeder license exists. A home hobby breeder of roof rats therefore needs no license at any volume, as long as every animal sold was produced and raised on the seller's own residence.

Sources: Kansas Department of Wildlife and Parks (via Cornell LII), Kansas Office of Revisor of Statutes (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Selling, offering for sale, or giving away a captive-bred roof rat is lawful. K.A.R. 115-20-3 expressly allows exotic wildlife to be 'sold, offered for sale or purchased' with no KDWP permit. A resident who sells only animals produced and raised on their own premises is exempt from the Pet Animal Act pet-shop license (K.S.A. 47-1701(t)(1)(B)); free adoption is likewise unregulated. A Pet Shop Operator license is required only for retail of animals NOT born on the seller's residence, for example reselling rats bought from outside breeders (K.S.A. 47-1701(t)(1); K.S.A. 47-1703). The Act's 'animal distributor' (dealer) license is written for dogs and cats only, so it does not reach a rodent seller.

Sources: Kansas Department of Wildlife and Parks (via Cornell LII), Kansas Office of Revisor of Statutes (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center)

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-13

Intrastate movement is unrestricted as long as the animal stays confined (K.A.R. 115-20-3 requires control at all times and no release). For import into Kansas, the Department of Agriculture exempts 'pocket pets' (rodents such as rats, hamsters, gerbils, and mice), along with zoo-to-zoo movements and non-poisonous reptiles, from the exotic-animal import permit. A separate rule, K.A.R. 9-7-1, provides that livestock and exotic animals shall not be imported into Kansas without a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection from an accredited veterinarian in the state of origin, subject to four listed exceptions (slaughter, public livestock market, special permit/movement agreement, and adjacent-county movement) that do not include pocket pets. The regulation itself sets no 30-day window; KDA guidance applies a 30-day standard CVI. How strictly the CVI is required for a single privately owned pet rodent is the one unsettled point and is best confirmed with the KDA Import Desk. Export is governed by the destination jurisdiction.

Sources: Kansas Department of Wildlife and Parks (via Cornell LII), Kansas Dept of Agriculture, Division of Animal Health, Kansas Department of Agriculture (via Cornell LII)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Exotic wildlife (including a non-native roof rat) must be confined or controlled at all times and must never be released onto the lands or into the waters of Kansas (K.A.R. 115-20-3). This is the core duty; releasing the animal is the prohibited act, not keeping it.
  • Keep the rat in a secure, escape-proof indoor enclosure
  • Never release a roof rat into the wild; release of confined exotic wildlife violates K.A.R. 115-20-3

Source: Kansas Department of Wildlife and Parks (via Cornell LII)

Pocket pets are exempt from the Kansas exotic-animal import permit, but K.A.R. 9-7-1 requires imported livestock and exotic animals to be accompanied by a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) from an accredited veterinarian in the state of origin (four listed exceptions do not cover pocket pets). Whether this is enforced on a single privately owned pet rodent is unsettled; confirm with the KDA Import Desk before importing.
  • Confirm with the KDA Import Desk (785-564-6616) whether a CVI is required for a single pet rodent
  • If required, obtain a CVI from a USDA-accredited veterinarian in the state of origin (KDA guidance uses a 30-day standard) certifying the animal free of clinical signs of infectious/contagious disease

Where: Kansas Department of Agriculture, Division of Animal Health (Import Desk)

Source: Kansas Dept of Agriculture, Division of Animal Health, Kansas Department of Agriculture (via Cornell LII)

A commercial Pet Shop Operator license (K.S.A. 47-1703) is required ONLY to retail animals not produced and raised on the seller's own residence (for example, reselling rats bought from other breeders). A resident home breeder selling only self-raised animals is exempt (K.S.A. 47-1701(t)(1)(B)), as is free adoption. Licensed pet shops are subject to KDA facility inspection and a documented veterinary-care program.
  • A resident selling only self-raised rats needs no license
  • If reselling bought-in stock or operating a non-residence retail premises, apply to the KDA for a Pet Shop Operator license and meet facility/veterinary-care standards

Where: Kansas Department of Agriculture, Animal Facilities Inspection (AFI) Program · Fees: Pet Shop Operator license set by KDA (commercial premises)

Source: Kansas Office of Revisor of Statutes (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center)

Official sources

  • K.S.A. 32-1301: Dangerous Regulated Animals Act (defines 'dangerous regulated animal' as big cats/bears/non-native venomous snakes; no rodents) — Kansas Office of Revisor of Statutes
  • K.A.R. 115-20-3: Exotic wildlife; possession, sale and requirements (non-native species may be imported/possessed/sold/purchased, no permit, no limit in time/number; must be confined and never released; (d) defines exotic wildlife) — Kansas Department of Wildlife and Parks (via Cornell LII)
  • K.A.R. 115-18-10: Importation and possession of certain wildlife; prohibition (prohibited list = aquatic species, monk parakeet, Asian raccoon dog; R. rattus absent) — Kansas Department of Wildlife and Parks (via Cornell LII)
  • K.S.A. 47-1701: Kansas Pet Animal Act definitions ((t)(1)(B) pet-shop exemption for home-raised animals sold by a resident; breeder/distributor licenses defined for dogs/cats only) — Kansas Office of Revisor of Statutes (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center)
  • K.A.R. 9-7-1: General import rule (livestock and exotic animals shall not be imported into Kansas without a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection; four listed exceptions do not include pocket pets) — Kansas Department of Agriculture (via Cornell LII)
  • Kansas Dept of Agriculture, Import & Export Regulations (zoo-to-zoo movements, pocket pets, and non-poisonous reptiles do not require an import permit; Import Desk 785-564-6616) — Kansas Dept of Agriculture, Division of Animal Health

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Kentucky? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Kentucky

Summary. Kentucky is one of the clearest 'yes' states for keeping a roof rat. Its exotic-wildlife rule, 301 KAR 2:082, names 'Domesticated races of rats (Rattus norvegicus or Rattus rattus) or mice (Mus musculus)' by binomial in the permit-exempt list, so importing, transporting, and possessing a captive-bred roof rat needs no state wildlife permit, and R. rattus is not on the inherently-dangerous prohibited-species list (Section 4). Keeping and breeding are unregulated at the state level: Kentucky's commercial pet-breeder bills and retail-sale bans cover only dogs and cats, not rodents. Two conditions attach to movement, not to keeping. First, the Department of Agriculture's animal-health rules require a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) for any animal imported into Kentucky (302 KAR 20:040) or offered for sale within Kentucky (302 KAR 20:065); rodents are not named for an exemption and are not named for an entry permit, so a CVI applies but no advance telephonic entry permit does. Giving a rat away for free is outside the for-sale CVI clause. Second, a strict reading of the exotic-mammal bite protocol (301 KAR 2:082 Section 6(8)) requires any exotic mammal that bites a person to be euthanized and its head submitted for rabies testing, with no written quarantine alternative for permit-exempt rodents; the actual epidemiological risk from a small rodent is negligible (CDC does not treat them as rabies vectors), but the rule offers no species-specific waiver. Never release a roof rat.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Kentucky-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Kentucky is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

301 KAR 2:082 lists 'Domesticated races of rats (Rattus norvegicus or Rattus rattus) or mice (Mus musculus)' among the animals that 'shall not require permits from the department for importation, transportation into Kentucky, or possession.' R. rattus is named by species, and it is absent from the Section 4 prohibited/inherently-dangerous list (which names the Gambian giant pouched rat, the multimammate rat (Mastomys), and nutria, but not R. rattus). No state wildlife permit, facility inspection, or fee applies to keeping one. General animal-cruelty law (KRS Chapter 525) still applies.

Sources: Kentucky Legislative Research Commission / KDFWR, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission, Kentucky Dept of Fish & Wildlife Resources, Cornell Legal Information Institute

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

Breeding is unregulated at the state level. Because possession is permit-exempt under 301 KAR 2:082, breeding needs no KDFWR permit, and Kentucky imposes no rodent-breeder license, quota, or facility standard. The commercial pet-breeder framework (KRS Chapter 258 and the 2023-2025 dog/cat breeder and retail-sale bills, e.g. SB 157, SB 122, HB 651) is confined to dogs and cats; rodents are outside its definitions. Federal USDA/AWA licensing can reach a large-scale breeder who ships wholesale or sight-unseen, but direct-to-consumer pet sales and hobby breeders under the de minimis threshold are federally exempt, and rats bred for research are excluded from the AWA entirely.

Sources: Kentucky Legislative Research Commission / KDFWR, Kentucky General Assembly, USDA APHIS

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

No state dealer/breeder license applies to selling or giving away captive-bred roof rats: Kentucky's retail pet-sale bans cover only dogs and cats (rodents and other 'pocket pets' are expressly outside them), and KRS Chapter 258 commercial-establishment licensing is dogs/cats. The one attached condition is a movement health document, not a business permit: 302 KAR 20:065 Section 1(2) provides that 'All animals offered for sale shall be accompanied by a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI), or other official movement document except for exemptions listed under each species of this administrative regulation or 302 KAR 20:040,' and the regulation lists no exemption for rodents or pocket pets. A captive-bred roof rat is a 'captive animal' under the 302 KAR 20:010 definition of 'Animal,' so a CVI from an accredited veterinarian is required to offer one for sale. Giving a rat away for free falls outside the 'offered for sale' clause. Enforcement of the CVI rule against casual hobbyist pet sales is questionable in practice, but the requirement exists in the text. General cruelty law (KRS Chapter 525) applies.

Sources: Kentucky Dept of Agriculture, Office of State Veterinarian, Kentucky Dept of Agriculture, Office of State Veterinarian, Kentucky General Assembly, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission / KDFWR

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-13

No KDFWR wildlife transportation/import permit applies: 301 KAR 2:082 exempts the domesticated race of R. rattus from importation and transportation permits by binomial. The attached condition is an animal-health document. 302 KAR 20:040 Section 1(2) provides that 'All animals shall be accompanied by a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) or other official movement document except for exemptions listed under each species section of this administrative regulation or 302 KAR 20:065,' and the entry regulation names no exemption for rodents or pocket pets. So bringing a roof rat into Kentucky (a move-in, or buying from an out-of-state breeder) requires a CVI issued in the state of origin within 30 days before entry. No advance telephonic entry permit is required: 302 KAR 20:040 reserves entry permits for specified livestock (cattle, swine, sheep, goats, ratites, camelids, cervids), and rodents have no such section. Export is governed by the destination state's rules; international movement is governed by federal CDC/USDA/USFWS rules (the CDC bars rodents of African origin). Never release a roof rat into the wild (301 KAR 2:082 Section 8 bars releasing exotic wildlife).

Sources: Kentucky Legislative Research Commission / KDFWR, Kentucky Dept of Agriculture, Office of State Veterinarian, Kentucky Dept of Agriculture, Office of State Veterinarian, USDA APHIS / CDC

Restrictions & responsibilities

A Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) is required to import a roof rat into Kentucky (302 KAR 20:040) or to offer one for sale within Kentucky (302 KAR 20:065). Rodents have no written exemption. The CVI is a vet-issued health document, valid about 30 days, certifying the animal is free of communicable disease. Giving a rat away free is outside the for-sale clause. No advance entry permit applies to rodents.
  • Have a USDA-accredited veterinarian examine the rat and issue a CVI (it records species, sex, age, and the seller's/buyer's or origin/destination details).
  • For import: obtain the CVI in the state of origin within 30 days before entering Kentucky.
  • For sale within Kentucky: have the CVI accompany the animal when offered for sale.
  • No telephonic entry permit is needed for rodents (entry permits apply only to listed livestock).

Forms: Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) · Where: Issued by a USDA-accredited veterinarian; the vet files a copy with the Office of the State Veterinarian (Kentucky Dept of Agriculture). · Fees: No state fee for the CVI; the issuing veterinarian charges an examination/paperwork fee.

Source: Kentucky Dept of Agriculture, Office of State Veterinarian, Kentucky Dept of Agriculture, Office of State Veterinarian, Kentucky Dept of Agriculture, Office of State Veterinarian

Exotic-mammal bite/rabies protocol: 301 KAR 2:082 Section 6(8) requires that if an exotic mammal bites a person (or shows rabies symptoms) the owner must have it killed in a way that preserves the brain and submit the head for rabies testing. R. rattus is a permit-exempt exotic mammal, so a strict reading applies this with no written quarantine alternative for domesticated rodents. The actual rabies risk from a small pet rodent is negligible and the CDC does not treat them as vectors, but the regulation provides no species-specific waiver.
  • Handle and socialize the rat to minimize bite risk.
  • If a bite occurs, contact the Office of the State Veterinarian and local health department; ask whether a 10-day quarantine alternative applies to a permit-exempt domesticated rodent before any euthanasia, since the text of Section 6(8) provides none.

Where: Cabinet for Health and Family Services / local health department; Office of the State Veterinarian.

Source: Kentucky Legislative Research Commission / KDFWR

Never release a roof rat into the wild. 301 KAR 2:082 Section 8 provides that, with narrow exceptions for pheasants and chukars, a person shall not release exotic wildlife into the wild, and R. rattus is an invasive species. Rehome responsibly. Check local county/city ordinances.

Source: Kentucky Legislative Research Commission / KDFWR

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • 301 KAR 2:082, Transportation and holding of live exotic wildlife (permit-exempt list names 'Domesticated races of rats (Rattus norvegicus or Rattus rattus) or mice (Mus musculus)'; prohibited species Section 4; exotic-mammal bite protocol Section 6(8); no-release Section 8) — Kentucky Legislative Research Commission / KDFWR
  • 301 KAR 2:082 (versioned text): permit-exempt rats subsection (rendered Section 6(10) in one renumbered version and Section 7(11) in another; both are the same 'Rattus norvegicus or Rattus rattus' provision) — Kentucky Legislative Research Commission
  • 301 KAR 2:082 (Cornell LII mirror): Section 7(11) 'Domesticated races of rats (Rattus norvegicus or Rattus rattus) or mice (Mus musculus)'; Section 6(8) exotic-mammal bite protocol; Section 8 no-release — Cornell Legal Information Institute
  • 301 KAR 2:082 Section 4 (Prohibited / inherently-dangerous species): names Gambian giant pouched rat (Cricetomys gambianus), multimammate rat (Mastomys), nutria; R. rattus absent. Simplified KDFWR list also published as a PDF. — Kentucky Dept of Fish & Wildlife Resources
  • 302 KAR 20:040, Entry into Kentucky (Section 1(2): all animals need a CVI except listed exemptions; no rodent exemption; entry permit only for listed livestock) — Kentucky Dept of Agriculture, Office of State Veterinarian
  • 302 KAR 20:065, Sale and exhibition of Kentucky origin animals in Kentucky (Section 1(2): all animals offered for sale need a CVI except listed exemptions; no rodent exemption) — Kentucky Dept of Agriculture, Office of State Veterinarian
  • 302 KAR 20:010, Definitions for 302 KAR Chapter 20 ('Animal' includes captive/pet animals, subjecting them to KDA movement rules; defines the CVI) — Kentucky Dept of Agriculture, Office of State Veterinarian
  • KRS Chapter 258 + 2023-2025 dog/cat breeder & retail-sale bills (SB 157, SB 122, HB 651, SB 56): commercial-breeder and retail-pet-shop regulation is limited to dogs and cats; rodents excluded — Kentucky General Assembly
  • USDA APHIS, Animal Welfare Act licensing (Class A breeder license applies to wholesale/sight-unseen dealers; direct-to-consumer and de minimis hobby sales exempt; research rats of genus Rattus excluded from AWA) — USDA APHIS
  • USDA APHIS, Bring a Pet Rodent into the United States (federal international-import rules; CDC bars rodents of African origin) — USDA APHIS / CDC

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Louisiana? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Louisiana

Summary. Louisiana has no law that prohibits keeping a captive-bred roof rat, and the lawful pathway is the same one the fancy rat (the domesticated Norway rat, R. norvegicus) already uses. The state wildlife code (La. R.S. 56:8) sorts wild quadrupeds into game (deer, bears, squirrels, rabbits), outlaw (coyotes, armadillos, feral hogs), protected (wolves, cougars, bobcats, foxes), and nongame (fur/skin animals such as nutria, mink, muskrat); R. rattus fits none. The 'potentially dangerous wild quadruped' ban (LAC 76:V-115) covers only big cats, bears, wolves, and primates, with no rodents. Local 'wild or exotic animal' ordinances (e.g. the Louisiana SPCA code for Orleans Parish) expressly exempt captive-bred 'laboratory rats... which have never known the wild' and the catch-all 'pocket pets or rodents,' which a multi-generation captive-bred roof rat fits. So keeping, hobby breeding, private rehoming, and direct retail sale are effectively legal at the state level. Commercial sale needs no LDWF license: the Nongame Quadruped Breeder/Exhibitor License covers only alligators, coyotes, and foxes and 'will not be issued for pets or the pet trade,' and federal AWA retail-pet-store sales of rats are exempt from USDA licensing. Parish ordinances vary, and releasing a roof rat is always prohibited (R.S. 56:20).

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Louisiana-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Louisiana is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-14

Keeping a captive-bred roof rat needs no Louisiana permit and follows the same route as the fancy rat. R. rattus is on no prohibited or dangerous list: the 'potentially dangerous wild quadruped' rule (LAC 76:V-115) lists only big cats, bears, wolves, and non-human primates, with no rodents, and the wildlife code's enumerated quadruped categories (La. R.S. 56:8: game, outlaw, protected, nongame) do not reach a non-native commensal rodent. Local 'wild or exotic animal' ordinances reinforce this: the Louisiana SPCA code (Orleans Parish) expressly permits 'laboratory rats... which have been bred and raised in captivity which have never known the wild, and pocket pets or rodents including, but not limited to, hamsters, gerbils, guinea pigs, chinchillas, sugar gliders or hedgehogs.' A captive-bred roof rat is a rodent and fits the 'pocket pets or rodents' catch-all, identical to the captive-bred Norway rat sold as the fancy rat. Confidence is medium, not high, because R. rattus is nowhere named by species and parish ordinances vary in wording and enforcement.

Sources: Louisiana Wildlife & Fisheries Commission (via Cornell LII), Louisiana Legislature, Louisiana SPCA (Orleans Parish animal control)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-14

Private hobby breeding of captive-born roof rats triggers no state wildlife license. The Nongame Quadruped Breeder License (La. R.S. 56:262) applies to 'imported or native nongame quadrupeds,' which the wildlife code (R.S. 56:8) defines as fur/skin animals such as alligators, beavers, mink, muskrats, nutrias, and foxes; a non-native commensal rodent with no pelt value falls outside it. LDWF confirms the nongame license covers only alligators, coyotes, and foxes and 'will not be issued for pets or the pet trade,' and the Game Breeder License (R.S. 56:171) covers wild game species (deer, squirrels, rabbits, game birds), not rodents. The state has no rodent or pocket-pet breeder license, so home breeding for the pet trade sits outside the licensing regime. No-release obligation applies (R.S. 56:20).

Sources: Louisiana Legislature, Louisiana Dept of Wildlife & Fisheries, Louisiana Legislature (via Justia), Louisiana Legislature

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-14

Both private rehoming and direct retail sale of captive-bred roof rats are unregulated by Louisiana wildlife law. The DR's open question (whether commercial sale needs a Nongame Quadruped Breeder License under R.S. 56:262) resolves against any license: LDWF states that license covers only alligators, coyotes, and foxes and 'will not be issued for pets or the pet trade,' and R. rattus lacks the fur/skin value the nongame definition (R.S. 56:8) requires. At the federal level, the Animal Welfare Act exempts 'retail pet stores' (a seller and buyer physically present so the buyer can observe the animal before purchase) from USDA licensing, and APHIS lists rats among the species this exemption covers, treating them like dogs, cats, rabbits, guinea pigs, and hamsters. So selling a roof rat face-to-face needs neither a state LDWF license nor a federal USDA license. Only a wholesale/sight-unseen operation (e.g. bulk online or supplying pet-store chains) could trigger USDA APHIS licensing; even then state law stays silent. Parish ordinances may add local limits.

Sources: Louisiana Legislature, Louisiana Dept of Wildlife & Fisheries, Louisiana Legislature, USDA APHIS (Federal Register)

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-14

Intrastate transport of a captive-bred roof rat is unrestricted: a roof rat is not a game quadruped (no transport tags, R.S. 56:125) and not a potentially dangerous wild quadruped (no escape plan or specialized enclosure), so it travels in an ordinary secure pet carrier with no state documentation. For interstate import, Louisiana's animal-health rules (LAC 7:XXI) require a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection and rabies proof for dogs and cats, and govern livestock and poultry, but do not list pet rodents, so the State Veterinarian requires no CVI, permit, or entry report for a privately owned pet rat crossing state lines. International import is governed federally by the CDC: the African rodent ban (42 CFR 71.56) reaches only rodents of African origin or African native habitat, and R. rattus is native to Asia, so it is not barred by that rule. Practical caveats not set by state law: commercial airlines/pet shippers often demand a recent health certificate as a private policy, and never release the animal (R.S. 56:20).

Sources: Louisiana Dept of Agriculture & Forestry (via Cornell LII), Louisiana Legislature, U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Louisiana Legislature

Restrictions & responsibilities

No Louisiana wildlife license applies to breeding or selling captive-bred pet roof rats. The Nongame Quadruped Breeder/Exhibitor License (La. R.S. 56:262) covers only alligators, coyotes, and foxes and 'will not be issued for pets or the pet trade'; R. rattus is not a fur/skin nongame quadruped. The state has no rodent or pocket-pet breeder license. Federally, direct retail sale of rats is exempt from USDA licensing under the AWA retail-pet-store exemption; only wholesale/sight-unseen sale could trigger a USDA APHIS license.
  • No state license needed for hobby breeding or face-to-face sale of captive-bred roof rats
  • If operating wholesale or selling sight-unseen at scale, check USDA APHIS dealer-license rules under the Animal Welfare Act

Where: Louisiana Dept of Wildlife & Fisheries (Wildlife Permits) for any state question; USDA APHIS Animal Care for wholesale federal licensing · Fees: No applicable state fee for pet rats

Source: Louisiana Legislature, Louisiana Dept of Wildlife & Fisheries, USDA APHIS (Federal Register)

Never release a roof rat into the wild. R.S. 56:20 forbids liberating any pen-raised or wild animal within the state without written permission of the LDWF secretary; a violation is a class four offense (R.S. 56:34). The roof rat is treated as an unprotected invasive pest the moment it is outside a cage. Keep it indoors in a secure enclosure.
  • Keep roof rats indoors in secure, escape-proof enclosures
  • Never release, abandon, or rehome a roof rat into the wild (R.S. 56:20, class four violation)

Where: Louisiana Dept of Wildlife & Fisheries

Source: Louisiana Legislature

Parish and municipal 'wild or exotic animal' ordinances vary. Many (e.g. the Louisiana SPCA code for Orleans Parish) expressly exempt captive-bred 'laboratory rats' and 'pocket pets or rodents,' which a captive-bred roof rat fits, but enforcement of the exact species can vary by parish and officer. Check your own parish/city code before keeping or selling.
  • Read your parish/municipal animal-control ordinance for any 'wild or exotic animal' rule and its pocket-pet/rodent exemption

Where: Local parish or municipal animal control

Source: Louisiana SPCA (Orleans Parish animal control)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • LAC 76:V-115, Possession of Potentially Dangerous Wild Quadrupeds, Big Exotic Cats, and Non-Human Primates (big cats/bears/wolves/primates only; no rodents) — Louisiana Wildlife & Fisheries Commission (via Cornell LII)
  • La. R.S. 56:8, Definitions (wildlife = all wild vertebrates; game/outlaw/protected/nongame quadruped categories; nongame = animals 'valuable for their skins or furs') — Louisiana Legislature
  • La. R.S. 56:262, Nongame quadrupeds; breeding, propagation, and exhibition (license for 'imported or native nongame quadrupeds'; breeder $50, exhibitor $20) — Louisiana Legislature
  • LDWF Nongame Quadruped Exhibitor and Breeder Licenses (covers alligators/coyotes/foxes only; 'will not be issued for pets or the pet trade') — Louisiana Dept of Wildlife & Fisheries
  • La. R.S. 56:171, Wildlife; business of raising and selling; breeder's license (wild game quadrupeds/birds; deer, squirrels, rabbits, game birds) — Louisiana Legislature (via Justia)
  • La. R.S. 56:20, Releasing game, fowl, or fish; no pen-raised or wild animal liberated within the state without the secretary's written permission (class four violation, R.S. 56:34) — Louisiana Legislature
  • Louisiana SPCA Animal Control FAQs (Orleans Parish 'wild or exotic animal' rule, exempting captive-bred 'laboratory rats... which have never known the wild, and pocket pets or rodents including, but not limited to, hamsters, gerbils, guinea pigs, chinchillas, sugar gliders or hedgehogs') — Louisiana SPCA (Orleans Parish animal control)
  • LAC 7:XXI, Animals and Animal Health (interstate import health requirements; CVI + rabies for dogs/cats; no pet-rodent rule) — Louisiana Dept of Agriculture & Forestry (via Cornell LII)
  • USDA APHIS Animal Welfare Act retail pet store / licensing exemption (9 CFR 1.1 'retail pet store' definition and 2.1 exemption list both include rats; direct retail sale not USDA-licensed) — USDA APHIS (Federal Register)
  • CDC, Bringing an Animal into the U.S. / African rodent importation ban (42 CFR 71.56; covers only rodents of African origin or African native habitat, not Asian-origin R. rattus) — U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Massachusetts? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Massachusetts

Summary. Massachusetts is a strict 'prohibited-unless-listed' state — and the roof rat is NOT on the list. Its exemption list (321 CMR 9.01) and domestic-animals list (321 CMR 9.02) name only the Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus) and its laboratory strains — Rattus rattus appears nowhere. So a roof rat is treated as a non-listed undomesticated mammal that may not be kept without a MassWildlife permit, and MassWildlife states it 'will not be issued a permit for keeping a wild animal as a pet.' The result: keeping, breeding, selling, and importing a roof rat are effectively prohibited here — purely because the species isn't named, while its near-twin the fancy rat is. A textbook 'species-not-domestication' gap and a prime advocacy target.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Massachusetts-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Massachusetts is silent. See United States.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Massachusetts Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (MassWildlife), written reply June 2026: confirmed that roof rats (Rattus rattus) are not a legal pet in Massachusetts, and directed us to the state's published 'Wildlife as pets' guidance. This confirms there is no general pet-keeping pathway for R. rattus in Massachusetts — even though its near-twin the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is exempt and fully legal. The barrier is that the species is simply absent from the state's exemption list, not a finding that domesticated roof rats are dangerous.
  • Massachusetts Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (MassWildlife), follow-up reply June 2026: confirmed that an educator may apply for a permit to possess roof rats, and provided the possession/importation application form. So while roof rats are not a general legal pet in Massachusetts, a documented educational or scientific keeper can apply to MassWildlife for a possession permit.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

R. rattus is not on the 321 CMR 9.01 exemption list nor the 321 CMR 9.02 domestic-animals list (both name only the Norway rat / laboratory rat derived from R. norvegicus). As a non-listed undomesticated mammal it may not be possessed without a MassWildlife license under M.G.L. c.131 §23 — and MassWildlife's own guidance states no permit is issued for keeping a wild animal as a pet, so there is no lawful pet pathway. Refined (assume-a-pathway re-audit): R. rattus isn't on the 321 CMR 9.01(12) exempt list (only R. norvegicus is), so possession needs a MassWildlife license under MGL c.131 §23 / 321 CMR 2.12 — BUT 2.12 requires DENIAL of applications to keep a wild animal 'as a pet' (MassWildlife: 'you will not be issued a permit for keeping a wild animal as a pet'). No private pet pathway; only a scientific/educational/commercial-propagator license (institutional). = restricted, not flat-prohibited. The operative trigger confirmed by Gemini DR (2026-06-10) is 321 CMR 9.02(2)(c): any vertebrate taxon not listed 'shall be presumed to be wild and shall be subject to the provisions of M.G.L. c. 131,' which is what subjects an unlisted R. rattus to the §23 licensing regime.

Sources: MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), Massachusetts General Court, MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife, MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Breeding an unlisted wild mammal requires a Class 4 Propagator's License under M.G.L. c.131 §23 / 321 CMR 2.12, which authorizes a holder to possess, maintain, propagate, buy, sell, or dispose of specified mammals — but acquisition is gated by an exhaustive application (scale diagrams/photos of enclosures, a written disposition plan and justification, documentary proof of professional husbandry qualifications, and a liability/inspection agreement). Critically, 321 CMR 2.12(9) MANDATES denial of any application to 'possess, maintain, propagate, or cultivate animals as pets,' or where the intent is 'purely on curiosity, impulse, novelty, or to provide personal amusement or entertainment.' There is therefore no hobby/small-breeder threshold: a Class 4 license for R. rattus is only structurally available for a certified non-pet purpose — scientific (recognized institution), educational (recognized institution), or commercial propagation for the agricultural/laboratory supply chain divorced from the pet trade. R. norvegicus needs none of this because it is exempt/domestic. Hobby/pet breeding is barred.

Sources: Massachusetts General Court, MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Commercial sale, offer for sale, barter, or transfer of a presumed-wild mammal requires a Class 6 Dealer's License or a Class 4 Propagator's License under 321 CMR 2.12(3) / M.G.L. c.131 §23. Because R. rattus is unlisted, the 'without a permit' privilege in 321 CMR 9.01 does not reach it. A second, independent barrier blocks the retail pet channel: under 330 CMR 12.00 (Licensing and Operation of Pet Shops), a licensed pet shop may sell only an 'Animal,' defined as a species that may be kept without a MassWildlife permit per 321 CMR 9.01/9.02 — so the roof rat falls outside what any pet shop may lawfully sell. The result is a closed regulatory loop: a Class 4/Class 6 holder may transfer R. rattus only to another permitted person or institution, permanently sequestering the species from public pet ownership. Private give-away/sale of a pet roof rat is not authorized; only a licensed non-pet dealer/propagator transfer is structurally possible.

Sources: Massachusetts General Court, MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Dept of Agricultural Resources (via Animal Legal & Historical Center)

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Cross-border movement of R. rattus is treated as importation of 'wildlife' under 321 CMR 2.15 regardless of captive-bred origin. No person may import a live mammal without an Importation Permit from the Director (321 CMR 2.15(2)); the application must be filed at least ten days in advance with the originating/destination facility details and a signed certification that the export is lawful in the origin jurisdiction, and the Director may deny under 321 CMR 2.15(10) where importation is 'detrimental to the fish and wildlife resources of Massachusetts... and is not in the public interest' (a real risk given the roof rat's invasive-pest reputation), and may require zoonotic-disease/parasite health certificates; illegal or diseased imports may be seized and humanely destroyed (321 CMR 2.15(22)). Once lawfully in-state under permit, transport is allowed only with the permit accompanying the animal and subject to Director-imposed caging/safety conditions. Liberation is ABSOLUTELY barred — never release; release of a non-native presumed-wild rodent is a serious violation. So transport is permit-gated and restricted, not unregulated. (The MDAR animal-health/CVI layer is secondary to the wildlife-import permit.)

Sources: Massachusetts General Court, MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), MA Dept of Agricultural Resources (via Cornell LII)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Because R. rattus is not on the Massachusetts exempt/domestic lists, there is no lawful way to keep it as a pet here — MassWildlife does not issue pet-keeping permits for wildlife. If you have a roof rat and move to Massachusetts, you cannot bring it; rehome it responsibly first. (The fancy rat, R. norvegicus, IS exempt and legal.)
  • Do not bring a roof rat into Massachusetts
  • If advocating: petition MassWildlife to add captive-bred R. rattus to the 321 CMR 9.02 / 9.01 lists

Where: Massachusetts Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (MassWildlife)

Source: MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife, MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Massachusetts. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Massachusetts

Massachusetts uses a "prohibited-unless-listed" system for keeping animals. The state's exemption list (321 CMR 9.01) and its domestic-animals list (321 CMR 9.02) name only the Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus) and the laboratory/fancy rat strains derived from it. The roof rat (Rattus rattus, also called the black rat) is not named on either list. The operative trigger is 321 CMR 9.02(2)(c): 'Any vertebrate taxa not listed in 321 CMR 9.02 shall be presumed to be wild and shall be subject to the provisions of M.G.L. c. 131.' The state therefore treats a roof rat as a non-listed wild mammal that cannot be kept without a MassWildlife license, and MassWildlife's guidance says it will not issue a permit to keep a wild animal as a pet. The practical result is that a tame, captive-bred roof rat is off-limits in Massachusetts because the species name is missing from a list, while its near-identical cousin the fancy rat is fully legal. This is a species-not-domestication gap, not a judgment that domesticated roof rats are dangerous or different to care for.

The ask: Ask MassWildlife to add captive-bred Rattus rattus to the 321 CMR 9.01 exemption list (subsection (12), List of Mammals) and/or the 321 CMR 9.02 domestic-animals list, the same regulatory route already used for the Norway rat / fancy rat. The controlling statute, M.G.L. c. 131 §23, lets the Director amend the list after a public hearing using four criteria. A domesticated, indoor-kept, captive-bred roof rat line appears to satisfy all four, and the Director is asked to weigh it against them: the roof rat is already established in the region, so an escaped tame animal adds little new ecological risk; it is no more dangerous or demanding to keep than the fancy rat the list already allows; and trade in a captive-bred line has little bearing on wild populations. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat (R. norvegicus), domesticated only in the 19th century (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/), so a captive-bred R. rattus is the same case one species over. Whether the four criteria are met is the Director's judgment after a public hearing; the request is only that the question be evaluated. This can be raised informally by email, or formally as a petition for rulemaking under G.L. c. 30A §4 directed to the Director of the Division of Fisheries & Wildlife and the Fisheries and Wildlife Board (Permit Section, 100 Cambridge Street, 6th Floor, Boston, MA 02114).

Where the lever really is: This is an agency lever, not a legislative one. The barrier is a regulation the agency itself writes and controls: the exemption list lives in 321 CMR 9.01, a MassWildlife regulation, and the enabling statute M.G.L. c. 131 §23 authorizes the Director of the Division of Fisheries & Wildlife to alter that list after a public hearing, applying four statutory criteria (no ecological harm from escape, no danger to people, care no harder than a common domestic animal, no impact on wild populations). The roof rat's absence is a gap: the species was never added. The agency has both the power and a built-in mechanism to fix it. The Norway rat / fancy rat got onto the list the same way, and sugar gliders, the four-toed hedgehog, and several chameleons and skinks were all later added to 321 CMR 9.01 through this process. The right move is to ask MassWildlife to add captive-bred R. rattus, either informally by writing to the Division or formally by filing a petition for rulemaking under the Massachusetts Administrative Procedure Act (G.L. c. 30A §4), which gives any interested person the right to ask an agency to amend a regulation and obliges the agency to consider it. The procedural path after a meritorious petition is: agency scientific review, then a public hearing noticed at least 21 days in advance in the Massachusetts Register, then a written comment period, then a Small Business Impact Statement, then a Fisheries and Wildlife Board vote, then final promulgation with the Secretary of the Commonwealth. A legislative bill is not the primary path here, because no statute names or bans the roof rat; the gap is administrative. If the species had been written into a statute by name, appealing to the agency would be pointless and the legislature would be needed, but that is not the situation in Massachusetts.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Massachusetts Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (MassWildlife) (executive / agency) — Mass.Wildlife@mass.gov
    MassWildlife writes and maintains the 321 CMR 9.01 exemption list and the 9.02 domestic-animals list, and under M.G.L. c. 131 §23 its Director can add a species to that list after a public hearing. This is the office with the actual power to fix the gap. Mass.Wildlife@mass.gov is the agency's official general inbox (verified on mass.gov); start here to ask for clarification and to request that captive-bred Rattus rattus be added, the same way Rattus norvegicus already is.
  • MassWildlife — formal Petition for Rulemaking under G.L. c. 30A §4 (public comment) — Mass.Wildlife@mass.gov
    If an informal request stalls, the Massachusetts Administrative Procedure Act (G.L. c. 30A §4) gives any interested person the right to file a written petition asking an agency to amend a regulation, and the agency must consider it. A petition to add captive-bred R. rattus to 321 CMR 9.01(12) forces the Division to formally consider the request and respond, and any list change triggers the public hearing required by M.G.L. c. 131 §23 — your chance to make the case on the record. Route the written petition to the Director of the Division of Fisheries & Wildlife and the Fisheries and Wildlife Board via the Permit Section, MassWildlife, 100 Cambridge Street, 6th Floor, Boston, MA 02114 (and copy the official Mass.Wildlife@mass.gov inbox). Board communications can also be addressed to the Chairman, Fisheries and Wildlife Board, 1 Rabbit Hill Road, Westborough, MA 01581.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Massachusetts Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (Director and Permit Section),

I am writing about a gap in the exemption list at 321 CMR 9.01. That list, and the domestic-animals list at 321 CMR 9.02, name the Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus) and its laboratory and fancy strains, but they do not name the roof rat (Rattus rattus, the black rat). Under 321 CMR 9.02(2)(c) any taxon not listed 'shall be presumed to be wild,' so because of that omission a tame, captive-bred roof rat cannot be kept in Massachusetts, even though its near-identical cousin the fancy rat is fully legal.

These are domesticated, captive-bred animals: selectively bred for tameness, kept entirely indoors as pets, and never released. They are not wild-caught and are no more demanding to care for than any common pet rodent.

I respectfully ask the Division to add captive-bred Rattus rattus to the 321 CMR 9.01 exemption list (subsection (12), List of Mammals) and/or the 9.02 domestic-animals list, the same route already used for the Norway rat and, more recently, for sugar gliders, the four-toed hedgehog, and several chameleons and skinks. Under M.G.L. c. 131 §23, a captive-bred domestic line appears to meet all four statutory criteria: (1) accidental release is unlikely to adversely affect the ecology of the Commonwealth, because the roof rat is already established in the region and a tame, captive-bred animal is poorly suited to surviving unaided; (2) the animal in captivity or escaped poses little danger to people by injury or disease; (3) its care is no more demanding in any major respect than common domestic animals; and (4) trade in a captive-bred line is unlikely to significantly affect wild populations. Whether these criteria are met is the Director's determination after a public hearing. I am asking that the question be evaluated, not assuming its outcome.

Please tell me the administrative procedure, designated recipient, and expected timeline for docketing such a request, and whether I should submit it as a formal petition for rulemaking under G.L. c. 30A §4 for a Fisheries and Wildlife Board hearing. I would also welcome the Division's view on whether the presumption of wildness under 321 CMR 9.02(2)(c) is rebuttable on a showing of domestication, or whether a full rulemaking is the only remedy. Thank you for your time.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your town]
[Your email]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • 321 CMR 9.01 — Exemption List (names only Norway Rat / R. norvegicus among rats; R. rattus absent) — MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)
  • 321 CMR 9.02 — List of Domestic Animals (laboratory rat derived from R. norvegicus only; 9.02(2)(c) presumes unlisted taxa wild) — MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)
  • M.G.L. c.131 §23 — propagation/dealing licenses; possession of undomesticated mammals; special exemption list + four criteria; alterable by Director after public hearing — Massachusetts General Court
  • G.L. c. 30A §4 — Administrative Procedure Act: any interested person may petition an agency to adopt, amend, or repeal a regulation — Massachusetts General Court
  • 321 CMR 2.12 — Artificial Propagation (Class 4 Propagator's / Class 6 Dealer's Licenses; 2.12(9) mandatory denial for pet/novelty purposes) — MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)
  • 321 CMR 2.15 — Importation, Liberation, and Transportation (2.15(2) import permit ≥10 days, 2.15(10) discretionary denial, 2.15(22) seizure; absolute liberation ban) — MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)
  • MassWildlife — Wildlife as pets ('will not be issued a permit... as a pet') — MA Division of Fisheries & Wildlife
  • 330 CMR 12.00 — Licensing and Operation of Pet Shops (sellable 'Animal' limited to species kept without a MassWildlife permit per 321 CMR 9.01/9.02) — MA Dept of Agricultural Resources (via Animal Legal & Historical Center)
  • 330 CMR 30.08 — Imported Animals (OCVI requirement) — MA Dept of Agricultural Resources (via Cornell LII)

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Maryland? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Maryland

Summary. Keeping, breeding, and selling a domesticated roof rat is legal in Maryland with no state permit. Maryland's 'dangerous animal' ban (Md. Criminal Law §10-621) lists big cats, bears, primates, and the like — no rodents — and the wildlife regulation (COMAR 08.03.09.03) expressly exempts 'domesticated rats and mice' from any import or possession restriction. No rodent-specific import certificate is mandated (Maryland's CVI/rabies rules cover only livestock, poultry, and dogs/cats/ferrets), though obtaining a general interstate CVI before importing is prudent and worth confirming with the State Veterinarian.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Maryland-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Maryland is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Md. Criminal Law §10-621(b)(1) lists the live animals a person may not possess, and no rodent appears on it. DNR's possession regulation COMAR 08.03.09.03(C) affirmatively states it does not prohibit possession of 'domesticated rats and mice,' which covers a captive-bred domesticated roof rat. No DNR captive-wildlife permit applies to domesticated rodents. Gemini DR-verified: rodents aren't in MD's dangerous-exotic ban (Crim. Law sec.10-621), but COMAR 08.03.09 requires a permit for 'live wildlife' with an exemption for 'domestic rats' that ISN'T taxonomically defined -- so whether captive-bred R. rattus qualifies (vs only R. norvegicus) is genuinely ambiguous and open to DNR officer interpretation.

Sources: Md. Code (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center), Maryland DNR (Division of State Documents)

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

§10-621 prohibits 'breed' only for the enumerated dangerous species; rodents are not enumerated. COMAR 08.03.09.03(C) exempts domesticated rats and mice from import/possession restrictions, and no DNR breeder license reaches domesticated rodents. (Federal USDA/AWA dealer licensing is a separate matter triggered only by commercial wholesale/sight-unseen thresholds — see United States.) Gemini DR-verified: private hobby breeding isn't state-regulated (game husbandry licenses cover game birds/mammals, not non-game rodents); county zoning/kennel/pet-shop rules are the layer.

Sources: Md. Code (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center), Maryland DNR (Division of State Documents)

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

§10-621 bars offering for sale/trade/barter/exchange only for the listed dangerous animals; rodents are not listed. DNR's sale/transfer rules apply to permit-acquired and native/regulated wildlife, not to captive-bred domesticated rodents exempted by COMAR 08.03.09.03(C). No Maryland state pet-dealer license is required for private rodent transfers. Gemini DR-verified: the state doesn't regulate rodent sales (the retail-sale ban targets dogs/cats); a LOCAL 'Commercial Animal Establishment' license is required and varies by county.

Sources: Md. Code (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center), Maryland DNR (Division of State Documents)

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

In-state transport of a domesticated rat is unregulated. For IMPORT, Maryland's rabies-import rule (COMAR 10.06.02.11) applies to dogs/cats/ferrets only, and MDA's admission rules require a CVI for livestock/poultry/dogs/cats/ferrets — there is no pet-rodent category. So no rodent-specific CVI is mandated, but a general interstate CVI is the customary document for any animal crossing state lines (note: since 2019 Maryland no longer accepts the federal APHIS 7001 'small animal' form), so confirm with MDA Animal Health before importing. Gemini DR-verified: importing any companion rodent needs an Interstate CVI issued within 30 days before entry (COMAR 15.14.05.01); private-traveler enforcement is historically lax but the ICVI is mandated.

Sources: Maryland Dept of Health (Division of State Documents), Maryland Dept of Agriculture — Animal Health Program, Maryland DNR (Division of State Documents)

Restrictions & responsibilities

No rodent-specific import certificate is required (Maryland's CVI/rabies rules cover only livestock, poultry, dogs/cats/ferrets), but a general interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection is the customary travel document — confirm with MDA Animal Health before importing a pet rat. Maryland no longer accepts the APHIS 7001 small-animal form (use an approved CVI form).
  • Confirm CVI expectations with MDA Animal Health before interstate movement

Where: Maryland Dept of Agriculture — Animal Health Program

Source: Maryland Dept of Agriculture — Animal Health Program

Never release a roof rat — it is a non-native species; rehome responsibly.

Source: Maryland DNR (Division of State Documents)

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Official sources

  • Md. Code, Criminal Law §10-621 — Dangerous-animal import/possession ban (no rodents listed) — Md. Code (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center)
  • COMAR 08.03.09.03 — exempts 'domesticated rats and mice' from import/possession prohibition — Maryland DNR (Division of State Documents)
  • COMAR 10.06.02.11 — Importation of Animals (rabies import certificate; dogs/cats/ferrets) — Maryland Dept of Health (Division of State Documents)
  • MDA Health Requirements Governing the Admission of Animals (CVI scope by species) — Maryland Dept of Agriculture — Animal Health Program

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.
