item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Maine? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Maine

Summary. Maine is a clear 'no' for the roof rat as the rule reads today, and the reason is one missing name on a list. The Department of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife (MDIFW) sorts every captive mammal into five buckets under 12 M.R.S. ch. 723 and 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7: Unrestricted, Restricted Category 1, Restricted Category 2, Prohibited, and Unclassified. The Unrestricted Species List names 'Brown Rat - Rattus norvegicus' (the fancy rat) and 'House Mouse - Mus musculus' by exact binomial, but it does not name Rattus rattus. A species that is not on the Unrestricted, Restricted, or Prohibited list is 'Unclassified,' and 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(4) states that 'A person may not possess any species that has not been categorized' and that an unclassified species 'will not be eligible for a permit under this chapter.' So the roof rat is not merely restricted-with-a-permit (as preliminary research assumed) and it is not on the named Prohibited list either; it sits in the Unclassified gap, which functions as a flat ban because no permit can be issued for it. Maine's 'wild animal' definition (12 M.R.S. Sec. 10001(69)) reaches a species 'wild by nature, whether or not bred or reared in captivity,' so a captive-bred, hand-tame roof rat is still treated as wildlife. There IS a pathway, but it is a list-fix, not a pet permit: Sec. 7.06(5) lets a person petition the MDIFW Captive Wildlife Technical Committee and Commissioner to categorize the species (ideally onto the Unrestricted List beside the fancy rat). Until that succeeds, keeping, breeding, selling/giving, and importing a roof rat are all prohibited. The fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is freely legal with no permit. Federal law adds a thin layer for movement/commerce: USFWS treats R. rattus as 'wildlife,' the USDA Animal Welfare Act licenses only wholesale/sight-unseen dealers (hobby and direct-to-consumer sales are exempt; lab rats of genus Rattus are excluded entirely), and the CDC bars rodents of African origin (not relevant to R. rattus, which is Asian in origin). Never release a roof rat.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Maine-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Maine is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

MDIFW's Unrestricted Species List names 'Brown Rat - Rattus norvegicus' and 'House Mouse - Mus musculus' by binomial but does NOT name Rattus rattus, and R. rattus is not on the Prohibited list either. Under the five-tier scheme it is therefore 'Unclassified,' and 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(4) provides verbatim: 'A person may not possess any species that has not been categorized. Any species which has not been identified as a Prohibited, Restricted, or Unrestricted species will not be eligible for a permit under this chapter.' So possession is unlawful AND no permit can be issued. The 'wild animal' definition (12 M.R.S. Sec. 10001(69): 'wild by nature, whether or not bred or reared in captivity, as distinguished from the common domestic animals') keeps a captive-bred, tame roof rat within MDIFW wildlife jurisdiction rather than treating it as a common domestic animal. The only lawful route to possession is to first petition MDIFW under Sec. 7.06(5) to categorize the species (best case onto the Unrestricted List beside the fancy rat).

Sources: Maine Legislature, Maine Legislature, Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife (via Cornell Legal Information Institute), Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Breeding (propagation) requires lawful possession plus a propagation permit, and an unclassified species is both barred from possession and ineligible for any permit under 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(4). Because R. rattus is unclassified, there is no lawful animal to breed and no propagation permit available, so breeding is prohibited. Even the simpler commercial pathway runs through the same gate: under Sec. 7.06(1) only species on the Unrestricted List may be traded by commercial pet shops, and a DACF commercial breeder/dealer or pet-shop license (7 M.R.S. ch. 739) does not override MDIFW species classification. Federal note: the USDA Animal Welfare Act licenses only wholesale/sight-unseen dealers (hobby and direct-to-consumer sales are exempt; rats of genus Rattus bred for research are excluded from the AWA), but that federal layer cannot make a state-prohibited species lawful to breed in Maine.

Sources: Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife (via Cornell Legal Information Institute), Maine Dept of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry (DACF), USDA APHIS

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Selling, bartering, or giving away a roof rat in Maine is barred by the same unclassified-species rule. 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(1) limits commercial pet shops and dealers to species on the Unrestricted List, and R. rattus is not on it; Sec. 7.06(4) makes possession of an unclassified species unlawful for any party, so neither a seller nor a private recipient can lawfully hold the animal. Unlike a state where only the commercial 'sale' is regulated, here the underlying possession is itself unlawful, so even a free transfer or adoption is prohibited because the recipient cannot lawfully possess the rat. (Were the species ever categorized as Restricted, an interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection within 30 days would attach to any transfer that involves moving the animal, but that condition is moot while possession is barred.)

Sources: Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife (via Cornell Legal Information Institute), Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, Maine Dept of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry (DACF)

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Importing or transporting a roof rat into or within Maine is unlawful while the species is unclassified. 12 M.R.S. Sec. 12152(1-A) provides that 'a person may not import wildlife into or possess wildlife in the State or receive or possess wildlife imported into the State' without a permit, and an unclassified species cannot obtain that permit (09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(4)). MDIFW expressly warns residents not to assume animals legally for sale in adjacent states or online are lawful to bring into Maine. If the species were ever categorized as Restricted, importation would then require a Wildlife Importation Permit (Category 2: $100 application + $27 permit) plus an interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) dated within 30 days, and a Category 2 possession permit ($27 + $27, valid two years) with a one-year-husbandry / 100-hours-experience requirement and Care-and-Housing standards (Sec. 7.17). Penalty for unlawful import/possession: each day is a separate Class E crime carrying a minimum fine of $50 plus an amount equal to twice the applicable permit fee (Sec. 12152(1-A)). Federal layer: USFWS treats R. rattus as 'wildlife,' and the CDC bars rodents of African origin (R. rattus is Asian in origin, so the CDC African-rodent bar does not apply). Never release a roof rat.

Sources: Maine Legislature, Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife (via Cornell Legal Information Institute), Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife (via Cornell Legal Information Institute), Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, USDA APHIS / CDC

Restrictions & responsibilities

Default ban via the 'Unclassified Species' rule. Because R. rattus is on none of MDIFW's lists, 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(4) makes it unlawful to possess and ineligible for any wildlife permit. There is no pet-permit application a keeper can file today; the only lawful route is to first get the species categorized (next entry). Unlawful possession/import is a Class E crime, each day a separate offense, minimum $50/day plus twice the applicable permit fee (12 M.R.S. Sec. 12152(1-A)).
  • Understand that no possession or import permit can be issued for R. rattus while it is unclassified.
  • Do not acquire or import a roof rat into Maine until the species is categorized; doing so is a per-day Class E crime and the animal can be confiscated.
  • Check local county/municipal ordinances as well; towns may further restrict animal keeping even if the species is later categorized.

Where: Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife (MDIFW), Wildlife Division

Source: Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife (via Cornell Legal Information Institute), Maine Legislature

Categorization petition (the only pathway). 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(5) lets a person petition MDIFW to review and categorize an unclassified species. The request is made on Department forms, the applicant bears the burden of proof, the Captive Wildlife Technical Committee evaluates it against the Sec. 7.06(3) criteria, and the Commissioner decides. Best outcome is adding captive-bred R. rattus to the Unrestricted List beside the fancy rat; a plausible conservative outcome is a Category 2 Restricted placement (then a Category 2 possession permit becomes available). Only after a successful categorization can any possession/import permit be sought.
  • Request the 'Request to Review or Change the Categorization of a Species' application form from the MDIFW Wildlife Division (info.ifw@maine.gov or by mail).
  • Compile biological, ecological, and husbandry evidence supporting the requested category (you bear the burden of proof under Sec. 7.06(5)).
  • Mail the completed application to: Wildlife Division, Inland Fisheries & Wildlife, 353 Water Street, Augusta, ME 04330.
  • If categorized as Category 2 Restricted, then apply for a Wildlife General Possession Permit (Cat 2) and, for any import, a Wildlife Importation Permit (Cat 2) plus a CVI dated within 30 days.

Forms: MDIFW Fish and Wildlife in Captivity (Species Categorization Requests + forms), Wildlife General Possession Permit Application - Category 2 Restricted Species ($27 application + $27 permit; one-year husbandry / 100-hours experience; CVI within 30 days), Wildlife Importation Permit Application - Category 2 Restricted Species ($100 application + $27 permit) · Where: Wildlife Division, Inland Fisheries & Wildlife, 353 Water Street, Augusta, ME 04330 (categorization request); fees payable to 'Treasurer, State of Maine'. · Fees: Categorization request: no fee stated on the captivity page. Post-categorization Category 2 possession permit: $27 application + $27 permit (valid two years). Category 2 importation permit: $100 application + $27 permit.

Source: Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife (via Cornell Legal Information Institute), Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife

Interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI). This would apply only IF the species were categorized as Restricted and an import permit issued: 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.11(1)C and the Cat 2 import/possession forms require an interstate health certificate / CVI issued by a veterinarian licensed in the state of origin, dated within 30 days of taking possession, with disease test results approved by the Maine DACF and DHHS. It is moot while the species is unclassified and possession is barred.
  • Applies only after a successful categorization to Restricted and issuance of a Category 2 import permit.
  • Then: obtain a CVI from a veterinarian licensed in the origin state, dated within 30 days of taking possession, including required disease statements.

Forms: Wildlife Importation Permit Application - Category 2 Restricted Species (CVI requirement on the instructions page) · Where: CVI issued by a veterinarian licensed in the state of origin; filed with the MDIFW import permit. Maine DACF / DHHS approve required disease statements. · Fees: No state fee for the CVI; the issuing veterinarian charges an examination/paperwork fee.

Source: Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife (via Cornell Legal Information Institute), Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife

Never release a roof rat into the wild. R. rattus is treated as an invasive species and disease vector in Maine (DACF pest/pesticide materials list 'Roof rat (Rattus rattus)' as a target pest), and releasing captive wildlife is unlawful. Rehome responsibly. Local county/municipal ordinances can further restrict animal keeping.

Source: Maine Dept of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry (DACF)

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Maine. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Maine

Maine sorts every captive mammal into five tiers under 12 M.R.S. ch. 723 and the MDIFW "Wildlife in Captivity" rules (09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7): Unrestricted, Restricted Category 1, Restricted Category 2, Prohibited, and Unclassified. The state's Unrestricted Species List names "Brown Rat - Rattus norvegicus," the domestic fancy rat sold in pet shops, and "House Mouse - Mus musculus," but it does not name "Rattus rattus," the domestic roof rat. The roof rat is also not on the named Prohibited list (which targets bears, big cats, wild canids, primates, and a short list of dangerous rodents). Because it is on no list, it is "Unclassified," and the rule (09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(4)) says "A person may not possess any species that has not been categorized" and that such a species "will not be eligible for a permit under this chapter." So a captive-bred, hand-tame pet roof rat is banned by default, and no permit can even be issued for it, while the fancy rat one species over is freely legal with no permit at all. This is not a behavioral or safety judgment about the animal; it is a gap in a list. The fancy rat already on the list is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated in the 19th century, and a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over.

The ask: Ask MDIFW to use its species-categorization process (09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06(5)) to add captive-bred domestic roof rats ("Rattus rattus") to the Unrestricted Species List, alongside the domestic Norway/fancy rat ("Rattus norvegicus") and the house mouse already on it, and in the meantime to provide a written determination of how the Department currently classifies Rattus rattus so keepers know where they stand. If the obstacle is the statute's "wild by nature" language (12 M.R.S. Sec. 10001(69)), the relevant question is domestication, not wild ancestry: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet Maine recognizes both as common domestic animals because what makes an animal domestic is generations bred for tameness, not the wild origin of its species. The fancy rat already on the list is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated in the 19th century (https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/), and a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense, one species over. Whether a captive-bred Rattus rattus is domesticated in the same sense as the fancy rat already on the list is a question for the Department to decide; the petitioner is not asking it to assume any particular answer.

Where the lever really is: This is an AGENCY problem, not a legislative one; the lever is MDIFW, not the Legislature. No Maine statute names, bans, or singles out the roof rat. The species is simply absent from the Unrestricted Species List that MDIFW creates and amends under 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, and the five-tier framework (12 M.R.S. ch. 723) delegates the species sorting to the Department. The Department has exercised that power before and maintains a standing process for it: Sec. 7.06(5) provides for a written "Request to Review or Change the Categorization of a Species," evaluated by the Captive Wildlife Technical Committee against the criteria in Sec. 7.06(3), with the Commissioner making the final decision. So the body that created the gap can close it administratively, no bill required. The petitioner should be candid that the outcome is not assured: the same Sec. 7.06(3) criteria weigh whether the species could survive in the Maine wild and whether it harbors agents harmful to people, livestock, or native wildlife, and Maine's DACF pest and pesticide materials describe the roof rat as an invasive disease vector. A realistic ask therefore offers MDIFW two acceptable outcomes: best case, add captive-bred R. rattus to the Unrestricted List beside the fancy rat; failing that, categorize it as a Restricted (Category 2) species so that a permitted pathway at least exists rather than a flat Unclassified ban. The Legislature is a fallback only if MDIFW declines both and a keeper wants parity codified.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Maine Department of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife (MDIFW) - Wildlife Division (Captive Wildlife) (executive / agency) — info.ifw@maine.gov
    MDIFW owns and amends the Unrestricted Species List and runs the Sec. 7.06(5) categorization-review process. Its 'Fish and Wildlife in Captivity' page describes the five tiers (including the 'Unclassified' category) and the 'Species Categorization Requests' process, with requests mailed to the Wildlife Division, Inland Fisheries & Wildlife, 353 Water Street, Augusta, ME 04330. This is the office that can actually fix the gap, by adding R. rattus to the Unrestricted List or by categorizing it into a Restricted tier so a permit becomes possible. Ask here for the categorization-request forms and for a written determination of how R. rattus is currently classified. General inbox info.ifw@maine.gov is confirmed on the official MDIFW contact page.
  • Maine State Legislature - Contact Your Legislator (House & Senate) (legislature) — official contact page
    FALLBACK ONLY, not the primary lever. No Maine statute names or bans the roof rat, so a bill is not needed to change an agency-maintained list; the cleanest path is the MDIFW categorization request. Use this only if MDIFW declines both to add R. rattus to the Unrestricted List and to categorize it into a permitted Restricted tier, and a keeper wants the fancy-rat/roof-rat parity codified or wants a legislator to ask the Department to act. Official 'find and contact your legislator' page for both chambers.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To: Maine Department of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife, Wildlife Division (Captive Wildlife)
Re: Request to categorize the captive-bred domestic roof rat (Rattus rattus), ideally onto the Unrestricted Species List

Dear MDIFW Wildlife Division,

I am writing about a gap in the Unrestricted Species List under 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7. The list names "Brown Rat - Rattus norvegicus," the domestic fancy rat sold in pet shops, and "House Mouse - Mus musculus," but it does not name "Rattus rattus," the domestic roof rat. Because the roof rat is on no list, I understand it is treated as an "Unclassified" species, which Sec. 7.06(4) says a person may not possess and which is not eligible for any permit. The fancy rat one species over is freely legal. The roof rats I am writing about are bred in captivity for generations, gentle, kept entirely indoors as family pets, and never released to the wild. They are kept no differently from the fancy rat.

This is a distinction based on which species name is on a list, not on how the animal lives or any risk it poses. If the concern is the statute's "wild by nature" language (12 M.R.S. Sec. 10001(69)), the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet Maine recognizes both as common domestic animals, because what makes an animal domestic is generations bred for tameness, not the wild origin of its species. The fancy rat already on your list is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated in the 19th century. I ask the Department to consider whether a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense as the fancy rat already on the list; I am not asking it to assume any particular answer.

Using the species-categorization process at Sec. 7.06(5), I respectfully request that the Department add captive-bred domestic roof rats ("Rattus rattus") to the Unrestricted Species List, parallel to the domestic Norway rat and house mouse already on it. If the Department concludes that some oversight is warranted, I would ask in the alternative that it categorize the captive-bred roof rat as a Restricted (Category 2) species, so that at least a permitted pathway exists rather than a flat Unclassified ban. Please also let me know the application forms required to initiate this review, and provide a written determination of how the Department currently classifies Rattus rattus, so keepers know where they stand in the meantime.

Thank you for your time and for maintaining these lists.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your town, Maine]
[Your email / phone]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • 12 M.R.S. Sec. 12152 - Permit to possess wildlife in captivity (Sec. 12152(1-A): 'a person may not import wildlife into or possess wildlife in the State or receive or possess wildlife imported into the State' without a permit; each day a separate Class E crime, minimum fine $50 plus twice the applicable permit fee) — Maine Legislature
  • 12 M.R.S. Sec. 10001 - Definitions (Sec. 10001(69) 'Wild animal' = 'a species of mammal, wild by nature, whether or not bred or reared in captivity, as distinguished from the common domestic animals'; Sec. 10001(71) 'Wildlife') — Maine Legislature
  • 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.06 - Classification of Species (Sec. 7.06(1) unrestricted species may be traded by commercial pet shops; Sec. 7.06(4) 'A person may not possess any species that has not been categorized... will not be eligible for a permit under this chapter, however a request may be made to review the categorization of a species subject to section 7.06(5)'; Sec. 7.06(3) categorization criteria; Sec. 7.06(5) petition pathway) — Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife (via Cornell Legal Information Institute)
  • 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7 (full text mirror) - Rules for Importation, Possession, Propagation, Rehabilitation, and Exhibition of Wildlife (confirms Sec. 7.06(4) unclassified language and Sec. 7.06(5) request-to-review verbatim; Sec. 7.11 importation/health certificate; Sec. 7.17 care and housing) — Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center)
  • 09-137 C.M.R. ch. 7, Sec. 7.17 - Care and Housing Requirements (minimum caging/standards for restricted species; the import health certificate/CVI requirement appears at Sec. 7.11(1)C) — Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife (via Cornell Legal Information Institute)
  • MDIFW Unrestricted Species List (PDF) - names 'Brown Rat - Rattus norvegicus' and 'House Mouse - Mus musculus' by binomial; contains NO Rattus rattus / roof rat / black rat / ship rat entry (verified by direct PDF text extraction) — Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife
  • MDIFW Fish and Wildlife in Captivity - describes the five tiers (incl. 'Unclassified'), the 'Species Categorization Requests' process (mail to Wildlife Division, Inland Fisheries & Wildlife, 353 Water Street, Augusta, ME 04330), and the warning not to assume animals legal in other states or online are legal in Maine — Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife
  • Wildlife General Possession Permit Application - Category 2 Restricted Species (PDF): $27 application + $27 permit (two-year term); one-year husbandry or 100 hours experience/training (BS substitutes 50 hours); CVI dated within 30 days of taking possession; mail with fee payable 'Treasurer, State of Maine' — Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife
  • Wildlife Importation Permit Application - Category 2 Restricted Species (PDF): $100 application + $27 permit; interstate CVI / health certificate required (verified by direct PDF text extraction) — Maine Dept of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife
  • State of Maine Animal Welfare Laws and Regulations (DACF Animal Welfare Program, Title 7) - commercial pet-shop/breeder/dealer licensing; a DACF license does not override MDIFW species classification — Maine Dept of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry (DACF)
  • Integrated Pest Management - RATS (DACF) - identifies 'Roof rat (Rattus rattus)' as a target invasive pest and disease vector in Maine (context for the categorization risk and the no-release rule) — Maine Dept of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry (DACF)
  • USDA APHIS Animal Welfare Act licensing - Class A breeder license applies to wholesale/sight-unseen dealers; direct-to-consumer and de minimis hobby sales exempt; rats of genus Rattus bred for research excluded from the AWA — USDA APHIS
  • USDA APHIS / CDC - Bring a Pet Rodent into the United States (federal international-import layer; CDC bars rodents of African origin under 42 CFR 71.56; R. rattus is Asian in origin) — USDA APHIS / CDC

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat, wild animal, wildlife in captivity, unrestricted species, unclassified species, Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI).

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Michigan? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Michigan

Summary. Michigan is a clean 'yes' state for keeping a roof rat, and the law treats it exactly the same as the ordinary fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus). No state rule names Rattus rattus, but every statute that could capture it instead exempts the whole order of rodents or names only other animals. The Pet Shops Act defines a regulated 'animal' as 'a mammal except livestock... and rodents,' so a rodent-only breeder or seller is not a pet shop and needs no MDARD license, inspection, or sale health certificate. The roof rat is not on Michigan's prohibited or restricted invasive-species list under NREPA Part 413 (the only prohibited mammals are nutria and wild/Russian boar), it is not a 'game' species under the exhaustive game list in MCL 324.40103 (so no DNR captive-game permit applies), and the Large Carnivore Act reaches only big cats and bears. Keeping, breeding, and selling or giving one away are therefore lawful and unregulated at the state level, subject only to general animal-cruelty law (MCL 750.50). The one concrete movement requirement is animal-health, not a possession or dealer permit: bringing a roof rat into Michigan from another state requires an official interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) signed by a USDA-accredited veterinarian in the state of origin, and Michigan issues no entry permit for nonnative domestic rodents (so no permit number is needed). Intrastate movement is unregulated. Never release a roof rat into the wild, which is an illegal 'introduction' of a nonnative mammal under NREPA Part 413. Local city, township, or county ordinances on rodent harborage and nuisance can add limits, especially for large indoor colonies.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Michigan-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Michigan is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

No Michigan statute bans or licenses keeping a roof rat, and three separate possession frameworks each exclude it. (1) The Large Carnivore Act (MCL 287.1101 et seq.) bans private possession only of big cats and bears, not small mammals. (2) NREPA Part 413 (MCL 324.41301 et seq.) makes it unlawful to possess a 'prohibited' or 'restricted' species, but the only prohibited mammals are nutria (Myocastor coypus) and wild/Russian boar (Sus scrofa Linnaeus); R. rattus is on neither the prohibited nor the restricted list. (3) DNR captive-wildlife rules reach only 'game,' and MCL 324.40103 defines game through an exhaustive list (the only game rodents are squirrel, muskrat, beaver, and woodchuck), so rats are not game and no captive-game permit applies. The species is also not native or department-introduced wildlife under MCL 324.43508. General animal-cruelty and sanitary-condition law (MCL 750.50) still applies to how the animal is kept.

Sources: Michigan Legislature, Michigan Invasive Species Program (DNR/MDARD/EGLE), Michigan Legislature, Michigan Legislature, Michigan Legislature

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Breeding pet roof rats is unregulated at the state level. Michigan licenses dog breeding (large-scale dog kennels under the Pet Shops Act) but has enacted no parallel rodent-breeder or small-mammal-propagation license. Because R. rattus is not 'game' under MCL 324.40103, the DNR captive-game propagation permit (MCL 324.42703) does not apply, and because it is not a prohibited/restricted species under NREPA Part 413 there is no invasive-species breeding ban. There is no numeric or revenue threshold that turns a rodent hobbyist into a regulated dealer under state law. Federal USDA/AWA licensing can reach a large-scale breeder who ships wholesale or sight-unseen or sells to research, but direct-to-consumer retail sales and de minimis hobby breeding are federally exempt, and rats of the genus Rattus bred for research are excluded from the AWA entirely.

Sources: Michigan Legislature, Michigan Legislature, Michigan Legislature, USDA APHIS

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Selling or giving away a roof rat is unregulated because of an explicit statutory carve-out. The Pet Shops Act (MCL 287.331 et seq.) requires an MDARD license to operate a 'pet shop' (a place where animals are sold, exchanged, or transferred), but MCL 287.331(d) defines the regulated 'animal' as 'a mammal except livestock as defined in 1937 PA 284, MCL 287.121 to MCL 287.131, and rodents.' Because the entire order of rodents is excluded, a person or business that breeds and sells roof rats is not a pet shop, needs no MDARD facility license or inspection, and is not bound by the Act's health-certificate-for-buyers requirement (which applies to dogs, cats, and ferrets). Unlike some states (e.g. Kentucky), Michigan has no intrastate sale CVI rule that reaches rodents, so no health document is required for an in-state sale or gift. Selling a prohibited invasive species would be unlawful under NREPA Part 413, but R. rattus is not on that list. General cruelty law (MCL 750.50) still applies.

Sources: Michigan Legislature, Michigan Legislature

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

No wildlife transport permit applies (R. rattus is not game and not a prohibited/restricted species), but a movement health document does. To import a roof rat into Michigan from another U.S. state, MDARD's published animal-movement policy for 'Other Species (Rabbits, Rodents, Reptiles and Amphibians)' requires that the rodent be accompanied by an official interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) filled out by a USDA-accredited veterinarian in the animal's state of origin. Michigan does not issue an entry permit for nonnative domestic rodents, so no permit number is required on the CVI. Intrastate movement within Michigan is unregulated (no movement document, testing, or waybill). International import is governed by federal CDC/USDA APHIS rules at the port of entry (the CDC bars rodents of African origin). Releasing a roof rat into the wild is prohibited: NREPA Part 413 (MCL 324.41305) bars introducing a nonnative mammal, and MCL 324.41301(1)(f) defines 'introduce' to mean to 'knowingly and willfully stock, place, plant, release, or allow the release of the organism in this state at any specific location where the organism is not already naturalized.'

Sources: Michigan Dept of Agriculture & Rural Development, Michigan Legislature, Michigan Legislature, USDA APHIS / CDC

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing a roof rat into Michigan from another state requires an official interstate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) signed by a USDA-accredited veterinarian in the state of origin. Michigan issues no entry permit for nonnative domestic rodents, so no permit number is needed. This applies on import only, not to keeping, intrastate movement, or an in-state sale or gift.
  • Before bringing the rat into Michigan, have a USDA-accredited veterinarian in the state of origin examine it and issue an official interstate CVI (the rat must be free of visual evidence of communicable disease).
  • Carry the CVI with the animal during transport into Michigan.
  • Do not request an entry permit number; Michigan does not issue one for nonnative domestic rodents.
  • No CVI is required for movement that stays entirely within Michigan.

Forms: MDARD - Other Species (Rabbits, Rodents, Reptiles and Amphibians) import requirements · Where: Issued by a USDA-accredited veterinarian in the state of origin; carried with the animal. Michigan Dept of Agriculture & Rural Development (MDARD), Animal Industry Division, administers the rule. · Fees: No state regulatory fee for the CVI; the issuing veterinarian charges their own examination/paperwork fee.

Source: Michigan Dept of Agriculture & Rural Development

Never release a roof rat into the wild. NREPA Part 413 (MCL 324.41305) bars introducing a nonnative mammal, and MCL 324.41301(1)(f) defines 'introduce' to include releasing or allowing the release of the organism where it is not already naturalized. Rehome responsibly. Local city, township, or county ordinances on rodent harborage and nuisance can add limits, especially for large indoor colonies, so check yours.

Where: Your county/city; MDNR for the no-release rule.

Source: Michigan Legislature

Husbandry is governed by general animal-cruelty law (MCL 750.50), which requires sufficient and proper care, adequate protection from the elements, and 'sanitary conditions' (a space free from health hazards, excessive animal waste, and overcrowding). This applies to any animal owner, including a roof-rat keeper or breeder.

Where: Enforced by local law enforcement / animal control.

Source: Michigan Legislature

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • MCL 287.331 - Pet Shops, Dog Pounds, and Animal Shelters Act, definitions (subsection (d): 'animal means a mammal except livestock as defined in 1937 PA 284, MCL 287.121 to MCL 287.131, and rodents'; subsection defining 'pet shop') — Michigan Legislature
  • MCL 324.41301 et seq. - NREPA Part 413 (Transgenic and Nonnative Organisms): definitions of 'prohibited species,' 'restricted species,' and 'introduce' (MCL 324.41301(1)(f)); no-introduction rule (MCL 324.41305). R. rattus is not listed. — Michigan Legislature
  • Michigan Invasive Species Program - Mammals / Prohibited and Restricted Species (the only prohibited mammals are nutria (Myocastor coypus) and wild/Russian boar (Sus scrofa Linnaeus); Rattus rattus is not prohibited or restricted) — Michigan Invasive Species Program (DNR/MDARD/EGLE)
  • MCL 324.40103 - NREPA definition of 'game' (exhaustive species list; the only game rodents are squirrel, muskrat, beaver, and woodchuck; rats and mice are not game) — Michigan Legislature
  • MCL 287.731 - Animal Industry Act (MDARD authority over importation of animals having potential to spread disease or endanger wildlife/humans; basis for the rodent import CVI rule) — Michigan Legislature
  • MDARD - Other Species (Rabbits, Rodents, Reptiles and Amphibians): import requires an official interstate CVI by a USDA-accredited vet in the state of origin; 'Michigan does not issue entry permits for nonnative domestic... rodents... no permit number is required' — Michigan Dept of Agriculture & Rural Development
  • MCL 750.50 - Michigan Penal Code (animal cruelty; duty of sufficient/proper care, adequate shelter, and 'sanitary conditions') — Michigan Legislature
  • MCL 287.1101 et seq. - Large Carnivore Act (private possession ban covers only big cats and bears, not small mammals) — Michigan Legislature
  • USDA APHIS - Animal Welfare Act licensing (Class A/B dealer license reaches wholesale/sight-unseen dealers; direct-to-consumer retail and de minimis hobby sales exempt; research rats of genus Rattus excluded from the AWA) — USDA APHIS
  • USDA APHIS - Bring a Pet Rodent into the United States (federal international-import rules; CDC bars rodents of African origin) — USDA APHIS / CDC

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat, nonnative domestic rodent, Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI).

Last reviewed 2026-06-14. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Minnesota? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Minnesota

Summary. Minnesota is one of the clearest 'yes' states for the roof rat, because the state names the species by binomial in its most permissive wildlife tier. DNR rule Minn. R. 6216.0270, subpart 4 reads: 'The following mammal is designated as an unregulated nonnative species: rat (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus),' and subpart 1 provides that 'These nonnative species are not subject to regulation under Minnesota Statutes, chapter 84D.' So both the roof rat and the fancy rat sit outside the invasive-species possession, propagation, sale, and transport controls of chapter 84D, with no species trap. The exotic-pet 'regulated animals' law (Minn. Stat. 346.155) reaches only big cats (Felidae), bears, and nonhuman primates, so no rodent needs an exotic-animal permit. Keeping and breeding are unregulated at the state level: the commercial-breeder licensing law (Minn. Stat. 347.57) defines 'animal' as 'a dog or a cat' and does not reach rodents, and there is no state pet-shop or pet-dealer license for small mammals. The one real condition attaches to movement, not to ownership: the Board of Animal Health requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) for any mammal imported into Minnesota (the import rule names no exemption for rodents or pocket pets), and beginning July 1, 2026 that CVI must be electronic (eCVI). Whoever keeps a roof rat is also bound by the codified pet-rodent care standards of Minn. Stat. 346.41 (caging, flooring, water, ventilation, transport). Never release one (it is a nonnative species, and abandonment is also a cruelty offense under Minn. Stat. 343.21); check local city ordinances.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Minnesota-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Minnesota is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Minn. R. 6216.0270, subp. 4 designates 'rat (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)' as an 'unregulated nonnative species,' and subp. 1 provides that 'These nonnative species are not subject to regulation under Minnesota Statutes, chapter 84D.' Because chapter 84D holds the state's prohibitions on possessing, importing, purchasing, selling, and propagating invasive species, naming R. rattus in the unregulated tier removes every ecological barrier to keeping one. Separately, the exotic-pet 'regulated animals' law, Minn. Stat. 346.155, defines 'regulated animal' as only Felidae (except domestic cats), bears, and nonhuman primates, so no rodent requires an exotic-animal registration, insurance, or microchip. No DNR or other state permit is needed to keep a captive-bred roof rat. The keeper is bound by the codified pet-rodent care standards of Minn. Stat. 346.41 and by general anti-cruelty law (Minn. Stat. 343.21).

Sources: Minnesota DNR / Office of the Revisor of Statutes, Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes, Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes, Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Breeding is unregulated at the state level. As an 'unregulated nonnative species' (Minn. R. 6216.0270), the roof rat is exempt from chapter 84D propagation bans, so no DNR permit applies to breeding. The state's Commercial Breeder Law (Minn. Stat. 347.57-347.64) defines a 'commercial breeder' for dogs and cats only: Minn. Stat. 347.57 ties the definition to producing 'litters of puppies or kittens,' and the chapter's 'animal' means 'a dog or a cat.' There is no state-level commercial-rodent-breeder license, per-animal fee, or facility inspection, whether a hobbyist produces one litter a year or a larger operation produces many. Federal USDA/AWA licensing can reach a wholesale or sight-unseen dealer, but breeders selling directly to the public face-to-face are covered by the AWA retail-pet-store exemption regardless of volume, and rats of the genus Rattus bred for research are excluded from the AWA entirely.

Sources: Minnesota DNR / Office of the Revisor of Statutes, Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes, USDA APHIS

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Selling or giving away a captive-bred roof rat needs no state permit. As an unregulated nonnative species, R. rattus is exempt from the chapter 84D ban on selling and purchasing invasive species (Minn. R. 6216.0270). Minnesota has no state-level pet-shop or pet-dealer license for small mammals; the state's agricultural dealer licenses (Minn. Dept of Agriculture) apply only to livestock market agencies, stockyards, and meatpackers, and the 'pet lemon law' consumer protections (Minn. Stat. 325F.791) cover only dogs and cats. State law imposes no transaction limit on a private breeder rehoming or selling rats directly. Two caveats: a commercial retail storefront must obtain a local municipal pet-shop license where one exists (for example Minneapolis and St. Paul license pet shops); and the pet-rodent care standards of Minn. Stat. 346.41 bind whoever holds the animals. Unlike Kentucky, Minnesota's import/sale CVI requirement is framed around importation of mammals (Board of Animal Health), not around the in-state act of offering an animal for sale, so a purely intrastate sale/transfer is not what triggers the CVI.

Sources: Minnesota DNR / Office of the Revisor of Statutes, Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes, City of Saint Paul, City of Minneapolis

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Intrastate transport (moving a roof rat between Minnesota locations) is unregulated for an unregulated-nonnative species, subject only to the transport-enclosure provisions of Minn. Stat. 346.41 (a chew-proof container giving fresh air, room to stand and turn, and food/water on trips over six hours). Importing a roof rat into Minnesota from another state or country is the restricted case: the Board of Animal Health's import rule and official import guidance state that 'All birds and mammals imported into Minnesota, unless specifically exempted below, must be accompanied by a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI),' and the listed exemptions name only specific livestock and dog/cat/ferret situations, with no exemption for rodents or pocket pets. So a roof rat brought into the state must travel with a CVI issued by an accredited veterinarian in the state of origin (typically within 30 days before entry), attesting the animal shows no clinical signs of infectious, contagious, or communicable disease. No advance import permit, and no rabies or TB/brucellosis testing, applies to a rodent. Beginning July 1, 2026, the Board requires all import/export CVIs to be electronic (eCVI); paper certificates are no longer accepted. International movement is governed by federal CDC/USDA rules (the CDC bars rodents of African origin). Never release a roof rat into the wild: it is a nonnative species and abandonment is also a cruelty offense (Minn. Stat. 343.21, subd. 5).

Sources: Minnesota Board of Animal Health / Office of the Revisor of Statutes, Minnesota Board of Animal Health, Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes, Minnesota DNR / Office of the Revisor of Statutes, USDA APHIS / CDC

Restrictions & responsibilities

A Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) is required to import a roof rat into Minnesota. The Board of Animal Health requires that all birds and mammals imported into the state be accompanied by a CVI unless specifically exempted, and the listed exemptions name no rodents or pocket pets. The CVI is a vet-issued health document attesting the animal shows no clinical signs of communicable disease. No CVI is required for in-state (intrastate) movement, and no advance import permit or rodent lab testing applies. Beginning July 1, 2026 the CVI must be electronic (eCVI).
  • Before importing, have a USDA-accredited veterinarian in the state of origin examine the rat and issue a CVI (records species, sex, age, number of animals, and origin/destination details).
  • Obtain the CVI typically within 30 days before entry into Minnesota.
  • For movement on or after July 1, 2026, ensure the certificate is an electronic CVI (eCVI); paper certificates are no longer accepted.
  • No advance import permit and no rabies/TB/brucellosis testing apply to a rodent.
  • Confirm with the Board of Animal Health whether any disease screening beyond a visual exam is expected for a pet rodent, and how the eCVI workflow accommodates a single private pet import.

Forms: Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) / eCVI · Where: Issued by a USDA-accredited veterinarian in the state of origin; the veterinarian forwards a copy to the origin-state animal health officials for transmittal to the Minnesota Board of Animal Health. · Fees: No state fee for the CVI; the issuing veterinarian charges an examination/paperwork fee.

Source: Minnesota Board of Animal Health / Office of the Revisor of Statutes, Minnesota Board of Animal Health

Codified pet-rodent care standards. Minn. Stat. 346.41 sets enforceable husbandry requirements for rodents that bind whoever holds the animal (owner or seller): daily fresh food; clean potable water by free choice or sufficient quantity; enclosure of materials strong enough to prevent escape or injury by chewing; a solid floor impervious to moisture, or a wire/mesh floor constructed to prevent injury to feet and legs (preventing bumblefoot); cleaning of the entire surface area and removal of excreta; ventilation minimizing drafts, odors, and moisture; sufficient floor space and height for exercise; outdoor shade if confined outdoors; and transport containers that prevent escape/injury, provide fresh air without injurious drafts, and allow standing/turning with food and water on trips over six hours. Failure to meet these is neglect under the anti-cruelty law.
  • House the rat in a chew-resistant, fully cleanable enclosure with safe flooring, good ventilation, and room to exercise.
  • Provide fresh food daily and clean water by free choice.
  • For transport, use a chew-proof container with fresh air and room to stand and turn; supply food and water on trips over six hours.

Where: Enforced by local animal control, local law enforcement, or the Board of Animal Health.

Source: Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes

Never release a roof rat into the wild. R. rattus is a nonnative species; releasing or letting a nonnative animal escape into a free-living state is contrary to Minnesota's invasive-species framework (Minn. Stat. 84D.01 defines 'introduction' as placement, release, or escape into a free-living state). Abandoning any animal is separately a cruelty offense under Minn. Stat. 343.21, subd. 5 ('No person shall abandon any animal'). Rehome responsibly. Local city or county ordinances may add limits on possession or sale, so check the ordinances for your municipality (e.g. Minneapolis, St. Paul).

Source: Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes, Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes, Minnesota DNR / Office of the Revisor of Statutes

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Minn. R. 6216.0270, Unregulated Nonnative Species (subp. 4: 'rat (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)'; subp. 1: 'These nonnative species are not subject to regulation under Minnesota Statutes, chapter 84D.') — Minnesota DNR / Office of the Revisor of Statutes
  • Minn. Stat. 84D.01, Definitions (Invasive Species): defines 'unregulated nonnative species' (subd. 18) and 'introduction' as placement, release, or escape into a free-living state (subd. 9) — Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes
  • Minn. Stat. 346.155, Possessing Regulated Animals: 'regulated animal' = Felidae (except domestic cats), bears, and nonhuman primates; no rodents — Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes
  • Minn. Stat. 346.41, Rodents (Pet and Companion Animal Welfare Act): codified care standards for pet rodents (food, water, enclosure, flooring/mesh, sanitation, ventilation, space, outdoor shade, transport containers) — Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes
  • Minn. Stat. 343.21, Overworking or Mistreating Animals (subd. 5: 'No person shall abandon any animal'; neglect/abandonment penalties) — Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes
  • Minn. Stat. 347.57, Commercial Breeders; Definitions: 'commercial breeder' is defined around 'litters of puppies or kittens' and 'animal' means 'a dog or a cat'; rodents are outside Minn. Stat. 347.57-347.64 — Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes
  • Minn. Stat. 97B.651, Unprotected Mammals and Birds: unprotected wild mammals may be taken, possessed, bought, sold, or transported in any quantity (R. rattus is not a game/protected species) — Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes
  • Minn. R. 1721.0040, Certificates of Veterinary Inspection: contents/submission of the CVI (must attest no clinical signs of infectious, contagious, or communicable disease and that movement requirements are met) — Minnesota Board of Animal Health / Office of the Revisor of Statutes
  • Animal Imports (official import guidance): 'All birds and mammals imported into Minnesota, unless specifically exempted below, must be accompanied by a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI)'; exemptions list only specified livestock and dog/cat/ferret situations (no rodent/pocket-pet exemption); eCVI mandate effective July 1, 2026 — Minnesota Board of Animal Health
  • Pet Shop License (Saint Paul): commercial retail pet-shop storefronts within the city require a municipal Pet Shop License (state has no rodent pet-shop license, so this defaults to municipalities) — City of Saint Paul
  • Pet Shop License (Minneapolis): commercial retail pet-shop storefronts within the city require a municipal pet-shop license — City of Minneapolis
  • USDA APHIS, Animal Welfare Act licensing: retail-pet-store exemption covers face-to-face direct-to-consumer sales regardless of volume; wholesale/sight-unseen dealers need a license; rats of the genus Rattus bred for research are excluded from the AWA — USDA APHIS
  • USDA APHIS / CDC, Bring a Pet Rodent into the United States (federal international-import rules; CDC bars rodents of African origin) — USDA APHIS / CDC

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat, unregulated nonnative species, Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI).

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Missouri? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Missouri

Summary. Keeping, selling, giving away, and moving a roof rat within Missouri is legal with no state permit. The Wildlife Code reaches all mammals (the general prohibition in 3 CSR 10-4.110 bars taking, selling, possessing, propagating, or releasing any wildlife unless a rule allows it), but 3 CSR 10-9.110(2) carves out 'mammals not native to Missouri,' which may be 'bought, sold, possessed, transported, and exhibited without permit.' R. rattus is non-native, is not federally endangered, is not on the Class II dangerous-wildlife list (3 CSR 10-9.240), and is not on the prohibited-species list (3 CSR 10-4.117 names the multimammate rat/mouse, genus Mastomys, but NOT genus Rattus). The Animal Care Facilities Act (RSMo 273.325) defines a regulated 'animal' as a dog or cat only, so no state breeder or pet-shop license reaches rats. Two real conditions attach to movement, not to ownership: bringing a rat INTO Missouri requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) within 30 days because the Dept of Agriculture treats it as an exotic/miscellaneous animal (2 CSR 30-2.010), and the Wildlife Code's general prohibition bars ever releasing one to the wild. One narrow textual quirk: the 3 CSR 10-9.110(2) carve-out lists buy/sell/possess/transport/exhibit but omits 'propagate' (which the very next subsection uses for fish), so breeding is best read as bundled with the unconditional right to possess and sell but is not spelled out; this is an open question for the MDC, not a known restriction. Check your city or county ordinance.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Missouri-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Missouri is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

The Wildlife Code's general prohibition (3 CSR 10-4.110) bars possessing any wildlife, 'including wildlife raised or held in captivity,' unless a rule allows it, but 3 CSR 10-9.110(2) provides that, except for federally endangered species and species on the prohibited (3 CSR 10-4.117) or Class II (3 CSR 10-9.240) lists, 'mammals not native to Missouri' may be 'bought, sold, possessed, transported, and exhibited without permit.' R. rattus is a non-native mammal, is not federally endangered, is not a Class II dangerous wild animal, and is not on the prohibited-species list (3 CSR 10-4.117 names genus Mastomys, not genus Rattus). No state wildlife permit, facility inspection, or fee applies to keeping one. General animal-cruelty law (RSMo Chapter 578) still applies.

Sources: Missouri Dept of Conservation (via Cornell LII), Missouri Dept of Conservation (via Cornell LII), Missouri Dept of Conservation (via Cornell LII), Missouri Dept of Conservation, Missouri Revisor of Statutes

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

No state license reaches breeding pet rats. The Animal Care Facilities Act defines a regulated 'animal' as 'any dog or cat' (RSMo 273.325(1)), so the Dept of Agriculture has no jurisdiction to license, inspect, or set facility standards for rat breeders regardless of scale, and there is no rodent-breeder license, hobbyist threshold, or quota in Missouri. On the conservation side, the right to breed is best read as bundled with the unconditional right to 'possess' and 'sell' a permit-exempt non-native pet under 3 CSR 10-9.110(2). One textual quirk: the 9.110(2) verb list (bought, sold, possessed, transported, exhibited) omits 'propagated,' a word the very next subsection (9.110(3)) does use for fish and crayfish, while the baseline 3 CSR 10-4.110 prohibits propagating any wildlife unless allowed. Read strictly that leaves captive breeding textually unaddressed rather than affirmatively authorized, so this is routed to the MDC as an open clarification (see contacts), not treated as a ban. General cruelty/care law (RSMo Chapter 578) applies. Federal USDA/AWA licensing can reach only a large-scale wholesale/sight-unseen dealer; direct-to-consumer and de minimis hobby sales are exempt and rats of genus Rattus bred for research are excluded from the AWA.

Sources: Missouri Revisor of Statutes, Missouri Dept of Conservation (via Cornell LII), Missouri Dept of Conservation (via Cornell LII), Missouri Revisor of Statutes, USDA APHIS

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

3 CSR 10-9.110(2) expressly authorizes non-native mammals to be 'bought, sold... without permit,' so no Class I/II/III Wildlife Breeder Permit or Commercial Wildlife Dealer Permit is needed to sell or give away R. rattus, provided the animal was lawfully sourced and not taken from the wild. On the agricultural side, the Animal Care Facilities Act's pet-shop and dealer licensing turns on the 'animal' = dog or cat definition (RSMo 273.325), so a vendor, hobbyist, or storefront dealing only in rats is not a regulated 'pet shop' and needs no state dealer/animal-business license. Sale or free transfer of a roof rat within Missouri is treated as an ordinary transfer of personal property, subject only to general consumer-protection and tax law plus animal-cruelty law (RSMo Chapter 578).

Sources: Missouri Dept of Conservation (via Cornell LII), Missouri Revisor of Statutes, Missouri Revisor of Statutes

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Intrastate transport within Missouri needs no permit: 3 CSR 10-9.110(2) expressly authorizes transporting non-native mammals without a Wildlife Code permit, so an owner may carry a roof rat for veterinary care, exhibition, or relocation inside the state with no documentation. Importation across the state line is the attached condition. The Dept of Agriculture governs animals entering Missouri under 2 CSR 30-2.010 and classifies a non-native rodent as an exotic/miscellaneous animal; 2 CSR 30-2.010(14)-(15) require that all miscellaneous and all exotic animals entering Missouri be accompanied by an official Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) issued within 30 days prior to movement, showing an individual listing of the scientific and common name and a description (sex, age, weight, coloration). No advance entry permit applies to a pet rodent. Export is governed by the destination state's rules; international movement is governed by federal CDC/USDA/USFWS rules (the CDC bars rodents of African origin). Never release a roof rat to the wild (3 CSR 10-4.110 bars liberating captive wildlife without the director's written authorization).

Sources: Missouri Dept of Conservation (via Cornell LII), Missouri Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII), Missouri Dept of Conservation (via Cornell LII), USDA APHIS / CDC

Restrictions & responsibilities

A Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) is required to import a roof rat INTO Missouri (2 CSR 30-2.010). The Dept of Agriculture treats a non-native rodent as an exotic/miscellaneous animal, and all such animals entering the state must be accompanied by an official CVI issued within 30 days before movement, individually listing the scientific (Rattus rattus) and common name plus a description (sex, age, weight, coloration). No CVI applies to movement entirely within Missouri, and no advance entry permit applies to a pet rodent.
  • Have a USDA-accredited veterinarian in the state of origin examine the rat and issue a CVI listing its scientific and common name and a physical description.
  • Obtain the CVI within 30 days before crossing into Missouri.
  • Carry the CVI with the animal during the move; the consignor and consignee physical addresses must appear on it.
  • No telephonic entry permit is needed for pet rodents (advance entry permits are reserved for listed livestock).

Forms: Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) · Where: Issued by a USDA-accredited veterinarian in the state of origin; Missouri Dept of Agriculture, Animal Health Division, oversees entry. · Fees: No state fee for the CVI; the issuing veterinarian charges an examination/paperwork fee.

Source: Missouri Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII), Missouri Dept of Agriculture, Animal Health Division

Never release a roof rat to the wild. 3 CSR 10-4.110 bars liberating any wildlife, including 'wildlife raised or held in captivity,' without the written authorization of the director of the Dept of Conservation, and R. rattus is an invasive species. Releasing one (including an escape or a misguided attempt to 'free' a pet) violates the Wildlife Code, an offense punishable as a misdemeanor. Use secure caging and rehome responsibly. Check local city/county nuisance-animal ordinances.

Source: Missouri Dept of Conservation (via Cornell LII)

Textual ambiguity in the propagation right: 3 CSR 10-9.110(2) authorizes non-native mammals to be bought, sold, possessed, transported, and exhibited without permit but omits the word 'propagated,' which the next subsection (9.110(3)) does use for fish and crayfish, while the baseline 3 CSR 10-4.110 prohibits propagating any wildlife unless allowed. Read strictly, captive breeding of non-native pet mammals is textually unaddressed rather than affirmatively authorized. In practice the MDC almost certainly treats breeding as bundled with the right to possess and sell an unregulated house pet, but the code text does not say so. This is a clarification to seek, not a known restriction (no rat-breeder license exists under either the Wildlife Code or the ACFA).
  • Breed under the standard non-native-mammal possession exemption; no state breeder license exists for rats.
  • If certainty is needed, ask the MDC in writing whether the omission of 'propagated' in 3 CSR 10-9.110(2) restricts captive breeding of permit-exempt non-native mammals, or whether it is implicit in the right to possess and sell.

Where: Missouri Dept of Conservation (Wildlife Code interpretation).

Source: Missouri Dept of Conservation (via Cornell LII), Missouri Dept of Conservation (via Cornell LII)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • 3 CSR 10-9.110, General Prohibition; Applications (Section (2): 'mammals not native to Missouri' may be 'bought, sold, possessed, transported, and exhibited without permit,' except federally endangered species and those on 3 CSR 10-4.117 / 3 CSR 10-9.240; Section (3) authorizes fish and crayfish to be 'bought, sold, transported, propagated, taken, and possessed,' showing 'propagated' is omitted for mammals) — Missouri Dept of Conservation (via Cornell LII)
  • 3 CSR 10-9.110 (official Missouri Secretary of State PDF of the current 3 CSR Chapter 10-9 rules) — Missouri Secretary of State / Dept of Conservation
  • 3 CSR 10-4.110, General Prohibition; Applications (Section (1): no wildlife, 'including wildlife raised or held in captivity,' may be molested, taken, transported, bought, sold, possessed, propagated, imported, exported, or liberated to the wild except as the rules permit) — Missouri Dept of Conservation (via Cornell LII)
  • 3 CSR 10-4.117, Prohibited Species (Section (1): prohibited species may not be imported, exported, transported, sold, purchased, or possessed alive without the director's written approval; Section (2)(A) Mammals names the multimammate rat/mouse genus Mastomys, flying foxes, mongooses, raccoon dogs, brushtail possums; genus Rattus is NOT listed) — Missouri Dept of Conservation (via Cornell LII)
  • 3 CSR 10-9.240, Class II Wildlife (inherently dangerous animals: large carnivores, bears, venomous reptiles, etc.; no rodents listed, so R. rattus is not a Class II 'dangerous wild animal') — Missouri Dept of Conservation
  • 2 CSR 30-2.010, Health Requirements Governing the Admission of Livestock, Poultry, Miscellaneous, and Exotic Animals Entering Missouri (Section (14)(A) miscellaneous animals and Section (15)(A) exotic animals must be accompanied by an official CVI, individually listing scientific/common name and description; all animals entering Missouri need a CVI issued within 30 days prior to movement) — Missouri Dept of Agriculture (via Cornell LII)
  • Missouri Dept of Agriculture, Certificates of Veterinary Inspection / Livestock Movement Requirements (practical CVI guidance: 30-day validity, accepted electronic CVI formats, physical-address requirement) — Missouri Dept of Agriculture, Animal Health Division
  • RSMo 273.325, Animal Care Facilities Act, Definitions ('animal' means 'any dog or cat' used or intended for research, teaching, testing, breeding, exhibition, or as a pet; 'pet shop' definition references that dog/cat-limited 'animal,' so rodent breeders/dealers are unregulated by the ACFA) — Missouri Revisor of Statutes
  • RSMo Chapter 578, Miscellaneous Offenses (animal-cruelty/neglect/abandonment statutes apply to any living vertebrate, the only clear legal parameters governing how kept/bred rats must be treated) — Missouri Revisor of Statutes
  • USDA APHIS, Animal Welfare Act licensing (Class A breeder license applies to wholesale/sight-unseen dealers; direct-to-consumer and de minimis hobby sales exempt; rats of genus Rattus bred for research are excluded from the AWA) — USDA APHIS
  • USDA APHIS / CDC, Bring a Pet Rodent into the United States (federal international-import rules; the CDC bars rodents of African origin) — USDA APHIS / CDC

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat, Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI).

Last reviewed 2026-06-14. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.
