item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in North Dakota? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › North Dakota

Summary. North Dakota is one of the most permissive states for keeping a roof rat, and is even more open than most because rats are not merely unlisted, they are named exempt. North Dakota splits animal regulation between Game and Fish (wildlife) and the Department of Agriculture's State Board of Animal Health (livestock and nontraditional livestock). A captive-bred roof rat is outside Game and Fish jurisdiction because NDCC 20.1-01-02(59) provides that 'Wildlife does not include domestic animals as defined by section 36-01-00.1 or birds or animals held in private ownership.' It then falls to the Board of Animal Health, whose nontraditional-livestock rule, NDAC 48.1-09-01-02, sorts species into three licensed categories and a separate exempt list. Rats are not in Category 1, 2, or 3; they are on the exempt list at 48.1-09-01-02(4)(h), which states that, unless the state veterinarian determines otherwise on disease or human-health grounds, 'Rats' are 'exempt from the importation permit and certificate of veterinary inspection requirement' that NDAC 48.1-09-02-01 otherwise imposes on nontraditional livestock. So no nontraditional-livestock license applies (those attach only to Category 2 and 3 under 48.1-09-01-03), and importing a pet rat needs neither a CVI nor an import permit. The rule says 'Rats' generically, with no binomial, so it covers Rattus rattus on the same footing as the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus). North Dakota also has no dog/cat-style commercial pet-breeder or pet-dealer license that reaches rodents, so breeding and selling or giving a roof rat are unregulated at the state level. The only firm legal lines are the general animal-cruelty and abandonment statutes (NDCC ch. 36-21.2): never release or abandon a roof rat. Local city or county ordinances can still add limits.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the North Dakota-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where North Dakota is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Keeping a captive-bred roof rat needs no state license or permit. Game and Fish has no jurisdiction because NDCC 20.1-01-02(59) provides that 'Wildlife does not include domestic animals as defined by section 36-01-00.1 or birds or animals held in private ownership,' and a pet rat is held in private ownership. The Board of Animal Health then governs it as nontraditional livestock, but rats are not placed in any of the licensed categories: NDAC 48.1-09-01-02 lists Category 1 (turkeys, ducks, rabbits, ratites, chinchilla, hedgehog, degus, and the like), Category 2, and Category 3, and separately at 48.1-09-01-02(4) provides that, 'Unless the state veterinarian determines it is necessary based on disease incidence information or human health or safety concerns, the following are exempt from the importation permit and certificate of veterinary inspection requirement,' listing 'Rats' at (4)(h). Nontraditional-livestock licenses, facility inspections, and fencing attach only to Category 2 and Category 3 (48.1-09-01-03), so none apply to a rat. R. rattus is also absent from the only prohibited-import provision, 48.1-09-01-02(5)(a) ('Skunks and raccoons may not be imported into the state for any purpose'). General animal-cruelty law (NDCC ch. 36-21.2; cruelty is a class C felony under 36-21.2-03) still applies.

Sources: North Dakota State Board of Animal Health / ND Legislative Assembly (NDAC), North Dakota Legislative Assembly (NDCC), North Dakota Department of Agriculture, North Dakota Legislative Assembly (NDCC)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Breeding is unregulated at the state level. Because rats are exempt from the nontraditional-livestock framework (NDAC 48.1-09-01-02(4)(h)), the Category 2/3 license, facility-inspection, fencing, identification, and annual-inventory duties (NDAC 48.1-09-01-03 and following) do not apply, and North Dakota has no separate state breeder permit for small companion rodents. North Dakota's commercial framework regulates 'domestic animals' as defined by NDCC 36-01-00.1 (dog, cat, horse, bovine animal, sheep, goat, bison, farmed elk, llama, alpaca, swine) and licensed nontraditional livestock; rats fall in neither set, so hobby and larger-scale rat breeding are not licensed by the state. Federal USDA Animal Welfare Act licensing can reach a breeder who ships wholesale or sells sight-unseen, but direct-to-consumer pet sales and de minimis hobby breeders are federally exempt, and rats of the genus Rattus bred for research are excluded from the AWA entirely.

Sources: North Dakota State Board of Animal Health / ND Legislative Assembly (NDAC), North Dakota Legislative Assembly (NDCC), USDA APHIS

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Selling or giving away a captive-bred roof rat is unregulated at the state level. North Dakota's livestock-dealer licensing and bonding rules cover commercial agricultural livestock, not exempt pet rodents, and the state has no dog/cat-style retail pet-shop or commercial-pet-breeder license that reaches rats. The nontraditional-livestock transfer paperwork (itemized bill of sale, manifest, or CVI at transfer, and the auction permit) applies to Category 2 and Category 3 animals under NDAC 48.1-09-01-03(7); rats are exempt and have no such requirement. Unlike Kentucky, North Dakota does not impose a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection to offer an animal for sale in state: the CVI/import-permit duty sits in NDAC 48.1-09-02-01 and is keyed to importation, and rats are expressly exempt from it (48.1-09-01-02(4)(h)). So both sale and free rehoming are lawful with no state permit. General cruelty law (NDCC ch. 36-21.2) applies.

Sources: North Dakota State Board of Animal Health / ND Legislative Assembly (NDAC), North Dakota Legislative Assembly (NDCC), North Dakota Department of Agriculture

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Importing, exporting, and moving a pet roof rat within North Dakota needs no state CVI or permit. The general rule, NDAC 48.1-09-02-01, provides that 'Nontraditional livestock may be imported into North Dakota only after the owner... obtains a certificate of veterinary inspection... [and] obtains an importation permit number from the office of the state veterinarian.' But NDAC 48.1-09-01-02(4) carves rats out of exactly that requirement: 'Unless the state veterinarian determines it is necessary based on disease incidence information or human health or safety concerns, the following are exempt from the importation permit and certificate of veterinary inspection requirement,' naming 'Rats' at (4)(h). Game and Fish has no transport authority over a privately owned rat because it is not 'wildlife' (NDCC 20.1-01-02(59)). So a move-in or an out-of-state purchase can cross the border with no pre-arrival paperwork, and intrastate movement is likewise unregulated. Export is governed by the destination state's rules (some states prohibit or restrict R. rattus); international movement is governed by federal CDC/USDA/USFWS rules (the CDC bars rodents of African origin). Never release a roof rat into the wild.

Sources: North Dakota State Board of Animal Health / ND Legislative Assembly (NDAC), North Dakota State Board of Animal Health / ND Legislative Assembly (NDAC), North Dakota Legislative Assembly (NDCC), USDA APHIS / CDC

Restrictions & responsibilities

Never release or abandon a roof rat. NDCC 36-21.2-04(1) provides that 'Any person that willfully engages in the abandonment of an animal is guilty of a class A misdemeanor,' and 'abandonment' is defined as relinquishing custody or control with no intent to reclaim and without placing the animal with another person able and willing to care for it. R. rattus is a non-native, invasive species, so releasing one is both unlawful and ecologically harmful. Rehome responsibly to a person who accepts the animal. Check your city/county ordinances, which can add local limits.

Source: North Dakota Legislative Assembly (NDCC)

Latent state-veterinarian override. The rats exemption at NDAC 48.1-09-01-02(4) opens with 'Unless the state veterinarian determines it is necessary based on disease incidence information or human health or safety concerns.' This means the State Veterinarian / Board of Animal Health could, by order or policy, impose a CVI, import permit, quarantine, or other condition on rats if a disease or human-health concern arose. The override has not been invoked against rats. Separately, NDAC 48.1-09-01-03(11) lets the board quarantine, at the owner's expense, any animal it determines poses a significant threat to wildlife, domestic animals, or human health.
  • No action is required while the exemption stands.
  • For certainty before importing or breeding at scale, ask the Office of the State Veterinarian in writing to confirm that the 'Rats' exemption (48.1-09-01-02(4)(h)) covers Rattus rattus and that no disease-based override is currently in effect.

Where: North Dakota State Board of Animal Health / Office of the State Veterinarian.

Source: North Dakota State Board of Animal Health / ND Legislative Assembly (NDAC)

Optional commercial layer for packaged feed only. Selling the live rat triggers no state registration, but if you manufacture and distribute your own packaged rat food, treats, or seed mix, that product must be registered as a 'specialty pet food' with the North Dakota Department of Agriculture before distribution (NDCC ch. 4.1-41). This regulates the feed product, not the animal.
  • If selling your own packaged rat diet, register each product as specialty pet food with the NDDA before distributing it in state.
  • Submit product labels for truth-in-labeling review (the NDDA uses an online License Application and Renewal Services portal).

Where: North Dakota Department of Agriculture, Pet Food Program. · Fees: Roughly $50 per in-state product and $100 per out-of-state product per two-year cycle (verify current fees with NDDA).

Source: North Dakota Department of Agriculture

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • NDAC ch. 48.1-09-01 (Nontraditional Livestock - Definitions and General Requirements): 48.1-09-01-01(15) wildlife-excludes-private-ownership definition; 48.1-09-01-02 categories (Category 1/2/3) and the exempt list at (4) naming 'h. Rats' as 'exempt from the importation permit and certificate of veterinary inspection requirement' unless the state veterinarian determines otherwise; prohibited imports at (5)(a) (skunks and raccoons; R. rattus absent); 48.1-09-01-03 Category 2/3 license/inventory/quarantine requirements — North Dakota State Board of Animal Health / ND Legislative Assembly (NDAC)
  • NDAC ch. 48.1-09-02 (Nontraditional Livestock - Importation Requirements): 48.1-09-02-01 requires a certificate of veterinary inspection and an importation permit number from the Office of the State Veterinarian before nontraditional livestock may be imported (this is the requirement that rats are exempted from by 48.1-09-01-02(4)(h)) — North Dakota State Board of Animal Health / ND Legislative Assembly (NDAC)
  • NDCC 20.1-01-02 (Title 20.1 Game, Fish, Predators, and Boating - Definitions): subsection 59 'Wildlife means any member of the animal kingdom... Wildlife does not include domestic animals as defined by section 36-01-00.1 or birds or animals held in private ownership.' — North Dakota Legislative Assembly (NDCC)
  • NDCC 36-01-00.1 (Title 36 Livestock - State Board of Animal Health, definitions): defines 'domestic animal' as dog, cat, horse, bovine animal, sheep, goat, bison, farmed elk, llama, alpaca, or swine (rats excluded), and defines nontraditional livestock — North Dakota Legislative Assembly (NDCC)
  • NDCC ch. 36-21.2 (Treatment of Animals): 36-21.2-03 animal cruelty (class C felony); 36-21.2-04 animal abandonment ('Any person that willfully engages in the abandonment of an animal is guilty of a class A misdemeanor') with the definition of 'abandonment'; pest/vermin/animal-damage-control exemptions in each section — North Dakota Legislative Assembly (NDCC)
  • NDDA Non-Traditional Livestock page: lists Arachnids, Invertebrates, Tropical freshwater and saltwater fish, Gerbils, Guinea pigs, Hamsters, Mice, Rats, Sugar gliders as exempt from non-traditional-livestock and importation requirements; summarizes Category 1 (no license), Category 2, Category 3 (license) — North Dakota Department of Agriculture
  • NDDA Livestock Licensing page (livestock-dealer licensing and bonding for commercial agricultural livestock; does not reach exempt pet rodents) — North Dakota Department of Agriculture
  • NDDA Commercial Feed and Pet Food Registration guidelines (specialty pet food product registration under NDCC ch. 4.1-41; only relevant if a seller distributes their own packaged rat food) — North Dakota Department of Agriculture
  • USDA APHIS, Animal Welfare Act licensing (Class A breeder license applies to wholesale/sight-unseen dealers; direct-to-consumer and de minimis hobby sales exempt; research rats of genus Rattus excluded from AWA) — USDA APHIS
  • USDA APHIS, Bring a Pet Rodent into the United States (federal international-import rules; CDC bars rodents of African origin) — USDA APHIS / CDC

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat, nontraditional livestock, certificate of veterinary inspection (CVI).

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Nebraska? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Nebraska

Summary. Nebraska is one of the clearest 'yes' states for keeping a roof rat. Its statute defining 'wild mammals' (Neb. Rev. Stat. 37-246) EXCLUDES 'the black rat' by name, alongside the house mouse, the Norway rat, the fallow deer, and feral domestic dogs and cats. 'The black rat' is the common name for Rattus rattus, so the species is identically situated to the fancy rat (R. norvegicus, 'the Norway rat'), which is excluded in the same clause. Because the Captive Wildlife Permit requirement (37-477(1)) and the prohibited inherently-dangerous list (37-477(2): wolf, skunk, Felidae, Ursidae) are both scoped to 'wild mammals,' the roof rat falls entirely outside the Nebraska Game and Parks Commission's wildlife permitting system, so keeping and breeding are unregulated at the state level. Two conditions attach to commerce and movement, not to ownership. First, selling rats through a retail storefront makes the seller a 'pet shop' (rodents are listed in the 54-626 definition of 'pet animal'), which needs a Department of Agriculture pet shop license (54-627; $125, premises inspection, written veterinary-care plan); casual sales and free gifting are outside that license. Second, importing an animal into Nebraska requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (23 NAC 21-004), and a pet roof rat is handled under the Department's generic 'Exotics (not bovid or cervidae)' import line, which calls for a CVI plus a pre-entry import permit number unless an approved electronic CVI (eCVI) is used. Intrastate movement and export are unregulated by the state. Never release a roof rat into the wild.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Nebraska-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Nebraska is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Neb. Rev. Stat. 37-246 defines 'wild mammals' but excludes by name 'the fallow deer, the house mouse, the Norway rat, the black rat, the feral domestic dog, and the feral domestic cat.' 'The black rat' is the common name for Rattus rattus. The Captive Wildlife Permit requirement at 37-477(1) reaches only 'any wild birds, any wild mammals, any nongame wildlife in need of conservation... or any wildlife determined to be an endangered or threatened species,' and the prohibited inherently-dangerous list at 37-477(2) is 'any wolf, any skunk, or any member of the families Felidae and Ursidae.' Because R. rattus is statutorily not a wild mammal, neither the permit nor the prohibited list applies, so no state permit, registration, fee, or facility inspection is required to keep one. General animal-cruelty law still applies.

Sources: Nebraska Legislature, Nebraska Legislature, Michigan State Animal Legal & Historical Center

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Breeding is unregulated at the state level. Because R. rattus is excluded from 'wild mammals' (37-246), the captive-wildlife system (37-477) imposes no propagation permit on it. Nebraska's commercial-breeder framework, the Commercial Dog and Cat Operator Inspection Act (Neb. Rev. Stat. 54-625 et seq.), defines 'Commercial dog breeder,' 'Commercial cat breeder,' and 'Casual breeder' exclusively in terms of dogs and cats, so there is no 'commercial rodent breeder' license category and no state rodent-breeding quota, fee, or facility standard. Hobby or large-scale rat breeding triggers no Nebraska license. Federal USDA/AWA licensing can reach a large wholesale/sight-unseen dealer, but rats of the genus Rattus bred for use as pets sold direct-to-consumer fall outside that federal layer (and research rats are excluded from the AWA entirely).

Sources: Nebraska Legislature, Nebraska Legislature, USDA APHIS

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Giving a roof rat away or selling a few casually (direct from a private home, no storefront) is unregulated: the 'Dealer' license under the Commercial Dog and Cat Operator Inspection Act is defined only for 'buying for resale or selling or exchanging dogs or cats,' so a person trading rodents is not a 'dealer.' The one attached condition is the pet shop license. Neb. Rev. Stat. 54-626 defines 'Pet animal' to include 'rodents' and defines 'Pet shop' as 'a retail establishment which sells pet animals and related supplies,' and 54-627 provides that 'A person shall not operate as a... pet shop unless the person obtains the appropriate license,' carrying a one-time $125 license fee, a premises inspection, and (under 23 NAC 18-007) a written veterinary-care plan. So selling roof rats through a retail establishment requires a Department of Agriculture pet shop license, while casual private sales and free gifting do not. (Roof rats are also outside the Dog and Cat Purchase Protection Act 'lemon law,' which covers only dogs and cats.) General cruelty law still applies.

Sources: Nebraska Legislature, Nebraska Legislature, Nebraska Dept of Agriculture / Cornell Legal Information Institute, Nebraska Legislature

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-14

Intrastate movement of a lawfully held pet roof rat is entirely unregulated, and Nebraska imposes no exit permit on export (the destination jurisdiction's rules govern). The attached condition is on IMPORT. 23 NAC 21-004.01 provides that 'Animals must comply with all applicable requirements to enter the state. Animals entering the state which are not in compliance are subject to enforcement actions and may be quarantined at the expense of the owner... or immediately returned to the state of origin.' Because 'the black rat' is excluded from 'wild mammals' (37-246), import is governed by the Department of Agriculture's animal-health rules, not by a Game and Parks wildlife embargo. The Department's published Summary of Import Requirements does not list rodents by name; a pet roof rat falls under the generic 'Exotics (not bovid or cervidae)' line, which requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) plus a 'Pre-Entry Import Permit number... unless using an approved eCVI.' A CVI is generally valid for 30 days before entry. International import is governed by federal CDC/USDA/USFWS rules (the CDC bars rodents of African origin). Never release a roof rat into the wild.

Sources: Nebraska Dept of Agriculture / Cornell Legal Information Institute, Nebraska Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian), Nebraska Dept of Agriculture, Nebraska Legislature, USDA APHIS / CDC

Restrictions & responsibilities

Operating a retail establishment that sells roof rats makes you a 'pet shop' (rodents are 'pet animals' under Neb. Rev. Stat. 54-626), which requires a Department of Agriculture pet shop license under 54-627: a one-time $125 fee, a premises pre-inspection, and a written veterinary-care plan (23 NAC 18-007). Casual private sales and giving rats away free are outside this license.
  • Determine whether you are operating a 'retail establishment' (storefront/commercial) selling pet animals; casual/private sales and free gifting are not pet shops.
  • If a pet shop: submit the Pet Shop/Dealer application to the Nebraska Department of Agriculture with the one-time $125 license fee.
  • Arrange a pre-licensing facility inspection by the Department.
  • Establish a written veterinary-care plan with a Nebraska-licensed attending veterinarian (23 NAC 18-007) and keep escape-proof, sanitary enclosures.

Forms: Nebraska Pet Shop/Dealer License Application · Where: Nebraska Department of Agriculture, Animal Health (Commercial Dog and Cat Inspection Program). · Fees: One-time $125 license fee, plus annual fees based on the number and nature of animals harbored.

Source: Nebraska Legislature, Nebraska Legislature, Nebraska Dept of Agriculture / Cornell Legal Information Institute

Importing a roof rat into Nebraska requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) and, under the Department of Agriculture's generic 'Exotics (not bovid or cervidae)' import line, a pre-entry import permit number unless an approved electronic CVI (eCVI) is used. The CVI is a vet-issued health document valid about 30 days. There is no CVI requirement for in-state movement and no exit permit for export.
  • Have a USDA-accredited veterinarian in the state of origin examine the rat and issue a CVI within 30 days before entering Nebraska.
  • Obtain a pre-entry import permit number from the Nebraska Department of Agriculture (or use a veterinarian on an approved eCVI system, which routes the data and can satisfy the permit step).
  • Confirm with the State Veterinarian whether a single relocating pet rodent's pre-entry permit is required or whether the CVI alone suffices, and whether any disease attestation must appear on the CVI.
  • No CVI is needed for moving a lawfully held rat within Nebraska.

Forms: Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) · Where: Issued by a USDA-accredited veterinarian in the state of origin; pre-entry import permit issued by the Nebraska Department of Agriculture, Bureau of Animal Industry. · Fees: No state fee for the CVI; the issuing veterinarian charges an examination/paperwork fee.

Source: Nebraska Dept of Agriculture / Cornell Legal Information Institute, Nebraska Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian), Nebraska Dept of Agriculture

Never release a roof rat into the wild. R. rattus is an invasive commensal pest in Nebraska, and Animal Damage Control statutes (Neb. Rev. Stat. 81-2,236) authorize cooperative eradication of 'injurious commensal and field rodents.' Releasing a captive rat is an illegal introduction of an invasive pest. Rehome responsibly. Local (Lincoln/Omaha/county) ordinances may separately address rats; check your city.

Source: Nebraska Dept of Agriculture, Nebraska Legislature

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Neb. Rev. Stat. 37-246 - Wild mammals, defined (excludes 'the fallow deer, the house mouse, the Norway rat, the black rat, the feral domestic dog, and the feral domestic cat') — Nebraska Legislature
  • Neb. Rev. Stat. 37-477 - Certain animals kept in captivity; permit required; exceptions (subsec. (1) permit trigger for wild birds/wild mammals/nongame/endangered; subsec. (2) prohibited list: 'any wolf, any skunk, or any member of the families Felidae and Ursidae') — Nebraska Legislature
  • Neb. Rev. Stat. 37-479 - Captive wildlife permit; fee (not more than $30/year) and prohibited-act penalties (NOT the species list; that is in 37-477(2)) — Nebraska Legislature
  • NE Wildlife - Article 2, Game Law General Provisions (Animal Legal & Historical Center mirror of Chapter 37 definitions, incl. 37-246 wild-mammal exclusions) — Michigan State Animal Legal & Historical Center
  • Neb. Rev. Stat. 54-626 - Commercial Dog and Cat Operator Inspection Act; terms defined ('Pet animal' includes 'rodents'; 'Pet shop' = 'a retail establishment which sells pet animals and related supplies'; commercial breeder/dealer defined only for dogs and cats) — Nebraska Legislature
  • Neb. Rev. Stat. 54-627 - License requirements; fees; premises available for inspection (pet shop license, one-time $125 fee, premises inspection) — Nebraska Legislature
  • 23 Neb. Admin. Code ch. 18 sec. 007 - Humane handling, care, treatment of dogs and cats (licensed facilities must keep a written veterinary-care plan and effective pest control) — Nebraska Dept of Agriculture / Cornell Legal Information Institute
  • 23 Neb. Admin. Code ch. 21 sec. 004 - Importation of Animals ('Animals must comply with all applicable requirements to enter the state'; noncompliant animals quarantined or returned) — Nebraska Dept of Agriculture / Cornell Legal Information Institute
  • Nebraska Dept of Agriculture - Animal Imports portal (CVI/import-permit framework, Bureau of Animal Industry) — Nebraska Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian)
  • Nebraska Dept of Agriculture - Summary of Import Requirements (PDF). Rodents are NOT listed by name; a pet rat falls under 'Exotics (not bovid or cervidae)': CVI + 'Pre-Entry Import Permit number... unless using an approved eCVI' — Nebraska Dept of Agriculture
  • Neb. Rev. Stat. 81-2,236 - Director; cooperate with USDA APHIS in management and control of 'injurious commensal and field rodents' (basis for invasive-pest eradication and the no-release rationale) — Nebraska Dept of Agriculture
  • USDA APHIS, Animal Welfare Act licensing (Class A breeder license for wholesale/sight-unseen dealers; direct-to-consumer and de minimis hobby sales exempt; research rats of genus Rattus excluded from the AWA) — USDA APHIS
  • USDA APHIS, Bring a Pet Rodent into the United States (federal international-import rules; CDC bars rodents of African origin) — USDA APHIS / CDC

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat, Norway rat, Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI).

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in New Hampshire? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › New Hampshire

Summary. New Hampshire is one of the clearest 'yes' states for keeping a roof rat, and the reason is one explicit name on a list. The Fish and Game Department sorts captive wildlife into Prohibited, Controlled, and Non-controlled categories under N.H. Admin. Code Chapter Fis 800, and Fis 804.02(b)(7)(f) names 'Rats, domesticated (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)' by binomial in the non-controlled list. Fis 804.02(a) provides that 'A permit to possess wildlife shall not be required for any person to possess wildlife designated as non-controlled,' so possessing, breeding, and importing a captive-bred roof rat needs no state wildlife permit. There is no species trap: the roof rat (R. rattus) has identical standing to the fancy rat (R. norvegicus), the two being named together in the same clause. The Fis 806 propagation permit applies only to controlled species, so hobby and personal breeding are entirely unregulated by Fish and Game; Fis 803.03(a) likewise exempts non-controlled species from any wildlife import permit. The one commercial touchpoint is the Department of Agriculture's 'pet vendor' license (RSA 437; N.H. Admin. Code Agr 1701): transferring small mammals 'to the public' at volume requires that business license, and RSA 437:1 counts transfers made 'with or without a fee or donation,' so free adoption can count toward the threshold; rats sold strictly as documented feeders are excluded from the count (Agr 1701.03). For interstate movement, neither the Agr 2100 import rules nor USDA APHIS name pet rodents for a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection, so no CVI is clearly required, though the State Veterinarian retains broad disease authority and the law is silent rather than expressly exemptive. The single firm prohibition is release: R. rattus is not on the non-controlled release-exempt list and is an invasive exotic mammal, so releasing one into the wild without a permit (which would not be granted) is barred, and animal-cruelty law applies as well. Never release a roof rat.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the New Hampshire-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where New Hampshire is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

N.H. Admin. Code Fis 804.02(a) provides that 'A permit to possess wildlife shall not be required for any person to possess wildlife designated as non-controlled,' and Fis 804.02(b)(7)(f) lists 'Rats, domesticated (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)' among the non-controlled mammals. R. rattus is named by species alongside the fancy rat, and it is not on the Fis 804.03 prohibited list or the Fis 804.05 controlled list. So no state wildlife permit, registration, facility inspection, or fee applies to keeping one (the Fis 804.01 cage/enclosure standards bind only controlled/prohibited permit holders). RSA 207:1 defines 'wild animals' as all animals other than domestic, and although 'wildlife' reaches species 'whether raised in captivity or not normally found in a wild state,' the Fis 804.02 listing is the dispositive exemption that removes the regulatory burden from a captive-bred domesticated rat. General animal-cruelty law (RSA 644:8) still applies.

Sources: NH Fish and Game (via Cornell Legal Information Institute), NH Fish and Game Department, NH General Court, NH General Court

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Breeding is unregulated by Fish and Game. The Fis 806 propagation-permit regime (annual veterinary inspection, annual Propagation of Wildlife Report) applies only to species 'designated as controlled for these purposes pursuant to Fis 804.05' (Fis 806.01(b)). Because R. rattus is non-controlled under Fis 804.02, it falls entirely outside Fis 806, so a hobbyist or small-scale breeder needs no Fish and Game propagation permit, inspection, or report. The act of breeding is distinct from the commercial act of distributing the offspring: transferring the resulting rats at volume can bring the Department of Agriculture pet-vendor license into play (see sell_give), but the breeding itself is not licensed by the state.

Sources: NH Fish and Game (via Cornell Legal Information Institute), NH Fish and Game Department

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

No Fish and Game sale permit applies to a non-controlled mammal. The one attached condition is a volume-triggered business license from the Department of Agriculture, not a species restriction. RSA 437:1(IV) defines a 'Pet vendor' to include any entity that transfers 'small mammals customarily used as household pets to the public in quantities set in rules adopted by the department, with or without a fee or donation required, and whether or not a physical facility is owned by the licensee in New Hampshire... between January 1 and December 31 of each year,' and 'Transfer' is the 'transfer of ownership of live animals or birds... to a member of the public.' The quantity is set by N.H. Admin. Code Agr 1701.02 at 'Two hundred small mammals' per year. Rats are small mammals, so transferring 200 or more roof rats to the public in a calendar year (free transfers count) requires a pet-vendor license; below 200, selling or giving is unregulated. Rodents sold strictly as feeders are excluded from the count if the seller keeps a signed buyer statement (Agr 1701.03), but without that documentation they count toward the threshold. General cruelty law (RSA 644:8) applies.

Sources: NH General Court, NH General Court, NH Dept of Agriculture, Markets & Food (via Cornell Legal Information Institute), NH Dept of Agriculture, Markets & Food (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center), NH Fish and Game (via Cornell Legal Information Institute)

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-14

No Fish and Game import permit is required: Fis 803.03(a) provides that 'A permit to import wildlife shall not be required for any person to import wildlife designated as non-controlled,' and R. rattus is non-controlled. Fis 803.01(a) routes imported wildlife through any applicable Department of Agriculture, USDA, and USFWS requirements, but the agriculture import rules (N.H. Admin. Code Chapter Agr 2100) enumerate Certificate of Veterinary Inspection and entry-permit requirements species-by-species (bovines, sheep, goats, swine, dogs/cats/ferrets, equine, poultry, household birds, cervidae, camelidae, ratites, yaks) and do not mention rodents, small mammals, or pocket pets. USDA APHIS states it 'does not have any animal health requirements related to bringing (importing) a pet rodent into the United States' and defers domestic interstate movement to the receiving state (the CDC bars rodents of African origin, which does not reach the Asian-origin R. rattus). So no CVI is clearly required to bring a pet roof rat into New Hampshire. Confidence is medium, not high, because the agriculture rule is silent rather than expressly exemptive, and the State Veterinarian retains broad authority under RSA 436 to quarantine or test domestic animals suspected of carrying reportable disease; high-volume commercial importers should confirm with the Division of Animal Industry. Releasing R. rattus into the wild is prohibited (RSA 207:14; see restrictions).

Sources: NH Fish and Game Department, NH Dept of Agriculture, Markets & Food (via Cornell Legal Information Institute), USDA APHIS / CDC, NH General Court

Restrictions & responsibilities

Pet-vendor license (volume-triggered business registration). Transferring 200 or more small mammals 'to the public' in a calendar year (N.H. Admin. Code Agr 1701.02; rats are small mammals) makes a person a 'pet vendor' under RSA 437:1 and requires a Department of Agriculture pet-vendor license. RSA 437:1 counts transfers 'with or without a fee or donation,' so free adoptions count; documented feeder-rodent sales are excluded (Agr 1701.03). Below 200/year there is no license. This is a business registration, not a species permit, and applies identically to fancy rats and other small mammals.
  • Track total small-mammal transfers to the public per calendar year (Jan 1 to Dec 31); free transfers count, documented feeder sales do not.
  • If you reach 200 in a year, file the Pet Vendor License Application with the Division of Animal Industry with the $200 annual fee.
  • Provide municipal zoning sign-off (RSA 437:3) certifying the facility conforms to local zoning, a veterinarian-signed disease-control program, and the required transfer records (source, dates, identifying marks).
  • If selling rats strictly as feeders, keep a buyer-signed statement that they are for feeding so they are excluded from the threshold (Agr 1701.03).

Forms: Pet Vendor License Application (NH Dept of Agriculture, Markets & Food) · Where: NH Department of Agriculture, Markets & Food, Division of Animal Industry (1 Granite Place South, Suite 211, Concord, NH 03301). · Fees: $200 non-refundable annual fee; license operates on a fiscal year expiring June 30. No fee applies below the 200-small-mammal threshold.

Source: NH General Court, NH General Court, NH Dept of Agriculture, Markets & Food (via Cornell Legal Information Institute), NH Dept of Agriculture, Markets & Food (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center), NH Dept of Agriculture, Markets & Food

Never release a roof rat into the wild. RSA 207:14 provides that 'No person shall import, possess, sell, exhibit, or release any live marine species or wildlife... without first obtaining a permit from the executive director,' and the director may refuse a permit posing a 'disease, genetic, ecological, environmental, health, safety, or welfare risk.' R. rattus is not on the Fis 805.02 non-controlled release-exempt list and is an invasive exotic mammal, so a release permit would not issue; release is effectively barred. Releasing a domesticated pet would also expose the owner to animal-cruelty/abandonment liability (RSA 644:8). Rehome responsibly and check local county/municipal ordinances.
  • Do not release a roof rat outdoors under any circumstances; if you can no longer keep it, rehome it to another keeper.
  • Check local town ordinances, which may add nuisance-rodent or animal-keeping rules.

Source: NH General Court, NH Fish and Game (via Cornell Legal Information Institute)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • N.H. Admin. Code Fis 804.02, Non-controlled Species - Possession (Fis 804.02(a): 'A permit to possess wildlife shall not be required for any person to possess wildlife designated as non-controlled'; Fis 804.02(b)(7)(f): 'Rats, domesticated (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)') — NH Fish and Game (via Cornell Legal Information Institute)
  • N.H. Admin. Code Chapter Fis 800, The Importation, Possession and Use of All Wildlife (adopted rule, eff. 2026-04-20): non-controlled possession Fis 804.02; import-permit exemption Fis 803.03(a); propagation permit limited to controlled species Fis 806.01(b); release rules Fis 805 — NH Fish and Game Department
  • N.H. Admin. Code Fis 805.02, Permits to Release Wildlife (non-controlled release exemptions are narrow; R. rattus is not release-exempt, so release requires a permit that would not issue for an exotic mammal) — NH Fish and Game (via Cornell Legal Information Institute)
  • RSA 207:1, Definitions ('Wild animals' = all animals other than domestic; 'Wildlife' reaches species whether or not raised in captivity that are normally found in a wild state) — NH General Court
  • RSA 207:14, Import, Possession, or Release of Wildlife ('No person shall import, possess, sell, exhibit, or release any live marine species or wildlife... without first obtaining a permit from the executive director'; permit may be refused for disease/ecological/health/safety/welfare risk) — NH General Court
  • RSA 437:1, Definitions ('Pet vendor' includes transfers of 'small mammals customarily used as household pets to the public in quantities set in rules adopted by the department, with or without a fee or donation required, and whether or not a physical facility is owned... between January 1 and December 31 of each year'; 'Transfer' = transfer of ownership to a member of the public) — NH General Court
  • RSA 437:3, Requirements (pet-vendor application, municipal zoning conformance sign-off, record-keeping of source/date/identifying marks, consent to inspection) — NH General Court
  • N.H. Admin. Code Agr 1701.02, License Required (pet-vendor thresholds: 30 dogs/cats/ferrets, 50 birds, 350 fish, 200 reptiles, 200 amphibians, 'Two hundred small mammals') — NH Dept of Agriculture, Markets & Food (via Cornell Legal Information Institute)
  • N.H. Admin. Code Agr 1701.03, License Exemption for Feeder Fish and Rodents (rodents typically sold as feed are excluded from the Agr 1701.02 count; the seller 'may have the buyer sign a statement that the fish or rodents being purchased are solely intended for the purposes of feeding,' and must obtain a license if records are not kept and a threshold is reached) — NH Dept of Agriculture, Markets & Food (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center)
  • N.H. Admin. Code Chapter Agr 2100, Importation of Bovines and Other Domestic Animals into New Hampshire (species-specific CVI/entry-permit rules for bovines, sheep, goats, swine, dogs/cats/ferrets, equine, poultry, household birds, cervidae, camelidae, ratites, yaks; rodents/small mammals/pocket pets not enumerated) — NH Dept of Agriculture, Markets & Food (via Cornell Legal Information Institute)
  • Pet Vending, NH Dept of Agriculture, Markets & Food (pet-vendor license overview, application, $200 annual fee, fiscal-year term) — NH Dept of Agriculture, Markets & Food
  • USDA APHIS, Bring a Pet Rodent into the United States ('Veterinary Services does not have any animal health requirements related to bringing (importing) a pet rodent'; domestic interstate movement set by the receiving state; CDC bars rodents of African origin) — USDA APHIS / CDC

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat, non-controlled species, pet vendor, Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI).

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in New Jersey? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › New Jersey

Summary. New Jersey is strict about exotic pets in general, but it expressly exempts the entire rat genus: its exempt-pet list (N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4) names 'Mice and Rats — Mus spp. and Rattus spp.' Because the exemption is written at the GENUS level, it covers Rattus rattus exactly as it covers the common fancy rat. So keeping and breeding a captive-bred roof rat is legal with no exotic/nongame permit (just cage it to prevent escape and never release it). Private rehoming/adoption is fine; COMMERCIAL selling triggers Fish & Wildlife pet-shop/dealer licensing. No pet-rat-specific state import certificate was found (the CVI rules cover livestock/poultry).

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the New Jersey-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where New Jersey is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4(a) lists species that 'may be possessed in this State without a permit,' and subsection (a)2.v lists 'Mice and Rats — Mus spp. and Rattus spp.' Because the exemption names the entire genus Rattus, captive-bred Rattus rattus falls within it and needs no exotic/nongame possession permit. The only condition (4.4(b)) is that the animal be caged to prevent escape. Rattus is absent from the permit-required list (7:25-4.3) and the potentially-dangerous-species list (7:25-4.8). Gemini DR-verified: N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4 exempts the entire genus Rattus from exotic-wildlife permitting (the model genus-level exemption).

Sources: NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

An exempt species under 7:25-4.4 is removed from the possession-permit scheme, and no NJ Fish & Wildlife rule imposes a hobby-breeding permit for an exempt pet rodent. Breeding is simply continued possession of exempt animals, so long as the no-escape housing rule (4.4(b)) is met and animals are never released (N.J.S.A. 23:4-63.3). Commercial-scale breeding for sale shifts into dealer/pet-shop licensing. Gemini DR-verified: no statewide hobby-breeder license for exempt rodents.

Sources: NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), NJ Revised Statutes (Justia)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Because Rattus spp. is exempt, transferring or giving an individual pet rat is not barred by the possession code. But anyone SELLING exotic/nongame wildlife commercially must hold the applicable NJ Fish & Wildlife permit — a Pet Shop–Retail Sales permit or an Animal Dealer–Wholesale permit ($100 each). Free adoption/rehoming via private transfer is the cleanest route and avoids the dealer question. Gemini DR-verified: private giving is unregulated; commercial sale needs a MUNICIPAL pet-shop license (local health dept), not a state exotic-dealer permit.

Sources: NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife, NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

Intrastate transport of a lawfully-possessed exempt pet is not restricted. New Jersey's animal-import / CVI scheme (N.J.A.C. 2:3) is limited to livestock and poultry and does not impose a CVI on pet rodents. The binding statewide rules are the no-release prohibition (N.J.S.A. 23:4-63.3) and the no-escape caging rule (7:25-4.4(b)). Confirm import expectations with the State Veterinarian, as no rat-specific rule was located. Gemini DR-verified: intrastate unregulated; import of companion rodents isn't subject to a state CVI (livestock/poultry/dogs-focused) - a practical-legal gray area; commercial carriers may still require a CVI.

Sources: NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII), NJ Revised Statutes (Justia)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Selling pet rats COMMERCIALLY requires a NJ Fish & Wildlife permit — a Pet Shop–Retail Sales permit (selling to individuals) or an Animal Dealer–Wholesale permit (selling to stores), $100 each, with recordkeeping. Private free adoption/rehoming does not.
  • For commercial sales: obtain the appropriate NJ Fish & Wildlife pet-shop/dealer permit
  • Private rehoming/adoption needs no permit

Forms: NJ Fish & Wildlife — Exotic & Nongame Wildlife Permit Applications · Where: NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife — Wildlife Permits Unit · Fees: $100 per permit

Source: NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife

Cage the rat to prevent escape (N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4(b)) and never release it (N.J.S.A. 23:4-63.3) — R. rattus is a non-native species. Rehome responsibly.

Source: NJ Revised Statutes (Justia), NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4 — Exempted species ('Mice and Rats — Mus spp. and Rattus spp.') — NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)
  • N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.3 — Exotic/nongame species requiring a permit (Rattus NOT listed) — NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)
  • N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.8 — Potentially dangerous species (rodents = prairie dogs & ground squirrels only) — NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife (via Cornell LII)
  • N.J.S.A. 23:4-63.3 — Possession/release of certain animals (no-release rule) — NJ Revised Statutes (Justia)
  • NJ Fish & Wildlife — Exotic & Nongame Wildlife Permit Applications (pet-shop/dealer permits) — NJ Division of Fish & Wildlife

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in New Mexico? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › New Mexico

Summary. New Mexico is a clear 'no' for the roof rat as the rule reads today, and the reason is one missing name on a list. The Department of Game & Fish (operating as the Department of Wildlife) regulates the importation and possession of live non-domesticated animals under NMSA 1978 Section 17-3-32 and 19.35.7 NMAC, sorting every non-domesticated species into four groups on the Director's Species Importation List. Group I species are 'designated semi-domesticated animals and do not require an importation permit'; Group IV species are 'dangerous, invasive, undesirable' and their importation is 'prohibited for the general public.' The critical default rule (19.35.7.10(A)(5)) is that 'any species of live non-domesticated animal not currently on the species importation list will be designated group IV until such time as another determination is made by the director.' The current list (dated January 3, 2023) names 'Rattus norvegicus / Rat, Common' (the fancy rat) and 'Mus musculus / Mouse, Common' in Group I, with no permit required, but it contains no entry for Rattus rattus anywhere. So the roof rat is not listed, defaults to Group IV, and is prohibited for the general public to keep, breed, sell or give away, or import, while the closely related fancy rat one species over is freely legal. There is a pathway, but it is a list-fix, not a pet permit: the rule's own language ('until such time as another determination is made by the director') and the Director's discretionary power to designate a species 'semi-domesticated' (19.35.7.7) let a keeper petition the Director to add captive-bred Rattus rattus to Group I beside the fancy rat. Group IV permits exist only for science, zoos, recovery programs, temporary events, service animals, or qualified experts, not for personal pets. The Livestock Board's CVI rules do not apply, because rodents are not 'livestock'. Never release a roof rat into the wild (19.35.7.19 bars releasing an imported animal without a release permit).

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the New Mexico-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where New Mexico is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

The roof rat is a non-domesticated species not on the Director's Species Importation List, so under 19.35.7.10(A)(5) it 'will be designated group IV until such time as another determination is made by the director,' and Group IV species are 'prohibited for the general public.' The current list (Jan 3, 2023) names 'Rattus norvegicus / Rat, Common' and 'Mus musculus / Mouse, Common' in Group I (no permit) but contains no Rattus rattus entry, confirmed by direct extraction of the official PDF. The Group IV exceptions are for scientific study, department-approved restoration/recovery, zoological display, temporary events/entertainment, service animal, or qualified expert; personal pet ownership is not among them, and the Department does not issue a Group IV pet-keeping permit. The 'domesticated animals' exemption in NMSA 17-3-32 does not reach R. rattus, because the Department has not designated it domesticated/semi-domesticated; the burden is on the importer to prove an animal is domesticated. The only lawful route to possession is first to obtain a Director's determination (19.35.7.7) adding captive-bred R. rattus to Group I (or to a permitted group). General animal-cruelty law applies. Never release (19.35.7.19).

Sources: New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish / State Records Center and Archives, Cornell Legal Information Institute, New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish, LE Field Operations Division / Special Use Permits Program, New Mexico Legislature (via Justia)

Breeding   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Breeding presupposes lawful possession, and the general public cannot lawfully possess a Group IV species. Because R. rattus is unlisted and defaults to Group IV (19.35.7.10(A)(5)), a private or commercial breeding program for the pet trade is prohibited. New Mexico offers no small-breeder, hobbyist, or residential exemption for Group IV wildlife, and its dedicated propagation framework is for game birds, not non-domesticated rodents. If an accredited zoo or research institution qualified for a Group IV permit, breeding might be allowed under the facility's approved containment and veterinary plans (19.35.7.12 requires a containment/confinement plan and an accredited-veterinarian health certificate), but that institutional route is not a pet-breeder pathway. Federal USDA/AWA licensing can reach a large-scale dealer who ships wholesale/sight-unseen, but cannot make a state-prohibited species lawful to breed in New Mexico.

Sources: New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish / State Records Center and Archives, New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish, LE Field Operations Division / Special Use Permits Program, USDA APHIS

Selling or giving away   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Transferring ownership of a Group IV species is among the most restricted activities. 19.31.10.10(C) makes it 'unlawful to purchase, possess, barter, transfer, transport, sell, or offer to sell any live animal listed as group II, III or IV on the directors species importation list or any protected species without a department issued permit or license.' Because R. rattus defaults to Group IV, both sale and free gifting are prohibited for the general public: even a free transfer is barred, because the recipient cannot lawfully possess a Group IV animal. No commercial pet store, wholesaler, or dealer can lawfully traffic in roof rats in New Mexico. (By contrast, for Group I species like the fancy rat, a pet store can hold a single annual commercial-importation permit covering multiple animals and the retail buyer needs no permit, the streamlined channel that is closed to R. rattus until it is moved to Group I.)

Sources: New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish / State Records Center and Archives, New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish / State Records Center and Archives, New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish, LE Field Operations Division / Special Use Permits Program

Transport & import   Prohibited

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Importing or transporting a roof rat into or within New Mexico is prohibited while the species defaults to Group IV. NMSA 1978 Section 17-3-32 makes it a misdemeanor to import any live animal without a Game & Fish permit (only 'domesticated animals' are exempt, which R. rattus is not), and 19.35.7.8 provides it is 'unlawful to import any live non-domesticated animal into New Mexico without first obtaining appropriate permit(s) issued by the director except those animals identified within the species importation list group I.' R. rattus is not Group I, so bringing one across the state line, even as a personal pet in a private vehicle, is unlawful; that Group IV import permit is not available to the general public. Internal transport is separately barred by 19.31.10.10(C) (unlawful to 'transport' a Group IV animal without a permit). The Livestock Board's CVI/import rules do not apply, because rodents are not 'livestock' (a standard CVI is legally insufficient here). Common carriers acting in their regular duties are exempt from the 'importer' definition (19.35.7.7), but that shields only the carrier; the sender and the receiver remain liable. Never release an imported animal without a release permit (19.35.7.19).

Sources: New Mexico Legislature (via Justia), New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish / State Records Center and Archives, New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish / State Records Center and Archives, USDA APHIS / CDC

Restrictions & responsibilities

Default Group IV prohibition. Because Rattus rattus is on no group of the Director's Species Importation List, 19.35.7.10(A)(5) designates it Group IV, 'prohibited for the general public.' There is no pet-keeping, breeding, or transfer permit a member of the public can obtain for it; Group IV permits are only for science, zoos, recovery programs, temporary events, service animals, or qualified experts. Do NOT acquire, import, or transfer a roof rat in New Mexico while it defaults to Group IV. Unlawful possession of a Group IV animal can lead to seizure and a misdemeanor charge.
  • Understand that no public pet-keeping or transfer permit exists for a Group IV species in New Mexico.
  • Do not acquire or import a roof rat into New Mexico until the species is reclassified by the Director; doing so is unlawful and the animal can be confiscated.
  • Check local county/city ordinances as well; municipalities may further restrict rodent keeping even if the species is later reclassified.

Where: New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish - Special Use Permits Program

Source: New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish / State Records Center and Archives, New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish / State Records Center and Archives

Director's determination (the only pathway). The Group IV default holds only 'until such time as another determination is made by the director' (19.35.7.10(A)(5)), and 19.35.7.7 gives the Director discretion to designate a species 'semi-domesticated' (Group I) where its members are 'commonly tamed, raised, bred or sold in captivity.' A keeper or breeder can petition the Director to add captive-bred Rattus rattus to Group I beside the fancy rat (best outcome), or, failing that, to a permitted group (Group II or III) so a permit pathway at least exists. Only after such a determination can keeping/breeding/transfer become lawful. The Department already lists 'Rattus norvegicus / Rat, Common' and 'Mus musculus / Mouse, Common' in Group I as the direct precedent.
  • Request the current Director's Species Importation List and a written statement of R. rattus's current group from the Special Use Permits Program (DGF.Permits@dgf.nm.gov).
  • Petition the Director, in writing, to make a determination adding captive-bred domesticated Rattus rattus to Group I, citing the Group I precedent for the fancy rat and house mouse and the 19.35.7.7 semi-domesticated definition.
  • If Group I is declined, ask in the alternative for placement in Group II or III so a permitted pathway exists.
  • If informal email fails, an Inspection of Public Records Act (IPRA) request can obtain internal NMDGF memos on the regulation of pet rodents.

Where: New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish - Special Use Permits Program, 1 Wildlife Way, Santa Fe, NM 87507 · Fees: No fee to petition for a determination. (For the separate Group IV institutional importation permits that are NOT available to pet keepers, the fee tier under 19.30.9 NMAC is $15 for 1-5 animals, $75 for 6-99, $300 for 100+, plus an optional $25 expedite fee.)

Source: New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish / State Records Center and Archives, New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish, LE Field Operations Division / Special Use Permits Program, New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish / State Records Center and Archives

Never release a roof rat into the wild. 19.35.7.19 provides that no person shall release from captivity an imported animal into New Mexico without a release permit from the director, and R. rattus is treated as an invasive species and disease vector (New Mexico is a high-plague state). Rehome responsibly. Check local county/city ordinances.

Source: New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish / State Records Center and Archives

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in New Mexico. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in New Mexico

New Mexico sorts every non-domesticated animal into four groups on the Department of Game & Fish 'Director's Species Importation List,' under NMSA 1978 Section 17-3-32 and 19.35.7 NMAC. Group I species are 'designated semi-domesticated animals and do not require an importation permit.' Group IV species are 'dangerous, invasive, undesirable' and 'prohibited for the general public.' The current list (dated January 3, 2023) names 'Rattus norvegicus / Rat, Common,' the domestic fancy rat sold in pet shops, and 'Mus musculus / Mouse, Common' in Group I, with no permit needed. It contains no entry for 'Rattus rattus,' the domestic roof rat. Because the roof rat is on no group, the rule's default clause (19.35.7.10(A)(5)) controls: 'any species of live non-domesticated animal not currently on the species importation list will be designated group IV until such time as another determination is made by the director.' So a captive-bred, hand-tame pet roof rat defaults to Group IV (prohibited), and the Group IV exceptions are for science, zoos, recovery programs, temporary events, service animals, or qualified experts, not personal pets, while the fancy rat one species over is freely legal with no permit at all. This is not a behavioral or safety judgment about the roof rat; it is a gap in a list. The fancy rat already on the list is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated in the 19th century, and a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over.

The ask: Ask the New Mexico Department of Game & Fish, in writing, to make a Director's determination adding captive-bred, domesticated Rattus rattus to the Director's Species Importation List as a Group I semi-domesticated animal (no permit), the same treatment already given to the fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) and the house mouse (Mus musculus). As a first step, request the current Director's Species Importation List and a written statement of what group Rattus rattus is in today, and whether captive-bred animals are treated differently from wild ones. This is a species-listing gap, not a domestication question: captive-bred roof rats are tame, raised entirely indoors, and never released, so they meet the rule's own definition of a species the Director may designate semi-domesticated, one 'commonly tamed, raised, bred or sold in captivity' (19.35.7.7). Domestication, not wild ancestry, is what the rule rewards: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are domestic, and the Department already extended Group I to the fancy rat and the house mouse despite their wild origins. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/), so a captive-bred roof rat qualifies on the same basis, one species over. Whether a captive-bred Rattus rattus is domesticated in the same sense as the fancy rat already on the list is a question for the Department to decide; the petitioner is not asking it to assume any particular answer.

Where the lever really is: This is an AGENCY problem, a species-listing gap, not a law-as-written problem, so the lever is the Department of Game & Fish, and the agency can fix it without legislation. The roof rat is named on no statutory prohibited list. Its prohibition is a regulatory default: 19.35.7.10(A)(5) provides that any species not on the Director's Species Importation List 'will be designated group IV until such time as another determination is made by the director.' Two facts make this an agency lever: (1) the same rule gives the Director discretionary power to designate a species semi-domesticated (Group I) 'in those instances where individual members of such species are commonly tamed, raised, bred or sold in captivity' (19.35.7.7), which captive-bred roof rats are, and which the Department already applied to the fancy rat and the house mouse; (2) because the Director assigns the list groups, the Director can move R. rattus off the Group IV default by a written determination, with no statutory change, which is exactly the 'another determination is made by the director' the rule contemplates. The statute (NMSA 17-3-32) only creates the import-permit requirement and exempts 'domesticated animals'; it does not itself list R. rattus as prohibited, which confirms the gap lives in the agency's list, where the agency holds the cure. The petitioner should be candid that the outcome is not assured: New Mexico is a high-plague state (Yersinia pestis is endemic in wild rodents) and state pest materials treat the roof rat as an invasive disease vector, so the Director could decline a Group I placement or instead place it in a permitted group (Group II or III). A realistic ask therefore offers the Department two acceptable outcomes: best case, add captive-bred R. rattus to Group I beside the fancy rat; failing that, place it in Group II or III so that at least a permitted pathway exists rather than a flat Group IV prohibition. The Legislature is a backstop only if the Department refuses both; the primary channel is a written petition or inquiry to NMDGF requesting a Director's determination and the current list.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • New Mexico Department of Game & Fish (Department of Wildlife) - Special Use Permits Program / Species Importation (executive / agency) — DGF.Permits@dgf.nm.gov
    Primary and decisive lever. The Special Use Permits Program (LE Field Operations Division) maintains the Director's Species Importation List and processes importation and special-use permits, and the Director has explicit regulatory authority (19.35.7.7) to designate a species semi-domesticated (Group I) by written determination, exactly the change needed for captive-bred R. rattus. Use the Special Use Permits inbox (DGF.Permits@dgf.nm.gov, shown on the Department's permits materials) to request the current list, ask what group R. rattus is in, and petition to add it to Group I. The general licensing/customer inbox ispa@dgf.nm.gov and the contact page are alternates.
  • Director's Species Importation List (official current PDF) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Verified official download of the current list (dated January 3, 2023). Read it first to confirm R. rattus is absent (and thus defaulting to Group IV) and to cite the exact Group I entries for the fancy rat ('Rattus norvegicus / Rat, Common') and the house mouse ('Mus musculus / Mouse, Common') as your precedent when you write to the Department.
  • New Mexico Legislature - Find My Legislator (legislature) — official contact page
    Secondary backstop ONLY. The agency can and should fix this itself, so go here only if the Department declines to make a Director's determination; your legislator can prompt the agency or, if ever needed, pursue a statutory clarification. Official tool to find and contact your own state representative and senator.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the New Mexico Department of Game & Fish, Special Use Permits Program (Director's Species Importation List):

I am writing about a gap in the Director's Species Importation List under 19.35.7 NMAC. The domesticated pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) does not appear on the list, so under 19.35.7.10(A)(5) it defaults to Group IV (prohibited for the general public), even though the closely related fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus / 'Rat, Common') and the house mouse (Mus musculus / 'Mouse, Common') are both Group I semi-domesticated and need no permit.

The captive-bred roof rats kept by hobbyists are tame, raised entirely indoors, and never released to the wild. They meet the rule's own definition of a species the Director may designate semi-domesticated, one 'commonly tamed, raised, bred or sold in captivity' (19.35.7.7). This is a listing gap, not a question of domestication. Domestication, not wild ancestry, is what the rule rewards: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are domestic, and the Department already placed the fancy rat and the house mouse in Group I despite their wild origins. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred roof rat qualifies on the same basis.

I respectfully request: (1) a copy of the current Director's Species Importation List and a written statement of what group Rattus rattus is in today, and whether captive-bred animals are treated differently from wild ones; and (2) that the Director make a determination adding captive-bred, domesticated Rattus rattus to Group I, on the same basis as the fancy rat. If the Department concludes some oversight is warranted, I would ask in the alternative that it place captive-bred Rattus rattus in Group II or III, so that at least a permitted pathway exists rather than a flat Group IV prohibition.

Thank you for your consideration.

[Your name]
[Your city, New Mexico]
[Your email]
Español
Al Departamento de Caza y Pesca de Nuevo Mexico, Programa de Permisos de Uso Especial (Lista de Importacion de Especies del Director):

Les escribo respecto a un vacio en la Lista de Importacion de Especies del Director, conforme a 19.35.7 NMAC. La rata de techo domesticada (Rattus rattus) no aparece en la lista, por lo que, segun 19.35.7.10(A)(5), queda por defecto en el Grupo IV (prohibida para el publico en general), aunque la rata fancy estrechamente emparentada (Rattus norvegicus / 'Rat, Common') y el raton domestico (Mus musculus / 'Mouse, Common') son ambos del Grupo I semidomesticados y no requieren permiso.

Las ratas de techo criadas en cautiverio que mantienen los aficionados son mansas, se crian totalmente en interiores y nunca se liberan a la naturaleza. Cumplen con la propia definicion de la norma de una especie que el director puede designar semidomesticada: aquella 'comunmente amansada, criada, reproducida o vendida en cautiverio' (19.35.7.7). Se trata de un vacio en la lista, no de una cuestion de domesticacion. Lo que la norma premia es la domesticacion, no la ascendencia silvestre: el perro desciende del lobo y el gato de un felido silvestre, y aun asi ambos son domesticos, y el Departamento ya coloco a la rata fancy y al raton domestico en el Grupo I pese a su origen silvestre. La rata fancy es la propia rata parda silvestre, domesticada apenas en el siglo XIX, de modo que una rata de techo criada en cautiverio califica sobre la misma base.

Solicito respetuosamente: (1) una copia de la Lista de Importacion de Especies del Director vigente y una declaracion por escrito sobre en que grupo se encuentra hoy Rattus rattus y si los animales criados en cautiverio reciben un trato distinto al de los silvestres; y (2) que el Director emita una determinacion para anadir a Rattus rattus domesticada y criada en cautiverio al Grupo I, sobre la misma base que la rata fancy. Si el Departamento concluye que se justifica alguna supervision, solicitaria en su lugar que coloque a la Rattus rattus criada en cautiverio en el Grupo II o III, de modo que al menos exista una via con permiso en lugar de una prohibicion absoluta del Grupo IV.

Gracias por su atencion.

[Su nombre]
[Su ciudad, Nuevo Mexico]
[Su correo electronico]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • 19.35.7 NMAC - Importation of Live Non-Domesticated Animals, Birds and Fish (19.35.7.7 definitions of non-domesticated/semi-domesticated and Director's discretion; 19.35.7.8 unlawful to import without permit except Group I; 19.35.7.10(A) Group I-IV definitions; 19.35.7.10(A)(5) unlisted species default to Group IV; 19.35.7.12 containment + veterinary requirements for permit holders; 19.35.7.19 no release without permit) — New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish / State Records Center and Archives
  • N.M. Admin. Code 19.35.7.7 (Cornell LII mirror): 'Non-domesticated animal' = 'any animal species that is wild by nature not listed as semi-domesticated or protected under chapter 17 NMSA, 1978'; 'Semi-domesticated animal' = the director may designate a species as such 'in those instances where individual members of such species are commonly tamed, raised, bred or sold in captivity' — Cornell Legal Information Institute
  • Director's Species Importation List (official PDF, dated January 3, 2023, 'Updated 2023') - Group I lists 'Mammal Rodent Muridae Rattus norvegicus Rat, Common I' and 'Mammal Rodent Muridae Mus musculus Mouse, Common I'; contains NO Rattus rattus / roof rat / black rat / ship rat entry and no genus/family catch-all (verified by direct PDF text extraction of all 27 pages); legend repeats the 19.35.7.10(A)(5) default-to-Group-IV rule — New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish, LE Field Operations Division / Special Use Permits Program
  • NMSA 1978 Section 17-3-32 - Importing game animals [live animals]; permits (misdemeanor to import any live animals/birds/fish without a Game & Fish permit, 'except domesticated animals or domesticated fowl or fish from government hatcheries'; annotation: 'the burden is on importer to prove' the animals were domesticated) — New Mexico Legislature (via Justia)
  • 19.31.10 NMAC Section 19.31.10.10(C) - Hunting and Fishing, Manner and Method ('It shall be unlawful to purchase, possess, barter, transfer, transport, sell, or offer to sell any live animal listed as group II, III or IV on the directors species importation list or any protected species without a department issued permit or license') — New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish / State Records Center and Archives
  • 19.30.9 NMAC - Game and Fish Licenses and Permits (importation/special-use permit fee tiers: $15 for 1-5 animals, $75 for 6-99, $300 for 100+, optional $25 expedite; applies to the institutional Group IV permits, not to a public pet permit, which does not exist) — New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish / State Records Center and Archives
  • 19.35.7 NMAC (full-text mirror) - Importation of Live Non-Domestic Animals, Birds and Fish (confirms the Group I-IV definitions, the 19.35.7.10(A)(5) unlisted-to-Group-IV default, 19.35.7.8 unlawful-import rule, and 19.35.7.19 no-release rule) — New Mexico Dept of Game & Fish (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center)
  • USDA APHIS, Animal Welfare Act licensing (Class A breeder license applies to wholesale/sight-unseen dealers; direct-to-consumer and de minimis hobby sales exempt; research rats of genus Rattus excluded from the AWA) — USDA APHIS
  • USDA APHIS / CDC, Bring a Pet Rodent into the United States (federal international-import layer; CDC bars rodents of African origin under 42 CFR 71.56; R. rattus is Asian in origin) — USDA APHIS / CDC

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat, rata de tejado, rata negra, non-domesticated animal, semi-domesticated animal, Director's Species Importation List, Group IV.
