item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Nevada? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Nevada

Summary. Nevada is permissive and the roof rat is almost certainly fine, with one wording gap that turns on interpretation rather than any ban. NRS 501.097 defines 'wildlife' as any wild mammal 'found naturally in a wild state... whether raised in captivity or not,' and the key exemption, NAC 503.140(1)(j), frees 'Domesticated races of rats and mice' from any NDOW permit or license to possess, transport, import, or export. That exemption is generic: unlike Kentucky or Virginia it names no species at all, so it neither singles out the fancy rat nor excludes the roof rat. R. rattus is NOT on Nevada's prohibited-species list (NAC 503.110 names only the African multimammate rat, genus Mastomys); the explicit prohibition of that one exotic rat genus while leaving R. rattus off strongly implies roof rats are not banned. NAC 503.140(3) expressly allows lawfully acquired exempt species to be sold in Nevada with no NDOW dealer license, and NAC 503.140(1) lets them be imported with no NDOW importation permit. The single open point is interpretive: NDOW has published nothing confirming that 'domesticated races of rats' reaches captive-bred R. rattus specifically, so all four activities read as unregulated by NDOW but remain officially untested. The Nevada Department of Agriculture's import rules (NAC 571) name no CVI or entry permit for small pet rodents. Two firm limits attach regardless: never release a roof rat (NAC 503.140(2) bars release; the wild roof rat is a declared vertebrate pest under NRS 555), and local Clark County / Las Vegas / Henderson business or breeder licensing applies to commercial activity regardless of species.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Nevada-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Nevada is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-14

NAC 503.140(1) provides that 'the following animals may be possessed, transported, imported and exported without a permit or license issued by the Department,' and item (j) is 'Domesticated races of rats and mice.' A captive-bred, multi-generational, tame roof rat is the natural fit for a 'domesticated race of rats,' so no NDOW possession license applies. Two facts reinforce a no-ban reading: R. rattus is absent from the NAC 503.110 prohibited-species list (which names the African multimammate rat, genus Mastomys (=Praomys), but no Rattus), and NRS 501.097 defines 'wildlife' as a wild mammal 'found naturally in a wild state... whether raised in captivity or not,' language that does not comfortably capture a domesticated captive line. The gap is that the exemption names no species at all, and NDOW has published no determination confirming it reaches R. rattus specifically rather than just the universally recognized fancy rat (R. norvegicus). Officially untested, so unregulated/unclear; the honest confidence in that unclear status is medium. General anti-cruelty law (NRS 574) still applies.

Sources: Nevada Legislature, Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII), Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII)

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-14

Breeding is unregulated by NDOW on the same footing as possession: if a captive-bred roof rat is a 'domesticated race of rats' exempt under NAC 503.140, propagation needs no state wildlife permit, and Nevada imposes no rodent-breeder license, quota, or facility standard at the state level. The Nevada Department of Agriculture does not run a state pet-shop or breeder licensing program for small rodents, and the USDA Animal Welfare Act generally exempts small-scale pet/feeder rodent breeders (and excludes laboratory Rattus from the Act entirely), reaching only wholesale/sight-unseen dealers. The same unmapped-exemption gap as 'keep' applies: if NDOW were to read R. rattus outside the exemption, the NAC 504 possession-license framework would apply instead. Commercial-scale breeding still needs local (Clark County / Las Vegas / Henderson) business or kennel/pet-shop licensing and zoning approval regardless of species.

Sources: Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII), Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII), USDA APHIS

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-14

NAC 503.140(3) provides that 'Except as otherwise provided in subsection 4, lawfully acquired species listed in this section may be sold in Nevada,' so if a captive-bred roof rat is within the 'domesticated races of rats and mice' exemption, private sale or free adoption needs no NDOW wildlife dealer permit. NAC 503.140(4) preserves all other applicable federal/state law and county/city ordinances, so a commercial seller still needs the relevant local business license, but the rats themselves carry no state-level sale restriction (Las Vegas microchipping/point-of-sale rules cover only dogs and cats, not small rodents). The same interpretive gap applies: the exemption that authorizes the sale names no species, so the conclusion rides on NDOW reading R. rattus into 'domesticated races of rats.' Officially untested.

Sources: Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII), Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII)

Transport & import   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-14

NAC 503.140(1) lets exempt species be 'transported, imported and exported without a permit or license issued by the Department,' so if a captive-bred roof rat is a 'domesticated race of rats,' there is no NDOW importation permit and no port-of-entry declaration. If an officer instead treated a roof rat as regulated wildlife, the restricted-species rules of NAC 503.110 would apply: NAC 503.110(3) reserves importation/possession permits for institutions (zoos, universities, research, aquaculture, educational nonprofits), and NAC 503.110(4) lets a restricted species be shipped through Nevada only with proof of lawful possession from the origin state, a health certificate, under 48 hours, and not unloaded or released. On the agriculture side, the Nevada Department of Agriculture's import rules (NAC 571) require CVIs/entry permits for listed livestock and certain companion animals (dogs/cats under NAC 571.080, rabbits, horses) and ban importing high-risk rabies vectors (NAC 571.075), but name no CVI or entry permit for small pet rodents; the NDA directs unlisted species to its permit office. So a pet roof rat reads as importable with no NDOW permit and no NDA CVI, subject to the same species-mapping gap. Never release a roof rat: NAC 503.140(2) bars releasing listed species into the wild, and the wild roof rat is a declared vertebrate pest under NRS 555.

Sources: Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII), Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII), Nevada Department of Agriculture, Division of Animal Industry, Nevada Legislature

Restrictions & responsibilities

Never release a roof rat into the wild. NAC 503.140(2) provides that 'Species listed in this section must not be released into the wild, except as otherwise authorized by the Department in writing,' and the wild roof rat is a declared vertebrate pest under NRS Chapter 555 (the NRS 555 definition of vertebrate pest expressly includes 'rat'). A released or escaped roof rat loses any pet-exemption protection and becomes subject to pest eradication. Keep roof rats strictly indoors in secure caging.
  • Keep roof rats strictly indoors in escape-proof caging; never release or abandon one.
  • Rehome responsibly to another keeper rather than releasing.

Source: Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII), Nevada Legislature

Commercial activity (a breeding operation or a retail seller) needs local municipal/county business licensing and zoning approval, regardless of species. NAC 503.140(4) preserves all applicable county/city ordinances. Cities such as Carlin and Elko require a kennel/pet-shop business license to operate commercially, and a high-volume operation in a residentially zoned area may need a home-occupation permit or variance. The rats themselves carry no state-level sale restriction; Las Vegas point-of-sale/microchipping rules (LVMC 7.42) apply only to dogs and cats, not small rodents.
  • If breeding or selling commercially, obtain the local city/county business license (and a kennel/pet-shop license where required).
  • Confirm residential zoning allows the activity, or seek a home-occupation permit/variance.
  • Private hobby keeping and free rehoming need no business license.

Where: Relevant city/county business-licensing office (e.g., City of Las Vegas, Clark County, City of Henderson, City of Elko). · Fees: Local business-license fees vary by jurisdiction; no NDOW fee applies to exempt species.

Source: Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII), City of Las Vegas

Interpretive caveat (latent, not a current barrier): NDOW has published no determination that the NAC 503.140(1)(j) exemption for 'domesticated races of rats and mice' reaches captive-bred R. rattus by name (the text names no species). If NDOW were ever to read R. rattus as regulated 'wildlife' under NRS 501.097, the NAC 504 possession-license framework would apply, and NAC 504.490 will not even issue a rehabilitation permit for 'rats.' The natural reading and the absence of R. rattus from the NAC 503.110 prohibited list both point the other way, so this is a gap to close with a written NDOW confirmation, not a present prohibition. Routed to NDOW as an open question.
  • For certainty, ask NDOW in writing to confirm the NAC 503.140 exemption includes captive-bred R. rattus (see contacts).
  • Keep acquisition records (breeder/source) showing the animal is a captive-bred domesticated line rather than wild-trapped.

Where: Nevada Department of Wildlife (Wildlife Diversity / Law Enforcement).

Source: Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII), Nevada Legislature, Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII)

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Official sources

  • NRS 501.097, 'Wildlife' defined: 'any wild mammal, wild bird, fish, reptile, amphibian, mollusk or crustacean found naturally in a wild state, whether indigenous to Nevada or not and whether raised in captivity or not.' — Nevada Legislature
  • NAC 503.140, Species for which certain permits and licenses are not required: subsection 1 lets listed animals 'be possessed, transported, imported and exported without a permit or license issued by the Department,' item (j) 'Domesticated races of rats and mice'; subsection 2 bars release into the wild; subsection 3 'Except as otherwise provided in subsection 4, lawfully acquired species listed in this section may be sold in Nevada'; subsection 4 preserves other federal/state law and county/city ordinances. — Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII)
  • NAC 503.110, Restrictions on importation, transportation and possession of certain species: prohibited-mammal list names '(6) Multimammate Rat or Mouse... All species in the genus Mastomys (=Praomys)'; no Rattus anywhere. Subsection 3 reserves restricted-species import/possession permits for institutions; subsection 4 sets the 48-hour through-transit rule (origin proof of lawful possession + health certificate, under 48 hours, not unloaded/released). — Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII)
  • NAC 504.490 (Issuance; general conditions): the Department will not issue a wildlife rehabilitation permit for 'Coyotes, foxes, skunks, raccoons, rats, mice, ground squirrels or bats' (relevant only if R. rattus were treated as regulated wildlife rather than a domesticated race). — Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners / NDOW (via Cornell LII)
  • Nevada Department of Agriculture, Import Requirements: CVIs/entry permits listed for livestock, horses, poultry, big cats, primates, rabbits, and CVIs for dogs/cats/ferrets, reptiles, etc.; small pet rodents (rats, mice) are not listed, with unlisted species directed to the permit office (775-353-3709 / entrypermits@agri.nv.gov). NAC 571 governs (571.075 import bans on fox/skunk/raccoon, 571.080 dogs/cats, 571.085 other species). — Nevada Department of Agriculture, Division of Animal Industry
  • NRS Chapter 555, Control of Insects, Pests and Noxious Weeds: the wild roof rat is a 'vertebrate pest' (the statutory definition of vertebrate pest expressly includes 'rat'); a released/escaped roof rat is subject to pest control, reinforcing the NAC 503.140(2) no-release rule. — Nevada Legislature
  • USDA APHIS, Animal Welfare Act licensing: Class A breeder licensing reaches wholesale/sight-unseen dealers; small-scale direct-to-consumer pet/feeder rodent breeders are de minimis exempt and laboratory rats of the genus Rattus are excluded from the AWA entirely. — USDA APHIS
  • City of Las Vegas Municipal Code (Title 6 business licensing; LVMC 7.42 point-of-sale/microchipping for dogs and cats only): a commercial seller needs a local business license, but small rodents are outside the dog/cat point-of-sale rules. — City of Las Vegas

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat, domesticated races of rats and mice, Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI).

Last reviewed 2026-06-14. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in New York? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › New York

Summary. Keeping, breeding, and selling pet roof rats is legal in New York — both statewide and in New York City. The state classifies Rattus rattus as 'unprotected wildlife,' which may be possessed and sold without restriction (ECL §11-0917(2)); it is not a prohibited 'wild animal' and not on the invasive-species list. NYC's Health Code bans only 'large rodents,' so small pet rats are allowed (a Class P pet-shop permit is needed only for commercial retail). Bringing a rat into NY from another state needs a 30-day vet health certificate; international movement is federally restricted.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the New York-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where New York is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

New York classifies Rattus rattus as 'unprotected wildlife,' which ECL §11-0917(2) says 'may be possessed, transported, bought and sold without restriction.' It is not a prohibited 'wild animal' (ECL §11-0512 / §11-0103(6)(e) lists primates, big cats, canids, bears, venomous reptiles, crocodilians — not rodents) and is not on the state invasive-species list (6 NYCRR Part 575). New York CITY allows it too: the NYC Health Code (Art. 161.01(b)(14)) bans only 'large rodents' (beaver, capybara, prairie dog, porcupine, etc.); small domestic rats are permitted.

Sources: NY State Senate (Consolidated Laws), NY State Senate, NYC DOHMH

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

No New York breeder license for rodents — the 'Pet Dealer' law (Agriculture & Markets Law Art. 26-A, §400) defines 'animal' as only dogs and cats, so breeding rats at any volume is outside it; only the general anti-cruelty rules apply. In NYC, hobby breeding is fine, but sanitation/nuisance rules (odor, escapes) apply.

Sources: NY Consolidated Laws

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Statewide, selling roof rats is legal — a retailer must just give buyers written/digital care instructions for 'small animals' (which the law lists as including rats), per General Business Law §391-t. In New York CITY, a commercial retail seller needs a Class P 'Pet Shop' permit (NYCHC §161.09); NYC's Local Law 132 (2024) banned the retail sale of dogs, cats, guinea pigs and rabbits, but rats remain sellable. Giving rats away or private/face-to-face placement needs no permit. (Federal USDA licensing applies to wholesale/sight-unseen sales — see United States.)

Sources: NY State Senate, NYC DOHMH

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Within New York, no permit is required. Bringing a rat INTO New York from another state requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (health certificate) issued within 30 days (1CRR-NY 67.2); no rabies vaccine is required for rodents, and enforcement against a private owner with a single pet is reportedly minimal. International import/export is restricted at the federal level (USFWS Form 3-177; CDC African-rodent ban) — see United States.

Sources: NY Dept. of Agriculture & Markets

Restrictions & responsibilities

In New York CITY, a commercial retail seller of rats needs a Class P 'Pet Shop' permit from DOHMH (facility inspections; integrated pest management). Rats remain legally sellable in NYC even after Local Law 132 (2024) banned retail sale of dogs/cats/guinea pigs/rabbits. Private/face-to-face placement and giveaways need no permit.
  • If running an NYC retail storefront, obtain a DOHMH Class P pet-shop permit

Forms: NYC Health Code Ch. 5 — Pet Shops · Where: NYC DOHMH · Fees: Municipal pet-shop permit fee

Source: NYC DOHMH

Statewide, a retailer selling rats must give the buyer written or digital care instructions for the species at the time of sale (GBS §391-t), and keep copies on file.

Source: NY State Senate

Bringing a rat into New York from another state requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) issued within 30 days by a USDA-accredited vet (1CRR-NY 67.2). No rabies vaccine is required for rodents.

Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Ohio

Summary. Keeping, breeding, and selling a roof rat is legal in Ohio. The Dangerous Wild Animals Act (ORC ch. 935, post-Zanesville) lists big cats, bears, primates, large constrictors and the like — no rodents. The roof rat is not native wildlife regulated by ODNR (it's actually named a nuisance pest), no Ohio prohibited/exotic list captures the genus Rattus, and Ohio's commercial breeder/dealer licensing (ORC ch. 956) is dogs-only. The one nuance is interstate IMPORT: Ohio's general animal-import rule likely requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection for an incoming pet rat (rodents aren't named in either the domestic or non-domestic import rule), so confirm with the State Veterinarian.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Oklahoma? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Oklahoma

Summary. Oklahoma is now AGENCY-CONFIRMED, and the answer is clean and favorable. The Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation (Wildlife Diversity Program together with its Law Enforcement Division) confirmed in writing (June 2026) that OAC 800:25-25-3(a)(25) exempts BOTH the Norway rat and the roof rat (Rattus rattus) from ODWC's import/export permit, its commercial breeder license, and its noncommercial breeder license. Keeping, breeding, and selling or trading roof rats are NOT prohibited and require NO ODWC permit; importing or exporting requires no permit and no health certificate. ODWC treats R. rattus as 'not normally found in the wild' (a non-native species) for purposes of that exemption, which resolves the earlier feral-population ambiguity in the keeper's favor. ODWC recommends standard biosecurity to prevent accidental escapes (never release one). The only open thread is the Oklahoma Department of Agriculture, Food & Forestry (ODAFF), which ODWC suggested contacting in case it enforces separate rules; that inquiry has been sent.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Pennsylvania? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Pennsylvania

Summary. Keeping, breeding, and rehoming a captive-bred roof rat appears legal in Pennsylvania with no permit. The state's 'exotic wildlife' permit list (34 Pa.C.S. §2961) covers only large carnivores (bears, big cats, wolves, coyotes), and the Game Commission's import/possession ban (58 Pa. Code §137.1) is a closed list that doesn't include any rat or rodent. One technicality: the Game Code's literal 'wild animal' definition could label any rat (even the common fancy rat) 'wildlife,' but no active rule turns that into a ban or permit for pet rodents — so it's best treated as legal-but-worth-confirming with the Game Commission. Importing a pet rat may call for a vet health certificate; never release one.

Preliminary — built from official sources but not yet agency-confirmed; a solid starting point. Know the local rule? Tell us.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Pennsylvania-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Pennsylvania is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

No Pennsylvania statute/regulation requires a permit to keep a pet rat. R. rattus is not 'exotic wildlife' (34 Pa.C.S. §2961 lists only large carnivores) and is not on the §137.1 possession-prohibition list (felids, canids, ursids, raccoons, nutria, skunks, primates, listed T&E/injurious). The only caveat: the literal §102 / 1 Pa.C.S. §1991 definition technically labels any non-(equine/bovine/sheep/goat/pig) mammal a 'wild animal,' but no active rule converts that into a rodent permit/ban.

Sources: Pennsylvania General Assembly, Pennsylvania General Assembly, PA Game Commission / PA Code & Bulletin

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

No propagation/breeding permit applies to pet rodents — the Game Commission's propagation and exotic-wildlife-dealer permits attach to enumerated game/furbearer and exotic-carnivore species, not rats. Breeding captive-bred roof rats is unregulated (same definitional caveat as keeping).

Sources: Pennsylvania General Assembly, PA Game Commission / PA Code & Bulletin

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling/giving a pet rat is not 'exotic wildlife dealer' activity (that permit covers only §2961 carnivores) and rats aren't on the §137.1 sale-prohibition list. A high-volume commercial animal dealer could fall under PA's Domestic Animal Law dealer license (3 Pa.C.S.; broad 'domestic animal' incl. captive wild animals), but ordinary private placement/free adoption is outside it.

Sources: Pennsylvania General Assembly, PA Game Commission / PA Code & Bulletin

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Intrastate transport isn't restricted. For IMPORT, PDA (Bureau of Animal Health) animal-health rules govern; a CVI is the general interstate mechanism but PDA notes not all states require a CVI for small/pocket pets, so treat it as recommended/possibly required and confirm with BAHDS. Game Commission §137.1 import-permit rules don't apply (rats aren't listed). Never release a pet rat (58 Pa. Code §137.1/§137.2).

Sources: PA Dept of Agriculture, BAHDS, PA Game Commission / PA Code & Bulletin

Restrictions & responsibilities

A veterinary health certificate (CVI) may be requested to bring a pet rat into Pennsylvania but isn't clearly required for pocket pets — confirm with PDA-BAHDS. Never release a pet rat into the wild (58 Pa. Code §137.1/§137.2) — it's illegal and ecologically harmful.

Where: PA Dept of Agriculture, Bureau of Animal Health & Diagnostic Services

Source: PA Dept of Agriculture, BAHDS, PA Game Commission / PA Code & Bulletin

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Pennsylvania

In Pennsylvania, keeping, breeding, and rehoming a captive-bred, domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) appears to be legal with no permit required. The state's "exotic wildlife" permit list (34 Pa.C.S. §2961) names only large carnivores: bears, big cats, wolves, and coyotes. The Game Commission's import/possession prohibition (58 Pa. Code §137.1) is a closed, enumerated list that contains no rat or rodent. The one snag is definitional. The Game Code's broad "wild animal" wording (34 Pa.C.S. §102, via 1 Pa.C.S. §1991) literally covers every mammal that is not a horse, cow, sheep, goat, or pig, which on paper would label even the ordinary pet "fancy" rat (Rattus norvegicus) "wildlife." No active rule turns that wording into a permit or ban for pet rodents, but the gap leaves owners unsure. The issue is not a law that bans the species. It is the absence of a written confirmation from the agency that captive-bred pet rats fall outside the exotic-wildlife and §137.1 schemes.

The ask: Ask the Pennsylvania Game Commission for a short written confirmation (an informal clarification letter or a formal declaratory ruling) stating that a captive-bred, domesticated roof rat kept as a pet is not regulated "exotic wildlife" under 34 Pa.C.S. §2961 and is not on the §137.1 importation/possession-prohibition list, and therefore may be kept, bred, and rehomed without an exotic-wildlife possession permit, an importation permit, or any other Commission authorization, notwithstanding the literal "wild animal" definition. On that definitional point, the same wording would also cover the common fancy rat, just as the dog (descended from the wolf) and the cat (descended from a wild felid) would fall under a literal wild-ancestry reading, yet all are treated as domestic because what matters is domestication, generations bred for tameness, not wild origin. The already-kept pet fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred R. rattus is the same case one species over. Whether a captive-bred R. rattus sits outside the wildlife scheme on that basis is for the Commission to confirm, not a result it is asked to presume. Separately, ask the PA Department of Agriculture (BAHDS) whether a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection is required to bring a pet rodent into the state. On domestication background, see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/.

Where the lever really is: This is a clarification problem, not a bad-law problem, so the lever is the agency, not the legislature. The statute and regulation that would have to list roof rats for a ban or permit to exist do not. 34 Pa.C.S. §2961 defines "exotic wildlife" as a short, closed set of large carnivores, and 58 Pa. Code §137.1 is a closed, enumerated import/possession list. Neither contains any rodent. There is no statutory list to add to and no on-point law being misapplied. The only live ambiguity is the over-broad definitional language in 34 Pa.C.S. §102 / 1 Pa.C.S. §1991, which the Commission does not enforce against pet rodents. The fix is a written agency clarification or declaratory ruling confirming that pets like R. rattus sit outside the exotic-wildlife and §137.1 scheme, which the Commission can issue without any legislative change. Going to the legislature would be the wrong tool, because there is no prohibition statute to repeal and no positive list to amend. A bill is worth considering only as a fallback if the Commission were to take the position that the literal "wild animal" definition bans or burdens pet rodents, which it currently does not. Use the legislature contact only in that contingency.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Pennsylvania Game Commission — Contact Us / staff inquiry form (executive / agency) — official contact page
    Official PGC public contact form (linked from the Commission's own Contact Information page) for routing a question to staff. Use it to request written confirmation that a captive-bred pet roof rat is outside the §2961 exotic-wildlife and §137.1 prohibition schemes and needs no Commission permit.
  • Pennsylvania Game Commission — License Division (executive / agency) — pgclicdiv@pa.gov
    Verified official Commission inbox (listed on the PGC Contact Information page) handling licensing/permit questions; the right place to ask, in writing, whether any exotic-wildlife or importation permit applies to a pet rodent — and to request that the answer be put in writing.
  • Pennsylvania General Assembly — Find My Legislator (fallback only) (legislature) — official contact page
    Official tool to identify and contact your state senator and representative. Use ONLY as a contingency — i.e., if the Commission ever asserts the literal 'wild animal' definition bans or burdens pet rodents — to seek a statutory clarification exempting domesticated pet rats. Not needed to fix anything today.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Pennsylvania Game Commission,

I am writing to request a written clarification about keeping a captive-bred, domesticated pet roof rat (Rattus rattus). I want to comply fully and would like the Commission's position in writing.

As I read the law, roof rats are not regulated 'exotic wildlife' under 34 Pa.C.S. §2961, which lists only large carnivores, and no rat or rodent appears on the closed importation/possession list in 58 Pa. Code §137.1. The only ambiguity I see is the broad 'wild animal' definition in 34 Pa.C.S. §102, which would literally reach even the common pet fancy rat, yet no active rule appears to apply it to pet rodents.

That same literal wording about wild origins would also reach the dog (descended from the wolf) and the cat (descended from a wild felid), which are recognized as domestic animals, because what makes an animal domestic is generations bred for tameness, not the wild ancestry of its species. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over. I raise this only to ask the Commission to confirm how the definition applies to a captive-bred pet rat, not to suggest any particular answer.

The rats I am asking about are captive-bred, hand-tame, kept entirely indoors as pets, and never released into the wild. The concern is the species label, not the animal's tameness.

Please confirm in writing that a captive-bred pet roof rat may be kept, bred, and rehomed without an exotic-wildlife possession permit, an importation permit, or any other Commission authorization. A short clarification letter or declaratory ruling would settle the question for responsible owners.

Thank you for your time.

[Your name]
[Your county / contact information]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

  • 34 Pa.C.S. §102 — definitions ('wild animals' = all mammals other than domestic per 1 Pa.C.S. §1991) — Pennsylvania General Assembly

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Puerto Rico? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Puerto Rico

Summary. In the U.S. territory of Puerto Rico, keeping and privately breeding a captive-bred roof rat ('rata negra', Rattus rattus) is legal without a wildlife permit. The DRNA wildlife regulation (Reglamento 6765, 2004) lists 'Rattus rattus' by binomial in its Apéndice 4, titled 'Especies exóticas de menor riesgo y elegibles para importación sin permiso', and Article 7.03 makes Apéndice 4 species eligible for 'importación, posesión y venta sin permiso'. The fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) sits in the same appendix with identical standing, so there is no species trap. Only captive-born animals may be imported or sold, and releasing any of them into the wild is flatly prohibited. Three conditions attach to commerce and movement, not to ownership. First, running a standing exotic-species buy/sell business (negocio de compraventa) needs DRNA's $150 dealer permit under Art. 7.01, because R. rattus carries no asterisk in Apéndice 4 and only single-asterisk agricultural/domestic species (cattle, dog, cat, pig) are exempt from that business permit; free private adoption and one-off private transfers are outside it. Second, importing the animal into the territory triggers the Puerto Rico Department of Agriculture's independent agricultural quarantine: a pre-shipment import permit plus a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection issued within 30 days, with exotic species also having to satisfy DRNA. Third, the layer is in flux: Ley Núm. 93-2025 (Ley para el Manejo de Especies Introducidas, signed Aug 1 2025) directs DRNA to write a new regulation sorting introduced species into prohibida / restringida / no restringida, and its statement of motives names the rata negra. No draft rule is posted yet, so the watch-item is prospective, not current.

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

DRNA Reglamento 6765 lists 'Rattus rattus' by binomial in Apéndice 4 ('Especies exóticas de menor riesgo y elegibles para importación sin permiso'), in the MAMÍFEROS section, with the Spanish name 'Rata negra' and the qualifier '(variedad de laboratorio)' and no asterisk. Art. 7.03(A) provides that Apéndice 4 species 'se consideran de menor riesgo... y son elegibles para importación, posesión y venta sin permiso', and that it is illegal only to possess exotics NOT listed in Apéndice 4. So a private individual may keep a captive-bred black rat with no wildlife permit, registration, facility inspection, or fee. The fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is in the same appendix with identical standing. Releasing the animal into the wild is flatly prohibited (Art. 7.03(A)).

Sources: Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales (DRNA), Microjuris al Día (mirror of the DRNA regulation), Asamblea Legislativa de Puerto Rico

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Art. 7.03(D) expressly permits 'la reproducción en cautiverio de las especies incluidas en el Apéndice 4', and requires prior DRNA permission ('permiso previo del Departamento') only for species followed by a double asterisk (**). R. rattus carries no asterisk in Apéndice 4, so private, non-commercial captive breeding of pet black rats needs no DRNA breeding permit, facility standard, or inventory report. The regulation also expects only captive-born individuals in commerce (Art. 7.03(B)). The fancy rat is treated identically.

Sources: Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales (DRNA), Microjuris al Día (mirror of the DRNA regulation)

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-14

Two layers. Free/private transfer: Art. 7.03(A) lets Apéndice 4 species be imported, possessed, and sold 'sin permiso', so giving a captive-bred black rat away or rehoming it through free vetted adoption needs no permit. Commercial business: Art. 7.01(B) requires a $150 permit to 'operar un negocio de compraventa de especies exóticas', and exempts only 'especies agrícolas o domésticas... aquellos animales marcados con un asterisco (*) en el Apéndice 4'. R. rattus (and R. norvegicus) carry no asterisk, so a standing buy/sell rattery needs the $150 DRNA dealer permit, plus a municipal patente, ARP use permit, Hacienda debt certificate, escape-proof facility, and is subject to surprise inspection (Art. 7.01(C)-(F), 7.02, 7.06). Only captive-born individuals may be sold (Art. 7.03(B)). The dividing line between a hobbyist who occasionally rehomes a litter and a 'negocio de compraventa' is not quantified in the text, which is the source of the medium confidence.

Sources: Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales (DRNA), Microjuris al Día (mirror of the DRNA regulation)

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-14

Intra-island transport of a permit-free Apéndice 4 animal is not separately restricted, provided it is secured (no risk of release; escape must be reported to DRNA within 24 hours, Art. 7.02(F)). IMPORT into Puerto Rico triggers two layers. DRNA: Art. 7.03(B) requires every shipment to carry a 'certificado veterinario' and limits import to captive-born individuals; because R. rattus is in Apéndice 4, no separate DRNA import permit is required. Puerto Rico Department of Agriculture (SAHO): even though PR is inside the U.S. customs zone, it runs an independent agricultural quarantine, the importer must obtain a prior import permit before shipping and present a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection issued within 30 days of shipment, and exotic species must also satisfy DRNA. Truly international import/export of the animal as 'wildlife' would add the U.S. federal USFWS layer (Form 3-177 declaration under 50 CFR Part 14) and the CDC bar on rodents of African origin. Release into the wild is prohibited (Art. 7.03(A)).

Sources: Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales (DRNA), Microjuris al Día (mirror of the DRNA regulation), Departamento de Agricultura de PR, Secretaría Auxiliar de Sanidad Animal (SAHO), U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, USDA APHIS / CDC

Restrictions & responsibilities

Operating a standing exotic-species buy/sell business (negocio de compraventa) in roof rats needs DRNA's $150 dealer permit under Art. 7.01, because R. rattus carries no asterisk in Apéndice 4 (only single-asterisk agricultural/domestic species are exempt). One-off private transfers and FREE vetted adoption of captive-bred black rats need no permit.
  • Determine whether the activity is a 'negocio de compraventa' (a standing buy/sell business) versus a private/free transfer; only the former triggers the permit.
  • If a business: file the DRNA dealer-permit application and pay $150 (certified check or money order to the Secretario de Hacienda, or in person at DRNA Recaudaciones).
  • Provide the supporting documents: municipal Patente, ARP use permit, Hacienda debt certificate, and ASUME negative certification if applicable (Art. 7.01(C)).
  • Maintain an escape-proof facility and post the permit and the list of species authorized for sale (Art. 7.01(D), 7.02); accept surprise DRNA inspections (Art. 7.06).
  • Sell only captive-born individuals (Art. 7.03(B)).

Forms: DRNA permiso de Negocio de Compraventa de Especies Exóticas (apply via DRNA Oficina de Licencias y Permisos) · Where: DRNA, Oficina de Licencias y Permisos Forestales, Vida Silvestre y Pesquerías (San Juan / Río Piedras). · Fees: $150 dealer permit (commercial buy/sell business only). Free/private transfer: no fee.

Source: Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales (DRNA), Microjuris al Día (mirror of the DRNA regulation)

Importing a roof rat into Puerto Rico needs a prior Puerto Rico Department of Agriculture (SAHO) import permit plus a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection issued within 30 days of shipment; only captive-born animals may be imported, and exotic species must also satisfy DRNA (Apéndice 4 already covers the DRNA side, so no separate DRNA import permit). Intra-island transport of a lawfully held rat is otherwise unregulated. Never release one (24-hour escape reporting to DRNA).
  • Obtain the PRDA/SAHO import permit BEFORE the animal is shipped (application to the SAHO veterinary diagnostic lab in Dorado).
  • Have a USDA-accredited veterinarian in the state/territory of origin issue a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection within 30 days of shipment, certifying the animal is free of communicable disease.
  • Carry the DRNA 'certificado veterinario' requirement (satisfied by the CVI) and ensure the animal is captive-born (Art. 7.03(B)).
  • For genuinely international shipments only, file the USFWS Form 3-177 wildlife declaration (50 CFR Part 14) and confirm the animal is not a rodent of African origin (CDC bar).

Forms: PR Dept of Agriculture (SAHO) animal-import requirements (permit + CVI), USFWS Form 3-177, Declaration for Importation or Exportation of Fish or Wildlife (international only) · Where: PR Dept of Agriculture, Secretaría Auxiliar de Sanidad Animal (SAHO), Laboratorio de Diagnóstico Veterinario, Dorado, PR; DRNA for the exotic-species side; USFWS wildlife inspection office for international shipments. · Fees: PRDA import permit fee (the DR reports $50; not confirmed in the extracted requirements text, confirm with PRDA). The issuing veterinarian charges for the CVI exam. No DRNA import-permit fee for Apéndice 4 species.

Source: Departamento de Agricultura de PR, Secretaría Auxiliar de Sanidad Animal (SAHO), Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales (DRNA), Microjuris al Día (mirror of the DRNA regulation), U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, USDA APHIS / CDC

Never release a roof rat into the wild. Reglamento 6765, Art. 7.03(A) prohibits releasing Apéndice 4 species into the environment of Puerto Rico, and Art. 7.02(F) requires reporting any escape to DRNA within 24 hours. Wild/feral R. rattus is a recognized invasive in PR (it also appears in Apéndice 2 as a harmful species). Rehome responsibly; check municipal ordinances.

Where: DRNA.

Source: Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales (DRNA), Microjuris al Día (mirror of the DRNA regulation)

WATCH-ITEM (prospective): Ley Núm. 93-2025 directs DRNA to adopt, within 180 days of Aug 1 2025 (Art. 10(b)), a regulation sorting introduced species into prohibida / restringida / no restringida (Art. 5), with a 30-day public-comment window on the list (Art. 5(x)). The statute's statement of motives names the rata negra. Art. 13 excludes species designated doméstica/naturalizada/de importancia agrícola by the Department of Agriculture. No implementing draft is posted yet (DRNA proposed-regs page checked 2026-06-14). If finalized adversely, it could change R. rattus's permit-free status.
  • Watch the DRNA 'Propuestas de Reglamento' page for the Ley 93-2025 draft and file a comment when it opens (see advocacy kit).
  • Ask the Department of Agriculture whether it has designated captive-bred Rattus rattus/norvegicus as 'doméstica' under Art. 13, which would exclude them from the new law entirely.

Where: DRNA (rulemaking); PR Dept of Agriculture (Art. 13 domestic determination).

Source: Asamblea Legislativa de Puerto Rico (via LexJuris)

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Puerto Rico

In Puerto Rico, keeping a captive-bred, tame pet roof rat ('rata negra', Rattus rattus) is currently legal. The species is named, with no restrictive asterisk, in Apéndice 4 of the DRNA wildlife regulation (Reglamento 6765), the list of lower-risk exotics eligible for import, possession, sale, and captive breeding without a permit (Art. 7.03). The fancy rat (R. norvegicus) sits in the same appendix with identical standing. Only releasing one into the wild is prohibited. The agency is reading the current rule correctly, and there is nothing for it to fix today. The issue is prospective: a 2025 statute, Ley Núm. 93-2025 (Ley para el Manejo de Especies Introducidas, signed Aug 1 2025), directs the DRNA to write a new regulation that will sort introduced species into 'prohibida', 'restringida', or 'no restringida', and the law's statement of motives names the rata negra. If that future regulation groups tame, captive-bred pet lines with feral pest populations, permit-free keeping could end. The risk is in a coming rule under a new law, not in any misreading of the current rule.

The ask: Both asks address the future rule, not the current status. (1) When the DRNA publishes its draft Ley 93-2025 classification regulation for public comment, ask in writing that Rattus rattus kept as a captive-bred pet be classified 'no restringida', or that captive-bred, indoor pet lines be expressly distinguished from feral and invasive populations, consistent with the species already being on Apéndice 4 and with Ley 93-2025 Art. 13, which excludes domestic and already-naturalized species as determined by the Department of Agriculture. (2) Ask your senator and representative for the same outcome: pet roof rats are domesticated companion animals, like the fancy rat already in Apéndice 4, and the implementing regulation should not strip permit-free status from keepers of captive-bred animals. These animals are captive-bred, hand-tame, kept strictly indoors, and never released; they are not the source of feral establishment. Domestication, not wild ancestry, is what defines a domestic animal: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic companions. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat (R. norvegicus), domesticated only in the 19th century (see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/), so a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated on the same footing, one species over.

Where the lever really is: This is a legislature/rulemaking lever, not an agency-misreading lever. The DRNA is applying its wildlife regulation correctly: Rattus rattus sits in Apéndice 4 of Reg. 6765 with no restrictive asterisk, so keeping, captive breeding, and private/free transfer are permit-free (Art. 7.03), and only release is prohibited. There is nothing for the agency to reinterpret now; writing to DRNA to clarify that the rat is legal would only confirm a status that is already correct, and could not change a law the agency is applying properly. The risk and the lever both lie upstream, in a new statute: Ley Núm. 93-2025 (verified, signed Aug 1 2025) directs DRNA to promulgate a regulation classifying introduced species as prohibida / restringida / no restringida (Art. 5), with the regulation due within 180 days of approval (Art. 10(b)), and the statute's statement of motives names the rata negra. The classification list carries a 30-day public-comment window before it is finalized (Art. 5(x)). DRNA's official 'Propuestas de Reglamento' page was fetched 2026-06-14 and shows NO posted draft implementing Ley 93-2025, so the comment window is not yet open. The two actions are: (a) watch the DRNA rulemaking page and file a comment when the draft appears, and (b) contact the legislature, because Ley 93-2025 is the enabling statute and legislators can shape both the mandate and the agency's posture. The science-based ask (captive-bred indoor pet lines are not the source of feral establishment, the species is already naturalized, and Art. 13 already excludes domestic and naturalized species) belongs in the rulemaking comment and in messages to legislators, not in a request for the agency to override its current correct reading.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • DRNA, Propuestas de Reglamento (official proposed-regulations / public-comment page) (public comment) — official contact page
    This is the official page where DRNA posts draft regulations for public comment. The Ley 93-2025 introduced-species classification rule will appear here, with its comment deadline and any public hearing. Checked 2026-06-14: the posted drafts are water-quality, tire-disposal, landfill, single-use-plastics, falconry, and a Condado lagoon reserve rule; NO Ley 93-2025 / introduced-species draft is posted, so the comment window is not yet open. When the draft appears, submit the comment asking that captive-bred pet Rattus rattus be classified 'no restringida' / distinguished from feral populations. This is the single most decisive touchpoint because it is where the actual rule gets written.
  • Directorio Legislativo, Oficina de Servicios Legislativos de Puerto Rico (official find-and-contact-your-legislator portal) (legislature) — official contact page
    Official OSLPR directory (2025-2028 term) that lets any member of the public look up and contact senators and representatives by name, district, or chamber, with phone and email on each profile. Because Ley 93-2025 is the enabling STATUTE behind the coming reclassification, legislators are the right audience for the message that pet roof rats are domesticated companion animals and the implementing rule should preserve permit-free keeping of captive-bred animals.
  • DRNA, Oficina de Licencias y Permisos Forestales, Vida Silvestre y Pesquerías (wildlife/exotic-species permits office) (executive / agency) — official contact page
    The substantive wildlife authority for exotic/introduced species and the office that will administer the Ley 93-2025 rule. Its public page (fetched 2026-06-14) lists only phone (787-999-2200, wildlife ext. 2750/2783) and a mailing address, NO official email or online form, so treat it as a monitoring/inquiry touchpoint (call or mail) to confirm the rule's status and timing, not as a lever to change the law it is correctly applying.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
Subject: Keep captive-bred pet roof rats classified as lower-risk under the Ley 93-2025 regulation

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing about the introduced-species classification regulation the DRNA must adopt under Ley Núm. 93-2025. I respectfully ask that the captive-bred domestic roof rat (Rattus rattus, 'rata negra') kept as a pet be classified 'no restringida', or that captive-bred, indoor pet lines be expressly distinguished from feral populations.

This is consistent with current law: the species is already in Apéndice 4 of Reglamento 6765 as a lower-risk exotic eligible for possession, sale, and captive breeding without a permit (Art. 7.03), and Ley 93-2025 (Art. 13) already excludes domestic and naturalized species as determined by the Department of Agriculture.

The animals I am writing about are captive-bred, hand-tame, kept strictly indoors, and never released. Like the fancy rat, which sits in the same Apéndice 4, the pet roof rat is a domesticated companion animal. It is not the source of any feral population; the distinction is the lineage and use, not the species name. Domestication, not wild ancestry, is what defines a domestic animal: the dog descends from the wolf and the cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic companions. The fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated on the same footing as the fancy rat already in Apéndice 4.

I ask that the forthcoming regulation preserve permit-free keeping of captive-bred pet roof rats. Please let me know when the draft regulation opens for public comment.

Thank you for your time and service.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your municipality, Puerto Rico]
[Your email]
Español
Asunto: Mantener a la rata negra de compañía criada en cautiverio como especie de menor riesgo en el reglamento de la Ley 93-2025

Estimado señor o señora:

Le escribo sobre el reglamento de clasificación de especies introducidas que el DRNA debe adoptar conforme a la Ley Núm. 93-2025. Respetuosamente solicito que la rata negra doméstica (Rattus rattus) criada en cautiverio y mantenida como mascota se clasifique como 'no restringida', o que las líneas de mascota criadas en cautiverio y mantenidas bajo techo se distingan expresamente de las poblaciones asilvestradas.

Esto es congruente con el derecho vigente: la especie ya figura en el Apéndice 4 del Reglamento 6765 como exótico de menor riesgo elegible para posesión, venta y reproducción en cautiverio sin permiso (Art. 7.03), y la propia Ley 93-2025 (Art. 13) excluye a las especies domésticas y naturalizadas según lo determine el Departamento de Agricultura.

Los animales a los que me refiero son criados en cautiverio, mansos, mantenidos estrictamente bajo techo y nunca liberados. Al igual que la rata fancy, que figura en el mismo Apéndice 4, la rata negra de compañía es un animal doméstico de compañía. No es el origen de ninguna población asilvestrada; la diferencia está en el linaje y el uso, no en el nombre de la especie. Lo que define a un animal doméstico es la domesticación, no su ascendencia silvestre: el perro desciende del lobo y el gato de un félido silvestre, y aun así ambos son reconocidos como animales domésticos de compañía. La rata fancy es la propia rata parda silvestre, domesticada apenas en el siglo XIX, de modo que una rata negra criada en cautiverio está domesticada en el mismo plano que la rata fancy que ya figura en el Apéndice 4.

Solicito que el reglamento próximo a adoptarse conserve la tenencia sin permiso de ratas negras de compañía criadas en cautiverio. Le agradeceré me informe cuándo el borrador del reglamento se abra a comentarios públicos.

Gracias por su tiempo y servicio.

Atentamente,
[Su nombre]
[Su municipio, Puerto Rico]
[Su correo electrónico]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Reglamento 6765 (DRNA, 2004), Reglamento para Regir la Conservación y el Manejo de la Vida Silvestre, las Especies Exóticas y la Caza en el ELA de Puerto Rico. Art. 7.01 (negocio de compraventa, $150; exención de especies con asterisco); Art. 7.03 (especies exóticas de menor riesgo del Apéndice 4, importación/posesión/venta sin permiso; reproducción en cautiverio); Apéndice 4 MAMÍFEROS lista 'Rattus rattus – Rata negra (variedad de laboratorio)' y 'Rattus norvegicus' sin asterisco. — Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales (DRNA)
  • Reglamento 6765, text-extractable mirror used to verify the Apéndice 4 listing and the Art. 7.01/7.03 asterisk mechanics (the DRNA-hosted copy is a scanned image; this mirror has an OCR/text layer). — Microjuris al Día (mirror of the DRNA regulation)
  • Ley Núm. 93 de 2025, Ley para el Manejo de Especies Introducidas (firmada 1 ago 2025). Art. 5 (clases prohibida/restringida/no restringida) y Art. 5(x) (comentario público 30 días); Art. 10(b) (reglamento en 180 días); Art. 13 (exclusión de especies domésticas/naturalizadas/agrícolas según el Departamento de Agricultura); exposición de motivos nombra 'la rata negra (Rattus rattus)' y 'la rata parda (Rattus norvegicus)'. — Asamblea Legislativa de Puerto Rico (via LexJuris)
  • Requisitos para la importación de animales a Puerto Rico (2024 update), DA-SAHO: permiso de importación previo + Certificado Veterinario (CVI) emitido dentro de 30 días; las especies exóticas deben cumplir además con el DRNA; solicitud al laboratorio en Dorado; contacto aperez@agricultura.pr.gov. — Departamento de Agricultura de PR, Secretaría Auxiliar de Sanidad Animal (SAHO)
  • Ley Núm. 241 de 1999, Nueva Ley de Vida Silvestre de Puerto Rico (enabling statute for Reg. 6765; DRNA authority over wildlife and exotic species). — Asamblea Legislativa de Puerto Rico
  • DRNA, Propuestas de Reglamento (official proposed-regulations / public-comment page). Checked 2026-06-14: no Ley 93-2025 / introduced-species draft posted; comment window not yet open. — Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales (DRNA)
  • USFWS Form 3-177, Declaration for Importation or Exportation of Fish or Wildlife (50 CFR Part 14). R. rattus is 'wildlife' to USFWS; a declaration is required for genuinely international import/export (not for domestic US-mainland-to-PR movement). — U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service
  • USDA APHIS / CDC, bringing a pet rodent into the United States (federal international-import layer; CDC bars rodents of African origin). — USDA APHIS / CDC

Search terms: Rattus rattus, rata negra, rata negra (variedad de laboratorio), roof rat, black rat, ship rat, rata parda (Rattus norvegicus), especies exóticas, Certificado Veterinario (CVI).

Last reviewed 2026-06-14. This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting. Spotted an error or an update? Let us know.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Rhode Island? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Rhode Island

Summary. Rhode Island is a clear species-not-domestication trap. Its regs (250-RICR-40-05-3) exempt ONLY the Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus) — naming it explicitly as a 'domestic animal' and on the Appendix A exempt list — and say nothing about Rattus rattus. By default (and by the doctrine 'expressing one excludes the other'), the roof rat is therefore an 'Exotic Wild Animal,' which is legal to keep but ONLY with a DEM Exotic Animal Possession Permit ($5 PER animal, a Rhode Island-licensed vet's commitment letter, and a DEM-approved written husbandry plan, plus escape-reporting and possible inspections). Rodents aren't in RI's flat-prohibited class (that's wild carnivores/primates), so a permit is obtainable. Breeding needs the possession permit for the parents; selling needs a Pet Shop License ($100 retail) or Dealer License (wholesale) — the hobby-breeder exemption is restricted to dogs and cats only. Import needs the possession permit approved ≥7 days ahead + a CVI counter-signed by the origin State Vet. So everything is legal-with-a-permit, and the disparity vs the fancy rat is the advocacy hook: petition DEM to add captive-bred R. rattus to the Appendix A exempt list.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Rhode Island-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Rhode Island is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

R. rattus is not on RI's 'domestic animal' list or Appendix A exempt list (which name only R. norvegicus), so by default it's an 'Exotic Wild Animal' (250-RICR-40-05-3.6(A)(8)). Rodents are not in the flat-prohibited class (wild carnivores w/o rabies vaccine, primates), so possession is permissible WITH a DEM Exotic Animal Possession Permit: $5 per specimen (one application per animal), a RI-licensed veterinarian's commitment letter, and a DEM-approved written husbandry plan secured BEFORE the permit issues; plus escape/death reporting and possible unannounced inspections (DEM has discretion to deny). Keeping without the permit = 'contraband' (seizure). The Norway rat needs none of this — the disparity is the advocacy point.

Sources: RI Dept of Environmental Management, RI DEM (via Cornell LII), RI DEM Division of Agriculture, Rhode Island General Assembly

Breeding   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-08

Breeding requires the Exotic Animal Possession Permit to legally hold the parent animals; commercial propagation for sale additionally requires a Pet Shop License (retail) or Dealer License (wholesale). Critically, RI's coveted 'hobby breeder' exemption (R.I. Gen. Laws §4-19-2) is restricted to DOGS AND CATS — there is no hobby exemption for rodents, so even small-scale home breeding of R. rattus for sale is treated as operating a Pet Shop. (Open: whether DEM requires a separate $5 possession application for each unweaned pup before transfer — see inquiry.)

Sources: RI Dept of Environmental Management, Rhode Island General Assembly, RI DEM Division of Agriculture

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

Commercial RETAIL sale to the public requires a Pet Shop License ($100/yr); WHOLESALE requires a Dealer License — the rodent seller can't use the dog/cat hobby exemption (§4-19-2). Even private, non-commercial transfer requires DEM authorization, and the RECIPIENT must independently obtain their own Exotic Animal Possession Permit before taking custody (permits are non-transferable). A pet shop in good standing can hold a species-level 'resale permit' (250-RICR-40-05-3.8) instead of per-animal permits, but the buyer still needs their own.

Sources: Rhode Island General Assembly, RI Dept of Environmental Management, RI DEM Division of Agriculture

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-08

IMPORT: you cannot just drive a roof rat into RI — the Exotic Animal Possession Permit application must reach DEM at least 7 days before shipment, accompanied by a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection from a federally-accredited vet in the origin state, COUNTER-SIGNED by the origin State Veterinarian, declaring freedom from infectious/zoonotic disease; DEM approves the point of entry and may impose case-by-case quarantine (R.I. Gen. Laws ch. 4-18). INTRASTATE: the permit is tied to the inspected/approved location and is non-transferable, so even moving the animal to a new RI address needs DEM written permission. Never release (escape must be reported immediately).

Sources: Rhode Island General Assembly, RI Dept of Environmental Management

Restrictions & responsibilities

Keeping a roof rat in RI requires a DEM Exotic Animal Possession Permit: $5 PER animal (one application each), a RI-licensed vet's commitment letter, and a DEM-approved written husbandry plan BEFORE issuance; escape/death must be reported; possible inspections. To IMPORT: file the permit application ≥7 days before shipment + a CVI counter-signed by the origin State Vet; DEM sets entry point + possible quarantine. Apply via the DAFE Permit Portal. Never release.
  • Line up a RI-licensed vet willing to give a commitment letter for ongoing DEM-required testing
  • Write a husbandry plan (enclosure/diet/enrichment) for DEM approval
  • File an Exotic Animal Possession Permit application ($5/animal) via the DAFE portal — ≥7 days before any import, with a counter-signed CVI

Forms: Exotic Animal Possession Permit Application · Where: RI DEM — Division of Agriculture & Forest Environment (DAFE) Permit Portal · Fees: $5 per animal (possession); $100/yr Pet Shop License (to sell)

Source: RI DEM Division of Agriculture, RI Dept of Environmental Management

Selling roof rats (or breeding them for sale) requires a Pet Shop License ($100/yr retail) or Dealer License (wholesale) — RI's hobby-breeder exemption is for dogs/cats ONLY, so it does not cover rodents. Buyers must each obtain their own possession permit.
  • For any sale/commercial breeding: obtain a Pet Shop License (retail) or Dealer License (wholesale) from DEM

Forms: Pet Shop License Application · Where: RI DEM — DAFE · Fees: $100/yr (Pet Shop)

Source: Rhode Island General Assembly, RI DEM Division of Agriculture

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Help change this

How to help in Rhode Island

In Rhode Island, keeping a pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) is legal but burdensome, while keeping the common "fancy rat" (the Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) is not regulated at all. The reason is wording, not biology. The state's wild-animal rules (250-RICR-40-05-3) name only the Norway rat as a "domestic animal" and put only the Norway rat on the Appendix A list of exempt animals. Because the regulation names one rat and is silent on the other, the captive-bred roof rat falls by default into the catch-all "Exotic Wild Animal" category. That triggers a DEM Exotic Animal Possession Permit: $5 per animal, a Rhode Island-licensed veterinarian's commitment letter, and a DEM-approved written husbandry plan before legal ownership, plus escape/death reporting and possible inspections. Two tame, captive-bred rats of nearly identical care needs are treated differently solely because of which species the list mentions.

The ask: Ask the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management (DEM) to add the captive-bred, domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) to the Appendix A list of exempt animals in 250-RICR-40-05-3.17, so it is treated the same as the already-exempt Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus). This is a regulatory fix DEM can make through its normal rulemaking process; it does not require a new law. The relevant fact is domestication, not wild ancestry. The dog descends from the wolf and the house cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic animals because of generations bred for tameness. The already-exempt Norway rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred R. rattus is the same case one species over. That is the question the Division is asked to weigh, not a conclusion it is asked to reach. Point to states that already do this: New Jersey exempts the whole genus, and Wyoming names both rat species. Until then, individual keepers can apply for the Exotic Animal Possession Permit through the DEM DAFE portal, and anyone who wants to be heard on a future rule change can subscribe to the Secretary of State's rulemaking notices to catch the next public-comment window. On domestication background, see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/.

Where the lever really is: This is an agency problem, and the lever is the agency (DEM), not the legislature. The roof rat is not named on any statutory prohibited list. It falls into the "Exotic Wild Animal" default because DEM's own regulation, 250-RICR-40-05-3, names only Rattus norvegicus as exempt (in the definitions and on the Appendix A list at 3.17) and is silent on Rattus rattus. Appendix A is a DEM-controlled regulatory list, not a fixed item in the General Laws, so DEM has authority to amend it through ordinary rulemaking. In the 2026 cycle (notice filed 04/13/2026, comment period through 05/20/2026, hearing mid-May) DEM proposed and processed amendments to this Part, banning tegus and giant African land snails and clarifying dealer exemptions, which shows the agency routinely revises this list. The right move is a written request or administrative petition to DEM's Division of Fish & Wildlife (the unit that authors Appendix A) to add captive-bred R. rattus to the exempt list, reinforced by participating in DEM's annual public-comment window for this Part. Going to the General Assembly would be the wrong door, because there is no statute banning the roof rat to repeal; the fix lives in a regulation DEM writes and can change. If DEM declines on invasive or structural-pest grounds, that is a policy judgment to address via the comment record, not a sign the lever was wrong.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • RI DEM — Division of Fish & Wildlife (general division inbox) (executive / agency) — DEM.DFW@dem.ri.gov
    This is the DEM division that authors and maintains the Appendix A exempt-animal list in 250-RICR-40-05-3. Send the request here to add captive-bred Rattus rattus to the exempt list. Verified as the official, non-personal division inbox on DEM's live Fish & Wildlife page (phone 401-789-0281).
  • RI DEM — Division of Agriculture & Forest Environment (DAFE) Permit Portal (executive / agency) — official contact page
    The official portal for filing the Exotic Animal Possession Permit (and Pet Shop/Dealer licenses) that a roof-rat keeper currently needs while the rule stands. Use it both to comply today and as the formal contact point for permit questions about the species.
  • RI Secretary of State — Rulemaking notice subscription (public comment) — official contact page
    The official statewide system to be notified the moment DEM opens its next public-comment window on 250-RICR-40-05-3. DEM amends this Part on roughly an annual cycle (it did so in 2026), so subscribing lets you submit a formal comment supporting the roof-rat exemption when the window reopens.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management, Division of Fish & Wildlife:

I am writing to ask DEM to add the captive-bred, domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) to the Appendix A list of exempt animals in 250-RICR-40-05-3.17.

Under the current rule, the closely related Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus) is named as a domestic animal and listed as exempt, but the roof rat is not mentioned. Because of that silence, a tame pet roof rat defaults into the "Exotic Wild Animal" category and requires a possession permit, a veterinarian's commitment letter, and an approved husbandry plan, while an essentially identical pet Norway rat requires nothing. This difference comes from which species the list names, not from any difference in the animals.

The roof rats kept as pets are captive-bred, hand-tamed, housed indoors in secure cages, and never released to the wild. They are kept the same way as the fancy rats already exempt under your rule. What makes an animal domestic is its breeding history, not its wild origins. The dog descends from the wolf and the house cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic animals because of generations bred for tameness. The exempt Norway rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over. New Jersey exempts the entire genus and Wyoming names both rat species, so there is precedent for harmonizing the two.

I respectfully ask the Division to add captive-bred Rattus rattus to the Appendix A exempt list, or to advise how I may petition for that amendment and when the next public-comment period on this Part will open.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

[Your name]
[Your town, Rhode Island]
[Your email]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • 250-RICR-40-05-3 — Importation & Possession of Wild Animals (§3.6 definitions; §3.11 Exotic Animal Possession Permit; only R. norvegicus 'domestic') — RI Dept of Environmental Management
  • 250-RICR-40-05-3.17 Appendix A — Exempt Exotic Animals (lists Norway Rat (R. norvegicus); R. rattus NOT listed) — RI DEM (via Cornell LII)
  • R.I. Gen. Laws ch. 4-18 — Importation of Wild Animals (7-day pre-approval, CVI, quarantine, penalties) — Rhode Island General Assembly
  • R.I. Gen. Laws ch. 4-19 — Animal Care (Pet Shop/Dealer licenses; hobby exemption dogs/cats only; 'Animal' includes rodent) — Rhode Island General Assembly
  • Exotic Animal Possession Permit Application ($5/specimen; husbandry plan; vet commitment) — RI DEM Division of Agriculture
  • Pet Shop License Application ($100/yr; 'Animal' includes rodent; home-breeding exemption = canine/feline only) — RI DEM Division of Agriculture

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in South Carolina? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › South Carolina

Summary. South Carolina does not regulate keeping pet rodents. Its only exotic-pet ban (Title 47, ch. 2) reaches just large wild cats, non-native bears, and great apes; its carnivore-sale ban (§47-5-50) doesn't touch rodents; and the wildlife-import chapter expressly EXEMPTS 'rats and mice' imported for the pet trade from any permit (§50-16-60). So keeping, breeding, and selling/giving a captive-bred roof rat is effectively legal and unregulated. Two soft points: the universal no-release rule, and confirming with Clemson Livestock-Poultry Health whether any health certificate applies to interstate pet-rodent transport. The one genuine open question is whether the generic phrase 'rats and mice' is read to include the R. rattus species specifically.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the South Carolina-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where South Carolina is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

South Carolina has no permit requirement to keep a pet rodent. The only categorical exotic-pet ban (SC Code §47-2-10 / §47-2-30) reaches only large wild cats, non-native bears, and great apes — rodents are not within it. SCDNR's restricted-non-native list (Reg. 123-152) is tegu-centric and does not list rats. Gemini DR-verified: R. rattus is an unprotected commensal rodent; no captive-wildlife permit is required for non-native rodents kept as pets (SC Code 50-16-10/-60).

Sources: South Carolina Legislature, South Carolina Dept of Natural Resources

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

No South Carolina law licenses or restricts breeding pet rodents — the breeder statutes cover dogs (and registrable companion dogs/cats) only. DNR's pet-import exemption for 'rats and mice' (§50-16-60) signals the pet-trade is unregulated. Breeding is unregulated rather than expressly permitted. Gemini DR-verified: no state breeder/facility license for small mammals.

Sources: South Carolina Code (Justia), South Carolina Legislature

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

The wild-carnivore-sale ban (§47-5-50) doesn't reach rodents, and the pet-sale disclosure law applies only to dogs/cats. DNR's importation chapter expressly exempts 'rats and mice … imported for sale as pets' from the permit requirement (§50-16-60). No state license is needed to sell or give pet rats, though local business-license rules may apply. Gemini DR-verified: 50-16-60 exempts 'rats and mice' for the pet trade; no state pet-shop/dealer license.

Sources: South Carolina Code (Justia), South Carolina Legislature

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-07

For wildlife-import purposes, §50-16-60 places 'rats and mice' on the no-DNR-permit list, and the §50-16-20 import-permit species list excludes rodents. Animal-health import is run by Clemson Livestock-Poultry Health; its CVI/rabies rules center on livestock/poultry/dogs/cats/ferrets, with no published rule imposing a CVI on pet rats — but confirm before interstate movement. Never release a non-native rat. Gemini DR-verified: Clemson Livestock-Poultry Health requires a 30-day CVI for wildlife/exotics entering SC, even though SCDNR waives the wildlife import permit for 'rats and mice'; within-state movement unregulated.

Sources: South Carolina Legislature, Clemson Livestock-Poultry Health (State Veterinarian)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Never release or let escape a roof rat — Title 50 ch. 16 prohibits releasing imported wildlife, and R. rattus is itself an established invasive. Rehome responsibly.

Source: South Carolina Legislature

  • SC Code §50-16-60 — Exemption for certain wildlife imported as pets ('rats and mice') — South Carolina Code (Justia)
  • SC Code Title 47, ch. 2 — Large Wild Cats, Non-Native Bears, Great Apes (limited exotic ban) — South Carolina Legislature
  • SCDNR — Restrictions on Non-native Wildlife (Reg. 123-152) — South Carolina Dept of Natural Resources
  • South Carolina Animal Import Requirements — Clemson Livestock-Poultry Health — Clemson Livestock-Poultry Health (State Veterinarian)
