item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in South Dakota? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › South Dakota

Summary. South Dakota is now agency-clarified, and the news is favorable. Preliminary research feared a 'prohibited-by-default' reading: a statutory gate (SDCL 40-3-24) bars possessing any nondomestic mammal unless the Animal Industry Board's rules allow it, and Order Rodentia is absent from those rules. But the South Dakota State Veterinarian (Animal Industry Board) confirmed in writing (June 2026) that the Board has NO AUTHORITY over the possession of rodents at all — so that gate is not applied to a pet roof rat, and possession is effectively unregulated rather than prohibited. The one concrete requirement the State Vet gave: IMPORTING a roof rat into South Dakota requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) plus an import permit number. The State Veterinarian further confirmed (June 2026) there is no other state-level regulator: LOCAL (city/county) authorities would have jurisdiction in most places, so the only thing to check is your municipal animal ordinance.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the South Dakota-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where South Dakota is silent. See United States.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • South Dakota Animal Industry Board (State Veterinarian), written reply June 2026: the Board has NO authority over the possession of roof rats or any other mammals in the Order Rodentia. Importing them into South Dakota requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) and an import permit number.
  • SD State Veterinarian follow-up (June 2026): no state agency regulates roof rat possession; LOCAL (city/county) authorities would have jurisdiction in most places. The import requirement (CVI + import permit number) is the standard small-animal process.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

The SD Animal Industry Board (State Veterinarian) confirmed in writing (June 2026) that it has NO authority over the possession of any mammals in Order Rodentia. That dispels the preliminary 'prohibited-by-default' concern (the SDCL 40-3-24 nondomestic-mammal gate is administered by the AIB, which says it does not reach rodents). So keeping a pet roof rat is effectively unregulated by the state animal-health authority. Labeled 'unregulated/unclear' because the law is silent (no affirmative pet-rodent rule), not because it is restricted. Follow-up clarification (June 2026): the State Veterinarian confirmed there is no state-level possession rule and that LOCAL (city/county) authorities would have jurisdiction in most places, so check your municipal ordinance.

Sources: South Dakota Legislature / Animal Industry Board, SD Animal Industry Board (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center)

Breeding   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-09

Because the Animal Industry Board disclaims authority over rodent possession, the SDCL 40-3-25 captive-nondomestic-mammal framework does not reach roof rats, and no SD rule specifically governs hobby breeding of pet rodents. Effectively unregulated by the state animal-health authority; commercial-scale breeding could implicate general business/USDA layers, but no SD-specific rodent breeding permit exists.

Sources: South Dakota Legislature / Animal Industry Board, SD Animal Industry Board (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center)

Selling or giving away   Unregulated / unclear

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-09

With the AIB disclaiming authority over rodents, the nondomestic-mammal dealer/auction permit framework (ARSD 12:68:18) does not apply to roof rats, and no SD rule specifically bars selling or giving them. Effectively unregulated at the state level; standard federal USDA dealer rules would only bite at wholesale/sight-unseen scale, not face-to-face placement.

Sources: SD Animal Industry Board (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center)

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-09

The SD State Veterinarian confirmed (June 2026) that importing a roof rat into South Dakota requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) and an import permit number. Internal movement of a lawfully-held pet is otherwise unrestricted. Never release a nonnative.

Sources: South Dakota Animal Industry Board, South Dakota Legislature / Animal Industry Board

Restrictions & responsibilities

At the STATE level, keeping/breeding/giving a roof rat is unregulated (the Animal Industry Board has no authority over rodent possession). The State Veterinarian confirmed that LOCAL city/county authorities would have jurisdiction in most places, so check your municipal animal ordinance. Never release.
  • Check your city/county animal-control ordinance for any pet-rodent or exotic-animal limits

Where: Your municipal / county animal control

Source: SD Animal Industry Board (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center)

Keeping, breeding, and giving/selling a roof rat are not regulated by the SD Animal Industry Board (it confirmed it has no authority over rodent possession). The one requirement: to IMPORT a roof rat into South Dakota you need a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) and an import permit number. Never release a roof rat.
  • Before bringing a roof rat into SD: obtain a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) and an import permit number
  • Contact the SD Animal Industry Board for the import permit number

Where: South Dakota Animal Industry Board

Source: South Dakota Animal Industry Board

The rule here isn't settled yet. Use our step-by-step guide to confirm with your agencies and send us what you find.

Official sources

  • SDCL 40-3-24/40-3-25/40-3-1(3) — nondomestic-mammal possession gate + AIB authority + 'domestic animal' definition (AIB confirms it does not reach Rodentia) — South Dakota Legislature / Animal Industry Board
  • ARSD Chapter 12:68:18 — Nondomestic Animal Control (permit orders enumerated; Rodentia absent) — SD Animal Industry Board (via MSU Animal Legal & Historical Center)
  • SD Animal Industry Board — Animal Movement & Imports (CVI + import permit number required to import) — South Dakota Animal Industry Board

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Tennessee? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Tennessee

Summary. Tennessee classifies wildlife into five mutually exclusive classes (TCA §70-4-403), and the roof rat lands in Class III — the residual catch-all 'all species not listed in other classes,' which 'requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture.' A DR correction: the statute does NOT enumerate 'rats, mice'; non-native rodents qualify purely through that residual clause. Because R. rattus is non-native (so not Class II/IV), not inherently dangerous (not Class I), and has not been elevated to the injurious Class V list, keeping, breeding, and selling/giving a captive-bred roof rat is entirely unregulated by TWRA — and the law draws no distinction between R. rattus and the fancy rat (R. norvegicus). The only state layer is animal-health: importing a rodent across state lines needs a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (normally valid 30 days), and a June 4, 2026 TDA emergency screwworm order tightens that to a 7-day CVI plus entry permit for animals from infested/high-risk states. Never release one — it is a banned invasive release.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Tennessee-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Tennessee is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

TCA §70-4-403(3) defines Class III as the residual class that 'requires no permits except those required by the department of agriculture, and includes all species not listed in other classes.' R. rattus is non-native (so not Class II/IV), is not inherently dangerous (not Class I), and is absent from the injurious Class V list, so it defaults to Class III. No TWRA possession permit, registration, facility inspection, or fee is required to keep one as a pet; ordinary proof of legal (non-wild) origin such as a bill of sale or breeder receipt suffices.

Sources: Tennessee General Assembly (via Justia), TWRA (via TN Secretary of State)

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

TWRA commercial propagation permits are required only for Class I or Class II wildlife, so no propagation permit applies to a Class III roof rat (TCA §70-4-403(3); Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 1660-01-37-.06). Tennessee's Commercial Breeder Act (TCA Title 44 ch. 17 pt. 7) covered only unsterilized dogs and cats and expired under its sunset clause on June 30, 2014, leaving no active state breeder license for rodents. Hobby and commercial rat breeding are unregulated by the state; large wholesale operations selling to labs or pet-store chains may still need federal USDA Animal Welfare Act licensing (see United States), and local zoning may apply to a home business.

Sources: Tennessee General Assembly (via Justia), TWRA (via Cornell LII), Tennessee General Assembly (via Animal Legal & Historical Center)

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

No TWRA sale/transfer permit applies to a Class III rodent — the 'Commercial Use of Wildlife' rule (Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 1660-01-17-.01) restricts only endangered, threatened, or native species and contains no bar on buying/selling/bartering legally obtained non-native wildlife. The TDA Livestock Dealer License (TCA Title 44 ch. 10) applies only to traditional livestock (cattle, swine, sheep, goats, horses, poultry), so pet rodents are exempt. Selling or gifting roof rats is therefore unregulated by state agencies; only local municipal/county zoning for a home-based commercial business may apply.

Sources: TWRA (via Animal Legal & Historical Center), TN Dept of Agriculture, Tennessee General Assembly (via Justia)

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Intrastate transport needs no health certificate, CVI, or TWRA permit, and TWRA importation rules expressly exempt Class III wildlife (Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 1660-01-15-.01(h)). But the TDA asserts jurisdiction over all animals crossing the state line: under Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 0080-02-01, an animal entering Tennessee must be free of communicable disease and accompanied by a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (normally valid 30 days). The June 4, 2026 TDA 'Order of the State Veterinarian' for New World Screwworm applies to all warm-blooded mammals — explicitly including 'Class III animals as classified by Tenn. Code Ann. §70-4-403(3)' — and, for animals from infested/high-risk states, requires a CVI issued within 7 days, the statement 'All animals listed on the CVI have been inspected and are free from screwworm larvae infestation,' freedom from open wounds, and a prior entry permit number from the State Veterinarian's Office. A lawful pathway plainly exists; transporting without the required CVI risks civil penalties up to $500.

Sources: TWRA (via TN Secretary of State), TN Dept of Agriculture (via TN Secretary of State), TN Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian), TN Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian), Tennessee General Assembly (via Justia)

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing a pet rodent into Tennessee from out of state requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) from an accredited vet in the origin state, declaring the animal free of communicable disease. Normally valid 30 days; the TDA is phasing out fillable-PDF CVIs in favor of electronic CVIs (eCVI) after June 30, 2026. No CVI is needed for movement entirely within Tennessee.
  • Have an accredited veterinarian in the origin state examine the rat and issue a CVI before crossing the state line
  • Prefer an electronic CVI (GlobalVetLink / VSPS / Vet Sentry) — PDF CVIs not accepted after June 30, 2026
  • Carry the CVI during transport into Tennessee

Forms: Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI / eCVI) · Where: Issued by an accredited veterinarian in the state of origin; TN Dept of Agriculture (Office of the State Veterinarian) oversees import compliance · Fees: Veterinary exam/CVI fee set by the issuing vet; no state filing fee

Source: TN Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian), TN Dept of Agriculture (via TN Secretary of State)

EMERGENCY (effective June 4, 2026): the TDA New World Screwworm order applies to all warm-blooded mammals, including Class III pets. For rodents originating from a screwworm-infested or USDA high-risk state, the standard 30-day CVI is insufficient — a 7-day CVI with a specific screwworm-free inspection statement, freedom from open wounds, and a pre-issued entry permit number (plus prophylactic-treatment declaration for infested zones) are required. Confirm your origin state's current status with the TDA on the day of shipment.
  • Check whether the origin state is currently an infested/high-risk state (status is fluid — confirm with TDA on shipment day)
  • If high-risk: obtain a CVI issued within 7 days of entry bearing the screwworm-free inspection statement; ensure the animal has no open wounds
  • If from an infested zone: obtain a prior entry permit number from the State Veterinarian's Office and a prophylactic-treatment declaration on the CVI

Forms: CVI (issued within 7 days) with screwworm inspection statement, Entry permit (infested-zone origins) · Where: Tennessee Dept of Agriculture — Office of the State Veterinarian (entry permits); accredited vet issues the CVI · Fees: No state fee for the order; veterinary CVI fee applies. Civil penalties up to $500 per violation for non-compliant transport.

Source: TN Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian), TN Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian)

No state breeder or dealer license is required for rodents (Commercial Breeder Act expired 6/30/2014; Livestock Dealer License covers traditional livestock only). A large-scale commercial breeder operating from a residence may still need a generic local business license, and federal USDA Animal Welfare Act licensing applies to wholesale / sight-unseen sales to labs or pet-store chains (see United States).
  • Verify with your county clerk / city whether a generic business license is needed for a home-based animal husbandry enterprise
  • If selling wholesale or sight-unseen, check federal USDA AWA licensing

Where: Local county clerk / municipal licensing (business license); USDA APHIS (federal wholesale) · Fees: Set locally / federally

Source: Tennessee General Assembly (via Animal Legal & Historical Center), TN Dept of Agriculture

It is a serious violation of Tennessee wildlife law to release any wildlife — including unregulated Class III animals — into the wild, and the roof rat is a highly invasive non-native pest. Intentional release or abandonment could trigger both wildlife violations and municipal nuisance-abatement fines. Rehome responsibly; never release.

Source: Tennessee General Assembly (via Justia), Shelby County Health Department

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Tenn. Code Ann. §70-4-403 — Classifications of wildlife (Class III = residual 'all species not listed'; no TWRA permit) — Tennessee General Assembly (via Justia)
  • Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 1660-01-18-.03 — Classes of Wildlife (R. rattus absent from Class I/V lists) — TWRA (via TN Secretary of State)
  • Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 1660-01-15-.01 — Animal Importation (Class III wildlife exempt from TWRA import permit, subsec. (h)) — TWRA (via TN Secretary of State)
  • Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 1660-01-17-.01 — General Provisions for Commercial Use (restrictions only for endangered/threatened/native) — TWRA (via Animal Legal & Historical Center)
  • Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 1660-01-37-.06 — Propagation Permits (Class I/II only) — TWRA (via Cornell LII)
  • Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 0080-02-01-.02 &.14 — Animal Health: CVI required for animals entering the state — TN Dept of Agriculture (via TN Secretary of State)
  • Import Requirements for Animals — Class III definition, CVI (30-day), eCVI transition — TN Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian)
  • Order of the State Veterinarian (June 4, 2026) — New World Screwworm interstate movement (7-day CVI, entry permit, applies to Class III) — TN Dept of Agriculture (State Veterinarian)
  • Tenn. Code Ann. §44-17-703 — Commercial Breeder Act (dogs/cats only; expired 6/30/2014) — Tennessee General Assembly (via Animal Legal & Historical Center)
  • Tenn. Code Ann. §44-10-203 — Livestock Dealer Licensing (traditional livestock only; rodents exempt) — TN Dept of Agriculture
  • Rodent Control / Urban & Rural Sanitation — feral R. rattus nuisance/eradication (no captive-keeping ban) — Shelby County Health Department

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Texas? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Texas

Summary. Texas does not regulate keeping, breeding, or selling pet roof rats at the state level, now confirmed in writing by TPWD (June 2026): as a non-native exotic rodent, Rattus rattus falls outside TPWD's 'nongame' wildlife rules (indigenous species only), the 'dangerous wild animal' law, and TAHC's 'exotic livestock' (hooved-animal) entry rules. A retail storefront still needs the local city's pet-shop license, wholesale/sight-unseen sales trigger federal USDA licensing, and international movement is federally restricted (roof rats are 'wildlife'). Releasing one is illegal.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Texas-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Texas is silent. See United States.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • Texas Parks & Wildlife Department (Wildlife Permits Office), written reply June 2026: because roof rats (Rattus rattus) are not native to Texas, no TPWD permit is required to keep them. All TPWD permits regulate the possession, transport, and display of native/indigenous species only, so a non-native roof rat is entirely outside TPWD's permit scope.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Texas regulates exotic-pet possession by banning specific hazardous species, not by a permit list. Rattus rattus is a non-native rodent, so it is outside TPWD's 'nongame' wildlife rules (which cover only species INDIGENOUS to Texas, TPWC §67.001) and is not a listed 'dangerous wild animal' (Health & Safety Code ch. 822). No state possession permit is required. (Local ordinances may cap how many pets a household may keep.)

Sources: Texas Statutes, Texas Statutes

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

There is no Texas breeder license for rodents — the Dog or Cat Breeders Act (Occupations Code ch. 802) covers only dogs and cats. Hobby and commercial rat breeding are unregulated by the state. (Federal USDA licensing still applies to WHOLESALE or sight-unseen sales — see United States.)

Sources: Texas Statutes

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-06

Selling or giving roof rats is unregulated by the state: the TPWD Commercial Nongame Dealer permit applies only to INDIGENOUS wildlife (31 TAC §65.325), so it doesn't cover non-native rats. Two layers still apply: a retail storefront needs the local city's pet-shop license, and wholesale or sight-unseen sales trigger federal USDA licensing (see United States).

Sources: Texas Parks & Wildlife, Texas Statutes

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-06

Within Texas and across state lines, no state permit or health certificate is required for pet rats: rodents are exempt from TAHC's 'exotic livestock' entry rules (those cover hooved animals) and from the DSHS rabies transport ban (rodents are low-risk). Airlines typically require a vet health certificate to fly. International import/export is restricted at the FEDERAL level (USFWS Form 3-177; CDC African-rodent ban) — see United States.

Sources: TAHC, Texas DSHS

Restrictions & responsibilities

A retail pet-store storefront needs the local city's Pet Shop License / commercial animal establishment permit (sanitation, zoning, records). Rules vary by municipality (Houston, Austin, Dallas, etc.). Private/face-to-face placement and giveaways do not need a state license.
  • Check your city's animal-establishment / pet-shop licensing if running a storefront

Where: Your city's animal control / code enforcement · Fees: Set locally

Source: Texas Parks & Wildlife

Releasing or abandoning a roof rat is illegal in Texas — it is criminal abandonment under the animal-cruelty law (Penal Code §42.092), and they are an invasive non-native species. Rehome responsibly (shelter, rescue, or new owner); never release.

Source: Texas Statutes

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • Tex. Parks & Wildlife Code §67.001 — 'nongame' = species INDIGENOUS to Texas (excludes R. rattus) — Texas Statutes
  • Tex. Health & Safety Code ch. 822 — Dangerous Wild Animals (rats not listed) — Texas Statutes
  • Tex. Occupations Code ch. 802 — Dog or Cat Breeders Act (dogs/cats only) — Texas Statutes
  • 31 TAC §65.325 / TPWD Commercial Nongame — applies only to indigenous wildlife — Texas Parks & Wildlife
  • Texas Animal Health Commission — Entry Requirements (rodents/pocket pets exempt from CVI) — TAHC
  • 25 TAC §169 / DSHS — rabies transport ban (foxes/skunks/coyotes/raccoons only; rodents low-risk) — Texas DSHS
  • Tex. Penal Code §42.092 — Cruelty to Nonlivestock Animals (abandonment) — Texas Statutes

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Utah? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Utah

Summary. Utah classifies birds and mammals species-by-species, and the roof rat falls through a gap created by a 2023 rule rewrite. The Division of Wildlife Resources' Bird and Mammal Classification Table 3b-1 (May 1, 2023, incorporated by Utah Admin. Code R657-3b) lists the Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus — the common pet 'fancy rat') as a domestic animal 'not covered under this rule,' but Rattus rattus appears nowhere on it. The table's default makes every unlisted species 'presumed prohibited' and requires a DWR assessment before collection, importation, or possession is authorized. Critically, this is NOT an absolute ban: a lawful pathway exists — a Certificate of Registration (COR) obtained through a case-by-case variance (R657-3a-9) or a species reclassification petition (R657-3a-8) — so keeping, breeding, selling, or importing a captive-bred roof rat is restricted rather than flatly prohibited. Before 2023, the old rule R657-3(32) jointly exempted 'Rats, Norway and Black (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)' as non-COR pets; the May 2023 simplification kept only the Norway rat, making this a textbook agency-fixable species/enumeration trap.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Utah-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Utah is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Bird and Mammal Classification Table 3b-1 (incorporated by Utah Admin. Code R657-3b) lists 'Rat, Norway / Rattus norvegicus' as a domestic animal not covered by the rule, but does NOT list Rattus rattus. The table's header makes every unlisted species 'presumed prohibited... require an assessment before... possession will be authorized,' and R657-3b-8 requires a Certificate of Registration before collecting/possessing any prohibited or controlled species. So possessing a captive-bred roof rat is not automatically illegal — a lawful COR pathway exists via a species assessment / variance — but it cannot proceed without prior DWR authorization, and unauthorized possession is a violation of Utah Code 23A-5-309. Restricted, not prohibited.

Sources: Utah Division of Wildlife Resources, Utah Division of Wildlife Resources, Utah Division of Wildlife Resources, Utah State Legislature

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

R657-3b-13 requires a Certificate of Registration before propagating any species classified as prohibited or controlled. Because R. rattus is unlisted on Table 3b-1 (presumed prohibited pending assessment), breeding can't proceed without a favorable DWR assessment and a COR that affirmatively authorizes propagation — which 'may contain stipulations to prevent detrimental impacts to wild populations, the environment, or human health or safety.' No exemption applies (the table names R. norvegicus, not R. rattus). A lawful pathway exists, so this is restricted; the DR notes the propagation burden is higher than mere possession given the species' pest-manual classification.

Sources: Utah Division of Wildlife Resources, Utah Division of Wildlife Resources, Utah Division of Wildlife Resources

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Utah Code 23A-5-309 bars collecting, possessing, transporting, donating, transferring, or exporting protected wildlife except as authorized by a rule, proclamation, or Wildlife Board order. Because R. rattus is unlisted / presumed prohibited, any sale or gift is lawful only to a recipient who already holds the necessary DWR COR for the species — transferring to an unregistered Utah resident implicates both parties. A commercial storefront additionally needs local municipal pet-shop/dealer licensing and zoning approval, which the COR application requires be resolved first. A pathway exists (transfer between COR holders), so restricted, not prohibited.

Sources: Utah State Legislature, Utah Division of Wildlife Resources, Utah Division of Wildlife Resources

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Intrastate movement of an unlisted/presumed-prohibited mammal triggers a COR (R657-3b-11); even moving a legally held roof rat between Utah counties must be covered by the COR. Importation compounds the requirement: a COR is required before importing (R657-3b-10), and UDAF Rule R58-1-13 makes it unlawful to import any species prohibited under R657-3, requiring a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) plus a UDAF entry permit for any animal that needs a DWR COR. A lawful path exists (COR + CVI + entry permit), so restricted. Never release a roof rat.

Sources: Utah Division of Wildlife Resources, Utah Dept of Agriculture & Food, Utah Division of Wildlife Resources

Restrictions & responsibilities

Because R. rattus is unlisted on Table 3b-1 (only the Norway rat is domestic-exempt), it is 'presumed prohibited' and requires a DWR Certificate of Registration before possession, breeding, sale, or import. The COR is reached either through a case-by-case Request for Variance (R657-3a-9) or a statewide Request for Species Reclassification (R657-3a-8). Both require an interagency review (DWR + Dept. of Agriculture & Food + Dept. of Health & Human Services). Contact the DWR Wildlife Registration office BEFORE acquiring any animals.
  • Contact the DWR Wildlife Registration / COR office (dwrregistration@utah.gov) about classification and a species assessment for captive-bred R. rattus
  • File a Request for Variance (R657-3a-9) for personal possession/breeding, OR a Request for Species Reclassification (R657-3a-8) to restore R. rattus to the noncontrolled/domestic-exempt list ($200 each)
  • If a variance/assessment is granted, apply for the COR ($10 handling + $75 personal or $150 commercial; $30 renewal) and meet caging/husbandry/inspection stipulations
  • Resolve local municipal/county zoning and pet-shop/dealer licensing first (required before the COR application)
  • For import: obtain a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection and a UDAF entry permit (R58-1-13)
  • If denied: request agency action before the Wildlife Board within 30 days (R657-2)

Forms: Utah DWR Certificate of Registration (Wildlife Registration office), DWR COR Application (birds & mammals), DWR Fee Schedule (licenses, permits & miscellaneous) · Where: Utah Division of Wildlife Resources — Wildlife Registration / COR office, 1594 W. North Temple, Suite 2110, Box 146301, Salt Lake City, UT 84114-6301 (import permit: Utah Dept of Agriculture & Food, Animal Industry) · Fees: Species reclassification or variance request $200 each; COR $10 handling + $75 personal / $150 commercial issuance, $30 renewal, $10 amendment; UDAF CVI + entry permit fees for import.

Source: Utah Division of Wildlife Resources, Utah Division of Wildlife Resources, Utah Division of Wildlife Resources, Utah Division of Wildlife Resources, Utah Dept of Agriculture & Food

Never release or abandon a roof rat in Utah. The state classifies Rattus rattus in its Vertebrate Pest and Structural Pest manuals as a highly destructive non-native invasive pest and a zoonotic-disease vector; release of a held animal would compound the criminal exposure under Utah Code 23A-5-309 and the ecological concerns that drive the COR review. Rehome only to a lawfully authorized (COR-holding) recipient.
  • Keep roof rats strictly indoors; never release
  • Rehome only to a COR-authorized recipient

Source: Utah State Legislature, Utah Division of Wildlife Resources

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in Utah. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Help change this

How to help in Utah

Utah classifies birds and mammals species-by-species, and the domesticated roof rat (Rattus rattus) falls through a gap. The Division of Wildlife Resources' Bird and Mammal Classification Table 3b-1 (under Admin. Rule R657-3b) names the Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus, the species behind the common pet 'fancy rat') as a domestic animal 'not covered' by the rule and fully exempt. Rattus rattus appears nowhere on that table. Under the rule, any unlisted species is 'presumed prohibited' and requires a DWR assessment and authorization before it can be possessed, bred, sold, or imported. A captive-bred, tame roof rat is not flatly illegal. A lawful pathway exists (a Certificate of Registration obtained through a variance or species reclassification), but the rat cannot be legally kept without a prior DWR determination. This is an enumeration gap, not a decision that roof rats are dangerous. The near-identical fancy rat is exempt by name, while the roof rat is missing. The gap is recent. Until the May 1, 2023 rule rewrite, the old rule R657-3(32) jointly listed 'Rats, Norway and Black (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)' as exempt domestic pets, so for over a decade captive-bred roof rats had the same unregulated status as fancy rats. The 2023 simplification carried only the Norway rat onto the new Table 3b-1 and dropped the roof rat, with no record of any finding that domesticated roof rats are dangerous.

The ask: Restore captive-bred, domestic-lineage Rattus rattus to Table 3b-1 as a noncontrolled/domestic-exempt species, alongside the Norway rat that is already listed and that the roof rat shared a line with under the pre-2023 rule. Specifically: (1) ask DWR in writing whether the post-2023 omission of R. rattus from Table 3b-1 was intentional, and whether captive-bred R. rattus can be grouped with R. norvegicus as a domestic commensal-rodent strain rather than treated as an unlisted species needing individual assessment; and (2) file or support a Request for Species Reclassification under R657-3a-8 ($200 fee) to amend Table 3b-1 to list captive-bred R. rattus as noncontrolled/domestic-exempt, restoring its pre-2023 status. The relevant question is domestication, not wild ancestry. The dog descends from the wolf and the house cat from a wild felid, yet both are treated as domestic animals because of generations bred for tameness rather than wild origins. The already-exempt Norway-rat fancy rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred R. rattus is the same case one species over. That is the question the Division is asked to weigh, not a result it is asked to reach. Because the classification lives in an administrative rule that DWR controls, not a statute, DWR (through the Wildlife Board's rulemaking process) is the body that can fix it. On domestication background, see https://blonderoofrat.com/how-the-sewer-rat-became-the-fancy-rat/.

Where the lever really is: This is the agency/rule branch, fixable through the Division of Wildlife Resources, not the legislature. The restriction comes from an administrative classification choice, not a statute that bans roof rats. The Utah Code (Title 23A, Wildlife Resources Code) delegates species-classification authority to the DWR and Wildlife Board. The list lives in Admin. Rule R657-3b and its incorporated Bird and Mammal Classification Table 3b-1 (May 1, 2023), both of which the DWR drafts and the Wildlife Board adopts. Nothing in statute names or prohibits the roof rat. It is absent from a table, which triggers the rule's default that an unlisted species is presumed prohibited. The Norway rat (the fancy rat's species) is named as domestic-exempt on the same table, and the same table jointly listed both rats until the May 2023 rewrite, which shows the table is the right instrument and the omission is an enumeration gap, not a policy judgment that roof rats are uniquely dangerous. The fix is an agency action: a written classification determination from the DWR Certificate of Registration office, and/or a Request for Species Reclassification under R657-3a-8 (Utah Code 63G-3-601 separately lets any person petition an agency to amend a rule) to add captive-bred R. rattus back to Table 3b-1. Two caveats. First, the legislature is not the primary lever, because the classification is administrative code, not statutory text, and petitioning lawmakers would redirect to DWR. Second, the DR notes the roof rat is entrenched in Utah's own pest manuals as an invasive structural pest, so the reclassification panel (DWR plus Dept. of Agriculture & Food plus Dept. of Health & Human Services) will require a strong biosecurity and domestic-lineage case; the realistic near-term win may be a personal-use variance (R657-3a-9) rather than statewide reclassification. Start with the agency, which can both interpret the gap and rewrite the table.

Where to send it (more than one channel helps):

  • Utah Division of Wildlife Resources — Wildlife Registration / Certificate of Registration (COR) office (executive / agency) — dwrregistration@utah.gov
    The COR office administers Rule R657-3b and Table 3b-1 — the exact instrument that lists the Norway rat as domestic-exempt and omits the roof rat — and processes both variance requests (R657-3a-9) and species reclassification petitions (R657-3a-8). Ask in writing whether the post-2023 omission of R. rattus was intentional and whether captive-bred R. rattus can be grouped with R. norvegicus or restored to the noncontrolled list. Verified contact (DR): dwrregistration@utah.gov; phone 801-538-4701 / 385-332-6154; mail to 1594 W. North Temple, Suite 2110, Box 146301, Salt Lake City, UT 84114-6301.
  • Utah DWR — Request for Species Reclassification (Utah Admin. Code R657-3a-8) (executive / agency) — dwrregistration@utah.gov
    The formal channel to restore captive-bred R. rattus to Table 3b-1's noncontrolled/domestic-exempt list — the same list it shared with R. norvegicus before May 2023. A reclassification petition ($200 fee) compels an interagency review (DWR + Dept. of Agriculture & Food + Dept. of Health & Human Services) and a formal Wildlife Board recommendation on the record, rather than an informal staff answer. If granted it legalizes the species statewide; if denied, the applicant may request agency action before the Wildlife Board within 30 days (R657-2).
  • Utah Office of Administrative Rules — Petition for Rulemaking (Utah Code 63G-3-601) / Public Notice Website (public comment) — official contact page
    Any person may petition a state agency to amend an existing rule under Utah Code 63G-3-601 (Office of Administrative Rules, rules.utah.gov, phone 801-957-7110). If DWR opens any rulemaking touching R657-3b or Table 3b-1, the proposed-rule notice, comment-period dates (typically 30+ days), and agency contact are posted on the Utah Public Notice Website (utah.gov/pmn) and in the twice-monthly Utah State Bulletin — the place a well-supported species-addition comment lands on the formal record. No roof-rat-specific window is open now; watch this portal.

A starting-point message — please put it in your own words; a short personal note carries far more weight than an identical form letter:

English
To: Utah Division of Wildlife Resources, Wildlife Registration / Certificate of Registration Office
Re: Classification of captive-bred domestic roof rat (Rattus rattus) under Rule R657-3b / Bird and Mammal Classification Table 3b-1

Dear Wildlife Registration Office,

I am writing about a gap in Bird and Mammal Classification Table 3b-1. The table names the Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus), the species behind the common pet 'fancy rat', as a domestic animal not covered by R657-3b, but the closely related roof rat (Rattus rattus) is not listed, which leaves it presumed prohibited by default and assessable only through a Certificate of Registration.

This appears to be a recent and possibly inadvertent change. Until the May 1, 2023 rule rewrite, the prior rule R657-3(32) jointly exempted 'Rats, Norway and Black (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)' as non-COR domestic pets. The 2023 simplification carried over only the Norway rat and dropped the roof rat, with no published finding that domesticated roof rats are dangerous.

The animals at issue are captive-bred, selectively bred for tameness, kept strictly indoors as pets, and never released to the wild. They are domesticated companion rodents, no different in keeping from the Norway-rat fancy rat the table already exempts. What makes an animal domestic is its breeding history, not its wild ancestry. The dog descends from the wolf and the house cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic animals because of generations bred for tameness. The exempt Norway rat is itself the wild brown rat, domesticated only in the 19th century, so a captive-bred roof rat is the same case one species over. The distinction is species enumeration, not domestication or any public-safety concern.

I respectfully ask the Division to: (1) state in writing whether the post-2023 omission of R. rattus from Table 3b-1 was intentional, and whether captive-bred R. rattus is treated as unlisted and assessable or can be grouped with R. norvegicus as a domestic strain; and (2) advise what a Request for Species Reclassification under R657-3a-8 to restore captive-bred Rattus rattus to Table 3b-1's noncontrolled/domestic-exempt section would require. Thank you for your time and for considering this correction.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your city, Utah] / [Your email]

Did you take action, or get a response? Tell us — it helps the next person, and we track what actually works.

Official sources

  • Utah Admin. Code R657-3b — Certification of Registration: Birds and Mammals (COR before collecting/possessing/propagating/transporting prohibited-or-controlled species; unlisted = presumed prohibited) — Utah Division of Wildlife Resources
  • Bird & Mammal Classification Table 3b-1 (May 1, 2023) — lists Rattus norvegicus as domestic-exempt; Rattus rattus absent (default presumed prohibited) — Utah Division of Wildlife Resources
  • Utah Admin. Code R657-3a — Collection, Importation, Transportation, and Possession of Animals (species reclassification R657-3a-8; variance R657-3a-9) — Utah Division of Wildlife Resources
  • Utah Code 23A-5-309 — Taking, transporting, selling, transferring protected wildlife illegal except as authorized — Utah State Legislature
  • Utah Admin. Code R58-1-13 — Exotic Animals and Wildlife (UDAF: import barred for R657-3 prohibited species; CVI + entry permit required for COR animals) — Utah Dept of Agriculture & Food
  • Utah DWR Fees — licenses, permits & miscellaneous (reclassification/variance $200; COR issuance/renewal fees) — Utah Division of Wildlife Resources
  • Utah State Bulletin (2012/2015) — former rule R657-3(32) jointly exempted 'Rats, Norway and Black (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)' as non-COR pets (severed in May 2023 rewrite) — Utah Office of Administrative Rules

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Virginia? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Virginia

Summary. Virginia is one of the clearest 'yes' states for the roof rat. Its wildlife code (4VAC15-20-50) literally names 'Domesticated races of rats (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)' as DOMESTIC animals — which removes captive-bred pet roof rats from the 'wild animal' and 'nonnative (exotic)' categories and from the Department of Wildlife Resources' permitting. The genus does not appear on the predatory/undesirable nonnative list. So keeping, breeding, and selling/giving a pet roof rat is legal with no wildlife permit. The only conditional requirement is a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection when importing one from out of state for sale, adoption, or breeding (a personal move-in is exempt). Never release one — wild R. rattus is a designated nuisance.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Virginia-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Virginia is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Domesticated Rattus rattus is expressly defined as a 'domestic animal' in 4VAC15-20-50 (which lists 'Domesticated races of rats (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)'), removing it from the 'wild animal' and 'nonnative (exotic) animal' definitions and thus from DWR possession-permit requirements. The genus does not appear on the predatory/undesirable nonnative list (4VAC15-30-40). No permit is required to keep one. Gemini DR-verified: 4VAC15-20-50 explicitly lists 'Domesticated races of rats (R. norvegicus and R. rattus)' as domestic animals (protection applies to captive-bred lineage).

Sources: Virginia DWR / Code of Virginia, Virginia DWR / Code of Virginia

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Because the species is a domestic animal outside DWR jurisdiction, breeding needs no DWR wildlife/propagation permit (the breeding restriction in 4VAC15-20-50(B) names only foxes and rabbits, not rats). No species-specific Virginia breeding ban exists. Large-scale commercial breeding could implicate general VDACS animal-dealer/pet-shop provisions and local zoning — activity-scale rules, not species rules. Gemini DR-verified: no state breeder license for companion rodents; only general welfare standards apply.

Sources: Virginia DWR / Code of Virginia

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

DWR sale/possession permits (4VAC15-30-40) apply only to listed predatory/undesirable nonnative exotics; R. rattus is a domestic animal and not on that list, so no DWR sale permit applies. There is no Virginia prohibition on selling or giving away domestic pet rodents. Standard pet-dealer/consumer rules and the import-CVI-for-sale rule (below) apply to the transaction, not the species. Gemini DR-verified: legal; commercial sellers ('dealers') may need a LOCAL pet-shop/dealer permit (fee capped at $50).

Sources: Virginia DWR / Code of Virginia, VDACS / Office of the State Veterinarian

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-07

Intrastate transport of a domestic pet rat is unregulated by DWR. For IMPORT from another state, Code of Va. §3.2-5902 requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (dated within 10 days) for a pet animal — but it EXEMPTS animals merely passing through and animals brought in by a resident or someone moving to Virginia, EXCEPT when brought in to offer for public sale, trade, or promotion. So: personal move-in = no CVI; import to sell/adopt-out/breed-for-sale = CVI required. Gemini DR-verified: commercial import needs a CVI issued within 10 days; a resident relocating with a personal pet rat is exempt. Intrastate legal.

Sources: VDACS / Office of the State Veterinarian, VDACS Office of Veterinary Services

Restrictions & responsibilities

A Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (within 10 days) is required to import a pet roof rat into Virginia FOR SALE, adoption, breeding, or promotion. Bringing your own pet in when you move (personal ownership) is exempt, as is merely passing through.
  • For a personal move-in: no CVI needed
  • To import for sale/adoption/breeding: get a CVI within 10 days

Where: VDACS Office of Veterinary Services

Source: VDACS / Office of the State Veterinarian, VDACS Office of Veterinary Services

Although domestic in status, releasing any roof rat into the wild is prohibited (4VAC15-30-40(C) no-liberation rule), and wild R. rattus is a designated nuisance species (4VAC15-20-160). Never release; rehome responsibly.

Source: Virginia DWR / Code of Virginia, Virginia DWR / Code of Virginia

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • 4VAC15-20-50 — Definitions; 'Domesticated races of rats (Rattus norvegicus and Rattus rattus)' listed as domestic animals — Virginia DWR / Code of Virginia
  • 4VAC15-30-40 — Importation, possession, sale of nonnative (exotic) animals (genus Rattus absent; no-liberation clause) — Virginia DWR / Code of Virginia
  • 4VAC15-20-160 — Nuisance species designated (wild Black rat / Rattus rattus) — Virginia DWR / Code of Virginia
  • Code of Va. §3.2-5902 — CVI required for importation of certain pet animals (resident/transit exemptions) — VDACS / Office of the State Veterinarian
  • Virginia Animal Admissions Requirements (CVI for sale/adoption/breeding, not personal ownership) — VDACS Office of Veterinary Services

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › U.S. Virgin Islands

Summary. In the U.S. Virgin Islands, a roof rat is a non-indigenous 'vermin' species and may not be imported, introduced, kept, or propagated without the express written permission of the Commissioner — confirmed in writing by the Dept of Planning & Natural Resources (DPNR, June 2026). 12 V.I.C. §102 names 'roof (black) rat (Rattus rattus)' (and R. norvegicus) as vermin excluded from 'indigenous species,' and while §105(a) protects indigenous species, §105(d) SEPARATELY prohibits importing or introducing any species that does not naturally occur in the Territory without the Commissioner's written authorization. DPNR is not required to grant it and has a strong basis to deny on biosecurity, invasive-species, conservation, property-damage, and public-health grounds (the territory and USFWS run active rodent-eradication programs protecting endemic species such as the endangered Virgin Islands tree boa). A discretionary written-permission pathway technically exists, so the status is restricted rather than an absolute ban, but approval for live rats is unlikely; any permitted entry also needs a veterinary health certificate (19 V.I.C. §2709). Both Rattus species are treated identically — there is no species trap. Never release one.

Key points here are confirmed in writing by the responsible agency (see below).
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the U.S. Virgin Islands-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where U.S. Virgin Islands is silent. See United States.
Confirmed by the agencies.
  • U.S. Virgin Islands Department of Planning & Natural Resources (DPNR), Division of Fish & Wildlife, written reply June 2026: roof rats (Rattus rattus) and Norway rats (Rattus norvegicus) are 'vermin' under 12 V.I.C. §102(n) and are excluded from 'indigenous species' (§102(i)). While §105(a) regulates indigenous species, §105(d) separately prohibits importing or introducing into the Territory any species that does not naturally occur there without the express written permission of the Commissioner. Because both rat species are non-indigenous vermin, neither may be imported, introduced, kept, or propagated without that written authorization — and DPNR is not required to grant it and has a strong basis to deny on biosecurity, invasive-species, conservation, property-damage, and public-health grounds. Any animal permitted to enter must also carry a valid certificate of veterinary inspection (19 V.I.C. §2709).

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

DPNR confirmed in writing (June 2026) that keeping a non-indigenous vermin species is prohibited without the Commissioner's express written permission. Although 12 V.I.C. §105(a)'s take/possess prohibition reaches only indigenous species, §105(d) separately bars importing OR INTRODUCING any non-indigenous species without written authorization, and DPNR reads keeping a non-indigenous vermin as falling within that bar. R. rattus is named vermin (§102), so a private keeper needs the Commissioner's permission — which DPNR is not required to grant and has a strong basis to deny. A discretionary written-permission pathway exists, so this is restricted rather than an absolute ban.

Sources: V.I. Legislature (via Justia), VI DPNR Division of Fish & Wildlife, VI DPNR Division of Fish & Wildlife, DPNR Division of Fish & Wildlife (via St. Thomas Source)

Breeding   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

DPNR confirmed (June 2026) that PROPAGATION of non-indigenous vermin is prohibited without the Commissioner's express written permission under 12 V.I.C. §105(d) — this applies regardless of whether the animal was locally acquired or imported, correcting the earlier DR read that local breeding was unregulated. R. rattus is named vermin (§102) and both Rattus species are treated identically. A discretionary permission pathway exists, so restricted rather than prohibited; the V.I. Dept of Agriculture import permit additionally prints an absolute 'will not be allowed to breed' condition on imported specimens.

Sources: V.I. Legislature (via Justia), VI DPNR Division of Fish & Wildlife, VI Dept of Agriculture, Division of Veterinary Services, VI Dept of Agriculture, Division of Veterinary Services

Selling or giving away   Restricted

Confidence: Medium · Last verified 2026-06-10

DPNR's June 2026 reply did not separately address private transfer, but because keeping a non-indigenous vermin requires the Commissioner's written permission under 12 V.I.C. §105(d), any transfer is effectively limited to authorized keepers. A commercial storefront would also need a general business license from the Dept of Licensing & Consumer Affairs, and the no-release duty binds any recipient. Restricted.

Sources: V.I. Legislature (via Justia), VI DPNR Division of Fish & Wildlife, VI DPNR Division of Fish & Wildlife

Transport & import   Restricted

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

DPNR confirmed (June 2026) that importing or introducing a non-indigenous species requires the Commissioner's express written permission under 12 V.I.C. §105(d), which DPNR is not required to grant and has a strong basis to deny. On top of that territorial bar, the V.I. Dept of Agriculture requires its Non-Indigenous Animal Import Permit ($25/species, void 2 months), a 30-day veterinary health certificate (19 V.I.C. §2709), port custody/inspection, a live-food ban, and a no-breeding condition. Internal movement of a lawfully held, confined animal is permissible; release is strictly unlawful. A lawful (if discretionary and unlikely) pathway exists — restricted, not an absolute ban.

Sources: VI Dept of Agriculture, Division of Veterinary Services, VI Dept of Agriculture, Division of Veterinary Services, VI DPNR Division of Fish & Wildlife

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing a roof rat into the USVI from the mainland, Puerto Rico, or abroad requires the V.I. Dept of Agriculture Non-Indigenous Animal Import Permit, secured BEFORE the animal departs its origin. It carries a $25-per-species fee, a 30-day veterinary health certificate, port custody/inspection by Veterinary Services, an absolute live-food ban (no rodents imported as feeders), and a binding condition that the imported animal 'will not be allowed to breed.' The permit is void two months after issuance. Never release an exotic species into the wild.
  • Before the animal leaves its origin, file the Non-Indigenous Animal Import Application with the V.I. Dept of Agriculture, Office of the Director of Veterinary Services (Kingshill, St. Croix), listing scientific name (Rattus rattus), common name, color, sex, and number of animals, plus consignor/owner contacts and your USVI physical address
  • Pay the $25-per-species non-refundable fee by check or money order payable to the VI Department of Agriculture
  • Obtain an official veterinary health certificate from a licensed/accredited (or USDA) veterinarian within 30 days of travel; include the screwworm-free treatment statement if originating from a screwworm-endemic area
  • Time travel so the animal arrives while the permit is valid (void 2 months after issue) and the certificate is within its 30-day window
  • On arrival, leave the animal in the carrier's custody until a V.I. Dept of Agriculture Veterinary Services agent completes the port inspection and releases it
  • Comply with the permit conditions: import only as a companion pet (not live food), prevent the imported animal from breeding, keep it securely confined, and never release it

Forms: Non-Indigenous Animal Import Application (V.I. Dept of Agriculture, Division of Veterinary Services) · Where: V.I. Department of Agriculture, Office of the Director of Veterinary Services, RR 1 Box 10345, Kingshill, St. Croix, USVI 00850 (veterinaryservices@doa.vi.gov) · Fees: $25.00 non-refundable per species (check/money order payable to VI Department of Agriculture)

Source: VI Dept of Agriculture, Division of Veterinary Services, VI Dept of Agriculture, Division of Veterinary Services

Releasing or letting a roof rat escape into the wild is strictly prohibited under the V.I. Rules & Regulations, which name 'cats or rats' among exotic species barred from intentional or incidental introduction (to protect native species such as the endangered Virgin Islands tree boa). The duty of secure confinement transfers to any new owner. The territory and USFWS actively run rodent-eradication programs, so an escaped pet is treated as an invasive predator and carries severe penalties.
  • Keep the roof rat securely caged and indoors at all times
  • Never release or abandon it; if rehoming, pass the confinement duty to a vetted new owner

Source: VI DPNR Division of Fish & Wildlife, U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service / Federal Register

A storefront pet shop or a continuous, profit-seeking retail operation selling roof rats needs a standard business license from the V.I. Dept of Licensing & Consumer Affairs (DLCA); there is no rodent/small-exotic breeder license or numeric hobbyist threshold in V.I. law. Private, occasional, face-to-face placement or giveaways do not require a license.
  • If operating a commercial storefront or ongoing retail sales, obtain a general business license from the V.I. Dept of Licensing & Consumer Affairs

Where: V.I. Department of Licensing & Consumer Affairs (DLCA) · Fees: Set by DLCA

Source: VI DPNR Division of Fish & Wildlife

It appears you can't currently keep a roof rat as a pet in U.S. Virgin Islands. Please confirm with the official sources above before acting. If you'd like to see this change, you can contact your representatives and the responsible agencies, ask them to treat a domesticated Rattus rattus line fairly and tell us what you learn so we can help others.

Official sources

  • 12 V.I.C. §102 — Definitions ('indigenous species' excludes vermin incl. 'roof (black) rat (Rattus rattus)') — V.I. Legislature (via Justia)
  • 12 V.I.C. §105 — Protection of Indigenous Species (take/possess/sell prohibition reaches only indigenous species; DPNR text) — VI DPNR Division of Fish & Wildlife
  • V.I. Rules & Regulations Concerning Wildlife & Marine Sanctuaries (DPNR) — exotic-species framework; no-introduce/no-release (names 'cats or rats') — VI DPNR Division of Fish & Wildlife
  • Biologists Recruit Public to Confront Invasive Species in the V.I. (Exotic Pet Amnesty list — rats omitted) — DPNR Division of Fish & Wildlife (via St. Thomas Source)
  • Non-Indigenous Animal Import Application ($25/species fee; live-food ban; 'Animal will not be allowed to breed'; species ID required) — VI Dept of Agriculture, Division of Veterinary Services
  • State Regulations for the Virgin Islands (Animal Entry & Veterinary Rules) — import permit, 30-day health certificate, port custody/inspection, screwworm provision, destruction-without-compensation — VI Dept of Agriculture, Division of Veterinary Services
  • Endangered Status for the Virgin Islands Tree Boa (Federal Register) — roof rat as invasive threat; no-introduction rationale — U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service / Federal Register

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Vermont? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Vermont

Summary. Vermont is permissive and unusually explicit for the roof rat. Its 'prohibited-unless-listed' wildlife regime (10 V.S.A. §4709; Reg. 881 / 10 App. V.S.A. §18) bans possessing or importing a wild animal without a permit unless the species is on the Fish & Wildlife exemption lists — and the July 2025 Unrestricted Wild Animal List names Rattus rattus by exact scientific name (common name 'Domesticated rat'), right alongside Rattus norvegicus. So there is no species trap: keeping, breeding, importing, and transporting a roof rat need no Fish & Wildlife permit. Breeding is also outside commercial law (the 'Pet Dealer' rule covers only dogs/cats/wolf-hybrids), and home sales are exempt; only a non-residential retail storefront needs a state Pet Shop License. Keepers remain bound by animal-cruelty law (13 V.S.A. ch. 8) and may never release a roof rat.

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Vermont-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Vermont is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

10 V.S.A. §4709 bars possessing any wild animal without a Fish & Wildlife permit, but Reg. 881 (10 App. V.S.A. §18) exempts any species on the Unrestricted Wild Animal List. The July 2025 list names Rattus rattus to the exact species level (Genus Rattus / species rattus, common name 'Domesticated rat'), so no importation or possession permit is required to keep a roof rat. The earlier 'is rat = which species?' ambiguity is fully resolved by the explicit listing.

Sources: Vermont General Assembly, Vermont Fish & Wildlife Board, Vermont Fish & Wildlife Department

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Breeding roof rats is unregulated at the state level. Because R. rattus is on the Unrestricted List it falls outside the wild-animal permit scheme, and Vermont's commercial breeder law applies only to other species: a 'Pet Dealer' (20 V.S.A. §3901(7)) is defined strictly as someone selling cats, dogs, or wolf-hybrids from three or more litters — rodents are deliberately omitted, so a home breeder of any scale never triggers municipal Pet Dealer permitting. Commercial-scale sale from a storefront is handled under the Pet Shop license (see sell_give); federal USDA/AWA licensing can apply to wholesale/sight-unseen sales (see United States).

Sources: Vermont Fish & Wildlife Department, Vermont General Assembly, Vermont General Assembly

Selling or giving away   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Private/face-to-face sales and giveaways are unregulated: a roof rat breeder is exempt from the Pet Dealer rule (rodents excluded, 20 V.S.A. §3901(7)) AND from the Pet Shop rule when selling 'from a private dwelling' (20 V.S.A. §3901(11) explicitly excludes a private dwelling from the Pet Shop definition). Only a non-residential retail operation — a storefront, a flea-market booth, or a detached commercial building — is a 'Pet Shop' (rodents ARE included in that definition) and needs a state Pet Shop License with inspection. Status is set to legal_with_permit to capture that commercial-storefront layer; ordinary hobbyist placement needs no license. (Federal USDA/AWA licensing applies to wholesale/sight-unseen sales — see United States.)

Sources: Vermont General Assembly, Vermont General Assembly

Transport & import   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Because R. rattus is on the Unrestricted Wild Animal List, no Fish & Wildlife import permit is needed to bring or move one into/within Vermont (10 V.S.A. §4709; Reg. 881). The list's '(Captive Bred Only)' tag — which would trigger a statement-of-origin/CVI — is applied species-by-species and is NOT placed on either Rattus line, so no CVI is mandated by Fish & Wildlife for a pet roof rat. VAAFM's domestic-animal import rule (Rule #98074) requires a CVI in practice mainly for livestock, poultry, and rabies-vector species (dogs/cats/ferrets); private small companion rodents are not subject to border CVI enforcement. Never release a roof rat.

Sources: Vermont General Assembly, Vermont Fish & Wildlife Board, Vermont Fish & Wildlife Department, Vermont Agency of Agriculture, Food & Markets

Restrictions & responsibilities

Selling roof rats from a non-residential retail space — a storefront, a flea-market booth, or a detached commercial building (anything 'not part of a private dwelling') — makes the operation a 'Pet Shop' under 20 V.S.A. §3901(11) (rodents are included) and requires a state Pet Shop License plus a pre-licensing inspection, records, and caging standards. Selling/giving roof rats from your own home is exempt and needs no license.
  • If selling only from your private dwelling: no Pet Shop license needed — you're statutorily exempt.
  • If operating any non-residential retail space (storefront, flea-market booth, detached building): apply for a Pet Shop License and pass the pre-licensing inspection.
  • Confirm which agency currently processes the application during the Act 167 transition (legacy VAAFM Animal Health vs. the new DPS Division of Animal Welfare).

Where: Vermont Pet Shop licensing — currently transitioning from VAAFM (Animal Health Section) to the DPS Division of Animal Welfare (Act 167, phased 2024–2025) · Fees: Pet Shop license historically ~$150/yr (plus inspection); civil penalties up to $1,000/violation under Act 167. No fee for private-dwelling sales.

Source: Vermont General Assembly, Vermont General Assembly

A captive roof rat is the keeper's personal property and is protected by Vermont's animal-cruelty law (13 V.S.A. ch. 8 — §352 sustenance/care, no abandonment; §362 bars poisoning a captive animal). Releasing or abandoning a roof rat is both criminal cruelty and an illegal release of a non-native species — never release one. If you can no longer keep it, rehome it, surrender it to a shelter/rescue, or arrange humane euthanasia by a veterinarian.
  • Provide food, water, shelter, and veterinary care
  • Never release or abandon a roof rat — rehome or surrender responsibly

Source: Vermont General Assembly

Thinking about keeping or breeding a roof rat? Start with the care & husbandry guide, the interactive guides, or get in touch.

Official sources

  • 10 V.S.A. §4709 — Transport, importation, possession of wild animals; permit requirement — Vermont General Assembly
  • Reg. 881 / 10 App. V.S.A. §18 — Governing the importation and possession of wild animals (prohibited-unless-listed; exemption via Unrestricted List) — Vermont Fish & Wildlife Board
  • Unrestricted Wild Animal List (July 2025) — names Rattus rattus ('Domesticated rat') AND Rattus norvegicus; no '(Captive Bred Only)' tag on either — Vermont Fish & Wildlife Department
  • 20 V.S.A. ch. 194 — §3901 (Pet Dealer excludes rodents; Pet Shop includes rodents but excludes private dwelling), §3906 (Pet Shop license) — Vermont General Assembly
  • 20 V.S.A. §3681 — Pet dealer permit (municipal; dogs/cats/wolf-hybrids only) — Vermont General Assembly
  • Act 167 (H.626, 2024) — transfers pet-shop/welfare oversight from VAAFM to DPS Division of Animal Welfare — Vermont General Assembly
  • 13 V.S.A. ch. 8 — Animal cruelty (§352 care/no abandonment; §362 poisoning a captive animal) — Vermont General Assembly
  • VAAFM Rule #98074 — Rules Governing the Importation of Domestic Animals, Including Livestock and Poultry (CVI mainly for livestock/rabies-vector species) — Vermont Agency of Agriculture, Food & Markets

Search terms: Rattus rattus, roof rat, black rat, ship rat.

item.title: Is it legal to keep a roof rat in Washington? Keeping, Breeding & Selling
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Are Roof Rats Legal? Laws by Country & State › United States › Washington

Summary. Washington is now DR-verified and is cleanly legal at the state level. The wildlife statute excludes "old world rats and mice of the family Muridae" from the definition of "wildlife" (RCW 77.08.010(74)), so the roof rat (Rattus rattus) is outside WDFW jurisdiction with no species trap (R. rattus and R. norvegicus are treated identically), and it is on neither the dangerous-wild-animal list (RCW 16.30.010) nor the deleterious-exotic-wildlife list (WAC 220-640-200). Keeping, breeding, and selling are unregulated by the state (WSDA licenses no breeders; a rat sale is treated as personal property) — commercial breeding/retail defer to LOCAL zoning and animal-business codes. Importing one requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection as a "pocket pet" (WAC 16-54-170 / WSDA), but no exotic entry permit. Never release a roof rat (it is a recognized invasive species; WAC 220-450-010).

Cross-checked against official government sources.
legal note This is a research aid, not legal advice; rules change and are interpreted by local officials. Verify with the official source before acting.
National law also applies. These are the Washington-specific rules; United States’s national rules (for example, breeder/dealer licensing and import/export) apply on top of them, and this page’s answers inherit them only where Washington is silent. See United States.

Status by activity

Keeping / owning   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

The roof rat is excluded from the statutory definition of "wildlife" — RCW 77.08.010(74) excludes "old world rats and mice of the family Muridae" — so WDFW has no jurisdiction. It is also absent from the dangerous-wild-animal list (RCW 16.30.010) and the deleterious-exotic-wildlife list (WAC 220-640-200). No state permit, caging, or inspection (only general anti-cruelty, RCW 16.52). Local exotic-pet ordinances may still apply.

Sources: Washington State Legislature, WA Dept of Fish & Wildlife

Breeding   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

No state rodent breeder license: WDFW breeding rules cover only dangerous/deleterious species (neither covers R. rattus), and the WSDA does not license, register, or regulate breeders of any species. Hobby breeding is unrestricted; commercial breeding defers to LOCAL county/municipal animal-business and zoning codes.

Sources: WA Dept of Fish & Wildlife

Selling or giving away   Legal

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

No state pet-dealer license applies to rodents — a roof rat sale is treated as the sale of personal property, not classified wildlife. Statewide pet-dealer bills historically targeted dog/cat volume breeders, not rodents. Retail sale defers to a local business/pet-shop license; private transfer is unregulated.

Sources: WA Dept of Fish & Wildlife

Transport & import   Legal with a permit

Confidence: High · Last verified 2026-06-10

Intrastate transport of an owned pet is unregulated (only humane-transport rules, RCW 16.52.080). IMPORT into Washington requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection within 30 days, with the roof rat handled administratively as a "pocket pet" (WAC 16-54-170 / WSDA small-animal import) — no exotic entry permit needed via that route; rodents are exempt from rabies vaccination. Never release a roof rat.

Sources: Washington State Dept of Agriculture, WA Dept of Fish & Wildlife

Restrictions & responsibilities

Importing a pet rat ('pocket pet') into Washington requires a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (WSDA). No CVI for in-state movement.

Where: WA State Dept of Agriculture, Animal Health Program

Source: Washington State Dept of Agriculture

Never release a roof rat — it's a non-native species; rehome responsibly.

Source: WA Dept of Fish & Wildlife
